title: Dolly Parton’s peerless career turned country music cliches inside out  | Dolly Parton | The Guardian
description: Beneath the wig and rhinestones, Parton was the genius behind strings of classic songs from Jolene to I Will Always Love You that continue to inspire new artists
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: Beneath the wig and rhinestones, Parton was the genius behind strings of classic songs from Jolene to I Will Always Love You that continue to inspire new artists
Content: Dolly Parton performs at halftime during a game between the Dallas Cowboys and the Washington Commanders  in 2023 in Arlington, Texas.Photograph: Brandon Sloter/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDolly Parton performs at halftime during a game between the Dallas Cowboys and the Washington Commanders  in 2023 in Arlington, Texas.Photograph: Brandon Sloter/Getty ImagesDolly PartonDolly Parton’s peerless career turned country music cliches inside outAlexis PetridisBeneath the wig and rhinestones, Parton was the genius behind strings of classic songs from Jolene to I Will Always Love You that continue to inspire new artistsDolly Parton, US country star, actor and philanthropist, dies aged 80Dolly Parton dies aged 80 – latest updatesDolly Parton’s family say goodbye to their aunt, sister, grandmother - videoShare your tributes and memories of Dolly PartonTue 25 Aug 2026 14.07 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTShareIn December 1977,Dolly Partonsubmitted to an interview with ABC Television’s Barbara Walters, much against her friends’ advice. Walters was not noted for her deep love and understanding of country music. She was a notoriously tough cookie, a Boston-born, Sarah Lawrence-educated journalist who had battled scarcely believable sexism to become the first female co-host of an American news programme. The month before she met Parton, she had interviewed Anwar Sadat and Menachem Begin while they were working out the terms of the Egypt-Israel peace treaty.It was all a very long way from Parton’s world, and the interview has something of the anthropological exercise about it. Walters looks aghast as Parton shows her around her tour bus, her collection of wigs and her “hand-washable and wrinkle-free” stage outfits (“you really like this? To me, it seems like horror”), and sits impassively as Parton sings Coat of Many Colours to her: an impressive feat, given the song’s saga of rural poverty and homespun wisdom is the mother of all tearjerkers from an artist never averse to yanking at her audience’s heartstrings. She asks Parton if people from “where I come from” would call her a hillbilly; regards the singer’s outfit with a jaundiced eye and tells her “you don’t have to look like this”. And, most infamously, she enquires: “Do you ever feel that you’re a joke?”View image in fullscreenParton performing in 1981.Photograph: LGI Stock/Corbis/VCG/Getty Images“The joke’s on the public,” responds Parton, her smile never slipping. “I know exactly what I’m doing and I can change it any time … I’m sure of myself. I’m sure of my talent.”It was a TV appearance that told you a lot about public perceptions of Parton in the years when she surged from Nashville fame to international superstardom – an era when you could turn on British TV and find a Canadian duo called MacLean and MacLean performing a mocking song called Dolly Parton’s Tits – and also told you a lot about Parton herself, most notably that, beneath the wig and the rhinestones, she had rather more in common with Walters than anyone might have thought.View image in fullscreenParton with Porter Wagoner circa 1968 in Nashville, Tennessee.Photograph: Michael Ochs Archives/Getty ImagesOf course she was sure of her talent: by the time she sat down with Walters, she had already written a string of imperishable country standards: not just Coat of Many Colours, but Jolene, My Tennessee Mountain Home, Down from Dover, I Will Always Love You, Little Bird, Kentucky Gambler, Love Is Like a Butterfly, The Bargain Store, The Seeker. Of course she knew exactly what she was doing with her image, based – as she never tired of telling interviewers – on “the town tramp” back in Pittman Center, Tennessee. A woman whose first solo hit was called Dumb Blonde, she used it both to lure in a certain type of country fan (“rednecks with flat tops who bring women who wear short skirts or tight pants,” as one 1970s journalist sniffily put it) and as a kind of glitzy, fluffy shield.Behind it, she could be subtly subversive. Years before the controversy around Loretta Lynn’s 1975 single The Pill highlighted the issue of Nashville’s sexism, Parton was writing songs of a distinctly feminist bent – Just Because I’m a Woman and When Possession Gets Too Strong among them – even if she always demurred from describing herself as such. She also had a line in songs that could give more conservative Nashville stars palpitations. Down from Dover was extraordinarily beautiful, but it seemed to simmer with empathic rage on behalf of its protagonist, an outcast unmarried mother, and concluded with a description of her giving birth to a stillborn baby. Her duet partner Porter Wagoner was so horrified that he urged her not to release it: she did, and it was summarily banned by country radio.And behind her image, she could be a model of smart, steely self-determination. If the country music establishment had a tendency to look down on her (the songwriter Tom T Hall once noted that he and Kris Kristofferson were the only two people in Nashville “who could describe Dolly Parton without using their hands”), she was abundantly aware of her own worth. The then-more-famous Wagoner was doing her a favour in 1967 when he adopted her as his duet partner, but Parton did most of the heavy lifting when it came to the pair’s songwriting, and left when it became apparent her success was beginning to outstrip his, occasioning a $3m lawsuit in the process. Moreover, she famously turned down Elvis Presley’s overtures to record the heart-rending song she wrote about the duo’s split, I Will Always Love You, when Presley’s manager indicated he wanted a cut of the songwriting royalties in return.View image in fullscreenDolly Parton in 1978.Photograph: Christian RoseShe was clearly possessed of a far greater artistic and commercial ambition than she was given credit for. The former was evidenced by 1973’s My Tennessee Mountain Home, an entirely self-penned autobiographical concept album that was rather less sentimental in its recollections than you might expect: “No amount of money could pay me to go back and live through it again,” she sang of her poverty-stricken rural upbringing on In the Good Old Days (When Times Were Bad). It ranks among the best things she ever released. Her daring became apparent around the time of the Walters interview, when Parton made a lunge for the pop mainstream, disregarding fears that it would alienate her existing audience.She scored a succession of huge pop hits: 1977’s Mann and Weill-penned Here You Come Again went to No 3 on the Hot 100, a chart on which Jolene had, incredibly, only peaked at No 60; three years later 9 to 5 hit No 1. She also transformed into an actor and dabbled in disco without losing her country essence. During her quest for mainstream success, she was as likely to essay a bluegrass version of the Beatles’ Help!, or a cover of Woody Guthrie’s Deportee (Plane Wreck at Los Gatos), or unleash upon the world Me and Little Andy, a song that anywhere other than Nashville would be regarded as a bit much – a childanda puppy snuff it in the final verse – as she was to release the winningly high-camp disco of Potential New Boyfriend. She really did know exactly what she was doing.In a sense, her moment as a mainstream crossover pop star was relatively short-lived. There was one more huge hit with 1983’s peerless Islands in the Stream, a Bee Gees-penned duet with Kenny Rodgers, but that moment had drawn to close by the time of 1987’s Rainbow. It seemed Parton had reached her limit with trying to cater to a broad audience – doggedly ploughing her way through its written-to-order contents, she sounded bored stiff, particularly when compared with the same year’s superb Trio, a collaboration with Emmylou Harris and Linda Ronstadt.View image in fullscreenDolly Parton in 1978.Photograph: Harry Langdon/Getty ImagesAnd besides, Rainbow’s commercial failure didn’t matter. Perhaps because she had never really turned her back on country – 1984’s Tennessee Homesick Blues opened with sound of Parton yodelling – Nashville welcomed her full-blooded return to the genre, with 1989’s Ricky Skaggs-produced White Limozeen. If she never scored another US Hot 100 hit, the broader celebrity she had established in the late 70s and early 80s never waned for the rest of her life. Tellingly, while promoting White Limozeen’s standout track, the insanely catchy and uproariously funny Why’d You Come in Here Lookin’ Like That?, she hosted Saturday Night Live: it would be a decade before another country star did so.In truth, Parton’s subsequent albums were of a decidedly mixed quality, at least until she returned to absolute basics: 1999’s Grammy-winning The Grass Is Blue kicked off a trio of stark, fantastic albums that dealt in bluegrass, Appalachian folk and country gospel, the music that she had “grown up surrounded by”. Thereafter, what she put out was hit-and-and miss: misjudged horrors including 2003’s post-9/11 collection of patriotic songs, For God andCountry, abutting albums as good as 2014’s Blue Smoke, although her voice sounded magnificent no matter the material. She was still more than capable of writing fantastic songs – but nothing that could eclipse the best of her 70s material.It didn’t really matter, because the best of her 70s material had long taken on a life of its own outside country music. Whitney Houston’s cover of I Will Always Love You became the biggest-selling single of all time by a female artist. At the last count, Jolene has been covered nearly 90 times: you could hear it rendered as noisy alt-rock by the White Stripes, synth-pop by Strawberry Switchblade, or a dubby post-club soundtrack by One Dove. Stars queued up to pay homage.View image in fullscreenParton attends the opening of the Country Music Hall of Fame and the museum’s show, Dolly Parton: Journey of a Seeker, in 2025.Photograph: Jason Kempin/Getty ImagesMeanwhile, in the 21st century, the full extent of Parton’s influence on pop became apparent. Younger stars queued up to pay homage of one kind or another. Taylor Swift, who knows a thing or two about pivoting away from country to pop, called her “a force of evolution and transformation in our industry”. Parton co-wrote Rainbowland on her goddaughter Miley Cyrus’s 2017 album Younger Now, and you didn’t have to analyse Sabrina Carpenter’s work too deeply to spot the influence. The fact that Carpenter’s 2024 smash Please Please Please sounded like something Parton might have written evidently didn’t escape Parton herself: she turned up duetting with Carpenter on a remixed version of the song, the swearing decorously omitted.As fans of Tammy Wynette or Patsy Cline would be quick to point out, Parton certainly wasn’t the first female country star to cross over into the pop charts, but she nevertheless seemed like the godmother of the pop-country that has swept the charts in recent years, which one Spotify playlist characterised as “Neon Cowgirl” (Parton was by far the oldest artist to make said playlist, rubbing shoulders with Swift, Carpenter, Chappell Roan, Kesha et al). When Beyoncé made a musical leap into country on Cowboy Carter, it somehow seemed inevitable that Parton would be involved, and so it proved: she delivered a spoken-word introduction to Beyoncé’s redux of Jolene. In fact, she seemed as present in pop music in the mid-2020s as she had been in the late 70s. The difference was that no one would have asked her if she was a joke. That question had been answered to everyone’s satisfaction a long time ago.Explore more on these topicsDolly PartonCountrycommentShareReuse this content

title: People’s bodies are changing in the age of Ozempic. How are we meant to talk about it? | Well actually | The Guardian
description: Discussing people’s bodies can be fraught. We asked eating disorder experts how to do so – or not – responsibly
Author: Madeleine Aggeler
Headline: Discussing people’s bodies can be fraught. We asked eating disorder experts how to do so – or not – responsibly
Content: The deluge of social media posts has only exacerbated the confusion and made it feel impossible to escape body discourse.Illustration: LUVLIMAGE/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe deluge of social media posts has only exacerbated the confusion and made it feel impossible to escape body discourse.Illustration: LUVLIMAGE/Getty ImagesWell actuallyPeople’s bodies are changing in the age of Ozempic. How are we meant to talk about it?Discussing people’s bodies can be fraught. We asked eating disorder experts how to do so – or not – responsiblyMadeleine AggelerTue 25 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 12.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the age of Ozempic and peoplebeing open about plastic surgery,discussionaboutpeople’s bodies isrife. At the same time, nobody seems quite sure how to talk about them, as shown by recent coverage of celebrities likeAriana Grande.It is a fraught topic. We asked eating disorder experts for guidelines to follow when talking about other people’s bodies, and how to do so without doing harm.Why does it feel particularly hard to talk about bodies right now?For experts in the field of eating disorders, the current ambivalence makes sense. “There’s a whiplash moment we’re stuck in,” says Dr Tom Hildebrandt, director of the Center for Eating and Weight Disorders at Mount Sinai hospital in New York.The body positivity movement of the 2010s saw a mainstream push to “accept all body sizes, shapes and types”, says Hildebrandt. Then, with the explosion of GLP-1s, progress toward body acceptance “took a hard right turn”, he says – once again, “the media went through its idealization of weight loss”.The vocabulary is different than it was before. Now, the focus is on “optimizing” one’s body and appearance, says Dr Ulrike Schmidt, professor of eating disorders at King’s College London.The deluge of social media posts has only exacerbated the confusion and made it feel impossible to escape body discourse.“The internet, specifically social media, has made commentary on the appearance of others more visible and widespread,” says Jessica Scheer, CEO of the National Eating Disorders Association (Neda). “Most of the commentary is speculative, and almost all of it is harmful.”Is it harmful to talk about someone’s body?“Everything is about context,” says Hildebrandt. “It means something different in your physician’s office than it does on a social media account for the whole world to see.”When considering how or whether to discuss bodies with other people, keep in mind that many people are unhappy with their bodies and appearance, says Schmidt. She points toa 2023 reportby the Butterfly Foundation, Australia’s national charity for eating disorders and body image issues, which found that 57% of young people were dissatisfied with how they look, and 49% said this had sometimes stopped them from attending school.“Even the seemingly most innocent and well-meaning comments about people’s body weight, shape or appearance have the potential for backfiring, sensitizing or hurting people,” she says. In her work as an eating disorder clinician, Schmidt says many of the people she sees recall comments about their bodies as the starting point of their eating disorder journey. Some of these comments were criticisms or warnings about changing bodies, while others were intended as compliments.“In clinic, we often hear that these kinds of congratulatory comments … made them think they are only acceptable, attractive and desirable if they are a certain weight or physique,” Schmidt says.How does one engage in body talk in a way that is not harmful?Body talk is ubiquitous, and it can be difficult not to engage. We asked experts how one might respond in various contexts.If an acquaintance or colleague brings up another person or celebrity’s body:When someone you aren’t very close to engages in body talk, you may not want to get involved. Often, discussing people’s bodies can be like talking about the weather, Hildebrandt says – a topic one turns to when there is nothing else to talk about. “But it’s a very low-level social connection; it doesn’t have much meaning to it.”In most cases, he says, people’s remarks about others’ bodies are not badly meant. They are more like a reflex, something we have been conditioned to believe is acceptable small talk. “I tell people to be bored by it,” says Hildebrandt. As soon as you signal that you’re not interested – by not engaging and changing the topic, for example – people will move on quickly,” Hildebrandt says.(Experts have noted that this is also auseful strategyif you feel activated by other people’s discussion of body shapes and sizes.)If a child criticizes their body or someone else’s:“If a young child says something negative about their body, it might be helpful to ask: ‘What makes you say that?’” says Schmidt.They might have made the comment because they are being bullied or teased by other children, or because they are mirroring the comments of an adult. “Depending on the origins of the comment, the response may need to be quite different,” Schmidt says.Hildebrandt tells his own children that public discussion of people’s bodies is “just trying to get your attention” and often features “lazy” messaging.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWell ActuallyPractical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good lifeEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“If someone’s going to try to sell me something based on somebody’s body type, they’re being lazy,” he says. “They’re just assigning a body value to get your attention.”The antidote, he says – in these conversations and in general – is to actively pursue other interests. It’s tough to simply “be less interested” in this prevalent topic, he says; “you have to be more interested in something else.”If an older relative criticizes or praises someone’s body:We may technically speak the same language as older relatives, but we may not always mean the same thing, Hildebrandt notes. For example, when you say “phone”, you mean a smartphone; “for your grandparents, it’s something that hangs on the wall.”This same language mismatch can happen in discussions about bodies. A grandparent’s remark about another person’s weight loss may be a comment about their overall success or an expression of concern about their wellbeing. Hildebrandt argues that it is more helpful to engage with their intended meaning as opposed to being overly literal and “ending up in a situation where there’s friction”.If people are discussing someone’s body on social media:Experts say it’s best not to comment in these public forums.“I see a lot of talk online about the harms of staying silent,” says Scheer. “However, making speculative comments about a person’s weight or physical appearance is not the antidote to silence.”In instances where a publicly speculated eating disorder may be the case, she says, “critical online discourse may be the digital reinforcement that fuels their continued behavior”.Is there ever a time when posting about someone else’s body on social media is valuable? “I haven’t heard of one yet,” says Hildebrandt.If you are struggling with seeing body discussions on social media,Neda recommends, among other things, limiting screen time and thinking critically about the media we are exposed to, including asking questions like: “Who created and profits from the message?”If you are worried about a friend or close relative:Speculating about a stranger’s health and worrying about a friend are two very different things. If you have concerns about a friend’s body image or eating behavior, experts recommend being direct and compassionate.“Be inquisitive, honest and open,” says Hildebrandt. “Don’t jump to a solution. Most people don’t want solutions – certainly not right off the bat. They want to be heard and understood, so being open and curious will get you the furthest.”Scheer also suggests focusing the conversation not on a person’s appearance, “but the other aspects that generally accompany an eating disorder, like social isolation and brain fog”.“None of us have the ability to control other people,” says Hildebrandt. “The other person is going to dictate whether the conversation goes further or not. If you’ve demonstrated that you can listen, hear and understand, then chances are you’re going to have more conversations.”Explore more on these topicsWell actuallyWeight-loss drugsBody imageHealthHealth & wellbeingSocial mediafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Airport Chaplain review – thoroughly bingeable TV about ‘Batman in a hi-vis vest’ | Television | The Guardian
description: This moreish show about a do-gooder keen to save the day stars Hugo Weaving and The Pitt’s Shabana Azeez … and it’s pressure-packed from the get-go
Author: Luke Buckmaster
Headline: This moreish show about a do-gooder keen to save the day stars Hugo Weaving and The Pitt’s Shabana Azeez … and it’s pressure-packed from the get-go
Content: Ground control … Hugo Weaving and Shabana Azeez in The Airport Chaplain.Photograph: Ben King/SBSView image in fullscreenGround control … Hugo Weaving and Shabana Azeez in The Airport Chaplain.Photograph: Ben King/SBSTelevisionReviewThe Airport Chaplain review – thoroughly bingeable TV about ‘Batman in a hi-vis vest’This moreish show about a do-gooder keen to save the day stars Hugo Weaving and The Pitt’s Shabana Azeez … and it’s pressure-packed from the get-goLuke BuckmasterTue 25 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHugo Weaving plays the eponymous airport chaplain in this pacy and moreish eight-part series, which was co-created by Elise McCredie and Jude Troy, and directed with jittery flair by Bonnie Moir and Tig Terera. In case you were wondering, yes, that profession reallydoesexist.I doubt the lives of real airport chaplains are anywhere near as frenetic as those of this show’s protagonist, Tobias Wallace (Weaving), whose existence is a testament to that old saying: “Not all heroes wear capes.” Sometimes, they wear hi-vis.The Airport Chaplain wastes no time establishing Tobias as a gallant do-gooder determined to save the day, as he rescues the toy rabbit of a distressed child. Tobias is a problem-solver, finding out-of-the-box solutions to all kinds of prickly situations, from locating lost baggage to transporting dead bodies, from intervening in cases of domestic violence to playing matchmaker, helping online lovers connect in real life. And sometimes, God forbid, he even provides spiritual counsel, such as helping a grieving son to deal with his father’s death.But most of all, Tobias is a spectacular busybody, inserting himself into virtually every problem in the airport. This might not be entirely realistic, but it certainly makes for interesting drama. We’re thrown into the thick of it from the first episode, in which Tobias receives a call from the control room and races to the aid of a panicked boy in a hoodie just as the police arrive. It very quickly becomes clear who is really in charge here, with the cops left looking useless as Tobias takes the reins. He’s a bit like Batman in an airport.But trouble arises when Tobias’s new boss arrives: terminal manager Mira Ansari-Cole (Shabana Azeez), who has not drunk the pastoral care Kool-Aid. During their first meeting, Mira isn’t impressed when Tobias describes his role as “primarily providing emotional, spiritual and practical support for passengers”. Nor is she thrilled when he knocks back her suggestion to file a daily work report, before abruptly leaving the meeting citing a “spiritual emergency”.The stage is set for a good ol’ fashioned war between management and an employee who views himself as absolutely integral to the viability of the organisation he works for. And as much as viewers may instinctively side with Tobias, most of us will surely see some merit in Mira’s scepticism, which gives her increasing desire to show him the door – a solid narrative foothold.Shabana Azeez: ‘The most disgusting thing I’ve seen on The Pitt? American coffee’Read moreJust as HBO’s hit medical dramaThe Pitt(also starring Azeez) reminds us of the power of hospitals as a central location, McCredie and Troy do something similar with airports; these are both places where virtually anybody can come through the door. In The Airport Chaplain, it is the exceptions that are the most interesting. While most people hurry from A to B, every now and then a character walks through the doors with a whole lot more going on. In the second episode, authorities – including Tobias, of course – deal with a man who has hidden Ethiopian honey in shampoo bottles. To me, this felt like a bit of a letdown; I was expecting something more sensational, like several kilograms of white powder inserted where the sun doesn’t shine.Maybe that comes later – only the first four episodes were made available to the press – but every single one is pressure-packed, making the show thoroughly bingeable; it is perfect forNetflix(where it will launch globally, with Australia getting it on SBS and SBS on Demand).Narratively, the structure feels a little scattered, though the writers (McCredie, Mithila Gupta, Sarah Bassiuoni and Vidya Rajan) do find a throughline that spans several episodes, in the story of a mysterious young woman, Asha Chawla (played by Kavitha Anandasivam), who is found in a prayer room, refusing to speak and without a passport or phone. Another recurring character is Cath Barnes (Claudia Karvan), a calm, pragmatic and sassy airline service manager who is good mates with the chaplain.Tobias is, of course, the glue binding the show together. Weaving – one of the giants of Australian screen and stage – exudes a great combination of gravitas and relatability. His presence has real oomph and dynamism, but without any heightened quality that suggests you would never encounter such a person in real life. If my luggage ever disappears, I want Tobias Wallace on the case.The Airport Chaplain is on Netflix, andSBSand SBS on Demand in AustraliaExplore more on these topicsTelevisionAustralian televisionNetflixSBSHugo WeavingClaudia KarvanreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Three years after his death, the Met goes after Mohamed Al Fayed. As for his enablers – well, you can’t rush things, can you? | Marina Hyde | The Guardian
description: The crimes he stands accused of required whole armies of facilitators. Don’t the victims deserve to see them face justice too, asks Guardian columnist Marina Hyde
Author: Marina Hyde
Headline: The crimes he stands accused of required whole armies of facilitators. Don’t the victims deserve to see them face justice too, asks Guardian columnist Marina Hyde
Content: The late Mohamed Al Fayed in Paris, June 2016.Photograph: Kamil Zihnioglu/APView image in fullscreenThe late Mohamed Al Fayed in Paris, June 2016.Photograph: Kamil Zihnioglu/APOpinionMohamed Al FayedThree years after his death, the Met goes after Mohamed Al Fayed. As for his enablers – well, you can’t rush things, can you?Marina HydeThe crimes he stands accused of required whole armies of facilitators. Don’t the victims deserve to see them face justice too?Tue 25 Aug 2026 09.35 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 14.03 EDTShareHow reassuring to learn that police investigating claims of sexual assault against Mohamed Al Fayed havehanded a fileto the Crown Prosecution Service, a mere three years after the former Harrods owner’s death at the age of 94, and just decades after the first survivors made reports of abuse. The CPS has said it won’t provide a timescale for any decision, to which we might remark: no shit. With this case, the one thing you could never accuse any of the authorities of is being bound by anything approaching a timescale.The story does, however, certainly have scale. So far, more than 400 allegations including rape, sexual assault, sexual exploitation and human trafficking have been made against Al Fayed byat least 156 women– abuse he got away with, having died without any charges ever being brought against him. The claimsspan the years 1977 to 2014. At least 21 women came forward while he was alive, and there have been extraordinary rundowns in news articles and documentaries about all the alleged enablers of his wicked behaviour, from lawyers to mouthpieces to security henchmen to the doctors who carried out “purity examinations” on his young female PAs.So, not to be a Debbie Downer – because any movement on this case is better than none – but perhaps that sense of scale is not immediately discernible from the file that has been sent to the CPS, which relates to a male suspect in his 80s and two indecent assaults on two women inLondon. The investigation remains ongoing, the Met confirms.View image in fullscreenAlleged victims of Mohamed Al Fayed (L-R) Gemma, Lindsay and Jen in London on 31 October 2024.Photograph: Benjamin Cremel/AFP/Getty ImagesOf course, other under-prosecuted criminal networks are available. During the full-spectrum coverage of the Jeffrey Epstein case, many asked how on earth so many blind eyes could be turned by so many people to so much flagrant abuse by someone who was known to haveserved prison timefor soliciting prostitution from a minor. People marvelled at the vast collective silence – yet anyone who couldn’t quite believe how it could happen should have been reassured that other vast collective silences were very much ongoing. Peter Mandelson’s now notoriousmessage of commiserationto his friend Jeffrey shortly before his 2008 incarceration – “it just could not happen in Britain” – always seems to me ironically resonant. Perhaps his lordship was right, though not in the way he meant.As the Epstein furore raged on earlier this year, several Al Fayed survivors wrote to me asking why this one case was dominating everything while another, still unresolved one – and so much closer to home – seemed to lack the turbocharge of outrage that pushes something from the places our society would rather forget into the ones where we have our (always belated) reckonings. The answer to that question is normally that significant numbers of people and institutions have a deeply vested interest innotgetting to the bottom of it.Met apologises for exposing 143 email addresses of Mohamed Al Fayed victimsRead moreIt would feel unwise to conclude anything other than that in this case. There has been no equivalent political pressure to let daylight in on Al Fayed’s activities. No one has got wall-to-wall news coverage for asking how he was able to operate an alleged criminal fiefdom in the centre of Knightsbridge, when allegations were repeatedly made and the rumours in rarefied circles were more than deafening. It was, it seems, just the way things were.And as indicated, for things to be that way for so long, there needed to be whole armies of enablers and hangers-on who facilitated abuse, or looked away, or closed down or ridiculed or trashed those who stepped out of line and said anything about it, including the alleged victims. Only one of Epstein’s helpers, Ghislaine Maxwell, has ever been brought to justice. Typically, no one bar the kingpin in what I think of as the sex-case industrial complex even faces so much as a charge – they simply melt back into society, into other jobs, into the ongoing conspiracy of silence.Today, the Al Fayed survivors’ group Justice for Fayed and Harrods Survivors issued a statementpointing outthat: “Survivors have spent decades either not being believed or being told that Fayed and those around him were too powerful and that nothing could be done – but today is an important reminder that the passage of time does not, by itself, put accountability beyond reach.” Yet with the best will in the world, the passage of time doesn’t exactly help, does it? Al Fayed himself died unscathed, and we all know that once things tip conveniently into the “historical” file, they are so much harder to prove.But there are things the public can get behind right now. What Al Fayed’s survivors want is the trafficking investigation they have been requesting for almost two years. As they point out, this was not one bad man, nor some form of corporate abuse. It was, they allege, a trafficking network involving multiple perpetrators and enablers and backed by the global movement of illicit funds. At least five survivors have already been confirmed by the Home Office as victims of modern slavery. Yet the Met has been accused of havingfailed in its legal dutyto offer the victims a referral to thenational referral mechanism(it’s understood the police didn’t believe they were obligated to),which identifies modern slavery victims. Yet again, all the running is being made by a survivors’ group. No One Abovewants confirmationthat human trafficking and modern slavery are the primary framework of the Al Fayed investigation, and to know that financial investigators are being utilised to determine how the network was funded and concealed.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt remains to be seen if any belated percentage of justice will be served in this case. Even if it is, we can expect all manner of blind-eye institutions to immediately resort to their happy place and trot out some trite platitude like “never again”. In fact, it would be more accurate to conclude the opposite. Always again. Always again, until society has the courage to realise that it so often takes a village to do bad things, as well as good ones.Marina Hyde is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.This article was amended on 25 August 2026. An earlier version said that the quotation about survivors not being believed was from No One Above; it was issued by Justice for Fayed and Harrods Survivors.Explore more on these topicsMohamed Al FayedOpinionCrimeMetropolitan policeLondonPoliceCrown Prosecution ServicecommentShareReuse this content

title: We asked our climate reporters to highlight one idea for positive change. We got a chronicle of global transformation | Climate crisis | The Guardian
description: There are countless initiatives around the world that can inspire people and spur them into action. Amid the devastation of the climate crisis, our journalists strive to highlight these stories of hope
Author: Bibi van der Zee
Headline: There are countless initiatives around the world that can inspire people and spur them into action. Amid the devastation of the climate crisis, our journalists strive to highlight these stories of hope
Content: How can positive ideas help shape a better world?Composite: Guardian Design/Getty Images/SOPA Images/Shutterstock/iStockPhoto/REXView image in fullscreenHow can positive ideas help shape a better world?Composite: Guardian Design/Getty Images/SOPA Images/Shutterstock/iStockPhoto/REXInside the GuardianClimate crisisWe asked our climate reporters to highlight one idea for positive change. We got a chronicle of global transformationThere are countless initiatives around the world that can inspire people and spur them into action. Amid the devastation of the climate crisis, our journalists strive to highlight these stories of hopeClimate campaign 2026: help us reach 30,000 acts of supportBibi van der ZeeTue 25 Aug 2026 08.27 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 11.02 EDTShareThe news is very often about the bad things (especially if you’re on the Guardian’s environment desk). Wildfires, floods, tipping points, billionaires making huge profits and buying themselves island refuges for the apocalypse … And yet, ticking along beside that is the steady pulse of what the rest of humanity is doing in response to the climate crisis. From housing developments with no cars to buildings made out of hemp, all over the planet people are ploughing ahead and changing their neighbourhoods and cities and the world.But as news stories typically need to be about new developments or things people didn’t previously know about, it can be hard to cover all those brilliant initiatives being undertaken in the background – no matter how cheering they are. Which is why, back in 2023, we decided to ignore the usual rules about what constitutes “news” and start writing about them anyway. Readers, we knew, would like to hear about them.And so was bornthe Alternatives, a weekly news column where we cover these different projects. We’re constantly amazed by some of the things we learn. Norway has heat pumps intwo-thirds of its homes. China’s sponge cities aretargeting 70% rainwater reuse. Paris is building agigantic cooling machine using river water. It feels as if the series is a vast chronicle of the transformations that are taking place everywhere, far faster than we sometimes realise.This year, as part of the Guardian’s annual climate support campaign, we are highlighting all of the work that our environment team does to bring readers positive ideas such as those above, providing hope that a better world is possible if we start acting on it.So, we asked our environment reporters around the world to share one big idea from their journalism – funded by you – that has helped drive or inspire some kind of positive change for the planet. Their answers are below.Climate campaign 2026: help us reach 30,000 acts of supportPetra StockClimate and environment reporter, Guardian AustraliaMany objections to wind turbines cite the impact on wildlife, such as birds and bats. But there are simple fixes and innovations that demonstrate there doesn’t need to be a trade-off between clean energy and safeguarding biodiversity. One such approach I reported – which involvesraising the “cut in” speedat which turbines start spinning – has the potential to save tens of thousands of native bats every year, with minimal impact on energy output.Ajit NiranjanEuropean environment correspondentSausage-hungry and schnitzel-loving Germany is not a likely place for plant-based food to boom, but it’s a case study in how individual green choices have a surprisingly powerful ripple effect. I reportedon the hospitals winning patients overas they change menus to enable healthier diets with more plants and less meat.Fiona HarveyEnvironmenteditorWhen everything seems wrapped in gloom, we need fresh thinking and some can-do attitude. That’s why I lovedinterviewing Mariana Mazzucato, one of the world’s leading economic and social thinkers, about her stimulating ideas of re-basing politics on the global common good. She shows that we can change the world for the better, including fixing the climate crisis, and though she advises global leaders , she also believes the joy we can bring to our daily lives – like carnivals and communal eating – can be just as powerful.Damian CarringtonEnvironment editorWhen I reported in 2020 thatmicroplastic pollution had been discovered at the top of Mount Everest, it showed that humanity’s litter had polluted the entire planet. But it also inspired a young researcher to set up anaward-winning project that is now recycling plasticin Nepal into much-needed insulation for homes and stopping the waste contaminating the high mountain nation.Jonathan WattsGlobal environment writerI covereda new reportby Thomas Piketty and co at the World Inequality Lab, which shows us that ajust and equitable world is possible. I alsohighlighted how new energyis bringing a new world order, with China dominating the energy transition with astonishing results, while fossil fuel fascists in the US try to turn back the clock.Gabrielle CanonSenior climate reporter, Guardian USA barley farm in the US Pacific Northwest had been quietly leeching pollutants into the nearby watershed. It has long been an issue along the southern Oregon coast, where 95% of the sprawling networks of wetlands were drained, diverted, or dried, and replaced by cattle ranges and crops. But when Karl Wenner acquired the land in 2021, he wanted to try something new. By restoring a wetland on just 28 of the farm’s 162 hectares, hecreated a welcome sanctuaryfor migrating and native birds that are disappearing from the area, endangered native fish who can be spotted swimming near rows of sprouting barley, and the plants that quickly soaked up the phosphorus, stopping run-off. The remarkable transformation was not only beneficial to the environment – it was a boon to business. The story showcased a symbiotic solution to one of the world’s most pressing environmental problems.This year’s Guardian climate support campaign highlights our unrivalled coverage of the climate emergency, including our reporting on the ideas and initiatives that can help tackle it.Please consider supporting it today.On Tuesday 20 October, join Damian Carrington, and our panel of experts—including Professor Andy Haines, Katie White MP, Asad Rehman, Shruti Suresh, Gareth Thomas and Amy Fairman for a hopeful and solutions-focused evening. Book ticketshereor atguardian.live

title: ‘I love rats but we can’t live with them’: the headache of rising rodent populations around the world | Climate crisis | The Guardian
description: Robert Corrigan has been dealing with the ‘smart’ rodents all his life – and believes there are better solutions to deal with the growing infestation in the world’s cities
Author: Isaaq Tomkins
Headline: Robert Corrigan has been dealing with the ‘smart’ rodents all his life – and believes there are better solutions to deal with the growing infestation in the world’s cities
Content: On the rise: a brown rat emerges from its hole.Photograph: Jakob Gunther/AlamyView image in fullscreenOn the rise: a brown rat emerges from its hole.Photograph: Jakob Gunther/AlamyClimate crisis‘I love rats but we can’t live with them’: the headache of rising rodent populations around the worldRobert Corrigan has been dealing with the ‘smart’ rodents all his life – and believes there are better solutions to deal with the growing infestation in the world’s citiesIsaaq TomkinsTue 25 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“The rodents have paid for every single bill I’ve ever had – every mortgage, every car payment, every pint of Guinness,” says Dr Robert Corrigan. “It’s been a great ride and I’m still at it.”New York-based Corrigan is one of the most respected voices in the world of rodentology. Now in his 70s, he has devoted his entire adult life to studying rats and our relationship with them.Last year, he and 10 other scientistspublished a paperdescribing the effect of global heating on rat populations. In 16 cities they found that rat numbers had increased dramatically, and there was a correlation between their numbers and rising temperatures.The two most common types of rat – the black and the brown – do not hibernate, which means in places with regular winters their reproduction slows down or even stops during cold periods. Here lies the problem, says Corrigan.View image in fullscreenRobert Corrigan in a New York alley on a rat observation mission.Photograph: Bobby Corrigan“When you have repeating warm winters, one after the other, the rats benefit,” he says. For many families of rats, the warmer temperatures may only offer a marginal advantage, but the problem escalates “when you start multiplying that little bit of extra rat production by hundreds of millions of rats”.Humans have been trying to control rats for centuries. Often an invasive species, they are vectors for disease,decimate crop yieldsand destabilise ecosystems as they hunt other species to extinction. At the other end of the spectrum, domesticated rats, descended from wild Norway rats, are often kept as affectionate pets.Now, more and more scientists and public servants around the world are trying to manage rats without filling their cities with harmful poisons. Methods for doing so range from contraceptives to robust public health regulations.The biggest issue with our current approach to rats– dumping poison on them and laying traps – is that we treat them like “any old vermin”, says Corrigan. They are in fact “smart mammals with mammal brains”.He should know. Corrigan first got to know rats while working as an exterminator in the sewers of New York City. He worked in the sewers to save up for graduate school, where he studied rodent pest management. There he then spent weekend after weekend camping out in barns to observe rats.“I saw things back then,” says Corrigan. “I saw kindness: that rat just brought food to another because it looked sick. I saw aggression: a bully would come around and attack other rats for no reason.”View image in fullscreenRats on the street in New York. Corrigan first got to know the rodents while working as an exterminator in the sewers of the US city.Photograph: Anadolu Agency/Getty ImagesHe describes his feelings towards rats as paradoxical: “Do I love that species and do I respect it as a scientist? Heck, yes. On the other hand I know that they cannot cohabitate with us because they can kill us.”Rats can carry pathogens that spill over into human populations. These include Weil’s disease,hantavirusornew variants of coronavirus.And yet, of all the methods used to control rat populations, poison is not one Corrigan would recommend. “It’s a band aid,” he says.There are compelling reasons to not throw everything at rodenticides, even though most experts – including Corrigan – do acknowledge their usefulness as a temporary corrective measure.Firstly, as with many public health issues, prevention is better than cure. Enforcing stricter public health regulations is often more effective than letting rat populations spiral and then dumping poison on them to regain control.Aside from the cruel, slow death they result in for rats, rodenticides are knownto harm other wildlifeand can end up being consumed by humans – in the US there are already thousands ofaccidental human rodenticide poisoningseach year.One hope for better managing rat populations are fertility controls, which are increasingly popular in the US following public concern about wildlife poisoning from rodenticides. Europe is slowly catching up as more experts champion the technology, which uses contraceptives to slow down rat population growth.“Developing new forms of birth control is the key to managing the soaring number of poison-resistant rats compassionately,” said Richard Parr, director of UK charity theCenter for Wild Animal Welfare. At the same time, he says outdated biocidal product regulation in the EU is “stifling innovation”. While the EU’s regulationis under review, it is not yet equipped to deal with new fertility control technology, creating uncertainty that deters investment.But Steven Belmain, professor of ecology at the University of Greenwich, maintains a scepticism about the idea that fertility controls are advanced enough to help.“People are sometimes quite naive thinking we can use fertility control. If you’ve got a rat in your house, you’re not going to feed it contraceptives and just let it live there with you,” he says.“Our restaurants, our hotels, our hospitals, our food warehouses will all just collapse without having any sort of poison management.”Back in New York, Corrigan is trying to find more evidence that fertility controls are a viable alternative to poisons, but ultimately believes infestations come from a failure of municipal politics. If one person has poor sanitation habits, it will cause an infestation that affects all.View image in fullscreenSteven Belmain is sceptical about about fertility controls:  ‘If you’ve got a rat in your house, you’re not going to feed it contraceptives and just let it live there with you.’Photograph: blickwinkel/Alamy“Cities are not strict enough on punishing people that ruin the block or the area or the province for everybody,” he says.But one significantly populated area stands out globally as one of the only places that has managed to almost entirely eradicate rats.Canada’s oil-rich western province of Alberta is the only place on Earth with a significant number of people, but a negligible rat population. At the centre of their success is collective effort, not fruitless chemical warfare.Karen Wickerson is the Alberta government’s rat and pest specialist. She runs a programme that has been operational since 1950 and is one of the most successful examples of invasive species management of the last century.After the second world war, Alberta was the breadbasket of Canada, which in turn was providing the allied forces with much-needed grain. So when rats were discovered on their eastern border with Saskatchewan, the provincial government took decisive action.“There was a rat patrol that went out and started eradicating all the infestations along the border. At that time there were probably six or seven hundred infestations a year,” says Wickerson. In 2025, Albertahad just five infestationsacross the province. While the local government does use anti-coagulants and traps to kill rats, the scale of the issue is almost non-existent thanks to a proactive population.From the very beginning, the Albertan government mobilised every citizen against rats: legislation was passed requiring them to control or report rodents on their property. At the same time a public education programme was launched: pamphlets were handed out, posters put up, and taxidermied specimens were placed in all the agriculture offices on the border.Wickerson has one of the posters from 1990 behind her on the wall. It shows a rat with glowing red pupils in the shape of the province, staring down menacingly at its onlooker.But even Albertans are nervous about the future of rat control. In 2026, people are taking more holidays outside of the province, bringing back rodent hitchhikers on their return. Even more significant is the development of urban areas, which creates more sanitation issues that can lead to infestation. Finally, Wickerson points out that last autumn was extremely warm, which undermines the natural protections they have as a cold province with tough winters.Hundreds of people around the world are trying to figure out a way to address increasing rat populations, and few are in doubt about the impact the climate crisis is having. Corrigan puts it simply: “Planet Earth is changing and the rats are benefiting.”Explore more on these topicsClimate crisisWildlifeAnimalsMammalsGlobal healthUrbanisationfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Dolly Parton, country star, actor and philanthropist, dies aged 80 after fighting cancer | Dolly Parton | The Guardian
description: Songwriter of I Will Always Love You, Jolene and 9 to 5 invested millions in child literacy, Covid-19 vaccine development and other causes
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Songwriter of I Will Always Love You, Jolene and 9 to 5 invested millions in child literacy, Covid-19 vaccine development and other causes
Content: Dolly Parton pictured in 2022.Photograph: NBC/Katherine Bomboy/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDolly Parton pictured in 2022.Photograph: NBC/Katherine Bomboy/Getty ImagesDolly PartonDolly Parton, country star, actor and philanthropist, dies aged 80 after fighting cancerSongwriter of I Will Always Love You, Jolene and 9 to 5 invested millions in child literacy, Covid-19 vaccine development and other causesAlexis Petridis on Dolly Parton’s peerless career that turned country music cliches inside outDolly Parton – a life in picturesCountry music legend Dolly Parton dies aged 80 – latest updatesShare your tributes and memories of Dolly PartonBen Beaumont-ThomasTue 25 Aug 2026 13.59 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 22.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDolly Parton, one of the greatest singer-songwriters in country music, who was also much cherished for her philanthropy, has died aged 80.Her death wasannouncedby nephew Brian Seaver on Instagram. “I have imagined the heaviness of this moment but haven’t truly felt it until now,” he said. “It is an honour, an honour that is mixed with absolute pride and great sadness.”Parton’s teamconfirmedthe singer died Tuesday “after bravely facing a brief battle with cancer.”“Dolly departed her Earthly life today at the Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center surrounded by loved ones,” the statement continued.Dolly Parton – a life in picturesRead moreSo gifted that she wrote two of the 20th century’s greatest songs – Jolene and I Will Always Love You – in a single day, Parton’s songwriting was characterised by its vivid storytelling, emotional acuity and melodic strength, all sung with strident clarity. From an eventual catalogue of hundreds of songs, she scored a record 25 US country No 1 singles and 47 albums in the country Top 10. She crossed over into the pop charts with 9 to 5, a US No 1 hit in 1980; balanced her music career with acclaimed acting, twice earning Golden Globe nominations for her roles; and donated more than 300m books to children through her Imagination Library literacy project.This was all done with considerable panache, rhinestoned glamour and towering hairdos, with her immortal assertion regarding her appearance – “it takes a lot of money to look this cheap” – the most quoted example of Parton’s ready wit.View image in fullscreenDolly Parton in 1976.Photograph: PAParton was born in poverty in a one-room cabin inTennessee, the fourth child to a mother who would have 12 children by the age of 35, and a father who was a farmer and construction worker. One of her best-loved songs, Coat of Many Colours, was about her mother creating patchwork clothes; Parton’s first guitar was cobbled together from a mandolin with bass guitar strings. Her first proper guitar was given to her aged eight by her uncle, and she went from singing in church to appearing on local television aged 10, to cutting her first record aged 13. That year, she appeared at the Grand Ole Opry, the concert hall in Nashville at the center of country music, and her performance was introduced by Johnny Cash. “I’ve always believed things would go well, and I dreamed that they would even before I was in high school,” she later said. “I always wanted to be a star. It just seemed natural to me.”After graduating high school in 1964, she moved to Nashville and started out as a songwriter rather than performer. The following year, she was signed as an artist and initially moulded as a pop singer, without success; after she was allowed to switch to country, she scored back-to-back hits and released her debut album Hello, I’m Dolly. In 1966, she married Carl Dean – who died in 2025, with the couple renewing their vows in 2016 to mark 50 years together.Beginning in 1967, a duet partnership with country singer and TV personality Porter Wagoner helped her star continue to ascend, and she had her first country No 1 in 1971 with the song Joshua.Jolene, her unforgettably raw and desperate plea to a rival lover, was released in 1973 and became her first UK success, reaching No 7. I Will Always Love You, written to Wagoner as a farewell after their creative partnership ended, was a country No 1 in 1974 and again via a re-recorded version in 1982, and would go on to be a huge pop success when revived by Whitney Houston for the soundtrack of The Bodyguard in 1992: it is still the bestselling single of all time by a woman, with an estimated 20m sales.In the mid 1970s, Parton broadened her sound, embracing pop-rock arrangements on songs such as 1977’s Light of a Clear Blue Morning – its accompanying album New Harvest … First Gathering was her first entry in the pop album chart. Later that year, its follow-up, Here You Come Again, reached the Top 20 and was her first million-selling LP, powered in part by its hit title track, which also won Parton the first of her 10 Grammy awards.The year 1980 was a peak in her success, with three back-to-back country No 1s, including 9 to 5, taken from the film of the same name, which Parton starred in alongside Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin, earning her an Oscar nomination for best original song. Parton would later write songs for a stage musical version of 9 to 5, in 2008.Another classic single came in 1983 – Islands in the Stream, a duet with Kenny Rogers, which topped the US pop charts – and a Christmas album with Rogers in 1984 went two times platinum. There were more notable film roles in the 1980s, too, opposite Burt Reynolds in The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas, Sylvester Stallone in Rhinestone, and an all-star female ensemble in Steel Magnolias.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenLinda Ronstadt, Dolly Parton and Emmylou Harris in 1987.Photograph: Paul Harris/Getty ImagesA landmark Parton album came in 1987 with Trio, an exquisitely harmonised, springwater-clear collaboration with Emmylou Harris and Linda Ronstadt, earning Parton her only nomination for album of the year at the Grammys. Another all-star trio recording came in 1993, with Tammy Wynette and Loretta Lynn on the album Honky-Tonk Angels, followed by a reunion with Harris and Ronstadt for Trio II in 1999, featuring a Grammy-winning cover of Neil Young’s After the Gold Rush.The turn of the century brought a trilogy of acclaimed bluegrass albums, and Parton would release 10 more LPs, the most recent being Rockstar in 2023. She was courted by a younger generation of stars, appearing with country artists such as Brad Paisley as well as pop singers such as Kesha, and her goddaughter Miley Cyrus. There were fewer acting roles, but she lent her voice to animated film Gnomeo and Juliet in 2011 and the following year appeared alongside Queen Latifah and more in the musical film Joyful Noise.Alongside her music and acting, Parton was an astute businesswoman and philanthropist. She founded the film and TV production company Sandollar, with former manager Sandy Gallin, which went on to produce hits such as Buffy the Vampire Slayer and the Father of the Bride film series. In 1986, she took a stake in the Silver Dollar City theme park in Tennessee and renamed it Dollywood, doubling its size over the next two decades, and a Dollywood-branded spa, cabin complex, theatre-restaurant concept and waterpark have since been opened.View image in fullscreenDolly Parton in Joyful Noise.Photograph: Van Redin/Publicity image from film companyThe Dollywood Foundation, funded through these business ventures and creative projects, was created in 1988, initially awarding college scholarships and running a program to help children complete high school in her native Sevier county, Tennessee. In 1995, Parton began her Imagination Library project, which sent an age-appropriate book to every child in the county every month until they were five. “My father could not read and write, and I saw how crippling that could be,” she explained. It expanded nationwide in 2000, internationally in 2006, and nearly 25m books are now distributed each year across the US, Canada, Australia, the UK and Ireland.In 2022, Jeff Bezos donated $100m (£83m) to the foundation. That year, Parton explained that as well as improving child literacy, “it’s the fact they get recognised. They get this little book with their little name on it in the mail, and they feel special. They start taking pride in themselves, and they know that somebody out there is thinking of [them].”View image in fullscreenDolly Parton receiving the Moderna vaccine she helped to fund.Photograph: @DollyParton/ReutersParton also set up a reserve in 2003 to help preserve the bald eagle; contributed $500,000 to the opening of a Sevier county hospital in 2006; coordinated relief efforts for people affected by the Smoky mountain wildfires of 2016; and contributed to an HIV/Aids charity album. She supported Black Lives Matter and transgender rights, opposing a North Carolina “bathroom bill” that restricted transgender people’s access to toilets (Parton was also nominated for an Oscar for her song in trans drama Transamerica, entitled Travelin’ Thru).She made a number of donations to Vanderbilt University’s medical center in Nashville, Tennessee, where her niece was treated for leukemia. The most high-profile of these was in 2020, when she donated $1m for research into Covid-19, which formed the basis for the eventual Moderna vaccine.2:19Dolly Parton’s family say goodbye to their aunt, sister, grandmother - videoIn May 2026, Partoncancelledher Las Vegas residency over health issues. A Broadway musical is alsoset to openlater this year after a run in Nashville.Explore more on these topicsDolly PartonCountryPop and rockTennesseenewsShareReuse this content

title: Labour MPs will push Burnham to back voting reform in first 100 days | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Nearly 100 Labour MPs support commission on changing the system used for Westminster election
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: Exclusive: Nearly 100 Labour MPs support commission on changing the system used for Westminster election
Content: Number 10 said Burnham remained committed to electoral reform in Labour’s next manifesto but stopped short of backing the new commission.Photograph: Kin Cheung/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNumber 10 said Burnham remained committed to electoral reform in Labour’s next manifesto but stopped short of backing the new commission.Photograph: Kin Cheung/AFP/Getty ImagesAndy BurnhamLabour MPs will push Burnham to back voting reform in first 100 daysExclusive: Nearly 100 Labour MPs support commission on changing the system used for Westminster electionWhy do some Labour MPs want electoral reform and will it happen?Jessica ElgotDeputy political editorTue 25 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham will face an immediate test of his backing for electoral reform in his first week in parliament as prime minister, with almost 100 Labour MPs supporting a bid for a new national commission.Burnham, a longtime advocate of electoral reform, will be asked to support the new commission into ditching first past the post in his first 100 days as prime minister.MPs have said the commission must report before the next election and hope to put electoral reform in Labour’s next manifesto. Number 10 said Burnham remained committed to electoral reform in Labour’s next manifesto but stopped short of backing the new commission..New polling of MPs by YouGov suggests the change is now supported by a majority in the Commons. Of those polled, 53% of MPs said they supported a review into first past the post – the current system of voting.An amendment to launch the commission has been backed by 185 MPs, including a number of former ministers and supporters of the previous prime minister, Keir Starmer.Whoever wins today’s elections, democracy is the loser under first past the post | Polly ToynbeeRead moreThe amendment has been tabled to the representation of the people bill, which returns to parliament for its remaining stages on 2 September. A Labour source said: “The representation of the people bill has been designed to deliver our manifesto commitments on votes at 16 and strengthen political donation rules to guard against foreign interference, and that’s what the government is prioritising.“Andy remains strongly committed to electoral reform, and has indicated this is a matter for a future party manifesto, given a mandate would need to be secured for it.”Burnham endorsed the call for a national commission on electoral reform at last year’s Labour conference, saying then as mayor of Greater Manchester that he backed “a manifesto commitment to a system of proportional representation to be introduced into Westminster elections in the next parliament.”The 98 Labour signatories to the amendment, tabled by Labour’s Alex Sobel include influential backbenchers such as Luke Akehurst and Chris Curtis, leading Labour centrists. Overall, MPs have signed from eight parties, as well as independents.Signatories also include MPs who have recently become ministers and ministerial aides – including the energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, communities minister Florence Eshalomi and the prime minister’s parliamentary private secretary and close ally Jo Platt.However, the newly appointed frontbench MPs may by convention withdraw support for backbench amendments once parliament returns.A new commission would not require legislation – meaning the amendment itself may end up out of scope of the bill. But MPs intend to use the amendment as a way of signalling to the prime minister the breadth of support for swifter reform.A national commission could consider a range of other proportional voting systems to replace first past the post, the current system for a general election in the UK which means the winners of the most votes in each constituency are elected. Other systems are used across the UK, including the Scottish parliament, the Welsh parliament and mayoral votes.In Scottish and Welsh elections, there are votes for a candidate and for a party, so additional members can be elected from a list alongside constituency representatives. In the recent Greater Manchester mayoralty, voters were given a first and second choice.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSobel said it was time for the prime minister to endorse the push – signed by more MPs than any other amendment in parliament. “Now we know a majority of MPs back this proposal, including a majority of Labour MPs. I know the prime minister is committed to reforming our electoral system and I and all the MPs who signed this amendment want to work with him to set the UK on a road towards fair, modern general elections,” he said.MPs told the Guardian that Burnham should announce the commission before the October budget. Rachel Blake, the former Treasury minister, said: “The PLP agrees with Andy Burnham that first past the post is broken, and that a national commission is the way to get a grip on it. The government should press ahead and launch this process within the prime minister’s first hundred days.”Akehurst, a member of Labour’s governing national executive committee, said: “Parliament is catching up with the public, most of whom already support electoral reform. Andy Burnham has a good track record on proportional representation, and it’s now hugely popular across the Labour party. He should seize this opportunity.”Labour MP Lizzi Collinge said first past the post “particularly devalues the votes of renters, young people and BAME people, and delivers parliaments that do not represent what most people voted for.”Another former Labour minister, Catherine Fookes, said first past the post “can’t cope with modern, multiparty politics. Andy Burnham has long talked about the need to move to a fair, proportional system. If he acts now by setting up a commission, he will find that most MPs support him from across parliament – and make good on his promise to rewire British politics.”A sixth Labour MP, Mike Reader, said that the poll of MPs showed there had been “a sea change in support for PR across Labour and the public. Most MPs know it is the fair thing for the country, it’s just a matter of how we get there. We hope Andy Burnham will now stick to his guns.”Labour members at the party’s annual conference in 2022 had previously backed a move towards proportional representation, which Burnham called a “historic vote” and said would be a move towards “a country that works for everybody, where everyone’s vote counts”.Campaign groups said they hoped Burnham would seize the moment for reform while he had a workable parliamentary majority. Make Votes Matter chief executive Emma Harrison said: “I’ve spoken alongside Andy in favour of proportional representation, I know he supports it – now he must show the public he deserves our trust.”The UK last rejected electoral reform in 2011 after a referendum was held to ask whether to change to an alternative vote system, where voters rank candidates in order of preference.Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamElectoral reformLabournewsShareReuse this content

title: UK to warn citizens to stock up on food amid threat from climate crisis and hostile states | Defence policy | The Guardian
description: Government resilience campaign aims to ensure people can cope in a national disaster, in order to free resources for most vulnerable
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: Government resilience campaign aims to ensure people can cope in a national disaster, in order to free resources for most vulnerable
Content: The fire-gutted remains of homes on Quarry Park Road on 17 August in Stourbridge, England after a wildfire that broke out across the West Midlands.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/GettyView image in fullscreenThe fire-gutted remains of homes on Quarry Park Road on 17 August in Stourbridge, England after a wildfire that broke out across the West Midlands.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/GettyDefence policyUK to warn citizens to stock up on food amid threat from climate crisis and hostile statesGovernment resilience campaign aims to ensure people can cope in a national disaster, in order to free resources for most vulnerableJessica ElgotandKiran StaceyTue 25 Aug 2026 12.55 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUK citizens will be told to stock up on tinned food and take steps to ensure they are prepared for national emergencies as part of a new government campaign to improve the nation’s resilience.The new campaign from the Cabinet Office will set out ways people can prepare for extreme weather events and potential attacks from hostile states, including stocking up on bottled water, sources told the Guardian.The aim will be to ensure most households have basic supplies and knowledge about how to cope in a crisis, in order to free up immediate government resources for the most vulnerable.Europe is the world’s fastest warming continent. What is to blame?Read morePlanning for a number of disasters, from cyber-attacks to extreme heat and flooding, has increased over the past few months after a number of incidents both in the UK and across the world. The plans, first reported by the FT, also include an internal reassessment of government preparations for a military attack by a hostile state affecting Britain.The Cabinet Office minister Louise Haigh, who is Andy Burnham’s de-facto deputy, is also understood to be coordinating crisis planning across departments in Whitehall to allow swifter assistance to affected communities.View image in fullscreenDrought is predicted to cause food shortages.Photograph: Maureen McLean/ShutterstockDuring his campaign to become Makerfield MP, Burnham spoke repeatedly about the threat of flooding to communities and the inadequacy of government planning and response.Burnham convened a Cobra meeting earlier this month to coordinate thegovernment’s response to the heatwave, amid a threat of spreading wildfires and drought warnings.The government was criticised, however, for its decision to send an emergency phone alert warning of wildfires last week, whichcharities and domestic abuse survivorssaid risked the safety of people who might be hiding secret phones.Haigh’s predecessor, Darren Jones, had said that work was under way on the so-called “war book” on how international conflict might affect the UK.The Cabinet Office said: “Safeguarding national security is the first priority of any government.“We’re committed to raising awareness of simple steps households can take to make themselves more resilient, as well as driving forward the home defence programme to build our country’s preparedness for various threats.”Burnham’s predecessor, Keir Starmer, warned shortly before he left office thatRussiacould attack a Nato country within four years, according to western intelligence assessments.View image in fullscreenVisiting Ukraine for a meeting with Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Monday, Burnham accused the Kremlin of ‘outrageous threats’ against the UK.Photograph: Ukrainian Presidency/SIPA/ShutterstockVisiting Ukraine on Monday,Burnham accused the Kremlin of “outrageous threats” against the UKas Russia warned of an escalation in tensions after the UK’s decision to present Ukraine with newly declassified blueprints to allow Kyiv to improve its production of long-range missiles.Vladimir Putin’s spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said the exchange would add “fuel to the fire” and scupper any moves towards a peace deal.Peskov said: “Britain is involved in this war on the side of the Kyiv regime.“Britain methodically and regularly adds fuel ‌to the fire, and methodically and regularly hatches schemes to prevent even the slightest progress in the peaceful settlement process.”Last week hackers linked toIranwere blamed for a cyber-attack that caused a British power plant to be temporarily shut down.The incident involved a small-scale energy generator, according to the UK government. It added that at no point was there a risk to the wider energy system, but it marks an apparent escalation in the threat posed by Iran to UK infrastructure.Explore more on these topicsDefence policyClimate crisisLouise HaighRussiaIranWildfiresAndy BurnhamnewsShareReuse this content

title: Canada announces retaliatory tariffs on wide range of US goods | Canada | The Guardian
description: Ottawa’s ‘focused response’ to levies imposed by Donald Trump on Canadian products comes after trade talks collapsed last week
Author: Leyland Cecco
Headline: Ottawa’s ‘focused response’ to levies imposed by Donald Trump on Canadian products comes after trade talks collapsed last week
Content: Canada announces 50% retaliatory tariffs on hundreds of US imports as trade war escalates – videoCanadaCanada announces retaliatory tariffs on wide range of US goodsOttawa’s ‘focused response’ to levies imposed by Donald Trump on Canadian products comes after trade talks collapsed last weekUS politics live – latest updatesLeyland Ceccoin TorontoTue 25 Aug 2026 12.17 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCanada has announced it will impose tariffs on a wide range of key American industries including cosmetics, dairy, wood products and outdoor equipment in the coming weeks, as it retaliates roughly “dollar for dollar” against levies imposed by the US.In a strong Canadian countermove to tariffs levied byDonald Trump, which took effect on Saturday after trade talks collapsed the day before, Canada’s finance and industry ministers on Tuesday called the measure a “focused response” to what they see as unfair trade practices.The White House claimed it was using section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to protest against “discriminatory” trade policies by Canada, including provincial bans on US alcohol – a ban that was only implemented in protest against tariffs imposed on Canadian goods last year.The prime minister,Mark Carney, had previously pledged a “dollar-for-dollar” response from his government after roughly 5% of exports to the US were singled out by the White House.The retaliatory Canadian measures will cover C$27.6bn ($19.9m) in imports and are meant to target key industries including steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper.The list from Ottawa has more than 700 items, ranging from from hockey sticks to ornamental fish and toilet paper to smoked lobster, with most of the tariffs set at 25% or 50%.A small group of items, including air conditioning units and tool parts, will face a lower 15% tariff. The levies will be effective starting 8 September and only apply to goods originating from the US.In announcing the retaliatory measures, the finance minister, François-Philippe Champagne, said the country was united in its fight against the US, telling attenders that Canada remained “masters of our own home”.The industry minister, Mélanie Joly, called on businesses and consumers to buy Canadian goods as part of a broader “resistance” movement in the trade war.“You have power,” she said.The government also announced more than C$7bn in support for businesses affected by the latest tariffs, adding to more than C$20bn in support announced over the past 18 months.Canada’s decision to retaliate means both countries have doubled down on a trade war that could cost billions.Earlier on Tuesday, Trump said he was giving “serious consideration” to changing the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” – reminiscent of his decision to rename the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. Otherspointed outthat Ontario, Canada’s most populous province, was named after the lake, not the other way around.Trump’s frustration with Ontario in particular stems from his feud with the province’s premier, Doug Ford, who called the president a “loser” and the “king of bankruptcies” and told the US president to “kiss my ass”. He also threatened to cut electricity and rare earth metal exports to the US.Trump called Ford a “flunky” of “Governor Carney” and warned “these clowns to ‘fall in line’ or, the consequences for Canada will be far WORSE!”Trump later alluded torevelationsthat his trade negotiators had looked to weaken French language rules, saying he would “never interfere” with Canadians speaking French, calling it a “lie … made up by a weak and ineffective Prime Minister in an attempt to gain political support”.Trump later added: “I love French Canadians!”Explore more on these topicsCanadaTariffsMark CarneyDonald TrumpQuebecTrump tariffsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham mulls insolvency law shake-up to help bring utilities under public control | Thames Water | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Rules on special administration seen as potential ‘roadblock’ to reshaping how UK’s essential services are run
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Exclusive: Rules on special administration seen as potential ‘roadblock’ to reshaping how UK’s essential services are run
