Content: Changes could trigger a legal challenge from creditors to Thames Water, who have promised to fight any attempt to change insolvency laws.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/SOPA Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenChanges could trigger a legal challenge from creditors to Thames Water, who have promised to fight any attempt to change insolvency laws.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/SOPA Images/ShutterstockThames WaterBurnham mulls insolvency law shake-up to help bring utilities under public controlExclusive: Rules on special administration seen as potential ‘roadblock’ to reshaping how UK’s essential services are runHelena HortonandKiran StaceyTue 25 Aug 2026 14.13 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham is considering ripping up the country’s insolvency laws to make it easier to bring key utilities such asThames Waterunder public control.Sources have told the Guardian the prime minister is considering a range of options as he seeks ways of delivering on his promise to radically reshape the way England’s water and Britain’s energy companies are run.One possibility, according to those briefed on his thinking, is to change the so-called special administration regime (SAR) to make it easier to put companies such as Thames Water into insolvency proceedings, and then take control of them afterwards.The move could pave the way for what Burnham has promised will be a10-year projectto take public control of utilities, but could trigger a legal challenge from creditors to Thames Water, who have promised to fight any attempt to change insolvency laws.From Scotland, I look at England’s water privatisation disaster. I wish you had done what we did | Devi SridharRead moreOne person briefed on the plans said: “Andy is completely committed to putting utilities such as energy and water companies into public control, and is looking at every option for how to achieve that. The special administration regime is one potential roadblock and his team is examining how they might have to change it to deliver on their promises.”A government source said: “Our water industry has not been working for people for far too long. That’s why this government is looking at how we can give the public more control and help keep bills as low as possible.”Burnham promisedin his first speechas prime minister to “build a new economy where we put life’s essentials back under stronger public control to make them affordable to you again”.In June, hetold the Guardianhe favoured public ownership for Thames Water, which is struggling with a £20bn debt. Emma Reynolds, the former environment secretary,said earlier this yearshe was opposed to a planned £10bn bailout by existing creditors because it did not offer value for money.Burnham was expected to make a speech on the water industry in his first few weeks in power, but was briefed by Downing Street officials on how expensive and legally fraught it could be to take public control of companies such as Thames Water.Ministers deniedreports on Tuesdaythat Burnham had shelved plans to take Thames into administration, but officials said that they were now taking their time to look at every possible route for doing so – including legislative change.Matthew Pennycook, the housing minister, said on Tuesday: “We are taking no options off the table when it comes to Thames Water … The water industry has been failing people for too long. We’ve seen rising bills while the number of serious pollution incidents are off the scale. We’ve got to do more.”While Burnham has been clear on his desire to take Thames into public ownership, officials say there are two big problems with the special administration regime as it stands.The first is that companies can only be taken into administration if they are insolvent or unable to provide a basic level of service. Owing to continued support from a group of creditors hoping to take ownership of the company, neither of these are the case.The second is that once a company enters administration, the administrator is under a legal duty to maximise returns to the creditors, meaning that it will be difficult for the government to take ownership without paying a significant price.The process is likely to be legally difficult because many of the creditors are US-based hedge funds with a history of taking an aggressive legal approach to protecting their investments.One possible solution is to use the upcoming water bill to change the terms of the special administration regime altogether.The plan has been put together by a group of Labour backbenchers, including the former environment committee members Helena Dollimore and Andrew Pakes, alongside the Good Growth Foundation thinktank.They are suggesting amending the water bill to introduce new triggers for special administration, including lower financial ones and new environmental metrics.They have also suggested a “bail in” mechanism, similar to that imposed on the banks after the financial crisis. This would force shareholders and creditors to be fully exposed to losses first, thus protecting taxpayers, and give ministers the power to impose losses on shareholders and haircuts on creditors. The process would also be run by regulators rather than the courts, to speed it up.Praful Nargund, the director of the Good Growth Foundation, said: “By putting emergency legislation in place now we can avoid litigation and ensure the special administration regime protects taxpayers, employees and customers from paying the price for shareholder failure.”Pakes said: “The challenge is stopping Thames driving the cost of a SAR up through legal challenges and making sure the costs are fairly represented. The difficulty of the SAR process highlights the failure of regulation to create the incentive for water companies to act faithfully.”However, this approach could still bring legal challenges, with the Thames creditors promising to bring a judicial review against any attempt to change the way the special administration process works.A source close to the creditors said: “Rejecting a fully funded £10bn turnaround plan and using legislation to force Thames Water into special administration and a new unfinanceable ownership model would be unprecedented and have an extremely negative read across to other struggling water companies.“It will only result in litigation and the transfer of huge costs and risk to customers and taxpayers, while irretrievably damaging investor confidence in UK-regulated sectors,” said the source.Explore more on these topicsThames WaterWater industryUtilitiesWater billsNationalisationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Badenoch plotted to remove Sunak as PM months before election, book claims | Conservatives | The Guardian
description: Anthony Seldon’s book alleges Badenoch asked fellow Tory ministers ‘if anyone was interested in changing the captain’
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Anthony Seldon’s book alleges Badenoch asked fellow Tory ministers ‘if anyone was interested in changing the captain’
Content: Rishi Sunak and Kemi Badenoch in the Commons in April 2023. Badenoch was in the cabinet throughout Sunak’s time as PM.Photograph: Jessica Taylor/UK Parliament/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRishi Sunak and Kemi Badenoch in the Commons in April 2023. Badenoch was in the cabinet throughout Sunak’s time as PM.Photograph: Jessica Taylor/UK Parliament/AFP/Getty ImagesConservativesBadenoch plotted to remove Sunak as PM months before election, book claimsAnthony Seldon’s book alleges Badenoch asked fellow Tory ministers ‘if anyone was interested in changing the captain’Peter WalkerSenior political correspondentTue 25 Aug 2026 11.05 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKemi Badenoch plotted with fellow Conservative cabinet ministers to remove Rishi Sunak as prime minister months before the general election, it has been claimed.Anthony Seldon, who has written political biographies of every prime minister since John Major, has alleged in a new book that Badenoch, who was business secretary at the time, phoned several other cabinet ministers to ask “if anyone was interested in changing the captain”.An ally of Badenoch, who is now the Conservative leader, described the claim as “total bollocks”.The book about Sunak’s time as prime minister, which is being serialisedin the Independent, says Badenoch did not respect Sunak, who she believed had been rude to her. Citing a series of sources, it says she sought to oust Sunak in 2023, when he faced considerable internal pressure over migration policy.It quotes one Conservative MP, who the book says is now a member of Badenoch’s frontbench team, as saying she was “a menace who orchestrated trouble in the cabinet” under Sunak.The book, titled Sunak at 10: The Last Conservative PM?, cites another unnamed “insider” as saying Badenoch “was actively looking at bringing Sunak down, constructing imaginary cabinets and offering jobs”.After Robert Jenrickresigned as immigration ministerin December 2023 over the details of Sunak’s plan to deport asylum seekers to Rwanda, the book says Badenoch discussed telling Sunak she would resign from the cabinet if he did not amend the policy, with some people recounting that Badenoch “had promised she would ‘take him out’”.It was at this point, the book says, that Badenoch contacted other cabinet ministers to see if any wanted a change in PM. It says she wanted “to avoid the image of wielding the knife”.Danny Kruger, a then Conservative MP who, like Jenrick, has since defected to Reform, told Seldon that Badenoch “definitely wanted” to remove Sunak and replace him “but was concerned about being a fag-end prime minister” given the looming election.Seldon says in the book that Badenoch decided against any challenge because she thought this would lead to her being blamed for an election defeat. It also says another reason for caution was Badenoch’s worry that she might lose a leadership contest to Penny Mordaunt, the then leader of the Commons.The book says the plotting prompted Sunak to condemn what he called “attention-seeking” rebels and he told allies: “They probably want me to tell them to fuck off so they can pontificate, but I have a country to run. I’m not going to rise to the bait.”Sunak said the impression of plotting and infighting pushed down the Tory vote and made the eventual election defeat in July 2024 even worse.Badenoch was in the cabinet throughout Sunak’s time as PM, first as trade secretary and then business secretary. She had stood to become Conservative leader in the 2022 internal party contest after Boris Johnson announced he was stepping down, finishing fourth behind Liz Truss, Sunak and Mordaunt. Sunak became prime minister without a contest after Truss’s premiership imploded in just 45 days.After the general election defeat, Badenoch became Tory leader, beating Jenrick in a vote of Conservative members.Dissatisfaction with Sunak was far from uncommon among Conservative MPs and ministers as the party headed towards what was seen as an inevitable election defeat, even if most accepted he had inherited a near-impossible situation.There was little appetite for yet another change of leader, however, which would have brought about a sixth Conservative prime minister inside eight years.Sunak’s office was contacted for comment.Explore more on these topicsConservativesKemi BadenochRishi SunakBiography booksnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘An enchanting oasis’: Venetian island with Napoleonic fort up for sale | Venice | The Guardian
description: Smaller than a football pitch, Crevan has a rich history – but how rich its buyer needs to be is strictly under wraps
Author: Angela Giuffrida
Headline: Smaller than a football pitch, Crevan has a rich history – but how rich its buyer needs to be is strictly under wraps
Content: There is  a private mooring along the island’s small internal canal, and a helipad.Photograph: Courtesy of LionardView image in fullscreenThere is  a private mooring along the island’s small internal canal, and a helipad.Photograph: Courtesy of LionardVenice‘An enchanting oasis’: Venetian island with Napoleonic fort up for saleSmaller than a football pitch, Crevan has a rich history – but how rich its buyer needs to be is strictly under wrapsAngela Giuffridain RomeTue 25 Aug 2026 09.21 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 14.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn island in theVenicelagoon boasting a Napoleonic fort and lush gardens is up for sale.Described as an “enchanting oasis of peace and beauty”, Crevan offers a “spectacular view” of Venice’s main island, but is far from its crowds.Located a few minutes by boat from the islands of Burano and Torcello and just slightly smaller than the size of a standard football pitch, Crevan was built in 1806 by the French military during the Napoleonic era as a strategic outpost to defend the northern Venetian lagoon from the Austrian empire.But in 1815 the island fell under Austrian rule before passing to the Italian state in 1866, after the annexation of Veneto to the Kingdom ofItaly. Crevan continued to serve a military purpose until after the first world war.After years of neglect, it was bought by a private owner and its buildings restored as residential properties.Map showing location of Crevan in Venice lagoonIts most prominent feature is the Napoleonic fort, converted by the current owner into a small villa with four bedrooms and surrounded manicured lawns and vegetable and fruit gardens and trees. There is also a private mooring along the island’s small internal canal, and a helipad.Crevan has been listed for sale by several top property agencies, includingLionard Luxury Real Estateand Dimora Italian Real Estate, an affiliate of Christie’s International. The asking price, however, is strictly reserved for interested buyers.“Crevan offers the privilege of withdrawing from the world without ever leaving the universal allure of Venice,” Dimitri Corti, the founder and chief executive of Lionard Luxury Real Estate, said in a press release. “What one acquires is not simply a residence and a piece of land, but space, privacy and an entire landscape to preserve.”But Crevan has competition. Isola Santa Cristina, another island in the Venetian lagoon that for decades was owned by the heir to the Swarovski crystal empire, was put up for sale at about €24m in June. The luxury retreat comes with a huge villa, a saltwater swimming pool and vineyards.An octagonal-shaped island close to the Venice lido and dating back to the 1500s, when it was built as a defence post by the Republic of Venice, is also on the market.Explore more on these topicsVeniceItalyEuropeHeritagenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘They make life much easier’: AI-powered shopping trolleys go on trial in Lancashire  | Morrisons | The Guardian
description: Customers give their verdicts as a Morrisons store becomes first in UK to test trolleys that scan, weigh and tally costs
Author: Raphael Boyd
Headline: Customers give their verdicts as a Morrisons store becomes first in UK to test trolleys that scan, weigh and tally costs
Content: Matthew Byrne pushes an AI-powered smart trolley. He says it has helped him to stick to his budget.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMatthew Byrne pushes an AI-powered smart trolley. He says it has helped him to stick to his budget.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianMorrisons‘They make life much easier’: AI-powered shopping trolleys go on trial in LancashireCustomers give their verdicts as a Morrisons store becomes first in UK to test trolleys that scan, weigh and tally costsRaphael BoydTue 25 Aug 2026 13.14 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 18.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLancashire has been the site of many British innovations throughout history, from the spinning jenny, which transformed textile production, to the creation of jelly babies.Now it has welcomed another first: AI shopping trolleys.AMorrisonsin Lancashire has become the first supermarket in the UK to trial the use of “smart trolleys” that allow customers to do their shopping without having to scan a single item.The AI-powered Caper smart trolleys, created by San Francisco-based Instacart, automatically register each item placed in the trolley, adding up the cost and recommending related products as you shop. Once finished, customers can scan their trolley screen rather than visiting a checkout.View image in fullscreenThe AI-powered Caper smart trolleys automatically register each item placed in the trolley.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianPreston is the first city in Britain to use them after the supermarket chain announced a deal to trial them at its location in Ashton-on-Ribble, to the west of the city.Amazon Fresh, which allowed shoppers to take items from the shelves and leave the shop without checking out, using cameras to charge directly to online accounts, failed to take off in the UK, with thecompany’s last physical British store closing in 2025. But Morrisons is more hopeful that its smart trolleys will be a success, with plans to put them in supermarkets across the country.The smart trolleys are already used in more than 100 cities across the world. They are similar in design and function to the Dash Cart used by Amazon’s Fresh stores, which still operate outside the UK.After the trolleys rolled into Ashton-on-Ribble last month, customer Matthew Byrne said they had “massively” helped him keep track of his shopping. Byrne is autistic and struggles to stick to set plans for what to get from the shops.“Having what I’ve bought on screen has been great. I have a habit of just grabbing things and throwing them in my trolley, and then wondering how I’m paying so much. It’s been amazing to visualise it and see it in real time. I came here with an £80 budget, and I’ve actually been able to stick to it.”Kaz Bond was disappointed to be forced to use a normal trolley for her latest shop due to a fault on her phone, having used them for every trip she has made to Morrisons since they became commonplace around four weeks ago.View image in fullscreenDebbie Files says the trolley was a ‘little bit confusing at first, but you get used to it pretty quickly’.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian“Honestly, I think they’re brilliant,” said Bond. “They make life much easier. I wouldn’t be that surprised if they’re everywhere before long. I reckon it’s the future.”Debbie Files had chosen Tuesday as the day to take a leap of faith and use the trolleys for the first time, albeit with the help of a Morrisons employee.“It was a little bit confusing at first, but you get used to it pretty quickly,” said Files. “It’s heavy, though. I’ve barely been able to turn it. I feel like I need a driving lesson to use it, but I got the hang of it. If they make a smaller one then that will get me to use it again.”Explore more on these topicsMorrisonsEnglandRetail industryShoppingSupermarketsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘It costs a lot of money to look this cheap’: Dolly Parton’s life in quotes | Dolly Parton | The Guardian
description: The late singer, actor and philanthropist leaves behind a life and career full of wisdom
Author: Guardian music
Headline: The late singer, actor and philanthropist leaves behind a life and career full of wisdom
Content: Dolly Parton circa 1983.Photograph: THA/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenDolly Parton circa 1983.Photograph: THA/ShutterstockDolly Parton‘It costs a lot of money to look this cheap’: Dolly Parton’s life in quotesThe late singer, actor and philanthropist leaves behind a life and career full of wisdomCelebrity tributes pour in for Dolly Parton: ‘a gift to the world’Alexis Petridis on Dolly Parton’s peerless career which turned country music cliches inside outDolly Parton – a life in picturesGuardian musicTue 25 Aug 2026 16.29 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 16.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBeloved musician, actor and philanthropist Dolly Parton hasdied at the age of 80after an incredible, one-of-a-kind career. The star was known for both her fierce wit and her unflappable positivity.Celebrity tributes pour in for Dolly Parton: ‘a gift to the world’Read moreIn a life filled with much-quoted gems of wisdom, here are some of her finest:On positivity“The way I see it, if you want the rainbow, you gotta put up with the rain.”“You have to work at being happy. Some people work at being miserable. If I wake up in the morning and don’t feel great or things are not great, I try to think about what I can do to make things work better, rather than just falling into that deep hole, because then you just go deeper and deeper.”“If you see someone without a smile today, give’em yours.”“If you’re feeling low, don’t despair. The sun has a sinking spell every night, but it comes back up every morning.”“They think I’m simple-minded because I seem to be happy. Why shouldn’t I be happy? I have everything I ever wanted and more. Maybe I am simple-minded. Maybe that’s the key: simple.”“Happiness is your commitment to appreciating all that is good in life.”“A positive attitude and a sense of humor go together like biscuits and gravy.”On her career“I’m not going to limit myself just because people won’t accept the fact that I can do something else.”“I always say I’ve dreamed myself into a corner. I’ve got to keep all those dreams alive. Every dream spins off into some something else.”“Don’t get so busy making a living that you forget to make a life.”“You’ll never do a whole lot unless you’re brave enough to try.”“I hope to die right in the middle of a song and right on the stage doing what I love to do. I hope to be about 120 when that happens.”View image in fullscreenDolly Parton in 2018.Photograph: 2018 Warner Bros Entertainment/Tina Rowden/Netflix“My music is so mine, it’s hard to turn it over to someone else. I have to be really involved in the production. It’s like someone else taking care of your kids– if they don’t treat them well, you’re going to be pissed off.”“I never tried quitting, and I never quit trying.”“Above everything else I’ve done, I’ve always said I’ve had more guts than I’ve got talent.”“I think in a way, my music has been almost like my ministry. Hopefully, it’s healing in some ways, just having a good sense of humor to be able to lift people up, to have songs that people can relate to.”On her looks“It costs a lot of money to look this cheap”Dolly Parton’s peerless career turned country music cliches inside out | Alexis PetridisRead more“People always ask me how long it takes to do my hair. I don’t know, I’m never there.”“I’m not offended by all the dumb blonde jokes because I know I’m not dumb – and I’m not blonde either.”“I have pretty good skin considering my age, and I think a lot of it is mineral oil and bacon grease.”“I describe my look as a blend of Mother Goose, Cinderellaand the local hooker!”“I’m not like a real person. I love being artificial. I think there’s a little magic in the fact that I’m so totally real, but look so artificial at the same time.”“I am a self-made woman, and I have the doctor bills to prove it.”View image in fullscreenDolly Parton circa 1997.Photograph: THA/Shutterstock“I’m no natural beauty. If I’m gonna have any looks at all, I’m gonna have to create them.”“A lot of people have said I’d have probably done better in my career if I hadn’t looked so cheap and gaudy. But I dress to be comfortable for me, and you shouldn’t be blamed because you want to look pretty.”“Those people who wake up and they’re just beautiful, they’re just born that way. Well, that ain’t me. I gotta work for everything I’ve got.”On relationships“I always love working with children. I never had children of my own. God has his purposes. God didn’t let me have children so everybody’s children could be mine. That’s kind of how I’m looking at it.”“Love is something sent from heaven above to worry the hell out of you.”“I was blessed to have family members who encouraged me to pursue my dreams. Whether it is your parents, or your uncles or your aunts or even the neighbor down the road, it’s important that kids have someone who encourages them to chase their rainbow.”“I often get myself in love trouble because I’m so passionate; I love so much and so deep.”“Love is like a butterfly: as soft and gentle as a feather, many-colored and full of cheer.”“I think everyone should be with who they love. I don’t want to be controversial or stir up a bunch of trouble but people are going to love who they are going to love. I think gay couples should be allowed to marry. They should suffer just like us heterosexuals.”Explore more on these topicsDolly PartonCountryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘So hacked off’: as election nears, New Zealanders despair at the main parties – and Opportunity knocks | New Zealand | The Guardian
description: National and Labour have passed government back and forth for years but many voters are no longer content with politics as usual
Author: Michelle Duff
Headline: National and Labour have passed government back and forth for years but many voters are no longer content with politics as usual
Content: ‘Clinging to the old ways ain’t gonna cut it’ – small parties are cutting into Labour’s and National’s share of the New Zealand vote.Photograph: Fiona Goodall/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Clinging to the old ways ain’t gonna cut it’ – small parties are cutting into Labour’s and National’s share of the New Zealand vote.Photograph: Fiona Goodall/Getty ImagesNew Zealand‘So hacked off’: as election nears, New Zealanders despair at the main parties – and Opportunity knocksNational and Labour have passed government back and forth for years but many voters are no longer content with politics as usualMichelle Duffin WellingtonTue 25 Aug 2026 19.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 19.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor decades, Mattie Wall mainly voted for Labour, one of New Zealand’s two major political parties. A former diplomat and project manager, the South Island-based retiree felt that the party with working class origins aligned with what was important to her: a thriving country, and the environment.This year she is among the New Zealanders who are peeling away from the Labour and National parties – which swing in and out of power every few terms – to vote for an untested party that has never held a parliamentary seat.“In the past, I didn’t feel the frustration I do now with politics,” said Wall, 76. “I’m so hacked off with both parties, with all parties really. We’ve got Trump 2.0, AI’s sudden [surge], increasing climate change impact – what are we waiting for, revolution or societal collapse? Clinging to the old ways ain’t gonna cut it.”As New Zealand prepares for an election in November, Wall is among the roughly5-8% of peopleaccording to recent polls who plan to vote for relative newcomers the Opportunity party. For her, its policies, including a land tax and a$370 a week universal basic income, represent pragmatism; a shake-up, but a sensible one. She is also impressed by Opportunity’s leader, businesswoman Qiulae Wong. “She’s intelligent, thoughtful, moderate, unpretentious, she speaks lay language and she’s a realist.”Wong, 38, is a sustainability consultant and mother-of-two from Auckland who returned to New Zealand in 2022after almost a decade working in London. Asked to define Opportunity, she said it looked to “market-driven solutions” while being committed to a low-emission future and evidence-based policy.The apparent rise of Opportunity – aself-described centrist partystarted three elections ago by economist and philanthropist Gareth Morgan – has injected an unexpected element of drama into the election race. The contest features a weakening right bloc, with National’s polling flagging at about 29%. National and Labour are seeing theirlowest combined support in 30 years, mirroring an international trend of minor parties gaining votes and influence.Polls have Opportunity winning more than the 5% threshold of seatsneeded to enter parliament under New Zealand’s mixed member proportional (MMP) system. It means Opportunity could get to choose who governs. Christopher Luxon, the National leader and prime minister, has ruled out working with Opportunity.The Post newspaper reportedOpportunity looks set to nab votes from right and left, with 20% of respondents voting National at the last election, 17% Labour, 12% the Greens and 8% NZ First. A quarter had last voted for Opportunity.Some put the shift down to a kind of mainstream malaise inNew Zealand politics. “Voters are less attached to parties than they used to be, and they’re more likely to shop around during elections,” said Massey University political scientist Richard Shaw. “They’re peeling off from everywhere; people’s attachment to parties is more elastic and the deep tribalism has gone.”Voters spoken to by the Guardian reflected this sentiment. “I don’t understand how a lot of people are surviving right now and that’s what drives my vote,” said Wellingtonian Gemma, 41, a former Green voter who will vote Opportunity for the first time. “Things can’t keep going in this direction.”‘Somewhere in the middle’Wong, the Opportunity leader, told the Guardian that polling was better than hoped but the party took nothing for granted. People told her they were fed up with “pendulum politics” – different governments coming into power and undoing the work of the last government at great cost. “They’re looking for something different because they’re frustrated, particularly with Labour and National for not having any big ideas or stable leadership to tackle some of the biggest challenges that we’re facing as a country.”View image in fullscreenQiulae Wong, the Opportunity party leader.Photograph: Hagen Hopkins/The GuardianWong said Opportunity would work with either party. New Zealanders needed stability when it came to climate legislation, healthcare funding models, and the education curriculum, she said. “It’s that back and forth which seems to be really holding us back in all aspects of New Zealand society … the solution is often somewhere in the middle.”Responding to criticism of Opportunity’s land tax proposal as untenable and liable to create fresh inequalities – the former Labour leader Helen Clarkcalls it “fantasy posing as policy” – Wong said the economy had to change and 70% of New Zealanders would be better off under the plan. It would introduce a tax of 1.75% on urban and 0.5% on rural land, is modelled to pull in NZ$24bn which would be used for the ‘citizen’s income,’ and is designed to drive house prices down by 10-15%.She did not expect it to happen immediately. “I’m realistic that as a new party coming into parliament demanding tax reform overnight is pretty unlikely. If we can get around the table with the other parties, there’s elements of this that will appeal to both the left and the right. It’s about supporting people who really need it.”Politics in New Zealand has historically been a two-party duopoly. Previously, the first past the post (FPP) voting system allowed parties to more easily win the majority of the house and govern alone.Since the introduction of New Zealand’s MMP system in 1996, voters get a party and an electorate vote. The first mainly determines how many seats a party gets in parliament. With 51% needed for a clear win, small parties often hold the balance of power. At the 2023 election, centre-right Nationalgot 38% of the vote, meaning it needed the New Zealand First and Act parties to form a coalition government.In August, Luxon said on Newstalk ZB thathe was open to holding a referendum on MMP, saying he wanted as many National ministers in cabinet as possible for a stable government, and not some “yahoo or numpty”. He denied he was talking about his current coalition partners, but many saw it ashis growing frustrationat managing them. He later told the Post it would be a “check-in” on democracy, as well as gauging support for a four-year governmental term.View image in fullscreenChristopher Luxon, prime minister in New Zealand’s incumbent National-led government.Photograph: Charlotte Graham-McLay/APShaw said the halcyon days for major parties had passed, and both Luxon and Labour party leader Chris Hipkins would be feeling the pressure of declining support. “They’re not the most successful any more, partly because of MMP but just because people shop around way more and the base vote for National and Labour is never going to be at 40% ever again.” Smaller parties were eating into major party territory. For example, the David Seymour-led Act party, with 0.5% of the vote in 2017,had received $1.8m in donations this year– just behind National – and was polling at 9%.With its positioning, Opportunity could continue to gain votes from everywhere – even if their centrism was a tactic, he said. “They’re quite clearly soft-left, they’re using the language of reconciliation and evidence and appealing to a different kind of political DNA in people and they’re resonating. They could absolutely kick on.”Still, some will always play it safe. Christine Hands, 77, who voted Labour in her first election in 1972, and for Jacinda Ardern twice, would never vote for a minority party. “I’ve never been a splinter party person. I’ll vote for National or Labour, depending on which is best for the country.” This time, for her, that’s National; a safe pair of hands who “haven’t mucked things up too much”.As for Opportunity? “I can see they’re quite charming, and people are thinking ‘a plague on both parties’, but their policies are as mad as a meat axe,” she said. “Then again, we survive everything. We always have.”Explore more on these topicsNew ZealandAsia PacificNew Zealand politicsNew Zealand election 2026featuresShareReuse this content

title: US Catholic churches see a record number of conversions: ‘It’s a real shift’ | Catholicism | The Guardian
description: After decades of declining religious affiliation, churches in southern California have seen an increase among gen Z
Author: Lynda Lin Grigsby
Headline: After decades of declining religious affiliation, churches in southern California have seen an increase among gen Z
Content: ‘I feel like it’s a dark time for a lot of people in the world, and I think that naturally is going to get people who reach for the light.’Photograph: Maggie ShannonView image in fullscreen‘I feel like it’s a dark time for a lot of people in the world, and I think that naturally is going to get people who reach for the light.’Photograph: Maggie ShannonCatholicismUS Catholic churches see a record number of conversions: ‘It’s a real shift’After decades of declining religious affiliation, churches in southern California have seen an increase among gen ZLynda Lin Grigsbyin Los Angeles and Santa BarbaraTue 25 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 10.03 EDTShareAlicia Martinez pulls on an oversized, chocolate-brown leather jacket – an incongruous choice for the July heat in Los Angeles. Later that day, she plans to see The Odyssey in a frigid theater. But first, there is mass.Martinez, 24, entersOur Savior Parish, the castle-like church beside her workplace, the University of Southern California. Inside, she dips her fingers in holy water, makes the sign of the cross on her forehead, and enters the main part of the church in hushed reverence.Seated in the pews, backed by the dancing light of stained-glass windows, she’s flanked by faith of all ages. Some wear chapel veils. Others sport USC-branded apparel. All huddle shoulder-to-shoulder. At summer’s peak at USC, a secular university synonymous with Hollywood and Trojan football, another institution is quietly gaining ground: the Catholic church.More than a year ago, the Catholic faith called to her like “a pounding noise in her heart”, Martinez said, even though she has Protestant roots. This year, she completed the Order of Christian Initiation of Adults program (OCIA), the Catholic church’s formal initiation process for adults.The parish growth mirrors a larger trend. In April, when the Catholic church traditionally registers new members, the Archdiocese of Los Angelesreported8,598 people preparing to be baptized or formally entering the church – the highest number of reported initiations for an archdiocese in the US, and a 54% increase from 2025. Across the US, the number of adults entering the Catholic church has climbed each year since the pandemic-low, according to asurveyof dioceses.View image in fullscreenAlicia Martinez at USC’s Our Savior Parish in Los Angeles, California.Photograph: Maggie ShannonThe increases have prompted talk of areligious revival. But experts say it’s too early to call it a trend. Religious disaffiliation and conversion are always in flux, says Michele Dillon, a sociology professor and dean of the College of Liberal Arts at the University of New Hampshire. Still, it’s an interesting moment for the church in the US, after decades of declining religious affiliation.Our Savior baptized 16 people this year, a record high, said Father Matt Wheeler, the pastor. Sixty-nine people enrolled in its OCIA program, a 57% increase from last year. Mass attendance grew so significantly that church leaders have, on occasion, redirected worshippers to an overflow area to watch a live stream.During mass, Wheeler often looks out at the sea of student faces and marvels to himself, “Wow. Nobody dragged these young adults here.”Martinez said that for her, the call ofCatholicismwas amplified by the loneliness of living in a big city, where she felt battles of good and evil were constantly unfolding before her eyes.“There’s so much wrong in the world,” said Martinez. She was drawn to Matthew’s Gospel, she said, which warns that as lawlessness increases, people’s love for one another will grow cold.For 20-year-old Kathryn Glavin, too, global crises – including war, injustice and division – lent urgency to the search for steadier ground in faith. For most of her life, she considered herself agnostic. Then, two years ago, the UC Santa Barbara student began noticing the Catholic church’s charitable work in her community. “I feel like it’s a dark time for a lot of people in the world,” said Glavin. “And I think that naturally is going to get people who reach for the light.” In April, Glavin was baptized atSt. Mark’s University Parishin Isla Vista, a student enclave cradled by UC Santa Barbara and the Pacific Ocean.View image in fullscreenThe annual Welcome Mass at USC’s Our Savior Parish in Los Angeles, California, which welcomes new students to the Catholic center on campus.Photograph: The GuardianAtSt Mark’s, interest in Catholicism is blossoming, said Father Ryan Thornton. Established in 1965 to serve UC Santa Barbara, a secular university, the church is located between three fraternity houses – right in the middle of student life. At first, the parish understood the growing interest in Catholicism as part of a Covid-era holdover when church gatherings were temporarily restricted. But six years later, the parish has seen its largest initiation class – 56 people, said Thornton.“That clearly can’t be about the pandemic because the difference is too far,” said Thornton. “So, then the question is, ‘Well, what’s happening now?’”Once popular reasons to join the Catholic church, such as family pressure or a plan to marry a Catholic partner, have largely fallen away. Today, becoming Catholic is an active choice, said Thornton.He and other church leaders suspect the new generations of faithful, many raised by non-religious parents, have emerged spiritually hungry from a steady diet of social media reels and Love Island watch parties. Catholicism offers a counterweight: rituals and a history that reaches far beyond the algorithm.“In some ways, the superficiality of our society – the Instagrammable life – has been tried and found wanting,” said Thornton.View image in fullscreenThe annual Welcome Mass at USC’s Our Savior Parish in Los Angeles, California, which welcomes new students to the Catholic center on campus.Photograph: Maggie Shannon/The GuardianThe increase in initiations in Los Angeles and Santa Barbara is set against a backdrop of adecades-long national shift away from organized religion. For decades, Catholicism in the US has lost more people than it has gained through religious switching – people who move to another religious tradition or no religion – according to Pew Research Centerstudies.But the “nones” – people who identify as atheist, agnostic, or “nothing in particular” – have leveled off in recent years, according to another Pew Researchstudy.Even if the increase in new Catholics reflects a new national shift, one strong year cannot reverse decades of gradual decline, said Maureen Day, a sociologist and theologian. Still, Day said, the local data could signal that religion is appealing to people in new ways – and the losses could begin to reverse.What could signal a true reversal is sustained participation in church life, said Day. But that is difficult to track, especially at university parishes, where students graduate and move away. No one calls their former pastor to report that they are still going to church, Thornton said.Publicly available data do not show which parishes drove the archdiocese-wide increase. But Dillon said parishes’ increases shouldn’t be dismissed.“It’s real,” said Dillon. “It’s a real observable shift in those individual parishes and dioceses.”Catholicism, with its centuries of tradition, elaborate rituals and thicket of rules, can intimidate newcomers. But parish leaders said it’s helped that participants these days have more accessible entry points. They listen toFather Mike Schmitz’spodcasts. They can pray in the car with theirHallowapp. And they can watchBishop Robert Barron’s YouTube channel. Our Savior Parish leaders are intentional about making the gospel relatable to a younger audience, said Wheeler. At a July mass, he referred the congregation to his latest Instagram reel.View image in fullscreenJohn Ceballos at USC’s Our Savior Parish in Los Angeles, California.Photograph: Maggie Shannon/The GuardianJohn Ceballos said that what’s made a difference for him is the gentler message at Our Savior Parish. Ceballos was baptized Catholic, but he stopped practicing in his 20s, in part, because of the fire-and-brimstone messaging.“It was like, ‘Oh, here we go. You know, we’re all going to hell,’” says Ceballos with a laugh. Now, at Our Savior Parish, he says mass is all about love and community. “Now, everybody’s good. Everybody’s a child of God.”This year, Ceballos, 50, was the oldest participant in Our Savior’s OCIA program. The age gap became a running joke:Do you even know what a fax machine is?But when they began studying Catholic teachings, the age gap fell away: everyone was a beginner.Near the end of mass at Our Savior Parish, Catholics come forward in a communion procession to receive what the church teaches is the body and blood of Christ. Even in the summer, when many USC students are away, the procession threads along the entire length of the church. As it stretches on, people kneeling in prayer shift on their knees. Others sit.Aidan Freire has attended mass at Our Savior Parish for two years. Although another parish is less than a mile away, he is drawn to this one because of its energy.“I feel like this parish is really good because everyone’s young,” said Freire, 19.To him, the clearest measure of the parish’s draw comes during Communion,which is reminiscent of another experience.“It’s like a TSA security line.”

title: Community-maxxing: gen Z are done with doomscrolling – and ready to socialise | Young people | The Guardian
description: Research shows young adults often feel isolated. So alongside embracing ‘grandma hobbies’, they want to get involved with the places they live and be good neighbours
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Research shows young adults often feel isolated. So alongside embracing ‘grandma hobbies’, they want to get involved with the places they live and be good neighbours
Content: Just remember to fibre-maxx, people …Photograph: Posed by models; Goodboy Picture Company/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJust remember to fibre-maxx, people …Photograph: Posed by models; Goodboy Picture Company/Getty ImagesPass notesYoung peopleCommunity-maxxing: gen Z are done with doomscrolling – and ready to socialiseResearch shows young adults often feel isolated. So alongside embracing ‘grandma hobbies’, they want to get involved with the places they live and be good neighboursTue 25 Aug 2026 12.59 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 14.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:Community-maxxing.Age:The portmanteau is recent, butHomo sapienshave always been social creatures.Appearance:Cosily communal.Community-maxxing? But I thought I was supposed to besolo-maxxing!Well, that means being single, so you could do both.Explain.Community-maxxing is seeking out regular in-person connections around you, often tied to shared interests.Vice reportsthat gen Z are “done doomscrolling” and are getting out in the world, sharing their passions, interests and “grandma hobbies” with like-minded folk by joiningbook groups,crafting circles,hikingandrun clubs.You’re telling megen Z have inventedsocialising?There’s more to it than that. Community-maxxing is also being a good neighbour, feeling part of the place you live in and being open to new connections.Can you give an example?At this summer’s Boomtown festival in the West Country,a group of Bristolian festival-goers welcomed Adam James, a young autistic fellow raver, who was attending his first festival alone, into their group for three days. They unquestioningly accepted James, giving him what he described as the best weekend of his life. “It’s what the community’s about, really,”James said.OK, that’s lovely. Good ongen Z.Community-maxxing is a way of combating loneliness and digitally enabled isolation, which are really problematic for their generation. “On an average day in 2023 one in 10 US young adults did not spend a single minute interacting face-to-face with another person,”the Financial Times reported earlier this month. Over here, Office for National Statistics research published last Novemberfound 33% of 16- to 29-year-olds felt lonely“often, always or some of the time”.That’s bleak – nowonder they’re cravingconnection.Yes, humans are social creatures – we need each other. “Community-maxxing … has become an accepted term in recent years to describe what therapists have known for decades: that individuals require repeated, quality social interaction to assist in developing a feeling of grounding and support,” therapist Stephanie Lewis told Vice.That’s true of everyone, surely, not just the youth.Yes, community-maxxing isn’t just for kids. You might have noticed there’s a renewed interest in communal living these days, frommulti-generational shared spacestoco-housing projectsandcommunities for older people.Hmm, I don’t think I’m up for joining a commune: I’m very particular about my towels.You can community-maxx however you like, in big or small ways.Suggestions onlineinclude “ask to borrow a tool instead of buying one”, “become a regular volunteer” and “chat to the person sitting next to you at your local cafe”. You could join a choir! Fix stuff at yourlocal repair cafe!Fine, but I still hate the word.How about IRL-core, community-coded, going social-mode, or people-pilled? We could get a group together in a nice local cafe to workshop this.Do say:“Gen Z are realising it takes a village to be a happy, fulfilled human.”Don’t say:“Sorry I missed pottery club – I’m solo-maxxing, so no one woke me after sleep-maxxing, and afterfibremaxxing,skin-maxxing and gym-maxxing, I was so tired I sleep-maxxed again.”Explore more on these topicsYoung peoplePass notesLonelinessfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘The day I disclose, my career is over’: the journalist facing an $800 daily fine to keep her sources secret | US press and publishing | The Guardian
description: If Catherine Herridge’s petition to the US supreme court fails, she’ll be on the hook for a daily fine until she discloses her sources – a case unsettling press freedom organizations
Author: Jeremy Barr
Headline: If Catherine Herridge’s petition to the US supreme court fails, she’ll be on the hook for a daily fine until she discloses her sources – a case unsettling press freedom organizations
Content: US press and publishing‘The day I disclose, my career is over’: the journalist facing an $800 daily fine to keep her sources secretIf Catherine Herridge’s petition to the US supreme court fails, she’ll be on the hook for a daily fine until she discloses her sources – a case unsettling press freedom organizationsJeremy Barrin WashingtonTue 25 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 12.42 EDTShareView image in fullscreenCatherine Herridge.Photograph: Caroline Gutman/The GuardianFor 18 days this summer, veteran journalist Catherine Herridge walked to her Washington DC mailbox and dropped off a check for $800. The money was required by law to cover a judge-imposed sanction after she was found in contempt of court in 2024 for refusing to disclose her sources. It fell to her 21-year-old son James to provide the moral support Herridge needed. “He understands the pressure that I’ve been under,” she said. “It was very hard, personally.”The check drop is now on hold. The judge who issued that order, Christopher R Cooper, has since clarified that Herridge doesn’t need to pay the fine until she has a chance to plead her case to the supreme court, which she petitioned late last week.If that petition is unsuccessful, and there is good reason to believe it will fail, then something rather extraordinary in American history will commence: Herridge will be on the hook for the daily fines until or unless she reveals her sourcing for a series of 2017 stories about the Chinese-American scientist Yanping Chen, who had been federally investigated – but not charged – over her ties to China’s military and whether a Virginia school she operated was secretly aiding the communist country.It’s a case that has unsettled not only Herridge and her family, but also the community of press freedom organizations that exist to ensure against the unthinkable – a reporter being forced to disclose confidential sources, shattering the foundation of national security reporting in the public interest.“Reporter-source confidentiality is the lifeblood of investigative journalism,” said Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at Freedom of the Press Foundation. “Whistleblowers in a position to expose abuses won’t trust journalists to protect them, and won’t come forward, if they believe reporters will be threatened with financial ruin for not outing them in court.”Unless the supreme court intervenes, or the matter is resolved via a settlement, that worst case scenario might be just around the corner.“I built my career on developing confidential sources, and the day I disclose, my career is over,” Herridge, 62, said in an interview last week in a law firm conference room a few blocks from the White House. “I mean, I’m finished. How can anyone trust me in the future? But it’s bigger than me. I’m in the last chapter of my career. This is really for people who have another 10 or 20 years ahead of them, and for another generation of journalists. It’s for their benefit.”View image in fullscreenCatherine Herridge: ‘This is really for people who have another 10 or 20 years ahead of them, and for another generation of journalists. It’s for their benefit.’Photograph: Caroline Gutman/The GuardianStill, she acknowledged, “the fines are designed to break you as a journalist, mentally and financially.”Although Herridge was found in civil contempt, if she refuses to pay the daily fine, she could be held in criminal contempt and put in jail.Herridge has only been able to pay the fees and litigate the case with the support of her former employer,Fox News, which has continued to cover her top-level legal representation even though she has not worked for the network in seven years.“This is a landmark first amendment case – probably one of the most important first amendment cases in two decades,” Herridge said. “And I have made a decision, with the backing of Fox, that I’m going to defend these principles.”She praised the network’s support, saying: “Fox News is doing something that other media organizations have not done: they are going to the mat for their reporter. They are going to the mat for the free press and the first amendment in an environment where other media outlets have settled. And I would not be where I am today unless they were paying my legal fees. This is something that would be crippling for any journalist.”In a statement, a Fox News spokesperson said: “Forcing journalists to unmask their sources under threat of government coercion sets a dangerous precedent that will chill investigative journalism and prevent future whistleblowers from holding the powerful accountable. We have remained steadfast in our support of Catherine Herridge in this gravely important battle to preserve press freedoms and will continue to fight this egregious assault on the first amendment.”There are no shortages of lawsuits involving journalists these days, withDonald Trumpa frequent filer of specious billion-dollar claims over reporting he doesn’t like.Herridge’s case is unique in part because she was not actually the target of the original lawsuit, which does not contest the accuracy of her reporting. Chen filed the case in 2018 under the Privacy Act, suing four government agencies – the FBI, the Department of Justice, the Department of Defense and the Department of Homeland Security – over what she said was the government’s “illegal and unwarranted public disclosure of her personal information” to a journalist (Herridge).After deposing numerous government officials, Chen’s team remained unable to find the source who provided the information – and lobbied a judge to force Herridge to cough up her source or sources. The judge, agreeing with Chen that Herridge was her only remaining avenue for providing the information she needed to litigate the case, ordered the journalist to reveal the information, something she has repeatedly refused to do.But Herridge, who is just a witness in the case, said she “doesn’t think it’s the role of a journalist to provide evidence against the government”.Press freedom advocates have seconded that argument.“Allowing civil litigants to commandeer journalists to help them prove their cases is arguably even more harmful than letting the government do so,” Stern said.But Chen’s team – led by attorney Andrew Phillips – has argued that her rights as a citizen should supersede any special privilege provided to a journalist, an argument that has been well received by the US court of appeals for the DC circuit.“Dr. Chen, like any other American citizen, is entitled to discover the identity of the federal official(s) who abused their access to an American’s private information and leaked it to cause her harm,” Phillips said in an email. “That type of unlawful conduct is exactly what the Privacy Act was designed to address. Rogue government officials who break the law and abuse their power to target private citizens should not be able to remain anonymous and free from consequences simply because they launder their unlawful conduct through a reporter.”Chen’s case has been aided by a lack of statutory protection for reporters operating in Washington DC, which unlike many US states does not have any sort of shield law that would moot the case.That’s why Herridge is hoping that the Supreme Court takes up the case. “If the lower court decision stands, it means that in Washington DC, where we do the bulk of the national security reporting, that journalists and sources will have the weakest protections of anywhere in the country,” she said. “For example, if I was reporting in Boston, this subpoena would’ve been thrown out years ago.”In a filing last month, Chen’s team asked the judge to implement graduated fines that could rise to $5,000 a day – and perhaps even more significantly, to bar Herridge from being reimbursed by a third party like Fox. The judge denied that motion, meaning that for the time being, the money will not ultimately have to come out of the Herridge family’s pockets.That is especially significant because, after being laid off by CBS News in 2024, Herridge no longer commands the network paycheck she did for decades. Instead, she is doing her own thing as an investigative journalist, without the guaranteed compensation and legal representation that comes with a full-time job.View image in fullscreenCatherine Herridge says she isn’t primarily concerned about getting back into the world of television news. She is instead focused on this case.Photograph: Caroline Gutman/The GuardianBut Herridge isn’t primarily concerned about getting back into the world of television news. She is instead focused on this case, and making sure that she can do some good for her chosen field – and the next generation of journalists – by ensuring that they won’t be forced to choose between bankrupting themselves or breaking their sacred promise to sources.Looking back on the decades of exclusive reporting she has done for the biggest television networks in the country, Herridge says of her current court battle: “It’s the most consequential thing that I’ve done in my career.”

title: Fishy business: who really profits when sardines go viral? - video | Portugal | The Guardian
description: Once a cheap store-cupboard staple, sardines are fast becoming a luxury food item. Last year, #SardineGirlSummer saw influencers promoting the health benefits of sardinemaxxing, while sardinecore became the must-have fashion trend. Now, demand is accelerating just as Morocco’s sardine stock has collapsed, causing shortages on supermarket shelves. The Guardian travels to Matosinhos in Portugal, the cultural home of the sardine industry, to investigate who is profiting from the boom, how it has affected local fishermen, and what sustainability looks like in an era of global heating
