title: The other Post Office scandal: how organised crime launders money on the high street | Crime | The Guardian
description: The long read: Hundreds of millions of pounds of dirty money are being deposited at post offices every year. So why are the police reluctant to investigate the scale of the problem?
Author: Oliver Bullough
Headline: The long read: Hundreds of millions of pounds of dirty money are being deposited at post offices every year. So why are the police reluctant to investigate the scale of the problem?
Content: Composite: Anaïs Mims/Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Anaïs Mims/Guardian Design/Getty ImagesThe long readCrimeThe other Post Office scandal: how organised crime launders money on the high streetHundreds of millions of pounds of dirty money are being deposited at post offices every year. So why are the police reluctant to investigate the scale of the problem?Last chance to buy the summer issue of The Long Read magazine, now with 15% off.Click hereto orderOliver BulloughTue 25 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 09.45 EDTShareLeicestershire police won’t say who first told them about Jigar Gheewala, but you can see why, once they had heard of him, they decided to find out more. Gheewala was unemployed, had no apparent income, yet lived in a £1.3m house and sent his three children to private school. “He was a declared bankrupt, with a bank account that was absolutely not reflective of what it should be,” said financial crime supervisor Laura Panter of Leicestershire police’s economic crime team. “That was our starting point.”Over the course of 2020, despite being on benefits, Gheewala’s bank account received more than £880,000 in cash in 200 different deposits. He was, it turned out, a money launderer, but not the kind you’ll see in the movies. Gheewala’s deposits had been made not in Liechtenstein or on Grand Cayman, but at various post office branches in Leicester, one thick wodge of banknotes after another.As banks haveclosed branchesall over Britain, post offices have quietly become central to how we move our money. In 2017, post offices began to accept deposits on behalf of banks, and those deposits now exceed £30bn a year. The way it works is straightforward. A customer hands over banknotes to be counted, then inserts a bank card and enters the pin, like a cashpoint in reverse. The post office system then communicates with the bank’s system, which credits the value of the cash to the account linked to the card.It is a simple system, whichPost OfficeLtd, the state-owned company that controls the branches, says provides a crucial service to businesses and individuals otherwise cut off from banking services. But the simplicity comes at a cost. It has eliminated many of the checks that previously stopped criminals from laundering their cash. In the same way you can use someone else’s card to take money from a cashpoint, provided you know the pin, you can use any bank card to make a deposit at the post office. The process is deliberately streamlined and, unlike at a bank, the post office operative (often referred to as postmaster or subpostmaster) has no way to access any of the account details, and thus no way to check if the person with the card is its holder, or whether this transaction is part of a suspicious pattern.Law enforcement agencies estimate that, alongside ordinary businesses’ takings, hundreds of millions of pounds of dirty money are being paid into the post office each year. This allows drug dealers and other criminals to bank their illicit wealth, and profit from their crimes, and to do so with the absolute minimum of effort. “The number of places where cash can come into the economy is vast now but, as bank branches continue to close, the number of places to pay it back in has necessarily become more restricted. You’ve got this sort of reverse funnel effect going on,” said a former Post Office employee with knowledge of how it organises financial services. “The bad guys are genuinely targeting post offices as one of the few places left where they can actually go to put money in.”Leicestershire police used Gheewala’s transactions to reconstruct how he operated. On a typical day, he might make his first cash deposit in the east of the city, at a post-office counter hosted by a convenience store; then it would be a five-minute drive to another store, with boxes of veg out the front, its windows obscured by decals of soft drinks and spirits, offering post office services alongside the scratchcards. A few minutes away was another branch, between a chemist and a fried chicken shop, before another short drive would bring him to a retail centre where the post office sat next to a bakery on a prosperous-looking residential street. A final drive north would take him to a convenience store among red-brick detached houses, and that was a morning’s work done: thousands of pounds deposited in an hour or so, bundles of criminal cash being paid into the most ordinary of locations.“When we started looking at this, we were then able to see other individuals in Leicestershire that were mimicking exactly the same activity,” said Panter. “What we were finding was there was quite a consistent pattern in terms of the deposit activity around post offices.”Panter and her colleagues’ investigation became Operation Kilo, which began in 2021 and culminated in December 2025 with Gheewala being sentenced to almost 12 years in prison, along with six co-conspirators. And this was not just a Leicester-based operation. Officers watched as couriers came to Leicester with bags full of cash earned by criminals from London and Yorkshire, stashing them in shops for Gheewala’s people to pick up. Each day’s haul would be distributed among a network of underlings, who trekked around the city’s post offices, paying rubber-band-bound stacks of banknotes into as many as 10 different accounts at each stop, using cards with the pins written on the back.The bank accounts into which the money was deposited belonged to ordinary people – “mules” in police jargon – who received small payments for renting them out, or to companies in Leicester’s garment business, where managers faked invoices to make the payments look legitimate. (Gheewala promised the mules £50 per £10,000 laundered, but in reality he often seems to have paid them less than that.) Gheewala controlled the whole operation from a laptop kept in an otherwise empty house, with all the account details and their passwords written down in a notebook. As soon as the money appeared online he would, using cryptocurrency exchanges, disperse it around the world.In two years, Gheewala’s groupmoved an astonishing £53m, allowing organised criminals to legitimise their earnings on an industrial scale. It’s not clear how much exactly Gheewala was charging for the service, although to judge by the lifestyle he was living, he was doing well out of it.His operation might have been big, but it wasn’t unique. Just a month after Gheewala’s conviction, two men werejailed in Birminghamfor an almost-identical scheme, in which they paid in up to £200,000 a day as they travelled between 10 post offices in the east of the city. In April, a man from Cheltenham was jailed for six years and eight months for controlling a network of mulespaying millions of poundsof cash into post offices in Bristol and Gloucestershire.And this has been going on for a while. Two men were jailed at Southwark crown court in 2024 for paying £26m into post offices in London and Manchester before their arrests in 2017. Studentshave been jailedin Scotland for paying criminal money into post offices, and there are other ongoing cases in which similar crimes are alleged.If it wasn’t for what has been going on elsewhere in the Post Office, this would be a major story. Instead, it has been largely ignored.ThePost Office Horizon scandalburst into the public consciousness thanks to 2024’s ITV drama Mr Bates vs the Post Office, but by that stage it had been dragging on for two decades. Post Office Ltd wrongly prosecuted hundreds of its post office operatives, despite senior figures knowing that the computer program that supposedly showed they had been committing fraud was faulty. Ex-post office operative Alan Bates’s landmark victory against his former employers in 2019 forced the government to overturn his and others’ convictions, and to promise to pay hundreds of millions of pounds in compensation.The scandal is one of Britain’s worst miscarriages of justice. One of its unfortunate side effects is that it has impeded investigations into how much money is being laundered via post office branches. Even if police officers are themselves confident that figures originating in Post Office Ltd’s Horizon software (a version of which isstill being used) are reliable, they are aware that many jury members will – for understandable reasons – be intensely sceptical. Documents released by the inquiry into the Horizon scandal show that, in 2024, just a few weeks after the ITV drama was first aired, a detective constable from Blackburn police station decided to halt an investigation into “large-scale money laundering, and possibly other fraud offences” via post office branches in Lancashire out of concern that defence lawyers would find it too easy to discredit evidence originating from the computer system.View image in fullscreenJigar Gheewala, who was sentenced to almost 12 years in prison for money laundering.Photograph: Leicestershire Police“After the Mr Bates TV show, it became a real hot potato and nobody wanted to get hold of it,” said one officer, who asked to remain anonymous. “For every case that’s brought, there are many more in the background. There is no real appetite to do anything unless it’s a slam dunk, because the public is on the side of the post office operatives.” So the problem remains. “It’s the way that you can pay money into the post office without checks, that’s the problem. It’s huge.”If you look at the raw numbers, you can see his point. In October 2020, cash deposits at post-office branches across the UKtotalled £1.9bn. That is £1.9bn for that single month, not the whole year. The following October, the sum was £2.2bn. That number kept rising each year until, by October 2025, it came to £2.9bn – an increase of 50% in just five years. Although Post Office Ltd then stopped publishing such detailed figures, the trend has continued. It boasted of a 10% increase in deposits in the first quarter of this year, meaning they have now almost certainly passed £3bn a month.What makes these numbers so astounding is that over the same period, cash usage among the general public has dropped sharply. Cash now accounts for fewer thanone in 10 transactionsin the UK. Yet cash deposits at the post office have gone sharply in the opposite direction.According to Post Office Ltd, the reason it stopped publishing monthly cash totals last year was because its post office operatives did not want to alert criminals to the amount of money they had on the premises. Branches are vulnerable to theft for the same reason they are wide open to money laundering. They are often just ordinary shops offering post-office services over the counter, and they lack the specialised equipment that would allow them to track who is on the premises, or to keep their employees safe.Back when Post Office Ltd was still publishing its monthly cash figures, it would accompany them with upbeat quotes about how much it was helping small businesses by providing banking services. While much of the increase is certainly being driven by the closure of bank branches, a senior police officer would regularly forward the figures to me, accompanied with a single emoji: 👀.Concerns about being seen to further victimise post office operatives has discouraged police officers from going on the record about the scale of the problem that they’re seeing. “I’m sure you appreciate that anything quotable is going to have to be suitably vanilla,” another senior officer told me. “It would need to be, you know, ‘we work in partnership’, ‘there are many perspectives’-type stuff.”The sensitivity is understandable, but it comes with dangers. By making it possible for organised criminals – drug dealers, human traffickers, thieves, fraudsters and others – to launder their earnings, and thus to keep their profits, the post office risks creating an entirely different scandal.The trial of Giuseppe Sangiovanni and seven of his alleged co-conspirators was due to start in May 2025 at Bristol crown court, and to run for several days. Sangiovanni was accused of running a scheme that laundered £2.2m via post office branches in Bristol and Gloucestershire over a few months of 2021. His alleged co-conspirators were accused of letting him move money through their bank accounts in return for small payments.On the first morning of the trial, however, Sangiovanni changed his plea to guilty and left the courtroom to await a fresh hearing, leaving his co-defendants behind. It quickly became clear that they were not criminal masterminds. I had only just arrived in Bristol and knew only the bare outlines of the case, but even I could tell their chances of escaping conviction were now close to nonexistent. If the prosecutors had all the transaction details, and the ringleader was admitting the charges, then the owners of the bank accounts through which the money had passed would find it all but impossible to convince a jury that nothing untoward had occurred.Technically, a trial was still scheduled, but it was so obviously not going to happen that the jury never even entered the courtroom. The two prosecution lawyers, far from wargaming the new reality, were using the break to discuss holiday destinations for their unexpected spell of spare time. The only people present who appeared not to realise the consequences of Sangiovanni’s decision were his co-defendants, who continued to sit in the dock like baby birds in smart casual, with only the haziest of ideas what was going on.The judge tried to help, encouraging them to discuss things with their lawyers. They whispered among themselves, until one at a time – over the course of many hours, and after many hearings were convened, suspended and convened again – they changed their pleas to guilty too. (They were not masterminds, as I say, and mostly received suspended sentences.)“They’re just run-of-the-mill local criminals. A couple of them weren’t really criminals at all. One that we didn’t charge was a single mum and, to a degree, was exploited,” said Detective Inspector Peter Highway of the south west regional organised crime unit. It was only while being interviewed by police that one defendant discovered that Sangiovanni had laundered more than £1m through his bank account. “He was a bit surprised by that number,” said Highway, “because he hadn’t done the deposits himself.”View image in fullscreenThe cast of Mr Bates vs the Post Office, broadcast on ITV in 2024.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockMoney laundering was criminalised in the UK in 1988 as part of a global effort to close loopholes in the financial system that were allowing criminals to keep their profits. Previously, it had been easy for criminals to walk into a bank and pay in cash, no questions asked, but the new laws obliged bankers to report suspicious transactions to law enforcement agencies. The theory was that, with bankers sending in a steady stream of suspicious activity reports, police officers would be able to see money being laundered in real time, freeze it and arrest its owners.The world has moved on since then and the most sophisticated crime, such as fraud, involves electronic money stolen from people’s bank accounts and moved in a bewildering variety of ways, involving shell companies, cryptocurrencies, secrecy jurisdictions and more. This requires equally advanced countermeasures from banks, which use AI-powered tools to spot the signs of criminal behaviour.At the street level, however, not much has changed: criminals still use cash, and the NationalCrimeAgency estimates that they launder about £12bn worth of banknotes in the UK each year, largely by presenting the money as the fruits of legitimate businesses. This is where branches of the post office come in.From the criminals’ point of view, post offices are quick and easy places to launder dodgy money. “There’s no requirement for ID verification, there’s no requirement for any kind of enhanced screening, there’s no centralised CCTV,” said the second senior police officer. We put a higher bar on buying alcohol than we do on money laundering via the post office.This is why Gheewala’s mules were able to go into a branch with a pocket full of bank cards, and pay bundles of cash into multiple accounts, one after another. “You definitely don’t want, in a post office that has already got queues out the door, to have a complicated financial transaction going on. So everything that the post office does for banking is done with simplicity in mind,” said the former Post Office employee.The trouble then is, as happened in Leicester, that criminals move money onwards as soon as it arrives in a bank account. Any reports that post office employees do make about the transaction will come too late for the bank to be able to freeze it. This defangs the UK’s entire anti-money-laundering strategy, which has always relied on being able to block suspicious transactions while officers investigate them.The criminal possibilities opened up by Post Office Ltd’s foray into banking were quickly obvious. In July 2020, the Post Office’s compliance committee noted £7m of questionable deposits had gone into 45 branches.In November that year, it discussed how £5-7m a week was being deposited at just two branches in east London, and said it was discussing with the banks what action to take.Sangiovanni and his co-defendants fell foul of this kind of scrutiny, after bank compliance officers spotted what amounted to millions of pounds of suspicious cash transactions at 27 post offices around Gloucestershire, and alerted the police who brought in first the mules, then Sangiovanni, for questioning. “He gave an account that he would go to a car park at Asda, and someone would give him a carrier bag full of cash, and he would then take it away, and then send them some crypto,” said Highway. “He didn’t feel that was suspicious. We did.”By the time officers from the south west organised crime unit moved in, however, the money was long gone. So, although they caught Sangiovanni, the criminals whose cash he was laundering got to enjoy the freshly laundered money. “Millions of pounds into the laundering, that’s a bit late in the day,” said Highway.It looks obvious how to close this gap in our defences against dirty cash. If the Post Office is going to act like a bank, it should collect the same kind of information as a bank, make the same kind of reports as a bank, and freeze transactions in the same way that banks do. In 2023, the regulators at the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) took a small step in this direction, by imposing limits on how much cash could be deposited at the post office at any one time. It was a logical step to take, but it ran into immediate controversy.The fact that two-thirds of bank branches have closed in the UK in the past decade has left businesses and individuals who still rely on cash heavily dependent on post-office branches to pay in their takings. Post Office Ltd used this fact to push back against the FCA’s deposit limits by saying they were penalising hard-pressed businesses that were just trying to stay afloat. “They are hurting legitimate customers and businesses who need support,” said Ross Borkett, Post Office Ltd’s then-head of banking, after the FCA’s changes were announced. Cash-intensive businesses, via the British Independent Retailers Association and the Independent Retail Consortium, mobilised a lobbying operation, writing to their MPs, who in turn held debates in parliament to highlight how few bank branches were left in their constituencies.View image in fullscreenLaw enforcement agencies estimate that hundreds of millions of pounds of dirty money are being paid into the post office each year.Photograph: Bank of England/PAAs a result, ministers promised to ensure that businesses and individuals still reliant on banknotes and coins would always be able to use them. In other words, the FCA’s cash limit is likely to be the last intervention to make payments at post offices harder.At a time when an increasingly large proportion of the population can’t access a physical bank branch, the 11,500 post-office branches in the UK will become ever-more central to a strategy of ensuring everyone can still use banknotes. Moving, securing and accepting cash is expensive though, which is one reason why the banks don’t much want to do it any more. Post offices don’t charge their customers for making deposits, however, so who is going to pay for it?The answer to that question is tied up in the legacy of the Horizon scandal. Post Office Ltd was already in significant financial difficulties before it began having to pay compensation to the hundreds of post office operatives that it had unfairly prosecuted. It has now had to distributemore than £1bn, pushing it into a deep annual loss.That is already a significant challenge for its long-term viability, but it is only half of the problem it faces. Post-office branches operate as independent businesses, but the amount of money operatives earned from providing post office services fell by almost 5% in the decade to 2023, in part thanks to fewer people sending letters. Meanwhile, post office operatives’ expenses have increased. So Post Office Ltd not only needs to find the money to pay compensation to the post office operatives it has wronged, but it must also simultaneously find a sustainable business model if it wants people to be post office operatives at all. And that is where banking comes in.Banks pay Post Office Ltd for providing services on their behalf, which helped it to post revenues of £309m from “banking and ATMs” in its 2024-5 accounts. That was more than a third of its revenues for that year, and only slightly less than it earned from handling the mail. In fact, Post Office Ltd may already be making more money from deposits and withdrawals than it does from its traditional business. As the former insider joked: “We should start calling it the Bank Office.”This isn’t just important for Post Office Ltd, but also for individual post office operatives, who earn a fee for every cash deposit they accept. “The post office operatives will be remunerated on the transactions that they have through their branch, so they will get a transaction fee,” Ben Woollard, the new head of banking at Post Office Ltd, told me. “As with any product, the more a post office operative or any business will deliver, then they will earn more income out of that.”Woollard argues that post-office branches are no different from any other business in being vulnerable to money laundering. He pointed out to me that anyone offering banking services receives annual training in how to recognise and tackle money laundering, and that the head office sends out alerts to branches in areas that appear to have a large number of suspicious transactions.But although any business that handles cash could be exploited by criminals, it is also true that few businesses handle banknotes in the volumes that routinely pass through post-office branches, making them more vulnerable to abuse than most. Post office operatives are also running a system that we know is already wide open to dirty money, and are rewarded proportionally to the raw total of money they put through it, so the temptation to look the other way or even to provide financial services to criminals must be ever-present.We have no idea how many insiders have given in to this temptation, and it looks likely that we will remain in the dark. The disastrous legacy of the Horizon scandal means there has been little appetite to investigate. With such a deeply flawed system, the best that police officers can hope for is to prosecute the more egregious offenders.So despite the success of Operation Kilo, Leicestershire police’s Detective Constable Catherine Richards wasn’t exactly optimistic that Gheewala’s conviction would change anything: “Crime is continuing,” she told me. “Money needs to be laundered. And, yeah, somebody else fills those boots, don’t they?”View image in fullscreenLast chance to buy the summer issue of The Long Read magazine, now with 15% offAI in the classroom, vending machines in the canteen, homeless people in the library, no one in the pub. title: Sex sells and wins votes – and the Democrats know it | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: Wonder why they’re posting flirty photos and wearing tight T-shirts? It’s a thirst trap strategy in motion, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: Wonder why they’re posting flirty photos and wearing tight T-shirts? It’s a thirst trap strategy in motion, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Content: A call to arms … Democratic Michigan senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed shows off his muscly physique.Photograph: Scott Olson/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA call to arms … Democratic Michigan senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed shows off his muscly physique.Photograph: Scott Olson/Getty ImagesOpinionUS politicsSex sells and wins votes – and the Democrats know itArwa MahdawiWonder why they’re posting flirty photos and wearing tight T-shirts? It’s a thirst trap strategy in motionTue 25 Aug 2026 10.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 14.03 EDTShareDespite being a card-carrying member of the International Order of Confirmed Homosexuals, I have spent quite a lot of time lately thinking aboutAbdul El-Sayed’sbiceps. I mean, have you seen them? The progressive Michigan senate nominee is jacked and he knows it. He almost always wears a tight black T-shirt to show off his muscles and incorporates a lot offitness contentin his campaign.I’m not the only one who has noticed El-Sayed’s prominent muscles. They have had a lot of coverage, and are seen as part of a wider attempt to rebrand the Democratic party. Which, I don’t need to tell you, has aserious imageproblem; a poll in March found that the party is looked on even less favourably than the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency. So, to make it look less like a party that is full of out-of-touch technocrats who sound as if they are reading from a 500-page PowerPoint presentation every time they try to explain anything, Democrats seem to be trying to up the sex appeal.“Democrats enter their thirst trap era,” News websiteAxios recently declared, summing up the phenomenon. The piece observed that the Democrats’ main TikTok page has given “the thirst trap treatment” to big names including El-Sayed, Zohran Mamdani and senator Jon Ossoff (“nicknamed‘Senator My Boo’ by internet fans”), by posting flirty photos and videos. Axios quotes a political analyst who explains that while female Democrats such as Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have had their share of screen time, the Dems’ TikTok page has made a “very intentional choice to feature the most attractive male members”.Fox News would appear toreluctantly agreewith the assessment that Democrats are leaning into good looks to win the midterms. “El-Sayed is out in these tight T-shirts,” Fox News host Ainsley Earhardt said in a discussion last week. “AOC with her pretty smile. She’s beautiful. She’s got the red lipstick. You have Mamdani, always smiling … It doesn’t make their philosophy any less dangerous, right?… even with a tight T-shirt, it’s still socialism and it fails.”Over on CNN there was a little more jubilation about the Democrats’ vibe shift. “Dems are hot again,” strategist Yemisi Egbewoleproclaimed. “They’re coming out of the closet as hot people and I’m so excited.” Egbewole added that it wasn’t just about physical attractiveness: “I think they’re learning from Trump. Entertainment really sells.”Sex sells too: it’s well established that votersaround the worldprefer good-looking candidates. But, while we may all be shallow deep down, some of us are shallower than others. A 2016studyfound that rightwing politicians in Europe, the US and Australia tended to be more attractive than their progressive counterparts. That’s partly because “low-information” conservative voters are particularly prone to choosing attractive candidates. “In low-information city elections, a beauty increase of one standard deviation attracts about 20% more votes for the average candidate on the right and about 8% more votes for the average candidate on the left,” an analysis of the study bythe Washington Post noted. Which raises the question: if looks really are so important to low-information rightwing voters, how did we end up with Donald Trump as president? (Woke 1.0 is over, haven’t you heard? It’s OK to say things like this now.)Social media may have brought a new visual element to politics, but the most famous anecdote about how looks can sway an election is almost 70 years old. In September 1960,70 million Americans watched Richard Nixon debate John F Kennedyin the first nationally televised debate between presidential candidates. Nixon had been the favourite going in but he had just been in hospital for a couple of weeks and looked terrible. JFK, on the other hand, was tanned and rested and had good stage makeup.You canquibblewith the conventional wisdom that Nixon lost that election on looks, but it certainly played a part. In hismemoir, Nixon wrote: “What hurt me the most in the first debate was not the substance of the encounter between Kennedy and me, but the disadvantageous contrast in our appearances. After the program ended, callers, including my mother, wanted to know if anything was wrong, because I did not look well.”In short: if thirst traps are what it takes to get the US on a better path, then so be it. Jacked candidates in tight T-shirts may seem like a cheap trick, but even Nixon’s mother would agree that it’s a sound political strategy.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The war on ‘loudcasting’ phones can be won, but it will take some very British nudging | Dan Hancox | The Guardian
description: Although mobiles blared in public are nothing new, this crop of headphone-dodging irritants are truly maddening. It’s time to take them on, says Dan Hancox, a writer and editor covering music, politics and cities
Author: Dan Hancox
Headline: Although mobiles blared in public are nothing new, this crop of headphone-dodging irritants are truly maddening. It’s time to take them on, says Dan Hancox, a writer and editor covering music, politics and cities
Content: Illustration: Anaïs Mims/Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenIllustration: Anaïs Mims/Guardian DesignOpinionEnvironmentThe war on ‘loudcasting’ phones can be won, but it will take some very British nudgingDan HancoxAlthough mobiles blared in public are nothing new, this crop of headphone-dodging irritants are truly maddening. It’s time to take them onTue 25 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 14.03 EDTShare‘Interesting cities can’t be quiet”, runs one of grime DJ and music industry thinkerElijah’sepigrams – and in its essential spirit, he is right. Silent, tidy, prim cities should be treated with suspicion. Any such atmosphere denotes that something has gone wrong at a macro level: either you’ve wound up in an authoritarian regime or, worse, Switzerland.But not all urban sounds are created equal, and some are more unwelcome than others. Take the tide of (Instagram, TikTok, YouTube) reels crashing on the shores of our collective attention on public transport, thanks to the astonishing number of grown adults who think it’s OK tosurf the slopwavewithout headphones.These rotters are accompanied by people taking their phone or video calls out loud on speakerphone. In the early days of mobile phones it was a widely agreed social truism that the white-collar workerunselfconsciously bellowing “I’m on the train!”into their BlackBerry was a grade-A public nuisance, plausibly worthy of throwing in the stocks. Well, at least then we were only being subjected to one end of the conversation.The spread of 5G across the country is making such unsolicited noise more possible and more common: “loudcasting”, the BBC called it in a recent in-depth look at the phenomenon. A public backlash is suddenly mounting. Never one to miss an opportunity for free press coverage, last week Wetherspoons boss Tim Martinbanned itfrom his pubs.It’s funny how social pressure points like this fade in and out of public view, as the technology that touches our lives evolves: 19 years ago, the same practice was christened “sodcasting” by Pascal Wyse in this newspaper – at that point there were no reels, no AI drivel, no streaming video calls, no such thing as an Instagram influencer, nor Instagram either. The moral panic back then was about tinny MP3s being played aloud from much more basic mobile phones – and the purported juvenile delinquency that had surely led to such a crisis.I probably annoyed a lot of Guardian readers that year, writing more than 2,000 wordsin defence of sodcasting: more precisely, in defence of teenagers playing music on their phones on the bus, the train or otherwise in public. There was something qualitatively different about that iteration, I would argue. It was a necessary claiming of public space by people who are often bullied out of it: adults-in-training, still working out how to exist in the outside world as independent beings, still learning to navigate their own social lives, and (an underrated asset, this) learning to enjoy musictogether, as a group activity. For the rest of us, this form of sodcasting amounted to an occasional, brief and usually joyful burst of alfresco music – and we could all do with hearing Crazy Cousinz and Giggs more often anyway.View image in fullscreen‘These days it always seems to be full-grown adults rather than teenagers taking calls on speakerphone or watching reels with no headphones.’Photograph: PjrTransport/AlamyThe 2010 furore about sodcasting followed a decade of punching down by Britain’s power-wielding adults against its most marginalised young people – the“chavs” and “hoodies”against whom New Labour and the tabloids collectively went to war, driven by the reactionary moralism of what was risibly called “the respect agenda”.A time of asbos, public spaces protection orders and curfews for young people.Interestingly – and admittedly anecdotally; this stuff isn’t easy to measure – sodcasting 1.0 seemed to disappear as a phenomenon after a year or two. New social behaviours that emerge in response to new popular technologies tend to do so: things settle down as a new consensus on how we should all use them is slowly reached, and reached collectively.Let’s hope that happens again, because what we are all hearing on buses and trains thanks to sodcasting 2.0 is measurably more antisocial and individualistic: for one thing, 2010’s groups of teen sodcasters weren’t changing songs every 10 seconds. For another – warning, more anecdotal analysis incoming – these days it always seems to be full-grown adults rather than teenagers taking calls on speakerphone or watching reels with no headphones. It is maddening behaviour to anyone who has experienced it: like being on a bus or a train with someone who is flicking TV channels, constantly.So, as Lenin once asked of matters of similarly grave importance: what is to be done? Last year, the Lib Demsproposed a £1,000 finefor sodcasting – an amusingly illiberal policy to make one of their centrepieces. For what it’s worth, I don’t think a fine is very useful, realistic or enforceable – though, God bless the ironclad French state, for it managed to find a way to do exactly that,fining a man €200(£170) for taking a call on loudspeaker on a station platform.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe truth is that we have more sane and effective options for shaping public behaviour in the form of nudge messaging. Transport for London has a strong history of this, via adverts on its trains, tubes and buses. In 2008, its Considerate Travel campaign seemed to help quieten down the mobile phone DJs and its currentAct Like a FriendandTravel Kindcampaigns aim to address hate crime, misogynistic creeps and encourage others to help passengers who may be unwell. Sodcasting 2.0 pisses me off no end, too, but I think people can change with a little nudging.Stefan Stern made anexcellent casein these pages recently that we should all remove our headphones – and turn off the content altogether – to hear and more fully participate in the noisy, messy city around us. Hopefully we can achieve this via social consensus, gentle persuasion, and without the soundtrack of someone broadcasting AI monkey videos. And if all else fails, well, sod it: let’s nudge the culprits into the stocks.Dan Hancox is a writer and editor covering music, politics and cities. His latest book is Multitudes: How Crowds Made the Modern WorldExplore more on these topicsEnvironmentOpinionPublic transportMobile phonesTfLPollutionAI (artificial intelligence)HeadphonescommentShareReuse this content

title: From ‘old people music’ to owning the streets: 60 years of Notting Hill carnival and me | Notting Hill carnival | The Guardian
description: As a child, being taken to the Caribbean celebration was a drag. But once sound systems arrived in the 1970s, it became an unmissable yearly pilgrimage offering a sense of freedom
Author: Lloyd Bradley
Headline: As a child, being taken to the Caribbean celebration was a drag. But once sound systems arrived in the 1970s, it became an unmissable yearly pilgrimage offering a sense of freedom
Content: ‘This wasourcarnival now’ … girls dancing on a street corner in 1975.Photograph: Richard Braine/Pymca/REX/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘This wasourcarnival now’ … girls dancing on a street corner in 1975.Photograph: Richard Braine/Pymca/REX/ShutterstockNotting Hill carnivalFrom ‘old people music’ to owning the streets: 60 years of Notting Hill carnival and meLloyd BradleyAs a child, being taken to the Caribbean celebration was a drag. But once sound systems arrived in the 1970s, it became an unmissable yearly pilgrimage offering a sense of freedomTue 25 Aug 2026 04.50 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 04.51 EDTShareMy earliest memories of theNotting Hill carnivalare of being mildly irritated. In its 1960s infancy, the event was strictly a Caribbean affair, transplanted to Ladbroke Grove as authentically as was practical. Its purpose was as obvious as its origins: giving Caribbean arrivals a chance to celebrate themselves by bringing the vibrancy of the home they left behind to these drab streets for a couple of days.Vital as this was – and it really was – it didn’t cut much ice with surly 10- or 11-year-olds like me, being dragged around behind parading steelbands. Yes, it was great to see so many Black people out in the open together and your mums and dads laughing and having a good time, but did we need to be here? There was football to be played and bikes to be ridden, yet so many of us were being forced to walk for what seemed like miles following “old people music”.Then as the 1970s got under way, everything changed. TheLondonsound systems that had been establishing themselves over the previous few years – Coxsone Outernational, Jah Shaka, 6X6, Sufferah HiFi, TWJ and so on – assumed a growing presence at carnival, under the flyover or on the street. They were operated by men and women not much older than us, who understood how the post-Windrush generation defined their Blackness as they came of age in London and how, although roots and heritage were always important, we didn’t need to simply recreate the Caribbean.View image in fullscreen‘Everything changed’ … Notting Hill Carnival in 1974.Photograph: Chris MilesThe sound systems played the same choice of music we heard at dances and parties or in our own record collections, so we could find the reggae, the lovers rock, the soul and funk that soundtracked our lives right there set up outside accommodating pubs, caffs or people’s front doors. The big plus point was the sound systems were static, meaning if you weren’t dropping some foot you could stand around with your hands in your pockets, always a teenager’s default setting. Indeed the only walking you were obliged to do would be if the music wasn’t up to it or there weren’t enough people – ie women – at that particular sound, so you’d find another one. This might involve a bit of float-following, but, then again, it might not.Refreshment was never a problem. Some Kentucky or a kebab when we were gathering at Turnpike Lane station, then load up with “supplies” before leaving, thus avoiding the so-called “carnival tax” temporarily inflating prices in Notting Hill off-licences. Our drinks of choice usually involved pre-mixing dark rum or Bacardi with Coca-Cola, or vodka with orange juice; beer was too heavy to lug around until they started selling it in those four packs held together with plastic rings. You’d drink a can, undo your belt, thread it through the empty ring and you were away. Some guys, more hardcore than me, would hang a pack off each hip then swagger round like a western gunslinger. (At this year’s Arsenal victory parade my son turned up with an insulated backpack containing rum, mixer, beer and ice that didn’t melt over the course of six hours, and I thought: “Wow! How we could have done with that at the carnival in the 70s!”)View image in fullscreen‘Everybody I knew went to work the following week with a bit of a spring in their step.’Photograph: PYMCA/Avalon/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesSuddenly, the Notting Hill carnival made sense. Youngsters came down in droves because this wasourcarnival now, and while we appreciated what it stood for historically, we wanted to enjoy ourselves, too. You wouldn’t dream of missing it. Carnival was the place to run into familiar faces who you probably didn’t know by name and might not have seen since last year’s event but you were glad to have a quick chat with.Just as the crowds swelled so did the area the event occupied. Sound systems would mostly set up outside the parade route, and by renting front gardens for the weekend there were smaller rigs as far as the canal up by Harrow Road to the north and Colville Terrace to the south – gentrification hadn’t been invented at that point – in between Ladbroke Grove and Chepstow Road. There were street dances of varying sizes everywhere, many doing a roaring trade selling drink or barbecue to the foolishly unprepared, and this takeover created one of the most attractive features of the weekend.In the early 1970s, when police harassment was commonplace, racist microaggressions were a part of everyday life and the hospitality industry wasn’t living up to its name, just being able to walk about such a large area of London seeing far more people that looked like you than didn’t, enjoying a drink and a dance or just pissing about and not being bothered by anybody was simply brilliant. It was as if we owned those streets for four days. Everybody I knew went to work the following week with a bit of a spring in their step. And most likely exhausted: back in such unregulated times, revelry tended to kick off on Friday evening and go through to Monday night and Tuesday morning, with sound systems playing until the J’ouvert celebrations welcomed the sunrise.View image in fullscreen‘An essentially self-regulating event was becoming subject to decisions being made elsewhere’ … Police arresting a young man during riots at the carnival in 1976.Photograph: Evening Standard/Getty ImagesSamba queens to sound systems: the riotous streets of Notting Hill carnival – in picturesRead moreMy peak carnival years were the early 1970s through to the early 1980s; the riot of 1976 changed things. How and why it kicked off is a different conversation, but the aftermath of overpolicing, increasing regulation and media that used violence and criminality as the starting point for reporting: all of this squeezed out a degree of the joyful anarchy and spontaneity that had made it so beautiful. Many people, especially out-of-towners, became scared to go and the tens of thousands that did were aware of a palpable tension, especially around 7pm when the police moved to shut down the sound systems.Naturally this changed the way we approached it, and perhaps the most dispiriting aspect of the shift was that an essentially self-regulating event was becoming subject to decisions being made elsewhere, giving the carnival the flavour of something being donetous rather thanbyus. It didn’t really matter how the content carried on evolving; the whole affair had become far too orderly. It doused the spark one bank holiday at a time, far from that untidy, magnificent era of mass-participation when anybody, just by showing up, knew they were genuinely contributing to the true essence of carnival.But of course the Notting Hill carnival kept going. And as it reaches its 60th anniversary it seems to have been regenerating in size and spontaneity again as the next generation bring back that joyful anarchy. May the streets feel like theirs.Explore more on these topicsNotting Hill carnivalSocial historyBlack British cultureReggaeSoulLondonRacecommentShareReuse this content

title: Food has turned into a class war – and it’s ruined my appetite | Zoe Williams | The Guardian
description: More than half of what Brits eat is ultra-processed. Now we’re a nation of food snobs – with no ingredient safe from judgment, writes Zoe Williams
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: More than half of what Brits eat is ultra-processed. Now we’re a nation of food snobs – with no ingredient safe from judgment, writes Zoe Williams
Content: Tempting …  the crispy pancake.Photograph: Jeff Gilbert/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.View image in fullscreenTempting …  the crispy pancake.Photograph: Jeff Gilbert/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.OpinionUltra-processed foodsFood has turned into a class war – and it’s ruined my appetiteZoe WilliamsMore than half of what Brits eat is ultra-processed. Now we’re a nation of food snobs – with no ingredient safe from judgmentTue 25 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 13.37 EDTShareLewis Bassett is a young sociologist and chef who I first encountered through his podcast, The Full English, where he thinks about the cultural meaning of, say, Delia Smith; gazpacho; whelks. This was thinking you didn’t know you needed until you heard it. Now he’s written a book of the same name, asking: why do we eat the way we do in Britain, and why do we think the way we do, even about the stuff we wouldn’t be caught dead eating?About 57% of all the food eaten in Britain is ultra-processed, which feels familiar from at least a decade of hand-wringing about it, but is radically defamiliarised when set against the rest of Europe. In France it’s 14%, and Italy is also in the teens. It’s amazing they don’t all live to be 150. And while this plainly has its roots in inequality, there is a hefty side order of attitude, which Bassett contemplates while working through the history of sourdough, curry and olive oil, and describing his own life cheffing in fancy kitchens and gastropubs.View image in fullscreenLewis Bassett … pondering the cultural meaning of whelks.Photograph: Lewis BassettBasically, we think posh food is pretentious; but what counts as “posh” constantly morphs, partly through the sheer cost of it, until even food that wasn’t posh before (like fish and chips) becomes posh, and therefore pretentious (also smaller portions: absolute sitcom signifier of despised posh food). I’m freestyling, of course, and you should read The Full English for the meat of Bassett’s argument, but it is fascinating to consider how any given ingredient is freighted with political self-fashioning.There are so many foods – the chickpea; the Findus crispy pancake; tomatoes; the Turkey Twizzler – that have had their moment as the thing some people hate other people for eating, and it’s all shorthand for a low-level class war, mediated through food. It amps up to a thousand when parents get involved.Bassett has this lovely, curious, unjudgmental thinking style, and concludes that “ours is a peculiar diet formed by a peculiar experience of modernity”. Still, you can’t help but think, if we could let go of some of the political and emotional charge around food, we’d end up eating things that were more delicious. I don’t mean Findus crispy pancakes – I know they’re ultra-processed. They were delicious, though.Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: From Scotland, I look at England’s water privatisation disaster. I wish you had done what we did | Devi Sridhar | The Guardian
description: Listening to debate, you’d think bringing English water companies into public ownership was a radical socialist idea. Here, we call it common sense, says chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh Devi Sridhar
Author: Devi Sridhar
Headline: Listening to debate, you’d think bringing English water companies into public ownership was a radical socialist idea. Here, we call it common sense, says chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh Devi Sridhar
Content: Environmental campaigners protest against Thames Water near the Rye River in High Wycombe, Buckinghamshire, 4 March 2026.Photograph: Maureen McLean/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenEnvironmental campaigners protest against Thames Water near the Rye River in High Wycombe, Buckinghamshire, 4 March 2026.Photograph: Maureen McLean/ShutterstockOpinionWater industryFrom Scotland, I look at England’s water privatisation disaster. I wish you had done what we didDevi SridharListening to debate, you’d think bringing English water companies into public ownership was a radical socialist idea. Here, we call it common senseProf Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of EdinburghTue 25 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 11.47 EDTShareEvery few months, there are more shocking headlines about the behaviour of England’s water companies. Thelatest are aboutthe ever-increasing pay of the chief executives and chief financial officers, which rose to a total of £25.3m across 14 companies over the past year. Meanwhile, people living in England struggle with rising water bills and untreated sewage being discharged (often illegally) on to beaches and in to lakes, and companies such as Thames Water areon the brink of insolvencyand want government backing.It’s not surprising that we’re in this situation: England’s water companies have long been accused of putting the interests of shareholdersabove those of customers. From their perspective, the privatisation of water has been an astounding success. Between 1991 and 2019,dividends to the shareholdersof the parent companies totalled £57bn, which averages out to more than £2bn every year. The majority of these private parentcompanies are foreign-owned, so the profits aren’t even kept in Britain.Lack of proper oversight creates a series of perverse incentives. If water companies can charge more for the same amount of water, they’ll do that. If they can dump untreated sewage in public waterways, they’ll do that, too.The root of the problem goes back to 1989 when Margaret Thatcher, then prime minister,privatised water in England. But right here, in the UK, there’s an example that shows that there is an alternative.Water companies circumventing bonus rules? What did ministers expect? | Nils PratleyRead moreUnlike England, Scotland chose to retain public ownership of Scottish Water and, between 2002 and 2019, the company invested35% more per household in infrastructurethan the privatised English water companies. It charges users 14% less and itdoesn’t pay dividends.While Scottish Water’s CEOpay package, which adds up to more than £500k,has beencriticised for being highrelative to other public sector employees, it’s relatively low compared with the private pay packets south of the border. More importantly, Scottish Water is accountable to people living in Scotland, as all profit is reinvested back into water and sanitation systems, instead of going to shareholders.I’ve lived in Scotland for over a decade and the water coming from taps is clean and delicious. Since 2018 Scottish Water’sYour Water Your Lifecampaign has been offeringfree drinking waterthrough a network of public water stations across the country. By 2022, the water dispensed at these would have filled the equivalent of15m plastic bottles. Water in people’s homes is paid for through local authorities charging council tax rather than customers receiving a bill from a private water-company.As a public health expert, I’ve found it hard not to think about England’s poor water infrastructure because I can see how, across the world, and especially in low-income countries, access to this vital resource is often a matter of life or death. It took thefather of epidemiology, John Snow, to identify dirty water as the cause of alarge cholera outbreak in London. Clean water isn’t a luxury: it’s necessary to human health and wellbeing.More recently, Chris Whitty, England’s chief medical officer, highlightedthe worrying public health problemof sewage in England’s waterways. He reminded water companies and their directors that human faeces is making people who swim or use the water on popular beaches and rivers sick.The normal logic of private efficiency might work in sectors of the economy where competition brings meaningful choice and innovation. Take cars: we can choose between different manufacturers, designs, fuel type and price; or even pharmaceutical companies, where competition encourages firms to develop different drugs and invest in risky research.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut what is the consumer choice in tap water?Wateris water: we just need it to be clean, and hopefully to taste good and be reliably delivered through functioning infrastructure. We need the waste we flush down our toilets to be treated and made safe through sanitation systems, before being released into nature again.Listening to the recent debates, you’d think that bringing English water companies back into public ownership was some kind of radical socialist idea. Guess what? That’s just normal life here in Edinburgh.If water and sanitation are treated as a commodity, then companies will of course look at how much they can squeeze consumers. But water isn’t something that you can choose to go without. It’s absolutely vital to human life – you’d die without it in about three days – and should be a basic part of public infrastructure provided by government.Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of EdinburghExplore more on these topicsWater industryOpinionWaterUtilitiesScotlandThames WaterWater billsHousehold billscommentShareReuse this content

title: As a doctor, I say this: before we even consider assisted dying, fix how we care for the most vulnerable | Zubir Ahmed | The Guardian
description: A person’s wish to die can be shaped by whether they have access to proper palliative care – and too many do not, says Labour MP and transplant surgeon Zubir Ahmed
Author: Zubir Ahmed
Headline: A person’s wish to die can be shaped by whether they have access to proper palliative care – and too many do not, says Labour MP and transplant surgeon Zubir Ahmed
Content: ‘A person’s wish to die does not happen in isolation from their circumstances.’Photograph: Rosemary Roberts/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘A person’s wish to die does not happen in isolation from their circumstances.’Photograph: Rosemary Roberts/AlamyOpinionAssisted dyingAs a doctor, I say this: before we even consider assisted dying, fix how we care for the most vulnerableZubir AhmedA person’s wish to die can be shaped by whether they have access to proper palliative care – and in England and Wales, too many do notZubir Ahmed is a transplant surgeon and former Labour ministerTue 25 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 08.30 EDTShareAs a doctor, I have spent much of my professional life caring for people at some of the most vulnerable moments they will ever face. I have seen the anxiety that surrounds the prospect of dying, and the desperate wish of patients and families to avoid unnecessary suffering.Naturally, we all want people facing the end of life to be treated with kindness and respect. But when considering the debate on assisted dying, true compassion demands that we ask a more fundamental question. What kind of society are we building if, before we’ve fixed the systems designed to care for people, we introduce a system designed to help them die? As a former health minister who has seen the system from the inside, I am able to say it is not ready or equipped to answer this question.Andy Burnham has been right to raise this as a priority issue at the start of his tenure as prime minister.Speaking at a care homerecently, he explained that assisted dying should not be introduced while Britain’s palliative care and social care systems remain under such strain. A choice between death without adequate care and a death prematurely self-induced is not a real choice.Indeed, as parliament prepares for yet another vote on assisted dying in England and Wales on 11 September, I fear that the offering has been somewhat mis-sold to the public. A state-controlled medicalised dying process is still a process – one where there remain risks of complication and suffering. The reality of assisted dying is more complex than the promise of a perfectly controlled death.Many people imagine a system where a person facing a terminal illness can choose the exact moment and manner of their death, free from distress. But the legislation does not and cannot provide that certainty. A patient who self-administers medication to begin the dying process may still experience complications. The process may take time; it may require medical intervention. It may not happen where or when the person imagined. The promise of absolute control can therefore become something different in practice: an appearance of choice that does not always deliver the agency people expect.I am far from the only medical professional to be worried about the prospect of assisted dying being available on the NHS. Among those raising concerns about the bill’s dozens of flaws have been theRoyal College of Physicians, theRoyal College of Psychiatrists, theComplex Life and Death Decisions (CLADD) group from King’s College London,theRoyal College of Pathologists, theBritish Geriatrics Societyand numerous other medical bodies and care authorities. The same concern comes up again and again: is it really a “free choice” when palliative care and social support fall short?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFrance’s ‘aid in dying’ law comes into effect after constitutional approvalRead moreA person’s wish to die does not happen in isolation from their circumstances. It can be shaped by whether they feel supported, whether they fear becoming a burden, whether their family is coping and whether they have access to the care they need. That is why the state of our care systems cannot be treated as a separate issue from assisted dying. Timely access to palliative and social care remains too often determined by where someone lives rather than what they need. For some families, excellent end-of-life support is available; for others, particularly in rural areas as well as constituencies experiencing high inequality, the experience is one of waiting, uncertainty and having to fight for services that should be guaranteed.A Labour government founded theNHSon a principle that remains as important today as it was at its creation: that healthcare should be there when people need it most, regardless of their circumstances. A postcode lottery in care cannot be ignored while debating a new legal pathway for people at the end of their life.In Scotland, this concern has been expressed clearly, and was an important reason why, in March, 85% of Labour MSPs voted against the legalisation of assisted dying in Holyrood. The bill introduced in Westminster by my colleague Kim Leadbeater, the Labour MP for Spen Valley, in October 2024 did not fare much better: too many concerns about patient welfare meant the House of Lords would not rubber-stamp the flawed text. And yet, on 11 September, MPs will be faced with yet another vote on assisted dying before the care systems are improved to a level which even makes that debate appropriate. Andy Burnham has his priorities right: this is the wrong debate at the wrong time. This is why I, and many others, will be voting against this bill, in pursuit of comfort, dignity and appropriate care for people who are vulnerable and dying.Zubir Ahmed MP is an NHS vascular and transplant surgeon, and served as the parliamentary under-secretary of state at the Department of Health and Social Care from 6 September 2025 to 12 May 2026.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Canadians do not seek a trade war – but nor will we be bullied by Donald Trump | Jen Gerson | The Guardian
description: A fundamental rupture in the values that have united North America is not a problem that can be wished away, says Canadian commentator Jen Gerson
Author: Jen Gerson
Headline: A fundamental rupture in the values that have united North America is not a problem that can be wished away, says Canadian commentator Jen Gerson
Content: An anti-US tariffs protest outside the US consulate in Vancouver in 2025.Photograph: Ethan Cairns/APView image in fullscreenAn anti-US tariffs protest outside the US consulate in Vancouver in 2025.Photograph: Ethan Cairns/APOpinionCanadaCanadians do not seek a trade war – but nor will we be bullied by Donald TrumpJen GersonA fundamental rupture in the values that have united North America is not a problem that can be wished away: this is a warning to the western allianceTue 25 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 08.30 EDTShareThe Canadians are exceedingly angry. I realise this can sometimes be difficult for foreigners to deduce, given our national struggle to express the full range of human emotion outside ice hockey riots. However, let me assure you that the prime minister Canadians saw take the stage on Saturday morning in the wake of the collapse in trade negotiations with the US was aMark Carneypractically vibrating with fury.“You’re at war when you get attacked. We got attacked,”he said, in arare press conferencethat was as candid and clear as he ever tends to be. “That’s fine … We’ve got the reserves, we’ve got the resilience, we’ve got the plan, we’ve got the focus. We’re gonna respond, we’re going to focus on what we can control and what we’re going to build.”Canada walked out of negotiations, with a deal apparently on the verge of completion, mere hours before50% tariffson a range of Canadian exports were due to kick in.Dollar-for-dollar retaliatory tariffs, scheduled to take effect on 8 September, will follow in turn. In a statement, Carneysaid thatlast-minute demands from the US were “uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal.” The USdenied this, insisting that it was Canadians who made last-minute demands.In subsequent interviews with Bloomberg, Canadian ambassador to the USMark Wiseman saidthere was no specific item that put a deal out of reach; rather, it was a range of issues in which the text that ultimately wound up on the page – or, at least the interpretation of that text – did not align with what the Canadians thought they had agreed to. The most contentious issues appear to be related to tariffs on autos, digital and cultural policy, and the US claiming the right to veto Canada’s attempts to form trade alliances with other countries. Meanwhile, Canadians have no reason to trust this administration not to unilaterally impose new tariffs on a whim – which it has done, repeatedly, and as recently as this week.In short, Carney noted, sometimes the US signature on trade deals is “written in pencil”.Canadian voters, who were pensive about the prospect of any new deal with the US in the first place, have come outstrongly in supportof the prime minister. Despite the fact that the deal’s collapse will almost certainly entail painful economic penalties, the mood is one of sustained and general anger toward the US not born merely of trade irritants – very few Canadians have opinions about rules of origin tariffs on auto parts, or softwood lumber protections, or supply managed dairy quotas. In cordial times, these are the ordinary frictions between close friends and neighbours.View image in fullscreenMark Carney and Donald Trump during a summit addressing the war in Gaza, 13 October 2025.Photograph: Evan Vucci/APRather, it’s an emotion born of a real and visceral sense of betrayal: that the people we trusted with shared security and military obligations, that the nation with which we allowed ourselves to grow economically interdependent, has turned on us. They are using ordinary trade irritants as an excuse to exercise mafioso-style dominance in the pursuit of our subjugation and maybe outright annexation. We know very well that this isn’t about trade.We are being trained to know our place in the new world order that the so-calledDunroe doctrineis seeking to impose on the western hemisphere.So how, exactly, are any of us supposed to respond when the US secretary of transportation, Sean Duffy, goes on Fox News in the aftermath of the collapse tosay things like: “We provide their security for them and they take advantage of us? President Trump was the first one to go and say ‘that’s not the kind of relationship friends should have’.”The US does not provide Canadian security – although many commentators, including myself, do criticise our lax military spending. The North American Aerospace Defense Command, orNorad, is a fully integrated entity of both the Canadian and US military. We have our own military, and our own police forces.How are we supposed to respond, exactly, when our large and once-admired neighbour to the southrepeatedly threatensto make us the “51st state”? Or when he postsgag photosof the whole of North America covered in a US flag – provocations we’re supposed to take “seriously but not literally”, as if that makes these threats less horrific or more acceptable.What does one do when one’s closest “friend” and “ally” repeatedlythreatens to disregardborder treaties? Or when the US’s actual behaviour aligns perfectly with the president’s threat to use “economic force“ to push us into becoming an American state?We don’t want to be an American state. And even if we did, we certainly wouldn’t want to be a state of whatever the US is choosing to become right now.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere is not a single Canadian who wants to start a war with the US. No country in Canada’s position storms out of a trade negotiation unless it has to. No country as small and dependent on the US tells the modern imperium to get lost, and risks the consequences thereof, unless there is no other option.What Carney – and Canada, for that matter – are trying to signal across the Atlantic is that the America we all built our expectations around is over. We cannot plan around the hope of a return to normal, even if Democrats regain power in Washington.Canada’s location and US-integrated economy mean that we will be the first to face the reality of whatever the US becomes. And if it is coming for us, no European ally – including the UK – can expect to remain untouched, regardless of whatever “special relationship” you imagine may insulate you.Personally, I simply cannot fathom the commentators and politicians in the UK who fail to understand this. Do you honestly imagine yourselves to be closer to the US militarily, geographically, economically, or culturally thanCanada? Guys, wearea little America, albeit with a steadier political system and the king on the money. If they are willing to vassaliseus, what sentiment of history or tradition remains to protectyou?A fundamental break in American values and objectives is not a problem that can be contained. It’s not a condition that can be ignored or wished away. Carney is seriouswhen he talks abouta historic “rupture in the world order”, as he did at Davos early this year.Canadians understand that maintaining our sovereignty and independence will entail consequences and sacrifices. We did not bring this trade war on ourselves; we have merely refused to comply in advance to the unreasonable demands of a bad-faith actor. We will be punished for it. We have accepted this. If nothing else, let the US’s retaliation be a warning to the rest of the western alliance. Run,run. Protect yourselves. Move faster.Jen Gerson is a Canadian commentator and co-founder ofThe Line. She lives in Calgary, AlbertaExplore more on these topicsCanadaOpinionDonald TrumpMark CarneyAmericascommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Trump’s economic threats: bullies can overplay their hand | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Tariffs on Canada, threats against Iran’s partners and bond market intervention show a president weaponising US power while making Americans poorer at home
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Tariffs on Canada, threats against Iran’s partners and bond market intervention show a president weaponising US power while making Americans poorer at home
Content: ‘The US president is willing to use state power to lower borrowing costs while hiking others through tariffs, war and cuts to social programmes.’Photograph: Will Oliver/UPI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘The US president is willing to use state power to lower borrowing costs while hiking others through tariffs, war and cuts to social programmes.’Photograph: Will Oliver/UPI/ShutterstockOpinionDonald TrumpThe Guardian view on Trump’s economic threats: bullies can overplay their handEditorialTariffs on Canada, threats against Iran’s partners and bond market intervention show a president weaponising US power while making Americans poorer at homeTue 25 Aug 2026 13.27 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 19.10 EDTShareThree moves in the last week have exposed the limits of Donald Trump’s economicbullying. The US slapped 50% tariffs on another$20bnof Canadian goods – then threatened the same rate on thecars, trucks, parts and steelthat America Inc depends on. On Monday, the Treasury secretary,Scott Bessent,menaced Iran’s trading partners with exclusion from the US financial network, hoping that coercion can deliver what months of war have not. And as the costs of war, tariffs andpro-billionairetax cuts helped send US bond yields higher, the Treasurysteppedin to tame long-term rates. These are not contradictory policies but a gamble: that US economic power can be repeatedly weaponised without reducing others’ willingness to depend on it.The Trump administration’s “D-day” sanctions are potentially the most consequential because they expose the scaffolding of American financial power. While markets shrugged off the immediatethreat, that calculation might change were the US to target a major Chineserefineryor bank. Such an escalation could spark a trade war with Beijing. The US has leverage. But China has pressure points –especially farmers in Republican states– that make using it costly. In the long run, there is a price to pay. Nations hold one another’s currencies partly because they trust the political relationship. Mr Trump is testing what happens when they don’t.View image in fullscreenScott Bessent.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersThe moves to control thebond marketare the most revealing. There is nothing new about Washington managing yields: the Federal Reserve has long been able to buytreasuries. What is new is Mr Bessent doing it so openly to deal with the fallout from failed policies. Mr Trump owns this: his tariffs raise input costs; his Iran war pushed up energy costs; his nonchalance aboutrising American grocery pricesreassures no one. When that mixture helps produce higher inflation expectations and rising long-end bond yields, Mr Trump’s team steps in to prevent interest rates ticking up.The US president is willing to usestate powerto lower borrowing costs while hiking others through tariffs, war and cuts to social programmes. Mr Bessent wants to stop rising long yields feeding into investment and Washington’s debt-interest bill. That hisformer mentorat George Soros’s hedge fund criticises him and wants bond markets to force spending cuts is not to be applauded. The better question for Mr Bessent is: why shield markets from the consequences of Mr Trump’s acts, but not households?The trade war with Canada is economically stupid andlegally dubious. In 2025, the Trump tariffsamountedto an average tax increase of $1,000 per US household. More than a quarter ofCanadian exportsto the US are now subject to significant tariffs orthreatenedwith tougher ones. Ottawa’s retaliation will start in September. North American production has been organised around such trade flows and tariffs will make US manufacturing more expensive, not less.Why Canada? Washington has largely given up trying to change China’seconomic model. Canada is seen as a soft target. The Guardian columnist Robert Reich issurelyright: Mr Trump picks on a friendly neighbour because that is what bullies do. This cannot go on. American economic power depends on other countries wanting to remain in a system the US dominates. Mr Trump thinks their dependence is his weapon. The more often he uses it against them, the harder theyshouldlook for the exit.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionTariffsCanadaUS economyMark CarneyUS politicsTrump administrationeditorialsShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on the French left: division makes Marine Le Pen’s path to the Élysée more straightforward | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Two years ago, progressive parties allied to see off the far right in a parliamentary election. Ahead of a seismic presidential election, that unity is missing
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Two years ago, progressive parties allied to see off the far right in a parliamentary election. Ahead of a seismic presidential election, that unity is missing
Content: The leader of Public Square, Raphael Glucksmann, ahead of a TV interview announcing  his candidacy for the 2027 French presidential election.Photograph: Julie Sebadelha/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe leader of Public Square, Raphael Glucksmann, ahead of a TV interview announcing  his candidacy for the 2027 French presidential election.Photograph: Julie Sebadelha/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionFranceThe Guardian view on the French left: division makes Marine Le Pen’s path to the Élysée more straightforwardEditorialTwo years ago, progressive parties allied to see off the far right in a parliamentary election. Ahead of a seismic presidential election, that unity is missingTue 25 Aug 2026 13.27 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 19.42 EDTShareIn the summer of 2024, as polls suggested that Marine Le Pen’s far-right Rassemblement National party would win a snap legislativeelectionrashly called by Emmanuel Macron, the perennially fragmented French left united to spectacular effect. The New Popular Front, whose name evokedLéon Blum’santi-fascist alliance in the 1930s, camefirstin a poll that delivered a hung parliament.Eight months before a presidential contest in which Ms Le Pen is the clear frontrunner, the prospect of a repeat performance appears close to zero. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leader of the hard-left France Unbowed, and Olivier Faure, the leader of the Socialist party (PS), have both ruled out the idea of backing a single candidate.Effortsby the Greens to broker talks between progressive parties have fallen on deaf ears.The obvious danger, as the most important election in the history of the Fifth Republic looms, is that chronic division will ease Ms Le Pen’s path to the Élysée. The 75-year-old Mr Mélenchon is a deeply polarising figure who has failed three times to reach the second round of a presidential race. But in a fractured field, the loyalty of his base among the young, the urban precariat and ethnic minority voters gives him a credible chance of making the runoff this time. At which point, pollspredict, France’s traditional “Republican front” against the far right would disintegrate, handing Ms Le Pen a crushing victory.Within the PS, the picture is one of confusion and debilitating internal rivalries. Raphael Glucksmann, the leader of Public Square, a small sister movement,declaredhis candidacy on Sunday and is favourite to win a joint primary. But senior figures such as the former president François Hollande are rumoured to be waiting to make their own move later on. The Greens aredividedover whether to offer support to Mr Mélenchon’s uncompromising leftism and reward his new emphasis on the environment, or back Mr Glucksmann’s more centrist strategy.View image in fullscreenJean-Luc Mélenchon.Photograph: Raphaël Lafargue/Abaca/ShutterstockAll of which makes Mr Glucksmann’s statedambitionto “rebuild the left” seem somewhat optimistic. A Parisian intellectual married to a famous television newsreader (who has taken leave for the duration of the campaign), he is polling at 10% and is unburdened by the aura of failure that has dogged the Socialist party in recent years. But if he becomes its presidential candidate, he will face the same challenge as his immediate predecessors: how to reconnect with alienated blue-collar towns that now vote for Ms Le Pen, while simultaneously courting Mr Mélenchon’s urban radicals and reassuring middle-class voters who deserted for Mr Macron.In 2022, the former Paris mayor Anne Hidalgo comprehensivelyflunkedthat test, receiving 1.75% of votes cast. A historic humiliation was partly the result of progressive voters calculating that Mr Mélenchon was the left candidate with the best chance of coming second, thus excluding Ms Le Pen from the runoff. But as the 2027 campaign begins in earnest, she enjoys a 20-point lead in the polls, and another place in the second round is all but assured.The question, therefore, is who can rally enough support from across the political spectrum to stop her becoming president. A united left would have had a far better chance of coming up with a convincing answer. But that is not the left France currently has.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
