title: Why the threat from the rampaging AI machine went ignored | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Letters: Jonathan Michie on his father’s efforts in the 1970s to map out concerns regarding widespread social coercion driven by automation. Plus a letter from Callum Brown
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Jonathan Michie on his father’s efforts in the 1970s to map out concerns regarding widespread social coercion driven by automation. Plus a letter from Callum Brown
Content: ‘AI is really not that smart, and a few well-chosen puzzles for it to solve expose its crippling obsession with data.’Photograph: Kilito Chan/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘AI is really not that smart, and a few well-chosen puzzles for it to solve expose its crippling obsession with data.’Photograph: Kilito Chan/Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)LettersWhy the threat from the rampaging AI machine went ignoredJonathan Michieon his father’s efforts in the 1970s to map out concerns regarding widespread social coercion driven by automation. Plus a letter fromCallum BrownTue 25 Aug 2026 12.44 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 12.55 EDTShareJill Lepore asks why nobody listened to warnings about the threats posed from the AI revolution (Democracy v the machine, 18 August). As she is a Harvard professor, her piece is understandably US-centric. But in 1972 there was an international gathering of AI researchers and others in Italy to tackle the ethical and social implications of AI.This “Serbelloni group” of global experts (they met at Villa Serbelloni on Lake Como) was led by my father, Donald Michie, the director of the University of Edinburgh’s department of machine intelligence. The group mapped out early concerns regarding potential political tyranny, the erosion of human autonomy and widespread social coercion driven by automation.Why did nobody listen? In part because the next year the UK cut research funding for machine learning, robotics and AI, following the Lighthill report, which had been established – it has since beendocumented– for this purpose. Researchers had instead to focus on more immediately industrial-relevant work. My father’s attempts to reconvene the Serbelloni group to include experts from the humanities thus proved unsuccessful.Jonathan MichieProfessor of innovation& knowledge exchange, University of OxfordJill Lepore rightly traces those welcoming the rampaging AI machine in a free market while modern humanists fear the unchecked machine. She mentions the underestimated American intellectual Lewis Mumford, who devoted most of his life to restraining the uninhibited city as a form of machine damaging people by the million. He hooked up with the British humanist Frederic J Osborn in a letter exchange that lasted over three decades, developing a sane town-planning system.Mumford was wise enough to see that the automatic machine had the capacity to make man passive and purposeless in the same manner as did living in the city, and humans must resist induced passivity of all kinds. So the myth still prevails. Beware – AI is really not that smart, and a few well-chosen puzzles for it to solve expose its crippling obsession with data, not with the humans’ forte, knowledge.Callum BrownProfessor emeritus in history, University of GlasgowHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Learning from lived experiences of poverty | Poverty | The Guardian
description: Letters: Carol Taylor and Howard Williamson respond to Katriona O’Sullivan’s article on the grinding reality of living in poverty
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Carol Taylor and Howard Williamson respond to Katriona O’Sullivan’s article on the grinding reality of living in poverty
Content: ‘Perhaps cheap toothbrushes should be free to our poorest citizens as a sensible public-health intervention.’Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Perhaps cheap toothbrushes should be free to our poorest citizens as a sensible public-health intervention.’Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesPovertyLettersLearning from lived experiences of povertyCarol TaylorandHoward Williamsonrespond toKatriona O’Sullivan’s article on the grinding reality of living in povertyTue 25 Aug 2026 12.44 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 12.55 EDTShareReading Katriona O’Sullivan’s article (Can anyone be too poor to buy a toothbrush? Yes – I know, because that was me, 19 August) reminded me of when I was a community worker at the Park Hill estate in Sheffield in the 1970s.When I (young and naive) asked the mums why they bought chips for their toddlers for lunch rather than spending the money on fresh fruit (I cringe now in embarrassment), they pointed out that a bag of chips was the price of a couple of apples and one of them filled the kids up. I began to understand, and to also see why they spent money on cigarettes. As O’Sullivan says, “a few bottles [of alcohol] can feel like an escape”.My work there gave me a lifetime of experience in a few months, which I’ve never forgotten.Carol TaylorMatlock, DerbyshireWhat an excellent piece by Katriona O’Sullivan – a very timely riposte to those who pass judgment from the comfort of their broadcasting pods. George Orwell made similar points in The Road to Wigan Pier – desperately poor people still tried (occasionally) to go to the cinema or buy ice-cream rather than spend their subsistence national assistance on tripe.It was – and is – a matter of human dignity and feeling that you are still living as a person, not as an automaton, as more fortunate people might expect you to be. Perhaps cheap toothbrushes should be free to our poorest citizens as a sensible public-health intervention.Howard WilliamsonTreforest, Rhondda Cynon TafHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Ulez has been a breath of fresh air for London | Air pollution | The Guardian
description: Letters: Sadiq Khan’s ultra-low emission zone in London is celebrated by Lorna Henderson, George Coleby and Leonard Neamtu after a study showed its health benefits for children
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Sadiq Khan’s ultra-low emission zone in London is celebrated by Lorna Henderson, George Coleby and Leonard Neamtu after a study showed its health benefits for children
Content: ‘Surely it is a human right to breathe clean air?’ writes Lorna HendersonPhotograph: PA Images/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Surely it is a human right to breathe clean air?’ writes Lorna HendersonPhotograph: PA Images/AlamyAir pollutionLettersUlez has been a breath of fresh air for LondonSadiq Khan’s ultra-low emission zone in London is celebrated byLorna Henderson, George ColebyandLeonard Neamtuafter a study showed its health benefits for childrenTue 25 Aug 2026 12.44 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 12.46 EDTShareIn light of the astonishing results achieved in lowering air pollution by the introduction of the ultra-low emission zone (Ulez) in London by Sadiq Khan (Ulez led to better lung size and function among London children, study finds, 18 August), should we now not extend this philosophy into every city in the UK to save lives?Surely it is a human right to breathe clean air? Why does Ofsted or the Department for Education not insist on air-quality monitors and give data for each school so parents are aware of the risks?Lorna HendersonNewcastle upon TyneThank you, Sadiq Khan, for showing what can be achieved when politicians ignore the loudest voices and stand up for what they believe and act in the interests of the whole population (Introducing Ulez was my hardest decision as mayor of London – but now we know its astonishing impact, 18 August). At a time when the government’s ability to do the right thing to protect the people of this country against the multiple threats posed by climate change, he has demonstrated that it is possible to truly lead in the face of self-interest and populism.George ColebyWorthing, West SussexIn the last decade, the fight for cleaner cities has become yet another culture war, and the ones suffering are the people living there every day. Sadiq Khan’s Ulez is an incredible way of addressing multiple issues such as traffic congestion, emissions and noise pollution, as well as creating space for pedestrians and cyclists.We can only hope this is taken further still and we’ll see more bicycle-friendly streets, more low-traffic neighbourhoods, more trees and improved public transport. We only have to look across the Channel and notice how Paris has transformed itself with similar measures. Let’s make it a friendly competition of who can make their capital a healthier, more livable city.Leonard NeamtuBucharest, RomaniaHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: There’s no place like a revered writer’s home | Museums | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to an editorial on preserving the homes of writers such as William Blake, Ted Hughes and William Wordsworth for the public
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to an editorial on preserving the homes of writers such as William Blake, Ted Hughes and William Wordsworth for the public
Content: William Wordsworth’s home Rydal Mount in the Lake District is open to the public.Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreenWilliam Wordsworth’s home Rydal Mount in the Lake District is open to the public.Photograph: AlamyMuseumsLettersThere’s no place like a revered writer’s homeReaders respond to an editorial on preserving the homes of writers such as William Blake, Ted Hughes and William Wordsworth for the publicTue 25 Aug 2026 12.44 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 12.55 EDTShareYour editorial (The Guardian view on writers’ houses: a museum of one’s own, 18 August) rightly laments that George Eliot has no publicly open home despite efforts to secure one. The same is true, remarkably, of William Blake, and he is at least as worthy a cause, and arguably even more influential.Poet, painter, printmaker and author of the words behind Jerusalem, Blake has no open home anywhere. Of his nine addresses,only two survive. In London, the apartment he rented is disappearing behind new development. The other, his cottage in Felpham, West Sussex, where he and his wife, Catherine, lived from 1800 to 1803 and experienced an outburst of creativity, is the only one that could ever open to the public.I am a trustee of the Blake Cottage Trust, which has spent two years saving it. In 2024 the roof was near collapse and the cottage was on Historic England’s at-risk register. Thanks to The National LotteryHeritageFund and other foundations, artisans have rebuilt the roof and removed a Victorian extension, returning the cottage to its original form. But much of the fabric still needs full conservation before the cottage is truly saved and can be opened to all, and that work costs a great deal of money.Raising it has not been easy. Even with the backing of the Heritage Fund and other trusts, we will need private philanthropy to fill a significant gap – and, as your article notes of Rydal Mount, heritage sites live or die on relevance and sustainability as much as repair.That’s why our ambition goes beyond bricks and thatch to include opening an arts and education centre near the cottage, conceived not just as somewhere to visit but as a living place of creativity and inspiration in its own right – one with year-round appeal for the local community as much as for returning visitors, and one that properly honours Catherine Blake too, who learned to read under William’s guidance and helped hand-print and colour the plates of his illuminated books.With the 2027 bicentenary of Blake’s death approaching, this is a moment when Guardian readers could make a real difference – to find out more, visitblakecottage.orgRichard ClemmowTrustee, The Blake Cottage TrustYour editorial gave a commendable overview of the important work that writers’ houses and museums have been doing to reconnect us with our literary heritage. Of course, turning a writer’s house into a museum is difficult, and not always viable. But this needn’t mean that the house cannot be saved for the nation and enjoyed by the public.The late poet laureate Ted Hughes was born in a tiny end-terrace house in Mytholmroyd, West Yorkshire. He claimed his first years there “shaped everything”. But the house is too small to accommodate tour groups (who would inevitably inconvenience the neighbours), and parking is limited to just a space or two on a residential street. So, when the house was saved 20 years ago byThe Elmet Trust, a local charity, it was opened to paying guests as a holiday cottage or writer’s retreat.This fully immersive experience goes beyond a visit to any museum. It places you in the poet’s shoes. Sleeping in the cosy attic room that Hughes shared with his older brother, or in the bedroom where he was born, inspires because it impresses upon us how humble his start in life was. Leaflets guide you to his favourite walks through the glorious Yorkshire woods and hillsides where he played as a child. His writings often described these places, or the views from his windows, and indeed the rooms in the house itself. There are no display cases, no text panels in sight. This is about lived experience.A George Eliot museum is indeed a worthy aspiration; a Ted Hughes museum scarcely less so. Yet while a museum is a fitting tribute to any great author, literary tourism at its best is about the readers and the fans as much as the writers. Interactive visitor centres such asSeamus Heaney HomePlaceare as vital a part of the future as traditional museums. Engaging with literary landscapes and walks is no less important – for health, for wellbeing, for our environment, for our imaginations. But surely nothing can beat stepping inside the world of a writer by staying in their home, for which, as Genevieve Fox reported in a Guardian travel article in 2021, the range of options is surprisingly large.Dr David RudrumSecretary, The Elmet TrustAlong with Rydal Mount and Dove Cottage, William Wordsworth also lived in two other Cumbrian houses which are open to the public. His childhood home, Wordsworth House in Cockermouth, owned by the National Trust, is currently only open for organised tours.The National Trustblames financial losses and low visitor numbers since the pandemic. Allan Bank in Grasmere, where Wordsworth lived briefly, is also owned by the National Trust, and open five days a week.But Rydal Mount was considered by Wordsworth to be his favourite home, and it’s where he lived for most of his life, until his death in 1850. I spent several years working for the Wordsworth family and curators, and the house has a fascinating history as well as a glorious location and exciting future. Wordsworth himself was only a tenant; the house was eventually bought by the family – his great-great-granddaughter Mary Henderson acquired it in 1969.Since then it’s seen the development of the five-acre gardens to plans drawn up by the poet. It has staged drama, music and poetry, co-hosted a film festival with the local cinema, and hosted weddings – including that of the poet’s great-great-great-great grandson Christopher Andrew. There was even, in the 1970s, a performance by the dance troupe Pan’s People when Miss UK contestants were filmed there.It will be exciting to see how the Wordsworth Trust, which acquired Rydal Mount in March, takes the life of the house forward. The challenge is to re-engage visitors with the life and work of the greatest of the Romantic poets, and poetry generally. The Wordsworth family initiated a successful poetry competition for Cumbrian school pupils and planned to roll this out nationwide. Perhaps that will bring a new generation to appreciate more than just Daffodils.Eileen JonesAuthor of Rydal Mount: The Story of Wordsworth’s HomeHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Celtic throw away four-goal aggregate lead to crash out of Champions League against Lask | Champions League | The Guardian
description: Callum McGregor opened the scoring in the first half to give Celtic a 4-0 aggregate playoff lead, but Lask fought back to win 5-4 after extra time
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Callum McGregor opened the scoring in the first half to give Celtic a 4-0 aggregate playoff lead, but Lask fought back to win 5-4 after extra time
Content: Samuel Adeniran of Lask celebrates scoring his team’s fifth goal against Celtic.Photograph: Christian Bruna/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSamuel Adeniran of Lask celebrates scoring his team’s fifth goal against Celtic.Photograph: Christian Bruna/Getty ImagesChampions LeagueCeltic throw away four-goal aggregate lead to crash out of Champions League against LaskPA MediaTue 25 Aug 2026 17.40 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 19.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCeltic threw away a four-goal lead in Austria as they missed out on theChampions Leaguefor the second year running. The Scottish champions looked to be cruising into the league stage when Callum McGregor put them 4-0 up on aggregate against Lask with a 21st-minute deflected strike.However, they went on to endure one of their all-time European lows with a 5-1 defeat in Linz delivering a £20m-plus blow.The Hoops had other chances in the first half but the Austrians gave themselves a lifeline when Moses Usor pounced on a loose pass from Benjamin Nygren to level on the night in the 32nd minute.The tie began to spiral out of Celtic’s control early in the second half as Robert Ljubicic and Samuel Adeniran netted from outside the box. Martin O’Neill’s side looked like they would cling on but Florian Flecker nodded home from close range in stoppage-time to spark an additional 30 minutes.Celtic had disappeared as an attacking force at half-time and Adeniran delivered the knockout blow that sends them into the Europa League.The Hoopsexited on penalties at the playoff stagelast season after failing to sign a proven striker before drawing a blank against Kairat Almaty. Fans will this year question the decision to sell Arne Engels just ahead of the first leg after they lost control in midfield in Austria.The quality of Celtic’s finishing had been the difference in Glasgow butLaskcreated chances throughout and the second leg started in similar fashion.Celtic looked to extend their lead. Mika Baur stabbed an early chance just wide and Kasper Høgh forced a couple of first-half saves from decent opportunities. McGregor opened the scoring in between those chances when he drilled a first-time shot in off a defender after Yang Hyun-jun had played a one-two with Kieran Tierney.The home side had exerted some pressure just before McGregor’s goal and they levelled following careless play from Nygren. The Austrian champions pulled a goal back three minutes after the restart when Usor outmuscled Auston Trusty and worked the ball inside for Ljubicic to drive home from 20 yards.View image in fullscreenDismayed Celtic players react to their capitulation against Lask.Photograph: Severin Aichbauer/SPP/ShutterstockCeltic endured some nervy moments before they conceded again in the 58th minute when Adeniran curled a wonderful first-time strike into the top corner from 25 yards.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCeltic were on the ropes. Several shots flew past Viljami Sinisalo’s goal before the Finn pulled off a great stop from Sascha Horvath. João Victor Tornich headed inches wide from the resulting corner.Adeniran fired off the underside of the bar and Celtic defended with four centre-backs as Liam Scales and Dane Murray came on to join Trusty and Cameron Carter-Vickers.With Luke McCowan, Reo Hatate and Sebastian Tounekti also off the bench, Carter-Vickers had to struggle on with cramp and Celtic could not hold out. Sinisalo made a great stop from a Tornich header but Flecker converted the rebound.Anthony Ralston replaced Carter-Vickers as extra-time allowed O’Neill to make a further change and Celtic appeared to stem the tide. However, Adeniran fired home from 25 yards with five minutes left after dispossessing McCowan and Celtic could not threaten after Sinisalo’s penalty save denied the striker his hat-trick.Explore more on these topicsChampions LeagueLaskCelticmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Serena Williams thrills New York crowd on US Open return with Alcaraz | US Open Tennis 2026 | The Guardian
description: Former women’s No 1 proves she’s no nostalgia act before star pairing crash out in mixed doubles quarter-finals
Author: Bryan Armen Graham
Headline: Former women’s No 1 proves she’s no nostalgia act before star pairing crash out in mixed doubles quarter-finals
Content: Carlos Alcaraz and Serena Williams enjoy competing in the mixed doubles.Photograph: Yuki Iwamura/APView image in fullscreenCarlos Alcaraz and Serena Williams enjoy competing in the mixed doubles.Photograph: Yuki Iwamura/APUS Open Tennis 2026Serena Williams thrills New York crowd on US Open return with AlcarazFormer women’s No 1 proves she’s no nostalgia act before star pairing crash out in mixed doubles quarter-finalsBryan Armen Grahamat Flushing MeadowsTue 25 Aug 2026 19.02 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSerena Williams’ US Open return lasted two matches and one afternoon Tuesday as she and Carlos Alcaraz followed a first-round win with a quarter-final defeat by Belinda Bencic and Flavio Cobolli in the headline attraction of the reimagined mixed doubles competition.Back inside Arthur Ashe Stadium 1,453 days afterthe defeat by Ajla Tomljanovicthat had appeared to end her career, Williams emerged from the tunnel at half past three to the roars of more than 10,000 spectators. As the 44-year-old American and Alcaraz warmed up in matching purple-and-black Nike kits, public-address announcer Andy Taylor rattled off her accolades one by one to a steadily rising wall of applause. Together they carried 30 grand slam singles titles, a record for a mixed-doubles team at a major.‘There was a lot of doubt and pain’: Arthur Fery on his dream Wimbledon run and the next stepRead moreThe tournament was still officially in qualifying week, but the crowds had already swelled to main-draw proportions. The scenes along the boardwalk from the Mets-Willets Point subway station to the Billie Jean King NationalTennisCenter looked like the middle weekend of the tournament. The No 7 train exhaled bursts of fans every few minutes. Vendors rolled enormous coolers through the crowd, selling cold water and canned soda. Jehovah’s Witnesses stood beside literature carts.Have you heard the good news? The Open was on a week early and Serena was back. Alcaraz, returningfrom a hiatus of his owndue to a wrist injury in the spring, wore a white sleeve and looked rusty from double-faulting on the opening point. The pair dropped three of the first four games, but won eight of the final nine games to beat the British-New Zealand pair of Lloyd Glasspool and Erin Routliffe 5-3, 4-1.“I never expected to be back on this court,” Williams said after the first match. “I never thought this would happen.”That momentum did not survive the quick turnaround, with Bencic and Cobolli ending their run 5-4 (4), 4-1. Yet Williams looked anything but a nostalgia act, flying to the net and reading points a stroke ahead. She even served the opening game of the quarter-final ahead of Alcaraz – a rarity in mixed doubles. When it was over after 55 minutes, Williams might have been second-guessing her decision to decline the singles wildcard organizers had kept open for her before giving it to Sofia Kenin.This was the bargain offered by the revamped mixed doubles championship: unprecedented star wattage, abbreviated matches and abrupt endings. Last year’s overhaul moved mixed doubles to a standalone slot before singles, cut the field to 16 and raised the top prize to $1m, favoring singles stars over the objections of doubles specialists. Early rounds use four-game sets, no-ad scoring and a 10-point decider. Only Wednesday’s final returns to six-game sets.Williams and Alcaraz were not the only star tandem caught by the format’s trapdoor. Top seeds Novak Djokovic andAryna Sabalenkalost in the opening match on Ashe to Katerina Siniakova and Henry Patten, who then fell to the married couple Elina Svitolina and Gaël Monfils.Svitolina and Monfils edged them 5-4 (6), 4-5 (3), 10-8, then kissed and embraced. Both have gone on deep singles runs here without winning the title. In Monfils’ final grand slam before retirement, they are two victories from a trophy and a seven-figure windfall when the event concludes on Wednesday night.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Happy wife, happy life,” Monfils said.The revamped event promised maximum attention for minimum wear and Williams delivered both. Her stay was fleeting, but long enough to make the US Open feel as though it had truly arrived ahead of schedule.Explore more on these topicsUS Open Tennis 2026US Open tennisSerena WilliamsCarlos AlcarazNovak DjokovicAryna SabalenkaTennisfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: De Zerbi hopes Sávio’s fresh start will help Spurs’ much-needed rebrand | Tottenham Hotspur | The Guardian
description: After an unacceptable performance against Brentford, head coach still believes they can avoid sinking feeling this season
Author: David Hytner
Headline: After an unacceptable performance against Brentford, head coach still believes they can avoid sinking feeling this season
Content: ‘Listen, I lost 3-0 in the first game in the Premier League … do you think for me it’s a problem if Savinho becomes Sávio?’ says Roberto De Zerbi.Composite: Guardian Pictures; Colorsport/Shutterstock; Tottenham Hotspur FC/Shutterstock; Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Listen, I lost 3-0 in the first game in the Premier League … do you think for me it’s a problem if Savinho becomes Sávio?’ says Roberto De Zerbi.Composite: Guardian Pictures; Colorsport/Shutterstock; Tottenham Hotspur FC/Shutterstock; Tom Jenkins/The GuardianTottenham HotspurDe Zerbi hopes Sávio’s fresh start will help Spurs’ much-needed rebrandAfter an unacceptable performance against Brentford, head coach still believes they can avoid sinking feeling this seasonDavid HytnerTue 25 Aug 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat’s in a name? Quite a bit, judging by the discussion at Roberto De Zerbi’s Tottenham press conference on Tuesday, shortly after the club hadcompleted the £75m signing of Savinhofrom Manchester City and the Brazil winger had let everybody know that he wanted to be called Sávio from now on. He will have that name on his Spurs shirt above his No 17, which he has taken over from Cristian Romero, the former captain who has moved to Atlético Madrid.The 22-year-old went by Sávio at various times before his two seasons at City but there was nonetheless speculation about the reasons for the reversion. Savinho translates roughly from the Portuguese as “little Sávio”. Was it him saying that he was now an older and more mature player?Football Daily | The Premier League soap opera is back – and Spurs are already hogging the narrativeRead moreOn the subject of theories, there is one about the fee, which could rise to £85m in add-ons. Even at £75m, it represents a record sale for City, who paid £30.8m to take Sávio from Troyes. Spurs are pushing to sign another attacker from City – Omar Marmoush, whose previous club Eintracht Frankfurt have a sell-on clause. Are Spurs paying more for Sávio in order to pay potentially less to City for Marmoush, which could reduce the liabilities to Eintracht?De Zerbi has plenty on his plate after Spurs’dismal 3-0 defeat at Brentfordon Saturday in their Premier League opener and before the Carabao Cup tie at home against Charlton on Wednesday night.“Listen, I lost 3-0 in the first game in the Premier League … do you think for me it’s a problem if Savinho becomes Sávio?” he said, turning to face his interpreter. “If Enrico [the interpreter] becomes Savinho, it’s a problem. If Savinho stays Sávio, nothing changes for me.”De Zerbi said the talks for Sávio had started three days after the end of last season. It has been a mini‑epic to get the deal over the line but well worth it, according to the Spurs manager, who rates Sávio as one of the best in the world for being able to get past his marker when one‑against‑one. The challenge for Sávio will be to improve his end product, particularly in terms of goals. He scored only seven for City in all competitions and only two in 53 Premier League appearances. Sávio is available for selection against Charlton, his paperwork having been completed in time.De Zerbi did get around to accepting that Sávio’s rebrand was part of a fresh start for the player. What is not in doubt is Spurs’ need for one after Brentford, when all the excitement around a summer of heavy spending turned to frustration; a very familiar sinking feeling.View image in fullscreenNew Tottenham signings Jan Paul van Hecke (left) and Sandro Tonali (right) after Spurs conceded their second goal during their 3-0 defeat at Brentford.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianIt is possible to explain away the shambles against Brentford, who were not only much more joined-up but appeared to want it more in the duels. De Zerbi has attempted to do so in that way beloved of managers, emphasising he is not making excuses, you understand, just stating facts.He had a completely new back four compared with his preferred unit from the end of last season; a new midfield pair, too. Up front from right to left, Mikey Moore, Richarlison and Mathys Tel were nobody’s idea of a trio to drive the push for Champions League football. De Zerbi was missing a host of players because of fitness issues, including Pedro Porro, Micky van de Ven, Mateus Fernandes and Dominic Solanke. Some of the issues can be traced to the slog of a pre-season tour to New Zealand and Australia, which De Zerbi continues to reference in irritated tones.Thesefactsdo not really wash. The performance against Brentford was unacceptable. There is the sense that it will work out for Spurs, mainly because they have De Zerbi and a collection of Premier League‑ready new signings. They have certainly put themselves under pressure for the visit of Charlton. A relevant statistic: Spurs have won one domestic home game in 2026 – against Everton on the final day of last season which enabled them to avoid relegation.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDe Zerbi made the point that he and the squad had “started the project right now, not last season”. Which was when he was parachuted in with seven games to go; he picked up 11 points to dodge the unthinkable. “Last season, we fought to stay up,” he said. The inference was that it would take rather more to become a proper team.On the other hand, the experiences of the previous campaign do offer reassurance. “Maybe last season was a tougher challenge to stay up than this season,” De Zerbi said. “I said to the players: last season, in a worse situation, we showed character, we showed balls. We showed pride and quality. Now we have to stay calm and to analyse better the situation – not to have an emotional reaction. We have to be intelligent.”What De Zerbi craves is consistency, which he defined as being five wins in a row. It seems a distant goal after Brentford but De Zerbi has faith. What it will take is a change to the collective mentality. “We have to get used to winning games and games and games – we have to change habits from the last two seasons,” he said.“For me, the Carabao Cup is like the Premier League. We are not in the condition to make differences [between the competitions]. We have to play well and get used to winning – and winning matches, not a match. We have to change the mood. And we can.”De Zerbi said that Porro and Van de Ven will return as substitutes against Charlton and Solanke may start. James Maddison is out for two weeks with a shoulder injury suffered against Brentford. De Zerbi has a decision to make on Sávio. Victory is non-negotiable.Explore more on these topicsTottenham HotspurRoberto De ZerbifeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Vuelta a España: Tadej Pogacar punishes peloton with mighty solo win on stage four | Vuelta a España | The Guardian
description: Tadej Pogacar put almost three minutes into the entire Vuelta a España field with a dominant victory on stage four to Andorra la Vella
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Tadej Pogacar put almost three minutes into the entire Vuelta a España field with a dominant victory on stage four to Andorra la Vella
Content: Tadej Pogacar after breaking clear in Andorra during stage four of the Vuelta.Photograph: Tim de Waele/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTadej Pogacar after breaking clear in Andorra during stage four of the Vuelta.Photograph: Tim de Waele/Getty ImagesVuelta a EspañaVuelta a España: Tadej Pogacar punishes peloton with mighty solo win on stage fourSlovenian powers to victory by more than three minutesLeader breaks rivals on brutal climb at halfway pointAgenciesTue 25 Aug 2026 12.03 EDTFirst published on Tue 25 Aug 2026 11.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTadej Pogacar arrived in red, lit the fuse on the climbs and turned stage four of theVuelta a España⁠into a private exhibition on Tuesday, powering away with almost 50km remaining to win alone in Andorra la Vella.The Slovenian, bidding to ⁠complete his Grand ⁠Tour collection by ​claiming the Vuelta for the first time, attacked on the road to the second climb and quickly reduced a high-altitude battle into ⁠a one-man procession.He began the final ascent with a lead of three minutes and 12 seconds and cruised over the last mountain pass before ⁠finishing in 2hr 40min 35sec. Jarno Widar won the sprint for second, 2min 39sec off the pace, with Felix ​Gall third.Seven years after his only previous ‌appearance in the Spanish ‌race, Pogacar underlined why he started as the overwhelming favourite having recently claimed afifth Tour de France title.The UAE Team Emirates rider now leads the general classification by 3min 21sec over compatriot Primoz Roglic of Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, with Spain’s Enric Mas of Movistar 11 seconds further back.Pogacar began patiently, sitting in the third peloton for much of the opening climb, around 32sec behind the group setting the pace. The ‌early attackers were reeled in on the descent from the first mountain pass, where Lorenzo Fortunato, of XDS Astana, crossed the summit of the ​Port d’Envalira first to collect maximum mountain points.View image in fullscreenThe peloton climbing to the Port d’Envalira earlier in stage four.Photograph: Tim de Waele/Getty ImagesThen came the coup de grace.With 50km to race, Pogacar surged clear uphill in familiar style. By the time he crossed the summit of the Collada de Beixalis, he had a lead of 1min 30sec over a chasing group including Mas, Roglic, Gall, ⁠Richard Carapaz and Oscar Onley.It was shaping up as Pogacar’s longest solo attack for stage victory ​in a Grand Tour. He ​had already produced long-range masterpieces this ​year at the Tour de France, where he attacked on the Col ​du Tourmalet and ‌rode the final 43km ​alone, and in ​previous Grand Tours including the 2019 Vuelta and the 2024 Giro d’Italia.On Tuesday, his pace was brutal and every climb saw the gap grow. With Embret Svestad-Bardseng pulling the chasing group, Pogacar stretched his advantage to nearly three minutes on the road to the later climbs.View image in fullscreenTadej Pogacar celebrates on the podium in Andorra la Vella.Photograph: Alexander Hassenstein/Getty Images“It’s super good because now I can be calm and confident for the next days,” said Pogacar. “We just keep going day by day and focus on each day after this, because it will be a little bit less stressful for sure.“[I didn’t] want to be also isolated against all the GC riders because they would all play against me – I tried with an attack on the climb and I just hoped that I could survive until the finish line. I saw that I could open the gap and I did it and it was pretty tough but a beautiful day out there.”Explore more on these topicsVuelta a EspañaCyclingTadej PogacarnewsShareReuse this content

title: Victor Torp seals Coventry’s Carabao Cup win at Plymouth in six-goal thriller | Carabao Cup | The Guardian
description: Second-half goals from Ephron Mason-Clark and Victor Torp dashed Plymouth’s comeback bid to give Coventry a 4-2 win in the Carabao Cup
Author: Ben Fisher
Headline: Second-half goals from Ephron Mason-Clark and Victor Torp dashed Plymouth’s comeback bid to give Coventry a 4-2 win in the Carabao Cup
Content: Victor Torp slots home Coventry’s fourth goal from the penalty spot.Photograph: Kieran McManus/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenVictor Torp slots home Coventry’s fourth goal from the penalty spot.Photograph: Kieran McManus/ShutterstockCarabao CupVictor Torp seals Coventry’s Carabao Cup win at Plymouth in six-goal thrillerBen Fisherat Home ParkTue 25 Aug 2026 16.59 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 20.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA midweek jaunt to Devon always had the makings of a tricky trip for a Coventry team focused on Premier League survival. Such feelings quickly evaporated when Frank Lampard’s side raced into a two-goal lead with just four minutes and six seconds on the clock, Taiwo Awoniyi opening his account for his new club before Jack Rudoni doubled Coventry’s advantage. But, ultimately, Coventry were made to toil before chalking up a welcome first victory of the season.Plymouth have form for a cup upset and another was brewing when Xavier Amaechi pulled Tom Cleverley’s side level nine minutes into the second half. Coventry, to their credit, roused once more, the substitute Ephron Mason-Clark regaining the lead before Victor Torp sealed progress to theCarabao Cupthird round from the penalty spot. “You’ve got to enjoy a win, always,” Lampard said. “A win is a big deal because it’s a nice feeling to take back on the bus for four hours.”Delap heads to Forest for £50m as Chelsea open talks to sell Jackson to Aston VillaRead moreThe 2,244 Coventry supporters, many of whom made the 444-mile round trip, cycled through the catalogue of songs after crisp finishes by Awoniyi and Rudoni. Then Lampard obliged when they craved a wave from a manager who led them back to the top flight after 25 years away. But the game did not turn into the non-event most would have envisaged. “It’s very easy to go: ‘Why don’t you just go 2-0 up and then beat Plymouth 5-0, 6-0?’” Lampard said. “I’ve played in these games many times with different teams and they can become awkward, especially when the flow of the game goes against you: the crowd turns, emotions catch up and all of a sudden the game feels very different. I thought we dealt OK with that, in the end.”Plymouth were suddenly liberated at 2-0 down. The Danish centre-back Mathias Ross sent a header wide from a free-kick and a couple of minutes later Oliver Irow read Harvey White’s flighted pass and the Tottenham loanee, 24 hours after signing, drove inside Joel Latibeaudiere and drilled past the Coventry goalkeeper Dan Bentley, another debutant. From there, aside from Awoniyi heading wide unmarked, Coventry had to withstand Plymouth pressure. After fumbling White’s shot from distance, Bentley diverted Will Evans’s rebound on to his left post.Cleverley knew the value of recording an upset, Lampard the damage of defeat. It must have crossed his mind when Amaechi levelled on 54 minutes. Amaechi swarmed Liam Kitching and pinched the ball after the Coventry defender got in a tangle and fired in. Plymouth introduced the homegrown academy graduates Tegan Finn and Caleb Roberts, joining the 17-year-old full-back Joe Mwaro, this his full debut, on the pitch. “I couldn’t be happier with the reaction and the quality we showed to make sure it was still a competitive game,” Cleverley said.View image in fullscreenJack Rudoni doubles Coventry’s lead from close range in the fifth minute.Photograph: Dan Mullan/Getty ImagesMason-Clark arrived for his first appearance of the season after a hamstring issue and added the fifth goal of an entertaining game. It was a galling goal from a Plymouth perspective. Tatsuhiro Sakamoto’s cross from the right caused problems, Mason-Clark at first failing to divert the ball goalwards. But Torp was alert to the ball dropping at the back post and squared to provide Mason-Clark the simplest of finishes, the forward poking in from inside the six-yard box.Lampard made a triple sub, Sidiki Cherif replacing Awoniyi for his debut, while Josh Eccles and Brandon Thomas-Asante also entered. Joe Edwards, the Plymouth midfielder, arrived from the bench but his first notable action was to inadvertently swipe at Thomas-Asante in the box when trying to clear the leftovers of a Coventry corner, giving the referee, Elliott Swallow, no choice but to award a penalty. Torp capped the scoring, thrashing the spot-kick into the top corner.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor Cleverley, this also represented a touchline duel with a friend and a former England teammate and he had spoken on the eve of the game of wanting English coaches like Lampard and Michael Carrick, another former teammate, to succeed. “If you do well in it, you’re great for a moment, if you don’t do so well, then you’re not,” Lampard said after. “If you have the English tag, I do think we’ve got a bit of a bracket of saying: ‘There’s another one [struggling].’ Hopefully we’re not idiots and we can show that over a period of time and do our jobs well.”Explore more on these topicsCarabao CupPlymouth ArgyleCoventry Citymatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Bruno Fernandes and Khadija Shaw land PFA Player of the Year awards | PFA Player of the Year awards | The Guardian
description: Manchester United’s Bruno Fernandes, Manchester City’s Nico O’Reilly and Khadija Shaw, and Arsenal’s Olivia Smith win big at the PFA awards
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Manchester United’s Bruno Fernandes, Manchester City’s Nico O’Reilly and Khadija Shaw, and Arsenal’s Olivia Smith win big at the PFA awards
Content: Bruno Fernandes (left) and Khadija Shaw with their PFA player of the year awards.Composite: Peter Byrne/PA; Shane Anthony Sinclair/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBruno Fernandes (left) and Khadija Shaw with their PFA player of the year awards.Composite: Peter Byrne/PA; Shane Anthony Sinclair/Getty ImagesPFA Player of the Year awardsBruno Fernandes and Khadija Shaw land PFA Player of the Year awardsFellow players pick Manchester United and Manchester City starsNico O’Reilly and Olivia Smith collect young players’ honoursPA MediaTue 25 Aug 2026 17.50 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 17.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleManchester United’s captain Bruno Fernandes has been crowned Professional Footballers’ Association Player of the Year as Manchester City’s Khadija Shaw won the women’s award for the second time.Playmaker Fernandes broke the record for Premier League assists during an outstanding 2025-26 campaign, setting up 21 goals as he surpassed Thierry Henry and Kevin De Bruyne.Celtic throw away four-goal lead to crash out of Champions League against LASKRead moreThe 31-year-old also scored nine times as United overcome a shaky first half of the campaign to finish third in the Premier League under Michael Carrick to earn a Champions League return.Fernandes was pleased to have been voted the winner by his fellow professionals. He said: “It is obviously a very proud moment. They are the ones you go on the pitch against and it’s probably not easy to vote for someone you play against, so it is a very good moment.”The Portugal international is the club’s first winner since Wayne Rooney took home the trophy in 2009-10, and adds to his Football Writers’ Association Footballer of the Year award from May.Shaw, who was also recognised by the FWA, scooped the PFA Women’s Player of the Year award for the second time. The 29-year-old claimed the trophy in 2023-24 and won it again having scored 21 goals on the way to a third consecutive Golden Boot and her maiden Women’s Super League title.Arsenal’s Olivia Smith picked up the women’s PFA Young Player of the Year title for the second campaign running, having won the 2025 crown for her exploits at Liverpool before continuing her form in the capital.Manchester City’s Nico O’Reilly was named men’s PFA Young Player of the Year following an outstanding campaign that ended with the versatile talent helping England to win World Cup bronze. The 21-year-old was part of the PFA Premier League Team of the Year along with City teammates Erling Haaland, Rayan Cherki and Antoine Semenyo.O’Reilly said: “I had a great season. I’m very proud of the season I had. I won two trophies with my club and managed to play at the World Cup with my country. I’m over the moon how it turned out.”Champions Arsenal had five representatives in David Raya, Gabriel, William Saliba, Jurriën Timber and Declan Rice, with Player of the Year Fernandes of United and Brentford’s Igor Thiago completing the team.The PFA WSL Team of the Year featured three players from triumphant City, with Shaw joined by teammates Kerstin Casparij and Yui Hasegawa.Mariona Caldentey, last year’s PFA Women’s Player of the Year, was joined in the XI by fellow Arsenal players Emily Fox and Alessia Russo. Tottenham defender Toko Koga and Manchester United’s Jess Park were also included in the team, as were the Chelsea trio of Hannah Hampton, Ellie Carpenter and Lauren James.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHayden Hackney, now of Everton, was named Championship PFA Players’ Player of the Year for his performances for defeated play-off finalists Middlesbrough.Dom Ballard, who scored a jaw-dropping effort for new club Bristol City at the weekend, collected the League One award for a goal-laden season at Leyton Orient.Swindon striker Aaron Drinan’s performances saw him collect the League Two award, while Lily Crosthwaite of Birmingham took the WSL2 player accolade.Sir Kenny Dalglish and Karen Carney received the PFA merit awards in recognition of their contribution to football. Dalglish enjoyed a success-laden career as a player with Celtic and Liverpool, and is Scotland’s most capped performer having represented his country on 102 occasions. The 75-year-old, who confirmed in June he was undergoing treatment for cancer, went on to enjoy a successful managerial career, leading Liverpool to three league titles before masterminding Blackburn’s Premier League triumph.Carney played 144 times for England, including being part of the Lionesses squad which finished third at the 2015 World Cup. Having come through the ranks at Birmingham, Carney won the quadruple with Arsenal in 2007 as well as a league and FA Cup double with Chelsea in 2018.Explore more on these topicsPFA Player of the Year awardsManchester UnitedManchester City WomenWomen's footballnewsShareReuse this content

title: Root reads from same old script in latest episode of England’s off-field soap opera | England cricket team | The Guardian
description: Captain followed trend of discussing nightclub incidents rather than cricket before the second Test against Pakistan
Author: Simon Burnton
Headline: Captain followed trend of discussing nightclub incidents rather than cricket before the second Test against Pakistan
Content: Joe Root said he led England through ‘conversations about what is expected from this group of players, what it means to play for England’.Photograph: Stu Forster/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJoe Root said he led England through ‘conversations about what is expected from this group of players, what it means to play for England’.Photograph: Stu Forster/Getty ImagesEngland cricket teamAnalysisRoot reads from same old script in latest episode of England’s off-field soap operaSimon BurntonCaptain followed trend of discussing nightclub incidents rather than cricket before the second Test against PakistanTue 25 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTShareEngland won the first game of their last Test series, againstNew Zealand at Lord’s, but between that match and the second Ben Stokes and Gus Atkinson were involved in aheadline-grabbing incidentat a London nightclub. “I’m angry, frustrated at having to sit here and talk through this,” Rob Key said a couple of days later.“I feel disappointed that I’m here talking about this because there’s so much we’ve tried to do, so much we’ve tried to learn from, and I believe that as a team, the way they’ve carried themselves in the lead‑up to last week’s game, the way they played that Test match – to then be now talking about this, is just incredibly frustrating.”England captain Joe Root ‘hacked off’ and ‘disappointed’ at Carse incidentRead moreEngland won the first game of this Test series, againstPakistan at Headingley, but between that match and the second Brydon Carse was involved in aheadline‑grabbing incidentat a Derby nightclub. “If I’m being brutally honest, I’m really hacked off. I’m really disappointed that after last week’s performance we’re sat here talking about something not related to it at all,” Joe Root said a couple of days later.“I look at all of the great things we did in that game – I thought the bowlers were outstanding, with the bat there were a couple of times we found ourselves under pressure and we worked our way through it. Every time we sit here and we’re talking about something off the field it’s really frustrating.”Two months and four days separated the two press conferences, a period in which a great deal changed for this team – the New Zealand series was lost, as was a coach and a captain – but also, it seems, nothing at all. So the frustration expressed by both Key and Root is also being felt, for different reasons, by those who have had to listen to them. Graham Gooch once famously asked Ian Botham, as it happens after a Test against Pakistan at Lord’s, where the teams will be reunited on Thursday: “Who writes your scripts?” Whoever is scripting the latest series of the soap opera needs to do a bit less recycling and get some fresh ideas.Root suggests that this is now guaranteed, given that since the squad reassembled in London he has led them through “conversations about what is expected from this group of players, what it means to play for England, what it takes to play for England … a very robust discussion about where we currently sit”. The players now know the standards of behaviour expected from them on and off the field. “I think there’s real clarity there, and now the guys can concentrate on focusing on what is important this week, and making sure we prepare properly and diligently for all the challenges that this surface and Pakistan are going to provide.”It is not just bewildering but damning that after Harry Brook’s run‑in with a bouncer in Wellington, after the first Ashes Test was followed by a squad‑break‑cum-stag-do in the Queensland beach resort of Noosa, after the then Test head coach Brendon McCullum promised to “use a firm grip to ensure that we are not making those same mistakes again”, and after Stokes’s and Atkinson’s night at Chelsea’s Rex Rooms, this was a job that still needed doing.View image in fullscreenJoe Root said of the Brydon Carse incident: ‘I don’t want to get caught up in digging up what’s happened. My concern is what happens moving from this point.’Photograph: Ben Whitley/PAKey, managing director of the England men’s side, was all smiles in the Lord’s sunshine as he watched the team train on Tuesday, apparently not feeling the sense of profound personal humiliation that the need for Root to lead a “robust discussion” might reasonably have provoked. “I don’t think it has to be rocket science,” Root said of a task that a succession of people older and more experienced than him have evidently bungled, if they attempted it at all. “It’s being clear what your responsibilities are as a player and then delivering on that time and time again.”More than 15 years after his Test debut, and with Stephen Fleming about to become the eighth interim or permanent coach under whom he has played, Root has certainly been through periods when the team had that clarity. But he would not be drawn on when, and under whom, it had been lost. “I don’t want to get caught up in digging up what’s happened before. My concern is what happens moving from this point,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“It’s not something you want to forget about in a week’s time, or six months’ time. This is something that we want to live and breathe every day and that’s what my focus is on. I don’t think it’s going to be helpful talking about what happened in that last period.”Root used the word “proud” a dozen times during his remarks to the press, and it is an emotion everyone associated with this team will want to enjoy with greater regularity. “I don’t know how long I’m going to play Test cricket for,” he said.“It sounds a bit of a cliche, but you want to leave the dressing room in a better place than where you found it. Well, this is the opportunity that lies ahead and we have to start acting on that straight away.”Explore more on these topicsEngland cricket teamJoe RootEngland v Pakistan 2026CricketanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Prime minister Andy Burnham ‘heartbroken’ after death of rugby league legend Billy Boston | Wigan Warriors | The Guardian
description: Sir Billy Boston, the Wigan Warriors legend who last year became the first rugby league player to be awarded a knighthood, has died at the age of 92
Author: Aaron Bower
Headline: Sir Billy Boston, the Wigan Warriors legend who last year became the first rugby league player to be awarded a knighthood, has died at the age of 92
Content: Billy Boston after he received his knighthood from King Charles in June 2025.Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAView image in fullscreenBilly Boston after he received his knighthood from King Charles in June 2025.Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAWigan WarriorsPrime minister Andy Burnham ‘heartbroken’ after death of rugby league legend Billy BostonBoston was one of the finest players in the sport’s historyWigan plan series of tributes in Thursday’s Hull KR clashAaron BowerTue 25 Aug 2026 11.26 EDTFirst published on Tue 25 Aug 2026 05.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy ­Burnham says he is “heart­broken” by the death of Sir Billy ­Boston after the prime minister led tri­butes to the rugby league icon.Boston died on Tuesday at the age of 92. He was one of the sport’s all‑time great players, scoring almost 500 tries during an illustrious career forWigan Warriorsand Great Britain, and last year became the first man in rugby league history to be knighted for his services to the game.His death comes just four days after the funeral of his wife of more than 70 years, Lady Joan Boston, who died last month. Burnham, a lifelong rugby league supporter who also served as president of the Rugby Football League, described Boston as a “giant of a man in every way”.The prime minister wrote: “Heartbroken to hear my friend Sir Billy Boston has died. Billy was one of the greatest rugby league players of all time but also one of the kindest and most down-to-earth people you could ever wish to meet.“He always had time for people and gave so much back to his adopted home, Wigan. I will miss him greatly and am thinking today of Billy’s ­family, still grieving the recent loss of his beloved wife Joan. A giant of a man in every way. Thank you, Billy, and rest in peace.”Boston joined Wigan in 1953 after starting his rugby career in his native Wales. He went on to score 478 tries in 488 games for the club, winning a plethora of honours for club and country. Only one man, the Warring­ton winger Brian Bevan, has more tries in the history of the sport than Boston.Less than a year after leaving Wales to begin a career in league, Boston became the first non-white player to be selected for Great Britain. He scored 36 tries in 18 games on that tour to Australia and New Zealand in 1954, and was part of the Lions’ World Cup-winning squad of 1960.View image in fullscreenBilly Boston scored 478 tries in 488 games for Wigan.Photograph: PABoston was awarded an MBE in 1996 but, last year, he became the first rugby league player to be knighted for services to the sport. That accolade was met with emotional ­celebrations in Wigan, the town in which he remained after retirement and where one of three statues – alongside those at Wembley and Cardiff – stands ­fea­turing Boston, which underlines his life and career.The Warriors are planning for an emotional occasion on Thursday evening when they host Hull KR in Super League, with a series of ­tributes planned to celebrate Boston’s life. Their head coach, Matt Peet, paid an emotional tribute on Tuesday while conducting his pre-match press duties. “It’s like he was on a different planet, really,” Peet said of Boston’s career.“I wish I could see more of him. I’ve seen bits of footage, but I think it’s more the legend when people talk about him in terms of the ­stories and players that played against him, ­players that played with him. It’s going to be a real tribute night on Thursday.Obviously, people are very upset and rightly so, but you’ve got to celebrate a life well lived. Everything that Billy represented and stood for.We have a responsibility to uphold the whole history of the club when you work at a club like this, but I think Billy’s top of the tree in terms of standing in the club’s history.”Kris Radlinski, the Wigan chief executive, said: “Today we mourn one of our greatest ever Warriors and rugby league’s first knight. Time moves on, as it must, but some names endure. Billy Boston will always be one of them. His place in the history of Wigan, and in the history of rugby league, is secure for ever.“I visited him on Sunday ­morning with Mandy [Johnston, Wigan’s administrator], held his hand and told him we loved him. Rest in peace, Billy. My friend, our Warrior and a true Wigan legend.”Eamonn McManus, the chair of Wigan’s biggest rivals, St Helens, described Boston as a “giant amongst giants”, said: “Sir Billy Boston was more than an all-time great of the sport of rugby league. His name both symbolised and transcended it. He was one of the greats for both Wigan and Great Britain in the golden era of our sport in the 1950s and 60s. He was a giant amongst giants.“He led and epitomised our sport’s and our communities’ ­pioneering example in breaking down racial ­barriers in this country and he should be remembered always for that. Although deeply saddened by his passing we should in equal measure celebrate his unparalleled contribution to our sport and to our society.”Explore more on these topicsWigan WarriorsRugby leaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: Xavi hopes time at the ‘university of football’ will end with Dutch success | Netherlands | The Guardian
description: Barcelona legend wants to emulate Johan Cruyff’s total football philosophy after taking over as the Netherlands head coach
Author: Arthur Renard
Headline: Barcelona legend wants to emulate Johan Cruyff’s total football philosophy after taking over as the Netherlands head coach
Content: Xavi Hernández began his playing career at the Barcelona academy, whose fundamentals are rooted in Dutch football.Photograph: EYE4images/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenXavi Hernández began his playing career at the Barcelona academy, whose fundamentals are rooted in Dutch football.Photograph: EYE4images/NurPhoto/ShutterstockNetherlandsXavi hopes time at the ‘university of football’ will end with Dutch successBarcelona legend wants to emulate Johan Cruyff’s total football philosophy after taking over as the Netherlands head coachArthur Renardin ZeistTue 25 Aug 2026 15.58 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“My feeling today is that I’m going to the university of football.” Those were Xavi Hernández’s opening words at his presentation asthe Netherlands coachon Tuesday. “I learned a lot from this university of football during my career as a player and as a coach. I have many connections with this country.”Those connections date back to when Xavi was drafted as a youngster into La Masia, the famed Barcelona academy whose fundamentals are rooted in Dutch total football, inspired by Rinus Michels and Johan Cruyff. Xavi’s first-team debut came under Louis van Gaal, and he spent many years under Frank Rijkaard before becoming one of the main pillars of the dream team under Pep Guardiola, who was hugely inspired by Cruyff.Xavi Hernández appointed head coach of the Netherlands on four-year contractRead moreXavi opened a Cruyff court – a multifunctional sport space for children – with Cruyff in his home town of Terrassa in 2014, and on Tuesday shared special memories of his time with Cruyff, who died in 2016. “With Johan in the last period of his life I had some meetings,” he said. “And he was always positive. Even when he was sick, he was positive. This is what I learned: always smiling. This is what I want to show here to the players. My first goal is to help them, and then enjoy the process. And we will be in a process to win.”Xavi says he wants to “dominate the game, to take the initiative with the ball and at the same time our goal is to show everybody a team with passion, with desire and ambition. And this is very important for me as a coach.”In theNetherlands, there has always been a strong emphasis on attacking football, which is why Xavi fitted the bill. The Catalan was asked whether he would use five defenders, as Van Gaal and Ronald Koeman did at times in recent years. “That this is not my idea,” he said. “We want to play in another system [like] 4-3-3, 4-2-3-1, 3-4-3. In those systems we can dominate the game more.”Xavi said he had spoken to Frenkie de Jong – whom he coached at Barcelona – and Virgil van Dijk. He added that he would speak again to Van Dijk, the captain, in the near future to hear his ambitions with the team.The 46-year-old was also clear he is willing to select players from the Saudi Pro League, something more relevant after Tijjani Reijnders moved from Manchester City to Al-Qadsiah last week. Two years ago, Koeman was clear when Steven Bergwijn moved to Al-Ittihad that the forward would no longer be selected because the league did not match the level he expected from his players.View image in fullscreenXavi Hernández said he wants to play attacking systems with the Netherlands to ‘dominate the game more’.Photograph: Stefan Koops/DeFodi Images/Shutterstock“It’s a good league as well,” Xavi said. “Maybe we choose some players from Saudi, from Eredivisie, Premier League, La Liga. I don’t care about the leagues, I care about the performances and the players.”Nigel de Jong, the director of elite football at the Dutch football federation (KNVB), had earlier been open about the process that led to Xavi’s appointment. He said he had first tested the waters with Guardiola, who indicated he did not want to take a job in the near future, before holding two meetings with Arne Slot, who eventually chose to remain a club coach.De Jong then invited Xavi to Amsterdam for a meeting also attended by Clarence Seedorf, a member of the KNVB’s supervisory board. The following day De Jong and Seedorf spoke at length with Michael Reiziger, the Netherlands’ under-21s coach, who played alongside Xavi at Barcelona for several years.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThey were considering promoting Reiziger in a way similar to Luis de la Fuente’s journey with Spain, his knowledge of the country’s upcoming talents regarded as a major plus. When the meeting with Reiziger became known in the Dutch media, there was an assumption the former full-back would become the national team coach. But then, on 12 August, the KNVB announced Xavi, a decision that seemingly came out of the blue.Xavi said drily that he was fine with the process. “Well, it’s not a bad position, after Guardiola and after Slot, no? At least you are at the podium. I don’t care if I’m the third [choice] or I’m the 10th. It’s a big honour to be here. He [De Jong] explained to me, very honestly: ‘We need your philosophy, we need to change with ambition, with passion.’ And we will work in this way.”First up for Xavi is a Nations League game against Germany in Amsterdam on 24 September, when he will face Jürgen Klopp, who is also starting a new job. “I feel excited, I feel motivated,” Xavi said, “because we are playing against Germany, one of the best teams in Europe, one of the best coaches in recent years.”Xavi, speaking in front of his staff, including Ruud van Nistelrooy, wants his team to adopt the Dutch style he saw as a young boy. “I remember when I was a kid, watching the Netherlands and watching good football,” he said, “and this is my way, this is my target.”Explore more on these topicsNetherlandsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: WSL academy teams to play in third tier after FA approves controversial plan | Women's football | The Guardian
description: Four Women’s Super League academy sides will play in tier three of the pyramid from next season
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Four Women’s Super League academy sides will play in tier three of the pyramid from next season
Content: Wolves celebrate promotion to the second tier after winning their FA Women's National League playoff in May.Photograph: Jan Kruger/The FA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWolves celebrate promotion to the second tier after winning their FA Women's National League playoff in May.Photograph: Jan Kruger/The FA/Getty ImagesWomen's footballWSL academy teams to play in third tier after FA approves controversial planFour WSL academy teams will play in WNL from 2027-28FA says move will raise standards and help young playersGuardian sportTue 25 Aug 2026 07.07 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFour Women’s Super League ­academy sides will play in the third tier of the ­pyramid from the ­2027-28 ­season afterthe ­controversial ­proposalwas approved by the ­Football ­Association’s board.The change forms part of what the FA described as a package of reforms to the Women’s National League “designed to strengthen the women’s football pyramid, raise standards across the league, and improve the development pathway for young players”.Data showed that young English players were getting significantly fewer competitive ­minutes than their counterparts across Europe’s leading leagues, the FA said.Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.WNL clubs will receive central funding for the first time and changes to the loan market will encourage clubs from the top two divisions to loan players to clubs in the third and fourth tiers.The WSL academy teams will not be eligible for promotion and will be chosen against criteria to be ­developed in the coming months, the FA said. With the third tier split into two geographical regions, it is expected that two academies will be placed in the northern division and two in the southern.Sue Day, director of women’s ­football at the FA, said:“For the game to continue moving forward, the FA Women’s National League must evolve alongside the professional game, and we need to create more opportunities for talented young English players to develop in senior football.”Explore more on these topicsWomen's footballWomen's Super LeaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Starting to wind me up’: Itauma rebuffs Hrgovic before world heavyweight title fight | Boxing | The Guardian
description: Moses Itauma has hit back at Filip Hrgovic’s taunt that he is a ‘delusional kid’ as the two men prepare to fight for the IBF world heavyweight title at the O2 Arena
Author: Donald McRae
Headline: Moses Itauma has hit back at Filip Hrgovic’s taunt that he is a ‘delusional kid’ as the two men prepare to fight for the IBF world heavyweight title at the O2 Arena
Content: Moses Itauma accused Filip Hrgovic of being a ‘talker’ before their fight at the O2 on Saturday.Photograph: James Fearn/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMoses Itauma accused Filip Hrgovic of being a ‘talker’ before their fight at the O2 on Saturday.Photograph: James Fearn/Getty ImagesBoxing‘Starting to wind me up’: Itauma rebuffs Hrgovic before world heavyweight title fightItauma can become second-youngest champion after Mike TysonHrgovic claims title victory for opponent would ‘ruin his soul’Donald McRaeTue 25 Aug 2026 14.18 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMoses Itauma has hit back at Filip Hrgovic’s taunt that he is a “delusional kid” and admitted that his Croatian rival is starting to annoy him as the two men prepare to fight for the IBF world heavyweight title on Saturday night at the O2 Arena in London.“I tell myself there’s nothing that this Hrgovic guy can do to get in my head but he’s starting to wind me up,” Itauma said on Tuesday evening. “In an interview earlier, apparently he said I wake up and I just hug trees. He’s really starting to annoy me.‘Not braggadocious, not swaggerdocious’: Moses Itauma on why he lets his fists do the talkingRead more“In my mind if somebody’s trying to get one up on you, or trying to get in your head, it’s because they’re not confident in themselves. Obviously Hrgovic is a talker. Before fights, he’s always said certain things – like he did to [Daniel] Dubois when he said he sees big muscles but not big balls. Then you see Dubois, in his mind, is raging. So Hrgovic has always been a talker. It’s just because English ain’t his first language that people don’t pay attention.”If Itauma beats Hrgovic, as expected, he will become thesecond-youngest world heavyweight championin history. Only Mike Tyson won the title at a younger age and Hrgovic said of the 21-year-old Itauma: “He’s a kid. He’s inexperienced. So, for him, it would be best to lose this fight because it’s going to ruin him, winning the world title. He’s already in the clouds. He’s already delusional. And it can ruin someone who’s not ready for that kind of fame, that kind of money.“It can ruin your soul, it can make you lose yourself and we’ve seen a lot of superstars and famous people who have lost themselves. They’re just lost in that crazy world of fame and money. He’s not ready for that. I think, for him, it would be best to lose this fight, to save his soul. Because what does it mean to achieve everything if you lose your soul and you lose yourself?”Itauma conceded that there is a semblance of truth in Hrgovic’s words: “Although it’s been annoying me, I hear that because I already know the level of success I’ve achieved and how I’m coping. I’ve always said I never wanted to be at Anthony Joshua or Tyson Fury level because I know how annoyed I get trying to be a normal person. Now I can’t imagine being at a level of Tyson Fury or Anthony Joshua. But, at the same time, if I’m going down this path, I don’t have a choice.”Asked if Hrgovic has a point that winning a world title at such a young age would be bad for his “soul”, Itauma replied: “I wouldn’t say he has a point but if I win this fight it might not be good for my soul. I can hear that. But that’s not the reason why I’m just gonna go in there and not win – for the sake of my soul. That’s not a good idea.”Pressed to explain why Itauma is “delusional”, Hrgovic said: “He went from youth level to professional, had a few fights and became a star. Everyone is clapping him on his back – [saying] you’re the best, you’re the next Muhammad Ali. You’re the new Mike Tyson. He’s just not, in reality. I’m very grateful for all the hard things I went through. It makes you a different person.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe 34-year-old Hrgovic, who has lost just once in a professional career stretching across nine years, said: “I’m in a much different position because of that experience, and the ups and downs in my life. I’m like a rock. Stable. Nothing can move me. I don’t care about fame. I don’t care about money. I don’t care about what people think. But we’ll see on Saturday.”Explore more on these topicsBoxingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Five more arrested over crash that killed seven people including two police officers | UK news | The Guardian
description: A total of 17 people have now been arrested over Saturday’s crash in which car drove wrong way along dual carriageway
Author: Raphael Boyd
Headline: A total of 17 people have now been arrested over Saturday’s crash in which car drove wrong way along dual carriageway
Content: A father and daughter pay their respects as floral tributes are left at Cleveland police central headquarters memorial garden in Hemlington.Photograph: Ian Forsyth/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA father and daughter pay their respects as floral tributes are left at Cleveland police central headquarters memorial garden in Hemlington.Photograph: Ian Forsyth/Getty ImagesUK newsFive more arrested over crash that killed seven people including two police officersA total of 17 people have now been arrested over Saturday’s crash in which car drove wrong way along dual carriagewayRaphael BoydTue 25 Aug 2026 09.20 EDTFirst published on Tue 25 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFive more people have been arrested by detectives investigating a crash that killed seven people, including two police officers.PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, were killed on Saturday when a Volkswagen Passat, which had been pursued by police, was driven the wrong way down the A66 near Middlesbrough and hit their marked armed response vehicle.All five occupants of the pursued car – Cole Robert Worthy, 17; Theo Rae, 17; Makai Saddington, 18; Michael Robert Cahill, 23; and Jacob Matusiak, 23 – were declared dead at the scene.Police have said the group had links to “serious and organised criminal activity” and that four of the five had a total of 37 previous convictions for offences such as possession of a bladed article, car theft, possession of drugs, racially aggravated intentional harassment, and numerous driving offences.The crash has led to greater scrutiny on an emerging trend of young people posting videos online of cars they are in being driven dangerously. One senior figure in the Police Federation of England and Wales said young people were “baiting police officers” with reckless driving.Paul Williams, the federation’s acting deputy national chair, told BBC Breakfast that reckless driving young people had become a “real problem” for responding officers.“Every day we can identify now numerous examples of young people sensationalising dangerous driving. Not just dangerous driving, but baiting police officers who are out there to protect the public,” said Williams.He added: “It’s a real problem. It’s causing officers concern. They shouldn’t have to be going out and worrying about whether they’re going to return home from their shift or not. But on top of that, wondering if they’re going to be plastered all over social media. It’s absolutely unacceptable and social media platforms need to take some action.”The five arrests on Tuesday came a day after Cleveland police announced 12 people, nine men and three women, had been arrested after officers said they received several reports of two vehicles, the VW Passat and a Volvo XC60, being driving dangerously at the time.Of those 12, four were arrested on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group and four on suspicion of possessing a firearm, while four of the suspects were also accused of possessing class A and B drugs with intent to supply.Two of the 12 people previously arrested have now appeared in court. Kai Beattie, 19, appeared at Teesside magistrates court charged with possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life. Cameron George, 26, was remanded in custody to appear at Teesside crown court on 21 September charged with drugs offences and possession of criminal property.The five arrested on Tuesday were a boy aged 16, an 18-year-old and a man of 21, all on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group; a 55-year-old on suspicion of assisting an offender and a 23-year-old on suspicion of making threats to kill.Road safety statistics up to 2025 also show a trend in dangerous driving for young people, particularly young men, being on the rise, with 77 people aged between 16 and 20 dying last year, compared with 65 the year before and 55 in 2016, the largest rise of any age group.The government has acknowledged the need to challenge social media companies that platform videos which encourage dangerous driving among people, with a Downing Street spokesperson saying on Monday that No 10 would give the regulator Ofcom its “full backing to take tough action” on any sites and apps that do not moderate or remove such content.The crash in Middlesbrough is one of several incidents involving people being killed or hospitalised due to a car trying to evade police that have occurred in the past fortnight across the UK, with a similar accident taking place in England on Tuesday, when a crash after a police pursuit in Warwickshire led to a man dying and a woman being hospitalised.In Ireland last week, another similar incident resulted in four people, including a seven-year-old boy, being hospitalised when a car containing five teenagers drove into them on the M9 in County Kildare to evade Garda. All five teenagers were killed.A fundraiser set up by Cleveland police federation for Blades’ and Clough’s families has exceeded £942,000 in donations.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content
