title: Two planned datacentres will have higher UK carbon emissions than ExxonMobil, analysis finds | Datacentres - UK | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Buckinghamshire and Bedfordshire sites predicted to emit 4.5m tonnes a year when fully running
Author: Pippa Neill
Headline: Exclusive: Buckinghamshire and Bedfordshire sites predicted to emit 4.5m tonnes a year when fully running
Content: Aerial view of the construction site for the proposed datacentre at Wapseys Wood in Buckinghamshire.Photograph: sdcm40campusView image in fullscreenAerial view of the construction site for the proposed datacentre at Wapseys Wood in Buckinghamshire.Photograph: sdcm40campusDatacentres - UKTwo planned datacentres will have higher UK carbon emissions than ExxonMobil, analysis findsExclusive: Buckinghamshire and Bedfordshire sites predicted to emit 4.5m tonnes a year when fully runningPippa NeillEnvironment reporterTue 25 Aug 2026 07.04 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe carbon emissions from just two planned datacentres in England will exceed all of the fossil fuel company ExxonMobil’s UK emissions, analysis has revealed.Experts have said this demonstrates the “serious threat” datacentres pose to the UK’s legally binding climate goals.Analysis by the non-profit group Foxglove reveals that when fully operational, the Wapseys Wood datacentre inBuckinghamshireand the Quest Park datacentre in Bedfordshire will use 1.3GW of power and will produce more than 4.5m tonnes of carbon emissions.ExxonMobil emitted3.9m tonnesin 2023, according to the global energy thinktank Ember.AI datacentres use a massive amount of electricity to power servers and cooling equipment, and to run facility systems. There are currently 315 datacentres in the queue to connect to the UK’s electricity grid, representing 73GW of demand. This is almost double the peak winter energy demand for the entire UK.Because of the long wait to connect to the grid, the Wapseys Wood and Quest Park datacentres are seeking to build their own on-site gas-fired power stations.Based on governmentfigureson the carbon intensity of electricity generation, Foxglove has calculated these projects will produce 4.577m tonnes of carbon emissions per year.A government spokesperson said these figures were “misleading” because of the assumption that both projects will run at 100% utilisation from day one, which they said was “not accurate”.Tom Hegarty, head of communications at Foxglove, said assuming a 100% utilisation rate followed standard industry practice.Kierra Box, a trade and environmental regulation campaigner at Friends of the Earth, said the aim was for datacentres to increase load and run at full capacity, and so it was “valid to look at those top level predictions”.The formerEnglandand Wales Green party leader Caroline Lucas described the projected emissions from these projects as “absolutely horrifying”, and said it should be ringing alarm bells right across government.The government says its own analysis shows there are multiple pathways for this rapid datacentre rollout to fit within theseventh carbon budget, which sets out how the government will reach its international climate targets.However there remains ahigh level of uncertaintyover how this will work.Toby Perkins, a Labour MP and chair of the Commons environmental audit committee, which is leading an inquiry into the environmental impact of datacentres, said this analysis was a “potent reminder that without the right measures in place, data centres could represent a serious threat to the environment and to our legally binding climate goals”.Oliver Hayes, head of policy at the campaign group Global Action Plan, said the two projects were “catastrophic for our carbon budgets”. He said the only way the rapid rollout of datacentres could fit within these budgets was if other elements of the economy were given much stricter carbon budgets.Sam Hunter-Jones, a ClientEarth lawyer, said every megawatt powering a datacentre connected to the grid was a megawatt that could not be used to replace fossil fuels elsewhere. “The reality is that unchecked datacentre growth is making the transition away from fossil fuels harder, not easier,” he said.The datacentres are two of the first to be fast-tracked through the government’s nationally significant infrastructure project (NSIP) regime. This regime allows developers to rapidly deliver infrastructure projects by bypassing local planning authorities with decisions instead handled by central government.Hayes said it was a “very worrying sign” that the government had allowed two gas-fired datacentres to apply into the NSIP regime. “I think that sends an extremely bad signal and demonstrates that they are not serious about addressing the emissions associated with datacentres,” he said, describing it as an “affront to local people”.Lucas also raised concerns about the projects being fast-tracked, and said it “insulates” them from local scrutiny.“In order to be able to make sensible decisions on which projects should go ahead and where they should be, we need to have more information in the public domain. We need to have more scrutiny, not less, and yet things like the NSIP regime are moving things in the opposite direction,” she said.A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: “Datacentres are a vital part of our economy and our everyday lives, helping us interact with the services we need, while driving growth and renewal for communities. We will enable the development and growth of new industries, such as datacentres, by building unprecedented amounts of clean power.”Wapseys Wood declined to comment. Quest Park did not respond to a request for comment.Explore more on these topicsDatacentres - UKGreenhouse gas emissionsAI (artificial intelligence)ExxonMobilClimate crisisComputingFossil fuelsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Expert witnesses challenge claim that Lindsay Clancy experienced psychosis | Massachusetts | The Guardian
description: One more day of testimony expected as closing arguments set for Thursday and jury likely to begin deliberations Friday
Author: Gabrielle Canon
Headline: One more day of testimony expected as closing arguments set for Thursday and jury likely to begin deliberations Friday
Content: Lindsay Clancy in Plymouth superior court, Plymouth, Massachusetts, on Tuesday.Photograph: Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger/APView image in fullscreenLindsay Clancy in Plymouth superior court, Plymouth, Massachusetts, on Tuesday.Photograph: Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger/APMassachusettsExpert witnesses challenge claim that Lindsay Clancy experienced psychosisOne more day of testimony expected as closing arguments set for Thursday and jury likely begins deliberations FridayGabrielle CanonTue 25 Aug 2026 17.23 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 18.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne more day of rebuttal testimony was expected this week in the trial against Lindsay Clancy, followed by closing statements likely on Thursday.The jury, which will likely begin deliberations on Friday, will decide whether theMassachusettsmother was experiencing postpartum psychosis when she killed her three children in January 2023.On Tuesday, prosecutors put two expert witnesses on the stand who challenged the arguments made by Clancy’s defense team – specifically, that Clancy committed the acts while suffering from postpartum psychosis – a mental illness that can cause hallucinations, mood swings, delusions and more, and was hearing a voice compelling her to do it. Her attorney Kevin Reddington has also claimed Clancy had bipolar disorder and was overmedicated.Tuesday’s testimonies capped off more than a month of testimony in a trial that has largely depended on opposing views from experts about Clancy’s mental health and her ability to understand the gravity of what she was doing.It’s not disputed that she strangled the children – Callan, 8 months, Dawson, three years old, and Cora, five years old, before she allegedly jumped from a second-floor window, which left her paralyzed from the waist down. But the outcome of the trial hinges on questions surrounding Clancy’s mental state at the time of the children’s deaths. The burden of proof is on the prosecution to show Clancy was not suffering from “a mental disease or defect” and that she had enough capacity to understand “the wrongfulness or criminality of her conduct”.Kirk Heilbrun, a forensic psychologist hired by prosecutors, initially took the stand on Friday andcontinued his testimony on Tuesdaymorning. He told the court he “did his best to have an open mind”, when he evaluated Clancy in April and that he believed she was “criminally responsible” for the deaths.Lindsay Clancy trial: psychologist says he doubts claim she was hallucinatingRead more“She retained an awareness of the illegality of killing others, including her children,” he said. “Her moral awareness of this killing was influenced by her strong desire to die and, if she was dead, not to leave her children behind.”Over nearly three days of testimony, the prosecution also focused on the timeline of events during the killings, asking Heilbrun to identify whether each step Clancy took was a decision – including her action to take the children down to the basement – in an attempt to convince the jury that these were planned murders. For each, he answered that they did.Under cross-examination, Heilbrun’s told the court he had been paid roughly $54,000 for the 180 hours he has worked on the case on behalf of the state, and that he will likely be paid more as the trial goes on. He also told Reddington that he didn’t have experience with postpartum mental health conditions.A recess was called at one point, after several heated exchanges between Heilbrun and Reddington during which Clancy’s attorney accused the psychologist of not reading her medical reports.Heilbrun’s testimony on Monday prompted a request for a mistrial from Reddington after the psychologist mentioned Clancy’s Catholic faith. The request was denied, but Judge William Sullivan admonished Heilbrun for the comment and instructed the jury to disregard the reference to “the religion that the defendant was raised with”, calling it “an absolutely inappropriate area of testimony”.After Heilbrun left the stand on Tuesday afternoon, prosecutors called forensic psychiatrist Gregory Saathoff, who is affiliated with the FBI and University of Virginia. Unlike Heilbrun, he claimed he was not paid for his testimony and had treated several women who have killed their children.Saathoff told the court that it was unusual that Clancy hadn’t reported hearing voices before the killings and that the voices ceased afterwards. He also said he found several inconsistencies in Clancy’s account of what happened.It is well documented that Clancy needed treatment for a mental health condition, and admitted herself to McLean, a psychiatric hospital in Massachusetts, a few weeks before the murders. Testimony from expert witnesses who were called by the defense had very different conclusions about her mental state.Dr Phillip Resnick, a forensic psychiatrist and expert in filicide, testified on Friday that Clancy was “clearly psychotic” on the day she killed her children and was not in control of her actions.“It was almost like she was a puppet and someone else was pulling the strings,” he said.That echoed another defense witness, Paul Zeizel, the psychologist who concluded Clancy “had no appreciation for the wrongfulness of her act”.Before the court adjourned for the day on Tuesday, Judge Sullivan told the jury that the presentation of evidence would conclude on Wednesday and that closing arguments would likely follow on Thursday. Deliberations are expected to begin on Friday. He encouraged jurors not to form their own conclusions until the very end.“You’ve heard a lot of evidence, but you haven’t heard all of it, right? And like I said before, you haven’t heard the closing arguments of the attorneys,” Sullivan said. “You haven’t heard the law that you’re going to have to apply to this. So you still have to keep an open mind.”In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsMassachusettsMental healthUS crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Father of USS Lincoln sailor detained by ICE released from detention | US immigration | The Guardian
description: Arrest of Luis Manuel Aviles, 48, sparked backlash as he was detained while his son, Joshua, was deployed in Middle East
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Arrest of Luis Manuel Aviles, 48, sparked backlash as he was detained while his son, Joshua, was deployed in Middle East
Content: Luis Manuel Aviles and his son Joshua Aviles, a US navy sailor onboard the USS Abraham Lincoln.Photograph: Joshua Aviles/Facebook/ReutersView image in fullscreenLuis Manuel Aviles and his son Joshua Aviles, a US navy sailor onboard the USS Abraham Lincoln.Photograph: Joshua Aviles/Facebook/ReutersUS immigrationFather of USS Lincoln sailor detained by ICE released from detentionArrest of Luis Manuel Aviles, 48, sparked backlash as he was detained while his son, Joshua, was deployed in Middle EastAssociated PressTue 25 Aug 2026 17.26 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 19.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe father of a US navy sailor who has been deployed in the Middle East for a record-breaking nine months onthe USS Abraham Lincolnaircraft carrier has been released from immigration detention, according to his family.Hisarrestsparked intense backlash after the Associated Press reported that his son was entering his ninth month on the Lincoln with the navy when his father was detained. The carrier had just set a US military record for uninterrupted time at sea and has raised concerns about supply shortages and deteriorating mental health among those serving onboard.Luis Manuel Aviles, 48, was arrested on Saturday after leaving his house to take his car to the mechanic, according to his wife, Argelia. She said her husband, a handyman in Key West, Florida, had a permit to work in the US. Originally from Nicaragua, he has lived in the US for 19 years.Wife of US soldier deported after Trump rollback on military family protectionsRead moreAviles’s arrest was thelatest in a stringof high-profile immigration arrests of the immediate family members of enlisted US soldiers as part of Donald Trump’s aggressive immigration crackdown. Elected officials recently launched a congressional investigation into the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) practice.Aviles’s son, Joshua, posted on Facebook on Tuesday that his father had been released from federal immigration custody. An immigration judge dismissed Aviles’s case on Monday, just hours after he was booked into an immigration detention center in Miami, according to Department of Justice records.The DHS didn’t offer comment to clarify why Luis Manuel Aviles was arrested – or subsequently released.Margaret Stock, an immigration attorney for military families, called the rapid succession of filed and dismissed charges “super unusual”.Joshua said in a Facebook post on Saturday that he had been working 12-hour days without a break since the USS Abraham Lincoln left US shores in November. The US navy confirmed that Aviles is enlisted and serves onboard the Lincoln, where his physically demanding duties include moving aircraft on the ship.The troubled vessel isin the processof being relieved in the Middle East by the USS George Washington.Explore more on these topicsUS immigrationUS militaryICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)Trump administrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Billie Piper stalker jailed for 12 months after breaching prevention order | Crime | The Guardian
description: Philip Jerome, 49, repeatedly tried to contact actor in hope they would begin a relationship, court hears
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: Philip Jerome, 49, repeatedly tried to contact actor in hope they would begin a relationship, court hears
Content: The court was told Philip Jerome had been trying to make contact with Billie Piper for more than eight years.Photograph: Anthony Harvey/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe court was told Philip Jerome had been trying to make contact with Billie Piper for more than eight years.Photograph: Anthony Harvey/ShutterstockCrimeBillie Piper stalker jailed for 12 months after breaching prevention orderPhilip Jerome, 49, repeatedly tried to contact actor in hope they would begin a relationship, court hearsSteven MorrisTue 25 Aug 2026 10.40 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA fan obsessed with Billie Piper has been jailed for 12 months after breaching a stalking prevention order.Philip Jerome, 49, from Winchester, had a sexual interest in the singer and actor, and repeatedly tried to get in touch with her in the hope they would end up in a relationship, a court in Hampshire was told.The court was told that Jerome had been attempting to make contact with Piper, whose television credits have included Doctor Who, for more than eight years. He was made subject to a restraining order in 2018 after attending Piper’s home, posting cards through her door and sending her letters by post.View image in fullscreenPhilip Jerome arriving at Basingstoke magistrates court to be sentenced for breaching the prevention order.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAHe breached this order within months by sending messages on Facebook to the star’s mother and sister, expressing a wish for them to meet up. He also attended Piper’s home and made comments about her choice of partner.In 2022, Jerome was jailed after turning up at a pop culture convention where he posed for a fan photograph with Piper twice on the same day, wearing different clothing the second time.When she recognised Jerome, he was ejected from the event by security. In the same year, he was made subject to a stalking prevention order.The court heard police carried out an inspection of Jerome’s devices in December 2025 and found four images of Piper saved on his phone, and that he had tagged 11 posts and images on X relating to her.He wrote: “I think I know which image probably made me fall for [Piper], the GQ awards, and made me want to meet her.”Anisa Alrubaie, prosecuting, told the court: “There are several instances where the defendant has been attempting to communicate with her by tagging her on X.”The prosecutor said Piper’s X account was organised by her personal assistant, who shielded her from critical posts. She continued: “She doesn’t generally inform Ms Piper of posts – there is a significant amount of negativity that is not relevant and she doesn’t need to be made aware.”Sentencing Jerome at Basingstoke magistrates, the district judge Kirsty Allman told him: “You have a sexual interest in Ms Piper. The motivation is to contact her in the hope she will engage in a relationship with you. This is delusional.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“You demonstrated an entrenched pattern of stalking and harassment offences, and failing to comply with court orders.”Caroline Bonavia, defending, said she accepted Jerome had shown a lack of remorse and empathy but said he had sought psychological support to stop him seeking “obsessive and unsuccessful relationships”.She also accepted that Piper had suffered because of Jerome’s behaviour over the years.Jerome pleaded guilty to four counts of breaching a stalking prevention order.Explore more on these topicsCrimeStalkingBillie PiperHampshireEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Climate damage would obliterate any economic benefits of new North Sea fields, analysis shows | Fossil fuels | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Economic harm of CO2 pollution from Rosebank and Jackdaw forecast to far outweigh any boost to UK
Author: Damian Carrington
Headline: Exclusive: Economic harm of CO2 pollution from Rosebank and Jackdaw forecast to far outweigh any boost to UK
Content: The argument that approving Rosebank and Jackdaw would cut bills and improve energy security is a ‘delusion’, say experts.Photograph: James Willoughby/SOPA Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe argument that approving Rosebank and Jackdaw would cut bills and improve energy security is a ‘delusion’, say experts.Photograph: James Willoughby/SOPA Images/ShutterstockFossil fuelsClimate damage would obliterate any economic benefits of new North Sea fields, analysis showsExclusive: Economic harm of CO2 pollution from Rosebank and Jackdaw forecast to far outweigh any boost to UKDamian CarringtonEnvironment editorTue 25 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 04.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe climate damage caused by developing the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gas fields under consideration by the UK government would destroy their economic benefits many times over, according to an analysis.It estimates the economic damage caused by the carbon pollution from the oil and gas produced would be between £119bn and £336bn in the coming decades, compared with the £28.7bn in value to the UK estimated by Adura, the fossil fuel company promoting the new fields.The assessment applies peer-reviewed research on how rising temperatures harm economies to the production estimates for the fields from the company. The figures are likely to be underestimates, as they do not include losses from amplified extreme weather, sea level rise or climate deaths. The analysis has been submitted to the Rosebank consultation and to an academic journal.View image in fullscreenProtesters last week calling on Andy Burnham to block the plans for Rosebank and Jackdaw.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockThe decision on whether to approveRosebank and Jackdawhas become highly controversial, with the oil industry, some energy leaders and rightwing political parties pushing for the go-ahead. Most centre and leftwing political parties,climate scientistsand environmental campaigners are opposed. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, also faces arevolt from Labour MPswho oppose the plans, while the former energy secretary Ed Miliband once called the Rosebank proposal “climate vandalism”.The argument that approving Rosebank and Jackdaw would reduce UK bills and improve energy security is a“delusion”, according to energy experts, as they are internationally traded commodities. Proponents of new drilling argue it would boost the UK economy, but the new analysis indicates this would be outweighed by long-term economic damage.“The numbers presented here show there’s going to be a very strong destruction of [economic] value above and beyond what Rosebank and Jackdaw could generate for the UK,” said Luke Hatton, at Imperial College London, who conducted the analysis. “The alternative is to really double down on clean energy technologies.” The UK’s net zero sector hasgrown three times fasterthan the overall UK economy in recent years.View image in fullscreenThe government’s official climate advisers have said ‘net zero is a more cost-effective path for the UK economy than continued reliance on fossil fuels’.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PARichard Sulley, of the University of Sheffield’s Grantham Centre for Sustainable Futures, who was not part of the study, said: “Expanding oil and gas production in the North Sea is not just an environmental crime but also economically illiterate. Climate change has already damaged the UK economy, with an estimated£4.4bn loss from this summer’s heatwavesalone.“Remaining tied to the use of fossil fuels keeps UK industries and consumers exposed to the international markets that set prices and will cost way more than it can ever deliver in growth.”Prof Ian Bateman, at the University of Exeter Business School, said: “This is an interesting study which shows the cumulative global climate damage of oil extraction and use is beginning to exceed its face value. When we add in the tax giveaways to the oil industry and compare this to the declining cost and zero climate damage of renewable energy then the economic case for leaving oil in the ground is overwhelming.”Adura, which is jointly owned by Shell and Norway’s Equinor, did not respond to a request for comment.View image in fullscreenActivists staging a protest outside Equinor’s offices in London in February.Photograph: Jack Taylor/ReutersA spokesperson for the Department forEnergySecurity and Net Zero said: “The North Sea remains a vital national asset, supporting jobs, growth and the UK’s energy security. Oil and gas will continue to play an important role in our energy system for decades to come, alongside transitioning to clean power to protect jobs and tackle the climate crisis.”The government’s official advisers, the Climate Change Committee,said in March: “Achieving net zero is a more cost-effective path for the UK economy than continued reliance on fossil fuels, bringing a net benefit to society.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionReform says we need to choose between climate and economy. It’s wrong | Larry ElliottRead moreTheanalysisusesresearch published in the journal Naturein March and production data submitted to the governmentby Adurato assess how much carbon dioxide pollution would result from Rosebank and Jackdaw and how much economic damage that would cause around the world.The economic damage is estimated for the period up to 2100 and the spread of estimates from £119bn to £336bn results from using ranges for how damages may increase in the future and are valued in today’s money. The analysis is based on additional CO2 being added to the atmosphere as evidence shows new oil and gas fields do notgenerally lead to other fields being shut down.If oil and gas production at Rosebank and Jackdaw is better than Adura’s central case, the climate damage range rises to £170bn-£482bn. Just 6% of this higher estimate would need to be felt in the UK to wipe out all the suggested economic gains within the country.Rosebank’s anticipated production accounts for the bulk of the damages – about 88%. It has been suggestedBurnham could approve Jackdawbut block Rosebank.Dr Rick Lupton, at the University of Bath, said: “The analysis is a reasonable piece of exploratory work based on real data and studies, but there are lots of assumptions involved in the specific numbers. The general point is sound: climate damage will certainly increase from exploiting these fields, and this may well be comparable or much larger than the economic benefits from the development, especially considering the mismatch between who benefits and who suffers the impacts.”The October cap on energy prices paid by UK energy customers is due to be thehighest in three years, driven by high gas prices due to the US-Israeli war on Iran.The Guardian’s climate forum 2026On Tuesday 20 October, join Damian Carrington, and our panel of experts—including Professor Andy Haines, Katie White MP, Asad Rehman, Shruti Suresh Gareth Thomas and Amy Fairman for a hopeful and solutions-focused evening.Book ticketshereor atguardian.liveExplore more on these topicsFossil fuelsOil (Environment)Oil (Business)Gas (Business)Gas (Environment)Climate crisisEnergynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Small changes can make a big difference’: how getting farmers, fishers and beavers together could save a Cornish river | Oceans | The Guardian
description: A local initiative is testing simple ways to stop algal blooms in the River Fal threatening some of England’s most biodiverse marine habitats
Author: Karen McVeigh
Headline: A local initiative is testing simple ways to stop algal blooms in the River Fal threatening some of England’s most biodiverse marine habitats
Content: Cornwall council organises boat trips on the River Fal as part of its strategy to reduce runoff. Photograph: Luke Gartside/The GuardianA local initiative is testing simple ways to stop algal blooms in the River Fal threatening some of England’s most biodiverse marine habitatsByKaren McVeighSeascape: the state of our oceans is supported byAbout this contentTue 25 Aug 2026 04.17 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 14.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn a rocky beach inCornwall, a group of wetsuit-clad freedivers and snorkellers are wading into the shallows. Below St Mawes Castle, built by Henry VIII to defend Falmouth harbour, they disappear in a swish of florescent pink and green fins.They are volunteers, trained by the CornwallWildlifeTrust to use underwater cameras and floating GPS devices to detect changes in marine habitats over time.Their work is vital because beneath the surface of Falmouth’s busy natural harbour, known as Carrick Roads, are two of the UK’s most biodiverse and carbon-rich marine habitats: lush seagrass meadows and purple-pink carpets of ancient maerl – a rare and fragile coral-like seaweed. They are some ofthe largest such beds in England.Parts of the slow-growing maerl beds, which stretch from St Mawes to St Just in Roseland, are believed to be up to 4,000 years old. They act as nurseries for commercially valuable species such as scallops and crab.Last year, however, divers found a “worrying deterioration” in the maerl beds, which were being smothered by algae, preventing much-needed sunlight getting to the seaweed. Algal blooms, fuelled by excess nutrients from agricultural runoff and sewage in the River Fal’s catchment area, are unfortunately also present today.View image in fullscreenTwo volunteers, Simon Tagney and Max Behnert, prepare to survey the seabed beneath the 16th-century St Mawes Castle. Photograph: Luke Gartside/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMax Behnert records on his compact camera as he swims through a forest of shallow thongweed, also known as sea spaghetti. Photographs: Luke Gartside/The GuardianSimon Tagney, 65, is a retired TV camera operator turned citizen scientist. “When I went down in March this year, everything looked newly polished and clean,” he says. “But going in today, there’s lot of filamentous algae on everything. A lot of the maerl is obscured by it. You can’t see the detail – it is like going into a dusty room.”The Cornwall Wildlife Trust is among several environmental organisations backing a new initiative from Cornwall council calledFal Rivers to Reef, which aims to work with farmers and landowners to restore nature, build climate resilience and reduce pollution from the river’s source in Goss Moor, through 22,000 hectares (54,000 acres) of farmland and woodland to Falmouth.A key driver of the scheme was catchment data from the Department for Environment Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) published in 2022, which identified rural farm pollution and waste from the water industry as the reason the Lower River Falfailed to achieve “good” ecological status. The new initiative aims to improve water quality and protect seagrass, maerl and the last remaining native oyster beds in Falmouth estuary, which are harvested from sail and oar boats.View image in fullscreenCornwall council is seeking to improve the Fal’s water quality by reducing farm runoff. Photograph: Luke Gartside/The Guardian“The Fal is full of nutrients and that can create mats of opportunistic algae that smothers seagrass like a blanket,” says Matt Slater, marine conservation officer at the trust, which has been forced to temporarily cancel a seagrass restoration project in Ardevora, on the Roseland peninsula, until the water quality improves.“We know that small changes by farmers can make a big difference in reducing runoff,” he says.About 14 miles (22km) from St Mawes, at Gare farm, over tea and home-baked cake, the tenant farmers Claire and Martin Tupper talk about their efforts to improve their soil and stop runoff, and the benefit they get from being involved in FalRiversto Reef.“We are not organic but it is the unseen pollution that is a concern,” says Martin, 63. They have long used “herbal leys” – a mixture of grasses, clover, legumes and herbs – to improve soil, cut down on fertilisers and improve drainage. And they have noticed the benefits: the lambs are growing faster and the mix attracts butterflies and dragonflies.View image in fullscreenClaire and Martin Tupper say advice about how to manage runoff has been invaluable for them at Gare farm. Photograph: Karen McVeigh/The GuardianWith the council’s help, they have also taken other steps, including relocating a gate away from a slope where it was causing excess runoff.And they are restoring an ancient orchard, a key source of biodiversity, which had lain neglected “because I was on my own and it wasn’t earning”, says Martin. “We didn’t know how to access that kind of help.”Claire, 62, says: “You want to do the right thing but you don’t necessarily know the right people to talk to. The support has been invaluable.”As part of Fal Rivers to Reef, the council runs workshops, get-togethers and recently, a boat trip on the estuary to get farmers, fishers and conservationists to better understand each other’s perspective.Jason Pascoe, 56, one of a score of native oyster “sail-and-oar” fishers left in Cornwall, says silt washing down the river from development, farming and heavier rain is creating more mud in the river and threatening the fishery.View image in fullscreenJason Pascoe goes looking for oysters. Photograph: Luke Gartside/The Guardian“One of the biggest problems for the oyster fishery is silt,” says Pascoe. “The oyster shells need to be clean and the larvae need clean substrate to build those shells.”Chris Jones, a beef farmer, says he has made a big change to his farm that could help Pascoe and his fellow fishers if taken up more widely.Since introducing beavers to an enclosure on his land in 2017, the animals have saved him from drought, he says, reducedflooding in the village of Ladock by cutting peak discharge through the site by half and the floodwater transit time from 10 to 90 minutes, and improved the native oyster beds downstream by trapping silt.Jones, who wasbehind a change in the law allowing beavers to be released in Englandafter witnessing benefits on his land, says: “This idea of looking at a river from its source to the sea is the only sensible way of doing it.”As he approaches the beaver enclosure, where water trickles through a series of dams, the soil is moist and the trees are covered in lichen and moss, Jones stops, takes off his shoes and socks and disappears into the reeds. He emerges holding his walking stick aloft, where a good 60cm (2ft) of silt and mud from the water remains.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenChris Jones, left, believes reintroducing more beavers into the region could help; Amie and Jim Pascoe say planting trees is an important part of the solution. Photographs: Karen McVeigh/The Guardian“It’s the most extraordinary thing,” Jones says, grinning. “These little dams act as silt traps; the silt is associated with nitrates and phosphates and pathogens. These beavers are a really good, very cheap – if not free – nature-based solution to achieve better water quality.”That the scheme brought him together with Pascoe, who lives in the nearby village of Coombe , has been hugely beneficial, he says. “If we have enough beavers out there holding enough silt, it has the potential to make his job better. It is amazing.”View image in fullscreenFarmers in the region have been encouraged to increase planting to help reduce runoff and increase biodiversity. Photograph: Luke Gartside/The GuardianJones is in the process of applying for a licence to release 150 beavers into the county. He acknowledges the fear of many farmers that they could damage trees and crops, but says these concerns can be easily addressed.Meanwhile, at Court farm in Philleigh, on the Roseland peninsula, Jim Pascoe, a fourth-generation arable farmer, and his daughter Amie Pascoe are among 48 farmers and landowners in the Fal Rivers to Reef cluster. Planting trees has provided one solution to the problem of runoff pollution, they say.“Forty or 50 years ago, you ploughed every ditch, every bit of land you could get your hands on,” says Jim, 77.Now, driving around his 105 hectares, he can now point to the orchard of 100 fruit trees and 5.5 hectares of woodland, created with the help of the planting projectForest for Cornwall. With existing woodland, the farm now boasts a hundred-acre wood, extending a buffer to help stop runoff entering the estuary.Forest for Cornwall exists alongside Fal Rivers to Reef, with the mission of planting 8,000 hectares of new trees across the county. This month, the council won£8.7m in additional Defra fundingfor it.The Pascoes have also built a two-mile public walkway through the ancient woodland, “to the estuary’s edge, where you get a terrific chorus of bird life”, says Jim.Amie, 47, who works in public relations, says: “We’ve spent our whole lives walking, riding in the woods and swimming in the river. I wanted to share that.”View image in fullscreenAlgae on the banks of the River Fal. Photograph: Luke Gartside/The GuardianThe Pascoes’ neighbour, Philip Marsden, an author who has 18 hectares he has turned into woodland and wildflower meadows, says the key to the success of the farm element of Fal Rivers to Reef is that it is “farmer led”.He says: “Farmers don’t have time to look into funding. There is huge untapped potential for nature recovery.”Delta blues: why estuaries are the canaries in the climate crisis coalmineRead morePhilippa Hoskin, nature recovery manager at Cornwall council, has a 25-strong, mostly externally funded team and key members are able to “speak farmer”, she says. This has helped communities engage with the wider aims of the project, she adds.The source-to-sea initiative is a long-term project so may yet encounter unforeseen obstacles along the way, one of those beingthe potential environmental impacts of aproposed development at Falmouth Docks. But for now, a joined-up approach is paying dividends.Loic Rich, Cornwall’s cabinet member for environment and climate change, says: “Here, you’ve got the people with the vision, you’ve got the farmers, you’ve got the fishers. Everybody’s together in the same room. It’s the ideal way to manage a landscape.”Explore more on these topicsSeascape: the state of our oceansOceansRiversFarmingMarine lifeFarm animalsWildlifefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Going with the grain: how restoring biodiversity led one farmer back to heritage wheat | Farming | The Guardian
description: Henry Astor looked back to his grandfather’s time for the inspiration to find older varieties that could help nature on his Cotswold farm
Author: Tomé Morrissy-Swan
Headline: Henry Astor looked back to his grandfather’s time for the inspiration to find older varieties that could help nature on his Cotswold farm
Content: Henry Astor mills his own flour on Bruern Farms, near Burford, Oxfordshire. Heritage wheat provides far more nutritious and digestible bread. Astor also finds it ‘fundamentally exciting’ to form a relationship with a baker by growing and milling the flour they use.Photograph: Sam Frost/The GuardianView image in fullscreenHenry Astor mills his own flour on Bruern Farms, near Burford, Oxfordshire. Heritage wheat provides far more nutritious and digestible bread. Astor also finds it ‘fundamentally exciting’ to form a relationship with a baker by growing and milling the flour they use.Photograph: Sam Frost/The GuardianThe age of extinctionFarmingGoing with the grain: how restoring biodiversity led one farmer back to heritage wheatHenry Astor looked back to his grandfather’s time for the inspiration to find older varieties that could help nature on his Cotswold farmThe age of extinction is supported byAbout this contentTomé Morrissy-SwanTue 25 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 03.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is the earliest harvest Henry Astor can remember. But walking through the scorched wheatfields of his Cotswolds farm, signs of life are everywhere – swarms of insects, kaleidoscopic wildflower meadows, bushy hedgerows several metres wide. A yellowhammer perches on a nearby tree.There are 18 otherred-listed birdson the farm, says Astor, who this year ringed 23 barn owls, three kestrels, two little owls as well as goshawk chicks. “Last winter we had clouds of goldfinch, chaffinch and greenfinch,” he says. Britain has lost73 million birds since 1970; but at Bruern Farms, a small but welcome reversal is taking shape.Between 30,000 and 40,000 trees have been planted over the past decade, many as part of a flood-mitigation scheme, some in a 17-hectare (42-acre) agroforestry section interspersing wheat with heritage fruits such as Cox’s pippin and Blenheim orange apples. Wildflower meadows are rebuilding soil fertility.As part of his obligations as a member of theNorth East Cotswold Farmer Cluster, which Astor co-founded, a plot is left for bird feeding, to boost populations. According to the cluster co-chair, Tim Field, this has resulted in flocks of linnets, goldfinch and chaffinch across 40 farms involved in the feeding project, while one farm has seen more than 400 teal feeding among watercress in a wetland area.View image in fullscreenApple trees in a multi-crop field at Bruern Farm.Photograph: Sam Frost/The GuardianCatastrophicbiodiversity losssince the postwar “green revolution” has been well documented. Wheat played its part, as heritage grains and mixed populations gave way to vast monocultures of dwarf wheat. Several initiatives are attempting to reverse course with nature-friendly farming, the farms in Astor’s farmer cluster among them.In all, Astor and neighbouring farmers have 800 hectares of floodplain meadow under restoration, while 3,000 hectares have been set aside for flood mitigation along the River Evenlode, including Bruern Farms’ land.Despite this progress, Field is one of those unconvinced by the government’srecently announced “30 by 30” nature restoration plans.“Farmer groups aren’t getting the recognition they deserve, yet we are proof that when farms are aggregated by purpose, we can be more powerful for landscape restoration at scale than has ever been achieved by public or [environmental NGO]-driven schemes.”Astor grew up on the 490-hectare farm his grandfather bought in 1936, but left for a career as a documentary maker and in advertising. In 2017 he returned, with his wife and three young sons, to run the farm. “My father said let the farm manager farm it, do not get involved,” Astor recalls.View image in fullscreenHarvested fields at Bruern Farm.Photograph: Sam Frost/The GuardianThat might initially have been the plan, but the farm Astor returned to was not the one he remembered. When the Milk Marketing Board was abolished in 1994, causing prices to plummet, Bruern ditched dairy. It went from being a mixed farm to wholly arable, farmed by contractors who, Astor says, “don’t really care about trees or hedgerows or nature; it’s a business, they just want maximum yield”.Yet profits were minimal. Astor says wheat farmers grow a commodity that decreases in value each year, while the costs of machinery and chemicals rise – most recently, fuel and fertiliserincreased sharplyduring the Iran war.View image in fullscreenSacks of flour await shipping.Photograph: Sam Frost/The GuardianBruern Farms’ transition from conventional to heritage wheat, grown with the environment in mind, happened in stages. First came an “awakening” at a supermarket. “A bag of crappy flour was £1.20, or £1,200 a tonne. I’m selling wheat at 15p a kilo. Who is taking that money?” Astor thought.In 2020, he was approached by Fielden whisky to grow heritage grains, including red lammas, orange devon and kent old hoary, on 140 hectares. It led him down a “rabbit hole”, sourcing the likes of miller’s choice, a “population wheat” from the South East Grain Alliance. Before modern wheat was introduced there was variety, he says. “They’d have ‘population wheat’ – 30-40 varieties [grown together], which I do today. It builds disease resistance, weather resistance; you have diversity in the field, and much longer roots, so you’re reaching the minerals.”Proponents say heritage wheat is also more nutrient-dense, has a protein structure that results in more digestible bread and, when stoneground, retains more of its nutrients than conventional wheat.View image in fullscreenAstor built up connections with local bakeries to sell on his flour.Photograph: Sam Frost/The GuardianIn 2021, Helen Evans, a baker at the now-closed Flor in London, inquired about Astor’s conventional wheat, which he still grows on some of his land but hopes to phase out. “I didn’t know anything about baking,” says Astor.At this point, he was still sending his grain to a nearby mill for processing. Commercial mills reject approximately 60% of the conventional grain sent to them for being too low in protein, and Astor began to wonder why he was accepting this when his flour was clearly in demand.Astor began personally delivering 300kg of flour a week to Flor. He did not make a profit, but the idea of bypassing wholesalers took shape. He contacted local bakeries and bought a mill. “There was something fundamentally exciting about the idea of growing something, milling it, then having that relationship with a baker,” says Astor.Astor says his goal is to mill 500 tonnes a year, which will allow him to reduce his cropping by half, promote biodiversity on the remaining land, reduce carbon emissions and run a viable business.View image in fullscreenAstor packs flour at the mill.Photograph: Sam Frost/The GuardianNow supplying more than 40 bakeries, Astor operates the mill as a separate business, paying his farm more than it would receive on the commodity market: £800 instead of £600 a tonne for heritage grain. Last year, the bakery chain Gail’s introduced its Bruern Farms sourdough, which is being launched on Ocado in September, followed by Waitrose in November.But simply changing the crop will not solve everything. When Astor sent soil samples to an expert last year, they said it was low in minerals, due in part to the area’s heavy clay, which makes drainage an issue and microbial activity sluggish.He hopes to boost the soil through natural means, such as volcanic ash and microbial teas. He applies minimal fertiliser, and the farm has not used pesticides in 15 years, preferring “intensive intercropping”, with wildflowers to attract predators that feed on aphids.View image in fullscreenThe farm uses wildflowers to attract aphid predators.Photograph: Sam Frost/The GuardianCarlos Guerra, a soil expert at the University of Coimbra in Portugal, supports this approach. He says modern wheat monocultures have “simplified soils as much as they have simplified landscapes – reducing plant and root diversity, weakening microbial communities, and increasing vulnerability to erosion, compaction and organic-matter loss”.Replacing these systems with a diversity of cultures, as well as eliminating pesticides, planting wildflower meadows, reducing soil disturbance and using organic or microbial preparations, “can help rebuild soil structure, biodiversity and nutrient cycling”.Astor hopes his system can be replicated throughout the country, which he believes would make farms profitable and boost food security.His vision is nostalgic. The farm of his childhood was a “self-sufficient community”: a mixed farm supporting several families. “I’m not interested in farming the way my father farmed – 100% arable with subsidies and chemicals. I’m interested in farming the way my grandfather farmed.“There was a connection to the village,” he says. “The community were eating the food we were growing on the farm.”View image in fullscreenAstor rents out land to a local restaurant so it can grow its own produce.Photograph: Sam Frost/The GuardianFor Astor, this is not just talk. The shop and cafe employ 15 people and the farm supports rural enterprise. A 1.2-hectare market garden is run by a nearby restaurant. One local couple has 150 sheep on the land; another young woman is building a separate flock of Herdwicks. The sheep are integrated into the rotation, helping fertilise the fields.This year, Astor harvested 190 tonnes of heritage wheat, up from 48 last year. He expects to reach the golden 500 figure by 2028.“I have three missions,” he says. “Growing nutritional food, feeding the community, and increasing biodiversity.”Find moreage of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reportersRebecca Ratcliffe,Phoebe WestonandPatrick Greenfieldin the Guardian app for more nature coverage.Explore more on these topicsFarmingThe age of extinctionFood (Environment)BiodiversityBirdsAnimalsWildlifeConservationfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: London bus drivers resume strike over heatwave working amid fears over air con deal  | Public transport | The Guardian
description: Drivers concerned that bus operator’s offer to retrofit cabs on 730 buses will not be complete by next summer
Author: Joanna Partridge
Headline: Drivers concerned that bus operator’s offer to retrofit cabs on 730 buses will not be complete by next summer
Content: Unite union and bus operator Arriva North London reached a deal during last week’s talks but some drivers rejected the offer saying it did not go far enough to solve the problem of working in heatwaves.Photograph: Guy Smallman/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenUnite union and bus operator Arriva North London reached a deal during last week’s talks but some drivers rejected the offer saying it did not go far enough to solve the problem of working in heatwaves.Photograph: Guy Smallman/Getty ImagesPublic transportLondon bus drivers resume strike over heatwave working amid fears over air con dealDrivers concerned that bus operator’s offer to retrofit cabs on 730 buses will not be complete by next summerJoanna PartridgeTue 25 Aug 2026 11.59 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLondon bus drivers have resumed strike action over having to work in high temperatures, amid fears that proposed improvements to air conditioning will not be complete by next summer.About 1,500 members of the Unite union working across north London andEssexare taking part in the four-day strike from Tuesday to Friday, after industrial action earlier this month. Further stoppages are planned for the coming weeks.The Unite union and bus operator Arriva North London reached an agreement during talks last week, but some drivers rejected the company’s offer, with workers deciding it did not go far enough to solve theproblem of working in hot weather.The Guardian understands many are concerned that proposals to improve the air-conditioning system across Arriva North London’s fleet of 730 buses may not be finished by next summer.Bus drivers havereported “excessive in-cab heat”for years, saying poor or faulty cooling was allowing temperatures to rise above 30C.Temperatures have often exceeded 40C during this year’srecord run of five heatwavesand there are concerns that such conditions could return in 2027.Bus drivers have reported the air-cooling system in their cabs has only managed to reduce temperatures by about 2C-3C, putting them at extra risk of fatigue and also causing some to suffer health problems including heat exhaustion, heatstroke and dehydration.The Unite general secretary, Sharon Graham, said: “London bus drivers do a vital job, but are putting themselves at risk due to these appalling conditions.“Arriva can fully afford to make meaningful changes our members can accept. Until that happens, strike action will continue and our members at Arriva North London will continue to have the full backing of Unite.”Drivers at eight bus garages – at Barking, Edmonton, Enfield, Grays, Palmers Green, Stamford Hill, Tottenham, and Wood Green – first went on strike on 14 and 18 August, which Unite said had led to delays and cancellations for more than 40 bus routes in the capital.Drivers at three of these garages voted against the new offer put forward by Arriva. The union members have resumed their strike.A spokesperson for Arriva London said: “We are disappointed that this strike is going ahead when five out of eight of our north London garages have said they don’t want [a strike]. We have already reached agreement with Unite officials on every demand – and we continue to seek feedback from Unite to understand what concerns remain at the three garages that voted to strike.”They added: “The safety and wellbeing of our colleagues and customers will always be our highest priority and measures have been introduced this summer to help drivers cope with extreme heat, while we are also investing in air conditioning upgrades for driver cabs across our London fleet.”Arriva, along with other transport operators and Unite, are members ofTransportfor London’s extreme weather taskforce, which has been established to find a solution to weather challenges.Further bus driver strikes are planned for eight occasions during September and October.Explore more on these topicsPublic transportTransportIndustrial actionLondonEssexTrade unionsExtreme heatnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘He’s box office’: Gary Lineker admits wanting Roy Keane to join The Rest Is Football | Gary Lineker | The Guardian
description: Podcast co-host says tongue-in-cheek that ex-Manchester United captain would like to sign up for his show
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: Podcast co-host says tongue-in-cheek that ex-Manchester United captain would like to sign up for his show
Content: Gary Lineker’s The Rest is Football has a new deal with Netflix after its popularity during the World Cup.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGary Lineker’s The Rest is Football has a new deal with Netflix after its popularity during the World Cup.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesGary Lineker‘He’s box office’: Gary Lineker admits wanting Roy Keane to join The Rest Is FootballPodcast co-host says tongue-in-cheek that ex-Manchester United captain would like to sign up for his showMichael SavageMedia editorTue 25 Aug 2026 13.59 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith an all-conquering podcast empire and a new deal that will make his football punditry show a regular fixture on Netflix, there seems little left forGary Linekerto wish for.However, while the former Match of the Day presenter is full of praise for Alan Shearer and Micah Richards – the fellow pundits on his The Rest Is Football show – Lineker has admitted to admiring a combative figure playing for his main rivals.Asked which of the plethora of football pundits he would want to poach, Lineker admitted that Roy Keane’sbrutal delivery and viral rantsmeant the former Manchester United captain would be his dream signing.“He’s box office,” Lineker said during an appearance at the Edinburgh TV festival, before joking that, analytically, the Irishman “doesn’t give you that much”.“He’s bloody good at being Roy Keane,” he said. “I’ve met Roy a few times. He’s really sweet … he just plays a character and he’s good at it. He’s really good at it, and he obviously knows his [stuff]. I was kidding about the analytical thing, a little bit.”Keane is a member of a podcast team that has emerged as Lineker’s main opposition – Gary Neville’s The Overlap operation, which includes the Stick to Football show. Soon after The Rest Is Football signed up with Netflix,Stick to Football announced a similar deal with Disney.While the rivalry is good natured, a tongue-in-cheek Lineker couldn’t help but add a slice of football needle, saying Keane “probably would” sign up for his show.“You’ve got Gary [Neville] and his team, you’ve got Piers Morgan and his team [making the World Cup Uncensored] show, and they’re just trying to copy,” Lineker joked. “They’re trailing in our wake and I wish them all the very best. There is room, particularly in football. There’s a lot of competition.”The deals bringing football podcasts to the world’s biggest streaming services are a sign of a thirst for sport content. Given the huge expense of live sporting rights, punditry has become a popular option.The Rest is Football appeared in Netflix’s daily top 10 charts on every day of its 40-day run of daily episodes filmed during the World Cup, and the US company has opted to continue their partnership during the domestic season.The Rest is Football obtained more than 7m monthly streams for its content alone last season, leading Lineker to joke that Neville’s outfit was “languishing miles behind”.Lineker was interviewed on stage about his transition from footballer to presenter to media mogul, as the co-founder of successfulpodcast stable, Goalhanger. During the appearance, he explained why he continued to speak out on political issues,particularly Gaza.In the last week, the Telegraph criticised him for reposting a video of Tony Greenstein, an anti-Zionist who was cleared last week of inviting support for Hamas. In the video, the activist said: “Zionism is in the tradition of the Nazis who persecuted Jews.”11:01Gary Lineker calls for Burnham to introduce wealth tax - The LatestLineker said: “I don’t think I speak much about politics, although politics is involved in everything that I speak about.“I think ultimately you need to live with yourself and if I see things that upset me in humanitarian terms, then I find it quite upsetting, and it triggers me to use a platform that I would never have had before … People can disagree and that’s absolutely fine.”Explore more on these topicsGary LinekerPodcastingDigital mediaPodcastsEdinburgh International Television FestivalShareReuse this content

title: NHS England to offer women ‘gamechanging’ free home testing kits for cervical cancer   | Cervical cancer | The Guardian
description: NHS has target of eliminating the cancer by 2040, but up to 4 million eligible women are not up to date with screening
Author: Andrew Gregory
Headline: NHS has target of eliminating the cancer by 2040, but up to 4 million eligible women are not up to date with screening
Content: The kits (not pictured) contain a swab to collect a sample to be posted back to the NHS free and tested for high-risk human papillomavirus.Photograph: Grace Cary/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe kits (not pictured) contain a swab to collect a sample to be posted back to the NHS free and tested for high-risk human papillomavirus.Photograph: Grace Cary/Getty ImagesCervical cancerNHS England to offer women ‘gamechanging’ free home testing kits for cervical cancerNHS has target of eliminating the cancer by 2040, but up to 4 million eligible women are not up to date with screeningAndrew GregoryHealth editorTue 25 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 10.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMillions of women inEnglandwho have missed cervical screening appointments will be offered free home testing kits on the NHS.The move comes amid concerns thatonly two-thirds of women attend in-person cervical screening appointmentswhen asked to do so, leaving as many as 4 million women not up to date.The rollout is being described as a “gamechanger”, offering a “discreet and convenient option” to encourage more women to get screened.The kits contain a swab to collect a sample from the vagina. This is then posted back to theNHSfree, where it is tested in labs for high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV).If high-risk HPV is detected, patients will then be asked to attend a cervical screening appointment with a clinician.View image in fullscreenHuman papillomavirus under the microscope.Photograph: Bsip Sa/AlamyHPV is a group of viruses that can be passed on through sexual contact and cause no symptoms. About 13 high-risk types of the virus are known to cause 99.7% of cervical cancers.Starting on Tuesday, eligible women between 30 and 65 who have not attended screening appointments will be sent invitations via the NHS app, text message, email or letter.They will then be able to order a kit through the app or website. The scheme is part of the NHS’s target of eliminating cervical cancer by 2040.Dr Sue Mann, national clinical director for women’s health at NHS England, said: “Screening saves thousands of lives each year by preventing cancers and catching them earlier, but only around two-thirds of women are attending cervical screening appointments when invited by the NHS.“Offering millions of women an alternative test they can do from the comfort of their own homes will be a gamechanger – making it easier than ever for them to get tested for HPV.”Women aged between 24 and 64 are invited for cervical screening every five years, or more often if HPV is detected.The latest figures from NHS England show 68.8% of eligible women are up to date with cervical screening, below the 80% target. It means about 4 million women are not up to date, according to NHS estimates.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“There are lots of reasons that may stop women from getting their cervical screening – embarrassment, lack of time, or worries about discomfort – and these kits provide a discreet and convenient option we hope will encourage more women to take up the life-saving test,” said Mann.“So, if you’re invited to take part, please order a test – it’s a simple swab you can do at home in minutes.”Athena Lamnisos, chief executive of the Eve Appeal, welcomed the move, saying that self-testing at home would be a “step-change” for many women.Michelle Mitchell, chief executive ofCancerResearch UK, said: “Cervical screening is a powerful tool that saves lives – it can prevent cervical cancer or spot it at an earlier stage when treatment is more likely to be successful.“While it’s best for cervical screening to be done by a nurse or doctor, there are barriers that make it challenging for some people to attend. At-home HPV self-testing kits will help more people take part in a way that works for them.”Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, said the aim was to make it as easy and convenient as possible for women to keep up with their screening. She said: “This is the future NHS we are building – there for all of us when we need it, and acting as early as possible to stop preventable deaths.”Explore more on these topicsCervical cancerCancerNHSHealthEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Yorkshireman believed to be first Briton to die fighting for Russia against Ukraine | UK news | The Guardian
description: Bradley Townsend reportedly killed by a drone on 10 June in Donetsk region after joining up with separatists
Author: Raphael Boyd
Headline: Bradley Townsend reportedly killed by a drone on 10 June in Donetsk region after joining up with separatists
Content: Bradley Townsend, 33, is thought to have been killed by a remote-controlled drone.Photograph: Unpixs/YouTubeView image in fullscreenBradley Townsend, 33, is thought to have been killed by a remote-controlled drone.Photograph: Unpixs/YouTubeUK newsYorkshireman believed to be first Briton to die fighting for Russia against UkraineBradley Townsend reportedly killed by a drone on 10 June in Donetsk region after joining up with separatistsRaphael BoydTue 25 Aug 2026 05.51 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA man from SouthYorkshireis believed to be the first British citizen to die fighting for Russia in its war against Ukraine.Bradley Townsend, a 33-year-old fisher from Barnsley, left Britain in April to join up with Russian separatists in eastern Donbas to aid in their invasion ofUkraine, despite having no previous combat experience or familiar ties to eastern Europe. Alongside 49-year-old Ben Stimson and 39-year-old Aiden Minnis, Townsend was granted Russian citizenship for joining the country’s military campaign.He is believed to have been killed by a remote-controlled first-person-view drone near Lyman, a city in Donetsk, on 10 June. He appeared in videos posted to social media by pro-Russian accounts, including one seemingly owned by Stimson, who was jailed in the UK in 2015 prior to Russia’s full scale invasion for travelling to join pro-Russian troops to fight in the region.Although Townsend’s death was only widely reported on Monday, unconfirmed reports that he had been killed began circulating in June. One pro-Russian report, seen by LBC, described Townsend as a “warrior in a holy war” who had “sacrificed his life for the cause”.Back in his native Yorkshire, his death was met with sadness and frustration. One former friend posted that Townsend, who was understood to have had struggled with mental health and addiction, was a “normal guy” who had been “indoctrinated” by people who “saw his vulnerability as an opportunity to recruit him into their twisted cause”, while another said that he had been “brainwashed” by his fellow British defectors.In videos taken after he had joined up with Russian forces, Townsend could be seen describing himself as a “normal working-class lad from Yorkshire” and laughing with Stimson and Minnis as the trio drank and played cards. He had also posted that the Donbas miners had donated to miners in Yorkshire during strikes in the 1980s, before he was born, and he intended to “repay that favour”.In a post after his death, Minnis described Townsend as “our beloved comrade-in-arms” who went “into the storm and fell on the battlefield” while comparing Ukrainians to Nazis, a common analogy used in Russian propaganda.In the same post, Minnis said that Townsend “sacrificed his life for our cause. His service was brief but he blazed the brightest star”.Townsend, who reportedly told his family he was travelling to Romania when he left Britain in April, also defended his decision to go to Russia on social media, while acknowledging he would be “persecuted” if he ever went home.In a post he wrote: “I came with the idea that I probably wouldn’t be able to go home. I’d definitely get persecuted if I went back. I’m not here for a suicide mission, but I understand that’s what can happen. This was my own decision, I wasn’t pushed into anything.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTom Tugendhat, the former Conservative MP and security minister who served in Iraq and Afghanistan, expressed his sympathies to Townsend’s family but described his actions as “unbelievably stupid” and “extremely misguided”, adding: “No question about it, it’s criminal because you’re engaging in an army that is committing the most barbarous war crimes that the world has seen in decades.”The Foreign Office is supporting Townsend’s family.Explore more on these topicsUK newsYorkshireRussiaUkraineEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Dogs blink more often when they see owners blinking, study finds | Animal behaviour | The Guardian
description: Scientists say research suggests blinking may have acquired a social relevance in interactions between dogs and people
Author: Nicola Davis
Headline: Scientists say research suggests blinking may have acquired a social relevance in interactions between dogs and people
Content: A dog winking. ‘This study shows how socially sensitive our dogs are to subtle cues, such as blinking, on our faces,’ one researcher said.Photograph: Jaromir Chalabala/AlamyView image in fullscreenA dog winking. ‘This study shows how socially sensitive our dogs are to subtle cues, such as blinking, on our faces,’ one researcher said.Photograph: Jaromir Chalabala/AlamyAnimal behaviourDogs blink more often when they see owners blinking, study findsScientists say research suggests blinking may have acquired a social relevance in interactions between dogs and peopleNicola DavisScience correspondentTue 25 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStare into a dog’s eyes and you may encounter a bemused expression. But researchers have found that dogs blink more often when they see their owners doing so, suggesting there may be more to the mutual gaze than meets the eye.Scientists have previously found that dogsturn on the puppy eyeswhen humans look at them, and that their brains candistinguish happy human facesfrom other expressions – even telling apart fearful faces from those that are angry or sad.But while previous work has suggested dogs and humans maysynchronisetheir blinking, and dogs may blink more when interacting with their owners rather than a familiar trainer, questions have remained over whether human blinking affects how often dogs bat their eyelids.Dr Chiara Canori, the first author of the new study, from the University of Parma, said: “What we wanted to do here was experimentally isolate the human blink and separate it from all the other things that normally happen during a real social interaction, which has never been done before.”Writing in the journalRoyal Society Open Science, Canori and colleagues report how they analysed recordings of 35 dogs of different breeds as each was shown two types of video.Both videos lasted 40 seconds and showed three people, one at a time: the dog’s owner and two unfamiliar humans. In one video, the humans each blinked once every three seconds, and in the other video they looked straight ahead without blinking.The results reveal dogs blinked more often when the on-screen humans blinked than when they did not. Further analysis found dogs only increased their rate of blinking when they were shown their owners blinking compared with when they displayed a still gaze – with the effect not seen for strangers.“This suggests that the social relevance of the partner matters,” said Canori, adding that the results were not explained by dogs looking at their owners for longer. The team found no evidence that the dogs synchronised their blinking with that of humans.Canori said the findings suggested blinking – an important mechanism for protecting the eye and keeping it moist – may have acquired a social relevance.“As of today, however, we cannot say that a dog deliberately blinks in order to convey a particular message,” she said. “It may provide subtle feedback about attention or engagement and perhaps help coordinate an interaction with another individual, particularly with a socially important partner.”Canori stressed that owners should not interpret an individual blink as having a specific, fixed meaning. “Our study does not show that every time a dog blinks it is deliberately ‘saying’ something,” she said. “What our work suggests is that this apparently simple and automatic behaviour can nevertheless be influenced by the social context.Dogsappear sensitive to blinking in other individuals, and their own blinking can change depending on who they are interacting with.”Dr Laura Cuaya, of the University of Vienna, who was not involved in the work, welcomed the findings but noted that the study’s design revealed more about how dogs perceive human blinks than whether they use blinking as a communicative cue.“Still, this study shows how socially sensitive our dogs are to subtle cues, such as blinking, on our faces,” she said. “I would be very interested to see researchers measure in their next studies whether our blinking behaviour changes when we interact with our dogs in social contexts.”Explore more on these topicsAnimal behaviourDogsPetsAnimalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Wife of US soldier deported after Trump rollback on military family protections | US military | The Guardian
description: Cristy Maryori Villafranca-Trejo, deported to Honduras, is latest military spouse to face removal amid Trump 2.0
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Cristy Maryori Villafranca-Trejo, deported to Honduras, is latest military spouse to face removal amid Trump 2.0
Content: Army Sgt Hedar Leonel Turcios Juarez, whose wife, Cristy Maryori Villafranca-Trejo, was deported, at home in El Paso, Texas, on 21 July 2026.Photograph: Ryan Romero/APView image in fullscreenArmy Sgt Hedar Leonel Turcios Juarez, whose wife, Cristy Maryori Villafranca-Trejo, was deported, at home in El Paso, Texas, on 21 July 2026.Photograph: Ryan Romero/APUS militaryWife of US soldier deported after Trump rollback on military family protectionsCristy Maryori Villafranca-Trejo, deported to Honduras, is latest military spouse to face removal amid Trump 2.0Associated PressTue 25 Aug 2026 16.23 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 19.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe wife of an active-dutyUS soldierwas deported on Monday to her nativeHonduras, according to her family and the federal Department of Homeland Security (DHS).Cristy Maryori Villafranca-Trejo is at least the seventh spouse or parent of an active-duty US soldier to be deported under the immigration crackdown duringDonald Trump’s second presidency.The Associated Press has found more than 50 cases in which immediate family members of US troops were placed in federal immigration detention after theTrump administrationrolled back protections for military families. In some instances, the DHS has released military spouses after media attention and advocacy by congressional leaders.Father of USS Lincoln sailor detained by ICE released from detentionRead moreVillafranca-Trejo’s husband, army Sgt Hedar Leonel Turcios Juarez, said he has been struggling to manage his military duties since she was detained on 11 July outside a Walmart near Fort Bliss, Texas, where he is stationed. Since then, he’s had to care for their six-year-old daughter without his wife’s help. Instead of training in the mornings, he takes his daughter to first grade – and he said he has already had to postpone a planned assignment at another base.“I don’t know if I will be able to continue with this,” Turcios Juarez said of his army career. “I have to make a plan to make sure I can still fulfill my military responsibilities – but also take care of my family.”The DHS confirmed Villafranca-Trejo’s deportation, saying she had “received due process”.Villafranca-Trejo, who has no known criminal record and entered the US in 2016 at age 18, was issued a final order of removal by an immigration judge in 2017 after failing to appear at a hearing, according to the DHS. Villafranca-Trejo’s husband said she had not received a notice for the hearing she missed and did not realize she had been ordered deported until they went to apply for her green card after marrying in 2022.Originally fromHonduras, Turcios Juarez became a US citizen in 2024 after enlisting two years earlier.Villafranca-Trejo’s motion to reopen her case was denied last May and an appeal before the Board of Immigration Appeals remained pending, according to her attorney. She had also been waiting for about a year for a decision on her application for military parole-in-place, a program that allows the immediate family of US troops to remain in the country to apply for a green card.“We were following the rules,” Turcios Juarez said. “We did everything we could on our side to fix this problem.”Prior to Trump’s second administration, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) would typically allow immediate family members of US troops to adjust their legal status even if they had been issued a final order of removal, according to Dan Gividen, who served as ICE deputy chief counsel from 2016 to 2019 under Trump.“If you’ve got an active-duty military member that’s married to someone now, and that’s going to give her the opportunity to get a green card, you wouldn’t detain them, much less execute the removal order,” Gividen said.JP Caballero, a spokesperson for congresswoman Veronica Escobar, a Democrat representing El Paso, said Escobar had opened a congressional inquiry into Villafranca-Trejo’s case and visited her at the Camp East Montana detention facility in Texas earlier this month.“My heart breaks for her, her children and the soldier who must feel so betrayed by the country he is sacrificing for,” Escobar said in a statement. “There are far too many families like theirs who are being targeted instead of supported.”Turcios Juarez said he was unsure how he would care for his daughter without his wife. He still hasn’t figured out how to tell his daughter what has happened. But he says he still wants to keep serving his country.“I love what I do, I want to keep doing this,” he said of the army. “I just don’t know how I am going to keep doing this.”Explore more on these topicsUS militaryUS immigrationTrump administrationDonald TrumpICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)US politicsHondurasnewsShareReuse this content

title: At least 47 killed and dozens kidnapped in gang attack near Haiti capital | Haiti | The Guardian
description: Gang leader threatens to kill hostages after attack in Kenscoff in which homes were also set alight
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Gang leader threatens to kill hostages after attack in Kenscoff in which homes were also set alight
Content: People walk past a burnt vehicle on Monday after the deadly violence in Kenscoff.Photograph: Clarens Siffroy/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople walk past a burnt vehicle on Monday after the deadly violence in Kenscoff.Photograph: Clarens Siffroy/AFP/Getty ImagesHaitiAt least 47 killed and dozens kidnapped in gang attack near Haiti capitalGang leader threatens to kill hostages after attack in Kenscoff in which homes were also set alight‘A massacre’: Haiti gangs carrying out mass killingsAssociated Press in Port-au-PrinceTue 25 Aug 2026 13.35 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 13.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt least 47 people were killed and more than 50 others kidnapped when armed men attacked a once peaceful community near Haiti’s capital at the weekend, the UN has said.A gang leader has threatened to kill the hostages if authorities kill any gang members as they try to secure the community of Kenscoff, nestled in the hills above Port-au-Prince.Sunday’s attack pierced the belief that security in theCaribbeancountry was improving. Romain Le Cour, the head of Haiti observatory at the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, said: “This is a major political and security test – for the government, for the police and for the international mission alike.”In a video posted on social media, the gang leader warned the director of Haiti’s national police, Vladimir Paraison, not to use drones to repel gangs in the area. “Paraison, if any of our soldiers are hurt, I will kill all of them,” he said, referring to the hostages.He identified himself as Izo 2, a reference to Izo, or Johnson André, one of Haiti’s most powerful gang members.
