Le Cour said Izo 2 was also known as Didi and led the armed group in Kenscoff on behalf of and in coordination with Izo and other gang leaders. “He’s running a kind of franchise cell for other gangs,” he said.Le Cour said the aim of the attack could be to force Haiti’s police and the UN-backed gang suppression force to disperse even more of their limited resources. “They don’t have enough personnel,” he said. “If you force them to deploy more troops, it would inevitably be at the expense of other areas.”The attack may also be a show of force and a message to Haiti’s government and police as the country prepares to hold general elections on 13 December, the first in more than a decade.Le Cour said: “This is a message to the government and the police that their claims of protection do not match reality. The gangs are saying: when we choose to attack, we can, and we will succeed.”View image in fullscreenWomen mourn at the site of the attack in Kenscoff.Photograph: Patrice Noel/ReutersThe first major attack on Kenscoff occurred in January 2025 and since then there have been sporadic attacks in the mountains surrounding the city centre. Sunday’s attack was the largest yet.At least five of the 47 people killed were children, according to the UN integrated office in Haiti, known as BINUH.Guns, gangs and drought: how crime and the climate crisis are reshaping HaitiRead moreKenscoff’s mayor, Jean Massillon, said two government employees were among those killed, including his cousin who served as his security detail.He said members of Viv Ansanm, a powerful gang coalition that the US has designated as a foreign terrorist organisation, also set fire to 25 homes.Massillon said gangs were still roaming Kenscoff’s periphery. “The atrocity of this crime reminds us that we have to continue working stronger every day to bring peace to the community,” he said. “I’m optimistic that the state will continue working to eradicate the gangs in Kenscoff.”Some survivors accused the government of not providing enough protection before the attack. The police rejected the accusations.Le Cour said that if police and armoured vehicles were indeed stationed in Kenscoff before the attack, it was concerning. “You let the gangs come in even if you had everything in place?” he said.Armed men control an estimated 70% of Port-au-Prince and swaths of land in Haiti’s central region and beyond, and gang violence has displaced a record 1.5 million people across Haiti. More than 3,050 people were reported killed from January to June and another 1,400 injured, according to UN statistics released on Tuesday.Explore more on these topicsHaitiCaribbeanAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: CIA director John Ratcliffe reportedly on Moscow visit | CIA | The Guardian
description: Unannounced trip reported by US media is said to be Ratcliffe’s first known visit to Russia as CIA chief
Author: Peter Beaumont
Headline: Unannounced trip reported by US media is said to be Ratcliffe’s first known visit to Russia as CIA chief
Content: John Ratcliffe was sworn in as director of the CIA in January 2025.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJohn Ratcliffe was sworn in as director of the CIA in January 2025.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesCIACIA director John Ratcliffe reportedly on Moscow visitUnannounced trip reported by US media is said to be Ratcliffe’s first known visit to Russia as CIA chiefPeter BeaumontTue 25 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe CIA director, John Ratcliffe, has made an unannounced visit to Moscow, US media reported, after flight data showed an American military aircraft flew to the Russian capital, where a US diplomatic motorcade was later spotted.CBS News quoted sources familiar with the situation as confirming Ratcliffe’s trip, saying it was his first known visit to Russia asCIAchief. Axios separately confirmed the visit, quoting a US official.The Financial Times reported that the Trump administration had asked Kyiv to pause its long-range strikes on major Russian cities during the course of the visit.There was no immediate comment from the CIA or the White House.Data from Flightradar24 showed a US military C-17 travelling from the US to Latvia and then on to Moscow. The tracker showed that the flight originated from Joint Base Andrews in Maryland, best known for hosting Air Force One.The C-17 Globemaster III is a large military transport aircraft that the US air force website says can be used for strategic and tactical airlift and airdrop missions as well as aeromedical evacuations.Ratcliffe’s reported visit comes as US-brokered talks aimed at ending Russia’s invasion of Ukraine have stalled. However, earlier this month Moscow freed a former US marine detained since 2022, amid concerns about his health.The reason for the visit is unclear but the CIA has mediated in recent US-Russia detainee exchanges and was involved in the 2024 prisoner exchange that secured the release of theWall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovichand the marine veteran Paul Whelan.Some speculation has focused on the war in Iran, which remains a bone of contention between Moscow and Washington. On Monday the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, announced a new economic sanctions strategydesigned to isolate Iran.Explore more on these topicsCIARussiaUS foreign policyEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: VW workers boo boss as he urges them to ‘pull together’ amid job cuts | Volkswagen (VW) | The Guardian
description: Oliver Blume faces workforce at German HQ as carmaker struggles against Chinese competition and US tariffs
Author: Kate Connolly
Headline: Oliver Blume faces workforce at German HQ as carmaker struggles against Chinese competition and US tariffs
Content: Oliver Blume, pictured at the International Motor Show last year, said VW wanted to guarantee a future for all of the company’s factories.Photograph: Kai Pfaffenbach/ReutersView image in fullscreenOliver Blume, pictured at the International Motor Show last year, said VW wanted to guarantee a future for all of the company’s factories.Photograph: Kai Pfaffenbach/ReutersVolkswagen (VW)VW workers boo boss as he urges them to ‘pull together’ amid job cutsOliver Blume faces workforce at German HQ as carmaker struggles against Chinese competition and US tariffsKate Connollyin BerlinTue 25 Aug 2026 11.47 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe chief executive of Volkswagen has faced boos and whistles of protest at the company’s headquarters after telling thousands of workers that a comprehensive reorganisation, which could include job losses and factory closures, is vital for its future.As Oliver Blume urged more than 10,000 workers on Tuesday to “pull together”, saying drastic restructuring measures at the struggling manufacturer were essential, they held up banners and shouted slogans, including: “Our jobs are not your balance sheet adjustments”.Blume said in Wolfsburg, northern Germany: “Our plan for the future is the largest transformation programme in our company’s history. To make this happen, everyone needs to pull together now.”The chief executive was speaking for the first time since details about plans formass job losses and possible factory closureswere made public.One of the goals of the proposed restructure was to guarantee a future for all plants at Europe’s largest carmaker, he said at the start of a tour of VW plants. “Our aim is to create viable prospects for all locations within the next six to 12 months.”Blume’s restructuring plans have yet to be approved by theVW group’s powerful supervisory board, which represents the labour force, as well as the state of Lower Saxony, the home of VW, and shareholders.The meeting, widely described by attenders as heated, was not open to the media. But witnesses – some of whom had to watch proceedings on a live stream outside the main meeting room owing to overcapacity – reported that Blume had said half of the expected job cuts, often cited at about 50,000, would take place in Germany. He reportedly said the other half would be made internationally, across a total of approximately 170 companies.Blume stressed that the worldwide job cuts plan was not a target, but a “theoretical calculation” and that it was based on the company’s costs, which he said were “about 30% above the average of comparable companies”. He said the executive board was “fully behind the future plan”, which involved bringing VW’s costs down in line with its competitors to make it sustainable for the future.Instead of forced job cuts, Blume said management wanted to rely on voluntary personnel measures as much as possible, including phased retirement, mutual agreements, and what he called “natural attrition and a restrictive hiring policy”.Blume described frequently proposed factory closures as the “last and most costly resort”. Among the proposals to keep factories open, VW’s manufacturing could switch towards the defence industry, and it could produce electric vehicles that are for sale in China, but not Europe yet, at its German factories.The manufacture of cars at VW’s plant in Osnabrück is due to end, possibly as soon as next year. At plants in Emden, Zwickau, Neckarsulm and Hanover, there are no plans for manufacturing from 2030.Daniela Cavallo, the head of VW’s works council, said opposition to factory closures was strong, calling them an “integral part” of the company.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Our trust in this company’s executive board, and in particular in its CEO Oliver Blume, has been damaged, not yet beyond repair, but nevertheless damaged,” she said, according to extracts from her speech shared with media by the works council.She accused Blume of being vague about the company’s plans. “It’s impossible to work with a CEO who doesn’t tell his people what’s going on,” she said.VW faces increasing pressure from rampant Chinese competition in Europe, decreasing sales in China and hefty US tariffs. Even before that, it was struggling for years with falling profits and overproduction in Europe.Last week, Blume described the situation at VW as “more than critical”. Previous cost-cutting measures, such as an average reduction of 20% in costs at its German factories last year, were insufficient.He said VW was too big, too slow and too complex. Blume is to attend eight more works council meetings over the coming days, in Braunschweig, Emden, Zwickau, Chemnitz, Dresden, Kassel-Baunatal, Salzgitter, and Hanover.Explore more on these topicsVolkswagen (VW)Automotive industryManufacturing sectorGermanyEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Gold price hits three-month high amid fears over Iran war and Trump economy | Gold | The Guardian
description: Bitcoin rises above $80,000 for the first time since May amid uncertainty over US fiscal plans
Author: Joanna Partridge
Headline: Bitcoin rises above $80,000 for the first time since May amid uncertainty over US fiscal plans
Content: The gold price tends to rise at times of uncertainty.Photograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe gold price tends to rise at times of uncertainty.Photograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersGoldGold price hits three-month high amid fears over Iran war and Trump economyBitcoin rises above $80,000 for the first time since May amid uncertainty over US fiscal plansJoanna PartridgeTue 25 Aug 2026 04.18 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 14.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGold prices hit their highest level in more than three months on Tuesday as continued conflict in the Middle East and ongoing political uncertainty fuelled the latest rally in the precious metal.Goldis viewed as a safe haven by investors and its price tends to rise at times of uncertainty.The metal has risen by about 15% so far during August, reaching $4,651 (£3,410) an ounce during Asian trading hours on Tuesday, before falling back slightly. This put gold on track for its best monthly performance in almost 30 years, since September 1999.Gold hits highest level in three months as traders worry about US inflation and bond market jitters – business liveRead moreThe price of gold began to rise in early August amid optimism that the US and Iran weregetting closer to restoring a ceasefirein the Middle East and reopening the strait of Hormuz. While this did not happen, the price of gold has continued to climb.Gold price chartThe latest rises came as investors awaited US inflation data and aclosely watched speechfrom the new US Federal Reserve chair, Kevin Warsh, amid anxiety in government bond markets over inflation and Donald Trump’s tax and spending plans.“Looking ahead, we expect dips in gold to be ⁠well-supported from buyers looking for gold to make its way towards the next ​upside resistance at $4,900/$5,000,” said Tony Sycamore, a market analyst at the broker IG.Bitcoin price chartThe price of bitcoin climbed above $80,000 (£58,680) on Tuesday, taking the cryptocurrency to a three-month high not seen since mid-May, which analysts attributed to a weakening US dollar and similar factors that were driving gold higher.The biggest rally in gold since the 1970s began in 2025, after Trump firstannounced the introduction of tariffson imported goods, prompting fears of disruption to global trade.The price topped $4,000 an ounce forthe first time last October, beforepassing $5,000 in Januaryand reaching a record high at the end of that month, partly fuelled by shifts in US policy, as well as political uncertainty elsewhere, includingin Franceand Japan.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHowever, many investors were surprised to see the price fall back again earlier this year, reaching $3,942 in late June, despite the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.War and geopolitical uncertainty would usually raise the gold price, making the fall counterintuitive. However, analysts said the US-Iran conflict has also driven oil prices higher, along with expectations of higher inflation and interest rate rises, which are factors that can subdue the gold price, outweighing demand for it as a safe store of wealth.There is renewed appetite for gold among investors as a “hedge against unclear US fiscal plans”, as a “hedge against inflation, amid questions over the Fed’s willingness, or ability, to fight inflation independently” and as a hedge against worries about the AI boom, according to Ipek Ozkardeskaya, a senior analyst at the Swiss banking group Swissquote.It comes as Trump hasannounced fresh tariffson cars and crucial raw materials from Canada, marking the latest deterioration in relations between the two neighbours, while the US hasthreatened to impose severe sanctionsagainst any country or entity maintaining economic ties with Iran.Explore more on these topicsGoldCommoditiesBitcoinCryptocurrenciesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Meta goes on trial as Silicon Valley faces a growing backlash | Technology | The Guardian
description: Also: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman expressed his surprising sympathy over the construction of datacenters across the country
Author: Blake Montgomery
Headline: Also: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman expressed his surprising sympathy over the construction of datacenters across the country
Content: Meta went on trial last week for allegedly designing platforms that are addictive for children.Photograph: Vicki Behringer/ReutersView image in fullscreenMeta went on trial last week for allegedly designing platforms that are addictive for children.Photograph: Vicki Behringer/ReutersTechScape newsletterTechnologyMeta goes on trial as Silicon Valley faces a growing backlashAlso: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman expressed his surprising sympathy over the construction of datacenters across the countryBlake MontgomeryTue 25 Aug 2026 07.21 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 08.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m Blake Montgomery, US tech editor at the Guardian, writing to you from a sunny park in New York City, which was supposed to endure rain all weekend but in fact delivered the best weather of the year.Why Meta’s big American backlash happened in courtA blockbuster case against Meta went to trial a week ago in Oakland, California, just north of the US tech company’s headquarters inSilicon Valley. California and 28 other US states are suing the £1tn ($1.36tn) company for allegedly designing products that are addictive for children, and hiding that information from the public.The courtroom has already seen minor fireworks. On the witness stand, a whistleblower who worked extensively withMark Zuckerbergaccused the CEO of lying to the public about his commitment to child safety. The prosecutor who opened the case framed her argument around four words that start with the letter H: Meta “hooks” in users, “holds” them on its platforms for as long as possible, “harvests” their data and then “hides” the truth from the public. She contended that this business model “worked especially well for kids”. More pyrotechnics are expected. Zuckerberg himself is expected to face tough questions on the stand, as is the CEO of Instagram.Meta has denied all allegations. Liza Crenshaw, a spokesperson for the company, said: “Rather than sticking to the facts or the law, the states have instead decided to chase an outlandish payout.”The trial presents a major challenge for Meta, not in the least, because in the United States, it’s proceedings like these that regulate the tech industry.China regulates tech by crackdown; the UK and Europe regulate the industry with legislation – Brussels’ prescriptive stipulations have become global defaults. But in the US, it’s mostly the courts that set the boundaries. They move much faster and with the vindictive authority that Americans often crave in response to harms. The slow wheels of democratic debate and bill drafting feel ill-suited to respond to Zuckerberg’s mantra of “move fast and break things”.Read more:Hook, hold, harvest and hide: Meta’s alleged strategy laid out in first week of landmark trialMeanwhile, US regulators have famously, obviously, andavowedlyhad difficulty keeping pace with the innovations that arise from Silicon Valley. As one Republican representative told a quantum computing expert during a 2018 hearing on Capitol Hill: “I can understand about 50% of the things you say.” Members of Congress would undoubtedly say the same about AI today.“Courts have the ability to force these changes much quicker than legislation. Courts have this authority to say, ‘Look, you either comply with these orders … or you stop doing business in our state’. States have the ability to enforce that. I think for these companies this is a real point of reckoning,” said Laura Marquez-Garrett, an attorney with the Social Media Victims Law Center, which is representing individual plaintiffs suing Meta and other social media companies in thousands of cases inCalifornia. Her organization was deeply involved in Meta’s first loss of a social media addiction trial in March in Los Angeles.Will this trial bring Meta’s moment of accountability? Maybe.Other tech companies have faced significant government lawsuits in recent years, and come away only stronger. Google faced perhaps the most significant antitrust litigation of the 2020s, losing its antitrust case against the US Department of Justice last year. The penalty was not divesting the Chrome browser but a “slap on the wrist”, critics said.But in the 1990s, a coalition of US states sued tobacco companies and secured a settlement that banned a laundry list of marketing tactics, including advertising on transit or anywhere outdoors, paid product placement for cigarettes, cartoon mascots, branded apparel and nearly all free distribution of cigarettes. You’d never see a tobacco company’s name on a US sports stadium today.Like those tobacco suits, the states’ suit against Meta may force the company to operate its social networks in less harmful ways and to keep them out of the hands of children. The states are explicitly asking the court that Meta be forced to change the design of its products to make them safer for children.“These AGs have a real chance at fixing the product,” said Marquez-Garrett.Read more:‘I always considered social media evil’: big tobacco whistleblower on tech’s addictive productsOpenAI makes safety moves‘We are hitting a different chapter’: OpenAI leader warns of threat of ‘persistent’ AI cyber-attacksOpenAI announces slowing pace of development after hack by rogue agentOpenAI launches ChatGPT for Teens with stronger safeguardsThe week the US data center backlash reached a fever pitchView image in fullscreenThe Pennhurst Asylum seasonal haunted house in Spring City, Pennsylvania, US.Photograph: Matthew Hatcher/Bloomerberg via Getty ImagesThe political champions of datacenters in the US are turn coatings to detractors. It’s knives out in the US datacenter backlash.Democrats who fast-tracked the development of these gargantuan fortresses of AI are now implementing restrictions on them. Republicans who trumpeted calls for their unrestricted construction are hastily rolling out plans to constrain them.Josh Shapiro, Democratic governor of Pennsylvania, rolled out restrictions for large datacenters last week. Just two months ago,the Guardianreported on how he was fast-tracking them and cutting red tape. Greg Abbott, Republican governor of Texas, said this weekend that the datacenter industry has “dug its own grave”. In November 2025, he called his state the “epicenter of AI development”. A Republican running for a contested Senate seat in Texas, Ken Paxton, debuted an anti-AI action plan over the weekend, though it was marked as “made with AI” on X.Read more:How the fight over US datacenters is scrambling this state’s politics: ‘We don’t want it’skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt’s no wonder: more than 70% of Americans oppose the construction of datacenters in their cities, per a poll released byGallupthree months ago. In just one year, the percentage of respondents saying they “strongly oppose” a datacenter being built near their homes more than doubled, according to polling by the climate news group Heatmap.Conservative media in the US has likewise taken notice.Fox Newson Thursday: “Silicon Valley is losing the datacenter fight, risking a repeat of a classic failure.”The Daily Wire, often a bellwether for young Republicans’ opinions, on Monday: “Silicon Valley created the datacenter backlash.”Donald Trump, always liable to turn on an ally and usually an extremely adept reader of political winds, is standing by the tech industry’s multitrillion-dollar infrastructure buildout.“Communities that don’t take a datacenter, they’re making a mistake,” the US president said in an interview with his former fixer and once-mortal nemesis Michael Cohen last week.Silicon Valley is extremely worried. The tech industry is all-in on AI, so much so that the entire US economy is as well, and the success of AI is predicated on access to enough computing power. No datacenters, no chips, no computing power, no AI, no profit, no economy.What to do when faced with a spiraling political threat?Some companies are playing nice. They’responsoringcommunity celebrations or pledging major community investments. They’re hosting listening sessions and making promises about how many jobs their projects will guarantee. Running de facto political campaigns for infrastructure projects is a big change for an industry accustomed to moving at the speed of bytes.Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, expressed some surprising empathy on apodcastlast month. His company has a range of partnerships across the US for hundreds of billions of dollars’ worth of datacenter construction.“I understand emotionally why people don’t want datacenters in their back yard in the same way that I don’t really want a nuclear power plant next to my house, even though I know it’s a super safe thing,” he said.Other Silicon Valley insiders are feeling hostile. Garry Tan, CEO of the influential startup incubator Y Combinator,wrote on Xthis weekend, “Reminder: the datacenter discourse is a documented psyop and they’re winning.” Alexis Ohanian, tech investor and co-founder of Reddit, wrote of the discourse: “It’s been brilliantly executed ngl [not gonna lie]. Facts are not gonna win this, esp at this point, it’s gotta be on emotional appeal.”In July, entrepreneur and Shark Tank host Kevin O’Leary accused opponents of his planned Utah datacenter of acting on behalf of the Chinese government. He later said he had “no evidence” for the claim and apologized for it, as did Fox News’ own hosts.The US’ adversaries have taken note of the heated debate and fanned the flames of fury. OpenAIdisclosedin early July that Chinese and Russian propagandists, including state-owned media, had used its tools to create materials circulated on X, including a cartoon tycoon holding bags of cash and smoking a cigar, encouraging pushback against datacenters.Reworked: A Guardian series about AI and the future of work‘Digging the grave of my profession’: the Hollywood creatives training AI to do their jobsWill AI give you the job? Automated hiring tools spark discrimination and secrecy lawsuitsThe wider TechScapeAfter more than 15 years of laptops in the classroom, do Australian schools need a rethink?Crypto bank part-owned by Trump family offers depositors way to ‘gain favor’ with White House, experts sayDid someone wearing Meta Glasses film you today? Are you sure?Explore more on these topicsTechnologyTechScape newsletterMetaOpenAICaliforniaDatacenters – USWest CoastSocial medianewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Lego sales jump 21% to nearly £5bn, helped by World Cup and F1 ranges | Retail industry | The Guardian
description: Danish toymaker also scores success with KPop Demon Hunters, Star Wars and botanicals products
Author: Sarah Butler
Headline: Danish toymaker also scores success with KPop Demon Hunters, Star Wars and botanicals products
Content: Lego sales rose by 21% as World Cup products including this figurine of Kylian Mbappe (front) and Lionel Messi (back) helped draw new customers.Photograph: Patrick T Fallon/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLego sales rose by 21% as World Cup products including this figurine of Kylian Mbappe (front) and Lionel Messi (back) helped draw new customers.Photograph: Patrick T Fallon/AFP/Getty ImagesRetail industryLego sales jump 21% to nearly £5bn, helped by World Cup and F1 rangesDanish toymaker also scores success with KPop Demon Hunters, Star Wars and botanicals productsSarah ButlerTue 25 Aug 2026 07.29 EDTFirst published on Tue 25 Aug 2026 04.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLego sales have risen by more than a fifth as tie-ups with the football World Cup, Formula One and the hit film KPop Demon Hunters as well as its flower-based and Star Wars kits drive demand.The toymaker said its revenues had increased by 21% to 41.9bn Danish kroner (£4.8bn) in the first six months of 2026, driven by strong growth in the Americas, Europe and the Asia-Pacific regions, offsetting stalled sales in China.Sales by its clients to consumers rose by 22% as it produced World Cup kits, including mini figures of players such as Harry Kane and even building kits of superstar players, including Cristiano Ronaldo and Lionel Messi which were retailing forup to £159.99.Net profit increased 32% to 8.6bn Danish kroner (£1bn) as the group launched 330 new products including its hi-tech Smart Play kit, withbricks that emit soundsand light.Lego launches Pokémon ‘smart’ bricks equipped for interactive battlesRead moreNiels B Christiansen, the chief executive of Lego Group, said: “We are very pleased with our strong start to 2026 and the excitement we see for the Lego brand. Our portfolio of products offers something for everyone, and culturally relevant brand experiences continue to drive demand across the globe. Our success in the market means we can maintain high investment levels in growth and sustainability for both the short and long term.”He said the World Cup was “a breakthrough for us” in providing “exciting sets” linked to football and “an example of us bringing the Lego brand close to a passion point and interest for many people”.He said Lego was expanding solar energy capacity at all of its factories. In June, it began constructing its largest solar installation so far in Billund, Denmark – its main headquarters and the home of the original Legoland park. The site, which will begin operating next year, will feature 160,000 panels able to produce 99 GWh a year. It is designed to match the company’s electricity needs in the town.View image in fullscreenThe Lego version of Cristiano Ronaldo.Photograph: Tom Little/ReutersLego also said it was also continuing its global shift towards using paper bags in its packaging and expected that to be completed next year.Increased use of recycled plastic in the bricks is also helping to offset rising costs of virgin plastic driven by the impact of the crisis in the Middle East which has driven up the price of oil.The company said it did expect to see costs rise in the second half of the year as the cost of fuelling its lorries rose as well as raw materials but said there would not be a “material impact” on the business.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLego has led a resurgence in the toy market in the past year, as adults look for an alternative entertainment to phones and TV screens.Christiansen said sales to both children and adults were increasing and there was a “nice synergy” between the two groups as when “more adults get excited about the brand they become super ambassadors” by buying the kits for children and young people.“Kidults”(buyers aged 12 and over) are spending spare cash on expensive Lego sets and collectible figurines. This group isbehind £1 in every £3 spent on toysin the UK, and these buyers spent 10% more in 2025 than the year before according to a study by the market research company Circana.With toys linked to a wide range of interests, from sports such asFormula Oneto hit films and TV shows including KPop Demon Hunters and Stranger Things, the British Toy and Hobby Association has said there appears to be an “evolving era of play, where toys are increasingly embedded in wider cultural moments, enjoyed by all the family”.Explore more on these topicsRetail industryLegoToysnewsShareReuse this content

title: The cat that fought Mussolini: how the Wulz photography sisters weaponised the family pet | Photography | The Guardian
description: Wanda and Marion Wulz defied the unbridled patriarchy of fascist Italy by shooting dancers, fencers and other famous women – as well as their cat Mucincina
Author: Joanna Moorhead
Headline: Wanda and Marion Wulz defied the unbridled patriarchy of fascist Italy by shooting dancers, fencers and other famous women – as well as their cat Mucincina
Content: ‘Cats symbolise freedom’ …the famous I + Cat image, combining the faces of Wanda and Mucincina.Photograph: Wanda Wulz/Archivi Alinari-Collezione Zannier, FlorenceView image in fullscreen‘Cats symbolise freedom’ …the famous I + Cat image, combining the faces of Wanda and Mucincina.Photograph: Wanda Wulz/Archivi Alinari-Collezione Zannier, FlorencePhotographyThe cat that fought Mussolini: how the Wulz photography sisters weaponised the family petWanda and Marion Wulz defied the unbridled patriarchy of fascist Italy by shooting dancers, fencers and other famous women – as well as their cat MucincinaJoanna MoorheadTue 25 Aug 2026 10.12 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 12.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘In those fascist times,” says Federica Muzzarelli ofItalyin the 1920s and 30s, “women were not free. They were regarded as mothers and homemakers. But the Wulz sisters were determined to create their own destiny. They chose photography as a way of being independent – and to show through their images that women could live that way.”Muzzarelli is the curator of Wanda and Marion Wulz: Avant-Garde Photography in 20th Century Italy, a show about to open at theEstorick Collectionin London. The Wulz sisters experimented with blended and altered images more than half a century before Photoshop was invented. The most famous image to emerge from their studio was I + Cat, a self-portrait of Wanda superimposed on the face of the family pet. But the show aims to cast Marion in a new light, showing that she was no mere assistant, but rather equal to her sister in terms of photography, as they championed feminism in fascist Italy, keeping the idea of women’s emancipation alive at a time of unbridled patriarchal ideology.double quotation markFamous women wanted to be photographed by themWanda, born in Trieste in 1903, was a promising dancer and musician; Marion, two years her junior, had been to art school and wanted to paint. But after the pair inherited their father’s photographic studio, which had in turn been founded by his father, they realised it represented their best path to an autonomous future. “They photographed modern women, dancing, playing sports, doing gymnastics,” says Muzzarelli. Women who were artists, poets, writers and actors sat for the sisters. Among them were painter Leonor Fini and Olympic fencing champion Irene Camber.View image in fullscreenModern woman … fencer Irene Camber.Photograph: Marion Wulz/Archivi Alinari-Archivio Studio Wulz, FlorenceIn 1932, Wanda exhibited six works, including I + Cat in the National Exhibition of FuturistPhotography. The show was staged to mark 10 years since the fascist revolution but, contends Muzzarelli, Wanda was never interested in that . She just wanted to show, as the only woman taking part, that she was every bit as capable as the men.“She showed she had the ability and skill to create a photomontage,” says Muzzarelli. Her technique for I + Cat, which superimposed one negative on top of another, was invented in the mid-19th century, but Wanda used it in a new way, making one face hers and the other that of Mucincina, the family cat. Both negatives will be in the London show, as well as the finished work. “Wanda wanted to explore the idea of female identity, of the cat as a free creature, a symbol of freedom,” says Muzzarelli, who believes another picture Wanda showed in the 1932 exhibition – Futurist Breakfast, showing items from a woman’s dresser – was also included to make a feminist point.The exhibition was Wanda’s only foray into futurism, but the years that followed were the sisters’ heyday. They continued to live in the apartment block in central Trieste in which they had been born, and where their studio was based. It became the centre of an informal female salon.View image in fullscreen‘They wanted to look perfect’ … ballerina Alba Wiegele.Photograph: Marion Wulz/Archivi Alinari-Archivio Studio Wulz, Florence“For several years,” says Claudia Baroncini, director of the Fondazione Alinari per la Fotografia, which owns the sisters’ archive, “the fashion designer Anita Pittoni lived with them. With her, they created a kind of club of artists – women who wanted to experiment with new ways of living. So they were pushing a different sort of life alongside a different sort of photography. And of course, photography has always been about a fusion of ideas and reality. So they were living their art.”Their first role in the studio was as subjects – they were often dressed up and photographed by their father, Carlo, when they were children. So they were always acutely aware of self-image, of disguise, of what appearance symbolised. As portrait photographers they were experts at “improving” the look of their sitters. “They were very clever with negatives,” says Baroncini, “creating shadows to change the shape of someone’s mouth or eyes, or to improve the quality of their skin. You can see, looking at the negatives, how much work they did to make their prints perfect. And that meant famous women wanted to be photographed by them, because they wanted to look perfect.”They also photographed one another: the show will include Marion’s striking portrait of Wanda wearing motorcycle goggles and another of her dressed as Cleopatra, while Wanda’s shots of Marion include her wearing designs by Pittoni, along with an extraordinarily modern-looking closeup with shining eyes.In spring 1945, as the second world war ended, Trieste was liberated from fascist rule by the Yugoslav army. From the terrace of their apartment, Marion photographed tanks and soldiers – and later celebrations in the street when the Anglo-American troops arrived. “These images show she was fully part of the artistic partnership,” says Baroncini.Although the women worked until the 1970s, they never recaptured their early success. Money became a struggle and they closed their studio in 1981, while continuing to take photographs. After Wanda died in 1984, Marion – who lived another nine years – documented their life and work together in a series of diaries.“Their lives had been tough,” says Baroncini, “and they didn’t realise the importance of their work for the history of photography. Wanda had a brief burst of fame during the futurist period, but they would be very surprised to know that, more than 120 years after their births, they were being recognised as great photographers.”At theEstorick Collection, London, from 16 September to 20 DecemberExplore more on these topicsPhotographyItalyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Climate-saving wonder – or €240m vanity bauble that ages like milk? The rocks set to hit Rotterdam docks | Architecture | The Guardian
description: MVRDV – the firm behind Marble Arch Mound – says Rotterdam ROCKS! will inspire visitors to live sustainably. But in an era when the greenest building is the one that already exists, this tottering cairn looks set to misfire
Author: Catherine Slessor
Headline: MVRDV – the firm behind Marble Arch Mound – says Rotterdam ROCKS! will inspire visitors to live sustainably. But in an era when the greenest building is the one that already exists, this tottering cairn looks set to misfire
Content: ‘Flintstones-esque primitivism’ … a digital rendering of Rotterdam ROCKS!Illustration: MVRDVView image in fullscreen‘Flintstones-esque primitivism’ … a digital rendering of Rotterdam ROCKS!Illustration: MVRDVArchitectureClimate-saving wonder – or €240m vanity bauble that ages like milk? The rocks set to hit Rotterdam docksMVRDV – the firm behind Marble Arch Mound – says Rotterdam ROCKS! will inspire visitors to live sustainably. But in an era when the greenest building is the one that already exists, this tottering cairn looks set to misfireCatherine SlessorTue 25 Aug 2026 07.37 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 13.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘It looks like something Shrek would throw up,” sniffed one online commentator, unflatteringly comparing Rotterdam ROCKS!, the recently unveiled proposal for a waterfront site in Europe’s largest port, with the vomitings of a cartoon ogre. Designed by Dutch architectural firm MVRDV, which gave London the supremely underwhelmingMarble Arch Moundin 2021, Rotterdam ROCKS! (the use of EMPHATIC CAPITALS connoting an in-your-face energy) is the winner of a major architectural competition intended to create “a new world wonder”.But instead of a modern Hanging Gardens of Babylon or contemporary Colossus of Rhodes, MVRDV’s super slick renderings depict a pile of artificial “rocks” (or ROCKS!) stacked together in a humongously scaled tottering cairn, wreathed in suspiciously luxuriant foliage and sluiced by a preposterous waterfall.Conceived as a paying visitor attraction that will proselytise aspects of sustainability and green living, the €240m (£205m) project is the precocious brainchild of Dutch entrepreneurDon Ritzen, who made his reputation throughRockstart, a venture capital fund for green tech startups. Ritzen’s evangelising mission is to speed the world’s transition to a green economy via his non-profit organisationShift, which provided the impetus for a radical new landmark building – to be constructed on a site previously earmarked for football club Feyenoord’s new stadium.View image in fullscreen‘Turns architecture into a regenerative, urban ecosystem’ … a rendering of the central hall of Rotterdam ROCKS!Illustration: MVRDVThe project will anchor the Waterkant, a more architecturally humdrum large-scale urban development on the south bank of the Maas. Pulverised during the second world war, Rotterdam’s docklands have provided an obliging tabula rasa for architectural experimentation, but with its amped-up, Flintstones-esque primitivism, Rotterdam ROCKS! will be far and away the most conspicuously off piste offering to date.Hyperbole abounds. Described as “a stacked landscape of living rocks that turns architecture into a regenerative, urban ecosystem and a new landmark for the city: rocks that breathe”, the project incorporates the more prosaic functions of a hotel, conference centre, food court and viewing deck. Underpinning it all is an immersive experience called the Elysium, which will illustrate paradigms for sustainability and circular living, elevating them into “something individuals, companies and organisations can feel, experience and act on”.View image in fullscreenInspiring a new green gospel? … a rendering of the Elysium experience at Rotterdam ROCKS!Illustration: MVRDVIn theory, visitors forking out entrance fees between €20 and €45 will come away energised and motivated to spread a new green gospel that goes beyond recycling their rubbish and carbon-offsetting their short break flights. But in practice, it may well end up being just a wallet-sapping mooch around a weird-looking building, rather like visiting a funfair.Ifthe dismaying experience of the Marble Arch Moundis anything to go by, then MVRDV will have its work cut out. Optimistically conceived as a temporary artificial hill, softly studded with lush vegetation, the Mound was beset by cost overruns, shonky construction and visitor apathy. Its patchy flanks of stuck-on turf were describedby one criticas “more like an ensemble of ill-matched carpet tiles than a greensward”, prompting comparisons to those scrubby winter wonderlands that pop up every Christmas to disappoint yuletide revellers.View image in fullscreenBack to reality … Marble Arch Mound.Photograph: David Levene/the GuardianComputer-generated renderings are a perpetual hostage to fortune, and MVRDV went gangbusters on Rotterdam ROCKS!, doubtless in an attempt to seduce the competition jurors. But already some aspects of the design are being dialled down – the sluicing waterfall has been quietly aborted – as the chastening reality of how this absurd confection might actually be built begins to sink in. A non-computer generated image shows architect Winy Maas (the M of MVRDV) clutching a pile of moss-covered pebbles.Wider contradictions also abound. Ritzen clearly subscribes to history’s “great man” theory, in which idealistic outliers and entrepreneurs heroically save the world, and progress is impelled by “charismatic” individuals (the Musks and the Zuckerbergs) rather than the messy flailings of collective political and social endeavour.But in an era increasingly being reshaped by the mantra “the greenest building is the one that already exists”, the idea of a constructing a hugely costly vanity bauble that promises to age like milk seems like a stupendous misfire, calculated simply to stroke egos and stoke clickbait.View image in fullscreenDoubly damned … a rendering of Rotterdam ROCKS!Illustration: MVRDVWouter Vanstiphout, a leading Dutch architectural historian,summed it up: “It is as if MVRDV has allowed the entire fundamental contradiction between architecture and sustainability to implode in a gesture of ontological self-loathing, a metaphorical ruin of the very idea of architecture, collapsing under its own weight, gnawed at and overgrown by a nature that has turned against humanity out of spite.”The final irony was that Rotterdam ROCKS! was unveiled during the height of Europe’s infernal summer, when the existential consequences of the climate crisis became even more viscerally apparent, as wildfires immolated large tracts of hill and dale. Low-lyingNetherlands(the Maldives of Europe) is doubly damned, with over half its terrain also vulnerable to flooding. Nearly all of Rotterdam lies below sea level, so if things continue on the predicted hell-in-a-handcart trajectory, Rotterdam ROCKS! may well be under water some day. Which might be the best place for it.Explore more on these topicsArchitectureNetherlandsClimate crisisRegenerationfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rise of the Footsoldier: Retribution review – never-ending hardman-on-a-mission franchise heads to Ibiza | Movies | The Guardian
description: The seventh in the series takes longstanding lead gangster Tate, played to the hilt as always by Craig Fairbrass, to the White Isle to knock some heads together
Author: Catherine Bray
Headline: The seventh in the series takes longstanding lead gangster Tate, played to the hilt as always by Craig Fairbrass, to the White Isle to knock some heads together
Content: ‘These are very serious people’ and other dialogue gems … Craig Fairbrass in Rise of the Footsoldier: Retribution.Photograph: Evelyn Xing/Signature EntertainmentView image in fullscreen‘These are very serious people’ and other dialogue gems … Craig Fairbrass in Rise of the Footsoldier: Retribution.Photograph: Evelyn Xing/Signature EntertainmentMoviesReviewRise of the Footsoldier: Retribution review – never-ending hardman-on-a-mission franchise heads to IbizaThe seventh in the series takes longstanding lead gangster Tate, played to the hilt as always by Craig Fairbrass, to the White Isle to knock some heads togetherCatherine BrayTue 25 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe seventh instalment in this seemingly never-ending series opens with a line of voiceover from star Craig Fairbrass, summarising forthcoming proceedings nicely: “They killed my best friend, now they all have to die.” The real-life hardman Pat Tatemight have been murdered in his 30s in Essex in 1995, but that hasn’t proved a setback for his invincible fictionalised counterpart, played to the hilt throughout the entire franchise with hard-headed gusto by Fairbrass. In this one, Tate is in Ibiza, but rather than larging it, he’s intent on tracking down his enemies and exacting the titular retribution. Various arms dealers, guns for hire and, perhaps more unexpectedly, the CIA, provide a bit of grit in the oyster.The director here is series veteran Nick Nevern, having appeared in ROTF: Marbella in 2019, and stepped up to the director’s chair for 2023’s ROTF: Vengeance. Retribution is at its best when engaged in stylised slow-motion action sequences that play out like The Untouchables, if The Untouchables had a soundtrack influenced by Paul Oakenfold and was made on about 100th of the budget. Dialogue is not its strong point, and is mostly made up of interchangeable gangster film cliches. (It’s all, “These are very serious people” and “You remind me so much of her”.) You may not be ponying up to watch a Footsoldier movie on the basis that you’ll be hearing curlicued witticisms worthy of Oscar Wilde, but it is possible to write gangster-speak with a bit more zest. Even Nick Love’s The Business gave us: “The geezer was so hard even his nightmares were scared of him.”Dialogue issues might matter less if the whole thing was a bit more wham, bam, thank you m’am, but the overall run time is distinctly baggy – a few more double-crossings and colourfully accented lads with different agendas have found their way into the mix than can strictly be necessary; it’s Tate’s vengeance quest that should remain the backbone of the piece. It might be time for the demise of the footsoldier – or at least a film that sticks more strictly to the promise of its opening line.Rise of the Footsoldier: Retribution is in UK cinemas from 28 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmThrillersCrime filmsCrimereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Penny Lane Is Dead review – Aussie slasher comedy zips from Neighbours to nasty | Movies | The Guardian
description: Mia’Kate Russell’s 80s-set Ozsploitation horror is a tad slapdash, but the grungy gore and seething catfights save it from dud status
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: Mia’Kate Russell’s 80s-set Ozsploitation horror is a tad slapdash, but the grungy gore and seething catfights save it from dud status
Content: Deranged and oddly fetching … Tahlee Fereday and Bailey Spalding in Penny Lane is Dead.Photograph: ShudderView image in fullscreenDeranged and oddly fetching … Tahlee Fereday and Bailey Spalding in Penny Lane is Dead.Photograph: ShudderMoviesReviewPenny Lane Is Dead review – Aussie slasher comedy zips from Neighbours to nastyMia’Kate Russell’s 80s-set Ozsploitation horror is a tad slapdash, but the grungy gore and seething catfights save it from dud statusLeslie FelperinTue 25 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 04.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere is a muddled if energetic effort from Australian writer-director Mia’Kate Russell. There’s a little too much blurriness around the edges, making relationships and motivations slightly opaque, while the last-minute entrances and exits are a bit on the haphazard side. But as a study of seething girl-on-girl anger that leads to ultraviolence, it’s a gas.Set in Australia in 1986 (presumably because this means no mobile phones, and thus no calling for help), a trio of high-school besties prepares for a night of partying before the summer ends. Penny (Bailey Spalding) is planning to go to university to study law and asks her girlfriend Toni (Tahlee Fereday) to come with her. The two have only recently become lovers and they haven’t yet come out to their buddy Amy (Alexandra Jensen) – a sweet, childlike teen who still carries a stuffed tiger toy around for comfort.And they most certainly haven’t come out to Kat (Sophia Wright-Mendelsohn, daughter of Aussie actor Ben Mendelsohn) – an erstwhile friend with whom they haven’t hung out for a while and who they didn’t think would show up that evening. Except here she is, bearing cupcakes for each of them with insults piped on the top in icing. Kat, it turns out, has drugged Penny’s cake, so she passes out and Kat’s super-skeevy ex-con boyfriend Angus (Ben O’Toole) shows up with his leather-clad crew – and suddenly it all goes from an episode of Neighbours to The Last House on the Left.The bits where Wright-Mendelsohn and Fereday, both of them great, slug it out and hurl insults at each other are the best parts of the film, full of Catfight-style grudge-match malice. What’s more, director Russell started out as a film makeup artist, so makes sure the cast is smeared with red goo in such a way as to look both deranged and oddly fetching.Penny Lane Is Dead is on Shudder and AMC+ from 28 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmHorror filmsAustralian filmreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Zip Wire review – cancer-curing scientist is on the hook for cable-dangle thriller | Movies | The Guardian
description: This nonsensical film sees an OCD-afflicted scientist fending off assassins while hanging from an aerial wire, and fails to get pulses racing for even a minute
Author: Cath Clarke
Headline: This nonsensical film sees an OCD-afflicted scientist fending off assassins while hanging from an aerial wire, and fails to get pulses racing for even a minute
Content: Hangin’ out … MyAnna Buring in Zip Wire.Photograph: Signature EntertainmentView image in fullscreenHangin’ out … MyAnna Buring in Zip Wire.Photograph: Signature EntertainmentMoviesReviewZip Wire review – cancer-curing scientist is on the hook for cable-dangle thrillerThis nonsensical film sees an OCD-afflicted scientist fending off assassins while hanging from an aerial wire, and fails to get pulses racing for even a minuteCath ClarkeTue 25 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 03.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn this silly, low-adrenaline thriller, the title star is a rickety old zip wire bolted into the side of a mountain in the Italian Dolomites that was never intended for human use. It was constructed in the first world war to sling weapons and supplies hundreds of feet down the valley – and is still used to get the occasional goat off the mountain. But for the second half of this film, a world-famous British research scientist with an extreme fear of heights dangles from it, fighting off highly skilled assassins in increasingly preposterous ways.The scientist is Amy (MyAnna Buring); she has discovered a cure for lung cancer, and her drive is explained in syrupy hospital-ward flashbacks to her mother dying when she was a teenager. Amy also has OCD – she is so anxious about germs that she never takes off her rubber gloves, and has an assistant in her lab to do anything that involves touching or handling objects. (Like all the characters, she never gets beyond a stereotype.) Her research is bankrolled by a big pharma company, whose CEO is played by Saffron Burrows (now seemingly mandatory casting for ropey British thrillers).Amy’s gamechanging discoveries result in an old-school conspiracy, involving a notebook with her research written in code and a trio of contract killers. Which is how Amy ends up in the Dolomites (where everyone has an English accent), halfway across a zip line. Supposedly, a human body cannot remain in a state of maximum panic for more than 30 minutes, but Amy seems to bat away her terrible fear of heights in about five minutes flat. For the audience, you’ll be lucky if this gets your pulse racing for more than two of them.Zip Wire is on digital platforms from 31 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmThrillersreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Why isn’t there hip-hop in 3/4 time?’: the groups reinventing a Polish folk dance for the modern age  | Folk music | The Guardian
description: The oberek is a traditional dance beloved of state folk ensembles – but a new generation of musicians is reconfiguring its music into wild new forms, merging folk steps with electronics and the sound of Chicago footwork
Author: Jakub Knera
Headline: The oberek is a traditional dance beloved of state folk ensembles – but a new generation of musicians is reconfiguring its music into wild new forms, merging folk steps with electronics and the sound of Chicago footwork
Content: Spinning out … Tercet Imperial.Photograph: Marek Kita/PRView image in fullscreenSpinning out … Tercet Imperial.Photograph: Marek Kita/PRFolk music‘Why isn’t there hip-hop in 3/4 time?’: the groups reinventing a Polish folk dance for the modern ageThe oberek is a traditional dance beloved of state folk ensembles – but a new generation of musicians is reconfiguring its music into wild new forms, merging folk steps with electronics and the sound of Chicago footworkJakub KneraTue 25 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 07.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s 6pm on the first day of OFF festival in Katowice, and a crowd is gathering in front of one of the stages to watch newcomers Tercet Imperial. Sporting disco outfits of nylon jackets, tracksuits and Chicago Bulls caps, keyboardist Piotr Zabrodzki deploys resonant acid melodies, while drummer Jan Emil Młynarski plays a rapid, irregular rhythm that brings to mind the scattergun beats of footwork, the ghetto-house subgenre that grew out of Chicago in the late 90s.Not many of those jerking their limbs to the music in front of the stage are likely to realise that they are listening to a distinctly Polish sound: that of the oberek, a traditional dance in triple metre whose name derives from the Polish verb “to spin”, because it usually accompanies couples whirling across dancefloors in a circular motion.“We play traditional music, but on different instruments,” says lead singer Joanna Sztucka. On Tercet Imperial’s debut album, Prymat, the melodies and lyrics of traditional songs are woven into contemporary production: violins and a snare drum are replaced by synthesisers and drum pads. “It’s is an attempt to create an alternative history,” Młynarski says. “We’re doing it primarily for people who know nothing about traditional music and don’t need to know anything at all.”Tercet Imperial are part of a wider phenomenon.Far, far in Chicago. Footberk Suite, by drummer Gary Gwadera (real name: Piotr Gwadera), is a concept album about an imagined meeting of the oberek and Chicago footwork. Its genesis can be found in the influential footwork compilation Bangs & Works Vol 1,released by Planet Mu in 2010, which was an inspiration to Gwadera. “I suddenly realised that grooves and this pulse of footwork were typical of the oberek, and that I wanted to combine them,” he says. To record it, he used dżaz, a minimalist percussion kit from the Polish countryside, along with a Roland TR-808 and electronic pads.View image in fullscreenA gentle flow … Mateusz Kowalski.Photograph: Cezary Piwowarski / Nowa Tradycja FestivalMusician Mateusz Kowalski offers a different take on this traditional music with his groups Radical Polish Ansambl, Tęgie Chłopy and Warszawska Orkiestra Sentymentalna. On his first solo album, released last year under the name Sam Kowalski, he replaced the violin with a gitalele (a small instrument combining the features of a classical guitar and a ukulele) and slowed the tempo, with no percussion – transforming the oberek’s nervous phrasing into a gentle, melancholic flow reminiscent of Appalachian folk music.Elsewhere, Polish duoOplafirst translated the tripartite rhythms and raw energy of the oberek to electric guitar and drums, and later to electronic pads, adding effects and looped guitar parts. Polish-French jazz quartetLumpekssound like Ornette Coleman on a prolonged ramble through the Polish countryside. Suferi, meanwhile, combines oberek rhythms with electrified violin, an effects-laden guitar, and a hip-hop groove on the drums.Often, even a seasoned ear won’t immediately pick up on the traditional dance’s influences – and that’s precisely the point. As Kowalski explains, when releasing the self-titled album, he didn’t describe it as traditional music. “Rather, I wanted to say: listen without any preconceptions and see what this music does to you. The idea is for people to be surprised when they find out that this is traditional material,” he says.The new interest in Polish tradition and its creative expressions stems from the turbulent history of rural music in Poland. Before the second world war, it was part of everyday life – weddings, celebrations and rituals – and passed down by ear. But war and migration disrupted the continuity of music across regions. During the communist era, a state-sanctioned version of folklore emerged, represented by the state song-and-dance ensembles Mazowsze and Śląsk. After the country’s political transformation in the 1990s, Poland’s own brand of popular dance music, disco polo, took over the social function of the old village band. Incorporating some traditional folk elements into the framework of Italo disco rhythms, it was meant to be accessible, cheap, and suitable for weddings.Paradoxically, as the countryside moved away from traditional music, city dwellers began to seek it out again. The Dom Tańca social centre, established in Warsaw in the 1990s, played a key role in reviving traditional music. Young musicians sought out rural masters, recording and learning directly from them, while also reviving the tradition of village dances.View image in fullscreenThe Mazowsze ensemble takes a turn.Photograph: Mondadori Portfolio/Getty Images“For my generation, traditional music was initially something to be ashamed of. In fact, nobody in my circle knew anything about it,” says Gwadera. “I didn’t have the key to understanding that music, and I saw it as a bit of an embarrassment.”Opla’s Hubert Zemler admits that he had listened to Hindu raga before he heard his first interesting oberek. “For a long time, I associated folk music with Mazowsze and the Śląsk ensemble – a centralised, sanitised view of tradition. Obereks have a ternary, danceable metre; they’re round dances, and people used to play them for hours on end. But they didn’t make their way into disco polo or pop. Why isn’t there any hip-hop in 3/4 time?”Since 2020, this musical interest in the countryside has coincided with a broader “peasant turn” in Polish culture and the public debate. Books such as Adam Leszczyński’s A People’s History of Poland and Kacper Pobłocki’s Chamstwo, as well as the Netflix series 1670 (the recently released third season of which has been this year’s most popular Polish series) have shifted historical narratives away from royalty, nobility and the intelligentsia. They started debates about the peasant origins of most of Polish society: the experience of serfdom, the history of social mobility, the suppression of rural roots.View image in fullscreenRural revivalists … Tercet Imperial.Photograph: Marek KitaNowadays, says Gwadera, traditional music is increasingly “treated as part of our own heritage and the forgotten history of the majority of society – it has become a response to the need for a sense of community”.The oberek no longer needs to be a reference or a folkloric embellishment – it is becoming the language of modern creativity. Says Młynarski: “I’m convinced that if this old rural melodic tradition had survived and not been supplanted by disco polo and party music in the 1990s, people would still be playing it today – but on synthesisers and in tracksuits.”Tercet Imperial play Unsound festival in Kraków 8–11 October, Le Guess Who? in Utrecht 5–8 November and Unsound London 25–26 November 2026Explore more on these topicsFolk musicElectronic musicfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Great Dictator by Matthew Sweet review – the fabulous life of Barbara Cartland | Biography books | The Guardian
description: A brilliant new biography that does it subject the favour of taking her seriously – even if few else did
Author: Kathryn Hughes
Headline: A brilliant new biography that does it subject the favour of taking her seriously – even if few else did
Content: Barbara Cartland in the 70s.Photograph: Smith Archive/AlamyView image in fullscreenBarbara Cartland in the 70s.Photograph: Smith Archive/AlamyBook of the dayBiography booksReviewThe Great Dictator by Matthew Sweet review – the fabulous life of Barbara CartlandA brilliant new biography that does it subject the favour of taking her seriously – even if few else didKathryn HughesTue 25 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 19.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBarbara Cartland was famous for dictating her novels. With a pekingese clamped to her hot pink bosom she would lie back on a library couch and exhale a story about virginal girls taming wayward dukes, damaged airmen or misunderstood surgeons. Meanwhile Miss Savory, Mrs Smith or Mrs Morgan, picked for being unfidgety and sneezeless, would take everything down in immaculate Pitman shorthand. Cartland reckoned on being able to polish off 8,000 words a day. “In this way,” she told one of the many reporters who quizzed her on her astonishing productivity, “the typescript for an 80,000-word novel is finished in a fortnight.” At her peak she was pushing out 23 books a year which added up to 723 in total. Only Agatha Christie and William Shakespeare topped her lifetime sales of 750m.Cartland was a dictator in other ways, too. Husbands, dogs, houses and the local council were all expected to bend themselves to her indomitable will. Resistance, let alone opposition, was futile. The managing director of the company that printed her books suggested that she read Nietzsche on the perceptive grounds that they had a lot of ideas in common. Oddly, he also declared himself madly in love with her. Behind that marshmallowy exterior, all pink chiffon, candyfloss hair and soft, smudgy lines, there lurked sinews of high-tensile steel.Anyone expecting this biography of Barbara Cartland to be an amusing takedown of amonstre sacréalong the lines of Craig Brown’s witty 2017 decimation of Princess Margaret will be disappointed. Rather, Matthew Sweet pays his subject the compliment of absolute seriousness, regarding her as a cultural phenomenon whose extraordinary life, stretching the entire 20th century, deserves deep study. Sweet has had unfettered access to the cornucopia of material that Cartland left behind at Camfield Place, the Hertfordshire manor house where she lived until her death in 2000 at the age of 98. Conducting a fingertip search of her letters, scrapbooks and typescripts, Sweet has crafted a generous but clear-sighted account of a woman who was too often reduced to the status of a lazy joke.She was born in 1901 into the lower upper class. On her father’s side she was pure trade. James Cartland and Son was a Birmingham metalworkers turning out umbrella stands, crocodile-shaped inkwells, shelf brackets shaped like sea monsters and “pharaonic letterboxes embossed with meaningless hieroglyphs”. Her adored mother Polly, meanwhile, was Gloucestershire gentry and there had been the usual rows about marrying down. Cartland’s paternal grandfather killed himself when the business went bust and her father retreated into alcoholism, leaving Polly to manage the tricky business of getting her daughter launched into a life the family could no longer afford.Sweet suggests that this constellation of losses and compensations set the emotional template for Cartland’s adult life. Men were necessary but fragile and certainly best not relied upon. Having come out as a deb in 1919 into a world where there were not enough husbands to go round, Barbara set out to become financially self-sufficient by plunging into the only kind of work for which she was qualified. For the next decade she filed gossipy titbits about young London society to the Express, the Mirror and the Daily Mail.This was the world of the Bright Young Things, so often written up today as a madcap time of pyjama parties and midnight dashes to the continent. In fact, Cartland’s columns reveal a society still in shock from the first world war: fathers are dead (Cartland lost hers in the trenches in 1918), grand family houses have been sold, divorce is everywhere and life seems impossible without alcohol or drugs. The men whom Cartland stepped out with were not the heart-throb dukes and dashing airmen that she would later write about, but broken people without the language to express their desolation. “My contemporaries were ashamed to show emotion,” she observed with characteristic perception in her 1943 memoir The Isthmus Years. “We had all of us a horror of sympathy.”So instead she simply carried on with a brittle determination to make the best of things. After plenty of dalliances with men called things like Pingo Langrishe and Nigs Ratendone she made a tactical marriage to a dull man called Alexander McCorquodale who was heir to a printing fortune. When he retreated into drink – shades of her father – she effected a neat swap by divorcing, then marrying his paternal cousin. In this way there was no need to change her surname: she had replaced one Mr McCorquodale with another. It rankled that she never achieved a title until she herself was made a Dame in 1991. By contrast, her ambitious daughter, Raine, managed to insert herself into the peerage not once but three times through each of her carefully strategic marriages.The only man who really mattered to Cartland was her beloved younger brother, Ronald. They went on holiday together and endlessly discussed the cod-eastern philosophies that were all the rage in the 1920s: Ouspensky and Gurdjieff were favourites and Cartland retained a vague mysticism to the end of her life involving ghosts and spiritual healing. She also believed in flying saucers and the power of honey to cure just about anything.Brother and sister bonded too over politics, specifically a socially engaged, internationalist Toryism. Barbara bossed Ronald into parliament where he became a leading anti-appeaser. She in turn wrote one of the first of the tiny number of 1930s British novels that dealt specifically with the evils of Nazi antisemitism. Dangerous Experiment (1936) involves the improbable story of Lena Carrington who, after a shipwreck and a spell as the slave of a tribe of thunder-worshippers in the Caucasus, ends up in Germany where she is courted by a Nazi lover. In the end she breaks things off when she sees him mistreating a Jewish refugee.This, of course, is not the Barbara Cartland that most of us remember from the 80s and beyond. In what Sweet calls her “imperial phase” she was writing novels with paper-thin plots that she endlessly recycled. She was also a relentless self-promoter. Bed linen, candles and towels were all enthusiastically marketed under her name, although with remarkable restraint she drew the line at scented toilet paper. She also pulled off a promotion with Dewhurst the butcher, which offered customers one of six previously unpublished Cartland novels for every £12 they spent. The promotion was not a great success because of the sheer weirdness of “being given a copy of Desire in the Desert with a parcel of mince”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut when, in a stroke of fortune so improbable that even now it hardly seems real, her daughter, Raine, became Diana Spencer’s stepmother, Cartland sensed new opportunities for cross-pollination. She took to announcing “I invented virgins” and managed to imply that the royal wedding of 1981 was somehow her doing, despite being pointedly not invited. Raine, a chip off  the old block, made sure that the gift shop at the Spencer family seat, Althorp, stocked a full run of Barbara Cartlands.It would be easy to dismiss Cartland as a quirk, an aberration the likes of which we will not see again. But the great triumph of this brilliant book is the way that Sweet embeds her firmly in the economic, political, social and artistic transformations of the 20th century while charting the ways in which she also transcended them. Somehow, and this remains the deep mystery of it all, Barbara Cartland emerges as that rather admirable thing: an entirely self-made woman.The Great Dictator: a Life of Barbara Cartland by Matthew Sweet is published by Hodder & Stoughton (£25). title: Feminism for a World on Fire by Natasha Walter review – hope amid the hopelessness | Natasha Walter | The Guardian
description: A writer and activist links the climate crisis to battles for justice around the world in this vital book
Author: Samantha Ellis
Headline: A writer and activist links the climate crisis to battles for justice around the world in this vital book
Content: Natasha Walter.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianView image in fullscreenNatasha Walter.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianNatasha WalterReviewFeminism for a World on Fire by Natasha Walter review – hope amid the hopelessnessA writer and activist links the climate crisis to battles for justice around the world in this vital bookSamantha EllisTue 25 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 06.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt has become increasingly difficult to change our minds, to question our own views or to find common ground with people we disagree with, all of which makes Natasha Walter’s new book both refreshing and exhilarating.In her ebullient 1998 debut The New Feminism, Walter hailed Margaret Thatcher as a trailblazer. In this fiercer, bleaker work, she rips into the “glossy language of aspiration feminism”, “the message that the individual woman can do anything she wants if she only has the necessary courage”. That kind of feminism inspired an “explosion of books and films about pioneers and heroines, about bossy women and gutsy girls” which retold the feminist story as “a succession of isolated campaigns, led by outsize individuals”.Instead, Walter advocates for ecofeminism, and for solidarity and sisterhood, “narratives that focus less on howIwin on my own, and more on how we thrive together”. She’s serious about that “we”, marshalling stories from across the globe. Walter founded the charityWomenfor Refugee Women in 2006, directing it for the next 15 years. During that time she was struck by women’s complaints of environmental degradation, their despairing at the “heaps of toxic waste that had grown up behind their homes”. Meanwhile feminism was being commodified by companies like Missoni, which copied the pink pussy hats knitted, for nothing, by feminist protesters, and sold them for £140 apiece. And by Dove, which promised “real beauty” and inclusivity while making billions of single-use plastic shampoo sachets that, according to Greenpeace, have clogged up sewers and contributed to floods in places like the Philippines (Dove states that it has made an “agenda-setting commitment to tackle the global beauty industry’s plastic waste issue”).She also saw some feminists who had supported the charity switch their energies to focus solely on British women, who they insisted needed protecting from migrants. No wonder she invokes indigenous scholar and healer Yuria Celidwen’s belief that political journeys must start with grief. But she also draws hope from Holly Archer (not her real name), a victim of grooming, gang-rape and abuse who has set up a project in Shropshire supporting survivors and “refuses to let her story be exploited by those who would use it to drive hatred and division”.I’d forgotten until she reminded me here that the slide into dystopia in Margaret Atwood’s The Handmaid’s Tale starts with climate change. In real life, too, women suffer first and most from environmental collapse. Rising sea levels in Bangladesh send women travelling miles further to fetch fresh drinking water. In north-east Syria, the radical women of Rojava – who fought off the extreme misogynist forces of Islamic State and are resisting authoritarianism from the new Syrian government as well as attacks from Turkey – struggle to feed their families because of water scarcity and food shortages. Nevertheless, they are “building something new”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘Heat, floods and droughts make men more violent to women’: Natasha Walter on eco-feminism in a world on fireRead moreWalter travels there to interview them and finds “the most determined feminists I have ever met”. It’s exhilarating to meet them on these pages too. One of the most joyous moments in the book comes during a conversation with Bahiya Mourad, who set up amala jin,or women’s house, in 2011. For a while she and her comrades evaded the authorities’ attention because they seemed like harmless old women, but when the government did try to close them down, they beat them off with sticks. Part of their work involves helping women who want to marry against their parents’ wishes, and, says Mourad, “often we end up dancing at their weddings”. In a book that can sometimes feel hopeless, it’s a vital reminder that feminist joy is not about buying a £140 pink pussy hat, but about helping other women – and, maybe one day, celebrating with them when the seemingly impossible has been achieved.Samantha Ellis is the author of books includingChopping Onions on My HeartandHow to Be a Heroine.
