title: Triage by Claudia Rankine review – how should we respond to the world’s atrocities? | Claudia Rankine | The Guardian
description: The American poet and essayist weaves memoir, fiction, criticism and lyrical lament into a tale of friendship in an age of existential crisis
Author: Sarah Crown
Headline: The American poet and essayist weaves memoir, fiction, criticism and lyrical lament into a tale of friendship in an age of existential crisis
Content: Engaging with our present moment’s contradictions … Claudia Rankine.Photograph: Tanya MarcuseView image in fullscreenEngaging with our present moment’s contradictions … Claudia Rankine.Photograph: Tanya MarcuseClaudia RankineReviewTriage by Claudia Rankine review – how should we respond to the world’s atrocities?The American poet and essayist weaves memoir, fiction, criticism and lyrical lament into a tale of  friendship in an age of existential crisisSarah CrownTue 25 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Any resemblance to actual persons, living or dead, or actual events is purely coincidental,” writes the multi-award winning Jamaican-American poet, essayist and playwrightClaudia Rankinein the disclaimer to her latest work. “Unless it isn’t.” The pretzel-logic of this statement, its assertive ambiguity, sets the tone for a book that digs directly into the question of what we are to do with the idea of truth, when the world we live in is asking us “to hold, visually and emotionally, realities we do not yet have a viable system of language for”. In Triage, Rankine borrows from her personal history and from a world whose landscape now encompasses “the rise of fascism, the implementation through deportations of the Great Replacement theory, the starvation of devastated populations subjected to war and climate change”, and uses the material she gathers to pose a simple question. When faced with realities such as these, what do you do? Do you stand, or do you fall?The book begins with a friendship. Two young people – our narrator, and another she refers to only as “the theorist” – meet in college in the late 20th century, and are drawn to each other. They’re passionate; they’re idealistic; they’re committed to the activism of the time (“shantytowns were built on campus to protest apartheid South Africa”) and steeped in the texts and authors and philosophical conceits of the humanities. Over time, they develop a game. “When we spied each other during the day,” the narrator explains, “we had to collapse.”double quotation markThe years pass; the world becomes wilder, more brutal, less sane; the crises and disasters multiply and intertwineThis collapse is “literal, and on occasion, an inconvenience to those around us”: the pair fall to the ground “in the dirt, grass, on cement, wood”, all over campus. They become known for it (“Aren’t you the two who fall?”), even though they themselves don’t seem, fully, to understand what their falling means. That it is a response to the “toomuchness” of the world around them, to “all the fevered wretchedness we had no answers for”, is without question. But what exactly the response itself signifies is less clear. Looking back from a vantage point 40 or more years into the future, the narrator offers a range of possible interpretations: “a refusal of continuance”; “a way to say things were unaligned”; perhaps just “the easiest way to keep from breaking apart”. But between the narrator and the theorist, the meaning of the game is never definitively pinned down.And it is perhaps this ambiguity that exists between them, even at the heart of a game that binds them to each other, that eventually drives them apart. The years pass; the world becomes wilder, more brutal, less sane; the crises and disasters to which the theorist and the narrator could, or should, respond multiply and intertwine. In the face of this worsening world, what began as a hair’s-breadth difference in the interpretation of their college game widens into a chasm. On the one side, the narrator sees her role as one of witnessing: her purpose, as she perceives it, is to record the atrocities around her, to acknowledge them, to mark them and to grieve them. Her work takes her into art criticism, and she focuses on images of couches, because “within the collapse, [they] seemed a place to land”. The theorist, on the other hand, is not content with reaction; they are compelled to act. What matters about falling for them isn’t the collapse itself, but the fact that the act of collapsing pushes them to rise up, over and over again.Triage acknowledges the validity of both characters’ responses – the witnessing and bearing of grief versus the acts of intervention and remaking. The book itself is a fantastical hybrid – part memoir, part reportage, part essay, part lyrical lament – and the complexity of its construction both mirrors and engages with our present moment’s contradictions. But in the end, the question of what is the right, the proportionate, even the realistic response to the world’s atrocities becomes subsumed by the question of which is the hopeful one.Triage is a challenging book for challenging times: it forces us to look at the world around us without blinking. There may be, as the narrator suggests in one of her final conversations with the theorist, “no solutions, only recognitions”. But at the same time, Rankine is clear that the truth of that statement doesn’t render action redundant: the book proposes courses of action even if it doesn’t offer the false promise of success. “Trying in the face of defeat is a thing,” the theorist argues. “For you, loss is a state of grief; for me, it’s a state to refuse … Things are unachievable only when you need the road to be short.”Triage by Claudia Rankine is published by Allen Lane (£22).To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. title: A Pocket Full of Slagford – a retro-futurist take on Thatcher-era northern England | Games | The Guardian
description: Developer Patrick Grant was born in Australia and lives in New Zealand, but a childhood of British TV inspired him to set a comedy game in a bleak vision of the north
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Developer Patrick Grant was born in Australia and lives in New Zealand, but a childhood of British TV inspired him to set a comedy game in a bleak vision of the north
Content: Inspired by northern English culture … A Pocket Full of Slagford.Photograph: SlumpsView image in fullscreenInspired by northern English culture … A Pocket Full of Slagford.Photograph: SlumpsSummer games previewsGamesA Pocket Full of Slagford – a retro-futurist take on Thatcher-era northern EnglandDeveloper Patrick Grant was born in Australia and lives in New Zealand, but a childhood of British TV inspired him to set a comedy game in a bleak vision of the northElliot GardnerTue 25 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 19.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSomething is amiss in the dingy town of Slagford, and curious scamp Pip Bunting is the only one who can find out what. So quit your mithering, it’s time to discover just how grim it truly is up north.A Pocket Full of Slagford is an upcoming retro-styled 3D puzzle adventure game set in a surreal alternative-reality near-future northern England that never escaped the clutches of Thatcherism. The story follows the misadventures of a young local lad from the eponymous Slagford after he takes ownership of a mysterious relic that lets him wreak havoc on reality.It’s the passion project of Australia-born, New Zealand-based artist Patrick Grant, who formed solo-developer studio Slumps to create a game inspired by the point-and-click classics from the late 80s and early 90s, such asLucasArts’ catalogueandGrim Fandango.View image in fullscreenReminiscent of point-and-click adventures of the past … A Pocket Full of Slagford.Photograph: Slumps“They’re just a great format for narrative-heavy games, like an interactive story,” says Grant. “I like designing puzzles as well, so I always wanted to make a point-and-click. But from playing a lot, I know how samey they can be. From the start I was thinking about what I could do differently.”The result of Grant’s prototyping is what he describes as a “jigsaw sticker book kind of thing.” As you navigate the nasty industrial hellscape, you collect imprints of the game’s scenery. If, along the way, you spot a place where these imprints align, you can paste them into the world to solve puzzles. Grant is also committed to evoking the oft-forgotten CD-Rom era of the late ’90s, complete with looping CG-rendered backgrounds and janky 3D models with far too many sharp edges.Yet he’s keen to emphasise that his main focus is the narrative. While the trailer andSteam store pagefeature a fair few Yorkshire-isms, A Pocket Full of Slagford’s story and dialogue take inspiration from various aspects of northern English culture, despite Grant admitting to having never actually spent any real time in the area.“In the colonies we get a lot of BBC English programming,” he explains. “So when I was growing up there was so much British telly that I’d be watching. There’s this BBC miniseries from the 80s calledBoys from the Blackstuff, about this group of scousers getting up to mischief, set in the Thatcher years, just trying to make ends meet. It’s incredibly well written – this mix of sad and funny – against that whole big economic collapse. I got interested in that, reading about the Thatcher years.”That interest is what inspired A Pocket Full of Slagford’s bleak setting. While Grant says he wasn’t trying to make a political point when he went into the project, he’s not shying away from the issues of the time: “Because of that working-class setting, you end up naturally touching on points like the wealth disparity, which I show in the game, and the class conflict. Specifically, from watching stuff like Boys from the Blackstuff, or Billy Elliot, I was interested in the infighting that goes on within these classes.”Despite touching on these themes, Grant stresses that he’s going for a comedic, surrealist angle. As he puts it: “I was like, what if I set it in the future and, instead of coal, they’re mining shit out of the ground?” He may not be trying to make a political statement about Thatcherism, but some might say he has hit on an apt analogy.A Pocket Full of Slagford is in development forPC, with no confirmed release dateExplore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsPCfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Camping trips, grief and embarrassing your kids – the fringe shows embracing every facet of fatherhood | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Edinburgh comedies by Whisper Theatre, Lightning Rod Special and Olaf Falafel are exploring what it’s like to be a dad, from the hilarious and melancholic to the devastatingly accurate cringe
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: Edinburgh comedies by Whisper Theatre, Lightning Rod Special and Olaf Falafel are exploring what it’s like to be a dad, from the hilarious and melancholic to the devastatingly accurate cringe
Content: Best. Dads. Ever. … Britt Anderson and Richie Schiraldi in Well-Balanced Dads.Photograph: The Whisper Theatre CollectiveView image in fullscreenBest. Dads. Ever. … Britt Anderson and Richie Schiraldi in Well-Balanced Dads.Photograph: The Whisper Theatre CollectiveEdinburgh festival 2026Camping trips, grief and embarrassing your kids – the fringe shows embracing every facet of fatherhoodEdinburgh comedies by Whisper Theatre, Lightning Rod Special and Olaf Falafel are exploring what it’s like to be a dad, from the hilarious and melancholic to the devastatingly accurate cringeChris WiegandTue 25 Aug 2026 07.56 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 08.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a historic masonic lodge in Edinburgh’s New Town I find myself raising my hand. The call has gone out for fathers in the audience and I join our hosts, Dick and Dale, along with another volunteer on stage. It’s just us four guys at a campsite, practising trick shots with a baseball, busting some moves and shooting the breeze. But bubbling underneath is an existential crisis.This isWell-Balanced Dads, from Chicago’sWhisper Theatre Collective, created by Dick and Dale themselves – AKA Richie Schiraldi and Britt Anderson. They’re sporting headbands, bum bags and tank tops blazoned with “Best. Dad. Ever”, each with a different back print – one’s a power drill, the other’s a barbecue. Both have bushy moustaches and they supply us volunteers with our own. There are bursts of classic rock – Foghat, Kenny Loggins, Creedence Clearwater Revival – as we join them on a road trip and other volunteers are cast as hitchhikers.Fatherhood has given both our hosts a sense of pride and purpose but what happens now their kids have flown the nest, leaving each with just their wives (Mary and, er, Mary) and each other for company? Who is there to appreciate/disdain their dad jokes and dad dancing? We get a lot of both in this highly physical show, which also unexpectedly adds a sensual dads’ dream ballet to the mix, as Dick and Dale take a family-style holiday without the kids in tow.double quotation markYou too may find something in your eye – surely sawdust or something equally manlyThat means there’s a sweetly melancholic air to these proceedings as the dads play hide and seek, break out their best holiday shirts and end up regressing into children themselves, complete with “are we nearly there yet?” pleas to the hitchhikers. There’s a keen awareness that the Marys usually run the show at home – with the dads packing all the wrong stuff,a bit like when Bandit takes the kids to the pool in Bluey.The audience participation is refreshingly ridicule-free and the central bromance blossoms, filling the room with goodwill. Individual theatregoers are singled out as legends by the dads for their admirable qualities. “This guy,” marvels Schiraldi as he hovers over my seat, “hasn’t paid his taxes for 18 years!” (I have, honest!) It’s akin to the ribbing you get at a family gathering.Fathers in the audience will feel seen and may well momentarily cringe if, purely by example, they find these dads also bombastically quoting their favourite lines from Gladiator. You too may find something in your eye – surely sawdust or something equally manly – when Dick and Dale open up about how much they miss their kids and give them a call. One of the offspring heartbreakingly suggests a weekly rather than daily catchup; the other is beginning to show their own care and concern towards their father.View image in fullscreenParenting and pride … Scott R Shepherd and Alice Yorke in Lions.Photograph: Wide Eyed StudiosIt ends with one of the loveliest scenes I’ve experienced at this year’s fringe as Dick and Dale roam the audience offering fist-bumps, jokes, hugs and other dad business to anyone who needs them. (Yes, they’ve brought a tape measure.) It caps off an hour of gently serious silliness that I enjoyed just as much as my 12-year-old daughter, delighted to see her dad make a fool of himself on stage. But that’s one welcome side-effect of parenthood: becoming 100% unembarrassable.Over at Summerhall, another couple of legends have a show about parenthood and pride – that’s surely why it’s called Lions. This moustachioed double act blend the character comedy with more openly autobiographical material in a production by the US companyLightning Rod Specialthat aims to break down “the myths our fathers told themselves about becoming great men”.There are goofy jokes here, too, about brewskis, barbecue and baseball but the costumes are cravats, tweed and coiffed wigs. There are also echoes of A Christmas Carol and, as we arrive, writer-performers Alice Yorke and Scott R Sheppard are laying a candlelit table as if for a feast yet amid the bagels are a bike helmet, a trophy and assorted paraphernalia. This is a multilayered alternative to an Edinburgh cliche, “the dead dad show”, with each actor announcing – with disarmingly cheery gusto – that they’re here to relive that loss and uncover what kind of men they were.Directed and developed by Sarah Blush, Lions mashes together eras – the performers are just as likely to brandish quills as record voice notes. It captures the sense that dads always hail from an unrecognisable era for their children, will always seem a bit fusty and formal to them, no matter how hard they try not to.View image in fullscreenThese dad jokes are award-winning … Olaf Falafel.Lions dramatically deals with the approach and aftermath of death, channelling the over-caffeinated state of waiting in hospitals and how sorting the paperwork becomes a temporary job for the children. There’s a chilling section that brings to mind Forced Entertainment’s unforgettable First Night when they consider who in this audience might die next. The rawness of Yorke and Sheppard’s autobiographical tributes floored me, as did the list of life’s disappointments itemised by Yorke’s dad who wished he’d been braver. Both of these shows offer fatherly advice in different ways – I’m asked to share my old man’s own words of wisdom in Well-Balanced Dads, which by default is a message to my daughter.A supreme being, the nearly naked show and politics with paws: Edinburgh fringe pick’n’mixRead moreBoth productions also create comedy from the befuddled reactions of the performers’ parents to their offspring’s artistic pursuits.Olaf Falafelupturns that dynamic with his multimedia fringe hour I Used to Work in a Helium Balloon Factory Until they Let Me Go. He takes great delight in detailing his teenage daughters’ withering responses to a career in comedy that finds him spending hours a day editing squirrel videos, making his own janky Meta glasses from Gü pots and animating a man who used to “twerk on the ducks” to accompany a misheard Bon Jovi lyric.The difference here is that these dad jokes areregular award-winnersand there are also some affectionate, relatable dispatches from dadhood – who hasn’t amassed their own mountain of those hairbands strewn in every corner of the home? One of the many things I loved about the show is how Olaf (it just sounds weird to call him Falafel) breaks off for a passing observation on how adopting a daft mask can be freeing, not just on stage – like a newly acquired, increasingly sweaty joke shop moustache as you try out some dad dancing – but in daily life, too. That’s a top fatherly tip. And there’s a nice final touch as his daughter cheerily holds the bucket for the audience’s money. Maybe he’s not so embarrassing after all.Well-Balanced Dadsis at Braw Venues @ Hill Street, Edinburgh, until 30 August.Lionsis at Summerhall, Edinburgh, until 30 August.Olaf Falafel Presents: I Used to Work in a Helium Balloon Factory Until they Let Me Gois at Laughing Horse @ the Pear Tree, Edinburgh, until 30 August.Explore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreComedy (Stage)ClownsParents and parentingComedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Kemah Bob: Love Child review – Miss Fortunate’s follow-up is a superbly playful origin story | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: With icky and edgy jokes, the comedian offers an authentic inquiry into her childhood in her sophomore show
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: With icky and edgy jokes, the comedian offers an authentic inquiry into her childhood in her sophomore show
Content: Thinking aloud … Kemah Bob.Photograph: Paul GilbeyView image in fullscreenThinking aloud … Kemah Bob.Photograph: Paul GilbeyEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewKemah Bob: Love Child review – Miss Fortunate’s follow-up is a superbly playful origin storyPleasance Courtyard, EdinburghWith icky and edgy jokes, the comedian offers an authentic inquiry into her childhood in her sophomore showBrian LoganTue 25 Aug 2026 11.19 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 11.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAstandup’s debut show usually tells us who they are, then with their follow-up, they branch out.Kemah Bobhas done things the other way around. After2024’s Miss Fortunate, a wild shaggy dog story about a disastrous trip to Thailand, she now delivers that delayed “this is me” set, an open-hearted inquiry into how she got here and her origins as the child of a poor black family, the descendants of slavery, in the southern US.That inquiry is prompted by misgivings on Bob’s part, coolly laid out here, about her career in comedy – which she loves, but worries is infantilising, and (see the receipts from that successful last fringe run) financially precarious. Is she leading a grownup life – or should she start doing so? There’s a thinking-aloud authenticity to that exploration that is very endearing in Love Child. Her audience cheerfully used as a sounding board, she casts her gaze back across generations of Bobs, and her own journey to the UK, to work out what life she ought now to lead.‘Just so cheeky!’ Kemah Bob on FOC Fest, the celebration for femmes of colour in comedyRead morePart of the pressure, she jokes, comes from being the product of the first pregnancy her parents didn’t terminate. She measures her upbringing against the Adverse Childhood Experience test for early-life trauma and it doesn’t sound too traumatic because Bob is such a smiling and playful host, packing icky jokes about inheriting “dick-sucking lips” from her dad or, as an adult, sharing sex toys with her mum.She goes on to ruminate on what made her parents who they were (there’s a great joke about her father’s having never been taught to be a man) – and her grandad too, a promiscuous blues singer with an addictive personality just like Kemah’s. When this chronology loops back to the present-day party at which Bob first sets her scene, it’s a jolt. That framing device could use some buttressing but the material is strong, in a thoughtful, sprightly show.AtPleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Stage)Edinburgh festivalComedy (Culture)reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Kate Cheka: The Last Funny Woman review – pregnant standup calls for comedy industry to grow up | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Cheka considers her tendency to ‘live life like a joke’ in a frank hour, with her frustrations leaving a lasting impression
Author: Anya Ryan
Headline: Cheka considers her tendency to ‘live life like a joke’ in a frank hour, with her frustrations leaving a lasting impression
Content: Giving everything she has … Kate Cheka.Photograph: @ezztheticphotographyView image in fullscreenGiving everything she has … Kate Cheka.Photograph: @ezztheticphotographyEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewKate Cheka: The Last Funny Woman review – pregnant standup calls for comedy industry to grow upVoodoo Rooms, EdinburghCheka considers her tendency to ‘live life like a joke’ in a frank hour, with her frustrations leaving a lasting impressionAnya RyanTue 25 Aug 2026 06.24 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKate Cheka wasn’t supposed to be here. After her debut hour two years ago, she swore she would never do the fringe again. But now she’s back, mic in hand and eight months pregnant, walking us through her life’s greatest romantic escapades, from Marseille to Texas and Nepal to Berlin. She does it all with mountains of energy – if you thought the fringe was exhausting at the best of times, just imagine doing all this with a baby on board.But, as she will tell us later, maybe there’s a reason she wants to give everything she has to her last pre-birth show. In an hour that’s more storytelling than laugh-out-loud standup, she weaves in political eye-rolls, thoughts on the rise of the far right and her tendency to date white men with access to property.View image in fullscreenDisappointments laid bare … Kate Cheka.Photograph: @ezztheticphotographyThe world is pretty darn depressing. Still, she remains a “good time girl”, which has led to some drunken sexual encounters. “Most comedians write jokes,” she says, “I live life like a joke.” Her pregnancy story is held back until just the right moment.She does all this in the style of a pub catchup. But despite her giggling, girlish demeanour, Cheka has big, often unheard things to say about the state of comedy. Her career is not going well, she tells us. Even though she’s started booking slots on radio, she’s finding that her lefty political feelings are not being met with applause. Things are made harder by the fact she’s a Black, working-class comedian. She presents a bleak, uncomfortable picture.Courtney Büchner: One of the Girls review – all aboard for a rollercoaster relationshipRead moreCheka’s disappointment is laid bare. She has worked hard and won awards, and yet TV execs still lure her into Zoom calls, only to build up her dreams and cruelly crush them. Cheka deserves her comedy flowers. But the final 15 minutes of this show are anything but funny. The tears rolling down her cheeks should get the industry looking inward. Let’s hope there are more opportunities to hear Cheka, in all her glory.AtPBH’s Free Fringe @ Voodoo Rooms, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalFestivalsTheatreComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Soft Spot review – this wine-glass circus has a lot of bottle | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: A handstand artist and a juggler slide, toss, stack and stand on umpteen glasses – without a drop of wine in sight
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: A handstand artist and a juggler slide, toss, stack and stand on umpteen glasses – without a drop of wine in sight
Content: Smashing time … Stina Otterström and Arttu Lahtinen in Soft Spot.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSmashing time … Stina Otterström and Arttu Lahtinen in Soft Spot.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewSoft Spot review – this wine-glass circus has a lot of bottleZoo Southside, EdinburghA handstand artist and a juggler slide, toss, stack and stand on umpteen glasses without a drop of wine in sightChris WiegandTue 25 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis Swedish circus two-hander begins with the performers offstage, and what sounds like the high-pitched notes of a glass harp. But the wine glasses here – first six of them, then dozens – are used for acrobatic tricks rather than music.Stina Otterströmis a handstand artist,Arttu Lahtinenis a juggler. Together, they execute a series of increasingly fiddly, full-bodied duets. Otterström’s strength is immediately contrasted with the fragility of this most familiar, yet hazardous, of props. Her first inversions involve holding the stems between her toes, passing them from one foot to the other, or balancing their bases on her soles. Lahtinen gives us variations on the tablecloth pull-trick and the buzz wire game, balancing glasses on planks of wood that he glides perilously close around Otterström’s body. Empty glasses are expertly slid, tossed, stacked and stood upon. Have we no wine here?Exit review – a circus squad who really drive each other up the wallRead moreThis is a restrained hour presented by OLO Company and Cluster Arts. It could sometimes benefit from more of a showperson’s – or even a sommelier’s – flair. The abundantly skilled pair remain demure throughout, just the odd glance or smile acknowledging their feats, an occasional teasing amid their steadfast reliance on one another. For too long it plays in one register, without quite enough variation in Mika Forsling’s nevertheless appealing music. Any notion of narrative or autobiography is absent. That’s not necessarily a problem if you’re embracing a fuller variety of tricks and tones – as in Compagnie Nyash’s remarkableStoel, with a duo and 15 mismatched chairs that take on their own personalities. It’s harder to achieve with identikit glasses.If a richness of mystery or ritual is absent, then the fizz among the tricks includes the mock-solemn arrival of a brush to tidy up a breakage, unexpectedly supplemented by a pile of broken glasses. That crunchy noise is much more atmospheric than an earlier recorded sound effect. These shards are eventually swept around the stage to form a striking surround for the final tricks, performed barefoot (eek!) and dramatically lit by Jaakko Sirainen. That stylish sequence would sparkle alongside other cabaret acts – and the wit in the duo’s curtain-call speech shows this pair could create a happier hour.AtZoo Southside, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreCircusEdinburgh festivalJugglingreviewsShareReuse this content

title: John Irvin obituary | Movies | The Guardian
description: British film-maker and director of Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy who was described by Alec Guinness as having ‘balls behind the camera’
Author: Ryan Gilbey
Headline: British film-maker and director of Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy who was described by Alec Guinness as having ‘balls behind the camera’
Content: ‘I hate being pigeonholed, and I like to do the unexpected’: John Irvin, pictured in 1986.Photograph: Alex Bowie/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘I hate being pigeonholed, and I like to do the unexpected’: John Irvin, pictured in 1986.Photograph: Alex Bowie/Getty ImagesMoviesObituaryJohn Irvin obituaryBritish film-maker and director of Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy who was described by Alec Guinness as having ‘balls behind the camera’Ryan GilbeyTue 25 Aug 2026 11.37 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 11.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBouncing from war zone reportage to cold war espionage, Hollywood horror to Sherwood Forest swashbuckler,Harold Pinterto Arnold Schwarzenegger, the director John Irvin, who has died aged 86, was nothing if not eclectic.“I’m a bit split,” he said. “I like playing with expensive toys, yet I also like the miniatures. I hate being pigeonholed, and I like to do the unexpected.”He enjoyed his greatest success with the BBC mini-series Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy (1979), adapted fromJohn le Carré’s novel about the intelligence officer George Smiley’s efforts to winkle out a Russian mole. Smiley was played with clenched elegance and economy by the formidableAlec Guinness, who took to striking out lines in the script whenever he felt he could convey the necessary information by expression alone.“I was terrified, knowing I had to spend a year with him,” Irvin told Guinness’s biographer Piers Paul Read. On the first day of rehearsals, the director offered a suggestion that was rejected out of hand. After persuading Guinness to try the scene his way, Irvin was vindicated. “Very good, John,” the actor said. “Ten out of ten.”There was still Guinness’s trepidation to contend with. Phoning Irvin at 3am once shooting was under way, the actor fretted that he “hadn’t found Smiley” and recommended that the part be recast. On set a few hours later, Guinness walked off in the middle of filming. Irvin brought him back and stood his ground. “We’re going to do it in one take,” he said of the day’s first scene. “Do you understand?”When Guinness was later asked what he liked about Irvin’s directing style, he said: “Balls behind the camera.”View image in fullscreenAlec Guinness in Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy, 1979.Photograph: Maximum Film/AlamyThe series, described by its producer Jonathan Powell as “a sort of elegy for empire”, was seen at its peak by more than 8 million viewers (more than 15% of the UK population) and won several prizes, including best drama series in the Broadcasting Press Guild awards.Interviewing the director in 1986 for Films in Review, Louise Tanner wrote: “There is about Irvin just a hint of a Le Carré hero, the crisp diction, the quiet air of knowing his way around the lands east of Suez.”Irvin was unavailable to direct the follow-up, Smiley’s People, having been courted by Hollywood since before Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy. His 1977 Granada Television adaptation of Dickens’ Hard Times had impressed executives there.From moles, he moved on to dogs: The Dogs of War (1980), that is, adapted fromFrederick Forsyth’s novel and starring Christopher Walken as a mercenary helping to overthrow a west African dictator. Stark and uncompromising, the film was hated by Forsyth.Apparitions were next. Ghost Story (1981) featured an illustrious cast who were famous before Irvin was even born: Fred Astaire, Melvyn Douglas, John Houseman andDouglas Fairbanks Jrplayed friends harbouring a nasty secret. The New England winter was scarier than any of the film’s spectres, Irvin recalled. “When I finished the last shot, I said to Fred, ‘It’s all over. You can go home to Beverly Hills.’” Astaire replied: “Oh John, I’m so happy. I thought I was going to go home in a box.”Horses followed in Champions (1984), the story of the cancer-stricken jockey Bob Champion (John Hurt), then reptiles in Turtle Diary (1985), a low-key comedy adapted by Pinter fromRussell Hoban’s novel, withGlenda Jacksonand Ben Kingsley as shy naturalists who plot to liberate giant sea turtles. Irvin compared working with that cast to “driving a Ford Mustang and trading up to a Ferrari”.In directing Schwarzenegger in Raw Deal (1986), he might be said to have swapped the sports car for a bulldozer. One of the Austrian action hero’s interchangeable shoot-’em-up thrillers, the film cast him as an ex-FBI agent infiltrating the Chicago mob. Even Irvin admitted the movie was “not dealing with the great mysteries of life”.He had hoped for many years to direct a film about Vietnam, where he spent time while making aBBCOmnibus documentary about war photographers. (He had even been shot at on the Laotian border.) When he was offered Hamburger Hill (1987), which focused on the real-life 10-day battle to capture Dong Ap Bia in the A Shau Valley in 1969, it satisfied that desire.View image in fullscreenJohn Irvin on the set of Hamburger Hill in the Philippine jungle south of Manila, 1986.Photograph: Alex Bowie/Getty ImagesIrvin succeeded in his aim of “[getting] as close as possible to the experience of combat without thrills or moralising. I wanted the audience to be there.”Unfortunately, the audience was fatigued. Oliver Stone’s Platoon (1986) dominated the Oscars before Hamburger Hill had even been released, whileStanley Kubrick’s Full Metal Jacket (1987) pipped Irvin’s film to the post in the US. He claimed in 2021 that Kubrick had been toying with a later release date until he was secretly shown a print of Hamburger Hill by a colour grader working on both movies.Nevertheless, the criticPauline Kaelconsidered it to be superior to both Stone and Kubrick’s films. Irvin, she wrote, “has the pride of a director who knows what he’s doing”.John and his twin brother, David, were born in Wallasey – now Merseyside but then part of Cheshire – to Elsie (nee Bending) and Charles Irvin, a mechanical engineer. After the family moved to South Shields in Tyne and Wear, the brothers were educated at Durham school.Film bewitched John from an early age. “When I was a child, I used to organise my gangs into film units. I was brought up near Newcastle in the same town as Ridley Scott – there must be something about the smell of the fish queues that produces film directors.”He enrolled at the London School of Film Technique (now the London Film School), which was then housed above a butcher’s shop in Brixton, south London. Irvin said his mother cried for two days when she learned that he would not, as she had hoped, be pursuing a career as an architect.After working as an apprentice editor at Rank, he received a British Film Institute grant to make Gala Day (1963), a documentary about the Durham miners’ gala, which was then bought by the BBC. Irvin made other documentaries for the corporation as well as for his own company, Mithras Films, which he formed in 1962 with Maurice Hatton.These included The 26 (1966), about ex-miners who participated in the General Strike of 1926, and the Bafta-nominated Mafia No! (1967), which documented a protest march across western Sicily against organised crime. While making a film about the civil war in Yemen, Irvin lived with Bedouin tribespeople for four months. He was also a film adviser to the Jamaican government in 1963-64.By the end of the 1960s, his experiences convinced him to leave the documentary world behind. “I reached the point in Vietnam where I had simply seen too much suffering.”View image in fullscreenIrvin during a photocall at the 2008 Rome international film festival.Photograph: Tiziana Fabi/ AFP/Getty ImagesHe worked in British television throughout the next decade on series including the political drama The Nearly Man (1974-75), one of several collaborations with the writerArthur Hopcraft, who went on to adapt Hard Times and Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy.Irvin’s later movies included Next of Kin (1989), starringPatrick Swayzeand Liam Neeson as Appalachian brothers out for revenge. Just as Hamburger Hill got lost amid other Vietnam movies, so his Robin Hood (1991), with Patrick Bergin in the title role and Uma Thurman as Maid Marian, was overshadowed by Robin Hood: Prince of Thieves, which starred Kevin Costner and opened a month later to far greater fanfare.The Hells Angels provided unlikely inspiration for Irvin’s earthy take. “Robin and his men must have terrorised Nottingham like a motorbike gang,” he said. There wasn’t much the director could do, however, when Bergin fell ill, forcing the production to rely on stand-ins. “We had to hide the problem from the studio,” Irvin said, “because otherwise they would have stopped the production.”He continued to demonstrate his versatility. The chocolate-box prettiness of Widows’ Peak (1994), a whimsical comic mystery starringJoan Plowrightand Mia Farrow, and his adaptation of HE Bates’s A Month By the Lake (1995), with Thurman and Vanessa Redgrave, were followed by the hard-nosed thrillers City of Industry (1997), starring Harvey Keitel, andShiner(2000), with Michael Caine andMartin Landauas rival boxing promoters. He also returned to combat in the TV movie When Trumpets Fade (1998), set during the dying days of the second world war.Mandela’s Gun(2016) dramatisedNelson Mandela’s stint as a guerrilla fighter for the ANC.View image in fullscreenIrvin filming Mandela’s Gun (2016).Photograph: Mandela’s GunAt the time of his death, Irvin was working on Water from an Ancient Well, a documentary about his friend the South African musicianAbdullah Ibrahim, who died in June.“To me, being a director is the most privileged existence there is,” said Irvin. “It’s bloody hard work, but when it’s going well, it’s like having the best table in the restaurant.”He is survived by Emilie, Luke and Amy, the children from his marriage to Sophie (nee Litchfield), who died in 1991, and by two grandchildren, Finn and Isla.John Charles Greenway Irvin, film director, born 7 May 1940; died 11 August 2026Explore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsAction and adventure filmsDocumentary filmsHistorical drama (TV)DramaDocumentaryobituariesShareReuse this content

title: Kit Harington to replace Nicholas Hoult in HBO’s Harry Potter TV series | Harry Potter TV series | The Guardian
description: Actor best known as Jon Snow in Game of Thrones will now play Gilderoy Lockhart in show’s second season
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: Actor best known as Jon Snow in Game of Thrones will now play Gilderoy Lockhart in show’s second season
Content: Kit Harington will play the vain and inept defence against the dark arts teacher in the season based on Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets.Photograph: Gareth Cattermole/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKit Harington will play the vain and inept defence against the dark arts teacher in the season based on Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets.Photograph: Gareth Cattermole/Getty ImagesHarry Potter TV seriesKit Harington to replace Nicholas Hoult in HBO’s Harry Potter TV seriesActor best known as Jon Snow in Game of Thrones will now play Gilderoy Lockhart in show’s second seasonNadia KhomamiTue 25 Aug 2026 08.05 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKit Harington will replaceNicholas Houltin HBO’s Harry Potter television series, after the Skins actor left the production because of scheduling conflicts.Harington will play Gilderoy Lockhart, the vain and inept defence against the dark arts teacher, in the season based on Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets, the second novel in JK Rowling’s series. The casting change was announced just two weeks after Hoult was confirmed for the role.Hoult, who played Lex Luthor in the recent Superman film, was released from the Harry Potter production after its filming schedule conflicted with his other commitments.Harington is best known for playing Jon Snow in Game of Thrones, as well as a more recent appearance in the BBC/HBO drama Industry.The actor voiced Lockhart in Audible’s full-cast adaptation of The Chamber of Secrets, released in 2025. He said recently that he was a longstanding Harry Potter fan and described Lockhart as one of his favourite characters.“I’m thrilled,”Harington told Collider. “I’ve said a million times, for anyone who cares, that I’m a huge Potter fan.“I’ve got to be honest, he’s one of my favourite characters. So, to be offered to play him is a real dream. I think he’s going to be so fun. I got to play him in the audiobooks. That’s not the exact way I’ll play him in the show because it’s an audiobook, but I’ve had a taste of him and felt my way around him. He’s just a wonderful creation.”Harry Potter publisher to receive millions in Anthropic copyright settlementRead moreLockhart is a celebrity wizard and prolific author whose reputation is built on supposedly heroic exploits that, it emerges, were largely the work of other witches and wizards. He was previously played by Kenneth Branagh in the 2002 film adaptation.The HBO series is intended to retell Rowling’s seven-book story over multiple seasons, with each season expected to be based on a different novel. The first season, Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone, is due to premiere on 25 December. Production on the second season is scheduled to begin this autumn.The series stars Dominic McLaughlin as Harry, Arabella Stanton as Hermione Granger and Alastair Stout as Ron Weasley. John Lithgow plays Albus Dumbledore, Janet McTeer is Minerva McGonagall, Nick Frost plays Rubeus Hagrid and Paapa Essiedu plays Severus Snape.Harington’s appointment is the latest change to the cast. Gracie Cochrane, who plays Ginny Weasley in the first season, is also leaving the series and will be replaced for its second season.Hoult, along with other cast members, has faced some backlash for his decision to join the show from those opposed to Rowling’s views on sex and gender.Explore more on these topicsHarry Potter TV seriesKit HaringtonNicholas HoultnewsShareReuse this content
