title: ‘The whole world is becoming rightwing and anti-gay’: William Yang on 60 years of capturing LGBTQ+ life | Photography | The Guardian
description: Yang has taken more than 500,000 photographs since he first moved to Sydney in the late 1960s and now devotes most of his time to untangling the past
Author: Oliver Giles
Headline: Yang has taken more than 500,000 photographs since he first moved to Sydney in the late 1960s and now devotes most of his time to untangling the past
Content: ‘Now I couldn’t take a camera into a sauna’ … William Yang at the exhibition Inside the Mirage at the TarraWarra Museum of Art in Victoria.Photograph: Thomas McCammon for TarraWarra Museum of ArtView image in fullscreen‘Now I couldn’t take a camera into a sauna’ … William Yang at the exhibition Inside the Mirage at the TarraWarra Museum of Art in Victoria.Photograph: Thomas McCammon for TarraWarra Museum of ArtPhotography‘The whole world is becoming rightwing and anti-gay’: William Yang on 60 years of capturing LGBTQ+ lifeYang has taken more than 500,000 photographs since he first moved to Sydney in the late 1960s and now devotes most of his time to untangling the pastOliver GilesTue 25 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTShareAs a young adult, William Yang discovered that his family’s story was actually a murder mystery. His uncle, William Fang Yuen, was killed by an employee on the family’s farm in far north Queensland in 1922, but his mother refused to tell him the full story. In 1990, he travelled to Innisfail in search of the truth.One aunt told Yang that his uncle and the worker had got into a fight over a gambling debt, and the worker had stabbed him to death with a spear. A cousin said a gang was involved. A local woman, who had been a child at the time, remembered it as a card game gone wrong.Desperate for concrete evidence, Yang visited the local courthouse, where he was presented with a dusty box of documents. Inside, there were papers caked in his uncle’s blood.“He was holding these when he died,” the sprightly 82-year-old recently told a rapt crowd at TarraWarra Museum ofArtin Victoria, his photograph of the stained sheets of paper glowing on the screen behind him.View image in fullscreenBlood spattered documents, from William Yang’s My Uncle’s Murder series, in 2008.Photograph: William YangView image in fullscreenWilliam Fang Yuen and business partners, from William Yang’s My Uncle’s Murder series, in 2008.Photograph: William YangIt turns out there was no spear, no mafia, no game of poker. Piecing together the records, it seems Yang’s uncle had accused his employee of fiddling the farm’s accounts. They had an argument and Yang’s uncle was shot dead. The man was brought to trial, then acquitted in a decision that many believe was racist: Yang’s uncle was Chinese and his employee was white. “This verdict upset the Chinese at the time,” Yang told his audience. “They thought it was a great miscarriage of justice.”Yang’s account of his family’s story is part of TarraWarra’s exhibition Inside the Mirage, which features several artists whose work explores the diaspora experience in Australia. Seven of Yang’s trademark annotated photographs tell the story of his uncle’s death and how it traumatised his mother, who was 16 when it happened and raised Yang and his siblings to be “more Australian than the Australians.” On the final photo, of a transcript of the evidence that his mother gave during the trial, Yang has written: “I feel the legacy of this murder came down to me in that, while I was growing up, my ethnicity was suppressed.”Yang now devotes most of his time to untangling the past. He has taken between 500,000 and 1 million photographs since the late 1960s, when he first moved to Sydney. It was there that Yang came out as gay in his late 20s and became a documentarian of the city’s LGBTQ+ community, photographing individuals and events through the debauchery of the 1970s, the horror of the HIV/Aids crisis in the 1980s and 1990s, the growing acceptance and subsequent journey to gay marriage in 2017.Alongside these are photos documenting how Yang came to embrace his Chinese heritage – he says he “came out as Chinese” in his mid 30s – as well as his portraits of Australian cultural luminaries such as the writers Patrick White and Barbara Blackman; artists such as Brett Whiteley and Max Dupain; and actors like Cate Blanchett and Sam Neill.Open gallery|0The State Library of New South Wales has acquired about 50,000 of Yang’s negatives from the 1970s and is now negotiating with the photographer over his images from the 1980s and 1990s, which he is busy digitising. “So many photographers leave their negatives in a dusty, unsorted pile,” Yang says. “I’m digitising the negatives to give the photos a chance of life.”Yang still occasionally photographs events and is working on a book of nudes titled The Male Body, but spends most days organising his archive. The process has given him new insights into his own work. “Looking back, I think the strongest element in my collection is the gay events,” he says. “People used to tell me, ‘I wouldn’t worry about that gay stuff. It’s so marginalised. You’ll come to your senses and start photographing the real world.’ But it’s in the margins where I think the value of the work is.”Some of his favourite photos were taken in the late 1970s and early 1980s at Ken’s Karate Klub, a gay sauna in Sydney, where a drag queen invited him to capture the shows she put on beside the pool. “Now I couldn’t take a camera into a sauna,” he says. “I’d be run out the place!”View image in fullscreen‘The gay community had been invisible for thousands of years – now there was a chance to be visible’ … William Yang at TarraWarra.Photograph: Thomas McCammon for TarraWarra Museum of ArtAnother memorable event was a party where the hosts wheeled out a young man on a table, decorated like a cake. “You could eat the cream off him,” says Yang, grinning cheekily. “I don’t think people would do that nowadays … Social media has changed everything.”Back then, Yang says, people were not only happy to be photographed; they were hungry for it. “One of the revelations I had in the seventies was that the gay community had been invisible for thousands of years, and now there was a chance to be visible. That was generally seized on.”Increased visibility helped change the public perception of the LGBTQ+ community, which helped earn greater legal rights. When Yang waslast profiled by the Guardian, in 2016, he worried “that the times are more conservative now.” A year later, the result of the gay marriage plebiscite allayed his fears. “That was a huge victory,” Yang says now. “It was a cultural shift [proving] we had majority approval.”Today, Yang is once again concerned about politics. “I see that the whole world is becoming rightwing and anti-gay,” he says. Although politicians like Pauline Hanson are seeing theirpopularity rising, Yang says, on balance, “we’re extremely lucky that we live in Australia and have free expression.”At one point in his monologue at TarraWarra, Yang shared an old worry he once had, that he might not “fulfil his destiny” of becoming a photographer. His final slide featured aportrait of Yang painted by Kean Onn See, which was nominated for this year’s Archibald prize. In the painting, Yang sits in his archive, dwarfed by boxes full of his photographs documenting personal and societal change. The painting was displayed on banners around Sydney, putting Yang and his life’s work in the spotlight.“Remember when I felt I had not fulfilled my destiny?” Yang asked the crowd at the end of his talk. “Well, now I feel I have. At times I’ve struggled … But by and large, I feel I’ve done it. It’s a good feeling to be satisfied.”View image in fullscreenKean Onn See’s painting, ‘At the studio of William Yang’, which was nominated for the 2026 Archibald prize.Photograph: Jenni CarterInside the Mirage isshowing at TarraWarra Museum of Artuntil 1 November

title: ‘It looked stunning on Joanna Lumley!’ 10 writers on their biggest hair disaster | Beauty | The Guardian
description: From bowl cuts to extreme mullets, punk dos to bad dye jobs, a terrible hairstyle can never be forgotten – even decades after it has grown out
Author: Kate Lloyd
Headline: From bowl cuts to extreme mullets, punk dos to bad dye jobs, a terrible hairstyle can never be forgotten – even decades after it has grown out
Content: A professional hairdresser did this … Viv Groskop.Composite: Guardian Design; James KirkwoodView image in fullscreenA professional hairdresser did this … Viv Groskop.Composite: Guardian Design; James KirkwoodBeauty‘It looked stunning on Joanna Lumley!’ 10 writers on their biggest hair disasterFrom bowl cuts to extreme mullets, punk dos to bad dye jobs, a terrible hairstyle can never be forgotten – even decades after it has grown outKate Lloyd,Rich Pelley,Jeffrey Ingold,Carys Afoko,Joel Snape,Viv Groskop,Paula Cocozza,Polly Hudson,Daniel LavelleandAlexi DugginsTue 25 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 06.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘It reminds me of the botched Jesus fresco’View image in fullscreen‘If you squint it could be a trendy mullet’ … Kate Lloyd.Composite: Guardian Design; Courtesy of Kate LloydIt’s the late 1990s. Big, round, feathered fringes are a huge deal at my primary school. Most of my friends have one, influenced by Britney Spears or Emma Bunton. I, too, have a fringe. Mine, as you can see, appears more inspired by Kevin Keegan circa 1993.Of course, calling what I’m sporting here “a fringe” is an incredible understatement. If you squint it could be a trendy east London mullet. Otherwise, I look a bit like a Knight Templar. Or someone wearing a hat made out of their own hair, on top of their own hair.It may surprise you to learn this cut was not the result of a sleepover prank gone wrong. It was done by a professional – a hairdresser who lived up the road from my parents and came round to our house to cut my brother’s, my mum’s and my hair.Not a sleepover prank gone wrong.Photograph: Courtesy of Kate LloydWhen I first discovered these photos, I assumed the look must have been a one-off. Maybe I moved just as the hairdresser was trimming the top and the only way to salvage things was to evokePat Sharp. Or maybe it was the hair equivalent of that botched Jesus fresco restoration: every attempt to improve it only made it worse.It turns out I actually wore this hairstyle for almost a year, according to my mum. I have a photo of me in a summer dress – with a forehead that resembles a city skyline – where I’m probably seven. And there’s another where I’m wearing a primary school jumper, aged eight.My mum has no recollection of the hair being a problem. She was happy with the cut back then, she says. “You were a little girl!” is her defence now.Thankfully, I have no memory of actually sporting it. I have, however, spent most of my adult life feeling disproportionately stressed about going to the hairdresser. As they say, the body keeps the score.Kate Lloyd‘What has he done to his hair now?’View image in fullscreenRich Pelley goes full on Keith Flint.Composite: Guardian Design; Courtesy of Rich PelleyThey say you don’t appreciate something until you lose it – and that is never more true than with hair. After decades of treating mine as a disposable fashion accessory, it appears to have disposed of itself. Perhaps that’s why I look back so fondly on all the terrible things I did to it while I still had the chance.View image in fullscreenDreadlock days at university.Photograph: Courtesy of Rich PelleyThe first was a pudding-bowl haircut that my mum and I appeared to share in the early 80s. At school, I had shoulder-length curtains with a shaved undercut, held out of my face with an alice band – a look I imagined made me resemble a member of Radiohead, rather than a teenage girl waiting to wash her face. It required constant maintenance because the curtains had to fall at exactly the right angle: too far apart and you looked like a medieval monk, too close together and you couldn’t see where you were going.View image in fullscreen‘It accidentally made me look like my mum’.Photograph: Courtesy of Rich PelleyAt college, it was a number one all over with a line shaved through one eyebrow, like Robbie Williams in Take That – or so I believed. I thought it made me look dangerous. In reality, I resembled someone who had lost a brief but intense argument with an electric razor.At university, I had dreadlocks that made me look like Sonic the Hedgehog. For my first proper job, I went bleached blond, which accidentally made me look like my mum again, so that had to go. Then came a spiky mohawk: less Mr T, more startled parrot.The problem is that, for the people around me, the dramatic effect diminishes each time. When I brilliantly shaved the top half of my head to look like Keith Flint from the Prodigy for a 90s-themed fancy-dress party, nowhere near enough people said: “I can’t believe what you’ve done to your hair!” Or: “You’ve won first prize.” Instead, they presumably thought: “What has Rich done to his hairnow? What a berk.”That, out of all the haircuts, was probably my worst, although it faces extremely stiff competition. Unlike my other terrible hairstyles, this one had only ever been intended to last for one night. The next morning, my Keith Flint costume had gone back in the wardrobe, but unfortunately my hair remained the same, so I was forced into another brief but intense argument with an electric razor – and this time the razor won. I thought I looked like Jay-Z, but in reality I looked more like an escaped convict.Rich Pelley‘The technical term is: a terrible mess’View image in fullscreenJeffrey Ingold refused to get a haircut for three years.Composite: Guardian Design; Courtesy of Jeffrey IngoldMeet Jeff at age 15 in 2006. Yes, you can laugh. I’d honestly be insulted if you didn’t laugh. My hair looks like a cross between a bird’s nest and tumbleweed. I believe the technical term for it is a “terrible mess”.For about three years as a young teenager, I outright refused to get a haircut and just let my hair run wild. I would roll out of bed and without even so much as looking at a comb or a brush, walk out the door with an unkempt, knotty mess on my head.I wasn’t trying to be edgy or cool. Believe me, I was teased mercilessly for my bad hair. Kids would come up and ask if there was something living in there or complain to the teacher that my hair was a distraction in class. Or they would “joke” that my parents were so poor they couldn’t afford to get me a haircut. One day when I was walking home from school, a group of students tried to throw pieces of chewed gum into my hair.Still, I stubbornly brushed off any suggestions I should go to the hairdressers. That hairstyle was a masterclass in deflection and adolescent survival.The summer before I started secondary school, a small group of classmates had spread a rumour that I was gay. News to me at the time. I didn’t even know what “gay” meant except it was clearly something bad and shameful. Friends whom I would once play with in the streets shunned me. No one would return my calls to hang out.It was then that I decided to grow my hair. I walked into that first day of secondary school with the beginnings of my unruly, curly mane. I was almost unrecognisable to those who’d known me for years with an outdated mushroom cut.The classroom whispers about my sexuality were drowned out by incessant questions and commentary about my ever-growing untamed hair. I didn’t know much back then, but something told me it was better to be the kid with weird hair than it was to be the gay kid. My hair became my armour.I wore it proudly and only cut it when I got accepted to university in my final year of school. By then it reached the top of my chest. I could see the light at the end of a dark, lonely tunnel. I was finally getting out of my small town and going somewhere no one knew me. I no longer needed to hide behind my hair. Though the kids were right: I am gay.Jeffrey Ingold‘Babe, we can’t bleach it any more’View image in fullscreenCarys Afoko went blond for a summer.Composite: Guardian Design; Courtesy of Carys AfokoCast your mind back to June 2011. Beyoncé took to the Pyramid stage at Glastonbury for a historic performance. She was resplendent in a gold-sequinned cardigan and black ankle boots and had a cascade of honey blond curls. I had blagged my way to a bar job at the festival to see my idol and I was not disappointed. It was a near-religious experience. As I began the long trek home from Worthy farm in Pilton, Somerset, I knew one thing: I had to dye my hair blond.I had attempted to dye my hair at home once, with disastrous results. This time, I made my way to a salon in east London with a picture of Beyoncé on my phone. My hairdresser, a lovely New Zealander called Vernon, understood the vision, and within a couple of hours I had been transformed. So began a summer to remember. My honey blond curls and I went to more festivals, parties and art openings than I had ever gone to before. Blonds, I decided, did have more fun.Blond, it turned out, was also more work. My hair was weaker and drier than usual. It took only a couple of months for my very dark roots to peep through, then I was back to the salon to see Vernon. After a few months I noticed the warm, honey colour was morphing into something more brassy. A friend explained that I needed a special shampoo to maintain the colour, maybe even a toner. I bought a £4 purple shampoo from Boots and hoped for the best. I was already shelling out to get my roots done. I wasn’t made of money.The breaking point came after a two-week beach holiday. One minute I was sipping rum out of a coconut, the next the tropical sun had bleached my curls white blond. I barely wore sunscreen in those days; it hadn’t occurred to me to protect my hair. It wasn’t the look I was going for, but I liked it, until I went back to see Vernon.“Babe, we can’t bleach it any more. The condition is terrible,” he said, running his fingers through my fried curls. Instead, he cut my hair and sent me on my way with dark roots and a broken spirit.Over the months that followed I endured the worst hair days of my life, growing out the blond and returning to my natural dark brown. My hair broke easily and I learned the hard way that colouring your hair is a commitment: the only low-maintenance way to have blond hair is to be born with it.Carys Afoko‘I looked like a stage magician’View image in fullscreenJoel Snape or a futuristic pirate?Composite: Guardian Design; Courtesy of Joel SnapeIt’s hard to remember, in our post-God-of-War, post-Jeff-Bridges-from-Iron-Man era, that growing a massive beard, if you’re bald, was oncenotconsidered the cranial topiary slam-dunk it’s now assumed to be. Back when Shrek 2 was the hottest thing at the box office, skinhead-plus-facial-bush had a faint whiff of desperation about it. It looked a bit villainous, and opened you up to comparisons with those toys where you use a tiny magnet to drag iron filings across an eerily hairless man’s face. I simply wasn’t prepared to risk it.And so, dear reader, I experimented. Forced to shave my head in my early 20s after losing most of my hair terrifyingly prematurely, I riffled through a variety of looks. I tried stubble, I tried shorter beards, I tried the Van Dyke – named after the 17th-century Flemish painter Anthony van Dyck, whose subjects often sported the same sort of chin-patch. Think Cyrus the Virus, the baddie from Con Air. Once, in a dating profile, I tried a big hat (I am, I should say to any ladies who felt misled when I showed up, sincerely sorry). And then I triedthis.Quite honestly, I don’t know what I was going for here, with what I believe istechnicallyan extended goatee. Stage magician? High-end jewel thief? Futuristic pirate? I do remember that around this time I wrote a feature where I went undercover in a group of pickup artists, and so maybe their penchant for “peacocking” (having something distinct and memorable about one’s appearance, even if it’s ridiculous) rubbed off on me. It certainly draws the eye, like a bluebottle on a birthday cake. I just can’t believe I thought it looked good.In this photo, I’m at a press event on a boat in 2003. Within hours of getting back to shore, I also came back down to earth: reminded by friends and flatmates that having a head like an egg is still preferable to looking like someone Jason Bourne would threaten to throw off a balcony.The good thing about beards is that you can experiment with impunity: I got rid of this one the morning afterwards, and stuck to the full buzz cut – no facial topiary in sight – until the late 2010s. That’s when the beard plus bald combo started really coming into its own. With the odd blip for Halloween outfits, I’ve had a full-bore beard ever since: they’re perfect for the shaving-averse, and surprisingly easy to shape.In a sense, I’m very lucky – I have friends who’ve gradually gone just as bald as me over the intervening decade, but remain unable to grow more than the wispiest facial fuzz. And so, to any twentysomethings staring at their emerging scalp with horror right now, I’d like to say: keep the faith, itwillimprove, as long as you can grow a proper beard. Just don’t forget what Jeff Bridges did for us.Joel Snape‘My parents paid money for this’View image in fullscreenThis illustrates why virtually no one is allowed to cut my hair … Viv Groskop.Composite: Guardian Design; James KirkwoodEveryone knows that it’s a bad idea to get your hair cut on the same day that you are having your photograph taken. This picture operates as a public health reminder of this fact. On a personal level it also illustrates why virtually no one is ever allowed to cut my hair. In 40-plus years of adult life, only three hairdressers have gained sufficient trust to be allowed to use scissors in my vicinity. You can see why.This photograph must have been taken around 1977, when I was about three or four. I remember the photographer coming to set up at the house. Most people didn’t own cameras, and photographer home visits were just one of the exceptionally weird “normal things” people did in the 1970s.Another key recollection I have from around that time is an overriding fear of the Daleks and of Tom Baker (who was then the Doctor in Doctor Who). The photograph was taken in the room that housed the place where terror resided: the television. Now, a new, chilling dimension was added to the horror already contained within those four walls: the immortalisation of this haircut.This was the era of the fashionable “Purdey” or “pageboy” cut. It looked stunning on Joanna Lumley in The New Avengers. It was slightly less stunning on a moody toddler old enough to know how awful she looked but too young to do anything about it. Around this age, I must have learned about the idea of bowl haircuts: a cut-price, kitchen-table haircut achieved by putting a bowl on someone’s head and cutting around it. I knew I looked as if I had one.The truth, however, was worse. A professional hairdresser did this in a salon and my parents paid money for it. I recently asked my mum for more details of this historic misdemeanor and she replied: “It was done very badly.” You think?Viv Groskop‘My fringe was a dark heavy clump’View image in fullscreenCatalogue of disasters … Paula Cocozza with her Freemans-inspired fringe.Composite: Guardian Design; Courtesy of Paula CocozzaWhen I was 10, I decided to do the unthinkable. I asked my parents for short hair. Being a girl, this went against the traditional beauty ideals I was growing up with in my family. As a child of the 70s, I had artless long hair and no fringe. One of my happiest childhood memories is of sitting on my dad’s lap on Saturday evenings after my weekly hair wash and having him comb and dry my hair while we watched Starsky & Hutch.But I was increasingly fashion-conscious. I found a picture of a model with the hair I wanted, and tore it out of our Freemans mail order catalogue. She had a fringe and a brunette version of the style made famous by Diana, Princess of Wales, with slightly less layering.We picked the salon for practical reasons. It was halfway between school and home, in a parade of shops next to a chemist and a butcher’s. Mum took me in with my picture. We showed it to the hairdresser, who looked at it and nodded. I sat in the chair and soon chunks of long brown hair began to land on the floor. I was amazed by how much of it there was, and how sad it looked lying there. Possibly tuning into the momentousness of the occasion, for the duration of the appointment, the hairdresser’s hands didn’t stop shaking.Afterwards, while I was still in the chair and she held up the mirror for me to survey the results, I tried hard to work out how come the hair I saw on my head looked so unlike that of the model in the Freemans catalogue. My fringe was a dark heavy clump. There wasn’t much in the way of layering. In fact, it looked pretty much like the haircut my mum gave my younger brother every couple of months.“Did you see her hands were shaking the whole way through?” my mum said when we were back on the street. I made the best of it with a sequined headband worn around my forehead, but I started growing it out right then.I haven’t had short hair, or a fringe, or a change of colour, or asked a hairdresser to cut off more than a couple of inches since. My hair never strays far from my shoulders. Sometimes, I think there might be another version of me – had that experience gone better – wandering around with a pixie cut.Paula Cocozza‘A hushed silence came over the salon’View image in fullscreenDon’t take hair advice from your frenemies … Polly Hudson.Composite: Guardian Design; Courtesy of Polly HudsonThere is never a good time for a hair disaster, but having one during peak awkward, self-conscious teenage years was a test of character and resilience I could have done without. My makeover had seemed like a logical decision. At the age of 14 in 1989, I had elbow-length, thick, glossy hair in perfect condition, which I always wore pulled back in a ponytail. My best friend helpfully suggested I might as well have a short back and sides, because it would look really cool. Side note: this was how I learned about frenemies.The hairdresser thought I was joking when I told her what I wanted, which I should have paid more attention to, but my friend’s mind was made up: I was doing this. “Yes, I am sure, really,” I insisted.I knew it was a mistake from the first snip of the scissors, just a millisecond too late. I remember a hushed silence came over the whole salon, but maybe that’s just in my head. There was definitely no chat from my chair, no discussion of forthcoming holiday plans – I sat in shellshocked silence while the stylist followed my instructions, and scalped me.My mum came to collect me – and pay the bill – and announced her arrival with a piercing scream from the doorway. I looked over to see her hands clasped over her face in horror. “Your beautiful hair!” she cried, although not as much as I did when we got home.Styled by the hairdresser, my new ’do was horrendous, but at least had some bouncy life to it. When I tried myself, it was flat and positively Hitler-esque. To clarify: this was not the look I was going for.Somehow there was worse to come, though. “It’ll grow,” was how every conversation about my new hair ended, even those that had begun with people saying it wasn’t that bad. And yes, it did grow, but only the top. The sides stayed stubbornly short. It was like a mushroom, and I started having to put the long part in a little ponytail, which stuck straight up. Now I looked like a sumo wrestler, another image that was not centre stage on many teenage girls’ mood boards. The ends became dry and split – I should have had a trim, but this was tricky seeing as I was never, ever letting anyone cut my hair ever again.It took a full five years to look anything approaching normal again. I will probably be scarred by the experience for ever, but sometimes it’s an advantage. Every Traitors viewer is biannually tempted by fringe influencer Claudia Winkleman, and most live to regret it. Of course I’m not immune to the lure, but I remember too well the snail’s-pace pain of growing out a mistake, so will never succumb. I’ve learned the hard way.Polly Hudson‘Mum’s sneaky salad-bowl trims’View image in fullscreenDaniel Lavelle sported far worse styles in his teens.When I was six, in the early 90s, I was like a pinball pinging around restlessly, which meant getting me to sit still on a barber’s chair was as likely as an accidental death in Midsomer Murders.Even if my mum could have plonked me down in the hot seat, there is no way a barber would have risked taking his scissors to my permanently oscillating head.Consequently, my mum resorted to cutting my hair herself. On the rare occasions when she could get me to sit still, she would plonk a bowl on my head and cut any hair that poked out around the sides. This usually happened when my attention was focused on playing Super Mario Bros on the Nintendo Entertainment System. Mum would approach with the stealth of a super assassin: “The Shadow Hairdresser, Operation Haircut”. If she was lucky, the trim would happen without me noticing.I wish I could say these were my worst haircuts, but I did far worse things to my hair than my mum’s sneaky salad-bowl trims ever could. When teenage hormones kicked in, so did a demoralising preoccupation with my appearance.In my early teens, I boarded the Beckham bandwagon with the rest of my male peers: curtains, floppy fringe, baby mohawk, buzz cut and several others, until I finally understood what putting a silk hat on a pig meant.After that, I shifted from attempts to look attractive to making a statement. That statement was mostly, “No, teacher, I won’t do what you tell me”, in the form of shaved-in patterns and hair dye.Sadly, the only statement my hair makes now is that it’s had enough and doesn’t want to stick around.Daniel Lavelle‘An egg that’s grown some cress’View image in fullscreenDon’t get your haircut when you are drunk …Alexi Duggins.Composite: Guardian Design; Courtesy of Alexi DugginsI’ve essentially had the same haircut since I was 17 years old, so I am no stranger to intrusive thoughts about it being out of date – particularly given the style I have chosen. Now that the 00s are well and truly gone, do I just look like a human bog brush? Or as though I’ve jammed wet fingers into a wet plug socket? Or like someone left a Sid Vicious waxwork too close to a radiator? Like I said: intrusive thoughts.So obviously, when I came across a hairdressing stand at a London festival in 2013, I was very taken by it. It offered “hairdressing inspired by music”, with cuts themed to different musical playlists. “We create styles that make you stand out, not fit in,” it said, in promotional documentation that also required you to sign an “extreme cuts contract” (sample text: “We would like to make you aware that we have had no professional training in hairdressing”). This, I decided, was exactly the change I needed.View image in fullscreen‘A disco-era King Midas’.Photograph: Courtesy of Alexei DugginsI had drunk quite a lot of beer by this point.Fifteen minutes later, my hair had undergone a rough hacking. My stylist, for some reason, felt that what my coiffure chiefly required was to unevenly lose the hair at the sides and have the front teased up to delicately emphasise my receding hairline. Even through the beer, I was not impressed.“Honestly,” said the scissors wielder, “you’ll look at this cut tomorrow and think: ‘Wow, this is really good.’ Then she sprayed it so liberally with gold glitter that it looked like I had been styled by a disco-era King Midas.“Jesus!” laughed a friend the next day – once I’d washed the glitter out. “You look like an egg that’s grown some cress out of the top.” Other pals developed a fondness for poking their fingers into the patchier bits. My ears, I was repeatedly told, now stuck out in a way that would make me the bookies’ favourite to star in a Dumbo remake.All in all, it was not the finest bit of coiffure I’ve ever had. I did learn something, though. It turns out that there are worse things than looking like a human bog brush. Namely, getting your hair done while drunk.Alexi DugginsExplore more on these topicsBeautyMen's hairWomen's hairHair carefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to use up leftover party wine | Wine | The Guardian
description: Sauces, reductions, deglazing: our expert panel has plenty of options for making the most of undrunk vino – whether you’ve got just a capful or a whole carafe to get through
Author: Anna Berrill
Headline: Sauces, reductions, deglazing: our expert panel has plenty of options for making the most of undrunk vino – whether you’ve got just a capful or a whole carafe to get through
Content: ‘A novel concept’: leftover wine can go into everything from stews to desserts.Photograph: heliography/Stockimo/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘A novel concept’: leftover wine can go into everything from stews to desserts.Photograph: heliography/Stockimo/AlamyKitchen aideWineHow to use up leftover party wineSauces, reductions, deglazing: our expert panel has plenty of options for making the most of undrunk vino – whether you’ve got just a capful or a whole carafe to get throughAnna BerrillTue 25 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat can I do with wine left over from a party?Rob,by emailThis is a novel concept, perhaps, but the answer essentially comes down to the quantity: “If we’re talking dribbles of red or white, that’s simple,” says Jon Atashroo, head chef/owner ofWhere There’s Smokein North Yorkshire. “They go into sauces, whether that’s for pasta or to deglaze a pan before making a gravy.” Joe Otway, chef/co-owner ofHigher Groundin Manchester, couldn’t agree more: “Reducing wine, be it white or red, in the base of anything is generally a good idea.” Take something tomato-based, such as ragu or chilli, as an example: “Once you’ve sweated the vegetables and there’s caramelisation on the bottom of the pan, a glass of red wine will add acidity, depth and sweetness.” And remember, you can always freeze wine dregs for later use: simply pour into ice-cube trays and stash.Moving on to medium amounts, we’re talking “stewy, fish-type things”, Atashroo says, perhaps moules marinière. Another good option is pickling: “A basic recipe is one part caster sugar, one part white-wine vinegar and one part white wine. And if you’re pickling something like beetroot, cook it in that mix, while if you’re using cucumbers, say, they go in cold.” That said, a current Atashroo go-to is altogether sweeter: “Weigh some red wine, though I don’t see why it wouldn’t work with white wine, too, add 20% of its weight in sugar, and reduce to a syrup – you’re looking for the consistency of strawberry sauce.” The result is complex and acidic, “almost like reduced port”, and great for drizzling over vanilla ice-cream. While we’re talking desserts, few things are better than fruit (peaches, figs, pears) poached in wine, either.Larger amounts of excess wine could be fermented into vinegar, although Otway has an easier route if you have any natural cider vinegar (ie, one with a mother) to hand: “Add a couple of tablespoons of vinegar to, say, a third of a bottle of wine, cover with muslin, so oxygen can get to it but flies can’t, and put in a cupboard for a month.” That’ll give you “some really interesting results” as the vinegar takes on the characteristics of the wine: “It’s perfect for pepping up dressings for these never-ending salad days.”If Rob’s party was more of a sparkling affair, Alastair Walling, head chef atBar Blondiein London, would use every last drop in a beurre blanc: “Combine vinegar, shallots and a sprig of thyme in a small, heavy-based saucepan and gently reduce the liquid by half. Add champagne and some finely diced mushrooms, then reduce by half again.” Lift out the thyme, lower the heat and whisk in chilled butter a little at a time. But be warned: “Keep the sauce just below a simmer, otherwise it may split.” Season (with salt and white pepper) and spoon that lovely sauce all over some steamed fish.All that said, maybe the most obvious solution is simply to repurpose the wine in another drink, perhaps sangria: “Add a generous amount of brandy to red wine, plus some orange juice and slices of orange and lemon, and leave to infuse,” says Jonny Lake ofTrivetandLabombe by Trivetin London. Serve straight over ice or top with soda, then sip while you plan your next party.Got a culinary dilemma? title: Lloyds Bank is holding on to our urgently needed £5,500 | Banks and building societies | The Guardian
description: We want our balance back, but we can’t access the money to pay for essential repairs and settle an electricity bill
Author: Anna Tims
Headline: We want our balance back, but we can’t access the money to pay for essential repairs and settle an electricity bill
Content: The trouble started when online problems prevented the church opening a new business account.Photograph: Gary Hider/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe trouble started when online problems prevented the church opening a new business account.Photograph: Gary Hider/AlamyConsumer championsBanks and building societiesLloyds Bank is holding on to our urgently needed £5,500We want our balance back, but we can’t access the money to pay for essential repairs and settle an electricity billAnna TimsTue 25 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 13.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLast November, Lloyds Bank informed me, in my role as treasurer of my parish church, that the church account was to be closed and that I should open a new business account instead. This can only be done online, but a fault with their system prevented me – and local branch staff – from doing so.At the branch staff’s suggestion, I opened the new account with a different bank in early March. Since then, I’ve been trying in vain to get Lloyds to transfer the balance from the closed account.I’ve been repeatedly told to visit my local branch and repeatedly told that the money would arrive within weeks. At one point I was told that the bank had lost my identity verification documents and so had put the case at the bottom of the pile.We are owed nearly£5,500, which, for a congregation of 10in a village of 60 houses, is a significant sum. We have had to borrow from parishioners to pay for essential repairs and to settle the electricity bill.CI,YorkshireThe apparent indifference of Lloyds is outrageous. As was its energy spurt when it realised public exposure was pending.As soon as I questioned its inertia, it winged off a mea culpa acknowledging poor and inconsistent communications and offering £400 in goodwill, plus £96 in lost interest.What the letter from the executive complaints manager did not mention was the still-missing funds.So back I had to go to Lloyds, and off went another letter from the bank apologising for the omission.The money was transferred more than four months after the account was closed.A Lloyds spokesperson said: “We’re sorry the customer had such a difficult experience. We should have handled things better.”We welcome letters but cannot answer individually. Email us atconsumer.champions@theguardian.comor write to Consumer Champions, Money, the Guardian, 90 York Way, London N1 9GU. Please include a daytime phone number. title: Boat trips, swimming and seafood: 10 of the UK’s best harbour towns and villages  | Travel | The Guardian
description: From smoked kippers in Northumberland to dolphin spotting in Dorset and a palm-fringed village on a sea loch in the Scottish Highlands
Author: Rachel Dixon
Headline: From smoked kippers in Northumberland to dolphin spotting in Dorset and a palm-fringed village on a sea loch in the Scottish Highlands
Content: The historic Pittenweem harbour in East Neuk, Fife, where fish is sold on the quay.Photograph: Angus McComiskey/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe historic Pittenweem harbour in East Neuk, Fife, where fish is sold on the quay.Photograph: Angus McComiskey/AlamyGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.TravelBoat trips, swimming and seafood: 10 of the UK’s best harbour towns and villagesFrom smoked kippers in Northumberland to dolphin spotting in Dorset and a palm-fringed village on a sea loch in the Scottish HighlandsRachel DixonTue 25 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 02.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePittenweem, FifeThe historic harbour is the hub of this working East Neuk fishing port, home to a fleet of about 30 small trawlers and creel boats. Their catches are sold at the covered market on the quay each weekday morning, and served at the harboursideDory BistroandChip Ahoyat the Larachmhor pub. Pittenweem (which means “place of the cave”) also has a Victorian-eraswimming poolnext to the beach, which is filled by the tide twice a day. After falling into disrepair, it was saved by a local group called the West Braes Project and reopened in 2021, along with the crazy golf course. Early each August, there is an annualarts festivalwith exhibits by nearly 200 artists in harbourside spaces, heritage buildings, homes and studios. Pittenweem is flanked by two other pretty harbour villages,St MonansandAnstruther, while a third,Crail, is a little further north; the Fife Coastal Path links them all.The Bankin Anstruther has harbour-view rooms (doubles from £120 B&B).Carnlough, County AntrimView image in fullscreenCarnlough harbour featured in Game of Thrones as the Braavos canal.Photograph: Christopher Hill Photographic/AlamyThere has been a harbour in the village of Carnlough since the late 1700s, but the one standing today dates to 1853 (Game of Thrones fans may recognise it as the Braavos canal). It was built on the orders of the Marchioness of Londonderry to transport limestone from her quarries – the town hall’sHeritage Hubtells the full story. The old railway line between the quarry and harbour is now a footpath with panoramic views, leading to Cranny Falls. The harbour is the focal point of the village, which stands at the foothills of Glencoy – one of the nine glens, or glacial valleys, of Antrim – on Carnlough Bay. It bustles with local fishers, andboat tripsset sail daily (£10 adults, £6 children; trips last 45 minutes). TheTwilight coffeeshop, directly across from the harbour, serves brunch and has bunkhouse accommodation upstairs (sleeping 14). The recently refurbishedHarbourview hoteloffers more than 200 Irish whiskeys and hosts an annual whiskey festival (doubles from £120 B&B).Solva, PembrokeshireView image in fullscreenAt low tide, Solva harbour becomes a huge stretch of sand.Photograph: Ashley Cooper/Getty ImagesSolva’s ancient harbour is at the bottom of a steep-sided valley on St Brides Bay, a few miles from St David’s. At high tide, it is popular with paddleboarders, but at low tide it becomes a huge stretch of sand, with the River Solva meandering down the middle. Then, there are rock pools and caves to explore; prime fishing, crabbing and shrimping spots; and safe, shallow places to swim. The village is split into Lower Solva, by the harbour, and Upper Solva – there are fantastic views over both ends from the Gribin headland.Cafe on the Quayand theHarbour Innhave outdoor tables overlooking the water; theHats & Barrelsserves fresh fish, and seasonal lobster and crab; and theCambrian Innis a restaurant with five rooms (doubles from £140 B&B).Craster, NorthumberlandView image in fullscreenThe small harbour at Craster, known for its smokehouse and kippers.Photograph: Jim Monk/AlamyWhile Craster’s natural haven has been used by fishers for centuries, today’s harbour was built in 1906 as a memorial to a member of the Craster family and has the ruins of Dunstanburgh Castle, a mile’s (1.6km) walk away up the coast as a backdrop. Craster is perhaps best known for its kippers, andL Robson & Sonshas been producing them at its smokehouse overlooking the harbour since 1856. They are sold in the shop next door, while thePiper’s Pitchhut serves them in a bun, and theJolly Fishermanpub turns them into paté and puts them in a scotch egg. TheCottage Inn, just outside Craster, has 10 rooms (doubles from £105 room only), and theDunstanburgh Castle Innin neighbouring Embleton has 16 (doubles from £120 B&B). The market town of Alnwick is about seven miles away.Clovelly, DevonView image in fullscreenCar-free Clovelly harbour.Photograph: Nigel Hicks/Getty ImagesBrixham, on Devon’s south coast, is probably the county’s best-known harbour town – but the village of Clovelly, on the north coast, is well worth seeking out, too. It was once the property of William the Conqueror, and is still privately owned today (entry is £10.90 adults; £6.25 children). The tiny harbour stands at the foot of a 122-metre cliff, reached via the steep, cobbled main street (known as Up-along or Down-along). Cars are not allowed, so goods are transported by sledges and donkeys. TheRed Lion hotel, right on the quay, has 17 rooms, all with sea views (doubles from £225 B&B); the restaurant serves dishes such as wild hake and local lobster, while the snug bar offers haddock and chips. TheFisherman’s Cottage & Kingsley Museumis a 1930s time capsule, and there areannual festivalscelebrating seaweed, seafaring and seafood.Staithes, North YorkshireView image in fullscreenStaithes village and harbour.Photograph: Nigel Harris/Getty ImagesNorth Yorkshire is not short of busy harbour towns and fishing villages: see Scarborough, Whitby and Robin Hood’s Bay. But Staithes, a little further north, is less well known. The name means “landing place” in Old English; Vikings landed here, and it was once one of the busiest fishing ports in the north-east. Today, there are still a handful of cobles (a traditional fishing vessel), plus boats runningwildlife-watching trips, from which minke whales can be seen in August and September. The village is a steep jumble of cottages (largely white-washed and red-roofed, with the occasional electric blue pile), threaded with cobbled snickets (narrow alleys). TheCod & Lobsterpub is right on the harbour wall; and theEndeavour B&B(refurbished in 2022) has four rooms, one with harbour views (doubles from £120 B&B). There is an annualarts festival(this year running 11-13 September), and visitors can walk a mile or so along theCleveland Wayto the ruined harbour at the abandoned hamlet ofPort Mulgrave.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPorthleven, CornwallView image in fullscreenPorthleven is one of Cornwall’s quieter harbour towns.Photograph: Jory Mundy/Getty ImagesFrom mighty Falmouth to minuscule Mousehole, harbour hunters are spoiled for choice in Cornwall. But pretty Porthleven, on the Lizard peninsula, tends to have fewer crowds. Its double harbour, which opened in 1825, is said to have beenbuilt by French prisoners of warafter the battle of Waterloo. It is lined with pubs, restaurants and galleries; there is acraft marketmost days from Easter to the end of October, and a food festival in April. The 17th-centuryShip Innstraddles the harbour and the waters of Mount’s Bay; theMussel Shoalis a seafood shack right on the harbour head; andKota Kaiserves fusion food such as Cornish fish and chips with katsu curry sauce, wasabi tartare, Asian slaw and pea puree. TheHarbour Innis a recently refurbished pub with 15 rooms (doubles from £110 B&B).Lyme Regis, DorsetView image in fullscreenLyme Regis harbour, built from Portland stone.Photograph: Travel Pics/Getty ImagesLyme Regis’s harbour includesthe Cobb, a breakwater and jetty. The first written mention of it was in 1328, when it was damaged by storms, but today’s Cobb was built from blocks of Portland stone in the late 18th and 19th centuries. It is on the west side of the town (known locally as the Pearl of Dorset), so is great for a sunset stroll. You can often see seals in the harbour and dolphins just out to sea; there are daily boat trips in late spring and summer. The beaches are fertile ground forfossil hunters– especially at Monmouth, to the west of the Cobb, and East Cliff, to the east of the town – and have thrown up many amazing discoveries, including an ichthyosaurus excavated by the paleontological pioneer Mary Anning in 1812. TheCobb Armsis the closest pub to the harbour and has three rooms (doubles £155 B&B); while theHarbour Inn, a tiny bit farther north by the beach, serves Lyme Bay seafood.Lymington, HampshireView image in fullscreenLymington is a yachting hub.Photograph: Thomas Faull/Getty ImagesThis market town on the west bank of the River Lymington, at the edge of the Solent, was first mentioned in the Domesday Book, became a hotbed for salt manufacture in the medieval era and later a shipbuilding centre in the 19th century. Today, it is ayachting hub, with two marinas as well as the old town quay. Near theRoyal Lymington Yacht Clubare the town’sseawater baths– established in 1833 and still open for swimmers (plus paddleboarding and inflatable obstacle courses). There is alively marketalong the high street on Saturdays; while waterfront pubs and restaurants include theShip InnandThe Haven, and the recently reopenedMayflower, set a little back near the seawater baths, which has seven rooms (doubles from £100 B&B). TheWightlinkferry port is just outside the town at Lymington Pier, taking passengers to Yarmouth on the Isle of Wight, another historic harbour town (with a crossing of about 40 minutes).Plockton, the HighlandsView image in fullscreenPlockton sits in a sheltered bay.Photograph: Getty Images/iStockphotoPlockton, a planned harbour village built to support the herring industry in the early 1800s, is known as the Jewel of the Highlands. It sits in a sheltered bay on the banks of Loch Carron, with a mild climate that allows incongruous-looking palm trees to thrive, and wooded hills beyond. Visitors can buy fresh fish and prawns off the pier when the boats come in at about 3pm; go onsea-kayak toursandseal-watching trips(from spring until the end of October); and watch the annualsummer regattain July. ThePlockton Innserves local langoustines and other seafood; thePlockton hotelhas six rooms with loch views and five overlooking the gardens (doubles £180 B&B); andthe bunkhouseby the railway station has budget beds (£20pp, discounts for groups). It is about an hour’s drive over the bridge to the Isle of Skye and on to its pastel-painted harbour capital, Portree.Explore more on these topicsTravelUnited Kingdom holidaysScotland holidaysEngland holidaysWales holidaysNorthern Ireland holidaysWildlife holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tell us: do you think AI has made Google search better or worse?  | Google | The Guardian
description: As people grow used to AI chatbots, we’d like to hear your views about Google’s search engine
Author: Guardian community team
Headline: As people grow used to AI chatbots, we’d like to hear your views about Google’s search engine
Content: How do you feel about Google’s search engine now that articicial intelligence is at the front and center of it search bar?Photograph: Nicolas Economou/NurPhoto/REX/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenHow do you feel about Google’s search engine now that articicial intelligence is at the front and center of it search bar?Photograph: Nicolas Economou/NurPhoto/REX/ShutterstockGoogleTell us: do you think AI has made Google search better or worse?As people grow used to AI chatbots, we’d like to hear your views about Google’s search engineGuardian community teamTue 25 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGoogle has put artificial intelligence at the front and center of its search bar. The most-visited site on the internet still shows the same list of links to users, but they have to scroll past a summarized response from an AI chatbot, a featureGooglecalls AI Overviews. The change to what was once the gateway to the rest of the internet has been profound, and the browsing habits of billions of people are shifting.“AI is driving the most significant upgrade of the Google Search experience ever,” Liz Reid, Google’s vice-president of search,wrote last August. In May, the company saidmore AI is coming.As people grow accustomed to AI chatbots, they’re spending more time with Google’s and therefore more time on Google.com. Studies, media outlets and website owners alike are finding that people navigate less to sites beyond Google if an AI Overview can give them a good enough answer, even if the bot cites the sites that feed it. Clicks, also known as traffic, are often the most significant way a website earns money from advertising. Large US media companiesare suingGoogle, alleging that AI summaries have redirected and reduced traffic to their sites, cutting into their revenue.Google said it had not seen a decline in aggregate traffic and that such accusations are based on “flawed methodologies”. Reid, the company’s vice-president of search, wrote last year: “Total organic click volume from Google Search to websites has been relatively stable year-over-year.”We want to hear from you. title: Wife of US soldier deported after Trump rollback on military family protections | US military | The Guardian
description: Cristy Maryori Villafranca-Trejo, deported to Honduras, is latest military spouse to face removal amid Trump 2.0
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Cristy Maryori Villafranca-Trejo, deported to Honduras, is latest military spouse to face removal amid Trump 2.0
Content: Army Sgt Hedar Leonel Turcios Juarez, whose wife, Cristy Maryori Villafranca-Trejo, was deported, at home in El Paso, Texas, on 21 July 2026.Photograph: Ryan Romero/APView image in fullscreenArmy Sgt Hedar Leonel Turcios Juarez, whose wife, Cristy Maryori Villafranca-Trejo, was deported, at home in El Paso, Texas, on 21 July 2026.Photograph: Ryan Romero/APUS militaryWife of US soldier deported after Trump rollback on military family protectionsCristy Maryori Villafranca-Trejo, deported to Honduras, is latest military spouse to face removal amid Trump 2.0Associated PressTue 25 Aug 2026 16.23 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 19.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe wife of an active-dutyUS soldierwas deported on Monday to her nativeHonduras, according to her family and the federal Department of Homeland Security (DHS).Cristy Maryori Villafranca-Trejo is at least the seventh spouse or parent of an active-duty US soldier to be deported under the immigration crackdown duringDonald Trump’s second presidency.The Associated Press has found more than 50 cases in which immediate family members of US troops were placed in federal immigration detention after theTrump administrationrolled back protections for military families. In some instances, the DHS has released military spouses after media attention and advocacy by congressional leaders.Father of USS Lincoln sailor detained by ICE released from detentionRead moreVillafranca-Trejo’s husband, army Sgt Hedar Leonel Turcios Juarez, said he has been struggling to manage his military duties since she was detained on 11 July outside a Walmart near Fort Bliss, Texas, where he is stationed. Since then, he’s had to care for their six-year-old daughter without his wife’s help. Instead of training in the mornings, he takes his daughter to first grade – and he said he has already had to postpone a planned assignment at another base.“I don’t know if I will be able to continue with this,” Turcios Juarez said of his army career. “I have to make a plan to make sure I can still fulfill my military responsibilities – but also take care of my family.”The DHS confirmed Villafranca-Trejo’s deportation, saying she had “received due process”.Villafranca-Trejo, who has no known criminal record and entered the US in 2016 at age 18, was issued a final order of removal by an immigration judge in 2017 after failing to appear at a hearing, according to the DHS. Villafranca-Trejo’s husband said she had not received a notice for the hearing she missed and did not realize she had been ordered deported until they went to apply for her green card after marrying in 2022.Originally fromHonduras, Turcios Juarez became a US citizen in 2024 after enlisting two years earlier.Villafranca-Trejo’s motion to reopen her case was denied last May and an appeal before the Board of Immigration Appeals remained pending, according to her attorney. She had also been waiting for about a year for a decision on her application for military parole-in-place, a program that allows the immediate family of US troops to remain in the country to apply for a green card.“We were following the rules,” Turcios Juarez said. “We did everything we could on our side to fix this problem.”Prior to Trump’s second administration, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) would typically allow immediate family members of US troops to adjust their legal status even if they had been issued a final order of removal, according to Dan Gividen, who served as ICE deputy chief counsel from 2016 to 2019 under Trump.“If you’ve got an active-duty military member that’s married to someone now, and that’s going to give her the opportunity to get a green card, you wouldn’t detain them, much less execute the removal order,” Gividen said.JP Caballero, a spokesperson for congresswoman Veronica Escobar, a Democrat representing El Paso, said Escobar had opened a congressional inquiry into Villafranca-Trejo’s case and visited her at the Camp East Montana detention facility in Texas earlier this month.“My heart breaks for her, her children and the soldier who must feel so betrayed by the country he is sacrificing for,” Escobar said in a statement. “There are far too many families like theirs who are being targeted instead of supported.”Turcios Juarez said he was unsure how he would care for his daughter without his wife. He still hasn’t figured out how to tell his daughter what has happened. But he says he still wants to keep serving his country.“I love what I do, I want to keep doing this,” he said of the army. “I just don’t know how I am going to keep doing this.”Explore more on these topicsUS militaryUS immigrationTrump administrationDonald TrumpICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)US politicsHondurasnewsShareReuse this content

title: At least 47 killed and dozens kidnapped in gang attack near Haiti capital | Haiti | The Guardian
description: Gang leader threatens to kill hostages after attack in Kenscoff in which homes were also set alight
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Gang leader threatens to kill hostages after attack in Kenscoff in which homes were also set alight
Content: People walk past a burnt vehicle on Monday after the deadly violence in Kenscoff.Photograph: Clarens Siffroy/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople walk past a burnt vehicle on Monday after the deadly violence in Kenscoff.Photograph: Clarens Siffroy/AFP/Getty ImagesHaitiAt least 47 killed and dozens kidnapped in gang attack near Haiti capitalGang leader threatens to kill hostages after attack in Kenscoff in which homes were also set alight‘A massacre’: Haiti gangs carrying out mass killingsAssociated Press in Port-au-PrinceTue 25 Aug 2026 13.35 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 13.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt least 47 people were killed and more than 50 others kidnapped when armed men attacked a once peaceful community near Haiti’s capital at the weekend, the UN has said.A gang leader has threatened to kill the hostages if authorities kill any gang members as they try to secure the community of Kenscoff, nestled in the hills above Port-au-Prince.Sunday’s attack pierced the belief that security in theCaribbeancountry was improving. Romain Le Cour, the head of Haiti observatory at the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, said: “This is a major political and security test – for the government, for the police and for the international mission alike.”In a video posted on social media, the gang leader warned the director of Haiti’s national police, Vladimir Paraison, not to use drones to repel gangs in the area. “Paraison, if any of our soldiers are hurt, I will kill all of them,” he said, referring to the hostages.He identified himself as Izo 2, a reference to Izo, or Johnson André, one of Haiti’s most powerful gang members. Le Cour said Izo 2 was also known as Didi and led the armed group in Kenscoff on behalf of and in coordination with Izo and other gang leaders. “He’s running a kind of franchise cell for other gangs,” he said.Le Cour said the aim of the attack could be to force Haiti’s police and the UN-backed gang suppression force to disperse even more of their limited resources. “They don’t have enough personnel,” he said. “If you force them to deploy more troops, it would inevitably be at the expense of other areas.”The attack may also be a show of force and a message to Haiti’s government and police as the country prepares to hold general elections on 13 December, the first in more than a decade.Le Cour said: “This is a message to the government and the police that their claims of protection do not match reality. The gangs are saying: when we choose to attack, we can, and we will succeed.”View image in fullscreenWomen mourn at the site of the attack in Kenscoff.Photograph: Patrice Noel/ReutersThe first major attack on Kenscoff occurred in January 2025 and since then there have been sporadic attacks in the mountains surrounding the city centre. Sunday’s attack was the largest yet.At least five of the 47 people killed were children, according to the UN integrated office in Haiti, known as BINUH.Guns, gangs and drought: how crime and the climate crisis are reshaping HaitiRead moreKenscoff’s mayor, Jean Massillon, said two government employees were among those killed, including his cousin who served as his security detail.He said members of Viv Ansanm, a powerful gang coalition that the US has designated as a foreign terrorist organisation, also set fire to 25 homes.Massillon said gangs were still roaming Kenscoff’s periphery. “The atrocity of this crime reminds us that we have to continue working stronger every day to bring peace to the community,” he said. “I’m optimistic that the state will continue working to eradicate the gangs in Kenscoff.”Some survivors accused the government of not providing enough protection before the attack. The police rejected the accusations.Le Cour said that if police and armoured vehicles were indeed stationed in Kenscoff before the attack, it was concerning. “You let the gangs come in even if you had everything in place?” he said.Armed men control an estimated 70% of Port-au-Prince and swaths of land in Haiti’s central region and beyond, and gang violence has displaced a record 1.5 million people across Haiti. More than 3,050 people were reported killed from January to June and another 1,400 injured, according to UN statistics released on Tuesday.Explore more on these topicsHaitiCaribbeanAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: First Thing: Supreme court threatens midterms mail-in voting as it backs Trump plan | US news | The Guardian
description: US president has been obsessed with restricting the ability to vote by mail, despite using it himself
Author: Martin Belam
Headline: US president has been obsessed with restricting the ability to vote by mail, despite using it himself
Content: Election workers sort mail-in ballots.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenElection workers sort mail-in ballots.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesFirst Thing newsletterUS newsFirst Thing: Supreme court threatens midterms mail-in voting as it backs Trump planUS president has been obsessed with restricting the ability to vote by mail, despite using it himself. Plus, why we are still fascinated with Meg from the White StripesDon’t already get First Thing in your inbox? Sign up hereMartin BelamTue 25 Aug 2026 08.31 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 09.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGood morning. The US supreme court has sided with Donald Trump inhis effort to crack down on mail-in voting, though it is unclear whether or not his administration will be able to take action before the midterm elections in November. The court’s justices voted 6-3 along ideological lines to lift an injunction that a judge in Massachusetts had placed in June on an executive order issued by the president. But a second injunction remains in place, and the ruling leaves room for legal challenges.Trump has repeatedly likened voting by mail to cheating, despite his own use of it and overwhelming evidence that the system is secure. In March he ordered the government to create a “state citizenship list” of eligible voters, requiring that mail-in ballots only be delivered to people on that list. He also directed the justice department to prioritise investigations and prosecutions of state and local election officials who issue ballots to people deemed ineligible to vote in federal elections.What did the dissenting judges say?In a blistering dissent, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson wrote that the decision “needlessly injects chaos and uncertainty into the upcoming midterm elections”.How have rights organisations reacted?The president of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, Derrick Johnson, said: “Let this ruling be a reminder that democracy is never, ever guaranteed. We have to fight for it, we have to fight to keep it and we have to protect the rights we do have within it … they are trying to do everything they possibly can to make it difficult for you to vote.”Trump announces new 50% tariff on Canadian cars, trucks and steelView image in fullscreenCanada’s prime minister, Mark Carney.Photograph: Canadian Press/ShutterstockDonald Trump hasannounced a new 50% tariffon automobiles and crucial raw materials from Canada, the latest deterioration in trade relations between the two neighbours with traditionally strong economic ties. The US president said Canada had been “ripping off” the US for years and that it was “among the worst Nations in the World to deal with”.How has Canada reacted?The country’s prime minister, Mark Carney, told reporters that Trump’s announcement was largely expected. “It’s not a surprise for us that the US would take some form of reprisal to our response to their unjustified tariff,” he said. Carney has vowed to match the American tariffs “dollar for dollar”, and said Canada could not accept any proposed trade dealthat would weaken French language protections.US strikesvessel ineastern Pacific, killingtwo people in first attack in monthsView image in fullscreenUS navy personnel deployed in the Pacific.Photograph: Michelle Bir/AFP/Getty ImagesThe US military has struck a vessel in the Pacific Ocean, killing two people accused of drug trafficking. US Southern Command (SouthCom) said it had “executed a lethal kinetic strike on a low-profile vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Eastern Pacific”.SouthCom did not provide evidence of the vessel’s alleged involvement in drug trafficking.Monday’s strike marks the latest in a series since theTrump administrationlaunched what it described as a campaign targeting “narco-terrorists” smuggling drugs into the US. Numerous reports, however, indicate the strikes have done little to stem the flow of drugs into the country.US threatens severe sanctions against countries with economic ties to IranView image in fullscreenThe US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersThe US has threatened to impose severe sanctionsagainst any country or entity maintaining economic ties with Iran, hoping to achieve with economic measures what military means have so far failed to do. It is unclear, however, how far the Trump administration is prepared to go in confronting China, Iran’s biggest trading partner, which has signalled its resistance to US economic pressure to cut off links with an ally.Iran vowed retaliation against any country that takes part in the US-led isolation campaign.Launching what he called Operation Economic Outcast, the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, called it an unprecedented campaign and compared it with the D-day Normandy landings, a turning point in the second world war.In other news …View image in fullscreenColombia’s president, Abelardo de la Espriella.Photograph: Pablo R Seco/EPAColombia’s far-right president,Abelardo de la Espriella, has announced acrackdown on immigrants.The country continues to deal with the aftermath of a 7.4-magnitude earthquake that killed more than 300 people and destroyed more than 30,000 homes.US healthcare officials said a food-poisoning outbreak tied to alfalfa sproutshadsickened people in at least 15 states.Target haspulled a controversial Halloween costumeoff its shelvesafter criticism across social media that it resembled a racist caricature.A mental health advocate suspected of killing her police officer husbandwas found deadsix days after she disappeared from her Massachusetts home, authorities said.An independent arbitrator has ordered the Washington Post torehire the high-profile opinion columnistKaren Attiah, who was fired abruptly last September over social media comments about Charlie Kirk.Stat of the day: Trump administration plans to revoke 200,000asylum seekers’ visasView image in fullscreenDonald Trump and Marco Rubio.Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APA Department of State spokesperson said it was coordinating with the Department of Homeland Security “toidentify and revoke the non-immigrant visas of foreignerswho have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently”. Associated Press put the number of people potentially involved at as many as 200,000, which would be the largest single mass revocation of visas in US history.Culture pick: Seam me up, Scotty! After 60 years, Star Trek has had a muppet takeoverView image in fullscreenMuppets! In Space!Photograph: Jan Thijs/Paramount+The creators of Strange New Worldstalk about boldly sewingwhere no one has sewn before.Don’t miss this: Australia has just 12,000 sea lions left – and ‘carnage’ may await them as bird flu takes holdView image in fullscreenAn Australian sea lion.Photograph: Alastair Pollock Photography/Getty ImagesEverybody loves seals and sea lions – the dogs of the ocean – but in Australia there are fears that bird flu has jumped species and could endanger them.Lisa Cox investigates.… or this: Why we’re still so fascinated by Meg WhiteView image in fullscreenMeg White in 2003.Photograph: Patrick Rideaux/Rex FeaturesRecent incorrect attempts to reveal the White Stripes star’s whereabouts reflecthow much we’re still obsessedwith the one-of-a-kind drummer who did things her own way.Climate check: Nevada files lawsuit challenging federal plan for Colorado River revivalView image in fullscreenWater flows from the Glen Canyon dam down the Colorado River.Photograph: George Frey/Getty ImagesNevada has filed a federal lawsuitchallenging the Trump administration’s plan for the imperilled Colorado River, which threatens to cut roughly 20% of the water supplied to lower basin states – Nevada, Arizona and California – over the next two years. It could become the first of many court battles over the waterway that supplies 40 million people, dozens of tribes and 5.5m acres of farmland across the American west.Last Thing: Toddler invades pitch during Minnesota’s MLS win over San JoseView image in fullscreenA child walks on to the field during the MLS match.Photograph: Icon Sportswire/Getty ImagesA toddler interrupteda Major League Soccer match between Minnesota United and San Jose Earthquakes at the weekend by invading the pitch – a bizarre scene punctuated by an on-air analyst saying: “There’s a baby on the field.” There’san adorable videoof it to enjoy.Sign upSign up for the US morning briefingFirst Thing is delivered to thousands of inboxes every weekday.
