title: Colombia’s new president Abelardo de la Espriella announces immigration crackdown | Colombia | The Guardian
description: Far-right leader echoes ally Donald Trump and says operations to ‘track down illegal immigrants’ should begin this week, amid earthquake aftermath
Author: Tiago Rogero
Headline: Far-right leader echoes ally Donald Trump and says operations to ‘track down illegal immigrants’ should begin this week, amid earthquake aftermath
Content: Colombian president Abelardo de la Espriella says the operations against ‘illegal immigrants’ will involve police and the migration authority.Photograph: Pablo R Seco/EPAView image in fullscreenColombian president Abelardo de la Espriella says the operations against ‘illegal immigrants’ will involve police and the migration authority.Photograph: Pablo R Seco/EPAColombiaColombia’s new president Abelardo de la Espriella announces immigration crackdownFar-right leader echoes ally Donald Trump and says operations to ‘track down illegal immigrants’ should begin this week, amid earthquake aftermathTiago RogeroSouth America correspondentMon 24 Aug 2026 20.34 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleColombia’s far-right president, Abelardo de la Espriella, has announced a crackdown on immigrants, ordering authorities to detain and deport people who are in the country irregularly or have committed crimes.In office for just over two weeks, the millionaire former lawyer made the announcement on Sunday as the country continued to grapple with theaftermath of a 7.4-magnitude earthquakeon 10 August that killed more than 300 people and destroyed more than 30,000 homes.De la Espriella said the first joint operations involving the police and the migration authority should begin “this very week”.“Let the coordinated operations begin to track down illegal immigrants: first, those committing crimes; second, those who have not regularised their status and who will have to be deported immediately,” de la Espriella said during a cabinet meeting held on Sunday in Barranquilla, the Caribbean city that has in effect been turned into an alternative capital.US promises $1bn in security aid to Colombia as new rightwing president pledges drugs crackdownRead moreHe echoed the “Americans first” rhetoric of his ally, US presidentDonald Trump, saying that from now on it would be “Colombians first, Colombians second and Colombians third”.The Colombian president has joined other Trump-aligned leaders in the region who have also tightened migration rules,including Argentina’sJavier Milei and Chile’s José Antonio Kast.De la Espriella’s order is facing criticism from the opposition and human rights activists, who say it will end a migration policy that endured for more than a decade under both rightwing and leftwing governments and benefited above all migrants fleeing the humanitarian crisis in neighbouring Venezuela.Although he used the anti-immigration rhetoric characteristic of other far-right candidates during his campaign, his platform focused chiefly on his promise to pursue an iron-fist policy against criminal groups.In the same announcement, he also declared that all gangs involved in drug trafficking, illegal mining, extortion and smuggling were “terrorists and we will treat them as such. Whatever happens, we will defeat them, by reason or by force.”The president did not directly mention Venezuelans when discussing immigration, but they account for roughly 90% of all migrants in the country. Of the 2.8 million Venezuelans living in Colombia, about 848,000 are in an irregular situation, including 193,000 children and adolescents.Activist forced out of US after criticising Trump-aligned Colombian politicianRead moreThe leftwing senator María José Pizarro Rodríguez reposted the president’s announcement and asked whether he was “proposing a Colombian ICE against fellow Latin Americans”, in reference to the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). She added that the “order to deport irregular migrants is pure xenophobia and aporophobia”.“Instead of persecuting people fleeing poverty and violence, regularise their status. There are thousands of migrants who work hard and contribute to the economies of the countries that receive them,” she wrote.The Colombian newspaperEl Tiempo reportedthat sources within the migration department believe the agency does not have enough staff to carry out the operations De la Espriella has promised.Analysts have also noted that under Colombian law there is no such category as an “illegal” immigrant, as De la Espriella said, but rather migrants in an “irregular” situation, since being in the country without the proper documentation is not a crime.Explore more on these topicsColombiaThe far rightDonald TrumpAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Taiwan charges nine people for smuggling ‘high-end’ AI servers to China | Technology | The Guardian
description: Among those charged are two Super Micro employees and one from Nvidia, marking another flashpoint in US-China AI rivalry
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Among those charged are two Super Micro employees and one from Nvidia, marking another flashpoint in US-China AI rivalry
Content: An Nvidia H100 graphics processor chip at the company's headquarters in Santa Clara, California.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn Nvidia H100 graphics processor chip at the company's headquarters in Santa Clara, California.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesTechnologyTaiwan charges nine people for smuggling ‘high-end’ AI servers to ChinaAmong those charged are two Super Micro employees and one from Nvidia, marking another flashpoint in US-China AI rivalryAssociated PressTue 25 Aug 2026 15.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTaiwanese prosecutors charged nine people Monday, including one fromNvidiaand two from Super Micro, for illegally exporting “high-end AI servers” to mainland China, adding another wave of turbulence in the AI ​​rivalry between China and the United States.Prosecutors said the servers involved were graphics processing units known as “B300,” which have been banned from sale toChina.Seventy-four servers arrived in China successfully, according to the prosecutors. Of those, 50 were sent through Indonesia, 16 delivered directly to China and eight sent to Japan first, then Hong Kong, before they landed in mainland China.Trump-backed Ken Paxton unveils ‘Texas first’ datacenter plan aimed at ‘negative impact’Read moreAnother attempt involving 56 servers failed, and the servers remain in Taiwan, said the prosecutor’s office.AI infrastructure, including advanced semiconductors mostly made in Taiwan, has become a key point of competition between the US and China. Washington began imposing restrictions on Nvidia’s exports of advanced chips to China in 2022 and tightened them in subsequent years. In April 2025, the US required licenses for exports of Nvidia’s H20 chips to China before allowing some sales to resume later that year.Under export controls, any sale by Nvidia of high-end AI servers – the computer infrastructure that houses the chips needed to power AI systems – requires a strict review process, according to a document from Keelung District prosecutors’ office in Taiwan. The document also said purchases of more than eight high-end AI servers require company staff to conduct on-site checks to the clients.“We will work with the Taiwan authorities to help them resolve the allegations as quickly as possible,” Patrick Rutherford, an Nvidia spokesperson, said in a written statement.Super Micro said in a written statement that the arrests of two of its former employees were due to its cooperation with the Taiwanese authorities and the company will continue to work to “enhance its robust export compliance program to protect American innovation”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionProsecutors are seeking the maximum five-year sentences for four of the nine defendants, including Chang, an Nvidia manager identified just by his family name. Chang was the “key figure” responsible for “authorizing the release of the B300 GPUs” in this case but “demonstrated a clearly poor attitude following the offense”, the document said.Some of the defendants set up a company in Japan, which helped successfully transfer eight of the servers, prosecutors said. Some allegedly created fake websites and falsified information to evade export restrictions.Explore more on these topicsTechnologyAI (artificial intelligence)NvidiaChinaAsia PacificComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: China denounces US threat of sanctions over trade with Iran | China | The Guardian
description: Beijing says it will take ‘all necessary measures’ to protect its interests as US steps up efforts to isolate Tehran
Author: Julian Borger
Headline: Beijing says it will take ‘all necessary measures’ to protect its interests as US steps up efforts to isolate Tehran
Content: Lianyungang port in China. The country buys an estimated 80% of Iran’s oil exports.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLianyungang port in China. The country buys an estimated 80% of Iran’s oil exports.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesChinaChina denounces US threat of sanctions over trade with IranBeijing says it will take ‘all necessary measures’ to protect its interests as US steps up efforts to isolate TehranExplainer: could US sanctions threaten China-Iran ties?Julian BorgerSenior international correspondentTue 25 Aug 2026 13.11 EDTFirst published on Tue 25 Aug 2026 07.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChina has denounced thethreat of US sanctions for its trade with Iran, saying any such measures would be illegal, and warned it would take “all necessary measures” to protect its national interests.Beijing’s rejection of the US threat of secondary sanctions for any country or entity continuing to trade with Tehran had been predicted.Chinabuys an estimated 80% of Iran’s oil exports and has defied previous US efforts to limit the flow of revenue to the Tehran regime.Its statement of opposition raises the question of how far the Trump administration would be prepared to go in confronting China and its financial system in the drive to isolateIran.Chart showing Iranian oil exports to China from January 2025 to August 2026In making the sanctions threat on Monday, the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, announced an initial set of sanctions on 60 individuals, entities and vessels for alleged involvement in trade with Iran, but there were no Chinese financial institutions on the list, despite their involvement in financing the Iranian oil trade. The omission reflected US caution.China is the biggest buyer of Iran’s oil. Could US sanctions threaten those ties?Read moreAsked why the Trump administration had not declared immediate sanctions and had stopped short of naming potential sanctions targets, Bessent replied: “Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?”Financial and trade experts say the administration is well aware of the risk of Chinese retaliation before a scheduled summit next month between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping. China could strike back through financial markets or with limits on its export of critical minerals.The spokesperson for China’s foreign ministry, Lin Jian, told reporters on Tuesday: “Cooperation between China and Iran has always been conducted within the framework of international law and should not be interfered with or disrupted.8:57‘Economic D-day’: How desperate is Trump to end Iran war? - The Latest“China has already stated many times that it firmly opposes illegal unilateral sanctions. China will take all necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own rights and interests.”Iran has been economically wrecked by the war and the accompanying US blockade, but it maintained its defiance in response to Bessent’s threats of total isolation.The economy minister, Ali Madanizadeh, said on state television: “Our defence is no longer so defensive; the enemies should wait for an attack.”Graph showing number of transits through the strait of Hormuz from February to August 2026An oil tanker was reportedly hit on Tuesday by an unidentified projectile at the mouth of the strait of Hormuz. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre said the crew was safe and no environmental damage was immediately apparent. Only two commercial vessels were reported to have successfully made the transit through the narrow waterway on Monday.Iran and Oman, which sits on the southern shore of the strait, held talks on Tuesday aimed at agreeing joint management of the waterway between the two countries. Oman’s foreign minister, Badr al-Busaidi, said after the discussions had concluded that there were hopes that a temporary agreed route through the strait would be announced soon.A Pakistani delegation was also in Tehran, leaving on Tuesday after a day’s talks with Iranian leaders. The delegation was headed by the army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, who has led Pakistan’s mediation efforts in the Iran conflict. The Pakistani military said the Tehran talks were focused on reopening the strait of Hormuz. Amemorandum signed by the US and Iranin June was intended to reopen the strait pending further negotiations but thedeal collapsedwithin weeks.The declaration of what Bessent called Operation Economic Outcast suggests the prospects of a resolution to the conflict with Iran are still remote. It also suggests a lean towards economic measures and away from military force after a six-month war that has not brought about the intended Iranian capitulation.View image in fullscreenDonald Trump and Xi Jinping in Beijing in May. They are due to meet again next month.Photograph: Alex Wong/Getty ImagesOil prices fell about 4% to a one-week low on Tuesday after the US sanctions announcement, as traders appeared to see economic ​pressure as posing less risk to oil supplies than further military escalation. But the price per barrel of about $87 remained far above the prewar average.The US defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, said further military action was not off the table. “By no means are we foreclosing using ‌kinetic strikes anywhere in the ​strait of Hormuz or around Iran,” he ⁠told reporters on Monday.Bessent called the sanctions campaign unprecedented and compared it to the D-day Normandy landings, a turning point in the second world war.“Today, in that same spirit, we are launching an economic onslaught against Iran’s financial connections around the globe,” he said. “Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone.”He said the US had identified those that continued to deal with Iran and each violator would be given a deadline to cut ties or face US sanctions. He said the deadlines imposed would depend on individual circumstances.“Any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the US dollar system,” he said. “The clock just started ticking.”Persuasion, denial and bluster: Trump ‘stuck’ on Iran war ahead of electionsRead moreBessent said Trump was “making phone calls to world leaders with specific requests to cease their interactions with the regime”, but he did not specify whether the US president would talk to his Chinese counterpart.Sina Toossi, a senior non-resident fellow at the Center for International Policy, said: “After nearly six months without a military or diplomatic victory, Washington appears to be trying to accomplish through intensified economic strangulation what military force has so far failed to achieve. But Tehran is answering that zero-sum approach with one of its own.”In apparent anticipation of the US measures, the United Arab Emirates, a close US and Israeli ally, announced it was suspending trade ties with Iran. Turkey, another trading partner with Iran, which has been critical of the US-led campaign against the Islamic Republic, has yet to respond to the US threat of sanctions.Andrew Miller, a senior fellow at the Center for American Progress, said: “The announcement of new economic sanctions on Iran and those countries trading with it signals what is plain to all: this war has brought the United States no closer to eliminating Iran’s nuclear programme or crippling the Iranian regime. But while sanctions can be effective, it is highly unlikely they will produce a quick settlement favourable to the United States.”Explore more on these topicsChinaUS foreign policyIranUS-Israel war on IranAsia PacificMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Artist known for sculptures of Mao Zedong jailed for slandering ‘heroes and martyrs’ | China | The Guardian
description: Gao Zhen sentenced to three years in prison after already spending two years in detention
Author: Yu-chen Li
Headline: Gao Zhen sentenced to three years in prison after already spending two years in detention
Content: Artist Gao Zhen in 2019.Photograph: Kimberli Mäkäräinen/WikimediaView image in fullscreenArtist Gao Zhen in 2019.Photograph: Kimberli Mäkäräinen/WikimediaChinaArtist known for sculptures of Mao Zedong jailed for slandering ‘heroes and martyrs’Gao Zhen sentenced to three years in prison after already spending two years in detentionDanny Vincent in TaipeiTue 25 Aug 2026 07.53 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGao Zhen, a prominent Chinese artist known for provocative sculptures of the former leaderMao Zedong, has been sentenced to three years in prison after being found guilty of slandering China’s “heroes and martyrs”. The sentencing came two years after he was detained while visiting the country with his family, according to his wife and human rights groups.Thecase has attracted international condemnation, largely because the artworks at the centre of the case were created more than 10 years before China created the law under which Gao was charged.The law, which bans defamation of China’s heroes and martyrs, came into force in March 2018. Courts have previously used the law to charge people who challenge official accounts of Chinese history.Gao, 70, a Chinese citizen and US permanent resident, wasdetained on 26 August 2024after returning to China with his wife and son. Police later raided his studio near Beijing.In one of Gao’s most famous works with his brother Gao Qiang, they depict Mao kneeling. In another, a firing squad made up of seven Mao statues point rifles at Jesus.View image in fullscreenSculpture entitled Mao's Guilt by Gao Zhen, left, and his brother Gao Qiang, pictured in Beijing in 2009.Photograph: Shiho Fukada/The New York Times/Redux/eyevineGao’s wife, Zhao Yaliang, told the Guardian that the two years since her husband’s detention had been a painful ordeal for the family.“His arrest and trial should never have happened. We have had no choice but to wait in anguish … I am very sad that it’s going to be this long,” she said after the verdict.According to his wife, two of Gao’s relatives were allowed to enter the Sanhe city people’s court in Hebei province for the verdict, while she waited with their son and several friends outside.“For two years he has suffered in the detention centre, while my son, our closest family members and I have also endured this torment,” she said.Gao’s family said he had fainted in detention and was afflicted with back, knee and respiratory problems. His wife said Gao had sustained heatstroke during the summer and described experiencing a feeling of “being close to death”.Weiquanwang, a human rights monitoring network, said Gao had been sentenced for “infringing the reputation and honour of heroes and martyrs”. The rights network said Gao’s studio and property had been sealed and that friends and supporters had been silenced.Artworks made by Gao during his time in detention and seen by the Guardian include a series of colourful paper cuttings.“A body can be confined, but clarity of mind is harder to take away. Mentally he remains remarkably sharp and unbroken,” said Gao Qiang, who spent decades producing art with him as the Gao brothers.“Art should never be a crime scene waiting to be discovered,” he said.In a handwritten letter sent from detention to his young son, Gao wrote: “Dad’s eyesight isn’t very good, and I don’t have my glasses, so my handwriting isn’t very good.“I hope I can finish my work as soon as possible and return to you and Mum,” he wrote. “Son, remember: Dad will always love you!”Sophie Richardson, a longtime China human rights campaigner, said: “Gao has been prosecuted for conduct that has never been criminal, and his family has endured collective punishment at the hands of the authorities, and that is criminal.”Sarah Brooks, the China director for Amnesty International, said the decision to sentence Gao to a maximum three-year prison term illustrated “the authorities’ determination to deter others from engaging in independent artistic expression”.Gao’s wife and their young son have been unable to leave China since his detention. Human rights campaigners said his wife was stopped from travelling abroad based on national security grounds. His young son is a US citizen but has been unable to leave without his parents.The Chinese foreign ministry was approached for comment.Yu-chen Li contributed to reporting.Explore more on these topicsChinaCensorshipMao ZedongAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Like smoking a cigarette’: Indonesia chokes on haze as blazes intensify amid super ‘El Niño’ | Indonesia | The Guardian
description: In Indonesia’s Kalimantan, fires have ravaged tens of thousands of acres, with suffocating smoke reaching Malaysia and putting Singapore on alert
Author: Natasha May
Headline: In Indonesia’s Kalimantan, fires have ravaged tens of thousands of acres, with suffocating smoke reaching Malaysia and putting Singapore on alert
Content: A Manggala Agni firefighter works to extinguish a land fire in Ogan Ilir Regency, South Sumatra, Indonesia, on 15 August 2026.Photograph: Bagus Kurniawan/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA Manggala Agni firefighter works to extinguish a land fire in Ogan Ilir Regency, South Sumatra, Indonesia, on 15 August 2026.Photograph: Bagus Kurniawan/NurPhoto/ShutterstockIndonesia‘Like smoking a cigarette’: Indonesia chokes on haze as blazes intensify amid super ‘El Niño’In Indonesia’s Kalimantan, fires have ravaged tens of thousands of acres, with suffocating smoke reaching Malaysia and putting Singapore on alertNatasha MayTue 25 Aug 2026 00.17 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 00.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSuwadi can barely see five metres in front of him when he steps outside his home in Indonesian Borneo.Each breath, he says, feels “like smoking a cigarette”.It has been like this for weeks in Kalimantan, the Indonesian side of Borneo island, where fires have raged across tens of thousands of acres of land, including ancient rainforest, triggering a trans-boundary haze now threatening Malaysia and Singapore.In West Kalimantan there has been a spike in emergency room visits, with about 5,000 people arriving with respiratory symptoms each week since July, compared with 500 per week in the first half of the year, health ministry data shows.Children continue to go to school and adults to work, but many are suffering from the unhealthy effects of breathing in thick smoke, constantly. “What about babies, the elderly, and pregnant women who are exposed to this?” asks Suwadi.Some classes have been suspended, with parents urging schools to switch to online learning.View image in fullscreenTraffic on a haze-shrouded road in Palangka Raya city, Central Kalimantan, on 20 August 2026.Photograph: REINA/AFP/Getty ImagesFires each year in Kalimantan are often blamed on “slash and burn” techniques used to clear land for plantations that produce palm oil, of which Indonesia is the world’s largest producer.Authorities say this year’s “super” El Niño may be intensifying the blazes, with the weather phenomenon expected to peak in September.Experts have warned the worst could be yet to come as the dry season continues into October, and the rains that could extinguish the fires look unlikely before November.The haze is fast becoming a regional issue, with Malaysia and Brunei agreeing to raise it at Asean as thick smoke from forest and peatland fires drifts across the border.On Tuesday, the Malaysian capital, Kuala Lumpur, was the most polluted city on earth, followed by Jakarta, according to air quality monitoring company IQAir. Almost 600 schools in the Malaysian state of Sarawak on Borneo island closed due to hot and dry conditions. Singapore went on alert.On social media, Indonesians have tried to draw attention to the issue – highlighting the huge blazes in Kalimantan, and also in Sumatra, West Papua, and in Lombok where a fire destroyed a traditional Sade village over the weekend.altForestry ministry data shows that nearly 94,000 hectares (232,000 acres) have burned nationwide this July alone.On Monday, the Indonesian president,Prabowo Subianto, ordered authorities to revoke the business permits of corporations suspected of directing the land clearing, state news agency Antara reported. Indonesian police arrested 72 people suspected of starting fires in Borneo and Sumatra, with most accused of deliberately burning land to clear areas for plantations.The response comes as regional experts fear this could be another devastating fire year, with many of Indonesia’s most severe blazes occurring during El Niño cycles.In 2015, another El Niño year, more than 6m acres were burned, with trans-boundary haze again plaguing neighbouring Malaysia and Singapore.During a recent visit to the region, Prabowo promised government resources to contain the fires, including helicopters and water pumps.View image in fullscreenProtester in Jakarta, Indonesia, against recurring forest and land fires.Photograph: Faisal Ramadhan/NurPhoto/ShutterstockBut some Indonesians have expressed frustration at what they see as government inaction against the companies allegedly involved.Indonesia’s unique rainforests are home to peatland ecosystems, which should be naturally resilient to fire when water tables remain high.However, drainage networks built to clear land for pulp and oil palm plantations have robbed the soil of its natural capacity to retain water, experts say.Fires on degraded peatlands are more difficult to control because they burn deep underground, says Justin Sentian, a professor in climate change at Universiti Malaysia Sabahand. And they produce thick, acrid smoke.“If authorities only act after hotspots appear, they will forever be playing catch-up,” says Sentian. “True prevention must address the soil itself by halting the conversion of peatlands and actively restoring degraded areas.”On Monday another fire broke out near the factory where Suwadi works in Kalimantan. With houses burning and smoke everywhere, Suwadi says he is afraid for the future of the region.“The fire is getting dangerously close to homes,” he says, “People are [in] panic now.”With Agence France-Presse and Associated PressExplore more on these topicsIndonesiaWildfiresAsia PacificPrabowo SubiantofeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Australia may face a rush of datacentre construction as AI firms look to avoid upcoming rules, experts say | Australian politics | The Guardian
description: Regulations will require new sites to avoid pushing up power prices by building renewable energy plants and minimising water use
Author: Josh Taylor
Headline: Regulations will require new sites to avoid pushing up power prices by building renewable energy plants and minimising water use
Content: Anthony Albanese at a national cabinet meeting in Perth.Photograph: Matt Jelonek/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAnthony Albanese at a national cabinet meeting in Perth.Photograph: Matt Jelonek/Getty ImagesAustralian politicsAustralia may face a rush of datacentre construction as AI firms look to avoid upcoming rules, experts sayRegulations will require new sites to avoid pushing up power prices by building renewable energy plants and minimising water useFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJosh TaylorTechnology reporterTue 25 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 18.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePlanned datacentres around Australia may avoid strict new rules being proposed by Anthony Albanese if they can secure approvals in the coming months, amid growing calls for a moratorium.The prime minister is aiming to come to an agreement with national cabinet onfederal regulations for datacentresat a meeting on Wednesday.The rules will require datacentres to avoid pushing up power prices – including by bringing renewable energy to the grid to cover their electricity demands – while meeting their own connection costs and minimising water use.Developers will also need to ensure their datacentres are appropriately sized and located away from schools, homes, potential housing or agricultural locations.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailHowever, the rules will not be retrospective. This means any project that has been approved before the legislation passes next year will only be subject to existing state or territory laws.The AustralianEnergyMarket Operator (Aemo) reported on Tuesday there were 225 datacentres in development, and electricity demand from them was expected to grow from 5 to 34 terawatt hours by 2036.There is uncertainty over the number of projects that will ultimately go ahead. More than 40% of datacentre projects since Aemo’s 2025 report either dropped off the list or regressed in status.But some of the projects currently in the pipeline could receive approval before the new rules apply.The New South Wales government isnow considering a 90MW datacentreabout 9km from Sydney’s CBD. Named Project Mars, the three-storey centre will cover 22,000sqm near Lane Cove River under current plans.Goodman Group, the company behind the project, is consulting with the community about the proposal, amid strong local pushback in an area where five datacentres are already approved or being proposed.The project’s website states it will use existing power, and 3.5ML a day of water from Sydney Water should it go ahead. There will be 200kW-worth of solar panels on the building, but the company has limited information on more renewables to offset its power demands, stating it is “exploring opportunities to source additional renewable generation to support its proposed datacentre rollout in Australia.”Sasha Titchkosky, a representative of Lane Cove Responsible Planning group, said developers should consider the potential damage to their brand should they proceed with datacentre projects under the old rules. But she said governments should enact a moratorium on approvals until the new rules are in place.“At the very least, a moratorium on approvals in established residential areas … [it] seems to me that would be the responsible thing for governments to do,” Titchkosky said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I don’t think it’s an unreasonable ask, to actually have the government doing what they should be doing to protect the citizens.”Goodman Group was approached for comment.Prof Crystal Legacy, an urban planning researcher at the University of Melbourne, said developers would probably want to get in “before the new regulatory levers come into play.” She warned that state governments, which may try to fast-track applications before new rules come into effect, would do so “at your political peril.”“People are now noticing, and there’s always going to be a political backlash,” Legacy said.“We call people Nimbys, but I think that’s an unfair characterisation for people who are just concerned about the environmental impacts, as well as the amenity impacts of these massive datacentres.”The Greens have previously called for a moratorium on approvals until the new rules are in place.While Albanese works to get the states and territories to sign off on his proposed changes, the community pressure is likely to continue, with a federal inquiry into datacentres currently accepting submissions, along with state inquiries in NSW and Tasmania.Explore more on these topicsAustralian politicsDatacentres - AustraliaAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingEnergynewsShareReuse this content

title: One Nation’s Malcolm Roberts ‘in two minds’ about whether gay people should be equal | One Nation | The Guardian
description: Footage shows senator on stage at the Church and State conference responding to question about party’s director James Ashby
Author: Tory Shepherd
Headline: Footage shows senator on stage at the Church and State conference responding to question about party’s director James Ashby
Content: Footage released on Sunday showed One Nation leader Pauline Hanson and senator Malcolm Roberts on stage at the Church and State conference in June.Photograph: Mike Bowers/The GuardianView image in fullscreenFootage released on Sunday showed One Nation leader Pauline Hanson and senator Malcolm Roberts on stage at the Church and State conference in June.Photograph: Mike Bowers/The GuardianOne NationOne Nation’s Malcolm Roberts ‘in two minds’ about whether gay people should be equalFootage shows senator on stage at the Church and State conference responding to question about party’s director James AshbyFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastTory ShepherdTue 25 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 17.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne Nation’sMalcolm Robertstold a conference earlier this year that he was in “two minds” about whether gay people should have equal rights.In footage from June’s Church and State conference, released on Sunday, the senator can be seen responding to a question about James Ashby, the party’s director, who is gay.Both Roberts and the One Nation leader,Pauline Hanson, appeared at the conservative Christian conference.In the footage, Roberts described Ashby as bright, honest and straight.“Well, straight in one way,” he joked.An audience member then asked Roberts what Christians should think about Ashby.Roberts responded by referring to the late American bishop and gay rights advocate John Shelby Spong, citing him as saying that after women and black people were no longer recognised as “inferior”, gay people were next.“Now I’m in two minds about that,” Roberts said. “So I haven’t got a firm position on it myself other than I don’t, I’m not homosexual and I can’t, I can’t understand it.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email“But there have been a number of homosexuals who are very, very prominent in many, many fields throughout history. So all I know is that in this environment, James is not morally sound. But from what I’ve seen of him, his honesty, his integrity, his ability, he is sound.“So if you pardon me, I haven’t made up my mind, but there are a number of people in society in very prominent positions in the arts, sports, science, business, politics, who are homosexual.“And I don’t think we can afford to ban them. So it’s difficult.”The chief executive of Equality Australia, Anna Brown, said it was “genuinely shocking” that aOne Nationsenator would talk about “banning” people.One Nation’s immigration policy is hard to define – even by its own MPsRead more“As though something so incompatible with a democratic society could be an acceptable option,” she said.“The idea that One Nation or its senators think that this could be an idea that’s on the table, or even a matter of legitimate debate, is incredibly chilling.“And perhaps it’s worth reminding the senator that being gay and a person of deep faith are not mutually exclusive, and neither makes someone any more or less morally sound.”The organiser of the conference, Dave Pellowe, said in the same forum that “loud, screaming activists” had held American medical health professions to ransom “until they capitulated to delisting same-sex attraction as something that needed treatment, as an illness”.Roberts is also seen in the footage vowing to push for the party to adopt a blanket abortion ban,contradicting Hanson’s position.He also said he would push for the party to claim that life begins at conception.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion6:27Barnaby Joyce suggests One Nation could welcome some refugees while barring other migrants – videoIn an Instagram post from earlier this year, also from the conference, Hanson can be seen saying she “had to have a conversation” with the Farrer MP, David Farley, after he commented that the current immigration intake of 306,000 was “probably not” too much.As leader she sometimes had to “call the shots”, she said in the latest footage.Since Farley’s migration comments, there have beenmultiple contradictions and changesin the anti-immigration party’s policy.Church and State describes itself as a “Christian political education ministry” teaching people to look at political issues and candidates through the lens of Scripture.One Nation representatives have made frequent comments about homosexuality on other occasions.Earlier this month, the MP Barnaby Joyce described One Nation as “one of the gayest parties in Australia” after its failed candidate Parminder Singh described homosexuality as a mental illness.Hanson then saidshe didn’t like Mardi Gras and that “your own personal sexuality should be kept behind closed doors”.Ashby has said as a “gay bloke” he doesn’t like the rainbow flag.Jason Virgo, who is gay, was elected as a One Nation MP in the South Australian election in March, while his newly elected colleague in the upper house, Cory Bernardi, said he stood by his2012 commentslinking same-sex marriage to polygamy and bestiality.In the Church and State footage, Roberts also discussed various conspiracy theories and said family law changes made since 1975 – including the introduction ofno-fault divorce– were “tearing apart this country”.“It’s deliberate because they’re after the family. They’re after anything that can stand up to communism,” he said.Malcolm Roberts, James Ashby and One Nation did not respond to a request for comment.Explore more on these topicsOne NationMalcolm RobertsPauline HansonAustralian politicsLGBTQ+ rightsnewsShareReuse this content

title: FBI raided Spanish vacation rental of wealthy leftwing funder James ‘Fergie’ Chambers after his arrest | FBI | The Guardian
description: Lawyer Baltasar Garzón, representing Chambers, said case against his client is ‘very strange’ as US requests extradition
Author: Timothy Pratt
Headline: Lawyer Baltasar Garzón, representing Chambers, said case against his client is ‘very strange’ as US requests extradition
Content: James ‘Fergie’ Chambers in Tunis, Tunisia, on 8 February 2024.Photograph: Chedly Ben Ibrahim/NurPhoto via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJames ‘Fergie’ Chambers in Tunis, Tunisia, on 8 February 2024.Photograph: Chedly Ben Ibrahim/NurPhoto via Getty ImagesFBIFBI raided Spanish vacation rental of wealthy leftwing funder James ‘Fergie’ Chambers after his arrestLawyer Baltasar Garzón, representing Chambers, said case against his client is ‘very strange’ as US requests extraditionTimothy PrattTue 25 Aug 2026 16.57 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 18.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFBI agents raided the Ibiza,Spain, vacation rental of 41-year-old James “Fergie” Chambers, a US citizen and wealthy donor to leftwing and humanitarian projects worldwide, in the days following his arrest last month, the Guardian has learned.Baltasar Garzón,a human rights lawyer representing Chambers, revealed the details in an exclusive interview. Chambers is wanted for extradition by theTrump administrationfor alleged financial support ofHamas, as well as other charges.Arrest of American who has given $1m in aid to Palestine prompts fears of ‘growing repression from Trump’Read moreGarzón, one of Europe’s most famous human rights lawyers, characterized the case as “very strange, one of the most remarkable I’ve worked on”. He told the Guardian the indictment against Chambers was “pretty weak and diffuse”.The case centers on Chambers allegedly laundering $7.5m that he wired several years ago from a US bank account to Tunisia, where Chambers lived at the time, and allegedly using the money to support the Palestinian group. The exact details of the indictment against Chambers remain sealed.Chambers, heir to one of the richest families in the US, has supported a handful of humanitarian projects in Gaza with funds totaling more than $1m, a member of his legal teamsaidshortly after his 10 July arrest.It is the first known case of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas.Garzón spoke with the Guardian on Thursday shortly after his second visit with Chambers, now in his second month in a Spanish jail. The former judge and veteran human rights lawyer said theFBIdidn’t find anything in the raid.View image in fullscreenBaltasar Garzón on 4 November 2025 in Madrid, Spain.Photograph: Europa Press News/Europa Press/Getty ImagesHe also indicated that the road ahead for Chambers may be longer than what a Spanish official told the Guardian shortly after his arrest, potentially lasting months.First, US authorities have until Wednesday – 45 days after his arrest – to submit documentation supporting the extradition petition and the underlying indictment, which remains sealed, Garzón said.If the US doesn’t meet this deadline, the petition expires and Chambers is released. If the deadline is met, the Spanish government evaluates the paperwork over several weeks. After that, the case winds its way through various legal and government bodies. One thing being considered from the start of the process and forward is if the petition is politically motivated, which would allow the Spanish government to deny extradition.“It’s noteworthy that humanitarian aid and defending human rights is being criminalized,” Garzón said. “It’s a case of persecution … and they’re not going to be able to find one cent directed at terrorist or violent acts.”The Spanish lawyer’s five-decade career includes seeking the extradition from London of the former Chilean dictator Augusto Pinochet, as well as pursuing accountability for human rights abuses in Spain, Argentina and elsewhere.Chambers, a self-described communist and anti-imperialist, is heir of the Cox family, owners of Atlanta-based Cox Communications. As part of a settlement in which his family severed ties with him at the time, he sold stock back to his family worth about $250m in mid-2023. Since then he has been funding an estimated 100 projects in 20 countries, his partner, Stella Schnabel, an actor and activist, said last month.Schnabel said the funds at the center of the US charges actually went tobuythe popular football club Club Africain, and to pay off debt and past-due salaries as well as rebuilding a training center and building youth football fields.The club went on to win the Tunisian football leaguein May.Chambers has been extensivelyprofiledin US media and was interviewed on local TV news station in New Hampshire in late 2023 about a direct action against Elbit Systems, an Israeli defense contractor, staged by a group whose legal fees he paid, then called Palestine Action – a group proscribed in the UK as a “terrorist organization”.Garzón also revealed that the US indictment was filed in New Hampshire.Chambers’ public comments on Israel and Gaza are part of the context in which the case is unfolding, Garzón said. For example, a weekafter the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel, Chamberspostedon X about Israel’s response: “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’/ There’s nothing to be ‘punished’ for/ No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done *anything* wrong/ It’s simply genocide/ Like it has been.”He has also been a staunch critic of the US andtold a reporterin 2024: “I think the most important thing for the prosperity of humanity is the destruction of the US.”“[Chambers] is a person who is not aligned with the views of the US government,” Garzón said. “There’s a political context to all this.”Garzón’s visit with Chambers on Thursday lasted two hours. Spain has rejected requests to release him on bail to date but the issue could be revisited if the US submits its paperwork on time and the case continues, the attorney said.“His freedom is being denied,” Garzón said. “It’s incomprehensible to him … as a defender of human rights.”He also said funds have been at least temporarily halted to theSameer Projectin Gaza, which helped support a bakery producing thousands of loaves of free bread daily during Israel’s ongoing siege on the territory.On 10 August, the projectannounced a “pause”in its operations on Instagram. The three-year-old project also supplies food, water and medical care. “[T]ens of thousands of Palestinians will feel the effects,” said the announcement.Explore more on these topicsFBISpainUS crimeUS justice systemUS foreign policyEuropeTrump administrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: CIA director John Ratcliffe reportedly on Moscow visit | CIA | The Guardian
description: Unannounced trip reported by US media is said to be Ratcliffe’s first known visit to Russia as CIA chief
Author: Peter Beaumont
Headline: Unannounced trip reported by US media is said to be Ratcliffe’s first known visit to Russia as CIA chief
Content: John Ratcliffe was sworn in as director of the CIA in January 2025.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJohn Ratcliffe was sworn in as director of the CIA in January 2025.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesCIACIA director John Ratcliffe reportedly on Moscow visitUnannounced trip reported by US media is said to be Ratcliffe’s first known visit to Russia as CIA chiefPeter BeaumontTue 25 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe CIA director, John Ratcliffe, has made an unannounced visit to Moscow, US media reported, after flight data showed an American military aircraft flew to the Russian capital, where a US diplomatic motorcade was later spotted.CBS News quoted sources familiar with the situation as confirming Ratcliffe’s trip, saying it was his first known visit to Russia asCIAchief. Axios separately confirmed the visit, quoting a US official.The Financial Times reported that the Trump administration had asked Kyiv to pause its long-range strikes on major Russian cities during the course of the visit.There was no immediate comment from the CIA or the White House.Data from Flightradar24 showed a US military C-17 travelling from the US to Latvia and then on to Moscow. The tracker showed that the flight originated from Joint Base Andrews in Maryland, best known for hosting Air Force One.The C-17 Globemaster III is a large military transport aircraft that the US air force website says can be used for strategic and tactical airlift and airdrop missions as well as aeromedical evacuations.Ratcliffe’s reported visit comes as US-brokered talks aimed at ending Russia’s invasion of Ukraine have stalled. However, earlier this month Moscow freed a former US marine detained since 2022, amid concerns about his health.The reason for the visit is unclear but the CIA has mediated in recent US-Russia detainee exchanges and was involved in the 2024 prisoner exchange that secured the release of theWall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovichand the marine veteran Paul Whelan.Some speculation has focused on the war in Iran, which remains a bone of contention between Moscow and Washington. On Monday the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, announced a new economic sanctions strategydesigned to isolate Iran.Explore more on these topicsCIARussiaUS foreign policyEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: VW workers boo boss as he urges them to ‘pull together’ amid job cuts | Volkswagen (VW) | The Guardian
description: Oliver Blume faces workforce at German HQ as carmaker struggles against Chinese competition and US tariffs
Author: Kate Connolly
Headline: Oliver Blume faces workforce at German HQ as carmaker struggles against Chinese competition and US tariffs
Content: Oliver Blume, pictured at the International Motor Show last year, said VW wanted to guarantee a future for all of the company’s factories.Photograph: Kai Pfaffenbach/ReutersView image in fullscreenOliver Blume, pictured at the International Motor Show last year, said VW wanted to guarantee a future for all of the company’s factories.Photograph: Kai Pfaffenbach/ReutersVolkswagen (VW)VW workers boo boss as he urges them to ‘pull together’ amid job cutsOliver Blume faces workforce at German HQ as carmaker struggles against Chinese competition and US tariffsKate Connollyin BerlinTue 25 Aug 2026 11.47 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe chief executive of Volkswagen has faced boos and whistles of protest at the company’s headquarters after telling thousands of workers that a comprehensive reorganisation, which could include job losses and factory closures, is vital for its future.As Oliver Blume urged more than 10,000 workers on Tuesday to “pull together”, saying drastic restructuring measures at the struggling manufacturer were essential, they held up banners and shouted slogans, including: “Our jobs are not your balance sheet adjustments”.Blume said in Wolfsburg, northern Germany: “Our plan for the future is the largest transformation programme in our company’s history. To make this happen, everyone needs to pull together now.”The chief executive was speaking for the first time since details about plans formass job losses and possible factory closureswere made public.One of the goals of the proposed restructure was to guarantee a future for all plants at Europe’s largest carmaker, he said at the start of a tour of VW plants. “Our aim is to create viable prospects for all locations within the next six to 12 months.”Blume’s restructuring plans have yet to be approved by theVW group’s powerful supervisory board, which represents the labour force, as well as the state of Lower Saxony, the home of VW, and shareholders.The meeting, widely described by attenders as heated, was not open to the media. But witnesses – some of whom had to watch proceedings on a live stream outside the main meeting room owing to overcapacity – reported that Blume had said half of the expected job cuts, often cited at about 50,000, would take place in Germany. He reportedly said the other half would be made internationally, across a total of approximately 170 companies.Blume stressed that the worldwide job cuts plan was not a target, but a “theoretical calculation” and that it was based on the company’s costs, which he said were “about 30% above the average of comparable companies”. He said the executive board was “fully behind the future plan”, which involved bringing VW’s costs down in line with its competitors to make it sustainable for the future.Instead of forced job cuts, Blume said management wanted to rely on voluntary personnel measures as much as possible, including phased retirement, mutual agreements, and what he called “natural attrition and a restrictive hiring policy”.Blume described frequently proposed factory closures as the “last and most costly resort”. Among the proposals to keep factories open, VW’s manufacturing could switch towards the defence industry, and it could produce electric vehicles that are for sale in China, but not Europe yet, at its German factories.The manufacture of cars at VW’s plant in Osnabrück is due to end, possibly as soon as next year. At plants in Emden, Zwickau, Neckarsulm and Hanover, there are no plans for manufacturing from 2030.Daniela Cavallo, the head of VW’s works council, said opposition to factory closures was strong, calling them an “integral part” of the company.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Our trust in this company’s executive board, and in particular in its CEO Oliver Blume, has been damaged, not yet beyond repair, but nevertheless damaged,” she said, according to extracts from her speech shared with media by the works council.She accused Blume of being vague about the company’s plans. “It’s impossible to work with a CEO who doesn’t tell his people what’s going on,” she said.VW faces increasing pressure from rampant Chinese competition in Europe, decreasing sales in China and hefty US tariffs. Even before that, it was struggling for years with falling profits and overproduction in Europe.Last week, Blume described the situation at VW as “more than critical”. Previous cost-cutting measures, such as an average reduction of 20% in costs at its German factories last year, were insufficient.He said VW was too big, too slow and too complex. Blume is to attend eight more works council meetings over the coming days, in Braunschweig, Emden, Zwickau, Chemnitz, Dresden, Kassel-Baunatal, Salzgitter, and Hanover.Explore more on these topicsVolkswagen (VW)Automotive industryManufacturing sectorGermanyEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: UK officials prepare for potential Trump talks as Burnham plans New York trip | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: PM known to be keen to attend UN general assembly after meeting Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Ukraine
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: PM known to be keen to attend UN general assembly after meeting Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Ukraine
Content: Officials preparing for a first meeting between Andy Burnham and Donald Trump are understood to have stepped up their work.Composite: Kin Cheung/Getty Images; Tasos Katopodis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenOfficials preparing for a first meeting between Andy Burnham and Donald Trump are understood to have stepped up their work.Composite: Kin Cheung/Getty Images; Tasos Katopodis/Getty ImagesAndy BurnhamUK officials prepare for potential Trump talks as Burnham plans New York tripPM known to be keen to attend UN general assembly after meeting Volodymyr Zelenskyy in UkrainePeter WalkerandJessica ElgotTue 25 Aug 2026 10.17 EDTFirst published on Tue 25 Aug 2026 03.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUK officials are making preparations for a potential meeting between Andy Burnham andDonald Trumpafter the prime minister said he hoped to attend next month’s UN general assembly in New York.Burnham is known to be particularly keen to attend the annual gathering after meetingVolodymyr Zelenskyyin Kyiv on Monday, when he pledged to help drum up more international support for Ukraine.Any meeting with the US president, whether in New York or Washington, is notably more speculative. But British officials who had already begun planning for a first encounter are understood to be stepping up their work given Burnham’s expected trip.As part of a series of interviews in Kyiv during his first overseas trip as PM, Burnham told Bloomberg: “I’m looking forward to going to New York in September.”Speaking after a meeting with Zelenskyy, he said: “I’ve not fully confirmed the details yet, but it’s likely I will go, particularly after today’s discussion. Leaving today, I’m quite clear what I need to do in the next few weeks.”8:57Burnham hands secret missile technology to Ukraine in first foreign trip - The LatestChairing a meeting in Kyiv of the “coalition of the willing” group of countries that are supportingUkraine, Burnham urged the international community to do more to protect the country against Russian attacks, particularly with more US-made Patriot interceptor missiles.He told LBC in another interview: “We need to go further together … There is an urgent need for air defence support.” That was “the big takeaway” from his meetings with Zelenskyy, he said.The general assembly would be just one part of international efforts to generate more support for Ukraine, particularly in the form of missiles. The defence secretary, Wes Streeting, will co-chair a meeting of the Ukraine defence contact group in September. The group, which includes all 32 Nato members and 25 other countries, coordinates the supply of military assistance.Attending the UN gathering, which almost 200 world leaders will attend from 22 to 28 September, would give Burnham an opportunity to press the case about more support for Ukraine, as would a meeting with Trump.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham and Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv.Photograph: Ukrainian Presidency/Sipa/ShutterstockBurnham and the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, would discuss a series of other global issues at the assembly, including Gaza and the humanitarian crisis in Sudan. The meeting will coincide with the first anniversary of Keir Starmer’s decision to formally recognise a Palestinian state.It would give Burnham the opportunity to meet a number of other world leaders at once, though bilateral talks tend to be brief given the frenetic schedule of the gathering.The prime minister’s policy background is predominantly domestic, and since entering No 10 he has had to rapidly develop a foreign policy – thus far very similar to that of Starmer – and get to know world leaders.He joined a number of other European leaders, including the European council president, António Costa, in laying wreaths for Ukraine’s Independence Day in Kyiv on Monday.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBurnham’s visit to Kyiv marks a renewal of badly needed support for UkraineRead moreHe also used the trip to announce that the UK government would allow the European defence company MBDA to declassify information about British-made components of the Anglo-French Storm Shadow/Scalp missiles to help Ukraine build its own version.Burnham told Zelenskyy during their meeting that there would be“no change in the UK’s steadfast support” for Kyiv.He also urged Ukraine’s allies to send more Patriot missiles as Ukraine struggles under continued Russian bombardment, and co-chaired his first “coalition of the willing” meeting, where he said the group was doing everything it could to “dig into our own stocks and help others dig into their stocks”.Zelenskyy has pleaded for more US-made interceptor missiles in recent months as Kyiv’s stocks have diminished. Supplies of Patriots have been diverted to the Middle East since the the US and Israel launched their war against Iran, and Ukraine has received significantly fewer this year than in previous years.During his interview with Bloomberg, Burnham said he felt “really confident” the weaponry problem was fixable. “There are other players who could help in the mix who we have influence with. It’s probably going to be a solution that involves a lot of layers and a lot of negotiation,” he said.Russia has sought to capitalise on the shortage by increasing its ballistic missile strikes, killing at least 23 people and wounding more than 100 in the past three days.Moscow has alsothreatened unspecified retaliationfor what it says is the UK’s increased involvement in the conflict.Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamDonald TrumpUnited NationsVolodymyr ZelenskyyUkraineForeign policyEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: The whitewashing of the Green India Mission forest expansion project | World news | The Guardian
description: The flagship environmental project has achieved ‘negligible’ results. Why so little progress, and what are the risks as the planet gets hotter? Plus, fusion dance pioneer Usha Jey
Author: Niha Masih
Headline: The flagship environmental project has achieved ‘negligible’ results. Why so little progress, and what are the risks as the planet gets hotter? Plus, fusion dance pioneer Usha Jey
Content: Lush countryside in Indore, Madhya Pradesh – the state is home to India’s largest forest area.Photograph: Sagar Ghosh/AlamyView image in fullscreenLush countryside in Indore, Madhya Pradesh – the state is home to India’s largest forest area.Photograph: Sagar Ghosh/AlamyThis Is IndiaWorld newsThe whitewashing of the Green India Mission forest expansion projectThe flagship environmental initiative has achieved ‘negligible’ results. Why so little progress, and what are the risks as the planet gets hotter? Plus, fusion dance pioneer Usha JeyDon’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereNiha MasihTue 25 Aug 2026 05.03 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 05.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIndia set out to expand its forested areas a decade ago. Last week, however, we learned that the forest cover programme had barely taken root when thegovernment’s auditors released their findingsof the flagship Green India Mission. The shortfall of 97.57% from India’s initial pledge in 2014 was stark enough to alarm the government’s own auditor, who described the progress as “negligible”.Yet if you ask the government about forest cover, you’ll get a far greener picture.I’m writing this on the day theUK Met Officeissued a calamitous warning – 2027 could be the hottest year yet, on account of the strongest El Niño in more than a century. For India, a disrupted monsoon season puts agriculture and millions who depend on it at risk.Which makes the question of what’s happening to India’s green cover feel far more urgent than an academic disagreement over numbers. I went down the rabbit hole of reports, datasets and government’s parliamentary disclosures. Here’s what I found.1. Forest cover vforest coverThe government’s lastcomprehensive report from 2023(released a year later) touted that forest cover in India has grown since 2021. But other, independent, assessments have found thatforest cover is lowerthan what the government has claimed in recent years, or that ithas reduced.The discrepancy lies in some creative accounting. Last year, dozens of former civil servants wrote to the government criticising the forest report. They described its methodology asunreliable and nonscientific, pointing to the inclusion of smaller orchards, as well as coconut and rubber plantations, in the calculation of forest cover.“A lot of the discrepancies are coming from how and what we are counting as forests. We have broadened the definition to include a lot more,” Pooja Choksi, founder of environmental consultancy Ficus Research Consulting, told me.The government has defended its methodology, saying its definition is internationally accepted and includes tree-covered land outside forests as well as orchards and bamboo and palm plantations.2. Whose land is it anyway?Even as the government pledged to increase forestation, over the past five years India has approved the diversion of forest land for development projects covering an area roughly equivalent to the size of Hong Kong, according to data shared in parliament this month. The pace has accelerated, with the last financial year seeing the single largest chunk cleared yet.Mining was the single-biggest sector, accounting for 22% of all diverted forest land, followed by road works and irrigation projects.3. Ground zeroThe pressure on forests is concentrated in some states. Nearly a quarter of all forest land diverted nationwide since 2021 is in Madhya Pradesh, which is home to the country’s largest forest area. Its share is more than double that of the next state, Odisha. Arunachal Pradesh on the north-eastern border with China ranks third for forest diversions, according to government figures shared in parliament.Oneresearch teamthat mapped 28 years of satellite data from three central Indian coalmine regions, including two in Madhya Pradesh, found the damage from such projects extended far beyond disappearing trees. Water bodies shrank, soil quality degraded and the overall natural ecosystems diminished by 35%.View image in fullscreenCoalmining has affected forests and other ecosystems in areas such as Madhya Pradesh.Photograph: Sushil Chikane/Alamy4. The ‘great’ projectPerhaps nowhere is this trade-off more starkly visible than in the project proposed in the pristine Andaman and Nicobar Islands, which are home to protected Indigenous tribes.The central government has touted the Great Nicobar Project as a strategic necessity to strengthen India’s maritime and defence presence in the Indo-Pacific. The project would divert 13,075 hectares offorest landand cut down, conservatively, at least 700,000 trees to make way for a trans-shipment port, an international airport, a mega township and a power plant for their operation, at a combined cost north of$6.89 bn (Rs 90,000 crore). The project has already led tolegal challengesand pushback from the opposition Congress party and environmentalists.“Situated at the precise intersection of variable sea-level rise and sinking land, the Great Nicobar Project is not merely ecologically destructive or culturally erosive for the Indigenous populations – it is geologically impossible,” geoscientist CP Rajendran wrote inThe Wire, arguing that the government is using natural security as a pretext to push a commercial hub in one of the world’s most tectonically active zones.5. Is compensatory afforestation the answer?For many such development projects that divert forest land, the answer has been to pour substantial public funds into planting trees and creating forests elsewhere. But experts caution that this may not be as simple a solution as it may sound.Choksi, whose research focuses on biodiversity outcomes of restoration and tree-planting policies, said the rush to meet Paris Agreement targets has made India obsessed with “green cover” while ignoring other aspects of environmental policy.“We need to move away from this very one-dimensional view that everything is green cover. What is being planted and where it is planted has a huge influence. The third question being why is it being planted because different trees have different purposes,” Choksi said.A natural forest patch with 100 different species, she added, has very different ecological value to a plantation under the Green India Mission, which might have 20 species. “It does have biodiversity value, but it certainly does not have the same value as the diverse forest patches that we have across the country,” she said.All of this shows that the true health of India’s forests is not easy to assess, which is in itself concerning. Meanwhile, India’s biennial forest report was due in 2025. We’re still waiting.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is IndiaNiha Masih takes a look at the stories, ideas and news makers of modern IndiaEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat else we’re reading aboutView image in fullscreenChef Gaggan Anand has finally opened a restaurant in India, on Delhi’s Janpath Road.Photograph: Jack Taylor/AlamyGaga over RaGa| Gaggan Anand, once dubbed the most famous Indian chef in the world by theNew York Times, has finally opened a restaurant in India. RaGa, on Delhi’s upmarket Janpath Road,starts serving on 26 August.Surviving summer| What is it like to endure extreme heat in a city pushed beyond its capacity to cope? In a dispatch from Mumbai’s sweltering summer inEquator magazine, Aruna Chandrasekhar provides a dystopian glimpse of a climate-stressed future.Cost of reporting| Uttar Pradesh journalistAbhishek Upadhyay, among the first to report on the theft of donations at Ayodhya’s Ram Mandir Temple, has alleged police harassment and retaliation over his reporting.Guest shelfA recommendation from someone with great tasteView image in fullscreenGathering’s Roly Poly hand-painted jacket.Photograph: Gathering TextilesDiet Sabya(@dietsabya), the anonymous Indian fashion watchdog, spills the tea on his current obsession: “Gatheringby Haider Saleem is a very under-the-radar, slow-fashion brand that not enough people know about. There’s a lingering notion that Indian menswear-forward brands have to look a certain way or that they somehow can’t occupy the same conversation, say as The Row or Lemaire. Gathering proves otherwise. The clothes have this organic ease to them: earthy tones, flattering cuts, natural fabrics, with much of the dyeing done traditionally in Jaipur. The sort of brand you want to gate keep until everyone discovers it and you can say: “Oh, I’ve known them for ages.’”Count itA number worth knowingView image in fullscreenPatients in a makeshift care centre in New Delhi during Covid-19 – the PM Cares fund was set up in the early days of the pandemic.Photograph: Money Sharma/AFP/Getty ImagesRs8,452 croreThe Prime Minister’s Citizen Assistance and Relief in Emergency Situations Fund (PM Cares), set up during the coronavirus pandemic, had a balance of£647m (Rs 8,452 crore)at the end of the 2025 financial year, prompting questions about why such a large sum remained unused instead of being put towards relief work. Pradeep Bhandari, a spokesperson for the Bharatiya Janata party, countered the charge in adebate on Times Now, saying the PM Cares fund provides for long-term rehabilitation instead of immediate relief during disasters.Vibe checkView image in fullscreenActor Maitreyi Ramakrishnan, centre, with hybrid bharatham dancers in Usha Jey’s video Hide N Seek.Photograph: YoutubeFor choreographer and director Usha Jey(@usha_jey), learning bharatanatyam at the age of 20 was a way to connect to her culture. Jey, who is French and of Sri Lankan Tamil heritage, has since developed her own movement language. Hybrid bharatham, as she calls it, fuses the Indian classical dance form with hip-hop but is careful to retain the integrity of both. There is an interplay of abandon and elegance in her choreographic works. Actor Maitreyi Ramakrishnan features in her latest video,Hide N Seek. Directed by Jey and her longtime partner, Gavin Emishka, the film is a striking visual treat featuring two dance forms in fluid negotiation.Get in touchDo you have any thoughts or responses to this week’s newsletter? title: Labour MPs will push Burnham to back voting reform in first 100 days | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Nearly 100 Labour MPs support commission on changing the system used for Westminster election
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: Exclusive: Nearly 100 Labour MPs support commission on changing the system used for Westminster election
Content: Number 10 said Burnham remained committed to electoral reform in Labour’s next manifesto but stopped short of backing the new commission.Photograph: Kin Cheung/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNumber 10 said Burnham remained committed to electoral reform in Labour’s next manifesto but stopped short of backing the new commission.Photograph: Kin Cheung/AFP/Getty ImagesAndy BurnhamLabour MPs will push Burnham to back voting reform in first 100 daysExclusive: Nearly 100 Labour MPs support commission on changing the system used for Westminster electionWhy do some Labour MPs want electoral reform and will it happen?Jessica ElgotDeputy political editorTue 25 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham will face an immediate test of his backing for electoral reform in his first week in parliament as prime minister, with almost 100 Labour MPs supporting a bid for a new national commission.Burnham, a longtime advocate of electoral reform, will be asked to support the new commission into ditching first past the post in his first 100 days as prime minister.MPs have said the commission must report before the next election and hope to put electoral reform in Labour’s next manifesto. Number 10 said Burnham remained committed to electoral reform in Labour’s next manifesto but stopped short of backing the new commission..New polling of MPs by YouGov suggests the change is now supported by a majority in the Commons. Of those polled, 53% of MPs said they supported a review into first past the post – the current system of voting.An amendment to launch the commission has been backed by 185 MPs, including a number of former ministers and supporters of the previous prime minister, Keir Starmer.Whoever wins today’s elections, democracy is the loser under first past the post | Polly ToynbeeRead moreThe amendment has been tabled to the representation of the people bill, which returns to parliament for its remaining stages on 2 September. A Labour source said: “The representation of the people bill has been designed to deliver our manifesto commitments on votes at 16 and strengthen political donation rules to guard against foreign interference, and that’s what the government is prioritising.“Andy remains strongly committed to electoral reform, and has indicated this is a matter for a future party manifesto, given a mandate would need to be secured for it.”Burnham endorsed the call for a national commission on electoral reform at last year’s Labour conference, saying then as mayor of Greater Manchester that he backed “a manifesto commitment to a system of proportional representation to be introduced into Westminster elections in the next parliament.”The 98 Labour signatories to the amendment, tabled by Labour’s Alex Sobel include influential backbenchers such as Luke Akehurst and Chris Curtis, leading Labour centrists. Overall, MPs have signed from eight parties, as well as independents.Signatories also include MPs who have recently become ministers and ministerial aides – including the energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, communities minister Florence Eshalomi and the prime minister’s parliamentary private secretary and close ally Jo Platt.However, the newly appointed frontbench MPs may by convention withdraw support for backbench amendments once parliament returns.A new commission would not require legislation – meaning the amendment itself may end up out of scope of the bill. But MPs intend to use the amendment as a way of signalling to the prime minister the breadth of support for swifter reform.A national commission could consider a range of other proportional voting systems to replace first past the post, the current system for a general election in the UK which means the winners of the most votes in each constituency are elected. Other systems are used across the UK, including the Scottish parliament, the Welsh parliament and mayoral votes.In Scottish and Welsh elections, there are votes for a candidate and for a party, so additional members can be elected from a list alongside constituency representatives. In the recent Greater Manchester mayoralty, voters were given a first and second choice.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSobel said it was time for the prime minister to endorse the push – signed by more MPs than any other amendment in parliament. “Now we know a majority of MPs back this proposal, including a majority of Labour MPs. I know the prime minister is committed to reforming our electoral system and I and all the MPs who signed this amendment want to work with him to set the UK on a road towards fair, modern general elections,” he said.MPs told the Guardian that Burnham should announce the commission before the October budget. Rachel Blake, the former Treasury minister, said: “The PLP agrees with Andy Burnham that first past the post is broken, and that a national commission is the way to get a grip on it. The government should press ahead and launch this process within the prime minister’s first hundred days.”Akehurst, a member of Labour’s governing national executive committee, said: “Parliament is catching up with the public, most of whom already support electoral reform. Andy Burnham has a good track record on proportional representation, and it’s now hugely popular across the Labour party. He should seize this opportunity.”Labour MP Lizzi Collinge said first past the post “particularly devalues the votes of renters, young people and BAME people, and delivers parliaments that do not represent what most people voted for.”Another former Labour minister, Catherine Fookes, said first past the post “can’t cope with modern, multiparty politics. Andy Burnham has long talked about the need to move to a fair, proportional system. If he acts now by setting up a commission, he will find that most MPs support him from across parliament – and make good on his promise to rewire British politics.”A sixth Labour MP, Mike Reader, said that the poll of MPs showed there had been “a sea change in support for PR across Labour and the public. Most MPs know it is the fair thing for the country, it’s just a matter of how we get there. We hope Andy Burnham will now stick to his guns.”Labour members at the party’s annual conference in 2022 had previously backed a move towards proportional representation, which Burnham called a “historic vote” and said would be a move towards “a country that works for everybody, where everyone’s vote counts”.Campaign groups said they hoped Burnham would seize the moment for reform while he had a workable parliamentary majority. Make Votes Matter chief executive Emma Harrison said: “I’ve spoken alongside Andy in favour of proportional representation, I know he supports it – now he must show the public he deserves our trust.”The UK last rejected electoral reform in 2011 after a referendum was held to ask whether to change to an alternative vote system, where voters rank candidates in order of preference.Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamElectoral reformLabournewsShareReuse this content

title: UK to warn citizens to stock up on food amid threat from climate crisis and hostile states | Defence policy | The Guardian
description: Government resilience campaign aims to ensure people can cope in a national disaster, in order to free resources for most vulnerable
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: Government resilience campaign aims to ensure people can cope in a national disaster, in order to free resources for most vulnerable
