The WNBA is not being overrun by trans women but by straight men who cannot let women have a flourishing league of their own without mocking it, manufacturing controversy and making themselves the story. Some of loudest voices posing as defenders of female athletesopenly ridicule and try to humiliate themfor laughs,in some cases through sexualized stunts. There is something almost pitiable about men squandering their energy and influence on belittling women whose discipline, sacrifice and extraordinary achievement have carried them to the highest level of their profession. Misogyny has simply put on the costume of concern.In Kanter’s case, this was not simply a lone provocateur wandering into an arena. According to Talking Points Memo, the Trump-aligned America First Policy Institute (AFPI)promoted Kanter’s arrival, circulated footage of his ejection and began selling a $45 “Let Freedom Play” sweatshirt featuring him in a mock-up of the WNBA logo. An AFPI executive was seated a few rows behind him, although the organization did not answer questions about whether it bought his courtside seat. Kanter, who attended the 2024 State of the Union as House speaker Mike Johnson’s guest and has said he plans to run for Congress in 2028, has political ambitions of his own.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly for the 2026 WNBA seasonSign up toWNBA 30A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markBack then, he used attention to protect vulnerable people. Now he uses vulnerable people to attract attentionWhether or not there is a formal arrangement, the transaction is visible enough: Kanter lends the campaign the credibility of an 11-year NBA veteran and supplies a spectacle in which transgender people are the bait, while an organization embedded in Trump’s political network converts those assets into attention, merchandise and political capital. If it keeps voters staring at a nonexistent threat to theWNBAinstead of the corruption engulfing the administration in the run-up to the November midterms, the stunt has done its real work.Late in the third quarter of Sunday’s contest, Natasha Cloud, one of the most uncompromising athlete-activists of her generation, finally took therage bait. The Sky guard approached Kanter, yelling and pointing in his direction. Kanter stood, spread his arms and stepped on to the court before security intervened. As he was escorted away, he stopped near the basket to argue his case, then stretched out his shirt and tried to draw a response from the crowd. He had arrived ready to provoke and left performing martyrdom.Kanter did not suddenly discover the uses of spectacle on Sunday. In 2020, after marching with Black Lives Matter protesters in Boston, hetold the Guardianthat athletes should use their platforms “to spread good, and to spread the truth”. He had long understood publicity as a political tool, and with good reason: he believed international pressure helped secure his father’s acquittal. The difference is what the performance now serves.None of this diminishes the courage Kanter showed in opposing Erdoğan. The offer of US citizenship is not a contract for ideological obedience. Human rights are not a prize withdrawn when their beneficiary later behaves immorally, nor does surviving persecution bind anyone to a prescribed worldview.But suffering does not automatically make a person generous, either. And Kanter, more than most, should understand the mechanics of dehumanization: how a powerful movement marks a minority as dangerous, treats its identity as illegitimate and converts real human beings into totems of social decay. The scale of Erdoğan’s repression and an American culture-war stunt are not equivalent. The moral reflex behind them – identifying people with less power and making public sport of their vulnerability – should have been instantly recognizable to him. The least cynical reading, perhaps charitable to a fault, is that Kanter can recognize this kind of othering only when he is its target.US citizenship gave Kanter what he asked for in that Manhattan conference room: safety, a home and the freedom to speak without Erdoğan deciding the consequences. That freedom includes the right to make a cruel spectacle of himself, but it does not exempt the spectacle from judgment.“I try to be the voice of those innocent people,” Kanter said in 2017. I believed him then. On Sunday, he used that voice to make other innocent people feel smaller. What a waste.Explore more on these topicsWNBABasketballRecep Tayyip ErdoğanTurkeyTransgendercommentShareReuse this content

title: Angel Reese breaks two WNBA rebounding records in one night during Dream win | Atlanta Dream | The Guardian
description: The 24-year-old set a WNBA record with 26 rebounds in the Atlanta Dream’s 78-71 win over the Los Angeles Sparks on Monday, pushing her past the season record
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The 24-year-old set a WNBA record with 26 rebounds in the Atlanta Dream’s 78-71 win over the Los Angeles Sparks on Monday, pushing her past the season record
Content: Angel Reese is averaging 12.4 rebounds per game this season.Photograph: Brett Davis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAngel Reese is averaging 12.4 rebounds per game this season.Photograph: Brett Davis/Getty ImagesAtlanta DreamAngel Reese breaks two WNBA rebounding records in one night during Dream win24-year-old breaks single game and single season recordReese’s 26 rebounds help Atlanta to win over Los AngelesAssociated PressTue 25 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 09.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAngel Reese rebounded her way into the record books not once, but twice in one night. Reese set a WNBA record with 26 rebounds in the Atlanta Dream’s 78-71 win over the Los Angeles Sparks on Monday, pushing her past the season record in the same game.“Last time I was here, I didn’t miss any shots. Tonight I couldn’t hit [anything] so I knew I was going be able to get them on the rebounding side,” Reese said after the game. “I just want to be there for my team. Offensively, defensively, whatever it takes to win.”Reese surpassed Chamique Holdsclaw’s record of 24 rebounds, set in May 2003 for Washington. Reese now has 458 rebounds on the season, seven more than A’ja Wilson’s mark set in 2024.The 24-year-old secured her WNBA-leading 27th double-double of the season on a basket with 13.9 seconds left in the game – she also scored 11 points on the night.“That’s a talent,” Dream guard Allisha Gray said. “I’m just in awe watching her rebound.”A three-time WNBA All-Star, Reese set a rookie record with 13.1 rebounds per game and the all-time league record with 15 straight double-doubles with Chicago in 2024. She led the league in rebounding her first two seasons and is leading again this seasonat 12.4 per game.The Dream’s win on Monday completed a 4-0 West Coast trip for the team.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly for the 2026 WNBA seasonSign up toWNBA 30A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Angel’s been remarkable on this trip,” Atlanta coach Karl Smesko said. “You can see her getting better each month.”Explore more on these topicsAtlanta DreamWNBABasketballUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Another set of Sullivan brothers are making football waves in Bangladesh | Soccer | The Guardian
description: While Cavan and Quinn Sullivan star in MLS with the Philadelphia Union, brothers Ronan and Declan have connected with their South Asian heritage
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: While Cavan and Quinn Sullivan star in MLS with the Philadelphia Union, brothers Ronan and Declan have connected with their South Asian heritage
Content: Ronan and Declan Sullivan won the SAFF U-20 Championship with Bangladesh this year.Photograph: Courtesy Bangladesh Football FederationView image in fullscreenRonan and Declan Sullivan won the SAFF U-20 Championship with Bangladesh this year.Photograph: Courtesy Bangladesh Football FederationSoccerAnother set of Sullivan brothers are making football waves in BangladeshWhile Cavan and Quinn Sullivan star in MLS with the Philadelphia Union, brothers Ronan and Declan have connected with their South Asian heritageSanjay SujanthakumarTue 25 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 05.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRonan Sullivan had tried a panenka twice in his life. Both attempts were at practice on the other side of the world, and one hit the crossbar. But his twin brother, Declan, was hardly surprised when Ronan turned to him and told him he’d chip the fifth penalty of a shootout that could win a scoreless tournament final, as millions tuned in online to see hisBangladeshside play against India in the Under-20 South Asian Football Federation (SAFF) Championship.“He didn’t even need to say it. I knew he was gonna do that the whole time,” Declan remembered, sitting next to his brother on the couch of their dorm room at Saint Joseph’s University. “I knew that if he got the last pen to win it, he was gonna do that. That’s just the him thing to do.”Moments later the ball gracefully splashed into the back of the net, and the thousands in attendance on 3 April in Malé, Maldives erupted.‘They’re defeating nations who occupied’: inside Bangladesh’s World Cup love affair with Argentina and BrazilRead more“I wouldn’t have believed you if you told me it [would have] went like that,” Ronan said.Less than two years after he began exchanging messages on Instagram with the “Save Bangladesh Football” fan page, the brothers were celebrating a U-20 title, made possible by their maternal ancestry, as members of essentially the home team. (Bangladesh is the largest source of migrant workers in the Maldives.)“Flying in there alone was incredible. Like the water’s so blue. I’ve never seen anything like it. Like we go to Ocean City, New Jersey, where the water is brown, and it’s our favorite place ever,” Ronan said. “So when we saw this water, we were like, ‘Oh my gosh!’ It looked like the water from [the movie] The Waterboy. At the end [of the movie], that special water … I think it’s just Maldives water.”The story seems ripped from the pages of a Hollywood script. Two kids from Philadelphia with very Irish names who had never visited Bangladesh before their tryout for the country’s U-20 squad prior to the tournament, then returned to its crowded capital triumphantly. They allowed a few days for the media frenzy, and a few more for themselves to explore, enjoy the food and time with their grandmother, whom they’d only seen in the US until this trip.But this could be part of the opening scene for Bangladesh, ranked 181st by Fifa, with nearly 180 million people and, according to the United Nations, the world’s sixth-largest diaspora. The vast majority of it is concentrated in southern Asia or the Middle East, but there’s a well-established community in the UK, growing ones in the US and Italy, and pockets elsewhere in the West.“I think a lot of people saw what we did over there and saw how good of an experience that was, and now all of a sudden I’m seeing a lot of foreign players interested in playing for Bangladesh, a couple kids from England who are on pretty good academies over there, so we have talent all around the world. It’s just about utilizing that,” Declan said.The Sullivans are well known in Bangladesh, the US and beyond, and so too is former US men’s national team captain Thomas Dooley. The son of an American serviceman who grew up and played in Germany then joined the USMNT by happenstance, Dooley was announced as the head coach of the Bangladesh senior team seven weeks after the U-20 side brought a trophy home. He spent most of the coaching chapter of his life in Southeast Asia, where he heard about “a fanatic country in football” he is now leading into a new World Cup cycle.“We are a country of being fans. We need to change that. We need to be a country of playing football,” Dooley told the Guardian. “That’s what we need to be, and we need to find a way to do that.”View image in fullscreenThe Bangladesh U-20 national team celebrate winning the SAFF Championship.Photograph: Courtesy Bangladesh Football FederationRonan, Declan, and their brothers Quinn and Cavan – both attackers for the Philadelphia Union – were eligible to play for the US and Germany as well as Bangladesh. While Quinn was cap-tied by the USMNT last summer and Manchester-City bound Cavan is a top American prospect, the twins were more realistic bets for Bangladesh.“It all started with an Instagram DM, which is kind of crazy,” Declan recalled. The message came from that Save Bangladesh Football account. Initially confused that a fan page was encouraging them to come for a camp before they had a passport, Ronan and Declan soon realized the account was a legitimate asset and facilitator for the federation, eventually connecting the Sullivans to federation vice-president Fahad Karim when they expressed interest in the SAFF U-20 tournament.“[We had] a bit of time before college. It would be awesome to go play, represent the country, become more part of the culture,” Ronan said. The next three months were “a bit of a crazy process,” primarily because obtaining a Bangladeshi passport when their mother didn’t have one wasn’t straightforward. But in March the twins flew from New York to Delhi, then Delhi to Dhaka, easily the longest journey of their lives.There wasn’t a red carpet waiting for them, though. They had not been promised spots in the squad, arriving for a camp with more than 30 players, including three fellow “origin” players whom the Sullivans knew of and could easily communicate with. The manager spoke English too but on the pitch, to varying degrees, there was a language barrier.“When you’re foreign, it’s harder to get the ball at first because you don’t speak the language and maybe the guys weren’t super thrilled that we’re there. But once you get the ball a couple times and show what you can do, it helps out,” Ronan said. After a few days of training they were confident they’d make the roster, and socially their integration progressed.Dooley adamantly defends the right of players with Bangladeshi roots to choose their national team. His Asian coaching odyssey started in the Philippines, where he shrugged off many fans resistant to foreign-born recruits, and he’s encouraged by the culture of the Bangladesh senior team he’s inherited, highlighting the leadership and humility of Leicester City midfielder Hamza Choudhury.“Everybody was happy that Hamza came in, and they understand – the players understand that international players can help them because they can look up to them,” Dooley said. “What kind of attitude they have, the work ethic that they bring in. So everything, they can look up to them, how they handle stuff.”The more they search for players abroad, the more they find – not necessarily in a major European league but at a level that can raise the standard of the pool. But it’s a balancing act. Dooley is getting “thousands” of messages about players and acknowledges “we have to be careful,” noting the budgetary constraints.“It’s not everybody who sends a picture of a free kick that he does is a good player, or maybe can help us. We have good players in this country over here too that we can actually afford,” he said. “We are not spending $2,000, $3,000 on a player to bring him over, and he’s sitting on the bench. So if the players who are coming over are the ones that really can help us, otherwise we’re using that money and putting all the local players in the camp and train them twice a day for two weeks, and you will see that they’re getting much, much better.”Dooley says that coaching a decent group of players who can cover plenty of ground to change the way they think about the game – “most of the players, they don’t think, they play” – and to limit mistakes can improve the team 20 to 30%. He thinks climbing to the 150s of the FIFA rankings is certainly achievable.Of course, there’s a much bigger dream than that.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenCelebrations at the SAFF U-20 Championship in the Maldives.Photograph: Save Bangladesh Football/Courtesy Save Bangladesh FootballThe Instagram comment sections of all four Sullivan brothers have been flooded with Bangladeshi flags for years. The twins were checking their phones in the Maldives, absorbing as the buzz online reached a different stratosphere. They noticed the rivalry with India in particular.“They were making edits of me walking a dog that was painted like the Indian flag. Like it was crazy. There was a lot of heat there, for sure. A lot of tension,” Ronan said.The fervent support in the Maldives created an atmosphere they had never felt on the pitch, a surreal experience that carried into a heroes’ welcome in Dhaka.“That was a lot. Got a lot of flowers, met a lot of people. I feel like our team was the hot new thing in Bangladesh,” Declan said. Indeed, when the Sullivan twins walked around Dhaka they already stood out because, in Declan’s words, “we’re white, for everyone there at least.”“We met a bunch of people, and everyone was so happy and so grateful that we brought the trophy back to the country. Like they were really, really hype about that, and that’s not something you would see in America [for] youth soccer.”And you probably wouldn’t see a media presence at the airport for a senior national team almost anywhere, no matter the circumstances, comparable to what met Dooley at the airport when his group departed for a friendly against San Marino in June.“I thought we are going to the World Cup,” Dooley said. “I was like, this is amazing, and I cannot imagine [the scene] if we would qualify for the World Cup.”“I think the country would explode if we qualify for a World Cup,” Ronan said.It seems far-fetched. No country from the Indian subcontinent has ever appeared at a men’s or women’s World Cup. Its viral passion for international soccer continues to bechanneled towards South American giants.However, with further expansion of the men’s World Cup looking inevitable, and a bridge to their diaspora being built, a new dimension awaits this sport in Bangladesh. Something even greater awaits if a country from the subcontinent can qualify. While recruiting players is increasingly common in international sport, what it could unlock in this scenario is rare.“Whenever I think about the 64 team [World Cup], I’m thinking, ‘Look, if we get all these players, we have a chance to qualify.’ Like, that’s the dream. That’s the ultimate goal,” Declan said. He mentioned his friend, former Union academy teammate and Penn State winger Nehan Hasan, and Stanford striker Trevor Islam as possible additions, and hopes there will be many more candidates.“We have to convince them. We have to tell them you can actually leave a legacy here in this country,” Dooley said about eligible players.Dooley preaches qualifying for the Asian Cup (the Bangladesh men only have once in their history) or the World Cup is a process, but in the same breath he says “it can go fast”. He mentions 19-year-old winger and Fulham academy product Farhaan Wahid and 25-year-old Louie Watson, an attacking midfielder in the English fourth division, as the next potential pieces for his project. Choudhury and a New York Cosmos summer signing, Canada-born midfielder Shamit Shome, are the cornerstones. Dooley stresses that goalkeeper will be a key position to address.After their fall friendlies, the next notable step for the program will be the senior level SAFF Championship in Bangladesh in November. Bangladesh have won the tournament just once, as hosts in 2003. It’s Dooley’s main focus, but after that, he’s planning to be more involved in the development of the sport domestically. In his view, it’s a top-down mission: the success of the senior team drives the interest, sponsorship, and investment for a proper pyramid structure, with youth academies feeding adult leagues.Until he moves into an apartment in the affluent Gulshan area of Dhaka, Dooley is living at a hotel. He’ll look out the window at densely populated high-rise buildings, lamenting only a school or two in sight with a soccer field. This is the deeper challenge, one of infrastructure, culture and mindset for the next generation.“We would love to have the kids not want to be a fan of Argentina. They want to be a player to play against Argentina, against Brazil,” he said.Explore more on these topicsFootballUS sportsUSABangladeshfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Vuelta a España: Tadej Pogacar punishes peloton with mighty solo win on stage four | Vuelta a España | The Guardian
description: Tadej Pogacar put almost three minutes into the entire Vuelta a España field with a dominant victory on stage four to Andorra la Vella
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Tadej Pogacar put almost three minutes into the entire Vuelta a España field with a dominant victory on stage four to Andorra la Vella
Content: Tadej Pogacar after breaking clear in Andorra during stage four of the Vuelta.Photograph: Tim de Waele/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTadej Pogacar after breaking clear in Andorra during stage four of the Vuelta.Photograph: Tim de Waele/Getty ImagesVuelta a EspañaVuelta a España: Tadej Pogacar punishes peloton with mighty solo win on stage fourSlovenian powers to victory by more than three minutesLeader breaks rivals on brutal climb at halfway pointAgenciesTue 25 Aug 2026 12.03 EDTFirst published on Tue 25 Aug 2026 11.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTadej Pogacar arrived in red, lit the fuse on the climbs and turned stage four of theVuelta a España⁠into a private exhibition on Tuesday, powering away with almost 50km remaining to win alone in Andorra la Vella.The Slovenian, bidding to ⁠complete his Grand ⁠Tour collection by ​claiming the Vuelta for the first time, attacked on the road to the second climb and quickly reduced a high-altitude battle into ⁠a one-man procession.He began the final ascent with a lead of three minutes and 12 seconds and cruised over the last mountain pass before ⁠finishing in 2hr 40min 35sec. Jarno Widar won the sprint for second, 2min 39sec off the pace, with Felix ​Gall third.Seven years after his only previous ‌appearance in the Spanish ‌race, Pogacar underlined why he started as the overwhelming favourite having recently claimed afifth Tour de France title.The UAE Team Emirates rider now leads the general classification by 3min 21sec over compatriot Primoz Roglic of Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, with Spain’s Enric Mas of Movistar 11 seconds further back.Pogacar began patiently, sitting in the third peloton for much of the opening climb, around 32sec behind the group setting the pace. The ‌early attackers were reeled in on the descent from the first mountain pass, where Lorenzo Fortunato, of XDS Astana, crossed the summit of the ​Port d’Envalira first to collect maximum mountain points.View image in fullscreenThe peloton climbing to the Port d’Envalira earlier in stage four.Photograph: Tim de Waele/Getty ImagesThen came the coup de grace.With 50km to race, Pogacar surged clear uphill in familiar style. By the time he crossed the summit of the Collada de Beixalis, he had a lead of 1min 30sec over a chasing group including Mas, Roglic, Gall, ⁠Richard Carapaz and Oscar Onley.It was shaping up as Pogacar’s longest solo attack for stage victory ​in a Grand Tour. He ​had already produced long-range masterpieces this ​year at the Tour de France, where he attacked on the Col ​du Tourmalet and ‌rode the final 43km ​alone, and in ​previous Grand Tours including the 2019 Vuelta and the 2024 Giro d’Italia.On Tuesday, his pace was brutal and every climb saw the gap grow. With Embret Svestad-Bardseng pulling the chasing group, Pogacar stretched his advantage to nearly three minutes on the road to the later climbs.View image in fullscreenTadej Pogacar celebrates on the podium in Andorra la Vella.Photograph: Alexander Hassenstein/Getty Images“It’s super good because now I can be calm and confident for the next days,” said Pogacar. “We just keep going day by day and focus on each day after this, because it will be a little bit less stressful for sure.“[I didn’t] want to be also isolated against all the GC riders because they would all play against me – I tried with an attack on the climb and I just hoped that I could survive until the finish line. I saw that I could open the gap and I did it and it was pretty tough but a beautiful day out there.”Explore more on these topicsVuelta a EspañaCyclingTadej PogacarnewsShareReuse this content

title: At least one in four former NFL players in study suffered from degenerative brain disease CTE | NFL | The Guardian
description: At least one in four former NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021 was found to have had chronic ⁠traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a study says
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: At least one in four former NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021 was found to have had chronic ⁠traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a study says
Content: The NFL says it is committed to player safety.Photograph: Doug Pensinger/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe NFL says it is committed to player safety.Photograph: Doug Pensinger/Getty ImagesNFLAt least one in four former NFL players in study suffered from degenerative brain disease CTE215 of 235 donated brains showed signs of CTECondition can only be diagnosed after deathSymptoms include problems with memory and moodReuters andGuardian sportTue 25 Aug 2026 09.44 EDTFirst published on Tue 25 Aug 2026 07.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt least one in four former NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021 was found tohave had chronic ⁠traumatic encephalopathy(CTE), according to a study released on Tuesday.Out of the 878 former players who died during that time frame, 235 donated their brains for study, researchers said, with 215 ⁠of those donated brains ⁠found to have CTE, ​a degenerative disease that can only definitively be diagnosed after death. CTE is associated with repeated blows to the head, including concussions.Symptoms includedifficulty with attention and memory, dementia, mood disorders and headaches.AnNFLspokesperson said: “The NFL continuously strives to make the game of football safer, including by implementing ⁠strategies to reduce concussions and head impacts.Brain injuries and legal battles: the NFL’s persistent problem with CTERead more“The NFL remains committed to ensuring that the NFL community has access to a robust – and expanding – set of resources to enhance their physical and ⁠mental well being.“We encourage former players to utilize these resources to identify and seek treatment when they are concerned about ​their health.“The study’s lead author Daniel Daneshvar, the chair ‌of physical medicine and rehabilitation ‌at Mass General Brigham and an associate professor at Harvard Medical School, said that repeated traumatic brain injuries are ‌a known factor in elevated rates of neurodegenerative disease.“Similarly, we and others have shown that in NFL players, specifically, there is about a four times higher rate of death from neurodegenerative disease than the general population,” he added.The study from Mass General Brigham, Boston University and the Concussion + CTE Foundation also found dementia was common among brain donors, with researchers urging prevention measures that focus on cutting down on repetitive head impacts across all levels ‌of the sport.“The bulk of the head impacts that these former NFL players experienced didn’t occur at the NFL level. They occurred at the collegiate level … and at the high school ​level and in many cases the youth level. And all of those cumulative hits to the head added up to result in an increased risk,” Daneshvar said.A number of high-profile NFL players who took their own lives – including Junior Seau, Dave Duerson and Aaron Hernandez – were found to have had CTE when their brains were analyzed after their deaths.The NFL’s 2011 collective bargaining agreement limited the number of contact practices during the season. The Ivy League banned full-contact tackling during practices five years later.The US supreme court cleared the way for the NFL’s settlement of ⁠concussion-related lawsuits with thousands of retired players in 2016.“If the changes that have been ​implemented at the NFL level, including reducing ​the amount of contact in sports practices ​to less than one per week, were propagated at the collegiate, high school, and youth ​levels, athletes would be ‌better off,” said Daneshvar, ​who urged current and former ​athletes experiencing cognitive symptoms to seek a neurodegenerative disease expert evaluation.“We know that nearly 70% of head impacts are occurring in practice. So without changing a single minute of game time at any of those levels, we can be substantially reducing the cumulative head impact burden that these individuals are experiencing throughout their lives.”Explore more on these topicsNFLConcussion in sportUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: De Zerbi hopes Sávio’s fresh start will help Spurs’ much-needed rebrand | Tottenham Hotspur | The Guardian
description: After an unacceptable performance against Brentford, head coach still believes they can avoid sinking feeling this season
Author: David Hytner
Headline: After an unacceptable performance against Brentford, head coach still believes they can avoid sinking feeling this season
Content: ‘Listen, I lost 3-0 in the first game in the Premier League … do you think for me it’s a problem if Savinho becomes Sávio?’ says Roberto De Zerbi.Composite: Guardian Pictures; Colorsport/Shutterstock; Tottenham Hotspur FC/Shutterstock; Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Listen, I lost 3-0 in the first game in the Premier League … do you think for me it’s a problem if Savinho becomes Sávio?’ says Roberto De Zerbi.Composite: Guardian Pictures; Colorsport/Shutterstock; Tottenham Hotspur FC/Shutterstock; Tom Jenkins/The GuardianTottenham HotspurDe Zerbi hopes Sávio’s fresh start will help Spurs’ much-needed rebrandAfter an unacceptable performance against Brentford, head coach still believes they can avoid sinking feeling this seasonDavid HytnerTue 25 Aug 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat’s in a name? Quite a bit, judging by the discussion at Roberto De Zerbi’s Tottenham press conference on Tuesday, shortly after the club hadcompleted the £75m signing of Savinhofrom Manchester City and the Brazil winger had let everybody know that he wanted to be called Sávio from now on. He will have that name on his Spurs shirt above his No 17, which he has taken over from Cristian Romero, the former captain who has moved to Atlético Madrid.The 22-year-old went by Sávio at various times before his two seasons at City but there was nonetheless speculation about the reasons for the reversion. Savinho translates roughly from the Portuguese as “little Sávio”. Was it him saying that he was now an older and more mature player?Football Daily | The Premier League soap opera is back – and Spurs are already hogging the narrativeRead moreOn the subject of theories, there is one about the fee, which could rise to £85m in add-ons. Even at £75m, it represents a record sale for City, who paid £30.8m to take Sávio from Troyes. Spurs are pushing to sign another attacker from City – Omar Marmoush, whose previous club Eintracht Frankfurt have a sell-on clause. Are Spurs paying more for Sávio in order to pay potentially less to City for Marmoush, which could reduce the liabilities to Eintracht?De Zerbi has plenty on his plate after Spurs’dismal 3-0 defeat at Brentfordon Saturday in their Premier League opener and before the Carabao Cup tie at home against Charlton on Wednesday night.“Listen, I lost 3-0 in the first game in the Premier League … do you think for me it’s a problem if Savinho becomes Sávio?” he said, turning to face his interpreter. “If Enrico [the interpreter] becomes Savinho, it’s a problem. If Savinho stays Sávio, nothing changes for me.”De Zerbi said the talks for Sávio had started three days after the end of last season. It has been a mini‑epic to get the deal over the line but well worth it, according to the Spurs manager, who rates Sávio as one of the best in the world for being able to get past his marker when one‑against‑one. The challenge for Sávio will be to improve his end product, particularly in terms of goals. He scored only seven for City in all competitions and only two in 53 Premier League appearances. Sávio is available for selection against Charlton, his paperwork having been completed in time.De Zerbi did get around to accepting that Sávio’s rebrand was part of a fresh start for the player. What is not in doubt is Spurs’ need for one after Brentford, when all the excitement around a summer of heavy spending turned to frustration; a very familiar sinking feeling.View image in fullscreenNew Tottenham signings Jan Paul van Hecke (left) and Sandro Tonali (right) after Spurs conceded their second goal during their 3-0 defeat at Brentford.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianIt is possible to explain away the shambles against Brentford, who were not only much more joined-up but appeared to want it more in the duels. De Zerbi has attempted to do so in that way beloved of managers, emphasising he is not making excuses, you understand, just stating facts.He had a completely new back four compared with his preferred unit from the end of last season; a new midfield pair, too. Up front from right to left, Mikey Moore, Richarlison and Mathys Tel were nobody’s idea of a trio to drive the push for Champions League football. De Zerbi was missing a host of players because of fitness issues, including Pedro Porro, Micky van de Ven, Mateus Fernandes and Dominic Solanke. Some of the issues can be traced to the slog of a pre-season tour to New Zealand and Australia, which De Zerbi continues to reference in irritated tones.Thesefactsdo not really wash. The performance against Brentford was unacceptable. There is the sense that it will work out for Spurs, mainly because they have De Zerbi and a collection of Premier League‑ready new signings. They have certainly put themselves under pressure for the visit of Charlton. A relevant statistic: Spurs have won one domestic home game in 2026 – against Everton on the final day of last season which enabled them to avoid relegation.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDe Zerbi made the point that he and the squad had “started the project right now, not last season”. Which was when he was parachuted in with seven games to go; he picked up 11 points to dodge the unthinkable. “Last season, we fought to stay up,” he said. The inference was that it would take rather more to become a proper team.On the other hand, the experiences of the previous campaign do offer reassurance. “Maybe last season was a tougher challenge to stay up than this season,” De Zerbi said. “I said to the players: last season, in a worse situation, we showed character, we showed balls. We showed pride and quality. Now we have to stay calm and to analyse better the situation – not to have an emotional reaction. We have to be intelligent.”What De Zerbi craves is consistency, which he defined as being five wins in a row. It seems a distant goal after Brentford but De Zerbi has faith. What it will take is a change to the collective mentality. “We have to get used to winning games and games and games – we have to change habits from the last two seasons,” he said.“For me, the Carabao Cup is like the Premier League. We are not in the condition to make differences [between the competitions]. We have to play well and get used to winning – and winning matches, not a match. We have to change the mood. And we can.”De Zerbi said that Porro and Van de Ven will return as substitutes against Charlton and Solanke may start. James Maddison is out for two weeks with a shoulder injury suffered against Brentford. De Zerbi has a decision to make on Sávio. Victory is non-negotiable.Explore more on these topicsTottenham HotspurRoberto De ZerbifeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Victor Torp seals Coventry’s Carabao Cup win at Plymouth in six-goal thriller | Carabao Cup | The Guardian
description: Second-half goals from Ephron Mason-Clark and Victor Torp dashed Plymouth’s comeback bid to give Coventry a 4-2 win in the Carabao Cup
Author: Ben Fisher
Headline: Second-half goals from Ephron Mason-Clark and Victor Torp dashed Plymouth’s comeback bid to give Coventry a 4-2 win in the Carabao Cup
Content: Victor Torp slots home Coventry’s fourth goal from the penalty spot.Photograph: Kieran McManus/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenVictor Torp slots home Coventry’s fourth goal from the penalty spot.Photograph: Kieran McManus/ShutterstockCarabao CupVictor Torp seals Coventry’s Carabao Cup win at Plymouth in six-goal thrillerBen Fisherat Home ParkTue 25 Aug 2026 16.59 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 20.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA midweek jaunt to Devon always had the makings of a tricky trip for a Coventry team focused on Premier League survival. Such feelings quickly evaporated when Frank Lampard’s side raced into a two-goal lead with just four minutes and six seconds on the clock, Taiwo Awoniyi opening his account for his new club before Jack Rudoni doubled Coventry’s advantage. But, ultimately, Coventry were made to toil before chalking up a welcome first victory of the season.Plymouth have form for a cup upset and another was brewing when Xavier Amaechi pulled Tom Cleverley’s side level nine minutes into the second half. Coventry, to their credit, roused once more, the substitute Ephron Mason-Clark regaining the lead before Victor Torp sealed progress to theCarabao Cupthird round from the penalty spot. “You’ve got to enjoy a win, always,” Lampard said. “A win is a big deal because it’s a nice feeling to take back on the bus for four hours.”Delap heads to Forest for £50m as Chelsea open talks to sell Jackson to Aston VillaRead moreThe 2,244 Coventry supporters, many of whom made the 444-mile round trip, cycled through the catalogue of songs after crisp finishes by Awoniyi and Rudoni. Then Lampard obliged when they craved a wave from a manager who led them back to the top flight after 25 years away. But the game did not turn into the non-event most would have envisaged. “It’s very easy to go: ‘Why don’t you just go 2-0 up and then beat Plymouth 5-0, 6-0?’” Lampard said. “I’ve played in these games many times with different teams and they can become awkward, especially when the flow of the game goes against you: the crowd turns, emotions catch up and all of a sudden the game feels very different. I thought we dealt OK with that, in the end.”Plymouth were suddenly liberated at 2-0 down. The Danish centre-back Mathias Ross sent a header wide from a free-kick and a couple of minutes later Oliver Irow read Harvey White’s flighted pass and the Tottenham loanee, 24 hours after signing, drove inside Joel Latibeaudiere and drilled past the Coventry goalkeeper Dan Bentley, another debutant. From there, aside from Awoniyi heading wide unmarked, Coventry had to withstand Plymouth pressure. After fumbling White’s shot from distance, Bentley diverted Will Evans’s rebound on to his left post.Cleverley knew the value of recording an upset, Lampard the damage of defeat. It must have crossed his mind when Amaechi levelled on 54 minutes. Amaechi swarmed Liam Kitching and pinched the ball after the Coventry defender got in a tangle and fired in. Plymouth introduced the homegrown academy graduates Tegan Finn and Caleb Roberts, joining the 17-year-old full-back Joe Mwaro, this his full debut, on the pitch. “I couldn’t be happier with the reaction and the quality we showed to make sure it was still a competitive game,” Cleverley said.View image in fullscreenJack Rudoni doubles Coventry’s lead from close range in the fifth minute.Photograph: Dan Mullan/Getty ImagesMason-Clark arrived for his first appearance of the season after a hamstring issue and added the fifth goal of an entertaining game. It was a galling goal from a Plymouth perspective. Tatsuhiro Sakamoto’s cross from the right caused problems, Mason-Clark at first failing to divert the ball goalwards. But Torp was alert to the ball dropping at the back post and squared to provide Mason-Clark the simplest of finishes, the forward poking in from inside the six-yard box.Lampard made a triple sub, Sidiki Cherif replacing Awoniyi for his debut, while Josh Eccles and Brandon Thomas-Asante also entered. Joe Edwards, the Plymouth midfielder, arrived from the bench but his first notable action was to inadvertently swipe at Thomas-Asante in the box when trying to clear the leftovers of a Coventry corner, giving the referee, Elliott Swallow, no choice but to award a penalty. Torp capped the scoring, thrashing the spot-kick into the top corner.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor Cleverley, this also represented a touchline duel with a friend and a former England teammate and he had spoken on the eve of the game of wanting English coaches like Lampard and Michael Carrick, another former teammate, to succeed. “If you do well in it, you’re great for a moment, if you don’t do so well, then you’re not,” Lampard said after. “If you have the English tag, I do think we’ve got a bit of a bracket of saying: ‘There’s another one [struggling].’ Hopefully we’re not idiots and we can show that over a period of time and do our jobs well.”Explore more on these topicsCarabao CupPlymouth ArgyleCoventry Citymatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Carabao Cup roundup: Leeds beat Forest again, Brentford hit Birmingham for six | Carabao Cup | The Guardian
description: Dan James inspired Leeds’ second win at Nottingham Forest in three days, while Nathan Collins headed home twice as Brentford beat Birmingham 6-1
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Dan James inspired Leeds’ second win at Nottingham Forest in three days, while Nathan Collins headed home twice as Brentford beat Birmingham 6-1
Content: A joyous Dan James after scoring the opening goal for Leeds in their 2-0 win at Nottingham Forest.Photograph: News Images/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA joyous Dan James after scoring the opening goal for Leeds in their 2-0 win at Nottingham Forest.Photograph: News Images/NurPhoto/ShutterstockCarabao CupCarabao Cup roundup: Leeds beat Forest again, Brentford hit Birmingham for sixDan James sets Leeds on way, Nathan Collins doubles upPeterborough thump Watford 5-1, West Ham win 4-1PA MediaTue 25 Aug 2026 18.41 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 20.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLeedssecured a second win at Premier League rivalsNottingham Forestin three days to book a spot in the Carabao Cup third round. Dan James’s 50th-minute opener and a Neco Williams own goal earned a 2-0 victory for Daniel Farke’s side toback up Saturday’s1-0 league success.Before the weekend, the West Yorkshire club had not won at the City Ground since 1972. After defeat, new Forest manager Oliver Glasner said he is not a “magician”.“Right now, we are far away from where we want to be,” Glasner said. “The fact is that this team had a relegation battle for nine months. Very turbulent season and it ended with a huge effort to stay in the league, and this is our starting point.“It’s really very important not to blame anybody because sometimes I tell them facts and they say, ‘Oh, Glasner is complaining’. No, no, no. But then maybe your best midfielder [Elliot Anderson] leaves the club and now we expect we compete for European places because Oliver Glasner is in. Sorry, this is what I can’t deliver within six weeks. I’m no magician, no messiah, just hard work. That is what we have to do.”Victor Torp seals Coventry’s Carabao Cup win at Plymouth in six-goal thrillerRead moreCallum Wilson scored just six minutes into his full debut and captain Nathan Collins headed home twice asBrentfordhammeredBirmingham6-1 at St Andrew’s. Aaron Hickey, Mikkel Damsgaard and Igor Thiago were also on target for the Bees after Demarai Gray briefly cancelled out Wilson’s opener.League OnePeterboroughstormed into round three by thumping ChampionshipWatford5-1 at Vicarage Road. Hornets head coach Alessio Dionisi paid a heavy price for making 11 changes as James Clarridge’s own goal, Harry Leonard’s double and strikes from Bolu Shofowoke and Harrison Jones clinched an emphatic upset.Hullrequired penalties to beat second-tierStoke. The Tigers won 5-4 in the shootout after Kieran Dowell cancelled out Robert Bozenik’s goal in a 1-1 draw.Teenager Josh Ayala scored twice on his full professional debut asWest Hamcame from behind to thrash Championship rivalsSouthampton4-1. Taty Castellanos and Jarrod Bowen sealed the Hammers’ victory at St Mary’s after 19-year-old Ayala’s double overturned Léo Scienza’s opener.West Ham manager Nuno Espírito Santo saluted Ajala afterwards. “It is important for Josh,” he said. “He works hard every day in training to get chances in games. We are delighted he took the opportunity.”Marcelino Núñez scored a sensational goal from the halfway line as part of a brace to helpIpswichbeatLeicester3-1.Middlesbroughavenged last season’s exit at the hands ofDoncasterwith a 3-1 win thanks to goals from Kyle Joseph, Will Lankshear and Jeremy Sarmiento.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNorwichforward Ante Crnac marked his first appearance in 10 months after a serious knee injury by scoring the winner in a 2-1 victory atCardiff.Saheed Olagunju’s debut goal helpedWolvesbeatSheffield Wednesday2-0 at Hillsborough, while Ched Evans scored twice asFleetwoodthrashed League Two rivalsShrewsbury4-0.Romelle Donovan’s firstSheffield Unitedgoal secured a 2-1 victory at fellow Championship sideBlackburn.Leyton Orientwon 6-5 on penalties away toWalsallafter a goalless draw.Elsewhere,Lincolnwere 4-1 victors atBlackpool, Jake Cooper earnedMillwalla 1-0 success atCambridge, League OneBarnsleyovercame fourth-tierCrewe3-2 at Oakwell, andReadingeased to a 3-0 win atStevenage.Explore more on these topicsCarabao CupLeeds UnitedNottingham ForestBrentfordBirmingham CitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Bruno Fernandes and Khadija Shaw land PFA Player of the Year awards | PFA Player of the Year awards | The Guardian
description: Manchester United’s Bruno Fernandes, Manchester City’s Nico O’Reilly and Khadija Shaw, and Arsenal’s Olivia Smith win big at the PFA awards
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Manchester United’s Bruno Fernandes, Manchester City’s Nico O’Reilly and Khadija Shaw, and Arsenal’s Olivia Smith win big at the PFA awards
Content: Bruno Fernandes (left) and Khadija Shaw with their PFA player of the year awards.Composite: Peter Byrne/PA; Shane Anthony Sinclair/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBruno Fernandes (left) and Khadija Shaw with their PFA player of the year awards.Composite: Peter Byrne/PA; Shane Anthony Sinclair/Getty ImagesPFA Player of the Year awardsBruno Fernandes and Khadija Shaw land PFA Player of the Year awardsFellow players pick Manchester United and Manchester City starsNico O’Reilly and Olivia Smith collect young players’ honoursPA MediaTue 25 Aug 2026 17.50 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 17.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleManchester United’s captain Bruno Fernandes has been crowned Professional Footballers’ Association Player of the Year as Manchester City’s Khadija Shaw won the women’s award for the second time.Playmaker Fernandes broke the record for Premier League assists during an outstanding 2025-26 campaign, setting up 21 goals as he surpassed Thierry Henry and Kevin De Bruyne.Celtic throw away four-goal lead to crash out of Champions League against LASKRead moreThe 31-year-old also scored nine times as United overcome a shaky first half of the campaign to finish third in the Premier League under Michael Carrick to earn a Champions League return.Fernandes was pleased to have been voted the winner by his fellow professionals. He said: “It is obviously a very proud moment. They are the ones you go on the pitch against and it’s probably not easy to vote for someone you play against, so it is a very good moment.”The Portugal international is the club’s first winner since Wayne Rooney took home the trophy in 2009-10, and adds to his Football Writers’ Association Footballer of the Year award from May.Shaw, who was also recognised by the FWA, scooped the PFA Women’s Player of the Year award for the second time. The 29-year-old claimed the trophy in 2023-24 and won it again having scored 21 goals on the way to a third consecutive Golden Boot and her maiden Women’s Super League title.Arsenal’s Olivia Smith picked up the women’s PFA Young Player of the Year title for the second campaign running, having won the 2025 crown for her exploits at Liverpool before continuing her form in the capital.Manchester City’s Nico O’Reilly was named men’s PFA Young Player of the Year following an outstanding campaign that ended with the versatile talent helping England to win World Cup bronze. The 21-year-old was part of the PFA Premier League Team of the Year along with City teammates Erling Haaland, Rayan Cherki and Antoine Semenyo.O’Reilly said: “I had a great season. I’m very proud of the season I had. I won two trophies with my club and managed to play at the World Cup with my country. I’m over the moon how it turned out.”Champions Arsenal had five representatives in David Raya, Gabriel, William Saliba, Jurriën Timber and Declan Rice, with Player of the Year Fernandes of United and Brentford’s Igor Thiago completing the team.The PFA WSL Team of the Year featured three players from triumphant City, with Shaw joined by teammates Kerstin Casparij and Yui Hasegawa.Mariona Caldentey, last year’s PFA Women’s Player of the Year, was joined in the XI by fellow Arsenal players Emily Fox and Alessia Russo. Tottenham defender Toko Koga and Manchester United’s Jess Park were also included in the team, as were the Chelsea trio of Hannah Hampton, Ellie Carpenter and Lauren James.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHayden Hackney, now of Everton, was named Championship PFA Players’ Player of the Year for his performances for defeated play-off finalists Middlesbrough.Dom Ballard, who scored a jaw-dropping effort for new club Bristol City at the weekend, collected the League One award for a goal-laden season at Leyton Orient.Swindon striker Aaron Drinan’s performances saw him collect the League Two award, while Lily Crosthwaite of Birmingham took the WSL2 player accolade.Sir Kenny Dalglish and Karen Carney received the PFA merit awards in recognition of their contribution to football. Dalglish enjoyed a success-laden career as a player with Celtic and Liverpool, and is Scotland’s most capped performer having represented his country on 102 occasions. The 75-year-old, who confirmed in June he was undergoing treatment for cancer, went on to enjoy a successful managerial career, leading Liverpool to three league titles before masterminding Blackburn’s Premier League triumph.Carney played 144 times for England, including being part of the Lionesses squad which finished third at the 2015 World Cup. Having come through the ranks at Birmingham, Carney won the quadruple with Arsenal in 2007 as well as a league and FA Cup double with Chelsea in 2018.Explore more on these topicsPFA Player of the Year awardsManchester UnitedManchester City WomenWomen's footballnewsShareReuse this content

title: Delap heads to Forest for £50m as Chelsea open talks to sell Jackson to Aston Villa | Transfer window | The Guardian
description: Nottingham Forest to pay club record £45m plus £5m in add-ons, while West Ham’s Diouf is likely to join Brentford soon
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: Nottingham Forest to pay club record £45m plus £5m in add-ons, while West Ham’s Diouf is likely to join Brentford soon
Content: Liam Delap has struggled at Chelsea since his £30m move from Ipswich last summer.Photograph: Robbie Stephenson/PAView image in fullscreenLiam Delap has struggled at Chelsea since his £30m move from Ipswich last summer.Photograph: Robbie Stephenson/PATransfer windowDelap heads to Forest for £50m as Chelsea open talks to sell Jackson to Aston VillaForest to pay club-record £45m plus £5m in add-onsWest Ham’s Diouf likely to join Brentford soonJacob SteinbergTue 25 Aug 2026 14.42 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNottingham Forest have agreed a deal worth £50m to sign Liam Delap from Chelsea, who have also opened talks over selling Nicolas Jackson to Aston Villa.Xabi Alonso has made João Pedro and Danny Welbeck his main strikers this season, leaving his other frontmen to seek opportunities elsewhere.Forest were one of several clubs interested in Delap, who has struggled since joiningChelseafrom Ipswich for £30m last summer, and will pay a club record of £45m plus £5m in add-ons for the 23-year-old.Football transfer rumours: Manchester City and Spurs chase Cody Gakpo?Read moreDelap managed only one league goal last season and was hindered by injuries after leaving Ipswich. But the former Manchester City striker was a key target for Forest’s manager, Oliver Glasner, and has a chance to revive his career at the City Ground.Chelsea are focused on outgoings before the transfer window shuts next Tuesday and are also hoping to sell Jackson, who wason loan at Bayern Munich last season. The Senegal international is valued at £65m and has been earmarked by Villa as a potential replacement for Ollie Watkins, who is expected to join the Saudi Pro League side Al-Hilal.Chelsea are not willing to agree to another loan for Jackson and want his valuation met but Villa are likely to press for a favourable payment schedule to ensure they can afford a permanent deal. Atlético Madrid are also interested in the 25-year-old, who joined Chelsea from Villarreal in 2023. Unai Emery, Villa’s manager, worked with Jackson at Villarreal.West Ham’s clear out after relegation from the Premier League is expected to continue with El Hadji Malick Diouf joiningBrentfordfor about £35m. The clubs are in discussions over a deal for the left-back and an agreement is likely soon.Diouf wants to leave and was left out of the squad when Nuno Espírito Santo’s side continued their disappointing start to the Championship season by losing 2-1 at home against Charlton last Saturday.West Ham signed the Senegal international for £19m from Slavia Prague last year. Brentford have made four signings and are plan to strengthen further.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNuno, who is understood to be under growing pressure after West Ham’s flat start, has had his hand weakened by a host of players hoping to force their way out. The Mexico midfielder Edson Álvarez has not been involved in the first two league games and is the subject of interest from Olympiakos and Real Sociedad.Torino have had a bid rejected for the midfielder Soungoutou Magassa, who is on Crystal Palace’s shortlist. Marseille could sign the French centre-back Jean-Clair Todibo. West Ham have raised funds through the sales of Mateus Fernandes, Crysencio Summerville and Freddie Potts, and have loaned Aaron Wan-Bissaka toAston Villaand Niclas Füllkrug to Werder Bremen.Explore more on these topicsTransfer windowNottingham ForestChelseaAston VillaBrentfordWest Ham UnitednewsShareReuse this content

title: Women’s Super League 2026-27 preview No 5: Charlton Athletic | Charlton Women | The Guardian
description: Karen Hills’s side are a blend of knowhow and young talent and are ready to compete 20 years after their disbandment
Author: Sophie Downey
Headline: Karen Hills’s side are a blend of knowhow and young talent and are ready to compete 20 years after their disbandment
Content: Charlton players mob goalkeeper Sophie Whitehouse, who saved four penalties, after securing promotion to the WSL after the playoff match against Leicester at the Valley. Photograph: SPP/AlamyKaren Hills’s side are a blend of knowhow and young talent and are ready to compete 20 years after their disbandmentBySophie DowneyTue 25 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 19.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGuardian writers’ predicted position:14th (NB: this is not necessarily Sophie Downey’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)Last season’s position:3rd (WSL2)ProspectsJust under 20 years sinceCharlton’s successful women’s team were disbandedafter the men’s team’s relegation from the Premier League, they are finally back in the limelight and ready to make a name for themselves again.Karen Hills’s side impressed for much of last season, going on a 27-game unbeaten streak and possessing the meanest defence in WSL 2. A mid-season blip harmed their race for the title, however, and they lost out to Birmingham City on the final day of the season, ultimatelygoing through a playoffto achieve their goal of promotion. Beating Leicester in that game will have given Hills and her players confidence that they can compete. There will be no complacency, however, having seen how newly promoted sides have fared in recent history.Six players have departed since last season, including the influential Katie Bradley But they have been replaced with a blend of knowhow and exciting young talent. The arrival of Ashleigh Neville and Emily van Egmond will bring experience to Hills’s dressing room. Leah Davidson’s and Grace Johnston’s arrivals from Australia are intriguing moves. Meanwhile, Sophie Whitehouse was the hero of the previous campaign and Charlton will be looking to the goalkeeper to again lead from the back. It is the attacking side of the game that perhaps causes the most concern. Charlton managed only 31 goals last season, the lowest of the WSL2’s top six.Preparations got under way with a pre-season trip to Cádiz, a chance for a new-look side to come together. There is no doubt that the task to stay up is a challenging one, but a club that have defied the odds on more than one occasion will believe they can do it again.Graph showing Charlton’s finish in the Women’s Super League 2 in the past five seasonsOff-field pictureA record-breaking partnership has seen haircare brand Sofnfree become the women’s team’s official sleeve partner. The branding will feature on all playing and replica shirts this season, while content creation will be a focus as Charlton hope to access new and existing audiences. The club have also launched their first women’s-centric TikTok channel. The news, however, that ownership group Global Football Partners have put the club up for sale could cause a bit of instability in the short term.The managerReaching the Women’s Super League was part of the five-year plan Hills had when she was appointed in 2021, bringing a club close to her heart back into the limelight. The 51-year-old represented Chartlon for six years as a player, winning the FA Cup in 2005. This is the second time in Hills’s coaching career she has guided a team to the top flight, having previously done so with Tottenham in 2019, and watching Charlton walk out at the Valley against Liverpool on 6 September will inevitably be an emotional moment for her.View image in fullscreenKaren Hills has guided a club into the top flight for the second time after have done so with Spurs in 2019.Photograph: Tiego Grenho/AlamyStar signingOnly three months ago, Neville was lining up against Charlton in the promotion playoff. Now she is a fully fledged Addick, joining from Leicester on a two-year deal. The full-back brings with her a wealth of experience having made more than a century of appearances in the WSL. The majority of those were under Hills at Tottenham after arriving there from Coventry United. A tough-tackling, intuitive defender, Neville never shirks a challenge and has the ability to push forward. She will also be a strong leader in the dressing room.Stat attackDespite finishing third in WSL2, Charlton kept the joint-most clean sheets and conceded the fewest goals in the division. No club saved as high a percentage of their shots on target faced, with Whitehouse playing every minute. She saved four penalties in the playoff shootout, too.Graph showing Charlton had the best save percentage in Women’s Super League 2 with 70.8%Set for a breakthroughJohnston was named Charlton’s first signing of the summer during a transfer window that has seen many A-League players depart for Europe. The versatile young full-back arrives at the Valley hoping to make her mark on English football after three seasons with Perth Glory. She impressed during her time with her home town club, played every minute of last season, winning the club’s 2026 best young player award. Johnston’s form led to her being called up to the Young Matildas in 2023, representing the under-20s and now the under-23s. She was an integral member of the squad that won the Asean Women’s Championship last year.What they say …“I know what Karen’s about and vice versa; she knows what I bring. I’m really looking forward to working with her again” –Ashleigh NevilleWhere are they playing their home games?Charlton will play their home games at the Valley for a third consecutive season. Season-ticket sales started almost immediately after their successful promotion push. Alcohol will also still be allowed in the stadium, with an alcohol-free section established. Other fan activations include giving supporters the opportunity to sponsor a player.Explore more on these topicsWSL season previews 2026-27Charlton WomenWomen's Super LeagueWomen's footballfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Xavi hopes time at the ‘university of football’ will end with Dutch success | Netherlands | The Guardian
description: Barcelona legend wants to emulate Johan Cruyff’s total football philosophy after taking over as the Netherlands head coach
Author: Arthur Renard
Headline: Barcelona legend wants to emulate Johan Cruyff’s total football philosophy after taking over as the Netherlands head coach
Content: Xavi Hernández began his playing career at the Barcelona academy, whose fundamentals are rooted in Dutch football.Photograph: EYE4images/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenXavi Hernández began his playing career at the Barcelona academy, whose fundamentals are rooted in Dutch football.Photograph: EYE4images/NurPhoto/ShutterstockNetherlandsXavi hopes time at the ‘university of football’ will end with Dutch successBarcelona legend wants to emulate Johan Cruyff’s total football philosophy after taking over as the Netherlands head coachArthur Renardin ZeistTue 25 Aug 2026 15.58 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“My feeling today is that I’m going to the university of football.” Those were Xavi Hernández’s opening words at his presentation asthe Netherlands coachon Tuesday. “I learned a lot from this university of football during my career as a player and as a coach. I have many connections with this country.”Those connections date back to when Xavi was drafted as a youngster into La Masia, the famed Barcelona academy whose fundamentals are rooted in Dutch total football, inspired by Rinus Michels and Johan Cruyff. Xavi’s first-team debut came under Louis van Gaal, and he spent many years under Frank Rijkaard before becoming one of the main pillars of the dream team under Pep Guardiola, who was hugely inspired by Cruyff.Xavi Hernández appointed head coach of the Netherlands on four-year contractRead moreXavi opened a Cruyff court – a multifunctional sport space for children – with Cruyff in his home town of Terrassa in 2014, and on Tuesday shared special memories of his time with Cruyff, who died in 2016. “With Johan in the last period of his life I had some meetings,” he said. “And he was always positive. Even when he was sick, he was positive. This is what I learned: always smiling. This is what I want to show here to the players. My first goal is to help them, and then enjoy the process. And we will be in a process to win.”Xavi says he wants to “dominate the game, to take the initiative with the ball and at the same time our goal is to show everybody a team with passion, with desire and ambition. And this is very important for me as a coach.”In theNetherlands, there has always been a strong emphasis on attacking football, which is why Xavi fitted the bill. The Catalan was asked whether he would use five defenders, as Van Gaal and Ronald Koeman did at times in recent years. “That this is not my idea,” he said. “We want to play in another system [like] 4-3-3, 4-2-3-1, 3-4-3. In those systems we can dominate the game more.”Xavi said he had spoken to Frenkie de Jong – whom he coached at Barcelona – and Virgil van Dijk. He added that he would speak again to Van Dijk, the captain, in the near future to hear his ambitions with the team.The 46-year-old was also clear he is willing to select players from the Saudi Pro League, something more relevant after Tijjani Reijnders moved from Manchester City to Al-Qadsiah last week. Two years ago, Koeman was clear when Steven Bergwijn moved to Al-Ittihad that the forward would no longer be selected because the league did not match the level he expected from his players.View image in fullscreenXavi Hernández said he wants to play attacking systems with the Netherlands to ‘dominate the game more’.Photograph: Stefan Koops/DeFodi Images/Shutterstock“It’s a good league as well,” Xavi said. “Maybe we choose some players from Saudi, from Eredivisie, Premier League, La Liga. I don’t care about the leagues, I care about the performances and the players.”Nigel de Jong, the director of elite football at the Dutch football federation (KNVB), had earlier been open about the process that led to Xavi’s appointment. He said he had first tested the waters with Guardiola, who indicated he did not want to take a job in the near future, before holding two meetings with Arne Slot, who eventually chose to remain a club coach.De Jong then invited Xavi to Amsterdam for a meeting also attended by Clarence Seedorf, a member of the KNVB’s supervisory board. The following day De Jong and Seedorf spoke at length with Michael Reiziger, the Netherlands’ under-21s coach, who played alongside Xavi at Barcelona for several years.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThey were considering promoting Reiziger in a way similar to Luis de la Fuente’s journey with Spain, his knowledge of the country’s upcoming talents regarded as a major plus. When the meeting with Reiziger became known in the Dutch media, there was an assumption the former full-back would become the national team coach. But then, on 12 August, the KNVB announced Xavi, a decision that seemingly came out of the blue.Xavi said drily that he was fine with the process. “Well, it’s not a bad position, after Guardiola and after Slot, no? At least you are at the podium. I don’t care if I’m the third [choice] or I’m the 10th. It’s a big honour to be here. He [De Jong] explained to me, very honestly: ‘We need your philosophy, we need to change with ambition, with passion.’ And we will work in this way.”First up for Xavi is a Nations League game against Germany in Amsterdam on 24 September, when he will face Jürgen Klopp, who is also starting a new job. “I feel excited, I feel motivated,” Xavi said, “because we are playing against Germany, one of the best teams in Europe, one of the best coaches in recent years.”Xavi, speaking in front of his staff, including Ruud van Nistelrooy, wants his team to adopt the Dutch style he saw as a young boy. “I remember when I was a kid, watching the Netherlands and watching good football,” he said, “and this is my way, this is my target.”Explore more on these topicsNetherlandsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Manchester United confirm Carlos Baleba signing as midfield spend nears £150m | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: Manchester United have confirmed the signing of Carlos Baleba from Brighton on a contract to 2031
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Manchester United have confirmed the signing of Carlos Baleba from Brighton on a contract to 2031
Content: Carlos Baleba is the third midfielder to join Manchester United this summer, after Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos.Photograph: Manchester United/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCarlos Baleba is the third midfielder to join Manchester United this summer, after Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos.Photograph: Manchester United/Getty ImagesManchester UnitedManchester United confirm Carlos Baleba signing as midfield spend nears £150mCameroon international joins from BrightonHe says United are the ‘club of my dreams’PA Media andGuardian sportTue 25 Aug 2026 11.58 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleManchester United have completed the signing of the Brighton midfielder Carlos Baleba in a deal worth up to £70m. The Cameroon international is the third midfielder to join this summer, after Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans.Baleba has signed a five-year contract with the option to extend for 12 months after United agreed a £65m deal plus £5m in add-ons and a sell-on with Brighton. It takes the club’s spend on midfielders to about £148m.Savinho seals £75m Spurs move from Manchester City – and changes name to SávioRead moreSantos and Tielemans have arrived from Chelsea and Aston Villa respectively during a summer when Casemiro left and Manuel Ugarte sustained a serious knee injury.“It is an incredible feeling to join the club of my dreams,” Baleba said. “Playing at Old Trafford is always special but the opportunity to do so as a Manchester United player will be a real honour.“I cannot wait to work with Michael Carrick. His experience and knowledge of the game make him the perfect coach to help me to reach the highest level.“The ambition of everyone at the club is extremely clear, the future is hugely exciting, and I am determined to play my part in delivering the success that we are capable of together.”United made a move to bring in Baleba last summer but cooled their pursuit when Brighton made it clear he was not leaving. Baleba was not at his best last season but that did not put off United, who stepped up their interest in the 22-year-old a week ago.United’s director of football, Jason Wilcox, said: “Carlos is an elite midfielder with immense potential to develop further. He brings a unique combination of qualities that will really complement our squad.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We are delighted to further strengthen our midfield with the addition of another established senior international with a proven track record of performing in the Premier League.”Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitedBrighton & Hove AlbionTransfer windownewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Icon of our game’: All-Australian selection lifts ruck great Max Gawn into rarified air | AFL | The Guardian
description: Minor premiers Fremantle led the league with five All-Australian selections but all eyes were on record-breaking Melbourne skipper Max Gawn
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Minor premiers Fremantle led the league with five All-Australian selections but all eyes were on record-breaking Melbourne skipper Max Gawn
Content: Max Gawn was named in the AFL All-Australian team for a record-breaking ninth time on Tuesday.Photograph: Michael Willson/AFL Photos/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMax Gawn was named in the AFL All-Australian team for a record-breaking ninth time on Tuesday.Photograph: Michael Willson/AFL Photos/Getty ImagesAFL‘Icon of our game’: All-Australian selection lifts ruck great Max Gawn into rarified airMelbourne player awarded record-breaking ninth blazerAFL minor premiers Fremantle lead league with five selectionsAustralian Associated PressTue 25 Aug 2026 19.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMelbourne colossus Max Gawn has underlined his status as the greatest ruckman of the modern era, awarded an unprecedented ninth All-Australian blazer after another brilliant individual season.Gawn was named captain of the representative side, which also featured Demons teammate Kysaiah Pickett among a record five Indigenous players chosen.Essendon outline plan for James Hird after opting for Mark McVeigh as head coachRead moreMinor premiers Fremantle led the league with five selections, headlined by key forward Josh Treacy, one of nine players named for the first time.Gawn’s record-breaking ninth selection comes after the 34-year-old champion defied changes to ruck rules to maintain his status as the competition’s dominant ruckman.Gawn’s latest inclusion pushed him clear of fellow greats Gary Ablett Snr, Gary Ablett Jnr, Patrick Dangerfield, Lance Franklin, Robert Harvey, and Mark Ricciuto, who all have eight blazers. That group was joined by Western Bulldogs skipper Marcus Bontempelli.The humble Gawn said he was “incredibly lucky” to have the late Jim Stynes as a mentor, declaring lessons from his fellow Melbourne ruck great crucial in his rise to greatness.“It’s all about being the best version of yourself,” Gawn said on stage at Melbourne’s Centrepiece on Tuesday night. “It’s hard enough playing footy out there at the MCG trying to not be someone that you are. So to have that in the back of my mind every time I get on the ground allows me to be me.”Melbourne coach Steven King hailed Gawn as an “icon of our game” and the ruck star’s teammates lauded his remarkable contribution the club.“I listened to Kingy last week – I don’t know if this footy club would be where we are right now if it wasn’t for Max,” Demons forward Bayley Fritsch told AAP. “Everything we’ve been through, he stood tall. He spoke to you guys in the media when the times have been the toughest at this club.“He was here when we were beaten by Geelong by 200 points or whatever it was down the road [in 2011] and then he’s obviously won the flag [in 2021]. He’s 34, and when we need him, he’s at his best. It’s all about being the best version of yourself.”Melbourne midfielder and former St Kilda captain Jack Steele added: “It’s a nightmare to play against him and it’s unreal to rove to him. He’s clearly the best ruckman of all-time for a reason and certainly deserves a ninth jacket.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFrom the Pocket: AFL WeeklyJonathan Horn brings expert analysis on the week's biggest AFL storiesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAdelaide skipper Jordan Dawson was named vice-captain after producing an outstanding individual season in difficult circumstances, following the death of elder brother Jaryd in April. Dawson was picked alongside Gawn, Bontempelli and Brownlow medal favourite Nick Daicos in the midfield.The Sydney Swans scandal has left many outraged. But what happens if no police charges are laid? | Rana HussainRead moreTreacy was selected with fellow first-timers Luke Jackson and Murphy Reid as Shai Bolton and Jordan Clark rounded out the league-leading Dockers’ cohort of five. Reigning premiers Brisbane were the only other club with more than two players selected – Harris Andrews, Zac Bailey and young key forward Logan Morris.Coleman Medal winner Charlie Curnow was the only player selected from embattled Sydney. The Swans suspended five players who were also then ruled ineligible for All-Australian selection, including star trio Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner and Nick Blakey.Ten players retained their All-Australian spots from last year, including St Kilda playmaker Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera and Geelong star Bailey Smith.Explore more on these topicsAFLAustralian rules footballAustralia sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Starting to wind me up’: Itauma rebuffs Hrgovic before world heavyweight title fight | Boxing | The Guardian
description: Moses Itauma has hit back at Filip Hrgovic’s taunt that he is a ‘delusional kid’ as the two men prepare to fight for the IBF world heavyweight title at the O2 Arena
Author: Donald McRae
Headline: Moses Itauma has hit back at Filip Hrgovic’s taunt that he is a ‘delusional kid’ as the two men prepare to fight for the IBF world heavyweight title at the O2 Arena
Content: Moses Itauma accused Filip Hrgovic of being a ‘talker’ before their fight at the O2 on Saturday.Photograph: James Fearn/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMoses Itauma accused Filip Hrgovic of being a ‘talker’ before their fight at the O2 on Saturday.Photograph: James Fearn/Getty ImagesBoxing‘Starting to wind me up’: Itauma rebuffs Hrgovic before world heavyweight title fightItauma can become second-youngest champion after Mike TysonHrgovic claims title victory for opponent would ‘ruin his soul’Donald McRaeTue 25 Aug 2026 14.18 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMoses Itauma has hit back at Filip Hrgovic’s taunt that he is a “delusional kid” and admitted that his Croatian rival is starting to annoy him as the two men prepare to fight for the IBF world heavyweight title on Saturday night at the O2 Arena in London.“I tell myself there’s nothing that this Hrgovic guy can do to get in my head but he’s starting to wind me up,” Itauma said on Tuesday evening. “In an interview earlier, apparently he said I wake up and I just hug trees. He’s really starting to annoy me.‘Not braggadocious, not swaggerdocious’: Moses Itauma on why he lets his fists do the talkingRead more“In my mind if somebody’s trying to get one up on you, or trying to get in your head, it’s because they’re not confident in themselves. Obviously Hrgovic is a talker. Before fights, he’s always said certain things – like he did to [Daniel] Dubois when he said he sees big muscles but not big balls. Then you see Dubois, in his mind, is raging. So Hrgovic has always been a talker. It’s just because English ain’t his first language that people don’t pay attention.”If Itauma beats Hrgovic, as expected, he will become thesecond-youngest world heavyweight championin history. Only Mike Tyson won the title at a younger age and Hrgovic said of the 21-year-old Itauma: “He’s a kid. He’s inexperienced.
