So, for him, it would be best to lose this fight because it’s going to ruin him, winning the world title. He’s already in the clouds. He’s already delusional. And it can ruin someone who’s not ready for that kind of fame, that kind of money.“It can ruin your soul, it can make you lose yourself and we’ve seen a lot of superstars and famous people who have lost themselves. They’re just lost in that crazy world of fame and money. He’s not ready for that. I think, for him, it would be best to lose this fight, to save his soul. Because what does it mean to achieve everything if you lose your soul and you lose yourself?”Itauma conceded that there is a semblance of truth in Hrgovic’s words: “Although it’s been annoying me, I hear that because I already know the level of success I’ve achieved and how I’m coping. I’ve always said I never wanted to be at Anthony Joshua or Tyson Fury level because I know how annoyed I get trying to be a normal person. Now I can’t imagine being at a level of Tyson Fury or Anthony Joshua. But, at the same time, if I’m going down this path, I don’t have a choice.”Asked if Hrgovic has a point that winning a world title at such a young age would be bad for his “soul”, Itauma replied: “I wouldn’t say he has a point but if I win this fight it might not be good for my soul. I can hear that. But that’s not the reason why I’m just gonna go in there and not win – for the sake of my soul. That’s not a good idea.”Pressed to explain why Itauma is “delusional”, Hrgovic said: “He went from youth level to professional, had a few fights and became a star. Everyone is clapping him on his back – [saying] you’re the best, you’re the next Muhammad Ali. You’re the new Mike Tyson. He’s just not, in reality. I’m very grateful for all the hard things I went through. It makes you a different person.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe 34-year-old Hrgovic, who has lost just once in a professional career stretching across nine years, said: “I’m in a much different position because of that experience, and the ups and downs in my life. I’m like a rock. Stable. Nothing can move me. I don’t care about fame. I don’t care about money. I don’t care about what people think. But we’ll see on Saturday.”Explore more on these topicsBoxingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Prime minister Andy Burnham ‘heartbroken’ after death of rugby league legend Billy Boston | Wigan Warriors | The Guardian
description: Sir Billy Boston, the Wigan Warriors legend who last year became the first rugby league player to be awarded a knighthood, has died at the age of 92
Author: Aaron Bower
Headline: Sir Billy Boston, the Wigan Warriors legend who last year became the first rugby league player to be awarded a knighthood, has died at the age of 92
Content: Billy Boston after he received his knighthood from King Charles in June 2025.Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAView image in fullscreenBilly Boston after he received his knighthood from King Charles in June 2025.Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAWigan WarriorsPrime minister Andy Burnham ‘heartbroken’ after death of rugby league legend Billy BostonBoston was one of the finest players in the sport’s historyWigan plan series of tributes in Thursday’s Hull KR clashAaron BowerTue 25 Aug 2026 11.26 EDTFirst published on Tue 25 Aug 2026 05.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy ­Burnham says he is “heart­broken” by the death of Sir Billy ­Boston after the prime minister led tri­butes to the rugby league icon.Boston died on Tuesday at the age of 92. He was one of the sport’s all‑time great players, scoring almost 500 tries during an illustrious career forWigan Warriorsand Great Britain, and last year became the first man in rugby league history to be knighted for his services to the game.His death comes just four days after the funeral of his wife of more than 70 years, Lady Joan Boston, who died last month. Burnham, a lifelong rugby league supporter who also served as president of the Rugby Football League, described Boston as a “giant of a man in every way”.The prime minister wrote: “Heartbroken to hear my friend Sir Billy Boston has died. Billy was one of the greatest rugby league players of all time but also one of the kindest and most down-to-earth people you could ever wish to meet.“He always had time for people and gave so much back to his adopted home, Wigan. I will miss him greatly and am thinking today of Billy’s ­family, still grieving the recent loss of his beloved wife Joan. A giant of a man in every way. Thank you, Billy, and rest in peace.”Boston joined Wigan in 1953 after starting his rugby career in his native Wales. He went on to score 478 tries in 488 games for the club, winning a plethora of honours for club and country. Only one man, the Warring­ton winger Brian Bevan, has more tries in the history of the sport than Boston.Less than a year after leaving Wales to begin a career in league, Boston became the first non-white player to be selected for Great Britain. He scored 36 tries in 18 games on that tour to Australia and New Zealand in 1954, and was part of the Lions’ World Cup-winning squad of 1960.View image in fullscreenBilly Boston scored 478 tries in 488 games for Wigan.Photograph: PABoston was awarded an MBE in 1996 but, last year, he became the first rugby league player to be knighted for services to the sport. That accolade was met with emotional ­celebrations in Wigan, the town in which he remained after retirement and where one of three statues – alongside those at Wembley and Cardiff – stands ­fea­turing Boston, which underlines his life and career.The Warriors are planning for an emotional occasion on Thursday evening when they host Hull KR in Super League, with a series of ­tributes planned to celebrate Boston’s life. Their head coach, Matt Peet, paid an emotional tribute on Tuesday while conducting his pre-match press duties. “It’s like he was on a different planet, really,” Peet said of Boston’s career.“I wish I could see more of him. I’ve seen bits of footage, but I think it’s more the legend when people talk about him in terms of the ­stories and players that played against him, ­players that played with him. It’s going to be a real tribute night on Thursday.Obviously, people are very upset and rightly so, but you’ve got to celebrate a life well lived. Everything that Billy represented and stood for.We have a responsibility to uphold the whole history of the club when you work at a club like this, but I think Billy’s top of the tree in terms of standing in the club’s history.”Kris Radlinski, the Wigan chief executive, said: “Today we mourn one of our greatest ever Warriors and rugby league’s first knight. Time moves on, as it must, but some names endure. Billy Boston will always be one of them. His place in the history of Wigan, and in the history of rugby league, is secure for ever.“I visited him on Sunday ­morning with Mandy [Johnston, Wigan’s administrator], held his hand and told him we loved him. Rest in peace, Billy. My friend, our Warrior and a true Wigan legend.”Eamonn McManus, the chair of Wigan’s biggest rivals, St Helens, described Boston as a “giant amongst giants”, said: “Sir Billy Boston was more than an all-time great of the sport of rugby league. His name both symbolised and transcended it. He was one of the greats for both Wigan and Great Britain in the golden era of our sport in the 1950s and 60s. He was a giant amongst giants.“He led and epitomised our sport’s and our communities’ ­pioneering example in breaking down racial ­barriers in this country and he should be remembered always for that. Although deeply saddened by his passing we should in equal measure celebrate his unparalleled contribution to our sport and to our society.”Explore more on these topicsWigan WarriorsRugby leaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: England captain Joe Root ‘hacked off’ and ‘disappointed’ at Carse incident | England cricket team | The Guardian
description: England captain Joe Root says cricketers need to avoid ‘stupid mistakes’ after Carse was dropped from squad following handcuffs incident
Author: Simon Burnton
Headline: England captain Joe Root says cricketers need to avoid ‘stupid mistakes’ after Carse was dropped from squad following handcuffs incident
Content: Joe Root was brutally honest about England cricket’s image problem during a press conference at Lord’s.Photograph: Philip Brown/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJoe Root was brutally honest about England cricket’s image problem during a press conference at Lord’s.Photograph: Philip Brown/Getty ImagesEngland cricket teamEngland captain Joe Root ‘hacked off’ and ‘disappointed’ at Carse incidentRoot says cricketers need to avoid ‘stupid mistakes’Carse dropped from squad following handcuffs incidentSimon BurntonTue 25 Aug 2026 09.56 EDTFirst published on Tue 25 Aug 2026 09.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJoe Root has spoken of his desire to remodel England’s dressing room into a group that inspires “supporters to look at us and not just revere what we do on the field but off it as well” after the conduct of the nation’s cricketers was once again called into question following the emergence of videos showingBrydon Carse being escorted from a Derby nightclub in handcuffslate on Saturday night.The England captain said he was “really hacked off” to be forced once again to address player behaviour, after a string of similar stories over the past eight months. But he repeatedly and pointedly referred to Carse’s misdemeanour, which led to the 31-year-old being briefly arrested on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly before being de-arrested and released without charge, as an “isolated incident”.“I’m not trying to sit here and ask people to be saints,” he said. “I just think that if we don’t put ourselves in certain situations it’s not something we have to worry about.” The 35-year-old talked of the unwritten code of conduct that players will be expected to abide by: “It doesn’t have to be rocket science. As players you get judged on the decisions you make on the field and off it too. That’s the world that we’re living in.Carse’s night out shows Fleming must get a grip on this England squad immediately | Mark RamprakashRead more“It’s not the isolated incident itself, I think it is the fact that we continually keep making stupid mistakes away from the game, and it’s detracting from what we’re doing on the field.“Clearly we’re not portraying ourselves how we want to, and I think we’ve got an opportunity to build a culture that’s very strong, something that’s player-driven. Of course that’s not going to happen overnight. But we want to create something that we can be proud of and people that follow us can be proud of.“The most important thing is we take this opportunity. We have a chance to build something that lives alongside what we achieved [in beating Pakistan at Headingley] last week. I thought the way we played was exceptional and we have to align that with being exceptional off the field as well, and understand what that looks like and how we want to represent ourselves and our nation. We’re going to have to earn a lot of trust back, and it’s something we’re going to have to live and breathe consistently.”As the squad gathered ahead of the second Test against Pakistan, which starts at Lord’s on Thursday, and in the absence of their full-time coach, Stephen Fleming, who is due to arrive in the country next month, Root led what he termed “a very robust discussion” during which the group were reminded of their responsibilities as international cricketers.“There are certain things that I do believe should stay in a dressing room. It is a sacred place,” he said of that conversation. “But don’t worry, they are very clear of what is expected of them and how we need to go about things moving forward.”One of Root’s first acts after returning to the captaincy at the end of last month was to cancel the curfew that had been imposed on players after a string of embarrassing incidents over the winter.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I still don’t believe that’s the way to go,” he said on Tuesday. “I think it’s important that we create something bigger than that. It’s about having something long-lasting that we can pass on to the next generation of players. I might only be in this dressing room for a couple more years.“There’s a group of players there that are going to be around for the next 10, and they can live and breathe something and achieve something over that period of time. And this is where that can start. I’ve made it very clear what is expected of them.”Explore more on these topicsEngland cricket teamEngland v Pakistan 2026Joe RootCricketnewsShareReuse this content

title: Luka Dončić looks like a superstar adrift at the Lakers | Luka Dončić | The Guardian
description: The Slovenian is one of the best players on the planet. But factors largely beyond his control have started to turn his career into a slog
Author: Owen Lewis
Headline: The Slovenian is one of the best players on the planet. But factors largely beyond his control have started to turn his career into a slog
Content: Luka Dončić averaged more than 33 points a game last season.Photograph: Lynne Sladky/APView image in fullscreenLuka Dončić averaged more than 33 points a game last season.Photograph: Lynne Sladky/APLuka DončićLuka Dončić looks like a superstar adrift at the LakersThe Slovenian is one of the best players on the planet. But factors largely beyond his control have started to turn his career into a slogOwen LewisTue 25 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 05.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLuka Dončić must feel as though, these past few months, he’s been twirling in a washing machine. He announced a separation from his fiancee in March; reports followed of a prolonged custody battle over their two daughters. As Dončić plays in the NBA and his children live in Slovenia, he doesn’t see them much as is. But after the reports of the rift with his ex emerged, he started playing some of the best basketball of his life: he led the Los Angeles Lakers to a 15-2 record in March, a stretch that included a torrential 60-point display against the Miami Heat. Behind Dončić’s brightening star, the Lakers seemed to be sharpening into a real contender. Then Dončićtweaked his hamstringin April and the illusion shattered. He watched from the sidelines as the Lakers limped out of the playoffs with an inevitable second-round defeat to the Oklahoma City Thunder.Actually, Dončić must feel as if he’s been in turmoil for the past fewyears. He made his first – and so far only –NBAfinals in 2024, leading the Dallas Mavericks there with a barrage of awesome shotmaking. As the best offensive player on the court while playing through multiple injuries, Dončić and his Mavs lost to the far deeper Boston Celtics in five games. As thanks, the Mavericks traded Dončić to the Lakers, citing defensive concerns, when what had really doomed them against the Celtics was that no oneasidefrom Luka – who led his team in points, rebounds, assists and steals in that series – could play at the requisite level to win.From Showtime to Insurance Time: how the LA Lakers became a $12.5bn hedge fund playRead moreAnd what to make of Dončić’s Lakers tenure? He and Austin Reaves seem to be platonic soulmates. He’s played with LeBron James, his idol. And yet the team remained built in the afterimage of the LeBron-Anthony Davis Lakers, a far worse fit for Dončić than the Mavs were during his stint in Dallas. With a hard ceiling imposed upon them – not enough shooting, less defense – they’ve yet to make an impactful playoff run during his time in LA.Now Dončić may get his chance. James is gone, off to theclunky but alarmingly stacked Philadelphia 76ers.In his place the Lakers have, at long last, employed a center not named Deandre Ayton. Walker Kessler may transform the Lakers for the better; he may also need time to develop into what Dončić needs; he most definitely cost a lot of money. This is the first season in Los Angeles that Dončić will get to run the Lakers as truly his own team, which is a mixed blessing. Will the (hopefully) improved synergy be enough to take down, or even meaningfully threaten, the monstrous basketball ecosystems that are Thunder and Spurs? Probably not, in which case many will blame Dončić.So, is Dončić cursed? Born to be an MVP, but thrust into the same era as Nikola Jokić and Shai Gilgeous-Alexander. Perfect on the Mavs, but helpless in the clumsy, unfeeling hands of owner Miriam Adelson and Nico “Defense wins championships” Harrison. Totally in control of any offense, but constantly furious at and distracted by those pesky outside factors, the referees. A shade too uninterested on defense for anybody to ignore the deficiency. Traded to the Lakers, who took too long to mold themselves around him. Brilliant in the regular season, capable of being a supernova in the playoffs, but too often injured. Early in his Lakers tenure, ready to return to the court after healing from a hamstring injury, the franchisegets new owners.The clock’s ticking for the 27-year-old, and it’s not even his fault. How is it fair that one of the great pressure performers of his generation is primed for a James Harden-esque legacy? We should know by now to resist the immense gravitational pull of rings; they’re too elusive – and too reliant on the contributions of others – to be the main criteria by which to judge a player in a team sport. But if Dončić retires without an NBA title, it will be held against him. Likewise with his lack of an MVP award, despite the fact that Dončić’s lone crime is being a unicorn slightly smaller than Jokić, and being born too soon before Victor Wembanyama. By the time voter fatigue comes for Wemby, Dončić will be on the wrong side of 30.Sports are made for narratives, all the more attractive when subjectivity enters the conversation. The prevailing attitude is that there are winners and there are losers, and excepting the mostmythmakingly tragic bad luckeverybody pretty much deserves what they get. Within that framework each player is buttonholed into a tidy little story, while various factors such as “timing”, “teammates”, and “De’Aaron Fox had a high ankle sprain during the most recent playoffs” are ignored or shunned. You wonder how much Dončić’s story will acknowledge that he didn’t always have agency in his fate, at least not to this point.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly for the 2026 WNBA seasonSign up toWNBA 30A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe more interesting question is how he feels right now. This is a player with something approaching absolute power on the basketball court who a) doesn’t seem very happy when exercising said power, b) is so bothered by any and all refereeing that his complaints are the pet peeve of half the fanbase, c) has repeatedly found himself in impossible situations through no fault of his own, and d) is dealing with a difficult situation in his life off the court. Lost in the inevitable handwringing about thepressureon Dončić and the potential of himunderdeliveringon what seemed to be adestined legacyis the feeling that one of the best basketball players alive doesn’t seem very happy. Think of his reaction after thefamous game-winner over Rudy Gobert. That’s not self-satisfied or showy trash talk, he’s pissed off. Not to mention what his apparent discontentment says about the sport or the person. Perhaps this season Dončić will be able to conduct the team and the action the way he hopes, but I wonder if he’d trade that possibility for a measure of peace. To hijack a cliche, the best offense is a good defense.Explore more on these topicsLuka DončićNBALos Angeles LakersBasketballUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Never seen this level of objection’: Scotland pushes back against datacentre boom | Datacentres - UK | The Guardian
description: Holyrood ‘inching towards moratorium’ amid concerns over massive proposed developments in Auchtertool and beyond
Author: Aisha Down
Headline: Holyrood ‘inching towards moratorium’ amid concerns over massive proposed developments in Auchtertool and beyond
Content: A protest outside Holyrood in June against proposed datacentres across Scotland.Photograph: Ken Jack/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA protest outside Holyrood in June against proposed datacentres across Scotland.Photograph: Ken Jack/Getty ImagesDatacentres - UK‘Never seen this level of objection’: Scotland pushes back against datacentre boomHolyrood ‘inching towards moratorium’ amid concerns over massive proposed developments in Auchtertool and beyondAisha DownGlobal technology reporterTue 25 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 05.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a village 21 miles north of Edinburgh, a real estate consultancy plans to build a datacentre larger than the village itself – 35 metres high, with an area larger than 100 football pitches.Billed as the second-biggest datacentre in the world, the development in Auchertool, Fife, has attracted 1,600 objections.“The public pressure is huge,” said David Torrance, a member of the Scottish parliament representing the village. “I’ve never seen this level of objection to a local plan, and I have been in politics for 25 years.”Similar concernsare being echoed across Scotland, next to gargantuan planned developments in towns such asAirdrieand Larbert. In a matter of weeks, as the Scottish parliament comes back into session, the growing opposition could pose a challenge to Britain’s AI strategy.“The Scottish government is inchingtowards a moratorium,” said Kat Jones, director of the Edinburgh-based charity Action to Protect Rural Scotland. “MSPs return to parliament next week, after a summer in their constituencies where they have been hearing the concerns of local people about proposed hyperscale datacentres. They will be expecting action.”For months, UK officials have been encouraging would-be datacentre developers to consider Scotland. In April, Fintan Slye, the chief executive of the UK’s National Energy System Operator (Neso), told a London audience tolook north: “If in the audience you have a big datacentre and you want to go to Scotland, please come talk to me, we will help you,” he said.“They are coming up here because we are energy-rich, and we are water-rich, and England is in drought and the grid is struggling,” said Torrance.ButScotland, it turns out, isn’t having it. The proposal for Auchtertool is a behemoth: drawings show the 600MW datacentre towering over the village, dwarfing old stone houses and blocking the view of fields and forests.“How can you possibly ask people to accept that?” Torrance said. “You can see why the public is objecting.”Scotland has already started to take steps that could mean the Auchtertool datacentre – and dozens of others – may never be built.This week, Scotland’s minister for public finance issued a new set of directions to regulate datacentres in the country. The first of these requires planning authorities to notify the government when they receive an application for a datacentre larger than 50MW – in other words, anything more than a twelfth of the size of Auchtertool.View image in fullscreenInterior of a datacentre. Campaigners at Action to Protect Rural Scotland allege that ministers have failed to include the emissions from hyperscale AI datacentres in work looking at their impact on climate targets.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAThe minister has also required that certain datacentres, including Auchtertool, submit an environmental impact assessment. Their developers had previously argued that they were exempt.In some senses, these are “obvious, bare-minimum” rules, said Jones. They mean that Scotland is starting to closely follow developments that stand to drastically reshape the landscape and resource consumption of the entire country.The fact that giant datacentres can currently be built across Britain with little strategy and without government knowledge is a feature of an old and idiosyncratic planning regime; no one foresaw that giant tech companies would wish to litter the world with buildings the size of large monuments.But these restrictions are just the start. The Scottish parliament will return at the end of this month. Three days after the session commences, in early September, campaigners plan a massive demonstration against datacentres in Edinburgh.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThat demonstration will aim higher. Campaigners have been calling for Scotland to put in place a full moratorium on datacentre development, to give the public and authorities time to examine the plans that are in the pipeline. This summer, the national council of the Scottish National party passed a motion tofreezeall new datacentre projects that have not received planning permission.Several weeks ago, Police Scotland warned another datacentre developer that public anger over datacentres could lead to incursions and posed a security risk, in what appeared to be the first-ever such warning in the UK.A moratorium on datacentres could soon become policy. At the least, “you’ll see a lot more restrictions – and stronger guidance,” said Torrance.Datacentre developers have other plans. Data Vita, the company building the UK’s AI growth zone in Lanarkshire, has recently been awarded an investment package which includes a £202m guarantee from the National Wealth Fund – although the Guardian’s investigations have revealed thatits plans to power itself do not stand up.View image in fullscreenThe Data Vita datacentre being extended within the AI growth zone in Airdrie, North Lanarkshire.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianMeanwhile, Mark Wilson, chief executive of ILI Group, the company building the datacentre in Auchtertool, spoke to the BBC’sScotcastthis week and defended its plans, suggesting that Torrance’s angry constituents were perhaps ill-informed.“I understand how people can think in a rural area,” he said. “There’s a lot of misinformation out there, it’s mainly coming from overseas, from America.”His company was part of a “once-in-a-lifetime opportunity” for Scotland to “create long-term economic benefit”, he said, through the jobs created by building datacentres. He conceded that most of the datacentre developments currently in the planning pipeline in Scotland were unlikely to be built.“Scotland can be No1,” he said. “We can become a global hub for datacentres in Scotland.”Explore more on these topicsDatacentres - UKScotlandAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingScottish politicsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tell us: do you think AI has made Google search better or worse?  | Google | The Guardian
description: As people grow used to AI chatbots, we’d like to hear your views about Google’s search engine
Author: Guardian community team
Headline: As people grow used to AI chatbots, we’d like to hear your views about Google’s search engine
Content: How do you feel about Google’s search engine now that articicial intelligence is at the front and center of it search bar?Photograph: Nicolas Economou/NurPhoto/REX/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenHow do you feel about Google’s search engine now that articicial intelligence is at the front and center of it search bar?Photograph: Nicolas Economou/NurPhoto/REX/ShutterstockGoogleTell us: do you think AI has made Google search better or worse?As people grow used to AI chatbots, we’d like to hear your views about Google’s search engineGuardian community teamTue 25 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGoogle has put artificial intelligence at the front and center of its search bar. The most-visited site on the internet still shows the same list of links to users, but they have to scroll past a summarized response from an AI chatbot, a featureGooglecalls AI Overviews. The change to what was once the gateway to the rest of the internet has been profound, and the browsing habits of billions of people are shifting.“AI is driving the most significant upgrade of the Google Search experience ever,” Liz Reid, Google’s vice-president of search,wrote last August. In May, the company saidmore AI is coming.As people grow accustomed to AI chatbots, they’re spending more time with Google’s and therefore more time on Google.com. Studies, media outlets and website owners alike are finding that people navigate less to sites beyond Google if an AI Overview can give them a good enough answer, even if the bot cites the sites that feed it. Clicks, also known as traffic, are often the most significant way a website earns money from advertising. Large US media companiesare suingGoogle, alleging that AI summaries have redirected and reduced traffic to their sites, cutting into their revenue.Google said it had not seen a decline in aggregate traffic and that such accusations are based on “flawed methodologies”. Reid, the company’s vice-president of search, wrote last year: “Total organic click volume from Google Search to websites has been relatively stable year-over-year.”We want to hear from you. title: Taiwan charges nine people for smuggling ‘high-end’ AI servers to China | Technology | The Guardian
description: Among those charged are two Super Micro employees and one from Nvidia, marking another flashpoint in US-China AI rivalry
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Among those charged are two Super Micro employees and one from Nvidia, marking another flashpoint in US-China AI rivalry
Content: An Nvidia H100 graphics processor chip at the company's headquarters in Santa Clara, California.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn Nvidia H100 graphics processor chip at the company's headquarters in Santa Clara, California.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesTechnologyTaiwan charges nine people for smuggling ‘high-end’ AI servers to ChinaAmong those charged are two Super Micro employees and one from Nvidia, marking another flashpoint in US-China AI rivalryAssociated PressTue 25 Aug 2026 15.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTaiwanese prosecutors charged nine people Monday, including one fromNvidiaand two from Super Micro, for illegally exporting “high-end AI servers” to mainland China, adding another wave of turbulence in the AI ​​rivalry between China and the United States.Prosecutors said the servers involved were graphics processing units known as “B300,” which have been banned from sale toChina.Seventy-four servers arrived in China successfully, according to the prosecutors. Of those, 50 were sent through Indonesia, 16 delivered directly to China and eight sent to Japan first, then Hong Kong, before they landed in mainland China.Trump-backed Ken Paxton unveils ‘Texas first’ datacenter plan aimed at ‘negative impact’Read moreAnother attempt involving 56 servers failed, and the servers remain in Taiwan, said the prosecutor’s office.AI infrastructure, including advanced semiconductors mostly made in Taiwan, has become a key point of competition between the US and China. Washington began imposing restrictions on Nvidia’s exports of advanced chips to China in 2022 and tightened them in subsequent years. In April 2025, the US required licenses for exports of Nvidia’s H20 chips to China before allowing some sales to resume later that year.Under export controls, any sale by Nvidia of high-end AI servers – the computer infrastructure that houses the chips needed to power AI systems – requires a strict review process, according to a document from Keelung District prosecutors’ office in Taiwan. The document also said purchases of more than eight high-end AI servers require company staff to conduct on-site checks to the clients.“We will work with the Taiwan authorities to help them resolve the allegations as quickly as possible,” Patrick Rutherford, an Nvidia spokesperson, said in a written statement.Super Micro said in a written statement that the arrests of two of its former employees were due to its cooperation with the Taiwanese authorities and the company will continue to work to “enhance its robust export compliance program to protect American innovation”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionProsecutors are seeking the maximum five-year sentences for four of the nine defendants, including Chang, an Nvidia manager identified just by his family name. Chang was the “key figure” responsible for “authorizing the release of the B300 GPUs” in this case but “demonstrated a clearly poor attitude following the offense”, the document said.Some of the defendants set up a company in Japan, which helped successfully transfer eight of the servers, prosecutors said. Some allegedly created fake websites and falsified information to evade export restrictions.Explore more on these topicsTechnologyAI (artificial intelligence)NvidiaChinaAsia PacificComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump-backed Ken Paxton unveils ‘Texas first’ datacenter plan aimed at ‘negative impact’  | Texas | The Guardian
description: The Republican Senate candidate announced the plan with a graphic flagged as ‘Made with AI’
Author: David Smith
Headline: The Republican Senate candidate announced the plan with a graphic flagged as ‘Made with AI’
Content: Ken Paxton speaks to reporters in San Antonio, Texas, on 8 August 2026.Photograph: Bob Daemmrich/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenKen Paxton speaks to reporters in San Antonio, Texas, on 8 August 2026.Photograph: Bob Daemmrich/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockTexasTrump-backed Ken Paxton unveils ‘Texas first’ datacenter plan aimed at ‘negative impact’The Republican Senate candidate announced the plan with a graphic flagged as ‘Made with AI’US politics live – latest updatesDavid Smithin WashingtonTue 25 Aug 2026 13.54 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 15.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKen Paxton, a Republican candidate for the US Senate in Texas, has unveiled plans to tackle the “negative impact” ofdatacentersamid a growing backlash across the political spectrum.Paxton, endorsed byDonald Trumpbut facing a close contest against Democrat James Talarico, posted a “Texas first” datacenter plan on X with a graphic thatthe social media network flaggedas “Made with AI”.Republicans have been struggling to keep up with a shift in public opinion fueled by concerns that power- and water-hungry datacenters will push up energy costs and harm the environment. Some fear the issue could prove costly in November’s US midterm elections.Hakeem Jeffries defends his meeting with Trump envoy Jared KushnerRead moreAn Annenberg Public Policy Centersurveylast month found that 61% of Americans now oppose the building of a new datacenter in their area, an increase from 49% in March. This includes 69% of Democrats, 54% of Republicans and 53% of independents.Last yearGreg Abbott, the governor of Texas, dubbed his state the “epicenter of AI development”, but on Sunday he told ABC’s This Week program that tech companies “basically dug their own grave for the problem that’s been caused for them and that’s why they got the backlash they deserve”.On Monday his ally Paxton, currently the state attorney general inTexas, outlined a four-point plan that includes banning Chinese technology to power US datacenters, holding companies criminally liable if AI chatbots undermine children’s safety and cutting red tape to ensure datacenters do not raise Texans’ electricity bills.He also pledged to support Abbott’s state plan to ban new datacenters from rural neighborhoods, repeal sales tax exemptions and ensure they are adding to Texas’s electricity capacity rather than taking from it.Paxton said in a statement: “Texans deserve a fighter to lead and represent them as we address the growing presence of datacenters in Texas and stop their negative impact on our neighborhoods.“This plan will ensure that happens while putting Texas first, protecting our culture and land, and safeguarding our families and communities. My plan will also work to ensure that datacenters are not utilized to power Al platforms that endanger our children.”The move signals an effort by Paxton, a rightwing populist who defeated the incumbent US senator John Cornyn ina Republican primary runoff, to blunt attacks on what could be a potential electoral issue. His rival Talaricohas urged tighter regulationson datacenter development and an end to sweetheart tax deals for big tech companies.Talarico accused Paxton of trying to erase his history giving datacenter tax handouts. He said in a statement: “Ken Paxton has taken nearly half a million dollars from the datacenter industry, voted to flood Texas with datacenters by giving them billions in tax handouts, and has refused to use his power as attorney general to respond to Texans’ requests to block datacenter development in their communities.“Now he’s scared his ties to big datacenter companies will lose him the election, so he’s making a sad attempt to reverse course by releasing a plan he literally used AI to make.”The race is tight in what is traditionally a Republican stronghold. A Fox News poll in late July showed Talarico leading 51% to 48%. The Cook Political Reportdescribes the election as a toss-up.Paxton is struggling to overcome a series of political scandals. He was impeached in 2023 after being accused of corruption andlater acquitted in a trial in the Texas senate. He was also indicted on charges of felony securities fraud but the case was dismissed after a 2024 pretrial diversion agreement. Last year his wife of 38 years, Angela Paxton, filed for divorce “on biblical grounds”, citing adultery.Politicians are scrambling to adjust to the backlash against AI datacenters, which consume huge quantities of electricity and water, threaten to alter the landscape of local communities, and create relatively few jobs.Josh Shapiro, the Democratic governor of Pennsylvania, last yearchampioneda $20bn investment by Amazon but last weeksigned an executive orderhe said imposes the “strictest guardrails in the nation”. Bernie Sanders, an independent senator for Vermont,has urgedbig tech leaders to pause AI development.The Axios websitereportedthat the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned leading AI companies that voter discontent with the centers is endangering the party’s chances of defending a Senate seat in Ohio.Trump, however, remains supportive of the industry. Hetold Punchbowl Newsrecently: “I saw Texas the other day sort of is against datacenters. I think it’s a mistake. And I’m not taking positions, I just think it’s a mistake, because there are other communities that want it. When a community wants it, it means a lot of money is going to come into that community.”Explore more on these topicsTexasKen PaxtonDatacenters – USRepublicansUS SenateUS CongressUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Australia may face a rush of datacentre construction as AI firms look to avoid upcoming rules, experts say | Australian politics | The Guardian
description: Regulations will require new sites to avoid pushing up power prices by building renewable energy plants and minimising water use
Author: Josh Taylor
Headline: Regulations will require new sites to avoid pushing up power prices by building renewable energy plants and minimising water use
Content: Anthony Albanese at a national cabinet meeting in Perth.Photograph: Matt Jelonek/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAnthony Albanese at a national cabinet meeting in Perth.Photograph: Matt Jelonek/Getty ImagesAustralian politicsAustralia may face a rush of datacentre construction as AI firms look to avoid upcoming rules, experts sayRegulations will require new sites to avoid pushing up power prices by building renewable energy plants and minimising water useFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJosh TaylorTechnology reporterTue 25 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 22.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePlanned datacentres around Australia may avoid strict new rules being proposed by Anthony Albanese if they can secure approvals in the coming months, amid growing calls for a moratorium.The prime minister is aiming to come to an agreement with national cabinet onfederal regulations for datacentresat a meeting on Wednesday.The rules will require datacentres to avoid pushing up power prices – including by bringing renewable energy to the grid to cover their electricity demands – while meeting their own connection costs and minimising water use.Developers will also need to ensure their datacentres are appropriately sized and located away from schools, homes, potential housing or agricultural locations.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailHowever, the rules will not be retrospective. This means any project that has been approved before the legislation passes next year will only be subject to existing state or territory laws.The AustralianEnergyMarket Operator (Aemo) reported on Tuesday there were 225 datacentres in development, and electricity demand from them was expected to grow from 5 to 34 terawatt hours by 2036.There is uncertainty over the number of projects that will ultimately go ahead. More than 40% of datacentre projects since Aemo’s 2025 report either dropped off the list or regressed in status.But some of the projects currently in the pipeline could receive approval before the new rules apply.Datacentres in AustraliaThe New South Wales government isnow considering a 90MW datacentreabout 9km from Sydney’s CBD. Named Project Mars, the three-storey centre will cover 22,000sqm near Lane Cove River under current plans.Goodman Group, the company behind the project, is consulting with the community about the proposal, amid strong local pushback in an area where five datacentres are already approved or being proposed.The project’s website states it will use existing power, and 3.5ML a day of water from Sydney Water should it go ahead. There will be 200kW-worth of solar panels on the building, but the company has limited information on more renewables to offset its power demands, stating it is “exploring opportunities to source additional renewable generation to support its proposed datacentre rollout in Australia.”Sasha Titchkosky, a representative of Lane Cove Responsible Planning group, said developers should consider the potential damage to their brand should they proceed with datacentre projects under the old rules. But she said governments should enact a moratorium on approvals until the new rules are in place.“At the very least, a moratorium on approvals in established residential areas … [it] seems to me that would be the responsible thing for governments to do,” Titchkosky said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I don’t think it’s an unreasonable ask, to actually have the government doing what they should be doing to protect the citizens.”Goodman Group was approached for comment.Prof Crystal Legacy, an urban planning researcher at the University of Melbourne, said developers would probably want to get in “before the new regulatory levers come into play.” She warned that state governments, which may try to fast-track applications before new rules come into effect, would do so “at your political peril.”“People are now noticing, and there’s always going to be a political backlash,” Legacy said.“We call people Nimbys, but I think that’s an unfair characterisation for people who are just concerned about the environmental impacts, as well as the amenity impacts of these massive datacentres.”The Greens have previously called for a moratorium on approvals until the new rules are in place.While Albanese works to get the states and territories to sign off on his proposed changes, the community pressure is likely to continue, with a federal inquiry into datacentres currently accepting submissions, along with state inquiries in NSW and Tasmania.Explore more on these topicsAustralian politicsDatacentres - AustraliaAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingEnergynewsShareReuse this content

title: Two planned datacentres will have higher UK carbon emissions than ExxonMobil, analysis finds | Datacentres - UK | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Buckinghamshire and Bedfordshire sites predicted to emit 4.5m tonnes a year when fully running
Author: Pippa Neill
Headline: Exclusive: Buckinghamshire and Bedfordshire sites predicted to emit 4.5m tonnes a year when fully running
Content: Aerial view of the construction site for the proposed datacentre at Wapseys Wood in Buckinghamshire.Photograph: sdcm40campusView image in fullscreenAerial view of the construction site for the proposed datacentre at Wapseys Wood in Buckinghamshire.Photograph: sdcm40campusDatacentres - UKTwo planned datacentres will have higher UK carbon emissions than ExxonMobil, analysis findsExclusive: Buckinghamshire and Bedfordshire sites predicted to emit 4.5m tonnes a year when fully runningPippa NeillEnvironment reporterTue 25 Aug 2026 07.04 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe carbon emissions from just two planned datacentres in England will exceed all of the fossil fuel company ExxonMobil’s UK emissions, analysis has revealed.Experts have said this demonstrates the “serious threat” datacentres pose to the UK’s legally binding climate goals.Analysis by the non-profit group Foxglove reveals that when fully operational, the Wapseys Wood datacentre inBuckinghamshireand the Quest Park datacentre in Bedfordshire will use 1.3GW of power and will produce more than 4.5m tonnes of carbon emissions.ExxonMobil emitted3.9m tonnesin 2023, according to the global energy thinktank Ember.AI datacentres use a massive amount of electricity to power servers and cooling equipment, and to run facility systems. There are currently 315 datacentres in the queue to connect to the UK’s electricity grid, representing 73GW of demand. This is almost double the peak winter energy demand for the entire UK.Because of the long wait to connect to the grid, the Wapseys Wood and Quest Park datacentres are seeking to build their own on-site gas-fired power stations.Based on governmentfigureson the carbon intensity of electricity generation, Foxglove has calculated these projects will produce 4.577m tonnes of carbon emissions per year.A government spokesperson said these figures were “misleading” because of the assumption that both projects will run at 100% utilisation from day one, which they said was “not accurate”.Tom Hegarty, head of communications at Foxglove, said assuming a 100% utilisation rate followed standard industry practice.Kierra Box, a trade and environmental regulation campaigner at Friends of the Earth, said the aim was for datacentres to increase load and run at full capacity, and so it was “valid to look at those top level predictions”.The formerEnglandand Wales Green party leader Caroline Lucas described the projected emissions from these projects as “absolutely horrifying”, and said it should be ringing alarm bells right across government.The government says its own analysis shows there are multiple pathways for this rapid datacentre rollout to fit within theseventh carbon budget, which sets out how the government will reach its international climate targets.However there remains ahigh level of uncertaintyover how this will work.Toby Perkins, a Labour MP and chair of the Commons environmental audit committee, which is leading an inquiry into the environmental impact of datacentres, said this analysis was a “potent reminder that without the right measures in place, data centres could represent a serious threat to the environment and to our legally binding climate goals”.Oliver Hayes, head of policy at the campaign group Global Action Plan, said the two projects were “catastrophic for our carbon budgets”. He said the only way the rapid rollout of datacentres could fit within these budgets was if other elements of the economy were given much stricter carbon budgets.Sam Hunter-Jones, a ClientEarth lawyer, said every megawatt powering a datacentre connected to the grid was a megawatt that could not be used to replace fossil fuels elsewhere. “The reality is that unchecked datacentre growth is making the transition away from fossil fuels harder, not easier,” he said.The datacentres are two of the first to be fast-tracked through the government’s nationally significant infrastructure project (NSIP) regime. This regime allows developers to rapidly deliver infrastructure projects by bypassing local planning authorities with decisions instead handled by central government.Hayes said it was a “very worrying sign” that the government had allowed two gas-fired datacentres to apply into the NSIP regime. “I think that sends an extremely bad signal and demonstrates that they are not serious about addressing the emissions associated with datacentres,” he said, describing it as an “affront to local people”.Lucas also raised concerns about the projects being fast-tracked, and said it “insulates” them from local scrutiny.“In order to be able to make sensible decisions on which projects should go ahead and where they should be, we need to have more information in the public domain. We need to have more scrutiny, not less, and yet things like the NSIP regime are moving things in the opposite direction,” she said.A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: “Datacentres are a vital part of our economy and our everyday lives, helping us interact with the services we need, while driving growth and renewal for communities. We will enable the development and growth of new industries, such as datacentres, by building unprecedented amounts of clean power.”Wapseys Wood declined to comment. Quest Park did not respond to a request for comment.Explore more on these topicsDatacentres - UKGreenhouse gas emissionsAI (artificial intelligence)ExxonMobilClimate crisisComputingFossil fuelsnewsShareReuse this content
