title: A Pocket Full of Slagford – a retro-futurist take on Thatcher-era northern England | Games | The Guardian
description: Developer Patrick Grant was born in Australia and lives in New Zealand, but a childhood of British TV inspired him to set a comedy game in a bleak vision of the north
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Developer Patrick Grant was born in Australia and lives in New Zealand, but a childhood of British TV inspired him to set a comedy game in a bleak vision of the north
Content: Inspired by northern English culture … A Pocket Full of Slagford.Photograph: SlumpsView image in fullscreenInspired by northern English culture … A Pocket Full of Slagford.Photograph: SlumpsSummer games previewsGamesA Pocket Full of Slagford – a retro-futurist take on Thatcher-era northern EnglandDeveloper Patrick Grant was born in Australia and lives in New Zealand, but a childhood of British TV inspired him to set a comedy game in a bleak vision of the northElliot GardnerTue 25 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 19.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSomething is amiss in the dingy town of Slagford, and curious scamp Pip Bunting is the only one who can find out what. So quit your mithering, it’s time to discover just how grim it truly is up north.A Pocket Full of Slagford is an upcoming retro-styled 3D puzzle adventure game set in a surreal alternative-reality near-future northern England that never escaped the clutches of Thatcherism. The story follows the misadventures of a young local lad from the eponymous Slagford after he takes ownership of a mysterious relic that lets him wreak havoc on reality.It’s the passion project of Australia-born, New Zealand-based artist Patrick Grant, who formed solo-developer studio Slumps to create a game inspired by the point-and-click classics from the late 80s and early 90s, such asLucasArts’ catalogueandGrim Fandango.View image in fullscreenReminiscent of point-and-click adventures of the past … A Pocket Full of Slagford.Photograph: Slumps“They’re just a great format for narrative-heavy games, like an interactive story,” says Grant. “I like designing puzzles as well, so I always wanted to make a point-and-click. But from playing a lot, I know how samey they can be. From the start I was thinking about what I could do differently.”The result of Grant’s prototyping is what he describes as a “jigsaw sticker book kind of thing.” As you navigate the nasty industrial hellscape, you collect imprints of the game’s scenery. If, along the way, you spot a place where these imprints align, you can paste them into the world to solve puzzles. Grant is also committed to evoking the oft-forgotten CD-Rom era of the late ’90s, complete with looping CG-rendered backgrounds and janky 3D models with far too many sharp edges.Yet he’s keen to emphasise that his main focus is the narrative. While the trailer andSteam store pagefeature a fair few Yorkshire-isms, A Pocket Full of Slagford’s story and dialogue take inspiration from various aspects of northern English culture, despite Grant admitting to having never actually spent any real time in the area.“In the colonies we get a lot of BBC English programming,” he explains. “So when I was growing up there was so much British telly that I’d be watching. There’s this BBC miniseries from the 80s calledBoys from the Blackstuff, about this group of scousers getting up to mischief, set in the Thatcher years, just trying to make ends meet. It’s incredibly well written – this mix of sad and funny – against that whole big economic collapse. I got interested in that, reading about the Thatcher years.”That interest is what inspired A Pocket Full of Slagford’s bleak setting. While Grant says he wasn’t trying to make a political point when he went into the project, he’s not shying away from the issues of the time: “Because of that working-class setting, you end up naturally touching on points like the wealth disparity, which I show in the game, and the class conflict. Specifically, from watching stuff like Boys from the Blackstuff, or Billy Elliot, I was interested in the infighting that goes on within these classes.”Despite touching on these themes, Grant stresses that he’s going for a comedic, surrealist angle. As he puts it: “I was like, what if I set it in the future and, instead of coal, they’re mining shit out of the ground?” He may not be trying to make a political statement about Thatcherism, but some might say he has hit on an apt analogy.A Pocket Full of Slagford is in development forPC, with no confirmed release dateExplore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsPCfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Meta goes on trial as Silicon Valley faces a growing backlash | Technology | The Guardian
description: Also: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman expressed his surprising sympathy over the construction of datacenters across the country
Author: Blake Montgomery
Headline: Also: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman expressed his surprising sympathy over the construction of datacenters across the country
Content: Meta went on trial last week for allegedly designing platforms that are addictive for children.Photograph: Vicki Behringer/ReutersView image in fullscreenMeta went on trial last week for allegedly designing platforms that are addictive for children.Photograph: Vicki Behringer/ReutersTechScape newsletterTechnologyMeta goes on trial as Silicon Valley faces a growing backlashAlso: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman expressed his surprising sympathy over the construction of datacenters across the countryBlake MontgomeryTue 25 Aug 2026 07.21 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 08.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m Blake Montgomery, US tech editor at the Guardian, writing to you from a sunny park in New York City, which was supposed to endure rain all weekend but in fact delivered the best weather of the year.Why Meta’s big American backlash happened in courtA blockbuster case against Meta went to trial a week ago in Oakland, California, just north of the US tech company’s headquarters inSilicon Valley. California and 28 other US states are suing the £1tn ($1.36tn) company for allegedly designing products that are addictive for children, and hiding that information from the public.The courtroom has already seen minor fireworks. On the witness stand, a whistleblower who worked extensively withMark Zuckerbergaccused the CEO of lying to the public about his commitment to child safety. The prosecutor who opened the case framed her argument around four words that start with the letter H: Meta “hooks” in users, “holds” them on its platforms for as long as possible, “harvests” their data and then “hides” the truth from the public. She contended that this business model “worked especially well for kids”. More pyrotechnics are expected. Zuckerberg himself is expected to face tough questions on the stand, as is the CEO of Instagram.Meta has denied all allegations. Liza Crenshaw, a spokesperson for the company, said: “Rather than sticking to the facts or the law, the states have instead decided to chase an outlandish payout.”The trial presents a major challenge for Meta, not in the least, because in the United States, it’s proceedings like these that regulate the tech industry.China regulates tech by crackdown; the UK and Europe regulate the industry with legislation – Brussels’ prescriptive stipulations have become global defaults. But in the US, it’s mostly the courts that set the boundaries. They move much faster and with the vindictive authority that Americans often crave in response to harms. The slow wheels of democratic debate and bill drafting feel ill-suited to respond to Zuckerberg’s mantra of “move fast and break things”.Read more:Hook, hold, harvest and hide: Meta’s alleged strategy laid out in first week of landmark trialMeanwhile, US regulators have famously, obviously, andavowedlyhad difficulty keeping pace with the innovations that arise from Silicon Valley. As one Republican representative told a quantum computing expert during a 2018 hearing on Capitol Hill: “I can understand about 50% of the things you say.” Members of Congress would undoubtedly say the same about AI today.“Courts have the ability to force these changes much quicker than legislation. Courts have this authority to say, ‘Look, you either comply with these orders … or you stop doing business in our state’. States have the ability to enforce that. I think for these companies this is a real point of reckoning,” said Laura Marquez-Garrett, an attorney with the Social Media Victims Law Center, which is representing individual plaintiffs suing Meta and other social media companies in thousands of cases inCalifornia. Her organization was deeply involved in Meta’s first loss of a social media addiction trial in March in Los Angeles.Will this trial bring Meta’s moment of accountability? Maybe.Other tech companies have faced significant government lawsuits in recent years, and come away only stronger. Google faced perhaps the most significant antitrust litigation of the 2020s, losing its antitrust case against the US Department of Justice last year. The penalty was not divesting the Chrome browser but a “slap on the wrist”, critics said.But in the 1990s, a coalition of US states sued tobacco companies and secured a settlement that banned a laundry list of marketing tactics, including advertising on transit or anywhere outdoors, paid product placement for cigarettes, cartoon mascots, branded apparel and nearly all free distribution of cigarettes. You’d never see a tobacco company’s name on a US sports stadium today.Like those tobacco suits, the states’ suit against Meta may force the company to operate its social networks in less harmful ways and to keep them out of the hands of children. The states are explicitly asking the court that Meta be forced to change the design of its products to make them safer for children.“These AGs have a real chance at fixing the product,” said Marquez-Garrett.Read more:‘I always considered social media evil’: big tobacco whistleblower on tech’s addictive productsOpenAI makes safety moves‘We are hitting a different chapter’: OpenAI leader warns of threat of ‘persistent’ AI cyber-attacksOpenAI announces slowing pace of development after hack by rogue agentOpenAI launches ChatGPT for Teens with stronger safeguardsThe week the US data center backlash reached a fever pitchView image in fullscreenThe Pennhurst Asylum seasonal haunted house in Spring City, Pennsylvania, US.Photograph: Matthew Hatcher/Bloomerberg via Getty ImagesThe political champions of datacenters in the US are turn coatings to detractors. It’s knives out in the US datacenter backlash.Democrats who fast-tracked the development of these gargantuan fortresses of AI are now implementing restrictions on them. Republicans who trumpeted calls for their unrestricted construction are hastily rolling out plans to constrain them.Josh Shapiro, Democratic governor of Pennsylvania, rolled out restrictions for large datacenters last week. Just two months ago,the Guardianreported on how he was fast-tracking them and cutting red tape. Greg Abbott, Republican governor of Texas, said this weekend that the datacenter industry has “dug its own grave”. In November 2025, he called his state the “epicenter of AI development”. A Republican running for a contested Senate seat in Texas, Ken Paxton, debuted an anti-AI action plan over the weekend, though it was marked as “made with AI” on X.Read more:How the fight over US datacenters is scrambling this state’s politics: ‘We don’t want it’skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt’s no wonder: more than 70% of Americans oppose the construction of datacenters in their cities, per a poll released byGallupthree months ago. In just one year, the percentage of respondents saying they “strongly oppose” a datacenter being built near their homes more than doubled, according to polling by the climate news group Heatmap.Conservative media in the US has likewise taken notice.Fox Newson Thursday: “Silicon Valley is losing the datacenter fight, risking a repeat of a classic failure.”The Daily Wire, often a bellwether for young Republicans’ opinions, on Monday: “Silicon Valley created the datacenter backlash.”Donald Trump, always liable to turn on an ally and usually an extremely adept reader of political winds, is standing by the tech industry’s multitrillion-dollar infrastructure buildout.“Communities that don’t take a datacenter, they’re making a mistake,” the US president said in an interview with his former fixer and once-mortal nemesis Michael Cohen last week.Silicon Valley is extremely worried. The tech industry is all-in on AI, so much so that the entire US economy is as well, and the success of AI is predicated on access to enough computing power. No datacenters, no chips, no computing power, no AI, no profit, no economy.What to do when faced with a spiraling political threat?Some companies are playing nice. They’responsoringcommunity celebrations or pledging major community investments. They’re hosting listening sessions and making promises about how many jobs their projects will guarantee. Running de facto political campaigns for infrastructure projects is a big change for an industry accustomed to moving at the speed of bytes.Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, expressed some surprising empathy on apodcastlast month. His company has a range of partnerships across the US for hundreds of billions of dollars’ worth of datacenter construction.“I understand emotionally why people don’t want datacenters in their back yard in the same way that I don’t really want a nuclear power plant next to my house, even though I know it’s a super safe thing,” he said.Other Silicon Valley insiders are feeling hostile. Garry Tan, CEO of the influential startup incubator Y Combinator,wrote on Xthis weekend, “Reminder: the datacenter discourse is a documented psyop and they’re winning.” Alexis Ohanian, tech investor and co-founder of Reddit, wrote of the discourse: “It’s been brilliantly executed ngl [not gonna lie]. Facts are not gonna win this, esp at this point, it’s gotta be on emotional appeal.”In July, entrepreneur and Shark Tank host Kevin O’Leary accused opponents of his planned Utah datacenter of acting on behalf of the Chinese government. He later said he had “no evidence” for the claim and apologized for it, as did Fox News’ own hosts.The US’ adversaries have taken note of the heated debate and fanned the flames of fury. OpenAIdisclosedin early July that Chinese and Russian propagandists, including state-owned media, had used its tools to create materials circulated on X, including a cartoon tycoon holding bags of cash and smoking a cigar, encouraging pushback against datacenters.Reworked: A Guardian series about AI and the future of work‘Digging the grave of my profession’: the Hollywood creatives training AI to do their jobsWill AI give you the job? Automated hiring tools spark discrimination and secrecy lawsuitsThe wider TechScapeAfter more than 15 years of laptops in the classroom, do Australian schools need a rethink?Crypto bank part-owned by Trump family offers depositors way to ‘gain favor’ with White House, experts sayDid someone wearing Meta Glasses film you today? Are you sure?Explore more on these topicsTechnologyTechScape newsletterMetaOpenAICaliforniaDatacenters – USWest CoastSocial medianewslettersShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Trump’s economic threats: bullies can overplay their hand | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Tariffs on Canada, threats against Iran’s partners and bond market intervention show a president weaponising US power while making Americans poorer at home
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Tariffs on Canada, threats against Iran’s partners and bond market intervention show a president weaponising US power while making Americans poorer at home
Content: ‘The US president is willing to use state power to lower borrowing costs while hiking others through tariffs, war and cuts to social programmes.’Photograph: Will Oliver/UPI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘The US president is willing to use state power to lower borrowing costs while hiking others through tariffs, war and cuts to social programmes.’Photograph: Will Oliver/UPI/ShutterstockOpinionDonald TrumpThe Guardian view on Trump’s economic threats: bullies can overplay their handEditorialTariffs on Canada, threats against Iran’s partners and bond market intervention show a president weaponising US power while making Americans poorer at homeTue 25 Aug 2026 13.27 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 19.10 EDTShareThree moves in the last week have exposed the limits of Donald Trump’s economicbullying. The US slapped 50% tariffs on another$20bnof Canadian goods – then threatened the same rate on thecars, trucks, parts and steelthat America Inc depends on. On Monday, the Treasury secretary,Scott Bessent,menaced Iran’s trading partners with exclusion from the US financial network, hoping that coercion can deliver what months of war have not. And as the costs of war, tariffs andpro-billionairetax cuts helped send US bond yields higher, the Treasurysteppedin to tame long-term rates. These are not contradictory policies but a gamble: that US economic power can be repeatedly weaponised without reducing others’ willingness to depend on it.The Trump administration’s “D-day” sanctions are potentially the most consequential because they expose the scaffolding of American financial power. While markets shrugged off the immediatethreat, that calculation might change were the US to target a major Chineserefineryor bank. Such an escalation could spark a trade war with Beijing. The US has leverage. But China has pressure points –especially farmers in Republican states– that make using it costly. In the long run, there is a price to pay. Nations hold one another’s currencies partly because they trust the political relationship. Mr Trump is testing what happens when they don’t.View image in fullscreenScott Bessent.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersThe moves to control thebond marketare the most revealing. There is nothing new about Washington managing yields: the Federal Reserve has long been able to buytreasuries. What is new is Mr Bessent doing it so openly to deal with the fallout from failed policies. Mr Trump owns this: his tariffs raise input costs; his Iran war pushed up energy costs; his nonchalance aboutrising American grocery pricesreassures no one. When that mixture helps produce higher inflation expectations and rising long-end bond yields, Mr Trump’s team steps in to prevent interest rates ticking up.The US president is willing to usestate powerto lower borrowing costs while hiking others through tariffs, war and cuts to social programmes. Mr Bessent wants to stop rising long yields feeding into investment and Washington’s debt-interest bill. That hisformer mentorat George Soros’s hedge fund criticises him and wants bond markets to force spending cuts is not to be applauded. The better question for Mr Bessent is: why shield markets from the consequences of Mr Trump’s acts, but not households?The trade war with Canada is economically stupid andlegally dubious. In 2025, the Trump tariffsamountedto an average tax increase of $1,000 per US household. More than a quarter ofCanadian exportsto the US are now subject to significant tariffs orthreatenedwith tougher ones. Ottawa’s retaliation will start in September. North American production has been organised around such trade flows and tariffs will make US manufacturing more expensive, not less.Why Canada? Washington has largely given up trying to change China’seconomic model. Canada is seen as a soft target. The Guardian columnist Robert Reich issurelyright: Mr Trump picks on a friendly neighbour because that is what bullies do. This cannot go on. American economic power depends on other countries wanting to remain in a system the US dominates. Mr Trump thinks their dependence is his weapon. The more often he uses it against them, the harder theyshouldlook for the exit.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionTariffsCanadaUS economyMark CarneyUS politicsTrump administrationeditorialsShareReuse this content

title: Sex sells and wins votes – and the Democrats know it | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: Wonder why they’re posting flirty photos and wearing tight T-shirts? It’s a thirst trap strategy in motion, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: Wonder why they’re posting flirty photos and wearing tight T-shirts? It’s a thirst trap strategy in motion, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Content: A call to arms … Democratic Michigan senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed shows off his muscly physique.Photograph: Scott Olson/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA call to arms … Democratic Michigan senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed shows off his muscly physique.Photograph: Scott Olson/Getty ImagesOpinionUS politicsSex sells and wins votes – and the Democrats know itArwa MahdawiWonder why they’re posting flirty photos and wearing tight T-shirts? It’s a thirst trap strategy in motionTue 25 Aug 2026 10.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 14.03 EDTShareDespite being a card-carrying member of the International Order of Confirmed Homosexuals, I have spent quite a lot of time lately thinking aboutAbdul El-Sayed’sbiceps. I mean, have you seen them? The progressive Michigan senate nominee is jacked and he knows it. He almost always wears a tight black T-shirt to show off his muscles and incorporates a lot offitness contentin his campaign.I’m not the only one who has noticed El-Sayed’s prominent muscles. They have had a lot of coverage, and are seen as part of a wider attempt to rebrand the Democratic party. Which, I don’t need to tell you, has aserious imageproblem; a poll in March found that the party is looked on even less favourably than the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency. So, to make it look less like a party that is full of out-of-touch technocrats who sound as if they are reading from a 500-page PowerPoint presentation every time they try to explain anything, Democrats seem to be trying to up the sex appeal.“Democrats enter their thirst trap era,” News websiteAxios recently declared, summing up the phenomenon. The piece observed that the Democrats’ main TikTok page has given “the thirst trap treatment” to big names including El-Sayed, Zohran Mamdani and senator Jon Ossoff (“nicknamed‘Senator My Boo’ by internet fans”), by posting flirty photos and videos. Axios quotes a political analyst who explains that while female Democrats such as Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have had their share of screen time, the Dems’ TikTok page has made a “very intentional choice to feature the most attractive male members”.Fox News would appear toreluctantly agreewith the assessment that Democrats are leaning into good looks to win the midterms. “El-Sayed is out in these tight T-shirts,” Fox News host Ainsley Earhardt said in a discussion last week. “AOC with her pretty smile. She’s beautiful. She’s got the red lipstick. You have Mamdani, always smiling … It doesn’t make their philosophy any less dangerous, right?… even with a tight T-shirt, it’s still socialism and it fails.”Over on CNN there was a little more jubilation about the Democrats’ vibe shift. “Dems are hot again,” strategist Yemisi Egbewoleproclaimed. “They’re coming out of the closet as hot people and I’m so excited.” Egbewole added that it wasn’t just about physical attractiveness: “I think they’re learning from Trump. Entertainment really sells.”Sex sells too: it’s well established that votersaround the worldprefer good-looking candidates. But, while we may all be shallow deep down, some of us are shallower than others. A 2016studyfound that rightwing politicians in Europe, the US and Australia tended to be more attractive than their progressive counterparts. That’s partly because “low-information” conservative voters are particularly prone to choosing attractive candidates. “In low-information city elections, a beauty increase of one standard deviation attracts about 20% more votes for the average candidate on the right and about 8% more votes for the average candidate on the left,” an analysis of the study bythe Washington Post noted. Which raises the question: if looks really are so important to low-information rightwing voters, how did we end up with Donald Trump as president? (Woke 1.0 is over, haven’t you heard? It’s OK to say things like this now.)Social media may have brought a new visual element to politics, but the most famous anecdote about how looks can sway an election is almost 70 years old. In September 1960,70 million Americans watched Richard Nixon debate John F Kennedyin the first nationally televised debate between presidential candidates. Nixon had been the favourite going in but he had just been in hospital for a couple of weeks and looked terrible. JFK, on the other hand, was tanned and rested and had good stage makeup.You canquibblewith the conventional wisdom that Nixon lost that election on looks, but it certainly played a part. In hismemoir, Nixon wrote: “What hurt me the most in the first debate was not the substance of the encounter between Kennedy and me, but the disadvantageous contrast in our appearances. After the program ended, callers, including my mother, wanted to know if anything was wrong, because I did not look well.”In short: if thirst traps are what it takes to get the US on a better path, then so be it. Jacked candidates in tight T-shirts may seem like a cheap trick, but even Nixon’s mother would agree that it’s a sound political strategy.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsUS politicsOpinionUS midterm elections 2026DemocratsRepublicanscommentShareReuse this content

title: No, AI doesn’t mean the end of mathematics – at least not yet | Bruce Schneier and Kasra Rafi | The Guardian
description: Mathematicians are raising concerns that the technology could kill their profession. But they still have abilities AI doesn’t
Author: Bruce Schneier
Headline: Mathematicians are raising concerns that the technology could kill their profession. But they still have abilities AI doesn’t
Content: ‘Current AIs are very strong at searching and recombining existing ideas, but they are weak at building any deep and sustained new theory.’Photograph: Mlenny/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Current AIs are very strong at searching and recombining existing ideas, but they are weak at building any deep and sustained new theory.’Photograph: Mlenny/Getty ImagesOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)No, AI doesn’t mean the end of mathematics – at least not yetBruce Schneierand Kasra RafiMathematicians are raising concerns that the technology could kill their profession. But they still have abilities AI doesn’tTue 25 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 13.47 EDTShareEarlier this month, about 40 top mathematiciansgatheredat OpenAI’s offices to discuss the future of their profession. The meeting was off-the-record, but ifrecentarticlesbymathematiciansare any guide, it was mostly pretty glum. People fear for their jobs, their careers and the work they love.We think thecontraryviewis more likely, at least in the short-term. AI models are nowhere near as capable as experienced academic mathematicians.This isn’t to say that AIs aren’t producing stunning mathematical results at the level of PhD researchers. In mid-May, OpenAIannouncedthat its frontier AI model disproved the unit distance conjecture, a famous 80-year-old problem in discrete geometry. In July, Anthropic’s published two AI-derivedresultsin academic cryptanalysis. Earlier this month, OpenAIpublished10 new mathematical results from its latest AI model. And AnthropicpublishedClaude’s attempt to prove the century-and-a-half-old Riemann hypothesis.Welcome to the age of extreme job anxiety | Zoe WilliamsRead moreThese results are both a vivid demonstration of the amazing capabilities of frontier AI in 2026 and an illustration of their limitations. In general, these AI-powered advances in mathematics fall into one of two categories. Some are counterexamples to mathematical statements that people had been trying to prove. Others are novel applications of known techniques to existing problems that human experts either did not know or did not think of using.The counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture is the most notable example of the first kind. Once it had been found, checking it was quick and straightforward. The difficult part was finding it among a large number of possibilities. The AI seems to have combined some sort of intuition acquired through machine learning with extensive computational search, in order to find the right example.An example of the second kind is the unit-distance conjecture. It was motivated by an elegant construction, and most mathematicians expected it to be essentially optimal – so they generally tried to prove rather than disprove it. The counterexample brings in ideas from elsewhere in mathematics: algebraic number theory. If an expert with that background deliberately set out to find a counterexample, they would probably have succeeded. But there was no reason for someone with precisely that expertise to focus on this problem. Because of its scope, AIs don’t have those same limitations.These results are relatively low-hanging fruit for AI; none of them required developing an extensive new theory. This does not make the discoveries trivial, or the AI’s achievements less impressive. Choosing the right direction, and recognizing an unexpected connection between subjects, are themselves forms of creativity. They are the same sorts of capabilities that led to AIsplayingthe game of Go at the grandmaster level, or doing Nobel-prize levelchemistryin the area of protein folding.What happens when medical students rely on AI – and never develop their own judgment? | Simar Bajaj and Joseph SakranRead moreWhat we have not yet seen is an AI developing a substantial new conceptual framework in order to solve a mathematical problem. Much of mathematics proceeds by identifying the objects that are truly central to a question and then developing a theory that helps us understand them. Current AIs are very strong at searching and recombining existing ideas, but they are weak at building any deep and sustained new theory.This speaks to a more general limitation of current AI systems. They are creative in the sense that they can recombine existing ideas in novel ways. But they are not creative in others: they have not yet developed conceptually new theories or structures. And while theyhavelarger working memories than humans do, know more about more different things than any particular human does, and can process information faster than humans, can, true novelty is still largely beyond their reach.Of course, that distinction may not survive for very long. Predictions are notoriously hard, especially about the future of AI. None of these mathematical capabilities were explicitly designed for, or palled. They’re all emergent properties of increasingly capable AI models. We are both confident that someday we will see AI models that are capable of the type of creativity required to do novel mathematics. Will that be in a few months, a few years or a few decades? Of course we don’t know, but our guess is sooner rather than later.Bruce Schneier is a security technologist who teaches at the Harvard Kennedy School at Harvard University and University of Toronto’s Munk SchoolKasra Rafi is a professor of mathematics at the University of TorontoExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionMathematicsComputingEmploymentCareersOpenAIAnthropiccommentShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s justice department has found a new way for presidents to avoid accountability | Claire Finkelstein | The Guardian
description: A recent memo claiming executive privilege over communications with private advisers invites corruption
Author: Claire Finkelstein
Headline: A recent memo claiming executive privilege over communications with private advisers invites corruption
Content: ‘Equipping presidents with extensive power to block witnesses in legal proceedings is a dangerous practice.’Photograph: Samuel Corum/PI/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘Equipping presidents with extensive power to block witnesses in legal proceedings is a dangerous practice.’Photograph: Samuel Corum/PI/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockOpinionTrump administrationTrump’s justice department has found a new way for presidents to avoid accountabilityClaire FinkelsteinA recent memo claiming executive privilege over communications with private advisers invites corruptionTue 25 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 14.21 EDTShareArecent office of legal counselmemoon executive privilege maintains that private advisers to a president can avoid responding to a subpoena by asserting the president’s executive privilege. The ability of presidents to shield communications from public view through claims of executive privilege, whether their own or those of a senior adviser, was already apowerful toolfor presidents to avoid accountability. But if courts accept the OLC’s new interpretation of presidential privilege, it will be substantially harder to call witnesses to testify before Congress or in court proceedings regarding possible wrongdoing by the presidents.Equipping presidents with extensive power to block witnesses in legal proceedings is a dangerous practice that invites corruption by presidents and their advisers. Consider the former White House counsel Don McGahn’s 2019refusal to testifyin response to a subpoena by the House judiciary committee in connection with the special counsel Robert Mueller’s investigation into Donald Trump. McGahn didn’t come up with that idea on his own. It was the Trump White House thatsought to bar McGahnfrom testifying through an assertion of a type of executive privilege known as “testimonial immunity.” Ironically, Mueller was investigating whether Trump obstructed justice, among other things, bydemandingthat McGahn fire Mueller himself. Trump’s insistence that McGahn not testify, backed up by a2019 OLC opinion, effectively made the first Trump administration complicit in the very obstruction under investigation.Brett Kavanaugh has become Trump’s chief enabler on the supreme court | Sidney BlumenthalRead moreThe then federal district court judge Ketanji Brown Jackson ended up rejecting the claim of privilege andorderedMcGahn to testify. After the Trump administration appealed and judicial decisions flipped back and forth, the parties finallyreached a settlementpermitting McGahn to testify behind closed doors. But it was too little too late for Congress. The case reminds us that assertions of privilege by presidential advisers are not legally well-established, but such assertions are sufficient to throw sand in the gears of a congressional investigation, even if such assertions are legally highly tenuous.Other presidents have invoked claims of privilege or the closely related idea of immunity regularly, but more often than not they are rejected by courts. Bill Clinton, for example, invoked itnumerous timesunsuccessfully to try to avoid responding to questions from the special prosecutor Kenneth Starr as well as to avoid testifying in a lawsuit brought by Paula Jones. The courtfoundhe had no immunity against a subpoena requiring him to appear at a deposition.Richard Nixon tried toinvoke itto avoid having to turn over the infamous White House tapes to the White House special prosecutor Leon Jaworski, but the supreme courtruledhe had to turn them over anyway. Even Thomas Jefferson and George Washingtontried to invoke itin one form or another. But where courts have ruled, such claims do not usually prevail.OLC’s latest memo goes far beyond even the 2019 memo written to bolster the White House’s block on McGahn. That memo justified testimonial immunity using the claim that senior aides to the president “are an extension of the President and are likewise entitled to absolute immunity from compelled congressional testimony”. But that argument is inapplicable to private persons who consult with the president. While executive privilege and testimonial immunity are not identical, they are sufficiently alike that the rationale for their invocation is the same, and neither should apply to non-governmental advisers.The current memo is also concerning because of its lack of candor about the historical precedent for executive privilege. Consider what the memo says about thesubpoena issued to Thomas Jeffersonin 1807 during the trial of Aaron Burr, when Burr subpoenaed Jefferson to obtain documents to prove his innocence. Jefferson refused to appear and invoked executive privilege. Chief Justice Marshall insisted there “is no exception whatsoever” to an accused’s right to prove his innocence by seeking documents and testimony that would exempt him.Marshalldid acknowledgethe existence of a “privilege to withhold certain official paper[s] that ‘ought not on light ground to be forced into public view’”. But he did not believe the privilege applied.As retired US judges, we’re not used to speaking out. But we cannot be silent | Michael P Donnelly and Robert F OrrRead moreThe memo once again engages problematic legal reasoning when it discusses Nixon’s bid to avoid turning over the tapes.The memo claimsthe Nixon case shows that the court recognized “the privilege of confidentiality of Presidential communications”, which “derive[s] from the supremacy of each branch within its own assigned area of constitutional duties”. And while Nixon certainly asserted such a right, inUS v Nixonthe US supreme court vehementlyrejected that contentionand denied Nixon’s request.Commentators havespeculatedthat one of the likely explanations for the timing of the OLC memo is that the administration is getting ready for the House or Senate to change hands, and that the justice department is looking for a way to block the onslaught of investigations to follow. That the OLC would take an extreme position to further immunize presidents from congressional scrutiny is disturbing but hardly surprising. As withso many memosin recent years, the OLC has abandoned all pretense of interpreting the law impartially. Courts should accord OLC opinions no weight whatsoever in future cases.Misrepresenting legal sources is a violation of the rules of professional conduct for lawyers, as made clear by theModel Rules of Professional Conduct. The quality of OLC argumentation sets a standard for legal practice across the federal government, as well as in the private sector. It is critical for the profession to reject the sort of outcome-oriented analysis the OLC has engaged in here, and federal courts must play a role in ensuring such legal analysis does not become par for the course across the legal profession.Claire Finkelstein, a contributing writer to the Guardian, is the Algernon Biddle professor of law and professor of philosophy at the University of Pennsylvania and the faculty director of its Center for Ethics and the Rule of LawExplore more on these topicsTrump administrationOpinionDonald TrumpLaw (US)US politicsUS supreme courtcommentShareReuse this content

title: I once saw Enes Kanter speak truth to power. Now he only punches down | WNBA | The Guardian
description: Nearly a decade after I watched him defy Erdoğan at great personal cost, Kanter is using his hard-won freedom to turn transgender people into a national punchline
Author: Bryan Armen Graham
Headline: Nearly a decade after I watched him defy Erdoğan at great personal cost, Kanter is using his hard-won freedom to turn transgender people into a national punchline
Content: Ex-NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom and Natasha Cloud of the Chicago Sky yell at one another during the second half of Sunday’s game between the Indiana Fever and Chicago Sky.Photograph: Michael Reaves/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEx-NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom and Natasha Cloud of the Chicago Sky yell at one another during the second half of Sunday’s game between the Indiana Fever and Chicago Sky.Photograph: Michael Reaves/Getty ImagesWNBAI once saw Enes Kanter speak truth to power. Now he only punches downBryan Armen GrahamNearly a decade after I watched him defy Erdoğan at great personal cost, the ex-NBA player is using his hard-won freedom to turn transgender people into a punchlineTue 25 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.53 EDTShareNine years ago, I watched Enes Kanterask America to take him in. It was May 2017, inside the National Basketball Players Association’s offices in midtown Manhattan. Kanter had just returned from a frightening detention at Bucharest airport, where Romanian border police told him Turkey had canceled his passport. He’d just turned 25, an NBA center with a green card and no country he could safely call home.“I’m open for adoption,” he joked from the head of a table in a nondescript conference room, addressing a dozen reporters hastily summoned by his manager. Then he turned serious: “My next move is to just become an American citizen.”The previous 48 hours had unfolded like a John le Carré thriller. Kanter said his manager woke him at 2.30am in Jakarta where he’d been hosting a basketball clinic because Indonesian security forces were looking for him. He hurried to Singapore, then Frankfurt, only to be stopped in Romania. He feared being sent toTurkey, where he had grown up and whose national team he had represented. There, he said, no one might hear from him again. Department of Homeland Security officials and lawyers for the Oklahoma City Thunder and the players’ union helped get him back to the United States.Sitting in that room that Monday morning, I saw someone who had already paid a steep cost for the right to speak truth to power. Kanter calledRecep Tayyip Erdoğanthe “Hitler of our century”. He recounted daily death threats, a family placed in jeopardy by his opposition to Erdoğan and support for the president’s exiled rival, Fethullah Gülen, and parents he had stopped calling because he feared the government was tapping their phones. He said his father, Mehmet, a university professor, had been spat on at a supermarket. “I try to be the voice of those innocent people,” he told us.The reprisals only widened. Turkey issued warrants for Kanter and later sought an Interpol Red Notice and his extradition. He skipped NBA trips abroad, including a Knicks game in London, because he feared detention or assassination. His father was dismissed, detained and charged with membership in a terrorist organization before his eventual acquittal in 2020.In 2021, Kanter finally became an American citizen and legally added Freedom to his name. You didn’t have to squint hard to make out the symbolism. The dissident Turkey tried to render voiceless and stateless had found both an adopted home and a protected platform.On Sunday night, I found myself thinking about the young man from that news conference – and wondering what became of him. Back then, he used attention to protect vulnerable people. Now he uses vulnerable people to attract attention.View image in fullscreenEnes Kanter, seen through a video camera, speaks to reporters in New York on 22 May 2017 after returning to the US following his detention at a Romanian airport.Photograph: Eduardo Muñoz/Getty ImagesKanter was sitting courtside at the Chicago Sky’s game against the Indiana Fever in a shirt reading: “WOMAN noun. adult human female.” He had joined a rally outside the arena in support of Sophie Cunningham, the Fever guard who opposes transgender participation in women’s sports. In recent weeks, Kanter had also declared himself eligible for the 2027 WNBA draft, claiming to identify as a woman and posting workout videos about beginning his “transition”. (League sourceshave since saidhe is not eligible to play and dismissed his declaration as a publicity stunt the WNBA would not “give oxygen” to.)The crudity of the attemptedreductio ad absurdumwas matched only by the breathlessness of the response across the Maga right, where Kanter’s stunt was greeted as an intellectual masterstroke:BRILLIANT,GOT ‘EM,CHECKMATE.Fox News has not merelycovered Kanter’s bit uncritically; it hasplainly participated in the mockery. Take the premise of transgender inclusion, distort it into the spectacle of a former NBA player treating womanhood as a debating prop, and wait for the audience to laugh. Yet Kanter exposed no contradiction. The punchline was simply the existence of transgender people.No player assigned male at birth has ever competed in the WNBA. Whatever legitimate questions exist about eligibility rules, competitive balance and the place of biology in elite sport can be discussed without reducing them to a spectacle designed to humiliate those at the center of the debate. Kanter’s stunt depends on the idea that gender identity is inherently fraudulent and that trans women are simply opportunistic men waiting to invade women’s spaces. It has done nothing to clarify policy. It has merely turned a vulnerable minority into content – including many trans fans who have long regarded the30-year-old leagueas one of the few places in professional sport where they belong. At a moment when ESPN’s WNBA coverage is averaging 1.4 million viewers, up 16% from the same point last season, Kanter’s stunt has hijacked a feelgood story about the league’s growth and made a phantom threat the focus instead.The invasion rhetoric carries a bitter irony. The WNBA is not being overrun by trans women but by straight men who cannot let women have a flourishing league of their own without mocking it, manufacturing controversy and making themselves the story. Some of loudest voices posing as defenders of female athletesopenly ridicule and try to humiliate themfor laughs,in some cases through sexualized stunts. There is something almost pitiable about men squandering their energy and influence on belittling women whose discipline, sacrifice and extraordinary achievement have carried them to the highest level of their profession. Misogyny has simply put on the costume of concern.In Kanter’s case, this was not simply a lone provocateur wandering into an arena. According to Talking Points Memo, the Trump-aligned America First Policy Institute (AFPI)promoted Kanter’s arrival, circulated footage of his ejection and began selling a $45 “Let Freedom Play” sweatshirt featuring him in a mock-up of the WNBA logo. An AFPI executive was seated a few rows behind him, although the organization did not answer questions about whether it bought his courtside seat. Kanter, who attended the 2024 State of the Union as House speaker Mike Johnson’s guest and has said he plans to run for Congress in 2028, has political ambitions of his own.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly for the 2026 WNBA seasonSign up toWNBA 30A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markBack then, he used attention to protect vulnerable people. Now he uses vulnerable people to attract attentionWhether or not there is a formal arrangement, the transaction is visible enough: Kanter lends the campaign the credibility of an 11-year NBA veteran and supplies a spectacle in which transgender people are the bait, while an organization embedded in Trump’s political network converts those assets into attention, merchandise and political capital. If it keeps voters staring at a nonexistent threat to theWNBAinstead of the corruption engulfing the administration in the run-up to the November midterms, the stunt has done its real work.Late in the third quarter of Sunday’s contest, Natasha Cloud, one of the most uncompromising athlete-activists of her generation, finally took therage bait. The Sky guard approached Kanter, yelling and pointing in his direction. Kanter stood, spread his arms and stepped on to the court before security intervened. As he was escorted away, he stopped near the basket to argue his case, then stretched out his shirt and tried to draw a response from the crowd. He had arrived ready to provoke and left performing martyrdom.Kanter did not suddenly discover the uses of spectacle on Sunday. In 2020, after marching with Black Lives Matter protesters in Boston, hetold the Guardianthat athletes should use their platforms “to spread good, and to spread the truth”. He had long understood publicity as a political tool, and with good reason: he believed international pressure helped secure his father’s acquittal. The difference is what the performance now serves.None of this diminishes the courage Kanter showed in opposing Erdoğan. The offer of US citizenship is not a contract for ideological obedience. Human rights are not a prize withdrawn when their beneficiary later behaves immorally, nor does surviving persecution bind anyone to a prescribed worldview.But suffering does not automatically make a person generous, either. And Kanter, more than most, should understand the mechanics of dehumanization: how a powerful movement marks a minority as dangerous, treats its identity as illegitimate and converts real human beings into totems of social decay. The scale of Erdoğan’s repression and an American culture-war stunt are not equivalent. The moral reflex behind them – identifying people with less power and making public sport of their vulnerability – should have been instantly recognizable to him. The least cynical reading, perhaps charitable to a fault, is that Kanter can recognize this kind of othering only when he is its target.US citizenship gave Kanter what he asked for in that Manhattan conference room: safety, a home and the freedom to speak without Erdoğan deciding the consequences. That freedom includes the right to make a cruel spectacle of himself, but it does not exempt the spectacle from judgment.“I try to be the voice of those innocent people,” Kanter said in 2017. I believed him then. On Sunday, he used that voice to make other innocent people feel smaller. What a waste.Explore more on these topicsWNBABasketballRecep Tayyip ErdoğanTurkeyTransgendercommentShareReuse this content

title: Canadians do not seek a trade war – but nor will we be bullied by Donald Trump | Jen Gerson | The Guardian
description: A fundamental rupture in the values that have united North America is not a problem that can be wished away, says Canadian commentator Jen Gerson
Author: Jen Gerson
Headline: A fundamental rupture in the values that have united North America is not a problem that can be wished away, says Canadian commentator Jen Gerson
Content: An anti-US tariffs protest outside the US consulate in Vancouver in 2025.Photograph: Ethan Cairns/APView image in fullscreenAn anti-US tariffs protest outside the US consulate in Vancouver in 2025.Photograph: Ethan Cairns/APOpinionCanadaCanadians do not seek a trade war – but nor will we be bullied by Donald TrumpJen GersonA fundamental rupture in the values that have united North America is not a problem that can be wished away: this is a warning to the western allianceTue 25 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 08.30 EDTShareThe Canadians are exceedingly angry. I realise this can sometimes be difficult for foreigners to deduce, given our national struggle to express the full range of human emotion outside ice hockey riots. However, let me assure you that the prime minister Canadians saw take the stage on Saturday morning in the wake of the collapse in trade negotiations with the US was aMark Carneypractically vibrating with fury.“You’re at war when you get attacked. We got attacked,”he said, in arare press conferencethat was as candid and clear as he ever tends to be. “That’s fine … We’ve got the reserves, we’ve got the resilience, we’ve got the plan, we’ve got the focus. We’re gonna respond, we’re going to focus on what we can control and what we’re going to build.”Canada walked out of negotiations, with a deal apparently on the verge of completion, mere hours before50% tariffson a range of Canadian exports were due to kick in.Dollar-for-dollar retaliatory tariffs, scheduled to take effect on 8 September, will follow in turn. In a statement, Carneysaid thatlast-minute demands from the US were “uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal.” The USdenied this, insisting that it was Canadians who made last-minute demands.In subsequent interviews with Bloomberg, Canadian ambassador to the USMark Wiseman saidthere was no specific item that put a deal out of reach; rather, it was a range of issues in which the text that ultimately wound up on the page – or, at least the interpretation of that text – did not align with what the Canadians thought they had agreed to. The most contentious issues appear to be related to tariffs on autos, digital and cultural policy, and the US claiming the right to veto Canada’s attempts to form trade alliances with other countries. Meanwhile, Canadians have no reason to trust this administration not to unilaterally impose new tariffs on a whim – which it has done, repeatedly, and as recently as this week.In short, Carney noted, sometimes the US signature on trade deals is “written in pencil”.Canadian voters, who were pensive about the prospect of any new deal with the US in the first place, have come outstrongly in supportof the prime minister. Despite the fact that the deal’s collapse will almost certainly entail painful economic penalties, the mood is one of sustained and general anger toward the US not born merely of trade irritants – very few Canadians have opinions about rules of origin tariffs on auto parts, or softwood lumber protections, or supply managed dairy quotas. In cordial times, these are the ordinary frictions between close friends and neighbours.View image in fullscreenMark Carney and Donald Trump during a summit addressing the war in Gaza, 13 October 2025.Photograph: Evan Vucci/APRather, it’s an emotion born of a real and visceral sense of betrayal: that the people we trusted with shared security and military obligations, that the nation with which we allowed ourselves to grow economically interdependent, has turned on us. They are using ordinary trade irritants as an excuse to exercise mafioso-style dominance in the pursuit of our subjugation and maybe outright annexation. We know very well that this isn’t about trade.We are being trained to know our place in the new world order that the so-calledDunroe doctrineis seeking to impose on the western hemisphere.So how, exactly, are any of us supposed to respond when the US secretary of transportation, Sean Duffy, goes on Fox News in the aftermath of the collapse tosay things like: “We provide their security for them and they take advantage of us? President Trump was the first one to go and say ‘that’s not the kind of relationship friends should have’.”The US does not provide Canadian security – although many commentators, including myself, do criticise our lax military spending. The North American Aerospace Defense Command, orNorad, is a fully integrated entity of both the Canadian and US military. We have our own military, and our own police forces.How are we supposed to respond, exactly, when our large and once-admired neighbour to the southrepeatedly threatensto make us the “51st state”? Or when he postsgag photosof the whole of North America covered in a US flag – provocations we’re supposed to take “seriously but not literally”, as if that makes these threats less horrific or more acceptable.What does one do when one’s closest “friend” and “ally” repeatedlythreatens to disregardborder treaties? Or when the US’s actual behaviour aligns perfectly with the president’s threat to use “economic force“ to push us into becoming an American state?We don’t want to be an American state. And even if we did, we certainly wouldn’t want to be a state of whatever the US is choosing to become right now.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere is not a single Canadian who wants to start a war with the US. No country in Canada’s position storms out of a trade negotiation unless it has to. No country as small and dependent on the US tells the modern imperium to get lost, and risks the consequences thereof, unless there is no other option.What Carney – and Canada, for that matter – are trying to signal across the Atlantic is that the America we all built our expectations around is over. We cannot plan around the hope of a return to normal, even if Democrats regain power in Washington.Canada’s location and US-integrated economy mean that we will be the first to face the reality of whatever the US becomes. And if it is coming for us, no European ally – including the UK – can expect to remain untouched, regardless of whatever “special relationship” you imagine may insulate you.Personally, I simply cannot fathom the commentators and politicians in the UK who fail to understand this. Do you honestly imagine yourselves to be closer to the US militarily, geographically, economically, or culturally thanCanada? Guys, wearea little America, albeit with a steadier political system and the king on the money. If they are willing to vassaliseus, what sentiment of history or tradition remains to protectyou?A fundamental break in American values and objectives is not a problem that can be contained. It’s not a condition that can be ignored or wished away. Carney is seriouswhen he talks abouta historic “rupture in the world order”, as he did at Davos early this year.Canadians understand that maintaining our sovereignty and independence will entail consequences and sacrifices. We did not bring this trade war on ourselves; we have merely refused to comply in advance to the unreasonable demands of a bad-faith actor. We will be punished for it. We have accepted this. If nothing else, let the US’s retaliation be a warning to the rest of the western alliance. Run,run. Protect yourselves. Move faster.Jen Gerson is a Canadian commentator and co-founder ofThe Line. She lives in Calgary, AlbertaExplore more on these topicsCanadaOpinionDonald TrumpMark CarneyAmericascommentShareReuse this content

title: I’m not usually patriotic. But Pauline Hanson’s cheap nationalism has me rooting for multicultural Australia | Paul Daley | The Guardian
description: Patriotism can be angry and stridently militaristic – or it can be a gentle pride in the success of an experiment like multiculturalism
Author: Paul Daley
Headline: Patriotism can be angry and stridently militaristic – or it can be a gentle pride in the success of an experiment like multiculturalism
Content: ‘Australia’s cultural institutions are replete with [again true] stories that celebrate an enduring multicultural Australia,’ writes Paul Daley.Photograph: Down Under Digital/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Australia’s cultural institutions are replete with [again true] stories that celebrate an enduring multicultural Australia,’ writes Paul Daley.Photograph: Down Under Digital/AlamyOpinionPauline HansonI’m not usually patriotic. But Pauline Hanson’s cheap nationalism has me rooting for multicultural AustraliaPaul DaleyPatriotism can be angry and stridently militaristic – or it can be a gentle pride in the success of an experiment like multiculturalismTue 25 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 20.28 EDTSharePatriotism is always stubbornly absent in me on days of official national commemoration.Australia Day – Invasion Day – has always left me cold for its divisiveness, historical asymmetry and exclusivity. Anzac Day, an unofficial national day for many, has never raised a patriotic shiver in me.I admit to feeling more than a little buoyant on particular international sporting occasions. Australia flogging England, here or there, in an Ashes Test series gives me an anticolonial glow. But not exactly a patriotic high.But true stories of Australian multi-ethnicity that play out on sporting fields or in so many cultural spheres, stories that reinforce my faith in an Australia that would be altered irrevocably by thoseadvocatingmonoculturalism (or who at best supinelyequivocateabout it) do make me feel patriotic.Take the Socceroos and the football World Cup. They represented a modern nation that is built on an overwhelming rejection of the abhorrentWhite Australia policy.Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best readsThe blind racism and profound illogicality that underpins so much of One Nation’s so-called policies on economics, immigration and social cohesion were exposed by Pauline Hanson’s absurd proposition that the Socceroos (for all their racial diversity) represent an Australian monoculture. Get her a dictionary, please.The Socceroos embody and embrace a repudiation of thecheap nationalistic racial and religious prejudicethat some One Nation officials (and others) blithely parrot. It was reassuring to see a senior federal government figure,Penny Wong, robustly debunk such fever-dream jingoistic bunkum.Australia’s cultural institutions are replete with (again true) stories that celebrate an enduring multicultural Australia.While recently meandering through Sydney’s wonderful Australian National Maritime Museum (so much of which is dedicated to telling Australia’s multicultural migration story) a small exhibit stopped me in my tracks. It was a small, battered and blackened metal fry-pan with a plastic handle that was brought to Australia by a Vietnamese “boat person”, Tuyet Lu, who made the perilous journey to Darwin on a small fishing boat with her husband, former store owner Tan Than Lu (who fought for South Vietnam) and their children. They arrived in Darwin in November 1977 with few personal possessions, the pan among them.She cooked withthe panin South Vietnam. She cooked with it on the boat for her family and other refugees. After arriving in Darwin and during six months living at Brisbane’s Wacol migrant hostel, she used the pan to cook Vietnamese food in Australia.Six months later, they were granted Australian asylum.Some of us will remember the heated debate around the influx of thousands of Vietnamese asylum seekers arriving by boat from South Vietnam after the fall of Saigon. The last vestiges of the White Australia policy (the first act of the Australia’s commonwealth parliament in the white federation of 1901) had only recently been removed. The Vietnamese, like many others, were viewed by some as a threat to some nebulous Australian cohesion (despite the early federation’s bitter social and political divisions over – among other things – sectarianism, conscription, women’s suffrage, racial equity and, later, the appeasement of European fascism).skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI protested against Pauline Hanson 28 years ago – now my teenager is doing the same thing | Philippa ChandlerRead moreThose opposing the settlement of “boat people” from Asia in the late 1970s could not have foreseen today’s proliferation of Vietnamese restaurants in just about every suburban shopping district and country high street across the land. Vietnamese cuisine is now Australian! But that is the defiant reality – the strength against occasional odds and, yes, enduring racism in some social quarters – of the Australian social and migration amalgam.It is a fitting postscript that Tuyet Lu used her battered and blackened pan in restaurants that she and her husband came to own and run in Australia. A melting pot indeed.Patriotism can be angry and stridently militaristic. It can also take the form of a gentle pride in the success of an experiment like multiculturalism.It is no coincidence that those now advocating the impossibility of an Australian monoculture began political life three decades ago attacking First Nations peoples, promoting the fanciful fallacy that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people (among the earth’s most disadvantaged)had it too good.Indigenous antiquity on this continent – 60,000 years and counting of human civilisation’s unbroken connection with the land, seas and skies, and its wondrous manifestations today – has long been a bedrock of my quiet,reflective form of Australian patriotism.This all resonates for me, hands down, far more meaningfully than militarism or boisterouswe-grew-here-you-flew-herebrands of jingoistic, exclusionary nationalism.Paul Daley is a Guardian Australia columnistExplore more on these topicsPauline HansonOpinionOne NationRacecommentShareReuse this content

title: Three years after his death, the Met goes after Mohamed Al Fayed. As for his enablers – well, you can’t rush things, can you? | Marina Hyde | The Guardian
description: The crimes he stands accused of required whole armies of facilitators. Don’t the victims deserve to see them face justice too, asks Guardian columnist Marina Hyde
Author: Marina Hyde
Headline: The crimes he stands accused of required whole armies of facilitators. Don’t the victims deserve to see them face justice too, asks Guardian columnist Marina Hyde
Content: The late Mohamed Al Fayed in Paris, June 2016.Photograph: Kamil Zihnioglu/APView image in fullscreenThe late Mohamed Al Fayed in Paris, June 2016.Photograph: Kamil Zihnioglu/APOpinionMohamed Al FayedThree years after his death, the Met goes after Mohamed Al Fayed. As for his enablers – well, you can’t rush things, can you?Marina HydeThe crimes he stands accused of required whole armies of facilitators. Don’t the victims deserve to see them face justice too?Tue 25 Aug 2026 09.35 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 14.03 EDTShareHow reassuring to learn that police investigating claims of sexual assault against Mohamed Al Fayed havehanded a fileto the Crown Prosecution Service, a mere three years after the former Harrods owner’s death at the age of 94, and just decades after the first survivors made reports of abuse. The CPS has said it won’t provide a timescale for any decision, to which we might remark: no shit. With this case, the one thing you could never accuse any of the authorities of is being bound by anything approaching a timescale.The story does, however, certainly have scale. So far, more than 400 allegations including rape, sexual assault, sexual exploitation and human trafficking have been made against Al Fayed byat least 156 women– abuse he got away with, having died without any charges ever being brought against him. The claimsspan the years 1977 to 2014. At least 21 women came forward while he was alive, and there have been extraordinary rundowns in news articles and documentaries about all the alleged enablers of his wicked behaviour, from lawyers to mouthpieces to security henchmen to the doctors who carried out “purity examinations” on his young female PAs.So, not to be a Debbie Downer – because any movement on this case is better than none – but perhaps that sense of scale is not immediately discernible from the file that has been sent to the CPS, which relates to a male suspect in his 80s and two indecent assaults on two women inLondon. The investigation remains ongoing, the Met confirms.View image in fullscreenAlleged victims of Mohamed Al Fayed (L-R) Gemma, Lindsay and Jen in London on 31 October 2024.Photograph: Benjamin Cremel/AFP/Getty ImagesOf course, other under-prosecuted criminal networks are available. During the full-spectrum coverage of the Jeffrey Epstein case, many asked how on earth so many blind eyes could be turned by so many people to so much flagrant abuse by someone who was known to haveserved prison timefor soliciting prostitution from a minor. People marvelled at the vast collective silence – yet anyone who couldn’t quite believe how it could happen should have been reassured that other vast collective silences were very much ongoing. Peter Mandelson’s now notoriousmessage of commiserationto his friend Jeffrey shortly before his 2008 incarceration – “it just could not happen in Britain” – always seems to me ironically resonant. Perhaps his lordship was right, though not in the way he meant.As the Epstein furore raged on earlier this year, several Al Fayed survivors wrote to me asking why this one case was dominating everything while another, still unresolved one – and so much closer to home – seemed to lack the turbocharge of outrage that pushes something from the places our society would rather forget into the ones where we have our (always belated) reckonings. The answer to that question is normally that significant numbers of people and institutions have a deeply vested interest innotgetting to the bottom of it.Met apologises for exposing 143 email addresses of Mohamed Al Fayed victimsRead moreIt would feel unwise to conclude anything other than that in this case. There has been no equivalent political pressure to let daylight in on Al Fayed’s activities. No one has got wall-to-wall news coverage for asking how he was able to operate an alleged criminal fiefdom in the centre of Knightsbridge, when allegations were repeatedly made and the rumours in rarefied circles were more than deafening. It was, it seems, just the way things were.And as indicated, for things to be that way for so long, there needed to be whole armies of enablers and hangers-on who facilitated abuse, or looked away, or closed down or ridiculed or trashed those who stepped out of line and said anything about it, including the alleged victims. Only one of Epstein’s helpers, Ghislaine Maxwell, has ever been brought to justice. Typically, no one bar the kingpin in what I think of as the sex-case industrial complex even faces so much as a charge – they simply melt back into society, into other jobs, into the ongoing conspiracy of silence.Today, the Al Fayed survivors’ group Justice for Fayed and Harrods Survivors issued a statementpointing outthat: “Survivors have spent decades either not being believed or being told that Fayed and those around him were too powerful and that nothing could be done – but today is an important reminder that the passage of time does not, by itself, put accountability beyond reach.” Yet with the best will in the world, the passage of time doesn’t exactly help, does it? Al Fayed himself died unscathed, and we all know that once things tip conveniently into the “historical” file, they are so much harder to prove.But there are things the public can get behind right now. What Al Fayed’s survivors want is the trafficking investigation they have been requesting for almost two years. As they point out, this was not one bad man, nor some form of corporate abuse. It was, they allege, a trafficking network involving multiple perpetrators and enablers and backed by the global movement of illicit funds. At least five survivors have already been confirmed by the Home Office as victims of modern slavery. Yet the Met has been accused of havingfailed in its legal dutyto offer the victims a referral to thenational referral mechanism(it’s understood the police didn’t believe they were obligated to),which identifies modern slavery victims. Yet again, all the running is being made by a survivors’ group. No One Abovewants confirmationthat human trafficking and modern slavery are the primary framework of the Al Fayed investigation, and to know that financial investigators are being utilised to determine how the network was funded and concealed.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt remains to be seen if any belated percentage of justice will be served in this case. Even if it is, we can expect all manner of blind-eye institutions to immediately resort to their happy place and trot out some trite platitude like “never again”. In fact, it would be more accurate to conclude the opposite. Always again. Always again, until society has the courage to realise that it so often takes a village to do bad things, as well as good ones.Marina Hyde is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: As a doctor, I say this: before we even consider assisted dying, fix how we care for the most vulnerable | Zubir Ahmed | The Guardian
description: A person’s wish to die can be shaped by whether they have access to proper palliative care – and too many do not, says Labour MP and transplant surgeon Zubir Ahmed
Author: Zubir Ahmed
Headline: A person’s wish to die can be shaped by whether they have access to proper palliative care – and too many do not, says Labour MP and transplant surgeon Zubir Ahmed
Content: ‘A person’s wish to die does not happen in isolation from their circumstances.’Photograph: Rosemary Roberts/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘A person’s wish to die does not happen in isolation from their circumstances.’Photograph: Rosemary Roberts/AlamyOpinionAssisted dyingAs a doctor, I say this: before we even consider assisted dying, fix how we care for the most vulnerableZubir AhmedA person’s wish to die can be shaped by whether they have access to proper palliative care – and in England and Wales, too many do notZubir Ahmed is a transplant surgeon and former Labour ministerTue 25 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 08.30 EDTShareAs a doctor, I have spent much of my professional life caring for people at some of the most vulnerable moments they will ever face. I have seen the anxiety that surrounds the prospect of dying, and the desperate wish of patients and families to avoid unnecessary suffering.Naturally, we all want people facing the end of life to be treated with kindness and respect. But when considering the debate on assisted dying, true compassion demands that we ask a more fundamental question. What kind of society are we building if, before we’ve fixed the systems designed to care for people, we introduce a system designed to help them die? As a former health minister who has seen the system from the inside, I am able to say it is not ready or equipped to answer this question.Andy Burnham has been right to raise this as a priority issue at the start of his tenure as prime minister.Speaking at a care homerecently, he explained that assisted dying should not be introduced while Britain’s palliative care and social care systems remain under such strain. A choice between death without adequate care and a death prematurely self-induced is not a real choice.Indeed, as parliament prepares for yet another vote on assisted dying in England and Wales on 11 September, I fear that the offering has been somewhat mis-sold to the public. A state-controlled medicalised dying process is still a process – one where there remain risks of complication and suffering. The reality of assisted dying is more complex than the promise of a perfectly controlled death.Many people imagine a system where a person facing a terminal illness can choose the exact moment and manner of their death, free from distress. But the legislation does not and cannot provide that certainty. A patient who self-administers medication to begin the dying process may still experience complications. The process may take time; it may require medical intervention. It may not happen where or when the person imagined. The promise of absolute control can therefore become something different in practice: an appearance of choice that does not always deliver the agency people expect.I am far from the only medical professional to be worried about the prospect of assisted dying being available on the NHS. Among those raising concerns about the bill’s dozens of flaws have been theRoyal College of Physicians, theRoyal College of Psychiatrists, theComplex Life and Death Decisions (CLADD) group from King’s College London,theRoyal College of Pathologists, theBritish Geriatrics Societyand numerous other medical bodies and care authorities. The same concern comes up again and again: is it really a “free choice” when palliative care and social support fall short?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFrance’s ‘aid in dying’ law comes into effect after constitutional approvalRead moreA person’s wish to die does not happen in isolation from their circumstances. It can be shaped by whether they feel supported, whether they fear becoming a burden, whether their family is coping and whether they have access to the care they need. That is why the state of our care systems cannot be treated as a separate issue from assisted dying. Timely access to palliative and social care remains too often determined by where someone lives rather than what they need. For some families, excellent end-of-life support is available; for others, particularly in rural areas as well as constituencies experiencing high inequality, the experience is one of waiting, uncertainty and having to fight for services that should be guaranteed.A Labour government founded theNHSon a principle that remains as important today as it was at its creation: that healthcare should be there when people need it most, regardless of their circumstances. A postcode lottery in care cannot be ignored while debating a new legal pathway for people at the end of their life.In Scotland, this concern has been expressed clearly, and was an important reason why, in March, 85% of Labour MSPs voted against the legalisation of assisted dying in Holyrood. The bill introduced in Westminster by my colleague Kim Leadbeater, the Labour MP for Spen Valley, in October 2024 did not fare much better: too many concerns about patient welfare meant the House of Lords would not rubber-stamp the flawed text. And yet, on 11 September, MPs will be faced with yet another vote on assisted dying before the care systems are improved to a level which even makes that debate appropriate. Andy Burnham has his priorities right: this is the wrong debate at the wrong time. This is why I, and many others, will be voting against this bill, in pursuit of comfort, dignity and appropriate care for people who are vulnerable and dying.Zubir Ahmed MP is an NHS vascular and transplant surgeon, and served as the parliamentary under-secretary of state at the Department of Health and Social Care from 6 September 2025 to 12 May 2026.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
