title: From Scotland, I look at England’s water privatisation disaster. I wish you had done what we did | Devi Sridhar | The Guardian
description: Listening to debate, you’d think bringing English water companies into public ownership was a radical socialist idea. Here, we call it common sense, says chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh Devi Sridhar
Author: Devi Sridhar
Headline: Listening to debate, you’d think bringing English water companies into public ownership was a radical socialist idea. Here, we call it common sense, says chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh Devi Sridhar
Content: Environmental campaigners protest against Thames Water near the Rye River in High Wycombe, Buckinghamshire, 4 March 2026.Photograph: Maureen McLean/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenEnvironmental campaigners protest against Thames Water near the Rye River in High Wycombe, Buckinghamshire, 4 March 2026.Photograph: Maureen McLean/ShutterstockOpinionWater industryFrom Scotland, I look at England’s water privatisation disaster. I wish you had done what we didDevi SridharListening to debate, you’d think bringing English water companies into public ownership was a radical socialist idea. Here, we call it common senseProf Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of EdinburghTue 25 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 11.47 EDTShareEvery few months, there are more shocking headlines about the behaviour of England’s water companies. Thelatest are aboutthe ever-increasing pay of the chief executives and chief financial officers, which rose to a total of £25.3m across 14 companies over the past year. Meanwhile, people living in England struggle with rising water bills and untreated sewage being discharged (often illegally) on to beaches and in to lakes, and companies such as Thames Water areon the brink of insolvencyand want government backing.It’s not surprising that we’re in this situation: England’s water companies have long been accused of putting the interests of shareholdersabove those of customers. From their perspective, the privatisation of water has been an astounding success. Between 1991 and 2019,dividends to the shareholdersof the parent companies totalled £57bn, which averages out to more than £2bn every year. The majority of these private parentcompanies are foreign-owned, so the profits aren’t even kept in Britain.Lack of proper oversight creates a series of perverse incentives. If water companies can charge more for the same amount of water, they’ll do that. If they can dump untreated sewage in public waterways, they’ll do that, too.The root of the problem goes back to 1989 when Margaret Thatcher, then prime minister,privatised water in England. But right here, in the UK, there’s an example that shows that there is an alternative.Water companies circumventing bonus rules? What did ministers expect? | Nils PratleyRead moreUnlike England, Scotland chose to retain public ownership of Scottish Water and, between 2002 and 2019, the company invested35% more per household in infrastructurethan the privatised English water companies. It charges users 14% less and itdoesn’t pay dividends.While Scottish Water’s CEOpay package, which adds up to more than £500k,has beencriticised for being highrelative to other public sector employees, it’s relatively low compared with the private pay packets south of the border. More importantly, Scottish Water is accountable to people living in Scotland, as all profit is reinvested back into water and sanitation systems, instead of going to shareholders.I’ve lived in Scotland for over a decade and the water coming from taps is clean and delicious. Since 2018 Scottish Water’sYour Water Your Lifecampaign has been offeringfree drinking waterthrough a network of public water stations across the country. By 2022, the water dispensed at these would have filled the equivalent of15m plastic bottles. Water in people’s homes is paid for through local authorities charging council tax rather than customers receiving a bill from a private water-company.As a public health expert, I’ve found it hard not to think about England’s poor water infrastructure because I can see how, across the world, and especially in low-income countries, access to this vital resource is often a matter of life or death. It took thefather of epidemiology, John Snow, to identify dirty water as the cause of alarge cholera outbreak in London. Clean water isn’t a luxury: it’s necessary to human health and wellbeing.More recently, Chris Whitty, England’s chief medical officer, highlightedthe worrying public health problemof sewage in England’s waterways. He reminded water companies and their directors that human faeces is making people who swim or use the water on popular beaches and rivers sick.The normal logic of private efficiency might work in sectors of the economy where competition brings meaningful choice and innovation. Take cars: we can choose between different manufacturers, designs, fuel type and price; or even pharmaceutical companies, where competition encourages firms to develop different drugs and invest in risky research.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut what is the consumer choice in tap water?Wateris water: we just need it to be clean, and hopefully to taste good and be reliably delivered through functioning infrastructure. We need the waste we flush down our toilets to be treated and made safe through sanitation systems, before being released into nature again.Listening to the recent debates, you’d think that bringing English water companies back into public ownership was some kind of radical socialist idea. Guess what? That’s just normal life here in Edinburgh.If water and sanitation are treated as a commodity, then companies will of course look at how much they can squeeze consumers. But water isn’t something that you can choose to go without. It’s absolutely vital to human life – you’d die without it in about three days – and should be a basic part of public infrastructure provided by government.Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of EdinburghExplore more on these topicsWater industryOpinionWaterUtilitiesScotlandThames WaterWater billsHousehold billscommentShareReuse this content

title: The war on ‘loudcasting’ phones can be won, but it will take some very British nudging | Dan Hancox | The Guardian
description: Although mobiles blared in public are nothing new, this crop of headphone-dodging irritants are truly maddening. It’s time to take them on, says Dan Hancox, a writer and editor covering music, politics and cities
Author: Dan Hancox
Headline: Although mobiles blared in public are nothing new, this crop of headphone-dodging irritants are truly maddening. It’s time to take them on, says Dan Hancox, a writer and editor covering music, politics and cities
Content: Illustration: Anaïs Mims/Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenIllustration: Anaïs Mims/Guardian DesignOpinionEnvironmentThe war on ‘loudcasting’ phones can be won, but it will take some very British nudgingDan HancoxAlthough mobiles blared in public are nothing new, this crop of headphone-dodging irritants are truly maddening. It’s time to take them onTue 25 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 14.03 EDTShare‘Interesting cities can’t be quiet”, runs one of grime DJ and music industry thinkerElijah’sepigrams – and in its essential spirit, he is right. Silent, tidy, prim cities should be treated with suspicion. Any such atmosphere denotes that something has gone wrong at a macro level: either you’ve wound up in an authoritarian regime or, worse, Switzerland.But not all urban sounds are created equal, and some are more unwelcome than others. Take the tide of (Instagram, TikTok, YouTube) reels crashing on the shores of our collective attention on public transport, thanks to the astonishing number of grown adults who think it’s OK tosurf the slopwavewithout headphones.These rotters are accompanied by people taking their phone or video calls out loud on speakerphone. In the early days of mobile phones it was a widely agreed social truism that the white-collar workerunselfconsciously bellowing “I’m on the train!”into their BlackBerry was a grade-A public nuisance, plausibly worthy of throwing in the stocks. Well, at least then we were only being subjected to one end of the conversation.The spread of 5G across the country is making such unsolicited noise more possible and more common: “loudcasting”, the BBC called it in a recent in-depth look at the phenomenon. A public backlash is suddenly mounting. Never one to miss an opportunity for free press coverage, last week Wetherspoons boss Tim Martinbanned itfrom his pubs.It’s funny how social pressure points like this fade in and out of public view, as the technology that touches our lives evolves: 19 years ago, the same practice was christened “sodcasting” by Pascal Wyse in this newspaper – at that point there were no reels, no AI drivel, no streaming video calls, no such thing as an Instagram influencer, nor Instagram either. The moral panic back then was about tinny MP3s being played aloud from much more basic mobile phones – and the purported juvenile delinquency that had surely led to such a crisis.I probably annoyed a lot of Guardian readers that year, writing more than 2,000 wordsin defence of sodcasting: more precisely, in defence of teenagers playing music on their phones on the bus, the train or otherwise in public. There was something qualitatively different about that iteration, I would argue. It was a necessary claiming of public space by people who are often bullied out of it: adults-in-training, still working out how to exist in the outside world as independent beings, still learning to navigate their own social lives, and (an underrated asset, this) learning to enjoy musictogether, as a group activity. For the rest of us, this form of sodcasting amounted to an occasional, brief and usually joyful burst of alfresco music – and we could all do with hearing Crazy Cousinz and Giggs more often anyway.View image in fullscreen‘These days it always seems to be full-grown adults rather than teenagers taking calls on speakerphone or watching reels with no headphones.’Photograph: PjrTransport/AlamyThe 2010 furore about sodcasting followed a decade of punching down by Britain’s power-wielding adults against its most marginalised young people – the“chavs” and “hoodies”against whom New Labour and the tabloids collectively went to war, driven by the reactionary moralism of what was risibly called “the respect agenda”.A time of asbos, public spaces protection orders and curfews for young people.Interestingly – and admittedly anecdotally; this stuff isn’t easy to measure – sodcasting 1.0 seemed to disappear as a phenomenon after a year or two. New social behaviours that emerge in response to new popular technologies tend to do so: things settle down as a new consensus on how we should all use them is slowly reached, and reached collectively.Let’s hope that happens again, because what we are all hearing on buses and trains thanks to sodcasting 2.0 is measurably more antisocial and individualistic: for one thing, 2010’s groups of teen sodcasters weren’t changing songs every 10 seconds. For another – warning, more anecdotal analysis incoming – these days it always seems to be full-grown adults rather than teenagers taking calls on speakerphone or watching reels with no headphones. It is maddening behaviour to anyone who has experienced it: like being on a bus or a train with someone who is flicking TV channels, constantly.So, as Lenin once asked of matters of similarly grave importance: what is to be done? Last year, the Lib Demsproposed a £1,000 finefor sodcasting – an amusingly illiberal policy to make one of their centrepieces. For what it’s worth, I don’t think a fine is very useful, realistic or enforceable – though, God bless the ironclad French state, for it managed to find a way to do exactly that,fining a man €200(£170) for taking a call on loudspeaker on a station platform.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe truth is that we have more sane and effective options for shaping public behaviour in the form of nudge messaging. Transport for London has a strong history of this, via adverts on its trains, tubes and buses. In 2008, its Considerate Travel campaign seemed to help quieten down the mobile phone DJs and its currentAct Like a FriendandTravel Kindcampaigns aim to address hate crime, misogynistic creeps and encourage others to help passengers who may be unwell. Sodcasting 2.0 pisses me off no end, too, but I think people can change with a little nudging.Stefan Stern made anexcellent casein these pages recently that we should all remove our headphones – and turn off the content altogether – to hear and more fully participate in the noisy, messy city around us. Hopefully we can achieve this via social consensus, gentle persuasion, and without the soundtrack of someone broadcasting AI monkey videos. And if all else fails, well, sod it: let’s nudge the culprits into the stocks.Dan Hancox is a writer and editor covering music, politics and cities. His latest book is Multitudes: How Crowds Made the Modern WorldExplore more on these topicsEnvironmentOpinionPublic transportMobile phonesTfLPollutionAI (artificial intelligence)HeadphonescommentShareReuse this content

title: The Sydney Swans scandal has left many outraged. But what happens if no police charges are laid? | Rana Hussain | The Guardian
description: Behaviour we once might have shrugged off now makes us deeply uncomfortable. But discomfort alone cannot define the standard
Author: Rana Hussain
Headline: Behaviour we once might have shrugged off now makes us deeply uncomfortable. But discomfort alone cannot define the standard
Content: Sydney Swans supporters cheer during an AFL match as part of a double header with the club’s AFLW side at the SCG on Sunday.Photograph: Steven Markham/AAPView image in fullscreenSydney Swans supporters cheer during an AFL match as part of a double header with the club’s AFLW side at the SCG on Sunday.Photograph: Steven Markham/AAPOpinionAFLThe Sydney Swans scandal has left many outraged. But what happens if no police charges are laid?Rana HussainBehaviour we once might have shrugged off now makes us deeply uncomfortable. But discomfort alone cannot define the standardMon 24 Aug 2026 23.20 EDTLast modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 23.21 EDTShareThe public response to theSydney Swansscandal has been fascinating. Before we knew very much at all, people were ready to be outraged. Perhaps understandably so. One in five Australian women has experienced sexual violence since the age of 15.Put footballers, women, alcohol, and alleged assault in the same story and it’s as if we already know how it ends. Entitled athletes.Womenas collateral damage. Another sporting culture gone bad.There is something encouraging in that response. Behaviour we once might have shrugged off now makes us deeply uncomfortable. But our heightened sensitivity to violence against women is one thing. Filling in the gaps before we know the facts is another.As a woman who loves AFL, I feel palpable despair. Why did it take so long to put us at the centre of this story? | Jill StarkRead moreSo, as we wait for clarity while police investigate an alleged sexual assault – and park what we can not responsibly know or speculate about – there is another question worth asking. What are we actually angry about?The staying out late. The drinking. The reported adult entertainers. Bringing women back to the team hotel. Doing it in the lead-up to finals. Letting down teammates. Getting caught.All have become part of the public reaction. But if no crime occurred and we still think something went badly wrong, we need to be able to name what that something was.Talk to people around football, as I have this week, and the answers are revealing.For some, the bender isn’t the line that has been crossed. Neither are the adult entertainers. It’s the brazenness of bringing it all back to the team hotel, in the biggest month of the season, with your teammates’ year on the line.For others, the qualifier is simpler: after the season. Drink. Party. Hire adult entertainers if that’s your thing. Just don’t do it now.That raises an uncomfortable possibility. Some of the behaviour that shocked the public may not be considered particularly shocking inside parts of football. For some, the transgression was doing it at the wrong time, in the wrong place – and getting found out.The Swans, however, clearly decided a line had been crossed.Five players were stood downfor the remainder of the season, including finals, for breaching club standards, while a Victoria police investigation into an alleged sexual assault remained ongoing.If I could sit down with the Swans administrators, there is one thing I would want to understand: what, exactly, was the line for you?The club has been clear that its sanctions were separate from the police investigation and related to breaches of its standards. No one has been arrested or charged and the five players have reportedly denied any criminal wrongdoing. But what is less clear publicly is where that line actually lives. Player contracts, codes of conduct and team rules necessarily govern professional athletes, but we don’t know how explicitly the conduct at the centre of this incident is dealt with in those documents.There is a meaningful difference between breaking an explicit contractual rule, breaching a team protocol and falling short of a broader behavioural standard that requires the club to exercise judgment.The same is true of rules about bringing women or other guests back to a team hotel. Such rules might be designed around security, safeguarding, player welfare, preparation, privacy, teammates or reputation. The rationale matters. Otherwise, there is a risk that “standards” becomes shorthand for an inherited moral code about what respectable behaviour is supposed to look like, without ever interrogating why.Then there is the gut response. Listen to parents, fans and much of the public this week and the reaction is visceral:it feels gross. Seedy. Not OK.We shouldn’t dismiss that as pearl-clutching. Perhaps that discomfort tells us our standards sit somewhere higher than simply “not illegal”. But discomfort alone can’t define the standard. If it warrants ending five players’ seasons, we should be able to articulate what the line is, what harm it exists to prevent and whose values sit behind it.Because amid all the very real emotion, I think we’ve become entangled in three different conversations.The criminal line: whether a crime was committed.The workplace line: what standard was breached, why that standard exists and whether the consequence was proportionate.And the much murkier cultural line: what behaviour is accepted, tolerated or normalised long before either of those lines is crossed.We keep moving between the three as though they are interchangeable. They aren’t.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFrom the Pocket: AFL WeeklyJonathan Horn brings expert analysis on the week's biggest AFL storiesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe absence of a criminal charge would not erase a workplace breach. And dealing with a workplace breach doesn’t answer the deeper cultural question.Because perhaps that is the discomfort underneath all of this.Not simply what happened on one night, but what this night might tell us about a version of male sporting culture where heavy drinking and the sexualisation of women can sit alongside bonding, celebration and blowing off steam – and how much of it we tolerate until something goes spectacularly wrong.Not everything that makes up a culture is illegal. Legal is an extraordinarily low bar for culture.Of course, there is another response: footballers aren’t moral leaders. They’re athletes. We shouldn’t expect young men who are very good at kicking a football to raise our children or model our values.Except the industry doesn’t treat them that way. It sells their personalities, their stories, their reputations and our emotional attachment to them. Brands aren’t paying footballers solely for what they do with a Sherrin. They’re buying the influence attached to the person holding it.You can’t monetise someone’s influence and then declare it irrelevant when that influence becomes inconvenient.Sydney Swans’ tears flow after AFL football’s week in the sewer | Jonathan HornRead morePerhaps that’s why this story has become such a Rorschach test. Some see violence against women. Some see entitled athletes. Some see employees who let down their workplace. Some see a rotten culture. Others see adults making private choices that became humiliatingly public.Those are different objections requiring different solutions.If criminal charges follow, there is a process for that.But if they don’t, those of us who felt immediately and viscerally that something had gone wrong will have to decide whether there was nothing wrong after all – or finally get precise about what we were angry about in the first place.Because if we can’t name what was wrong, beyond what may or may not have been illegal, we have very little chance of making it better.Rana Hussain is a sports broadcaster, inclusion consultant and Basketball Australia directorInformation and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse is available from the following organisations. In Australia, support is available atFull Stop Australia(1800 385 578). In the UK,Rape Crisisoffers support on 0808 500 2222. In the US,Rainnoffers support on 800-656-4673. Other international helplines can be found atibiblio.org/rcip/internl.htmlExplore more on these topicsAFLOpinionSydney SwansAustralian rules footballAustralia sportWomenViolence against women and girlscommentShareReuse this content

title: Families need to openly talk to children about misogyny, consent and sexual violence. Here’s how to start | Stephanie Wescott and Jane Gilmore | The Guardian
description: All family members should feel safe to raise concerns, ask questions and cover topics without fear of shutdown or reprimand
Author: Jane Gilmore
Headline: All family members should feel safe to raise concerns, ask questions and cover topics without fear of shutdown or reprimand
Content: ‘Starting conversations about consent as early as possible, and having them as often as possible, is the best approach,’ write Stephanie Wescott and Jane Gilmore.Photograph: Maskot/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Starting conversations about consent as early as possible, and having them as often as possible, is the best approach,’ write Stephanie Wescott and Jane Gilmore.Photograph: Maskot/Getty ImagesOpinionGenderFamilies need to openly talk to children about misogyny, consent and sexual violence. Here’s how to startStephanie Wescott andJane GilmoreAll family members should feel safe to raise concerns, ask questions and cover topics without fear of shutdown or reprimandMon 24 Aug 2026 21.20 EDTShareThere have been multiple high-profile alleged incidents of sexual violence against women and girls in news headlines this month. Some of them involve teenage boys.Families might find themselves having – or thinking they need to have – discussions with their children about consent and sexual violence.We know parents have an important role to play in teaching their children about respectful sex and healthy relationships – and counteringharmful messagesthey may see online.But it can be difficult to know where to start.Before initiating the discussionThere are a few ways adults can prepare ahead of time.From the classroom to the locker room: nine days of ‘deeply disturbing’ sexual assault allegations shake AustraliaRead moreResearch suggests it’s important forparents to feel confidentwhen talking about consent and sexual violence so they can be clear about information and answer questions. Confidence also leads to better emotional regulation during these conversations. Ensuring you have a good level of knowledge yourself can support your level of confidence.Use accurate words instead of euphemisms and, particularly with teenagers, don’t try to soften the discussion by hiding from the realities of violence.According to the latestAustralian Bureau of Statistics data, nearly 30% of all sexual assaults reported to police in 2024 were against girls between 10 and 17 years old. The number of sexual assaults recorded nationally in 2024 also increased by 10% from 2023.Children and teenagers need to know the facts and risks, and to be in no doubt that their parents will support them through any experience.How to begin the discussionFamilies need to haveopen conversationswhen it comes to talking to children and young people about misogyny, rape and sexual violence. This means all family members should feel safe to raise concerns, ask questions and cover topics without fear of shutdown or reprimand.A good starting point is to ask children what they have read about in recentmedia reports, what they think about the issues and what their friends have said. This provides an opening to important conversations that are not just about young people’s own personal experiences.A possible way to do this might be to ask:There’s been so much in the news this week about [incident]. Have you seen it?Setting is importantIt’s important children and teenagers don’t feel as if they’re being confronted when adults initiate conversations.Instead of a more formal, sit-down discussion, you might choose to start a conversation in a more casual setting such asin the car or while doing chores.Keep the conversation open and don’t instructWhile parents should be clear about their values (for example, violence against women is never OK), asking questions and helping young people reach their own conclusions can bemore effectivethan giving instructions. These questions might include:what have you heard about (a particular incident)?how does it make you feel?do you have any questions you’d like to ask?Tone is important too. Try to keep the conversation calm, non-judgmental and open. Encourage your child to talk to you about concerning experiences and topics.Don’t play into harmful stereotypesAvoidreinforcing harmful messagesandgender stereotypessuch as “boys will be boys” or myths about rape (“women often lie about rape”, “men need sex from women”).double quotation markIt’s important children and teenagers don’t feel as if they’re being confronted when adults initiate conversationsIt’s crucial your child hears you reject these myths, even if they appear to agree with them. They might simply be testing your reactions.Discomfort is normalSex, violence and pornography can beconfronting and uncomfortabletopics, particularly between parents and children. Recognise thediscomfort is normalbut don’t let it become an excuse to avoid the topic.If you find it’s truly impossible to have these discussions with your children, find another responsible adult among your family or friends who is more able to be your deputy.Provide ongoing supportResearch suggestsfeminist approaches from parents(such as those that centre the safety of women and girls) as well as parental support forschool education initiativeson healthy relationships and consent help support violence prevention work.Outside the news cycle, adults can regularly support children to recognise sexism and misogyny in everyday situations, which, in turn, helps them recognise it in their own lives.For example, harmful “jokes” about women can normalise the misogyny thatunderpins violence. What one person thinks is just a silly line might sound like tacit permission to someone else. Adults should explicitly name and explain these harms when they arise.Help young people to think criticallyResearchshows exposure to misogynistic content on social media can lead to young people supporting misogynistic ideas.I am often asked how young boys could be rapists. For many adolescent men, the answer is entitlement | Chanel ContosRead moreIt’s essential parents and carers discuss therole social media companiesplay in spreading this content. Helping young peoplethink criticallyabout what they are seeing in their feeds can reduce the potential for harm.When should parents start discussions?While we tend to focus on building adolescents’ knowledge, starting conversations about consent asearly as possible, and having them as often as possible, is the best approach.Research suggestsyounger childrenbenefit from age-appropriate conversations about consent starting as soon as they are able to talk. This includes discussions about learning to trust their feelings and using correct anatomical words for body parts. It also includes teaching kids to respect other people’s boundaries and allowing them to make decisions about their own bodies, such as declining physical affection. Consent for little children is not about sex, it’s about physical affection such as hugs, and sharing toys and food.Remember, misogyny, sexual violence against women and consent are complex topics. You don’t have to cover every detail in every conversation. Ongoing and open communication is far more effective than one perfectly crafted conversation.Stephanie Wescott is a lecturer in humanities and social sciences at Monash University and Jane Gilmore is a PhD candidate at Monash University. title: Dolly Parton, country star, actor and philanthropist, dies aged 80 after fighting cancer | Dolly Parton | The Guardian
description: Songwriter of I Will Always Love You, Jolene and 9 to 5 invested millions in child literacy, Covid-19 vaccine development and other causes
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Songwriter of I Will Always Love You, Jolene and 9 to 5 invested millions in child literacy, Covid-19 vaccine development and other causes
Content: Dolly Parton pictured in 2022.Photograph: NBC/Katherine Bomboy/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDolly Parton pictured in 2022.Photograph: NBC/Katherine Bomboy/Getty ImagesDolly PartonDolly Parton, country star, actor and philanthropist, dies aged 80 after fighting cancerSongwriter of I Will Always Love You, Jolene and 9 to 5 invested millions in child literacy, Covid-19 vaccine development and other causesAlexis Petridis on Dolly Parton’s peerless career that turned country music cliches inside outDolly Parton – a life in picturesCountry music legend Dolly Parton dies aged 80 – latest updatesShare your tributes and memories of Dolly PartonBen Beaumont-ThomasTue 25 Aug 2026 13.59 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 22.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDolly Parton, one of the greatest singer-songwriters in country music, who was also much cherished for her philanthropy, has died aged 80.Her death wasannouncedby nephew Brian Seaver on Instagram. “I have imagined the heaviness of this moment but haven’t truly felt it until now,” he said. “It is an honour, an honour that is mixed with absolute pride and great sadness.”Parton’s teamconfirmedthe singer died Tuesday “after bravely facing a brief battle with cancer.”“Dolly departed her Earthly life today at the Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center surrounded by loved ones,” the statement continued.Dolly Parton – a life in picturesRead moreSo gifted that she wrote two of the 20th century’s greatest songs – Jolene and I Will Always Love You – in a single day, Parton’s songwriting was characterised by its vivid storytelling, emotional acuity and melodic strength, all sung with strident clarity. From an eventual catalogue of hundreds of songs, she scored a record 25 US country No 1 singles and 47 albums in the country Top 10. She crossed over into the pop charts with 9 to 5, a US No 1 hit in 1980; balanced her music career with acclaimed acting, twice earning Golden Globe nominations for her roles; and donated more than 300m books to children through her Imagination Library literacy project.This was all done with considerable panache, rhinestoned glamour and towering hairdos, with her immortal assertion regarding her appearance – “it takes a lot of money to look this cheap” – the most quoted example of Parton’s ready wit.View image in fullscreenDolly Parton in 1976.Photograph: PAParton was born in poverty in a one-room cabin inTennessee, the fourth child to a mother who would have 12 children by the age of 35, and a father who was a farmer and construction worker. One of her best-loved songs, Coat of Many Colours, was about her mother creating patchwork clothes; Parton’s first guitar was cobbled together from a mandolin with bass guitar strings. Her first proper guitar was given to her aged eight by her uncle, and she went from singing in church to appearing on local television aged 10, to cutting her first record aged 13. That year, she appeared at the Grand Ole Opry, the concert hall in Nashville at the center of country music, and her performance was introduced by Johnny Cash. “I’ve always believed things would go well, and I dreamed that they would even before I was in high school,” she later said. “I always wanted to be a star. It just seemed natural to me.”After graduating high school in 1964, she moved to Nashville and started out as a songwriter rather than performer. The following year, she was signed as an artist and initially moulded as a pop singer, without success; after she was allowed to switch to country, she scored back-to-back hits and released her debut album Hello, I’m Dolly. In 1966, she married Carl Dean – who died in 2025, with the couple renewing their vows in 2016 to mark 50 years together.Beginning in 1967, a duet partnership with country singer and TV personality Porter Wagoner helped her star continue to ascend, and she had her first country No 1 in 1971 with the song Joshua.Jolene, her unforgettably raw and desperate plea to a rival lover, was released in 1973 and became her first UK success, reaching No 7. I Will Always Love You, written to Wagoner as a farewell after their creative partnership ended, was a country No 1 in 1974 and again via a re-recorded version in 1982, and would go on to be a huge pop success when revived by Whitney Houston for the soundtrack of The Bodyguard in 1992: it is still the bestselling single of all time by a woman, with an estimated 20m sales.In the mid 1970s, Parton broadened her sound, embracing pop-rock arrangements on songs such as 1977’s Light of a Clear Blue Morning – its accompanying album New Harvest … First Gathering was her first entry in the pop album chart. Later that year, its follow-up, Here You Come Again, reached the Top 20 and was her first million-selling LP, powered in part by its hit title track, which also won Parton the first of her 10 Grammy awards.The year 1980 was a peak in her success, with three back-to-back country No 1s, including 9 to 5, taken from the film of the same name, which Parton starred in alongside Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin, earning her an Oscar nomination for best original song. Parton would later write songs for a stage musical version of 9 to 5, in 2008.Another classic single came in 1983 – Islands in the Stream, a duet with Kenny Rogers, which topped the US pop charts – and a Christmas album with Rogers in 1984 went two times platinum. There were more notable film roles in the 1980s, too, opposite Burt Reynolds in The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas, Sylvester Stallone in Rhinestone, and an all-star female ensemble in Steel Magnolias.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenLinda Ronstadt, Dolly Parton and Emmylou Harris in 1987.Photograph: Paul Harris/Getty ImagesA landmark Parton album came in 1987 with Trio, an exquisitely harmonised, springwater-clear collaboration with Emmylou Harris and Linda Ronstadt, earning Parton her only nomination for album of the year at the Grammys. Another all-star trio recording came in 1993, with Tammy Wynette and Loretta Lynn on the album Honky-Tonk Angels, followed by a reunion with Harris and Ronstadt for Trio II in 1999, featuring a Grammy-winning cover of Neil Young’s After the Gold Rush.The turn of the century brought a trilogy of acclaimed bluegrass albums, and Parton would release 10 more LPs, the most recent being Rockstar in 2023. She was courted by a younger generation of stars, appearing with country artists such as Brad Paisley as well as pop singers such as Kesha, and her goddaughter Miley Cyrus. There were fewer acting roles, but she lent her voice to animated film Gnomeo and Juliet in 2011 and the following year appeared alongside Queen Latifah and more in the musical film Joyful Noise.Alongside her music and acting, Parton was an astute businesswoman and philanthropist. She founded the film and TV production company Sandollar, with former manager Sandy Gallin, which went on to produce hits such as Buffy the Vampire Slayer and the Father of the Bride film series. In 1986, she took a stake in the Silver Dollar City theme park in Tennessee and renamed it Dollywood, doubling its size over the next two decades, and a Dollywood-branded spa, cabin complex, theatre-restaurant concept and waterpark have since been opened.View image in fullscreenDolly Parton in Joyful Noise.Photograph: Van Redin/Publicity image from film companyThe Dollywood Foundation, funded through these business ventures and creative projects, was created in 1988, initially awarding college scholarships and running a program to help children complete high school in her native Sevier county, Tennessee. In 1995, Parton began her Imagination Library project, which sent an age-appropriate book to every child in the county every month until they were five. “My father could not read and write, and I saw how crippling that could be,” she explained. It expanded nationwide in 2000, internationally in 2006, and nearly 25m books are now distributed each year across the US, Canada, Australia, the UK and Ireland.In 2022, Jeff Bezos donated $100m (£83m) to the foundation. That year, Parton explained that as well as improving child literacy, “it’s the fact they get recognised. They get this little book with their little name on it in the mail, and they feel special. They start taking pride in themselves, and they know that somebody out there is thinking of [them].”View image in fullscreenDolly Parton receiving the Moderna vaccine she helped to fund.Photograph: @DollyParton/ReutersParton also set up a reserve in 2003 to help preserve the bald eagle; contributed $500,000 to the opening of a Sevier county hospital in 2006; coordinated relief efforts for people affected by the Smoky mountain wildfires of 2016; and contributed to an HIV/Aids charity album. She supported Black Lives Matter and transgender rights, opposing a North Carolina “bathroom bill” that restricted transgender people’s access to toilets (Parton was also nominated for an Oscar for her song in trans drama Transamerica, entitled Travelin’ Thru).She made a number of donations to Vanderbilt University’s medical center in Nashville, Tennessee, where her niece was treated for leukemia. The most high-profile of these was in 2020, when she donated $1m for research into Covid-19, which formed the basis for the eventual Moderna vaccine.2:19Dolly Parton’s family say goodbye to their aunt, sister, grandmother - videoIn May 2026, Partoncancelledher Las Vegas residency over health issues. A Broadway musical is alsoset to openlater this year after a run in Nashville.Explore more on these topicsDolly PartonCountryPop and rockTennesseenewsShareReuse this content

title: Dolly Parton’s peerless career turned country music cliches inside out  | Dolly Parton | The Guardian
description: Beneath the wig and rhinestones, Parton was the genius behind strings of classic songs from Jolene to I Will Always Love You that continue to inspire new artists
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: Beneath the wig and rhinestones, Parton was the genius behind strings of classic songs from Jolene to I Will Always Love You that continue to inspire new artists
Content: Dolly Parton performs at halftime during a game between the Dallas Cowboys and the Washington Commanders  in 2023 in Arlington, Texas.Photograph: Brandon Sloter/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDolly Parton performs at halftime during a game between the Dallas Cowboys and the Washington Commanders  in 2023 in Arlington, Texas.Photograph: Brandon Sloter/Getty ImagesDolly PartonDolly Parton’s peerless career turned country music cliches inside outAlexis PetridisBeneath the wig and rhinestones, Parton was the genius behind strings of classic songs from Jolene to I Will Always Love You that continue to inspire new artistsDolly Parton, US country star, actor and philanthropist, dies aged 80Dolly Parton dies aged 80 – latest updatesDolly Parton’s family say goodbye to their aunt, sister, grandmother - videoShare your tributes and memories of Dolly PartonTue 25 Aug 2026 14.07 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTShareIn December 1977,Dolly Partonsubmitted to an interview with ABC Television’s Barbara Walters, much against her friends’ advice. Walters was not noted for her deep love and understanding of country music. She was a notoriously tough cookie, a Boston-born, Sarah Lawrence-educated journalist who had battled scarcely believable sexism to become the first female co-host of an American news programme. The month before she met Parton, she had interviewed Anwar Sadat and Menachem Begin while they were working out the terms of the Egypt-Israel peace treaty.It was all a very long way from Parton’s world, and the interview has something of the anthropological exercise about it. Walters looks aghast as Parton shows her around her tour bus, her collection of wigs and her “hand-washable and wrinkle-free” stage outfits (“you really like this? To me, it seems like horror”), and sits impassively as Parton sings Coat of Many Colours to her: an impressive feat, given the song’s saga of rural poverty and homespun wisdom is the mother of all tearjerkers from an artist never averse to yanking at her audience’s heartstrings. She asks Parton if people from “where I come from” would call her a hillbilly; regards the singer’s outfit with a jaundiced eye and tells her “you don’t have to look like this”. And, most infamously, she enquires: “Do you ever feel that you’re a joke?”View image in fullscreenParton performing in 1981.Photograph: LGI Stock/Corbis/VCG/Getty Images“The joke’s on the public,” responds Parton, her smile never slipping. “I know exactly what I’m doing and I can change it any time … I’m sure of myself. I’m sure of my talent.”It was a TV appearance that told you a lot about public perceptions of Parton in the years when she surged from Nashville fame to international superstardom – an era when you could turn on British TV and find a Canadian duo called MacLean and MacLean performing a mocking song called Dolly Parton’s Tits – and also told you a lot about Parton herself, most notably that, beneath the wig and the rhinestones, she had rather more in common with Walters than anyone might have thought.View image in fullscreenParton with Porter Wagoner circa 1968 in Nashville, Tennessee.Photograph: Michael Ochs Archives/Getty ImagesOf course she was sure of her talent: by the time she sat down with Walters, she had already written a string of imperishable country standards: not just Coat of Many Colours, but Jolene, My Tennessee Mountain Home, Down from Dover, I Will Always Love You, Little Bird, Kentucky Gambler, Love Is Like a Butterfly, The Bargain Store, The Seeker. Of course she knew exactly what she was doing with her image, based – as she never tired of telling interviewers – on “the town tramp” back in Pittman Center, Tennessee. A woman whose first solo hit was called Dumb Blonde, she used it both to lure in a certain type of country fan (“rednecks with flat tops who bring women who wear short skirts or tight pants,” as one 1970s journalist sniffily put it) and as a kind of glitzy, fluffy shield.Behind it, she could be subtly subversive. Years before the controversy around Loretta Lynn’s 1975 single The Pill highlighted the issue of Nashville’s sexism, Parton was writing songs of a distinctly feminist bent – Just Because I’m a Woman and When Possession Gets Too Strong among them – even if she always demurred from describing herself as such. She also had a line in songs that could give more conservative Nashville stars palpitations. Down from Dover was extraordinarily beautiful, but it seemed to simmer with empathic rage on behalf of its protagonist, an outcast unmarried mother, and concluded with a description of her giving birth to a stillborn baby. Her duet partner Porter Wagoner was so horrified that he urged her not to release it: she did, and it was summarily banned by country radio.And behind her image, she could be a model of smart, steely self-determination. If the country music establishment had a tendency to look down on her (the songwriter Tom T Hall once noted that he and Kris Kristofferson were the only two people in Nashville “who could describe Dolly Parton without using their hands”), she was abundantly aware of her own worth. The then-more-famous Wagoner was doing her a favour in 1967 when he adopted her as his duet partner, but Parton did most of the heavy lifting when it came to the pair’s songwriting, and left when it became apparent her success was beginning to outstrip his, occasioning a $3m lawsuit in the process. Moreover, she famously turned down Elvis Presley’s overtures to record the heart-rending song she wrote about the duo’s split, I Will Always Love You, when Presley’s manager indicated he wanted a cut of the songwriting royalties in return.View image in fullscreenDolly Parton in 1978.Photograph: Christian RoseShe was clearly possessed of a far greater artistic and commercial ambition than she was given credit for. The former was evidenced by 1973’s My Tennessee Mountain Home, an entirely self-penned autobiographical concept album that was rather less sentimental in its recollections than you might expect: “No amount of money could pay me to go back and live through it again,” she sang of her poverty-stricken rural upbringing on In the Good Old Days (When Times Were Bad). It ranks among the best things she ever released. Her daring became apparent around the time of the Walters interview, when Parton made a lunge for the pop mainstream, disregarding fears that it would alienate her existing audience.She scored a succession of huge pop hits: 1977’s Mann and Weill-penned Here You Come Again went to No 3 on the Hot 100, a chart on which Jolene had, incredibly, only peaked at No 60; three years later 9 to 5 hit No 1. She also transformed into an actor and dabbled in disco without losing her country essence. During her quest for mainstream success, she was as likely to essay a bluegrass version of the Beatles’ Help!, or a cover of Woody Guthrie’s Deportee (Plane Wreck at Los Gatos), or unleash upon the world Me and Little Andy, a song that anywhere other than Nashville would be regarded as a bit much – a childanda puppy snuff it in the final verse – as she was to release the winningly high-camp disco of Potential New Boyfriend. She really did know exactly what she was doing.In a sense, her moment as a mainstream crossover pop star was relatively short-lived. There was one more huge hit with 1983’s peerless Islands in the Stream, a Bee Gees-penned duet with Kenny Rodgers, but that moment had drawn to close by the time of 1987’s Rainbow. It seemed Parton had reached her limit with trying to cater to a broad audience – doggedly ploughing her way through its written-to-order contents, she sounded bored stiff, particularly when compared with the same year’s superb Trio, a collaboration with Emmylou Harris and Linda Ronstadt.View image in fullscreenDolly Parton in 1978.Photograph: Harry Langdon/Getty ImagesAnd besides, Rainbow’s commercial failure didn’t matter. Perhaps because she had never really turned her back on country – 1984’s Tennessee Homesick Blues opened with sound of Parton yodelling – Nashville welcomed her full-blooded return to the genre, with 1989’s Ricky Skaggs-produced White Limozeen. If she never scored another US Hot 100 hit, the broader celebrity she had established in the late 70s and early 80s never waned for the rest of her life. Tellingly, while promoting White Limozeen’s standout track, the insanely catchy and uproariously funny Why’d You Come in Here Lookin’ Like That?, she hosted Saturday Night Live: it would be a decade before another country star did so.In truth, Parton’s subsequent albums were of a decidedly mixed quality, at least until she returned to absolute basics: 1999’s Grammy-winning The Grass Is Blue kicked off a trio of stark, fantastic albums that dealt in bluegrass, Appalachian folk and country gospel, the music that she had “grown up surrounded by”. Thereafter, what she put out was hit-and-and miss: misjudged horrors including 2003’s post-9/11 collection of patriotic songs, For God andCountry, abutting albums as good as 2014’s Blue Smoke, although her voice sounded magnificent no matter the material. She was still more than capable of writing fantastic songs – but nothing that could eclipse the best of her 70s material.It didn’t really matter, because the best of her 70s material had long taken on a life of its own outside country music. Whitney Houston’s cover of I Will Always Love You became the biggest-selling single of all time by a female artist. At the last count, Jolene has been covered nearly 90 times: you could hear it rendered as noisy alt-rock by the White Stripes, synth-pop by Strawberry Switchblade, or a dubby post-club soundtrack by One Dove. Stars queued up to pay homage.View image in fullscreenParton attends the opening of the Country Music Hall of Fame and the museum’s show, Dolly Parton: Journey of a Seeker, in 2025.Photograph: Jason Kempin/Getty ImagesMeanwhile, in the 21st century, the full extent of Parton’s influence on pop became apparent. Younger stars queued up to pay homage of one kind or another. Taylor Swift, who knows a thing or two about pivoting away from country to pop, called her “a force of evolution and transformation in our industry”. Parton co-wrote Rainbowland on her goddaughter Miley Cyrus’s 2017 album Younger Now, and you didn’t have to analyse Sabrina Carpenter’s work too deeply to spot the influence. The fact that Carpenter’s 2024 smash Please Please Please sounded like something Parton might have written evidently didn’t escape Parton herself: she turned up duetting with Carpenter on a remixed version of the song, the swearing decorously omitted.As fans of Tammy Wynette or Patsy Cline would be quick to point out, Parton certainly wasn’t the first female country star to cross over into the pop charts, but she nevertheless seemed like the godmother of the pop-country that has swept the charts in recent years, which one Spotify playlist characterised as “Neon Cowgirl” (Parton was by far the oldest artist to make said playlist, rubbing shoulders with Swift, Carpenter, Chappell Roan, Kesha et al). When Beyoncé made a musical leap into country on Cowboy Carter, it somehow seemed inevitable that Parton would be involved, and so it proved: she delivered a spoken-word introduction to Beyoncé’s redux of Jolene. In fact, she seemed as present in pop music in the mid-2020s as she had been in the late 70s. The difference was that no one would have asked her if she was a joke. That question had been answered to everyone’s satisfaction a long time ago.Explore more on these topicsDolly PartonCountrycommentShareReuse this content
