title: ‘The whole world is becoming rightwing and anti-gay’: William Yang on 60 years of capturing LGBTQ+ life | Photography | The Guardian
description: Yang has taken more than 500,000 photographs since he first moved to Sydney in the late 1960s and now devotes most of his time to untangling the past
Author: Oliver Giles
Headline: Yang has taken more than 500,000 photographs since he first moved to Sydney in the late 1960s and now devotes most of his time to untangling the past
Content: ‘Now I couldn’t take a camera into a sauna’ … William Yang at the exhibition Inside the Mirage at the TarraWarra Museum of Art in Victoria.Photograph: Thomas McCammon for TarraWarra Museum of ArtView image in fullscreen‘Now I couldn’t take a camera into a sauna’ … William Yang at the exhibition Inside the Mirage at the TarraWarra Museum of Art in Victoria.Photograph: Thomas McCammon for TarraWarra Museum of ArtPhotography‘The whole world is becoming rightwing and anti-gay’: William Yang on 60 years of capturing LGBTQ+ lifeYang has taken more than 500,000 photographs since he first moved to Sydney in the late 1960s and now devotes most of his time to untangling the pastOliver GilesTue 25 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTShareAs a young adult, William Yang discovered that his family’s story was actually a murder mystery. His uncle, William Fang Yuen, was killed by an employee on the family’s farm in far north Queensland in 1922, but his mother refused to tell him the full story. In 1990, he travelled to Innisfail in search of the truth.One aunt told Yang that his uncle and the worker had got into a fight over a gambling debt, and the worker had stabbed him to death with a spear. A cousin said a gang was involved. A local woman, who had been a child at the time, remembered it as a card game gone wrong.Desperate for concrete evidence, Yang visited the local courthouse, where he was presented with a dusty box of documents. Inside, there were papers caked in his uncle’s blood.“He was holding these when he died,” the sprightly 82-year-old recently told a rapt crowd at TarraWarra Museum ofArtin Victoria, his photograph of the stained sheets of paper glowing on the screen behind him.View image in fullscreenBlood spattered documents, from William Yang’s My Uncle’s Murder series, in 2008.Photograph: William YangView image in fullscreenWilliam Fang Yuen and business partners, from William Yang’s My Uncle’s Murder series, in 2008.Photograph: William YangIt turns out there was no spear, no mafia, no game of poker. Piecing together the records, it seems Yang’s uncle had accused his employee of fiddling the farm’s accounts. They had an argument and Yang’s uncle was shot dead. The man was brought to trial, then acquitted in a decision that many believe was racist: Yang’s uncle was Chinese and his employee was white. “This verdict upset the Chinese at the time,” Yang told his audience. “They thought it was a great miscarriage of justice.”Yang’s account of his family’s story is part of TarraWarra’s exhibition Inside the Mirage, which features several artists whose work explores the diaspora experience in Australia. Seven of Yang’s trademark annotated photographs tell the story of his uncle’s death and how it traumatised his mother, who was 16 when it happened and raised Yang and his siblings to be “more Australian than the Australians.” On the final photo, of a transcript of the evidence that his mother gave during the trial, Yang has written: “I feel the legacy of this murder came down to me in that, while I was growing up, my ethnicity was suppressed.”Yang now devotes most of his time to untangling the past. He has taken between 500,000 and 1 million photographs since the late 1960s, when he first moved to Sydney. It was there that Yang came out as gay in his late 20s and became a documentarian of the city’s LGBTQ+ community, photographing individuals and events through the debauchery of the 1970s, the horror of the HIV/Aids crisis in the 1980s and 1990s, the growing acceptance and subsequent journey to gay marriage in 2017.Alongside these are photos documenting how Yang came to embrace his Chinese heritage – he says he “came out as Chinese” in his mid 30s – as well as his portraits of Australian cultural luminaries such as the writers Patrick White and Barbara Blackman; artists such as Brett Whiteley and Max Dupain; and actors like Cate Blanchett and Sam Neill.Open gallery|0The State Library of New South Wales has acquired about 50,000 of Yang’s negatives from the 1970s and is now negotiating with the photographer over his images from the 1980s and 1990s, which he is busy digitising. “So many photographers leave their negatives in a dusty, unsorted pile,” Yang says. “I’m digitising the negatives to give the photos a chance of life.”Yang still occasionally photographs events and is working on a book of nudes titled The Male Body, but spends most days organising his archive. The process has given him new insights into his own work. “Looking back, I think the strongest element in my collection is the gay events,” he says. “People used to tell me, ‘I wouldn’t worry about that gay stuff. It’s so marginalised. You’ll come to your senses and start photographing the real world.’ But it’s in the margins where I think the value of the work is.”Some of his favourite photos were taken in the late 1970s and early 1980s at Ken’s Karate Klub, a gay sauna in Sydney, where a drag queen invited him to capture the shows she put on beside the pool. “Now I couldn’t take a camera into a sauna,” he says. “I’d be run out the place!”View image in fullscreen‘The gay community had been invisible for thousands of years – now there was a chance to be visible’ … William Yang at TarraWarra.Photograph: Thomas McCammon for TarraWarra Museum of ArtAnother memorable event was a party where the hosts wheeled out a young man on a table, decorated like a cake. “You could eat the cream off him,” says Yang, grinning cheekily. “I don’t think people would do that nowadays … Social media has changed everything.”Back then, Yang says, people were not only happy to be photographed; they were hungry for it. “One of the revelations I had in the seventies was that the gay community had been invisible for thousands of years, and now there was a chance to be visible. That was generally seized on.”Increased visibility helped change the public perception of the LGBTQ+ community, which helped earn greater legal rights. When Yang waslast profiled by the Guardian, in 2016, he worried “that the times are more conservative now.” A year later, the result of the gay marriage plebiscite allayed his fears. “That was a huge victory,” Yang says now. “It was a cultural shift [proving] we had majority approval.”Today, Yang is once again concerned about politics. “I see that the whole world is becoming rightwing and anti-gay,” he says. Although politicians like Pauline Hanson are seeing theirpopularity rising, Yang says, on balance, “we’re extremely lucky that we live in Australia and have free expression.”At one point in his monologue at TarraWarra, Yang shared an old worry he once had, that he might not “fulfil his destiny” of becoming a photographer. His final slide featured aportrait of Yang painted by Kean Onn See, which was nominated for this year’s Archibald prize. In the painting, Yang sits in his archive, dwarfed by boxes full of his photographs documenting personal and societal change. The painting was displayed on banners around Sydney, putting Yang and his life’s work in the spotlight.“Remember when I felt I had not fulfilled my destiny?” Yang asked the crowd at the end of his talk. “Well, now I feel I have. At times I’ve struggled … But by and large, I feel I’ve done it. It’s a good feeling to be satisfied.”View image in fullscreenKean Onn See’s painting, ‘At the studio of William Yang’, which was nominated for the 2026 Archibald prize.Photograph: Jenni CarterInside the Mirage isshowing at TarraWarra Museum of Artuntil 1 November

title: The cat that fought Mussolini: how the Wulz photography sisters weaponised the family pet | Photography | The Guardian
description: Wanda and Marion Wulz defied the unbridled patriarchy of fascist Italy by shooting dancers, fencers and other famous women – as well as their cat Mucincina
Author: Joanna Moorhead
Headline: Wanda and Marion Wulz defied the unbridled patriarchy of fascist Italy by shooting dancers, fencers and other famous women – as well as their cat Mucincina
Content: ‘Cats symbolise freedom’ …the famous I + Cat image, combining the faces of Wanda and Mucincina.Photograph: Wanda Wulz/Archivi Alinari-Collezione Zannier, FlorenceView image in fullscreen‘Cats symbolise freedom’ …the famous I + Cat image, combining the faces of Wanda and Mucincina.Photograph: Wanda Wulz/Archivi Alinari-Collezione Zannier, FlorencePhotographyThe cat that fought Mussolini: how the Wulz photography sisters weaponised the family petWanda and Marion Wulz defied the unbridled patriarchy of fascist Italy by shooting dancers, fencers and other famous women – as well as their cat MucincinaJoanna MoorheadTue 25 Aug 2026 10.12 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 12.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘In those fascist times,” says Federica Muzzarelli ofItalyin the 1920s and 30s, “women were not free. They were regarded as mothers and homemakers. But the Wulz sisters were determined to create their own destiny. They chose photography as a way of being independent – and to show through their images that women could live that way.”Muzzarelli is the curator of Wanda and Marion Wulz: Avant-Garde Photography in 20th Century Italy, a show about to open at theEstorick Collectionin London. The Wulz sisters experimented with blended and altered images more than half a century before Photoshop was invented. The most famous image to emerge from their studio was I + Cat, a self-portrait of Wanda superimposed on the face of the family pet. But the show aims to cast Marion in a new light, showing that she was no mere assistant, but rather equal to her sister in terms of photography, as they championed feminism in fascist Italy, keeping the idea of women’s emancipation alive at a time of unbridled patriarchal ideology.double quotation markFamous women wanted to be photographed by themWanda, born in Trieste in 1903, was a promising dancer and musician; Marion, two years her junior, had been to art school and wanted to paint. But after the pair inherited their father’s photographic studio, which had in turn been founded by his father, they realised it represented their best path to an autonomous future. “They photographed modern women, dancing, playing sports, doing gymnastics,” says Muzzarelli. Women who were artists, poets, writers and actors sat for the sisters. Among them were painter Leonor Fini and Olympic fencing champion Irene Camber.View image in fullscreenModern woman … fencer Irene Camber.Photograph: Marion Wulz/Archivi Alinari-Archivio Studio Wulz, FlorenceIn 1932, Wanda exhibited six works, including I + Cat in the National Exhibition of FuturistPhotography. The show was staged to mark 10 years since the fascist revolution but, contends Muzzarelli, Wanda was never interested in that . She just wanted to show, as the only woman taking part, that she was every bit as capable as the men.“She showed she had the ability and skill to create a photomontage,” says Muzzarelli. Her technique for I + Cat, which superimposed one negative on top of another, was invented in the mid-19th century, but Wanda used it in a new way, making one face hers and the other that of Mucincina, the family cat. Both negatives will be in the London show, as well as the finished work. “Wanda wanted to explore the idea of female identity, of the cat as a free creature, a symbol of freedom,” says Muzzarelli, who believes another picture Wanda showed in the 1932 exhibition – Futurist Breakfast, showing items from a woman’s dresser – was also included to make a feminist point.The exhibition was Wanda’s only foray into futurism, but the years that followed were the sisters’ heyday. They continued to live in the apartment block in central Trieste in which they had been born, and where their studio was based. It became the centre of an informal female salon.View image in fullscreen‘They wanted to look perfect’ … ballerina Alba Wiegele.Photograph: Marion Wulz/Archivi Alinari-Archivio Studio Wulz, Florence“For several years,” says Claudia Baroncini, director of the Fondazione Alinari per la Fotografia, which owns the sisters’ archive, “the fashion designer Anita Pittoni lived with them. With her, they created a kind of club of artists – women who wanted to experiment with new ways of living. So they were pushing a different sort of life alongside a different sort of photography. And of course, photography has always been about a fusion of ideas and reality. So they were living their art.”Their first role in the studio was as subjects – they were often dressed up and photographed by their father, Carlo, when they were children. So they were always acutely aware of self-image, of disguise, of what appearance symbolised. As portrait photographers they were experts at “improving” the look of their sitters. “They were very clever with negatives,” says Baroncini, “creating shadows to change the shape of someone’s mouth or eyes, or to improve the quality of their skin. You can see, looking at the negatives, how much work they did to make their prints perfect. And that meant famous women wanted to be photographed by them, because they wanted to look perfect.”They also photographed one another: the show will include Marion’s striking portrait of Wanda wearing motorcycle goggles and another of her dressed as Cleopatra, while Wanda’s shots of Marion include her wearing designs by Pittoni, along with an extraordinarily modern-looking closeup with shining eyes.In spring 1945, as the second world war ended, Trieste was liberated from fascist rule by the Yugoslav army. From the terrace of their apartment, Marion photographed tanks and soldiers – and later celebrations in the street when the Anglo-American troops arrived. “These images show she was fully part of the artistic partnership,” says Baroncini.Although the women worked until the 1970s, they never recaptured their early success. Money became a struggle and they closed their studio in 1981, while continuing to take photographs. After Wanda died in 1984, Marion – who lived another nine years – documented their life and work together in a series of diaries.“Their lives had been tough,” says Baroncini, “and they didn’t realise the importance of their work for the history of photography. Wanda had a brief burst of fame during the futurist period, but they would be very surprised to know that, more than 120 years after their births, they were being recognised as great photographers.”At theEstorick Collection, London, from 16 September to 20 DecemberExplore more on these topicsPhotographyItalyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Camping trips, grief and embarrassing your kids – the fringe shows embracing every facet of fatherhood | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Edinburgh comedies by Whisper Theatre, Lightning Rod Special and Olaf Falafel are exploring what it’s like to be a dad, from the hilarious and melancholic to the devastatingly accurate cringe
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: Edinburgh comedies by Whisper Theatre, Lightning Rod Special and Olaf Falafel are exploring what it’s like to be a dad, from the hilarious and melancholic to the devastatingly accurate cringe
Content: Best. Dads. Ever. … Britt Anderson and Richie Schiraldi in Well-Balanced Dads.Photograph: The Whisper Theatre CollectiveView image in fullscreenBest. Dads. Ever. … Britt Anderson and Richie Schiraldi in Well-Balanced Dads.Photograph: The Whisper Theatre CollectiveEdinburgh festival 2026Camping trips, grief and embarrassing your kids – the fringe shows embracing every facet of fatherhoodEdinburgh comedies by Whisper Theatre, Lightning Rod Special and Olaf Falafel are exploring what it’s like to be a dad, from the hilarious and melancholic to the devastatingly accurate cringeChris WiegandTue 25 Aug 2026 07.56 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 08.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a historic masonic lodge in Edinburgh’s New Town I find myself raising my hand. The call has gone out for fathers in the audience and I join our hosts, Dick and Dale, along with another volunteer on stage. It’s just us four guys at a campsite, practising trick shots with a baseball, busting some moves and shooting the breeze. But bubbling underneath is an existential crisis.This isWell-Balanced Dads, from Chicago’sWhisper Theatre Collective, created by Dick and Dale themselves – AKA Richie Schiraldi and Britt Anderson. They’re sporting headbands, bum bags and tank tops blazoned with “Best. Dad. Ever”, each with a different back print – one’s a power drill, the other’s a barbecue. Both have bushy moustaches and they supply us volunteers with our own. There are bursts of classic rock – Foghat, Kenny Loggins, Creedence Clearwater Revival – as we join them on a road trip and other volunteers are cast as hitchhikers.Fatherhood has given both our hosts a sense of pride and purpose but what happens now their kids have flown the nest, leaving each with just their wives (Mary and, er, Mary) and each other for company? Who is there to appreciate/disdain their dad jokes and dad dancing? We get a lot of both in this highly physical show, which also unexpectedly adds a sensual dads’ dream ballet to the mix, as Dick and Dale take a family-style holiday without the kids in tow.double quotation markYou too may find something in your eye – surely sawdust or something equally manlyThat means there’s a sweetly melancholic air to these proceedings as the dads play hide and seek, break out their best holiday shirts and end up regressing into children themselves, complete with “are we nearly there yet?” pleas to the hitchhikers. There’s a keen awareness that the Marys usually run the show at home – with the dads packing all the wrong stuff,a bit like when Bandit takes the kids to the pool in Bluey.The audience participation is refreshingly ridicule-free and the central bromance blossoms, filling the room with goodwill. Individual theatregoers are singled out as legends by the dads for their admirable qualities. “This guy,” marvels Schiraldi as he hovers over my seat, “hasn’t paid his taxes for 18 years!” (I have, honest!) It’s akin to the ribbing you get at a family gathering.Fathers in the audience will feel seen and may well momentarily cringe if, purely by example, they find these dads also bombastically quoting their favourite lines from Gladiator. You too may find something in your eye – surely sawdust or something equally manly – when Dick and Dale open up about how much they miss their kids and give them a call. One of the offspring heartbreakingly suggests a weekly rather than daily catchup; the other is beginning to show their own care and concern towards their father.View image in fullscreenParenting and pride … Scott R Shepherd and Alice Yorke in Lions.Photograph: Wide Eyed StudiosIt ends with one of the loveliest scenes I’ve experienced at this year’s fringe as Dick and Dale roam the audience offering fist-bumps, jokes, hugs and other dad business to anyone who needs them. (Yes, they’ve brought a tape measure.) It caps off an hour of gently serious silliness that I enjoyed just as much as my 12-year-old daughter, delighted to see her dad make a fool of himself on stage. But that’s one welcome side-effect of parenthood: becoming 100% unembarrassable.Over at Summerhall, another couple of legends have a show about parenthood and pride – that’s surely why it’s called Lions. This moustachioed double act blend the character comedy with more openly autobiographical material in a production by the US companyLightning Rod Specialthat aims to break down “the myths our fathers told themselves about becoming great men”.There are goofy jokes here, too, about brewskis, barbecue and baseball but the costumes are cravats, tweed and coiffed wigs. There are also echoes of A Christmas Carol and, as we arrive, writer-performers Alice Yorke and Scott R Sheppard are laying a candlelit table as if for a feast yet amid the bagels are a bike helmet, a trophy and assorted paraphernalia. This is a multilayered alternative to an Edinburgh cliche, “the dead dad show”, with each actor announcing – with disarmingly cheery gusto – that they’re here to relive that loss and uncover what kind of men they were.Directed and developed by Sarah Blush, Lions mashes together eras – the performers are just as likely to brandish quills as record voice notes. It captures the sense that dads always hail from an unrecognisable era for their children, will always seem a bit fusty and formal to them, no matter how hard they try not to.View image in fullscreenThese dad jokes are award-winning … Olaf Falafel.Lions dramatically deals with the approach and aftermath of death, channelling the over-caffeinated state of waiting in hospitals and how sorting the paperwork becomes a temporary job for the children. There’s a chilling section that brings to mind Forced Entertainment’s unforgettable First Night when they consider who in this audience might die next. The rawness of Yorke and Sheppard’s autobiographical tributes floored me, as did the list of life’s disappointments itemised by Yorke’s dad who wished he’d been braver. Both of these shows offer fatherly advice in different ways – I’m asked to share my old man’s own words of wisdom in Well-Balanced Dads, which by default is a message to my daughter.A supreme being, the nearly naked show and politics with paws: Edinburgh fringe pick’n’mixRead moreBoth productions also create comedy from the befuddled reactions of the performers’ parents to their offspring’s artistic pursuits.Olaf Falafelupturns that dynamic with his multimedia fringe hour I Used to Work in a Helium Balloon Factory Until they Let Me Go. He takes great delight in detailing his teenage daughters’ withering responses to a career in comedy that finds him spending hours a day editing squirrel videos, making his own janky Meta glasses from Gü pots and animating a man who used to “twerk on the ducks” to accompany a misheard Bon Jovi lyric.The difference here is that these dad jokes areregular award-winnersand there are also some affectionate, relatable dispatches from dadhood – who hasn’t amassed their own mountain of those hairbands strewn in every corner of the home? One of the many things I loved about the show is how Olaf (it just sounds weird to call him Falafel) breaks off for a passing observation on how adopting a daft mask can be freeing, not just on stage – like a newly acquired, increasingly sweaty joke shop moustache as you try out some dad dancing – but in daily life, too. That’s a top fatherly tip. And there’s a nice final touch as his daughter cheerily holds the bucket for the audience’s money. Maybe he’s not so embarrassing after all.Well-Balanced Dadsis at Braw Venues @ Hill Street, Edinburgh, until 30 August.Lionsis at Summerhall, Edinburgh, until 30 August.Olaf Falafel Presents: I Used to Work in a Helium Balloon Factory Until they Let Me Gois at Laughing Horse @ the Pear Tree, Edinburgh, until 30 August.Explore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreComedy (Stage)ClownsParents and parentingComedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Climate-saving wonder – or €240m vanity bauble that ages like milk? The rocks set to hit Rotterdam docks | Architecture | The Guardian
description: MVRDV – the firm behind Marble Arch Mound – says Rotterdam ROCKS! will inspire visitors to live sustainably. But in an era when the greenest building is the one that already exists, this tottering cairn looks set to misfire
Author: Catherine Slessor
Headline: MVRDV – the firm behind Marble Arch Mound – says Rotterdam ROCKS! will inspire visitors to live sustainably. But in an era when the greenest building is the one that already exists, this tottering cairn looks set to misfire
Content: ‘Flintstones-esque primitivism’ … a digital rendering of Rotterdam ROCKS!Illustration: MVRDVView image in fullscreen‘Flintstones-esque primitivism’ … a digital rendering of Rotterdam ROCKS!Illustration: MVRDVArchitectureClimate-saving wonder – or €240m vanity bauble that ages like milk? The rocks set to hit Rotterdam docksMVRDV – the firm behind Marble Arch Mound – says Rotterdam ROCKS! will inspire visitors to live sustainably. But in an era when the greenest building is the one that already exists, this tottering cairn looks set to misfireCatherine SlessorTue 25 Aug 2026 07.37 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 13.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘It looks like something Shrek would throw up,” sniffed one online commentator, unflatteringly comparing Rotterdam ROCKS!, the recently unveiled proposal for a waterfront site in Europe’s largest port, with the vomitings of a cartoon ogre. Designed by Dutch architectural firm MVRDV, which gave London the supremely underwhelmingMarble Arch Moundin 2021, Rotterdam ROCKS! (the use of EMPHATIC CAPITALS connoting an in-your-face energy) is the winner of a major architectural competition intended to create “a new world wonder”.But instead of a modern Hanging Gardens of Babylon or contemporary Colossus of Rhodes, MVRDV’s super slick renderings depict a pile of artificial “rocks” (or ROCKS!) stacked together in a humongously scaled tottering cairn, wreathed in suspiciously luxuriant foliage and sluiced by a preposterous waterfall.Conceived as a paying visitor attraction that will proselytise aspects of sustainability and green living, the €240m (£205m) project is the precocious brainchild of Dutch entrepreneurDon Ritzen, who made his reputation throughRockstart, a venture capital fund for green tech startups. Ritzen’s evangelising mission is to speed the world’s transition to a green economy via his non-profit organisationShift, which provided the impetus for a radical new landmark building – to be constructed on a site previously earmarked for football club Feyenoord’s new stadium.View image in fullscreen‘Turns architecture into a regenerative, urban ecosystem’ … a rendering of the central hall of Rotterdam ROCKS!Illustration: MVRDVThe project will anchor the Waterkant, a more architecturally humdrum large-scale urban development on the south bank of the Maas. Pulverised during the second world war, Rotterdam’s docklands have provided an obliging tabula rasa for architectural experimentation, but with its amped-up, Flintstones-esque primitivism, Rotterdam ROCKS! will be far and away the most conspicuously off piste offering to date.Hyperbole abounds. Described as “a stacked landscape of living rocks that turns architecture into a regenerative, urban ecosystem and a new landmark for the city: rocks that breathe”, the project incorporates the more prosaic functions of a hotel, conference centre, food court and viewing deck. Underpinning it all is an immersive experience called the Elysium, which will illustrate paradigms for sustainability and circular living, elevating them into “something individuals, companies and organisations can feel, experience and act on”.View image in fullscreenInspiring a new green gospel? … a rendering of the Elysium experience at Rotterdam ROCKS!Illustration: MVRDVIn theory, visitors forking out entrance fees between €20 and €45 will come away energised and motivated to spread a new green gospel that goes beyond recycling their rubbish and carbon-offsetting their short break flights. But in practice, it may well end up being just a wallet-sapping mooch around a weird-looking building, rather like visiting a funfair.Ifthe dismaying experience of the Marble Arch Moundis anything to go by, then MVRDV will have its work cut out. Optimistically conceived as a temporary artificial hill, softly studded with lush vegetation, the Mound was beset by cost overruns, shonky construction and visitor apathy. Its patchy flanks of stuck-on turf were describedby one criticas “more like an ensemble of ill-matched carpet tiles than a greensward”, prompting comparisons to those scrubby winter wonderlands that pop up every Christmas to disappoint yuletide revellers.View image in fullscreenBack to reality … Marble Arch Mound.Photograph: David Levene/the GuardianComputer-generated renderings are a perpetual hostage to fortune, and MVRDV went gangbusters on Rotterdam ROCKS!, doubtless in an attempt to seduce the competition jurors. But already some aspects of the design are being dialled down – the sluicing waterfall has been quietly aborted – as the chastening reality of how this absurd confection might actually be built begins to sink in. A non-computer generated image shows architect Winy Maas (the M of MVRDV) clutching a pile of moss-covered pebbles.Wider contradictions also abound. Ritzen clearly subscribes to history’s “great man” theory, in which idealistic outliers and entrepreneurs heroically save the world, and progress is impelled by “charismatic” individuals (the Musks and the Zuckerbergs) rather than the messy flailings of collective political and social endeavour.But in an era increasingly being reshaped by the mantra “the greenest building is the one that already exists”, the idea of a constructing a hugely costly vanity bauble that promises to age like milk seems like a stupendous misfire, calculated simply to stroke egos and stoke clickbait.View image in fullscreenDoubly damned … a rendering of Rotterdam ROCKS!Illustration: MVRDVWouter Vanstiphout, a leading Dutch architectural historian,summed it up: “It is as if MVRDV has allowed the entire fundamental contradiction between architecture and sustainability to implode in a gesture of ontological self-loathing, a metaphorical ruin of the very idea of architecture, collapsing under its own weight, gnawed at and overgrown by a nature that has turned against humanity out of spite.”The final irony was that Rotterdam ROCKS! was unveiled during the height of Europe’s infernal summer, when the existential consequences of the climate crisis became even more viscerally apparent, as wildfires immolated large tracts of hill and dale. Low-lyingNetherlands(the Maldives of Europe) is doubly damned, with over half its terrain also vulnerable to flooding. Nearly all of Rotterdam lies below sea level, so if things continue on the predicted hell-in-a-handcart trajectory, Rotterdam ROCKS! may well be under water some day. Which might be the best place for it.Explore more on these topicsArchitectureNetherlandsClimate crisisRegenerationfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Seam me up, Scotty! After 60 years, Star Trek has had a muppet takeover. About time too | Television | The Guardian
description: Star Wars has embraced the magic of puppetry since the 70s, but Trekkers have been starved of any muppet action … until now. The creators of Strange New Worlds talk about boldly sewing where no one has sewn before
Author: Duncan Barrett
Headline: Star Wars has embraced the magic of puppetry since the 70s, but Trekkers have been starved of any muppet action … until now. The creators of Strange New Worlds talk about boldly sewing where no one has sewn before
Content: A major departure … Star Trek: Strange New Worlds comes over all puppet.Photograph: Jan Thijs/Paramount+View image in fullscreenA major departure … Star Trek: Strange New Worlds comes over all puppet.Photograph: Jan Thijs/Paramount+TelevisionSeam me up, Scotty! After 60 years, Star Trek has had a muppet takeover. About time tooStar Wars has embraced the magic of puppetry since the 70s, but Trekkers have been starved of any muppet action … until now. The creators of Strange New Worlds talk about boldly sewing where no one has sewn beforeDuncan BarrettTue 25 Aug 2026 04.17 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s life, Jim – but very muchnotas we know it.In fact, when it comes to the latest episode of Star Trek: Strange New Worlds, the life forms in question are less flesh-and-blood and more fabric-and-felt – as the series becomes the latest sci-fi show to embrace the magic of puppetry.Level-Five Transporter Accident follows in a longstanding Trek tradition that sees crew membersundergo unfortunate transformations while beaming up to the ship. This time, the crew suffers an even greater indignity: thanks to a spot of boldly sewing from the legendary Jim Henson’s Creature Shop, the Enterprise team are reconstituted into – quite literally – a bunch of muppets.“I thought it would be a big swing for us, but we spent a lot of time discussing how to do it as a Star Trek episode,” says Strange New Worlds showrunner Henry Alonso Myers. “Because I knew if it didn’t feel like Star Trek then it wouldn’t work.”It’s a major departure for the Trek franchise, which turns 60 next month. Across nearly 1,000 episodes and 13 movies, Star Trek has always eschewed the art of puppetry – in stark contrast to its cooler, younger siblingStar Wars. Luke Skywalker’s mentor Yoda in The Empire Strikes Back was just one of many iconic puppetcharacters who populated the original movie trilogy.View image in fullscreen‘A big swing’ … La’an Noonien-Singh (Christina Chong) and Una (Rebecca Romijn) in Level-Five Transporter Accident.Photograph: Jan Thijs/Paramount+“The Star Wars universe has a very tangible, lived-in quality, which was different to a lot of science fiction at the time,” says Brian Herring, the British puppeteer who operated lovable droid BB-8 in the most recent Star Wars movies. “Back in the 70s and 80s, George Lucas was using every trick in the book to populate that universe, and that included puppets as well as people in creature suits.” Ever since, sci-fi and puppetry have gone hand-in-glove, from ET to Little Shop of Horrors, Gremlins and beyond.View image in fullscreen‘I’ll be right here’ … ET.Photograph: Universal Pictures/AllstarMeanwhile, despite Star Trek’s six-decade commitment ‘to seek out new life’, the franchise has remained a puppet-free zone.“Star Trek made a big commitment to makeup early on,” says Dr Chris Nunn, assistant professor of film at the University of Birmingham. “So aliens would typically be played by human actors under heavy prosthetic masks, and that trend has continued.”So why the unexpected course-correction from a franchise about to enter its seventh decade? The answer, it turns out, is less about the magic of puppetry and more about the tropes of modern TV production.“Doing a puppet episode is a TV concept,” says Myers. “One of the things we try to do on Strange New Worlds is go for big swings that haven’t been done before in Star Trek.” (Hence an all-singing, all-dancing musical episode named Subspace Rhapsody and the part-animated Those Old Scientists.)For advice, Myers turned to former Angel showrunner Jeffrey Bell, who worked on the fan-favourite episode Smile Time, which sees its titular vampire, played by David Boreanaz, transformed into a puppet while investigating a sinister Sesame Street-style mystery.In Strange New Worlds, Myers flipped the format on its head, keeping Ethan Peck’s Spock as flesh and (green Vulcan) blood, while forcing the rest of the Enterprise crew to become chaotic, muppety versions of themselves.“Spock was the obvious character to run into this problem,” says Myers. “Because he’s so logical.” The episode’s director, Jordan Canning, agrees. “Spock was 100% the right choice,” she laughs. “He’s the ultimate straight man.”View image in fullscreen‘He’s the ultimate straight-man!’ Spock (Ethan Peck) and Erica Ortegas (Melissa Navia) in Star Trek: Strange New Worlds.Photograph: Jan Thijs/Paramount+Like the hit Star Wars TV series The Mandalorian, Strange New Worlds uses a giant LED screen known as the Volume rather than building physical stage sets. Sci-fi actors must be particularly adept at playing make-believe, but according to Canning, the puppets made things easier for Peck.“The Star Trek cast are amazing at working with their imaginations,” she says. “But when you have great puppeteers, you don’t really have to work at it. You can’t help but feel connected to those characters.”Myers agrees. “The fact that Ethan is physically interacting with the puppets, not just looking at a tennis ball on a stick, makes the whole thing feel more real,” he says.“It’s like Ryan Gosling in Project Hail Mary,” says Nunn. “That movie wouldn’t have worked if they’d added the alien in post. The fact that Gosling was reacting live in the moment is what made their relationship feel genuine.”For Dawn Dininger, one of five puppeteers who operates Grogu in The Mandalorian, it’s a double-edged sword. “The actors always forget that he’s a puppet.” she says. “They just think he’s a baby and start rocking him and playing with him. They never talk to us, even though we’re the ones controlling him. They forget we’re there.”View image in fullscreen‘Sigourney Weaver was starstruck by Baby Yoda!’ … Pedro Pascal as the Mandalorian and Signourney Weaver as Colonel Ward in The Mandalorian and Grogu.Photograph: Justin Lubin/Lucasfilm/Disney/APAlthough The Mandalorian notionally focuses on Pedro Pascal’s titular bounty hunter, it’s his puppet sidekick Grogu (AKA Baby Yoda) who steals the show – as evidenced by the not-so-subtle name-change for this year’s movie spin-off, The Mandalorian and Grogu.A puppet-fabricator by training, Dininger was unprepared for the cult status the character would almost instantly accrue. Now, when top Hollywood actors appear opposite the puppet – as Sigourney Weaver recently did – it’s the A-listers who are starstruck.“It’s like tagging along with a famous person!” laughs Dininger. “Nobody knows who you are, but they all know him, and they get excited as soon as they see him on set.”View image in fullscreen‘The actors think he’s a baby … they forget we’re here’ – a puppeteer on The Mandalorian and Grogu.Photograph: Nicola Goode/Lucasfilm/Disney/AP“I was under the table thinking, I can’t believe I’m interacting with Sigourney Weaver. Then afterwards I asked if I could get a photo, and she was like, ‘Well, yeah. Because I need a photo with Grogu.’ She couldn’t get over him. It was really cute.”It’s a stark contrast to the Star Wars prequels of the late 1990s, which had a heavy reliance on green screen and CGI. Controversially, puppet Yoda was replaced mid-trilogy by an eerily acrobatic digital doppelganger.“Suddenly Yoda’s jumping around,” remembers Nunn. “That was kind of freaky for those of us who grew up with the puppet.”By the time of the Star Wars sequel trilogy, practical skills were at the forefront again.“We see elements of physical craftsmanship,” says Nunn, “and I don’t think that’s rooted entirely in nostalgia. I think it’s also about the film-maker saying, ‘I really care about this.’”It might be a while before we find out if Star Trek will follow in Grogu’s rubbery footsteps. Strange New Worlds is ending next year, and Trek production is now on hold, waiting for the dust to settle from the Paramount-Skydance merger.In the meantime, though, the puppets are still out there. “They’re in storage,” says Canning. “Those puppets will always exist. I would love to get them out again and make some short films or a web series or something.“If the fans like it, let’s get them out again. Let the puppets play!”Star Trek: Strange New Worlds is on Paramount+Explore more on these topicsTelevisionStar TrekStar Wars: The Empire Strikes BackStar Wars: The Mandalorian and GroguStar WarsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Environmental violence’: inside the fight to save indigenous land from becoming a nuclear dumping ground | Documentary films | The Guardian
description: New documentary To Use a Mountain spotlights the pain and triumph of resisting government efforts to turn parts of rural US into disposal sites
Author: Andrew Lawrence
Headline: New documentary To Use a Mountain spotlights the pain and triumph of resisting government efforts to turn parts of rural US into disposal sites
Content: Peace activists standing at the entry to the Nevada National Security Site in To Use a Mountain.Photograph: To Use a Mountain, LLCView image in fullscreenPeace activists standing at the entry to the Nevada National Security Site in To Use a Mountain.Photograph: To Use a Mountain, LLCDocumentary films‘Environmental violence’: inside the fight to save indigenous land from becoming a nuclear dumping groundNew documentary To Use a Mountain spotlights the pain and triumph of resisting government efforts to turn parts of rural US into disposal sitesAndrew LawrenceTue 25 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 05.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNuclear energywas supposed to be our salvation, humanity’s chance to retool technology first conceived as a weapon of mass destruction into an engine of limitless prosperity. But even as the industry touted nuclear fission as an economic game-changer (never mind theastronomical startup costs), a safety paragon (never mind the spills atChornobyl,Three Mile IslandandFukushima) and harmless fodder for anAmerican comedy institution(never mind that glowing rod on Homer’s back or the three-eyed fish), there was no getting around the matter of what to do with all the toxic waste (never mind nuclear’s claimed green credentials).The stagnant state of that dirty business brought Casey Carter, the director of the new avant-gardedocumentarycalledTo Use a Mountain, back to his interview with a Washington state farmer who was part of a class-action lawsuit against the government over the release of radioactive material from theHanford nuclear reservation– site of the world’s first full-scale plutonium production reactor. The farmer’s words still echo, despite ultimately being cut to fit the film’s 90-minute runtime. “He joked that nuclear power is the only faith-based energy because everyone always asks, ‘Do you believe in it?’” Carter says. “He was like, ‘You don’t have to believe in solar. It’s just a pretty good idea.’”To Use a Mountain could exist as a coda toChristopher Nolan’sOppenheimer, showing how the Manhattan Project physicist’s fears about nuclear technology’s vast potential for devastation proved more justified than even he could have imagined. In particular, the film trains its lens on the passage of the 1982 Nuclear Waste Policy Act – which, among other things, placed six rural communities across the US in a derby of sorts to become the permanent site for more than 90,000 tons of high-level nuclear waste.The plan was for the waste to remain isolated for 10,000 years, and that humans would still be around to celebrate theReagan-era edictas a triumph. But the affected communities are more inclined to believe there may be no one left to parcel out due credit once the waste leaches into groundwater, pollutes the air and contaminates the food chain. Ultimately, Nevada’s Yucca Mountain, about a two-hour drive from Las Vegas, was selected as the nuclear burial site, but after decades of scheming and development, legal challenges and obstruction from activists and prominent politicians such asSenate majority leader Harry Reid, the Yucca Mountain project was halted – leaving the US with no permanent repository for its nuclear waste. (In the meantime, the federal government pays utility companiestens of billions of dollarsto hold on to their spent fuel until a place for it opens up.)‘Can we accept what we have done or not done?’: harrowing film follows doctors in GazaRead moreCarter’s documentary unspools like an art installation, steeped in mood and texture, as it urges viewers to reckon with the anxious state of play. Gone are the voice-of-God narrator, the talking-head experts and even basic chyrons; the subjects who appear on camera aren’t named until the film’s end credits. Instead, To Use a Mountain papier-maches reams of Department ofEnergy(DoE) surveys, analyses and internal memos on to contemporary footage of decaying storage sites and interviews with community members who speak to the personal and environmental damage those false starts have wrought. A sound bath that samples from salmon-rich rivers and one-room church worship only serves to further underscore the stakes.It’s a prevailing sense of doom established in shaky handheld shots that search the sky for danger, then paid off in archival footage of Oppenheimer’s bomb going off beneath desolate US landscapes before giving way to Hiroshima and Nagasaki. “I didn’t want to have a traditional journalistic conversation,” says Casey, stressing the importance of humanizing the communities and concerns that the energy department documents treat with clinical distance. “These people were written about, mapped and diagrammed in excruciating detail. The Department of Energy was looking at them through this purely utilitarian lens, just kinda scanning the American landscape and trying to figure out which place was disposable enough.”View image in fullscreenIan Zabarte on Yucca Mountain in To Use A Mountain.Photograph: To Use A Mountain, LLCNot surprisingly, the Department of Energy disposal list quickly homed in on sparsely populated rural communities that mining and farming industries had left behind. In some cases, those communities were largely made up of marginalized Black and brown people whose claims to the land date back generations. Advocates against the Yucca Mountain site argue that its designation as a DoE nuclear disposal ground disregards aUS government treaty obligationto the Western Shoshone tribe. The area’s history of seismic activity is another reason to be wary of Yucca’s structural integrity over the ensuing millennia.With impressionistic flourish, the film traces the arc of the resistance. Among others, it follows Ian Zabarte – a Shoshone principal who has lost family members to radiation-related diseases connected to the government’s nuclear testing on tribal lands. As he goes from testifying on Capitol Hill as a young man to hiking the desolate area decades later, Zabarte never wavers in his belief that Yucca belongs to the Shoshone, arguing effectively that eminent domain is just racism by another name. “It’s heavy, it’s tragic and unfortunately it’s an all-too-familiar state of affairs,” Carter says. “The amazing thing was having these conversations and really gaining a deeper understanding of the duration, persistence and willpower within these communities.”In one scene drawn from archival footage from Hanford, which was fully decommissioned in the 1980s and has since beendescribed as“the most contaminated place in the western hemisphere”, the film lowers viewers into a disused storage tank that has been leaking contaminants into the groundwater system and threatening the Columbia River – a lifeline to Portland, Oregon; Boise, Idaho; and scores of communities in between.View image in fullscreenCasey Carter, the director of To Use a Mountain.Photograph: To Use a Mountain, LLC“In traveling to these places, you realize each one of them has dealt with issues of environmental violence or racism even prior to being nominated as a potential nuclear waste storage facility,” Carter says. “It’s gut-wrenching to think about people encountering this level of treatment from their government. It really shows how much of this anger exists in many parts of rural America, not just Maga rural America. This film is just a tour of example after example.”Carter’s stylistic confidence suggests he’s been at this auteur thing for a while. But the truth is, To Use a Mountain is his first attempt at an ambitious, feature-length people’s history. A double major in physics and photography, Carter went to grad school for architecture in hopes of “unifying my left and right brain”, he says. That thirst for scientifically driven aesthetics, combined with formative years spent in the shadow of Oak Ridge national laboratory in east Tennessee, which alsofigured prominentlyin the Manhattan Project, compelled Carter to devote six years to retracing the US government’s slog-footed effort to bury its nuclear shame. In hindsight, there’s no missing those signatures in the CAD images Carter uses to depict Yucca Mountain and other disposal-site candidates.Doubtless, some audiences may be tempted to return the concerns raised in To Use a Mountain to the back burner – to file it under “not my problem” because the energy department hasn’t sized up their community or their local power plant hasn’t been designated a Superfund site yet. Never mind that just last month, Idaho, Louisiana, Oklahoma, Tennessee and Utah werenamedas finalists for “nuclear lifecycle innovation campuses” – federal sites that would handle spent fuel and waste management. The DoE plans to pick three host states by the end of this year. Oppenheimer’s existential dread is roaring back to the fore.Can we afford to be afraid of nuclear power?Read moreIf anything, Carter’s film is a reminder of how our unsolved nuclear problem connects to all the other existential threats that keep us doomscrolling through the night and calling on a higher power – God? The government? – to restore our faith that humanity can outlive the toxic waste it leaves behind. “When I started this film in the summer of 2018, Covid hadn’t happened,” Carter says. “War in Ukraine, Gaza and Iran hadn’t happened. Artificial intelligence hadn’t been invented yet. The big tech companies are advocating for microreactors to power datacenters. Even by taking this methodological approach to making the film, it’s still opened up to this kaleidoscope of impacts that touches on military history, the environmental impacts and human psychology and fear. There’s just a sprawling network of consequences associated with this material.”To Use a Mountain is out in the US now with UK and Australia release dates to followExplore more on these topicsDocumentary filmsNuclear wasteEnergyWasteNuclear powerNevadafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Triage by Claudia Rankine review – how should we respond to the world’s atrocities? | Claudia Rankine | The Guardian
description: The American poet and essayist weaves memoir, fiction, criticism and lyrical lament into a tale of friendship in an age of existential crisis
Author: Sarah Crown
Headline: The American poet and essayist weaves memoir, fiction, criticism and lyrical lament into a tale of friendship in an age of existential crisis
Content: Engaging with our present moment’s contradictions … Claudia Rankine.Photograph: Tanya MarcuseView image in fullscreenEngaging with our present moment’s contradictions … Claudia Rankine.Photograph: Tanya MarcuseClaudia RankineReviewTriage by Claudia Rankine review – how should we respond to the world’s atrocities?The American poet and essayist weaves memoir, fiction, criticism and lyrical lament into a tale of  friendship in an age of existential crisisSarah CrownTue 25 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Any resemblance to actual persons, living or dead, or actual events is purely coincidental,” writes the multi-award winning Jamaican-American poet, essayist and playwrightClaudia Rankinein the disclaimer to her latest work. “Unless it isn’t.” The pretzel-logic of this statement, its assertive ambiguity, sets the tone for a book that digs directly into the question of what we are to do with the idea of truth, when the world we live in is asking us “to hold, visually and emotionally, realities we do not yet have a viable system of language for”. In Triage, Rankine borrows from her personal history and from a world whose landscape now encompasses “the rise of fascism, the implementation through deportations of the Great Replacement theory, the starvation of devastated populations subjected to war and climate change”, and uses the material she gathers to pose a simple question. When faced with realities such as these, what do you do? Do you stand, or do you fall?The book begins with a friendship. Two young people – our narrator, and another she refers to only as “the theorist” – meet in college in the late 20th century, and are drawn to each other. They’re passionate; they’re idealistic; they’re committed to the activism of the time (“shantytowns were built on campus to protest apartheid South Africa”) and steeped in the texts and authors and philosophical conceits of the humanities. Over time, they develop a game. “When we spied each other during the day,” the narrator explains, “we had to collapse.”double quotation markThe years pass; the world becomes wilder, more brutal, less sane; the crises and disasters multiply and intertwineThis collapse is “literal, and on occasion, an inconvenience to those around us”: the pair fall to the ground “in the dirt, grass, on cement, wood”, all over campus. They become known for it (“Aren’t you the two who fall?”), even though they themselves don’t seem, fully, to understand what their falling means. That it is a response to the “toomuchness” of the world around them, to “all the fevered wretchedness we had no answers for”, is without question. But what exactly the response itself signifies is less clear. Looking back from a vantage point 40 or more years into the future, the narrator offers a range of possible interpretations: “a refusal of continuance”; “a way to say things were unaligned”; perhaps just “the easiest way to keep from breaking apart”. But between the narrator and the theorist, the meaning of the game is never definitively pinned down.And it is perhaps this ambiguity that exists between them, even at the heart of a game that binds them to each other, that eventually drives them apart. The years pass; the world becomes wilder, more brutal, less sane; the crises and disasters to which the theorist and the narrator could, or should, respond multiply and intertwine. In the face of this worsening world, what began as a hair’s-breadth difference in the interpretation of their college game widens into a chasm. On the one side, the narrator sees her role as one of witnessing: her purpose, as she perceives it, is to record the atrocities around her, to acknowledge them, to mark them and to grieve them. Her work takes her into art criticism, and she focuses on images of couches, because “within the collapse, [they] seemed a place to land”. The theorist, on the other hand, is not content with reaction; they are compelled to act. What matters about falling for them isn’t the collapse itself, but the fact that the act of collapsing pushes them to rise up, over and over again.Triage acknowledges the validity of both characters’ responses – the witnessing and bearing of grief versus the acts of intervention and remaking. The book itself is a fantastical hybrid – part memoir, part reportage, part essay, part lyrical lament – and the complexity of its construction both mirrors and engages with our present moment’s contradictions. But in the end, the question of what is the right, the proportionate, even the realistic response to the world’s atrocities becomes subsumed by the question of which is the hopeful one.Triage is a challenging book for challenging times: it forces us to look at the world around us without blinking. There may be, as the narrator suggests in one of her final conversations with the theorist, “no solutions, only recognitions”. But at the same time, Rankine is clear that the truth of that statement doesn’t render action redundant: the book proposes courses of action even if it doesn’t offer the false promise of success. “Trying in the face of defeat is a thing,” the theorist argues. “For you, loss is a state of grief; for me, it’s a state to refuse … Things are unachievable only when you need the road to be short.”Triage by Claudia Rankine is published by Allen Lane (£22).To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com.
