title: From ‘old people music’ to owning the streets: 60 years of Notting Hill carnival and me | Notting Hill carnival | The Guardian
description: As a child, being taken to the Caribbean celebration was a drag. But once sound systems arrived in the 1970s, it became an unmissable yearly pilgrimage offering a sense of freedom
Author: Lloyd Bradley
Headline: As a child, being taken to the Caribbean celebration was a drag. But once sound systems arrived in the 1970s, it became an unmissable yearly pilgrimage offering a sense of freedom
Content: ‘This wasourcarnival now’ … girls dancing on a street corner in 1975.Photograph: Richard Braine/Pymca/REX/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘This wasourcarnival now’ … girls dancing on a street corner in 1975.Photograph: Richard Braine/Pymca/REX/ShutterstockNotting Hill carnivalFrom ‘old people music’ to owning the streets: 60 years of Notting Hill carnival and meLloyd BradleyAs a child, being taken to the Caribbean celebration was a drag. But once sound systems arrived in the 1970s, it became an unmissable yearly pilgrimage offering a sense of freedomTue 25 Aug 2026 04.50 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 04.51 EDTShareMy earliest memories of theNotting Hill carnivalare of being mildly irritated. In its 1960s infancy, the event was strictly a Caribbean affair, transplanted to Ladbroke Grove as authentically as was practical. Its purpose was as obvious as its origins: giving Caribbean arrivals a chance to celebrate themselves by bringing the vibrancy of the home they left behind to these drab streets for a couple of days.Vital as this was – and it really was – it didn’t cut much ice with surly 10- or 11-year-olds like me, being dragged around behind parading steelbands. Yes, it was great to see so many Black people out in the open together and your mums and dads laughing and having a good time, but did we need to be here? There was football to be played and bikes to be ridden, yet so many of us were being forced to walk for what seemed like miles following “old people music”.Then as the 1970s got under way, everything changed. TheLondonsound systems that had been establishing themselves over the previous few years – Coxsone Outernational, Jah Shaka, 6X6, Sufferah HiFi, TWJ and so on – assumed a growing presence at carnival, under the flyover or on the street. They were operated by men and women not much older than us, who understood how the post-Windrush generation defined their Blackness as they came of age in London and how, although roots and heritage were always important, we didn’t need to simply recreate the Caribbean.View image in fullscreen‘Everything changed’ … Notting Hill Carnival in 1974.Photograph: Chris MilesThe sound systems played the same choice of music we heard at dances and parties or in our own record collections, so we could find the reggae, the lovers rock, the soul and funk that soundtracked our lives right there set up outside accommodating pubs, caffs or people’s front doors. The big plus point was the sound systems were static, meaning if you weren’t dropping some foot you could stand around with your hands in your pockets, always a teenager’s default setting. Indeed the only walking you were obliged to do would be if the music wasn’t up to it or there weren’t enough people – ie women – at that particular sound, so you’d find another one. This might involve a bit of float-following, but, then again, it might not.Refreshment was never a problem. Some Kentucky or a kebab when we were gathering at Turnpike Lane station, then load up with “supplies” before leaving, thus avoiding the so-called “carnival tax” temporarily inflating prices in Notting Hill off-licences. Our drinks of choice usually involved pre-mixing dark rum or Bacardi with Coca-Cola, or vodka with orange juice; beer was too heavy to lug around until they started selling it in those four packs held together with plastic rings. You’d drink a can, undo your belt, thread it through the empty ring and you were away. Some guys, more hardcore than me, would hang a pack off each hip then swagger round like a western gunslinger. (At this year’s Arsenal victory parade my son turned up with an insulated backpack containing rum, mixer, beer and ice that didn’t melt over the course of six hours, and I thought: “Wow! How we could have done with that at the carnival in the 70s!”)View image in fullscreen‘Everybody I knew went to work the following week with a bit of a spring in their step.’Photograph: PYMCA/Avalon/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesSuddenly, the Notting Hill carnival made sense. Youngsters came down in droves because this wasourcarnival now, and while we appreciated what it stood for historically, we wanted to enjoy ourselves, too. You wouldn’t dream of missing it. Carnival was the place to run into familiar faces who you probably didn’t know by name and might not have seen since last year’s event but you were glad to have a quick chat with.Just as the crowds swelled so did the area the event occupied. Sound systems would mostly set up outside the parade route, and by renting front gardens for the weekend there were smaller rigs as far as the canal up by Harrow Road to the north and Colville Terrace to the south – gentrification hadn’t been invented at that point – in between Ladbroke Grove and Chepstow Road. There were street dances of varying sizes everywhere, many doing a roaring trade selling drink or barbecue to the foolishly unprepared, and this takeover created one of the most attractive features of the weekend.In the early 1970s, when police harassment was commonplace, racist microaggressions were a part of everyday life and the hospitality industry wasn’t living up to its name, just being able to walk about such a large area of London seeing far more people that looked like you than didn’t, enjoying a drink and a dance or just pissing about and not being bothered by anybody was simply brilliant. It was as if we owned those streets for four days. Everybody I knew went to work the following week with a bit of a spring in their step. And most likely exhausted: back in such unregulated times, revelry tended to kick off on Friday evening and go through to Monday night and Tuesday morning, with sound systems playing until the J’ouvert celebrations welcomed the sunrise.View image in fullscreen‘An essentially self-regulating event was becoming subject to decisions being made elsewhere’ … Police arresting a young man during riots at the carnival in 1976.Photograph: Evening Standard/Getty ImagesSamba queens to sound systems: the riotous streets of Notting Hill carnival – in picturesRead moreMy peak carnival years were the early 1970s through to the early 1980s; the riot of 1976 changed things. How and why it kicked off is a different conversation, but the aftermath of overpolicing, increasing regulation and media that used violence and criminality as the starting point for reporting: all of this squeezed out a degree of the joyful anarchy and spontaneity that had made it so beautiful. Many people, especially out-of-towners, became scared to go and the tens of thousands that did were aware of a palpable tension, especially around 7pm when the police moved to shut down the sound systems.Naturally this changed the way we approached it, and perhaps the most dispiriting aspect of the shift was that an essentially self-regulating event was becoming subject to decisions being made elsewhere, giving the carnival the flavour of something being donetous rather thanbyus. It didn’t really matter how the content carried on evolving; the whole affair had become far too orderly. It doused the spark one bank holiday at a time, far from that untidy, magnificent era of mass-participation when anybody, just by showing up, knew they were genuinely contributing to the true essence of carnival.But of course the Notting Hill carnival kept going. And as it reaches its 60th anniversary it seems to have been regenerating in size and spontaneity again as the next generation bring back that joyful anarchy. May the streets feel like theirs.Explore more on these topicsNotting Hill carnivalSocial historyBlack British cultureReggaeSoulLondonRacecommentShareReuse this content

title: Kemah Bob: Love Child review – Miss Fortunate’s follow-up is a superbly playful origin story | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: With icky and edgy jokes, the comedian offers an authentic inquiry into her childhood in her sophomore show
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: With icky and edgy jokes, the comedian offers an authentic inquiry into her childhood in her sophomore show
Content: Thinking aloud … Kemah Bob.Photograph: Paul GilbeyView image in fullscreenThinking aloud … Kemah Bob.Photograph: Paul GilbeyEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewKemah Bob: Love Child review – Miss Fortunate’s follow-up is a superbly playful origin storyPleasance Courtyard, EdinburghWith icky and edgy jokes, the comedian offers an authentic inquiry into her childhood in her sophomore showBrian LoganTue 25 Aug 2026 11.19 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 11.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAstandup’s debut show usually tells us who they are, then with their follow-up, they branch out.Kemah Bobhas done things the other way around. After2024’s Miss Fortunate, a wild shaggy dog story about a disastrous trip to Thailand, she now delivers that delayed “this is me” set, an open-hearted inquiry into how she got here and her origins as the child of a poor black family, the descendants of slavery, in the southern US.That inquiry is prompted by misgivings on Bob’s part, coolly laid out here, about her career in comedy – which she loves, but worries is infantilising, and (see the receipts from that successful last fringe run) financially precarious. Is she leading a grownup life – or should she start doing so? There’s a thinking-aloud authenticity to that exploration that is very endearing in Love Child. Her audience cheerfully used as a sounding board, she casts her gaze back across generations of Bobs, and her own journey to the UK, to work out what life she ought now to lead.‘Just so cheeky!’ Kemah Bob on FOC Fest, the celebration for femmes of colour in comedyRead morePart of the pressure, she jokes, comes from being the product of the first pregnancy her parents didn’t terminate. She measures her upbringing against the Adverse Childhood Experience test for early-life trauma and it doesn’t sound too traumatic because Bob is such a smiling and playful host, packing icky jokes about inheriting “dick-sucking lips” from her dad or, as an adult, sharing sex toys with her mum.She goes on to ruminate on what made her parents who they were (there’s a great joke about her father’s having never been taught to be a man) – and her grandad too, a promiscuous blues singer with an addictive personality just like Kemah’s. When this chronology loops back to the present-day party at which Bob first sets her scene, it’s a jolt. That framing device could use some buttressing but the material is strong, in a thoughtful, sprightly show.AtPleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Stage)Edinburgh festivalComedy (Culture)reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Soft Spot review – this wine-glass circus has a lot of bottle | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: A handstand artist and a juggler slide, toss, stack and stand on umpteen glasses – without a drop of wine in sight
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: A handstand artist and a juggler slide, toss, stack and stand on umpteen glasses – without a drop of wine in sight
Content: Smashing time … Stina Otterström and Arttu Lahtinen in Soft Spot.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSmashing time … Stina Otterström and Arttu Lahtinen in Soft Spot.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewSoft Spot review – this wine-glass circus has a lot of bottleZoo Southside, EdinburghA handstand artist and a juggler slide, toss, stack and stand on umpteen glasses without a drop of wine in sightChris WiegandTue 25 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis Swedish circus two-hander begins with the performers offstage, and what sounds like the high-pitched notes of a glass harp. But the wine glasses here – first six of them, then dozens – are used for acrobatic tricks rather than music.Stina Otterströmis a handstand artist,Arttu Lahtinenis a juggler. Together, they execute a series of increasingly fiddly, full-bodied duets. Otterström’s strength is immediately contrasted with the fragility of this most familiar, yet hazardous, of props. Her first inversions involve holding the stems between her toes, passing them from one foot to the other, or balancing their bases on her soles. Lahtinen gives us variations on the tablecloth pull-trick and the buzz wire game, balancing glasses on planks of wood that he glides perilously close around Otterström’s body. Empty glasses are expertly slid, tossed, stacked and stood upon. Have we no wine here?Exit review – a circus squad who really drive each other up the wallRead moreThis is a restrained hour presented by OLO Company and Cluster Arts. It could sometimes benefit from more of a showperson’s – or even a sommelier’s – flair. The abundantly skilled pair remain demure throughout, just the odd glance or smile acknowledging their feats, an occasional teasing amid their steadfast reliance on one another. For too long it plays in one register, without quite enough variation in Mika Forsling’s nevertheless appealing music. Any notion of narrative or autobiography is absent. That’s not necessarily a problem if you’re embracing a fuller variety of tricks and tones – as in Compagnie Nyash’s remarkableStoel, with a duo and 15 mismatched chairs that take on their own personalities. It’s harder to achieve with identikit glasses.If a richness of mystery or ritual is absent, then the fizz among the tricks includes the mock-solemn arrival of a brush to tidy up a breakage, unexpectedly supplemented by a pile of broken glasses. That crunchy noise is much more atmospheric than an earlier recorded sound effect. These shards are eventually swept around the stage to form a striking surround for the final tricks, performed barefoot (eek!) and dramatically lit by Jaakko Sirainen. That stylish sequence would sparkle alongside other cabaret acts – and the wit in the duo’s curtain-call speech shows this pair could create a happier hour.AtZoo Southside, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreCircusEdinburgh festivalJugglingreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Kate Cheka: The Last Funny Woman review – pregnant standup calls for comedy industry to grow up | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Cheka considers her tendency to ‘live life like a joke’ in a frank hour, with her frustrations leaving a lasting impression
Author: Anya Ryan
Headline: Cheka considers her tendency to ‘live life like a joke’ in a frank hour, with her frustrations leaving a lasting impression
Content: Giving everything she has … Kate Cheka.Photograph: @ezztheticphotographyView image in fullscreenGiving everything she has … Kate Cheka.Photograph: @ezztheticphotographyEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewKate Cheka: The Last Funny Woman review – pregnant standup calls for comedy industry to grow upVoodoo Rooms, EdinburghCheka considers her tendency to ‘live life like a joke’ in a frank hour, with her frustrations leaving a lasting impressionAnya RyanTue 25 Aug 2026 06.24 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKate Cheka wasn’t supposed to be here. After her debut hour two years ago, she swore she would never do the fringe again. But now she’s back, mic in hand and eight months pregnant, walking us through her life’s greatest romantic escapades, from Marseille to Texas and Nepal to Berlin. She does it all with mountains of energy – if you thought the fringe was exhausting at the best of times, just imagine doing all this with a baby on board.But, as she will tell us later, maybe there’s a reason she wants to give everything she has to her last pre-birth show. In an hour that’s more storytelling than laugh-out-loud standup, she weaves in political eye-rolls, thoughts on the rise of the far right and her tendency to date white men with access to property.View image in fullscreenDisappointments laid bare … Kate Cheka.Photograph: @ezztheticphotographyThe world is pretty darn depressing. Still, she remains a “good time girl”, which has led to some drunken sexual encounters. “Most comedians write jokes,” she says, “I live life like a joke.” Her pregnancy story is held back until just the right moment.She does all this in the style of a pub catchup. But despite her giggling, girlish demeanour, Cheka has big, often unheard things to say about the state of comedy. Her career is not going well, she tells us. Even though she’s started booking slots on radio, she’s finding that her lefty political feelings are not being met with applause. Things are made harder by the fact she’s a Black, working-class comedian. She presents a bleak, uncomfortable picture.Courtney Büchner: One of the Girls review – all aboard for a rollercoaster relationshipRead moreCheka’s disappointment is laid bare. She has worked hard and won awards, and yet TV execs still lure her into Zoom calls, only to build up her dreams and cruelly crush them. Cheka deserves her comedy flowers. But the final 15 minutes of this show are anything but funny. The tears rolling down her cheeks should get the industry looking inward. Let’s hope there are more opportunities to hear Cheka, in all her glory.AtPBH’s Free Fringe @ Voodoo Rooms, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalFestivalsTheatreComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)reviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Librarians: A Very Serious Comedy! review – workplace meltdown borrows from classic sitcoms | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Well-tuned performances help along a familiar set of laughs as a rickety library gets a new manager and an inspection
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: Well-tuned performances help along a familiar set of laughs as a rickety library gets a new manager and an inspection
Content: Easy to classify … The Librarians.Photograph: Jonny RuffView image in fullscreenEasy to classify … The Librarians.Photograph: Jonny RuffEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewThe Librarians: A Very Serious Comedy! review – workplace meltdown borrows from classic sitcomsPleasance Courtyard, EdinburghWell-tuned performances help along a familiar set of laughs as a rickety library gets a new manager and an inspectionChris WiegandTue 25 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 00.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe sign says Plumstanton Library but this could be The Brittas Empire’s Whitbury New Town Leisure Centre, The Office’s Wernham Hogg or Torquay fleapit Fawlty Towers. Such is the instant familiarity of a failing workplace whose staff have a new manager and an inspector to contend with at once. It’s not only the books that are well worn in Matthew Howell and Jack Michael Stacey’s play. Acting head librarian Harry Wordsworth has even bought his own “best boss” mug like David Brent.Nevertheless it’s a frequently funny hour, with well-tuned performances. Harry (Matthew Howell) finds himself in charge when Peter, who has run the library for more than 25 years, pops his clogs in the Agatha Christie section. This death in the aisle is both a tragedy and mystery which the remaining staff stumble through, beset by dodgy electrics, dwindling visitors and a seemingly inevitable closure.Oafish Harry’s co-workers include Elaine (Billie Hamer), a stickler for the rules who can’t hear the word “fine” without reaching for her stamping device, and a man known chiefly as Work Experience (Jack Michael Stacey). Of course, the new boss (Jo Hartland) has been dispatched from London and is suspiciously viewed as a snob. Alliances are formed, plans are hatched and rivalry fills the air. As does a whiff ofMischief Theatre– the writers met when performing inThe Play That Goes Wrongand an am-dram company is referenced here with the acronym Prat. No prizes for guessing the typo that befalls “public library” but there’s a lovely twist I didn’t predict.Little Animals review – Motherland milquetoast creates a clever climate pleaRead moreAmy Milburn’s production heightens the calamities sufficiently so a simple act like fetching the inspector (James Watterson) a glass of water becomes a feat of physical comedy. It unfolds in an awfully British landscape of biscuits and sausage rolls, Mrs Miggins and Lord Lucan. There are some light political swipes, with an accidental new leader installed by misfiring tactical voting, yet you might expect more bite about the country’s rampant library cuts and closures. Breezily enjoyable – even if you prefer your comedy to be less easily classified.AtPleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 31 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreComedy (Stage)LibrariesComedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Ali G: Who Iz I? trailer reveals return of Sacha Baron Cohen’s prank-playing rudeboy | Movies | The Guardian
description: Comedian returns in new film, adding a retired US general to a list of pranked celebrities that include Buzz Aldrin and Donald Trump
Author: Laurence Phelan
Headline: Comedian returns in new film, adding a retired US general to a list of pranked celebrities that include Buzz Aldrin and Donald Trump
Content: Sacha Baron Cohen in the trailer for Ali G: Who Iz I?Photograph: Amazon MGM StudiosView image in fullscreenSacha Baron Cohen in the trailer for Ali G: Who Iz I?Photograph: Amazon MGM StudiosMoviesAli G: Who Iz I? trailer reveals return of Sacha Baron Cohen’s prank-playing rudeboyComedian returns in new film, adding a retired US general to a list of pranked celebrities that include Buzz Aldrin and Donald TrumpLaurence PhelanTue 25 Aug 2026 10.31 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 14.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first full trailer for Ali G: Who Iz I? has been released online, revealing some of the escapades and pranks – and their victims – that will appear in the second feature-length comedy starring the academically challenged west Staines rudeboy character created and played bySacha Baron Cohen.Sporting new dreadlocks but still wearing the clothing that was favoured by young white Britons copying US hip-hop and Black streetwear fashions in the 00s, Ali is back to contend with the issues of the day – as well as the pregnancy of his long-term girlfriend, Julie. In the 20 years since the character has been away, he says that “the world went to crap: there was Covid, wars and Ed Sheeran”.The trailer gives glimpses of pranks played on retired US army general Stewart Rodeheaver, and someone who may be the Canadian DJ and producer Deadmau5 at a music festival.Ali G first appeared on the UK comedy programme The 11 O’Clock Show in 1998, then in three series of Da Ali G Show in the early 00s, during which he interviewed unsuspecting politicians, academics, public figures and celebrities. He asked Buzz Aldrin if man will ever walk on the sun (perhaps during winter when it’s cold) and pitched a business idea for “ice-cream gloves” to Donald Trump. Da Ali G Show also featured the first appearances of Baron Cohen’s other best-known characters: the Kazakh TV reporter Borat Sagdiyev, and Brüno, an obtuse Austrian fashionista.Prince William? David Cameron? JD Vance? Celebrities brace – and Staines celebrates – ahead of new Ali G filmRead moreIn 2002, Ali G starred in the feature-lengthAli G Indahouse, a scripted story without any mockumentary elements or pranks that received a mixed critical reception but was a domestic success, earning more than £17m at the UK box office. Thefirst Borat film, however, was an international hit in 2006, making more than $260m (£200m) globally.Baron Cohen claimed to have retired both Ali G and Borat in 2007, citing the characters’ popularity and the concomitant difficulty of finding unaware new subjects to interview or prank. However, Borat returned in a2020 sequelthat included an interview withRudy Giuliani, and now Who Iz I? becomes the fifth film featuring characters from Da Ali G Show. (At present there are no rumours of a sequel to 2009 filmBrüno.)Ali G: Who Iz I? is scheduled for release in cinemas on 23 October.Explore more on these topicsFilmSacha Baron CohenComedy filmsComedynewsShareReuse this content

title: Artist known for sculptures of Mao Zedong jailed for slandering ‘heroes and martyrs’ | China | The Guardian
description: Gao Zhen sentenced to three years in prison after already spending two years in detention
Author: Yu-chen Li
Headline: Gao Zhen sentenced to three years in prison after already spending two years in detention
Content: Artist Gao Zhen in 2019.Photograph: Kimberli Mäkäräinen/WikimediaView image in fullscreenArtist Gao Zhen in 2019.Photograph: Kimberli Mäkäräinen/WikimediaChinaArtist known for sculptures of Mao Zedong jailed for slandering ‘heroes and martyrs’Gao Zhen sentenced to three years in prison after already spending two years in detentionDanny Vincent in TaipeiTue 25 Aug 2026 07.53 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGao Zhen, a prominent Chinese artist known for provocative sculptures of the former leaderMao Zedong, has been sentenced to three years in prison after being found guilty of slandering China’s “heroes and martyrs”. The sentencing came two years after he was detained while visiting the country with his family, according to his wife and human rights groups.Thecase has attracted international condemnation, largely because the artworks at the centre of the case were created more than 10 years before China created the law under which Gao was charged.The law, which bans defamation of China’s heroes and martyrs, came into force in March 2018. Courts have previously used the law to charge people who challenge official accounts of Chinese history.Gao, 70, a Chinese citizen and US permanent resident, wasdetained on 26 August 2024after returning to China with his wife and son. Police later raided his studio near Beijing.In one of Gao’s most famous works with his brother Gao Qiang, they depict Mao kneeling. In another, a firing squad made up of seven Mao statues point rifles at Jesus.View image in fullscreenSculpture entitled Mao's Guilt by Gao Zhen, left, and his brother Gao Qiang, pictured in Beijing in 2009.Photograph: Shiho Fukada/The New York Times/Redux/eyevineGao’s wife, Zhao Yaliang, told the Guardian that the two years since her husband’s detention had been a painful ordeal for the family.“His arrest and trial should never have happened. We have had no choice but to wait in anguish … I am very sad that it’s going to be this long,” she said after the verdict.According to his wife, two of Gao’s relatives were allowed to enter the Sanhe city people’s court in Hebei province for the verdict, while she waited with their son and several friends outside.“For two years he has suffered in the detention centre, while my son, our closest family members and I have also endured this torment,” she said.Gao’s family said he had fainted in detention and was afflicted with back, knee and respiratory problems. His wife said Gao had sustained heatstroke during the summer and described experiencing a feeling of “being close to death”.Weiquanwang, a human rights monitoring network, said Gao had been sentenced for “infringing the reputation and honour of heroes and martyrs”. The rights network said Gao’s studio and property had been sealed and that friends and supporters had been silenced.Artworks made by Gao during his time in detention and seen by the Guardian include a series of colourful paper cuttings.“A body can be confined, but clarity of mind is harder to take away. Mentally he remains remarkably sharp and unbroken,” said Gao Qiang, who spent decades producing art with him as the Gao brothers.“Art should never be a crime scene waiting to be discovered,” he said.In a handwritten letter sent from detention to his young son, Gao wrote: “Dad’s eyesight isn’t very good, and I don’t have my glasses, so my handwriting isn’t very good.“I hope I can finish my work as soon as possible and return to you and Mum,” he wrote. “Son, remember: Dad will always love you!”Sophie Richardson, a longtime China human rights campaigner, said: “Gao has been prosecuted for conduct that has never been criminal, and his family has endured collective punishment at the hands of the authorities, and that is criminal.”Sarah Brooks, the China director for Amnesty International, said the decision to sentence Gao to a maximum three-year prison term illustrated “the authorities’ determination to deter others from engaging in independent artistic expression”.Gao’s wife and their young son have been unable to leave China since his detention. Human rights campaigners said his wife was stopped from travelling abroad based on national security grounds. His young son is a US citizen but has been unable to leave without his parents.The Chinese foreign ministry was approached for comment.Yu-chen Li contributed to reporting.Explore more on these topicsChinaCensorshipMao ZedongAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Kit Harington to replace Nicholas Hoult in HBO’s Harry Potter TV series | Harry Potter TV series | The Guardian
description: Actor best known as Jon Snow in Game of Thrones will now play Gilderoy Lockhart in show’s second season
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: Actor best known as Jon Snow in Game of Thrones will now play Gilderoy Lockhart in show’s second season
Content: Kit Harington will play the vain and inept defence against the dark arts teacher in the season based on Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets.Photograph: Gareth Cattermole/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKit Harington will play the vain and inept defence against the dark arts teacher in the season based on Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets.Photograph: Gareth Cattermole/Getty ImagesHarry Potter TV seriesKit Harington to replace Nicholas Hoult in HBO’s Harry Potter TV seriesActor best known as Jon Snow in Game of Thrones will now play Gilderoy Lockhart in show’s second seasonNadia KhomamiTue 25 Aug 2026 08.05 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKit Harington will replaceNicholas Houltin HBO’s Harry Potter television series, after the Skins actor left the production because of scheduling conflicts.Harington will play Gilderoy Lockhart, the vain and inept defence against the dark arts teacher, in the season based on Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets, the second novel in JK Rowling’s series. The casting change was announced just two weeks after Hoult was confirmed for the role.Hoult, who played Lex Luthor in the recent Superman film, was released from the Harry Potter production after its filming schedule conflicted with his other commitments.Harington is best known for playing Jon Snow in Game of Thrones, as well as a more recent appearance in the BBC/HBO drama Industry.The actor voiced Lockhart in Audible’s full-cast adaptation of The Chamber of Secrets, released in 2025. He said recently that he was a longstanding Harry Potter fan and described Lockhart as one of his favourite characters.“I’m thrilled,”Harington told Collider. “I’ve said a million times, for anyone who cares, that I’m a huge Potter fan.“I’ve got to be honest, he’s one of my favourite characters. So, to be offered to play him is a real dream. I think he’s going to be so fun. I got to play him in the audiobooks. That’s not the exact way I’ll play him in the show because it’s an audiobook, but I’ve had a taste of him and felt my way around him. He’s just a wonderful creation.”Harry Potter publisher to receive millions in Anthropic copyright settlementRead moreLockhart is a celebrity wizard and prolific author whose reputation is built on supposedly heroic exploits that, it emerges, were largely the work of other witches and wizards. He was previously played by Kenneth Branagh in the 2002 film adaptation.The HBO series is intended to retell Rowling’s seven-book story over multiple seasons, with each season expected to be based on a different novel. The first season, Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone, is due to premiere on 25 December. Production on the second season is scheduled to begin this autumn.The series stars Dominic McLaughlin as Harry, Arabella Stanton as Hermione Granger and Alastair Stout as Ron Weasley. John Lithgow plays Albus Dumbledore, Janet McTeer is Minerva McGonagall, Nick Frost plays Rubeus Hagrid and Paapa Essiedu plays Severus Snape.Harington’s appointment is the latest change to the cast. Gracie Cochrane, who plays Ginny Weasley in the first season, is also leaving the series and will be replaced for its second season.Hoult, along with other cast members, has faced some backlash for his decision to join the show from those opposed to Rowling’s views on sex and gender.Explore more on these topicsHarry Potter TV seriesKit HaringtonNicholas HoultnewsShareReuse this content

title: Russian stadium says it will not host Kanye concerts – but promoter says shows have not been cancelled | Kanye West | The Guardian
description: The controversial rapper now known as Ye was due to play two huge shows at St Petersburg’s Gazprom Arena, which now states it cannot host performances for contractual reasons
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: The controversial rapper now known as Ye was due to play two huge shows at St Petersburg’s Gazprom Arena, which now states it cannot host performances for contractual reasons
Content: Kanye West pictured in 2024.Photograph: Scott Dudelson/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKanye West pictured in 2024.Photograph: Scott Dudelson/Getty ImagesKanye WestRussian stadium says it will not host Kanye concerts – but promoter says shows have not been cancelledThe controversial rapper now known as Ye was due to play two huge shows at St Petersburg’s Gazprom Arena, which now states it cannot host performances for contractual reasonsLaura SnapesTue 25 Aug 2026 07.06 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 14.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe St Petersburg stadium that was set to host two concerts by Ye – making the rapper formerly known asKanye Westthe biggest western act to play in Russia since start of the Ukraine war – has now said that the concerts will not take place at the venue, although the promoter has stressed that they have not been cancelled.Gazprom Arena had previously posted on social media saying that “the most influential musical artist of our time” would perform there on 10 and 11 October. “This is no joke!” the post stated. The event sold out immediately, including tickets priced at £1390 ($1896).The news came after countries including the UK, Italy, Poland, Switzerland, France and more blocked or sought to block concerts by Ye owing to public safety concerns over his prior antisemitic outbursts and expressions of sympathy towards nazism. In January, Yeissued an apologyfor his behaviour and discussed his mental health struggles. “I am not a Nazi or an antisemite,” he wrote. “I love Jewish people.”The Russian venue has now released a statement distancing itself from the concerts. “In light of the numerous inquiries received by Gazprom Arena regarding the organisation of a Kanye West concert, we hereby officially state: Gazprom arena was not, and is not, the organiser of this event. That role was handled by the Moscow-based concert agency Say Agency.“Gazprom Arena has not signed any contracts to lease the stadium for this event. No such contract exists. Consequently, the concert cannot take place at our venue.”On Telegram, Say Agency said that it was surprised by the announcement, learning the news at the same time as the public, but that “as of now, the Ye concert has not been cancelled”.Say Agency said that it announced the concerts after Gazprom arena approved an “official letter”, but said that the rental contract had not yet been signed ahead of its expiry later this week.The planned appearance has caused controversy outside Russia. Ye’s plan to play the country – following in the footsteps of Paul Oakenfold, DaBaby, Jason Derulo and Akon – flouts sweeping sanctions and calls for culture boycotts.Within Russia, politician Nikolay Novichkov called for the musician to be investigated for praising Hitler and said that the concerts should be cancelled unless he publicly declared “moral support for Russia and the special military operation”. Legislator Vitaly Milonov said Ye should perform traditional Russian songs at the planned concerts. “Maybe after this he’ll stop his disgusting antics and become a normal person,” he added.Say Agency previously released a statement acknowledging the controversy. “Not everything Kanye West said should be forgotten. Many people are talking about Kanye today. Many are trying to criticise him for words spoken during difficult times. But it’s easy to judge based on a single statement. It’s more difficult to listen to a person who has been changing the industry for decades. We listened, and we want to remind you.”Despite the controversy, fans have been undeterred from seeing Ye live when concerts have been allowed to proceed. He has recently performed to vast audiences in the US, Turkey, the Netherlands, Georgia, Albania, Portugal and Kazakhstan, with more dates planned for the US and Indonesia. The dates come in support of his 12th solo album, Bully, released in March.Explore more on these topicsKanye WestRussiaRapnewsShareReuse this content

title: Freddie Mercury’s ‘splendid things’ to go on display at V&A | Freddie Mercury | The Guardian
description: Eight costumes spanning Queen frontman’s career will feature in a free trail developed with his former fiancee
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: Eight costumes spanning Queen frontman’s career will feature in a free trail developed with his former fiancee
Content: Freddie Mercury, who would  have been 80 this autumn, in the Made in Heaven music video.Photograph: Simon FowlerView image in fullscreenFreddie Mercury, who would  have been 80 this autumn, in the Made in Heaven music video.Photograph: Simon FowlerFreddie MercuryFreddie Mercury’s ‘splendid things’ to go on display at V&AEight costumes spanning Queen frontman’s career will feature in a free trail developed with his former fianceeNadia KhomamiArts and culture correspondentTue 25 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 00.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEight famous costumes worn byFreddie Mercury, including the outfit featured on the cover of Queen’s debut album and the catsuit from the video for Bohemian Rhapsody, are to go on display at the V&A in London this autumn to mark what would have been the singer’s 80th birthday.Freddie Mercury | Splendid Things, a free trail developed with Mercury’s former fiancee and close friend Mary Austin, will run from 24 October 2026 to 17 January 2027. Austin is lending seven of the looks, which span Mercury’s career from the 1970s to his final years.Among them is a monochrome ensemble worn for an earlyQueengig at Imperial College and pictured on the cover of the band’s eponymous debut album. Also on display will be the “Mercury Wing” catsuit, designed by Wendy de Smet and worn during the A Night at the Opera tour in 1975-76, as well as in the groundbreaking Bohemian Rhapsody video.Mercury’s crown and cloak, designed by Diana Moseley and worn during Queen’s 1986 Magic Tour, will also feature. He wore the outfit for the band’s final live performance at Knebworth that year. The display will also include a costume from the Made in Heaven music video, as well as accessories and items from his personal wardrobe.View image in fullscreenFreddie Mercury in the crown and cloak designed by Diana Moseley that he wore in 1986.Photograph: Denis O’ReganThe trail takes its name from a remark Mercury made in 1978: “I like to be surrounded by splendid things. I want to lead a Victorian life surrounded by exquisite clutter.”Austin first met Mercury when she was 19 and he was 24, while they were both working around Kensington’s Biba fashion scene. Mercury, born as Farrokh Bulsara on 5 September 1946 in Zanzibar, was selling his artwork and vintage clothes from a stall in Kensington Market. They became engaged on Christmas Day 1973, the year Queen released their debut album.Their relationship ended in the mid-1970s, but they remained close for the rest of Mercury’s life. When he died in 1991, he left Austin his Kensington home, Garden Lodge, and his possessions.Austin has described Mercury’s clothes as central to the image he created as a performer. “The clothes were part of that exploration,” she said inA Life in Lyrics, due to be published in September. “Freddie understood early on that he wasn’t just wearing clothes; he was providing an image to match the scale of the space and the vastness of the crowd.”View image in fullscreenFreddie Mercury in the Made in Heaven music video.Photograph: Simon FowlerAustin said the clothes and costumes to be displayed at the V&A “tell a hugely important part” of Mercury’s story both on and off the stage: “Never mere accoutrements, his costumes and clothes were essential to his performances, creative vision, and wider self-expression, carefully designed to create a lasting visual and emotional impact that has reached across the generations and still reverberates today.”The installations have been designed by Tom Piper, whose work includes productions for the Royal Shakespeare Company, the Tower ofLondonpoppies and the V&A’s Alice: Curiouser and Curiouser and Taylor Swift | Songbook Trail.Each of the trail’s six stops will be staged differently, using sets, sound and lighting to evoke moments from Mercury’s career.Kate Bailey, the V&A’s senior curator of theatre and performance, said the display would explore Mercury’s “love of ‘splendid things’” and his interest in art, design and fashion.Explore more on these topicsFreddie MercuryQueenV&AMuseumsLondonPop and rockExhibitionsnewsShareReuse this content

title: The Airport Chaplain review – thoroughly bingeable TV about ‘Batman in a hi-vis vest’ | Television | The Guardian
description: This moreish show about a do-gooder keen to save the day stars Hugo Weaving and The Pitt’s Shabana Azeez … and it’s pressure-packed from the get-go
Author: Luke Buckmaster
Headline: This moreish show about a do-gooder keen to save the day stars Hugo Weaving and The Pitt’s Shabana Azeez … and it’s pressure-packed from the get-go
Content: Ground control … Hugo Weaving and Shabana Azeez in The Airport Chaplain.Photograph: Ben King/SBSView image in fullscreenGround control … Hugo Weaving and Shabana Azeez in The Airport Chaplain.Photograph: Ben King/SBSTelevisionReviewThe Airport Chaplain review – thoroughly bingeable TV about ‘Batman in a hi-vis vest’This moreish show about a do-gooder keen to save the day stars Hugo Weaving and The Pitt’s Shabana Azeez … and it’s pressure-packed from the get-goLuke BuckmasterTue 25 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHugo Weaving plays the eponymous airport chaplain in this pacy and moreish eight-part series, which was co-created by Elise McCredie and Jude Troy, and directed with jittery flair by Bonnie Moir and Tig Terera. In case you were wondering, yes, that profession reallydoesexist.I doubt the lives of real airport chaplains are anywhere near as frenetic as those of this show’s protagonist, Tobias Wallace (Weaving), whose existence is a testament to that old saying: “Not all heroes wear capes.” Sometimes, they wear hi-vis.The Airport Chaplain wastes no time establishing Tobias as a gallant do-gooder determined to save the day, as he rescues the toy rabbit of a distressed child. Tobias is a problem-solver, finding out-of-the-box solutions to all kinds of prickly situations, from locating lost baggage to transporting dead bodies, from intervening in cases of domestic violence to playing matchmaker, helping online lovers connect in real life. And sometimes, God forbid, he even provides spiritual counsel, such as helping a grieving son to deal with his father’s death.But most of all, Tobias is a spectacular busybody, inserting himself into virtually every problem in the airport. This might not be entirely realistic, but it certainly makes for interesting drama. We’re thrown into the thick of it from the first episode, in which Tobias receives a call from the control room and races to the aid of a panicked boy in a hoodie just as the police arrive. It very quickly becomes clear who is really in charge here, with the cops left looking useless as Tobias takes the reins. He’s a bit like Batman in an airport.But trouble arises when Tobias’s new boss arrives: terminal manager Mira Ansari-Cole (Shabana Azeez), who has not drunk the pastoral care Kool-Aid. During their first meeting, Mira isn’t impressed when Tobias describes his role as “primarily providing emotional, spiritual and practical support for passengers”. Nor is she thrilled when he knocks back her suggestion to file a daily work report, before abruptly leaving the meeting citing a “spiritual emergency”.The stage is set for a good ol’ fashioned war between management and an employee who views himself as absolutely integral to the viability of the organisation he works for. And as much as viewers may instinctively side with Tobias, most of us will surely see some merit in Mira’s scepticism, which gives her increasing desire to show him the door – a solid narrative foothold.Shabana Azeez: ‘The most disgusting thing I’ve seen on The Pitt? American coffee’Read moreJust as HBO’s hit medical dramaThe Pitt(also starring Azeez) reminds us of the power of hospitals as a central location, McCredie and Troy do something similar with airports; these are both places where virtually anybody can come through the door. In The Airport Chaplain, it is the exceptions that are the most interesting. While most people hurry from A to B, every now and then a character walks through the doors with a whole lot more going on. In the second episode, authorities – including Tobias, of course – deal with a man who has hidden Ethiopian honey in shampoo bottles. To me, this felt like a bit of a letdown; I was expecting something more sensational, like several kilograms of white powder inserted where the sun doesn’t shine.Maybe that comes later – only the first four episodes were made available to the press – but every single one is pressure-packed, making the show thoroughly bingeable; it is perfect forNetflix(where it will launch globally, with Australia getting it on SBS and SBS on Demand).Narratively, the structure feels a little scattered, though the writers (McCredie, Mithila Gupta, Sarah Bassiuoni and Vidya Rajan) do find a throughline that spans several episodes, in the story of a mysterious young woman, Asha Chawla (played by Kavitha Anandasivam), who is found in a prayer room, refusing to speak and without a passport or phone. Another recurring character is Cath Barnes (Claudia Karvan), a calm, pragmatic and sassy airline service manager who is good mates with the chaplain.Tobias is, of course, the glue binding the show together. Weaving – one of the giants of Australian screen and stage – exudes a great combination of gravitas and relatability. His presence has real oomph and dynamism, but without any heightened quality that suggests you would never encounter such a person in real life. If my luggage ever disappears, I want Tobias Wallace on the case.The Airport Chaplain is on Netflix, andSBSand SBS on Demand in AustraliaExplore more on these topicsTelevisionAustralian televisionNetflixSBSHugo WeavingClaudia KarvanreviewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: this heartwrenching drama about Indigenous child welfare will make you seethe with anger | Television | The Guardian
description: Flash-forward 18 years, when a grown-up woman confronts her adoptive mother. Plus: the Spanish Armada tries to overthrow Elizabeth I. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: Flash-forward 18 years, when a grown-up woman confronts her adoptive mother. Plus: the Spanish Armada tries to overthrow Elizabeth I. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Fighting to get her children back … Patti Little Bird.Photograph: ©Original Pictures Inc.View image in fullscreenFighting to get her children back … Patti Little Bird.Photograph: ©Original Pictures Inc.TV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: this heartwrenching drama about Indigenous child welfare will make you seethe with angerIn this week’s double bill , a grown-up woman confronts her adoptive mother. Plus: the Spanish Armada tries to overthrow Elizabeth I. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Priya Elan,Phil Harrison,Jack Seale,Ali CatterallandSimon WardellTue 25 Aug 2026 01.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLittle Bird9pm, Sky AtlanticA drama with minimal dialogue that can still stir such deep outrage is proof of its power. But there is a guttural cry in this week’s double bill that, somehow, makes you even angrier about the Sixties Scoop – the period when Canada removed Indigenous children from their families. Patti Bird is fighting to get her kids back while, flashing forward 18 years, Esther confronts her adoptive mother.Hollie RichardsonThe Great British Sewing Bee8pm, BBC OneIt’s music week and the wholesome sewing competition takes a risque turn, with a pattern challenge inspired by Madonna’s iconic cone bra. The material girls then need to get into teams to make outfits for pop groups, before creating a 70s disco-inspired outfit – which leads to lovely host Sophie Willan calling them her “Sewing Bee Gees”.HRSaving Lives at Sea8pm, BBC TwoForget about the calming nature of the shipping forecast, this dramatic series continues to follow lifeboat rescuers. Filmed around the “graveyard of the North Sea”, where ships regularly run aground due to the dangerous sand banks, this week, with a storm approaching, a yacht capsizes leaving its four passengers missing in the water.Priya ElanCelebrity MasterChef9pm, BBC OneJudge Giorgio Locatelli has seen enough of the fumbling celebrities. He’s donning his whites and stepping into the arena in a new feature that involves the chef cooking a signature dish (this time, pappardelle with pea puree and a butter sauce) while the contenders try to keep up.Phil HarrisonEmergency 24/79pm, BBC TwoThe immersive documentary, filmed at Southmead Hospital in Bristol, tracks a Tuesday afternoon that brings the A&E department two tricky patients: a man whose leg has been severed by a train; and another whose wound looks like a stabbing. It’s as much about teamwork and organisation as it is about medicine.Jack SealeThe Tudors with Rob Rinder and Ruth Goodman9pm, Channel 5View image in fullscreenHaving a blast … The Tudors with Rob Rinder and Ruth Goodman.Photograph: Channel 5It’s 1588: as the Spanish Armada speeds towards England to overthrow Elizabeth I, every male from seven to 60 nervously fingers their (mandatory) bow and arrows – and Blighty’s sailors prepare to repel boarders. Ruth and Rob compellingly relate the events. Plus, an important question: “I hate to ask,” says Ruth, “but where did the crew go to the toilet?”Ali CatterallFilm choiceArthur the King (Simon Cellan Jones, 2024), 10.40pm, BBC OneView image in fullscreenLeader of the pack … Mark Wahlberg in Arthur the King.Photograph: Album/AlamyMichael (Mark Wahlberg) used to be an adventure racer, competing in team endurance events that involve epic stretches of running, trekking, cycling and kayaking – but never won a contest. Irked by his failure, he comes out of retirement for the world championship in the Dominican Republic. As his ragtag group struggle through mud, forest and mountain, Michael realises they are being followed – and at times assisted – by a stray dog. Simon Cellan Jones’s fact-based adventure is Lassie-like in its dog-friendly emotional manipulation, but has plenty of rugged action for extreme sports fans.Simon WardellLive sportTennis: US Open, 3pm, Sky Sports Main Event.Day one of the mixed doubles tournament at Flushing Meadows.EFL Cup football: Nottingham Forest v Leeds, 7.30pm, ITV1.Preston v Everton is on Wed at 7pm on Sky Sports Main Event.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Feminism for a World on Fire by Natasha Walter review – hope amid the hopelessness | Natasha Walter | The Guardian
description: A writer and activist links the climate crisis to battles for justice around the world in this vital book
Author: Samantha Ellis
Headline: A writer and activist links the climate crisis to battles for justice around the world in this vital book
Content: Natasha Walter.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianView image in fullscreenNatasha Walter.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianNatasha WalterReviewFeminism for a World on Fire by Natasha Walter review – hope amid the hopelessnessA writer and activist links the climate crisis to battles for justice around the world in this vital bookSamantha EllisTue 25 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 06.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt has become increasingly difficult to change our minds, to question our own views or to find common ground with people we disagree with, all of which makes Natasha Walter’s new book both refreshing and exhilarating.In her ebullient 1998 debut The New Feminism, Walter hailed Margaret Thatcher as a trailblazer. In this fiercer, bleaker work, she rips into the “glossy language of aspiration feminism”, “the message that the individual woman can do anything she wants if she only has the necessary courage”. That kind of feminism inspired an “explosion of books and films about pioneers and heroines, about bossy women and gutsy girls” which retold the feminist story as “a succession of isolated campaigns, led by outsize individuals”.Instead, Walter advocates for ecofeminism, and for solidarity and sisterhood, “narratives that focus less on howIwin on my own, and more on how we thrive together”. She’s serious about that “we”, marshalling stories from across the globe. Walter founded the charityWomenfor Refugee Women in 2006, directing it for the next 15 years. During that time she was struck by women’s complaints of environmental degradation, their despairing at the “heaps of toxic waste that had grown up behind their homes”. Meanwhile feminism was being commodified by companies like Missoni, which copied the pink pussy hats knitted, for nothing, by feminist protesters, and sold them for £140 apiece. And by Dove, which promised “real beauty” and inclusivity while making billions of single-use plastic shampoo sachets that, according to Greenpeace, have clogged up sewers and contributed to floods in places like the Philippines (Dove states that it has made an “agenda-setting commitment to tackle the global beauty industry’s plastic waste issue”).She also saw some feminists who had supported the charity switch their energies to focus solely on British women, who they insisted needed protecting from migrants. No wonder she invokes indigenous scholar and healer Yuria Celidwen’s belief that political journeys must start with grief. But she also draws hope from Holly Archer (not her real name), a victim of grooming, gang-rape and abuse who has set up a project in Shropshire supporting survivors and “refuses to let her story be exploited by those who would use it to drive hatred and division”.I’d forgotten until she reminded me here that the slide into dystopia in Margaret Atwood’s The Handmaid’s Tale starts with climate change. In real life, too, women suffer first and most from environmental collapse. Rising sea levels in Bangladesh send women travelling miles further to fetch fresh drinking water. In north-east Syria, the radical women of Rojava – who fought off the extreme misogynist forces of Islamic State and are resisting authoritarianism from the new Syrian government as well as attacks from Turkey – struggle to feed their families because of water scarcity and food shortages. Nevertheless, they are “building something new”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘Heat, floods and droughts make men more violent to women’: Natasha Walter on eco-feminism in a world on fireRead moreWalter travels there to interview them and finds “the most determined feminists I have ever met”. It’s exhilarating to meet them on these pages too. One of the most joyous moments in the book comes during a conversation with Bahiya Mourad, who set up amala jin,or women’s house, in 2011. For a while she and her comrades evaded the authorities’ attention because they seemed like harmless old women, but when the government did try to close them down, they beat them off with sticks. Part of their work involves helping women who want to marry against their parents’ wishes, and, says Mourad, “often we end up dancing at their weddings”. In a book that can sometimes feel hopeless, it’s a vital reminder that feminist joy is not about buying a £140 pink pussy hat, but about helping other women – and, maybe one day, celebrating with them when the seemingly impossible has been achieved.Samantha Ellis is the author of books includingChopping Onions on My HeartandHow to Be a Heroine. title: The Great Dictator by Matthew Sweet review – the fabulous life of Barbara Cartland | Biography books | The Guardian
description: A brilliant new biography that does it subject the favour of taking her seriously – even if few else did
Author: Kathryn Hughes
Headline: A brilliant new biography that does it subject the favour of taking her seriously – even if few else did
Content: Barbara Cartland in the 70s.Photograph: Smith Archive/AlamyView image in fullscreenBarbara Cartland in the 70s.Photograph: Smith Archive/AlamyBook of the dayBiography booksReviewThe Great Dictator by Matthew Sweet review – the fabulous life of Barbara CartlandA brilliant new biography that does it subject the favour of taking her seriously – even if few else didKathryn HughesTue 25 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 19.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBarbara Cartland was famous for dictating her novels. With a pekingese clamped to her hot pink bosom she would lie back on a library couch and exhale a story about virginal girls taming wayward dukes, damaged airmen or misunderstood surgeons. Meanwhile Miss Savory, Mrs Smith or Mrs Morgan, picked for being unfidgety and sneezeless, would take everything down in immaculate Pitman shorthand. Cartland reckoned on being able to polish off 8,000 words a day. “In this way,” she told one of the many reporters who quizzed her on her astonishing productivity, “the typescript for an 80,000-word novel is finished in a fortnight.” At her peak she was pushing out 23 books a year which added up to 723 in total. Only Agatha Christie and William Shakespeare topped her lifetime sales of 750m.Cartland was a dictator in other ways, too. Husbands, dogs, houses and the local council were all expected to bend themselves to her indomitable will. Resistance, let alone opposition, was futile. The managing director of the company that printed her books suggested that she read Nietzsche on the perceptive grounds that they had a lot of ideas in common. Oddly, he also declared himself madly in love with her. Behind that marshmallowy exterior, all pink chiffon, candyfloss hair and soft, smudgy lines, there lurked sinews of high-tensile steel.Anyone expecting this biography of Barbara Cartland to be an amusing takedown of amonstre sacréalong the lines of Craig Brown’s witty 2017 decimation of Princess Margaret will be disappointed. Rather, Matthew Sweet pays his subject the compliment of absolute seriousness, regarding her as a cultural phenomenon whose extraordinary life, stretching the entire 20th century, deserves deep study. Sweet has had unfettered access to the cornucopia of material that Cartland left behind at Camfield Place, the Hertfordshire manor house where she lived until her death in 2000 at the age of 98. Conducting a fingertip search of her letters, scrapbooks and typescripts, Sweet has crafted a generous but clear-sighted account of a woman who was too often reduced to the status of a lazy joke.She was born in 1901 into the lower upper class. On her father’s side she was pure trade. James Cartland and Son was a Birmingham metalworkers turning out umbrella stands, crocodile-shaped inkwells, shelf brackets shaped like sea monsters and “pharaonic letterboxes embossed with meaningless hieroglyphs”. Her adored mother Polly, meanwhile, was Gloucestershire gentry and there had been the usual rows about marrying down. Cartland’s paternal grandfather killed himself when the business went bust and her father retreated into alcoholism, leaving Polly to manage the tricky business of getting her daughter launched into a life the family could no longer afford.Sweet suggests that this constellation of losses and compensations set the emotional template for Cartland’s adult life. Men were necessary but fragile and certainly best not relied upon. Having come out as a deb in 1919 into a world where there were not enough husbands to go round, Barbara set out to become financially self-sufficient by plunging into the only kind of work for which she was qualified. For the next decade she filed gossipy titbits about young London society to the Express, the Mirror and the Daily Mail.This was the world of the Bright Young Things, so often written up today as a madcap time of pyjama parties and midnight dashes to the continent. In fact, Cartland’s columns reveal a society still in shock from the first world war: fathers are dead (Cartland lost hers in the trenches in 1918), grand family houses have been sold, divorce is everywhere and life seems impossible without alcohol or drugs. The men whom Cartland stepped out with were not the heart-throb dukes and dashing airmen that she would later write about, but broken people without the language to express their desolation. “My contemporaries were ashamed to show emotion,” she observed with characteristic perception in her 1943 memoir The Isthmus Years. “We had all of us a horror of sympathy.”So instead she simply carried on with a brittle determination to make the best of things. After plenty of dalliances with men called things like Pingo Langrishe and Nigs Ratendone she made a tactical marriage to a dull man called Alexander McCorquodale who was heir to a printing fortune. When he retreated into drink – shades of her father – she effected a neat swap by divorcing, then marrying his paternal cousin. In this way there was no need to change her surname: she had replaced one Mr McCorquodale with another. It rankled that she never achieved a title until she herself was made a Dame in 1991. By contrast, her ambitious daughter, Raine, managed to insert herself into the peerage not once but three times through each of her carefully strategic marriages.The only man who really mattered to Cartland was her beloved younger brother, Ronald. They went on holiday together and endlessly discussed the cod-eastern philosophies that were all the rage in the 1920s: Ouspensky and Gurdjieff were favourites and Cartland retained a vague mysticism to the end of her life involving ghosts and spiritual healing. She also believed in flying saucers and the power of honey to cure just about anything.Brother and sister bonded too over politics, specifically a socially engaged, internationalist Toryism. Barbara bossed Ronald into parliament where he became a leading anti-appeaser. She in turn wrote one of the first of the tiny number of 1930s British novels that dealt specifically with the evils of Nazi antisemitism. Dangerous Experiment (1936) involves the improbable story of Lena Carrington who, after a shipwreck and a spell as the slave of a tribe of thunder-worshippers in the Caucasus, ends up in Germany where she is courted by a Nazi lover. In the end she breaks things off when she sees him mistreating a Jewish refugee.This, of course, is not the Barbara Cartland that most of us remember from the 80s and beyond. In what Sweet calls her “imperial phase” she was writing novels with paper-thin plots that she endlessly recycled. She was also a relentless self-promoter. Bed linen, candles and towels were all enthusiastically marketed under her name, although with remarkable restraint she drew the line at scented toilet paper. She also pulled off a promotion with Dewhurst the butcher, which offered customers one of six previously unpublished Cartland novels for every £12 they spent. The promotion was not a great success because of the sheer weirdness of “being given a copy of Desire in the Desert with a parcel of mince”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut when, in a stroke of fortune so improbable that even now it hardly seems real, her daughter, Raine, became Diana Spencer’s stepmother, Cartland sensed new opportunities for cross-pollination. She took to announcing “I invented virgins” and managed to imply that the royal wedding of 1981 was somehow her doing, despite being pointedly not invited. Raine, a chip off  the old block, made sure that the gift shop at the Spencer family seat, Althorp, stocked a full run of Barbara Cartlands.It would be easy to dismiss Cartland as a quirk, an aberration the likes of which we will not see again. But the great triumph of this brilliant book is the way that Sweet embeds her firmly in the economic, political, social and artistic transformations of the 20th century while charting the ways in which she also transcended them. Somehow, and this remains the deep mystery of it all, Barbara Cartland emerges as that rather admirable thing: an entirely self-made woman.The Great Dictator: a Life of Barbara Cartland by Matthew Sweet is published by Hodder & Stoughton (£25).
