title: John Irvin obituary | Movies | The Guardian
description: British film-maker and director of Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy who was described by Alec Guinness as having ‘balls behind the camera’
Author: Ryan Gilbey
Headline: British film-maker and director of Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy who was described by Alec Guinness as having ‘balls behind the camera’
Content: ‘I hate being pigeonholed, and I like to do the unexpected’: John Irvin, pictured in 1986.Photograph: Alex Bowie/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘I hate being pigeonholed, and I like to do the unexpected’: John Irvin, pictured in 1986.Photograph: Alex Bowie/Getty ImagesMoviesObituaryJohn Irvin obituaryBritish film-maker and director of Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy who was described by Alec Guinness as having ‘balls behind the camera’Ryan GilbeyTue 25 Aug 2026 11.37 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 11.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBouncing from war zone reportage to cold war espionage, Hollywood horror to Sherwood Forest swashbuckler,Harold Pinterto Arnold Schwarzenegger, the director John Irvin, who has died aged 86, was nothing if not eclectic.“I’m a bit split,” he said. “I like playing with expensive toys, yet I also like the miniatures. I hate being pigeonholed, and I like to do the unexpected.”He enjoyed his greatest success with the BBC mini-series Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy (1979), adapted fromJohn le Carré’s novel about the intelligence officer George Smiley’s efforts to winkle out a Russian mole. Smiley was played with clenched elegance and economy by the formidableAlec Guinness, who took to striking out lines in the script whenever he felt he could convey the necessary information by expression alone.“I was terrified, knowing I had to spend a year with him,” Irvin told Guinness’s biographer Piers Paul Read. On the first day of rehearsals, the director offered a suggestion that was rejected out of hand. After persuading Guinness to try the scene his way, Irvin was vindicated. “Very good, John,” the actor said. “Ten out of ten.”There was still Guinness’s trepidation to contend with. Phoning Irvin at 3am once shooting was under way, the actor fretted that he “hadn’t found Smiley” and recommended that the part be recast. On set a few hours later, Guinness walked off in the middle of filming. Irvin brought him back and stood his ground. “We’re going to do it in one take,” he said of the day’s first scene. “Do you understand?”When Guinness was later asked what he liked about Irvin’s directing style, he said: “Balls behind the camera.”View image in fullscreenAlec Guinness in Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy, 1979.Photograph: Maximum Film/AlamyThe series, described by its producer Jonathan Powell as “a sort of elegy for empire”, was seen at its peak by more than 8 million viewers (more than 15% of the UK population) and won several prizes, including best drama series in the Broadcasting Press Guild awards.Interviewing the director in 1986 for Films in Review, Louise Tanner wrote: “There is about Irvin just a hint of a Le Carré hero, the crisp diction, the quiet air of knowing his way around the lands east of Suez.”Irvin was unavailable to direct the follow-up, Smiley’s People, having been courted by Hollywood since before Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy. His 1977 Granada Television adaptation of Dickens’ Hard Times had impressed executives there.From moles, he moved on to dogs: The Dogs of War (1980), that is, adapted fromFrederick Forsyth’s novel and starring Christopher Walken as a mercenary helping to overthrow a west African dictator. Stark and uncompromising, the film was hated by Forsyth.Apparitions were next. Ghost Story (1981) featured an illustrious cast who were famous before Irvin was even born: Fred Astaire, Melvyn Douglas, John Houseman andDouglas Fairbanks Jrplayed friends harbouring a nasty secret. The New England winter was scarier than any of the film’s spectres, Irvin recalled. “When I finished the last shot, I said to Fred, ‘It’s all over. You can go home to Beverly Hills.’” Astaire replied: “Oh John, I’m so happy. I thought I was going to go home in a box.”Horses followed in Champions (1984), the story of the cancer-stricken jockey Bob Champion (John Hurt), then reptiles in Turtle Diary (1985), a low-key comedy adapted by Pinter fromRussell Hoban’s novel, withGlenda Jacksonand Ben Kingsley as shy naturalists who plot to liberate giant sea turtles. Irvin compared working with that cast to “driving a Ford Mustang and trading up to a Ferrari”.In directing Schwarzenegger in Raw Deal (1986), he might be said to have swapped the sports car for a bulldozer. One of the Austrian action hero’s interchangeable shoot-’em-up thrillers, the film cast him as an ex-FBI agent infiltrating the Chicago mob. Even Irvin admitted the movie was “not dealing with the great mysteries of life”.He had hoped for many years to direct a film about Vietnam, where he spent time while making aBBCOmnibus documentary about war photographers. (He had even been shot at on the Laotian border.) When he was offered Hamburger Hill (1987), which focused on the real-life 10-day battle to capture Dong Ap Bia in the A Shau Valley in 1969, it satisfied that desire.View image in fullscreenJohn Irvin on the set of Hamburger Hill in the Philippine jungle south of Manila, 1986.Photograph: Alex Bowie/Getty ImagesIrvin succeeded in his aim of “[getting] as close as possible to the experience of combat without thrills or moralising. I wanted the audience to be there.”Unfortunately, the audience was fatigued. Oliver Stone’s Platoon (1986) dominated the Oscars before Hamburger Hill had even been released, whileStanley Kubrick’s Full Metal Jacket (1987) pipped Irvin’s film to the post in the US. He claimed in 2021 that Kubrick had been toying with a later release date until he was secretly shown a print of Hamburger Hill by a colour grader working on both movies.Nevertheless, the criticPauline Kaelconsidered it to be superior to both Stone and Kubrick’s films. Irvin, she wrote, “has the pride of a director who knows what he’s doing”.John and his twin brother, David, were born in Wallasey – now Merseyside but then part of Cheshire – to Elsie (nee Bending) and Charles Irvin, a mechanical engineer. After the family moved to South Shields in Tyne and Wear, the brothers were educated at Durham school.Film bewitched John from an early age. “When I was a child, I used to organise my gangs into film units. I was brought up near Newcastle in the same town as Ridley Scott – there must be something about the smell of the fish queues that produces film directors.”He enrolled at the London School of Film Technique (now the London Film School), which was then housed above a butcher’s shop in Brixton, south London. Irvin said his mother cried for two days when she learned that he would not, as she had hoped, be pursuing a career as an architect.After working as an apprentice editor at Rank, he received a British Film Institute grant to make Gala Day (1963), a documentary about the Durham miners’ gala, which was then bought by the BBC. Irvin made other documentaries for the corporation as well as for his own company, Mithras Films, which he formed in 1962 with Maurice Hatton.These included The 26 (1966), about ex-miners who participated in the General Strike of 1926, and the Bafta-nominated Mafia No! (1967), which documented a protest march across western Sicily against organised crime. While making a film about the civil war in Yemen, Irvin lived with Bedouin tribespeople for four months. He was also a film adviser to the Jamaican government in 1963-64.By the end of the 1960s, his experiences convinced him to leave the documentary world behind. “I reached the point in Vietnam where I had simply seen too much suffering.”View image in fullscreenIrvin during a photocall at the 2008 Rome international film festival.Photograph: Tiziana Fabi/ AFP/Getty ImagesHe worked in British television throughout the next decade on series including the political drama The Nearly Man (1974-75), one of several collaborations with the writerArthur Hopcraft, who went on to adapt Hard Times and Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy.Irvin’s later movies included Next of Kin (1989), starringPatrick Swayzeand Liam Neeson as Appalachian brothers out for revenge. Just as Hamburger Hill got lost amid other Vietnam movies, so his Robin Hood (1991), with Patrick Bergin in the title role and Uma Thurman as Maid Marian, was overshadowed by Robin Hood: Prince of Thieves, which starred Kevin Costner and opened a month later to far greater fanfare.The Hells Angels provided unlikely inspiration for Irvin’s earthy take. “Robin and his men must have terrorised Nottingham like a motorbike gang,” he said. There wasn’t much the director could do, however, when Bergin fell ill, forcing the production to rely on stand-ins. “We had to hide the problem from the studio,” Irvin said, “because otherwise they would have stopped the production.”He continued to demonstrate his versatility. The chocolate-box prettiness of Widows’ Peak (1994), a whimsical comic mystery starringJoan Plowrightand Mia Farrow, and his adaptation of HE Bates’s A Month By the Lake (1995), with Thurman and Vanessa Redgrave, were followed by the hard-nosed thrillers City of Industry (1997), starring Harvey Keitel, andShiner(2000), with Michael Caine andMartin Landauas rival boxing promoters. He also returned to combat in the TV movie When Trumpets Fade (1998), set during the dying days of the second world war.Mandela’s Gun(2016) dramatisedNelson Mandela’s stint as a guerrilla fighter for the ANC.View image in fullscreenIrvin filming Mandela’s Gun (2016).Photograph: Mandela’s GunAt the time of his death, Irvin was working on Water from an Ancient Well, a documentary about his friend the South African musicianAbdullah Ibrahim, who died in June.“To me, being a director is the most privileged existence there is,” said Irvin. “It’s bloody hard work, but when it’s going well, it’s like having the best table in the restaurant.”He is survived by Emilie, Luke and Amy, the children from his marriage to Sophie (nee Litchfield), who died in 1991, and by two grandchildren, Finn and Isla.John Charles Greenway Irvin, film director, born 7 May 1940; died 11 August 2026Explore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsAction and adventure filmsDocumentary filmsHistorical drama (TV)DramaDocumentaryobituariesShareReuse this content

title: Rise of the Footsoldier: Retribution review – never-ending hardman-on-a-mission franchise heads to Ibiza | Movies | The Guardian
description: The seventh in the series takes longstanding lead gangster Tate, played to the hilt as always by Craig Fairbrass, to the White Isle to knock some heads together
Author: Catherine Bray
Headline: The seventh in the series takes longstanding lead gangster Tate, played to the hilt as always by Craig Fairbrass, to the White Isle to knock some heads together
Content: ‘These are very serious people’ and other dialogue gems … Craig Fairbrass in Rise of the Footsoldier: Retribution.Photograph: Evelyn Xing/Signature EntertainmentView image in fullscreen‘These are very serious people’ and other dialogue gems … Craig Fairbrass in Rise of the Footsoldier: Retribution.Photograph: Evelyn Xing/Signature EntertainmentMoviesReviewRise of the Footsoldier: Retribution review – never-ending hardman-on-a-mission franchise heads to IbizaThe seventh in the series takes longstanding lead gangster Tate, played to the hilt as always by Craig Fairbrass, to the White Isle to knock some heads togetherCatherine BrayTue 25 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe seventh instalment in this seemingly never-ending series opens with a line of voiceover from star Craig Fairbrass, summarising forthcoming proceedings nicely: “They killed my best friend, now they all have to die.” The real-life hardman Pat Tatemight have been murdered in his 30s in Essex in 1995, but that hasn’t proved a setback for his invincible fictionalised counterpart, played to the hilt throughout the entire franchise with hard-headed gusto by Fairbrass. In this one, Tate is in Ibiza, but rather than larging it, he’s intent on tracking down his enemies and exacting the titular retribution. Various arms dealers, guns for hire and, perhaps more unexpectedly, the CIA, provide a bit of grit in the oyster.The director here is series veteran Nick Nevern, having appeared in ROTF: Marbella in 2019, and stepped up to the director’s chair for 2023’s ROTF: Vengeance. Retribution is at its best when engaged in stylised slow-motion action sequences that play out like The Untouchables, if The Untouchables had a soundtrack influenced by Paul Oakenfold and was made on about 100th of the budget. Dialogue is not its strong point, and is mostly made up of interchangeable gangster film cliches. (It’s all, “These are very serious people” and “You remind me so much of her”.) You may not be ponying up to watch a Footsoldier movie on the basis that you’ll be hearing curlicued witticisms worthy of Oscar Wilde, but it is possible to write gangster-speak with a bit more zest. Even Nick Love’s The Business gave us: “The geezer was so hard even his nightmares were scared of him.”Dialogue issues might matter less if the whole thing was a bit more wham, bam, thank you m’am, but the overall run time is distinctly baggy – a few more double-crossings and colourfully accented lads with different agendas have found their way into the mix than can strictly be necessary; it’s Tate’s vengeance quest that should remain the backbone of the piece. It might be time for the demise of the footsoldier – or at least a film that sticks more strictly to the promise of its opening line.Rise of the Footsoldier: Retribution is in UK cinemas from 28 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmThrillersCrime filmsCrimereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Zip Wire review – cancer-curing scientist is on the hook for cable-dangle thriller | Movies | The Guardian
description: This nonsensical film sees an OCD-afflicted scientist fending off assassins while hanging from an aerial wire, and fails to get pulses racing for even a minute
Author: Cath Clarke
Headline: This nonsensical film sees an OCD-afflicted scientist fending off assassins while hanging from an aerial wire, and fails to get pulses racing for even a minute
Content: Hangin’ out … MyAnna Buring in Zip Wire.Photograph: Signature EntertainmentView image in fullscreenHangin’ out … MyAnna Buring in Zip Wire.Photograph: Signature EntertainmentMoviesReviewZip Wire review – cancer-curing scientist is on the hook for cable-dangle thrillerThis nonsensical film sees an OCD-afflicted scientist fending off assassins while hanging from an aerial wire, and fails to get pulses racing for even a minuteCath ClarkeTue 25 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 03.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn this silly, low-adrenaline thriller, the title star is a rickety old zip wire bolted into the side of a mountain in the Italian Dolomites that was never intended for human use. It was constructed in the first world war to sling weapons and supplies hundreds of feet down the valley – and is still used to get the occasional goat off the mountain. But for the second half of this film, a world-famous British research scientist with an extreme fear of heights dangles from it, fighting off highly skilled assassins in increasingly preposterous ways.The scientist is Amy (MyAnna Buring); she has discovered a cure for lung cancer, and her drive is explained in syrupy hospital-ward flashbacks to her mother dying when she was a teenager. Amy also has OCD – she is so anxious about germs that she never takes off her rubber gloves, and has an assistant in her lab to do anything that involves touching or handling objects. (Like all the characters, she never gets beyond a stereotype.) Her research is bankrolled by a big pharma company, whose CEO is played by Saffron Burrows (now seemingly mandatory casting for ropey British thrillers).Amy’s gamechanging discoveries result in an old-school conspiracy, involving a notebook with her research written in code and a trio of contract killers. Which is how Amy ends up in the Dolomites (where everyone has an English accent), halfway across a zip line. Supposedly, a human body cannot remain in a state of maximum panic for more than 30 minutes, but Amy seems to bat away her terrible fear of heights in about five minutes flat. For the audience, you’ll be lucky if this gets your pulse racing for more than two of them.Zip Wire is on digital platforms from 31 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmThrillersreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Why isn’t there hip-hop in 3/4 time?’: the groups reinventing a Polish folk dance for the modern age  | Folk music | The Guardian
description: The oberek is a traditional dance beloved of state folk ensembles – but a new generation of musicians is reconfiguring its music into wild new forms, merging folk steps with electronics and the sound of Chicago footwork
Author: Jakub Knera
Headline: The oberek is a traditional dance beloved of state folk ensembles – but a new generation of musicians is reconfiguring its music into wild new forms, merging folk steps with electronics and the sound of Chicago footwork
Content: Spinning out … Tercet Imperial.Photograph: Marek Kita/PRView image in fullscreenSpinning out … Tercet Imperial.Photograph: Marek Kita/PRFolk music‘Why isn’t there hip-hop in 3/4 time?’: the groups reinventing a Polish folk dance for the modern ageThe oberek is a traditional dance beloved of state folk ensembles – but a new generation of musicians is reconfiguring its music into wild new forms, merging folk steps with electronics and the sound of Chicago footworkJakub KneraTue 25 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 07.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s 6pm on the first day of OFF festival in Katowice, and a crowd is gathering in front of one of the stages to watch newcomers Tercet Imperial. Sporting disco outfits of nylon jackets, tracksuits and Chicago Bulls caps, keyboardist Piotr Zabrodzki deploys resonant acid melodies, while drummer Jan Emil Młynarski plays a rapid, irregular rhythm that brings to mind the scattergun beats of footwork, the ghetto-house subgenre that grew out of Chicago in the late 90s.Not many of those jerking their limbs to the music in front of the stage are likely to realise that they are listening to a distinctly Polish sound: that of the oberek, a traditional dance in triple metre whose name derives from the Polish verb “to spin”, because it usually accompanies couples whirling across dancefloors in a circular motion.“We play traditional music, but on different instruments,” says lead singer Joanna Sztucka. On Tercet Imperial’s debut album, Prymat, the melodies and lyrics of traditional songs are woven into contemporary production: violins and a snare drum are replaced by synthesisers and drum pads. “It’s is an attempt to create an alternative history,” Młynarski says. “We’re doing it primarily for people who know nothing about traditional music and don’t need to know anything at all.”Tercet Imperial are part of a wider phenomenon.Far, far in Chicago. Footberk Suite, by drummer Gary Gwadera (real name: Piotr Gwadera), is a concept album about an imagined meeting of the oberek and Chicago footwork. Its genesis can be found in the influential footwork compilation Bangs & Works Vol 1,released by Planet Mu in 2010, which was an inspiration to Gwadera. “I suddenly realised that grooves and this pulse of footwork were typical of the oberek, and that I wanted to combine them,” he says. To record it, he used dżaz, a minimalist percussion kit from the Polish countryside, along with a Roland TR-808 and electronic pads.View image in fullscreenA gentle flow … Mateusz Kowalski.Photograph: Cezary Piwowarski / Nowa Tradycja FestivalMusician Mateusz Kowalski offers a different take on this traditional music with his groups Radical Polish Ansambl, Tęgie Chłopy and Warszawska Orkiestra Sentymentalna. On his first solo album, released last year under the name Sam Kowalski, he replaced the violin with a gitalele (a small instrument combining the features of a classical guitar and a ukulele) and slowed the tempo, with no percussion – transforming the oberek’s nervous phrasing into a gentle, melancholic flow reminiscent of Appalachian folk music.Elsewhere, Polish duoOplafirst translated the tripartite rhythms and raw energy of the oberek to electric guitar and drums, and later to electronic pads, adding effects and looped guitar parts. Polish-French jazz quartetLumpekssound like Ornette Coleman on a prolonged ramble through the Polish countryside. Suferi, meanwhile, combines oberek rhythms with electrified violin, an effects-laden guitar, and a hip-hop groove on the drums.Often, even a seasoned ear won’t immediately pick up on the traditional dance’s influences – and that’s precisely the point. As Kowalski explains, when releasing the self-titled album, he didn’t describe it as traditional music. “Rather, I wanted to say: listen without any preconceptions and see what this music does to you. The idea is for people to be surprised when they find out that this is traditional material,” he says.The new interest in Polish tradition and its creative expressions stems from the turbulent history of rural music in Poland. Before the second world war, it was part of everyday life – weddings, celebrations and rituals – and passed down by ear. But war and migration disrupted the continuity of music across regions. During the communist era, a state-sanctioned version of folklore emerged, represented by the state song-and-dance ensembles Mazowsze and Śląsk. After the country’s political transformation in the 1990s, Poland’s own brand of popular dance music, disco polo, took over the social function of the old village band. Incorporating some traditional folk elements into the framework of Italo disco rhythms, it was meant to be accessible, cheap, and suitable for weddings.Paradoxically, as the countryside moved away from traditional music, city dwellers began to seek it out again. The Dom Tańca social centre, established in Warsaw in the 1990s, played a key role in reviving traditional music. Young musicians sought out rural masters, recording and learning directly from them, while also reviving the tradition of village dances.View image in fullscreenThe Mazowsze ensemble takes a turn.Photograph: Mondadori Portfolio/Getty Images“For my generation, traditional music was initially something to be ashamed of. In fact, nobody in my circle knew anything about it,” says Gwadera. “I didn’t have the key to understanding that music, and I saw it as a bit of an embarrassment.”Opla’s Hubert Zemler admits that he had listened to Hindu raga before he heard his first interesting oberek. “For a long time, I associated folk music with Mazowsze and the Śląsk ensemble – a centralised, sanitised view of tradition. Obereks have a ternary, danceable metre; they’re round dances, and people used to play them for hours on end. But they didn’t make their way into disco polo or pop. Why isn’t there any hip-hop in 3/4 time?”Since 2020, this musical interest in the countryside has coincided with a broader “peasant turn” in Polish culture and the public debate. Books such as Adam Leszczyński’s A People’s History of Poland and Kacper Pobłocki’s Chamstwo, as well as the Netflix series 1670 (the recently released third season of which has been this year’s most popular Polish series) have shifted historical narratives away from royalty, nobility and the intelligentsia. They started debates about the peasant origins of most of Polish society: the experience of serfdom, the history of social mobility, the suppression of rural roots.View image in fullscreenRural revivalists … Tercet Imperial.Photograph: Marek KitaNowadays, says Gwadera, traditional music is increasingly “treated as part of our own heritage and the forgotten history of the majority of society – it has become a response to the need for a sense of community”.The oberek no longer needs to be a reference or a folkloric embellishment – it is becoming the language of modern creativity. Says Młynarski: “I’m convinced that if this old rural melodic tradition had survived and not been supplanted by disco polo and party music in the 1990s, people would still be playing it today – but on synthesisers and in tracksuits.”Tercet Imperial play Unsound festival in Kraków 8–11 October, Le Guess Who? in Utrecht 5–8 November and Unsound London 25–26 November 2026Explore more on these topicsFolk musicElectronic musicfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Jill Gomez obituary | Opera | The Guardian
description: Soprano with razor-sharp articulation who created lead roles including the Duchess of Argyll in Powder Her Face
Author: Barry Millington
Headline: Soprano with razor-sharp articulation who created lead roles including the Duchess of Argyll in Powder Her Face
Content: Jill Gomez enjoyed her first major successes at Glyndebourne, appearing between 1969 and 1984.Photograph: United Archives GmbH/AlamyView image in fullscreenJill Gomez enjoyed her first major successes at Glyndebourne, appearing between 1969 and 1984.Photograph: United Archives GmbH/AlamyOperaObituaryJill Gomez obituarySoprano with razor-sharp articulation who created lead roles including the Duchess of Argyll in Powder Her FaceBarry MillingtonTue 25 Aug 2026 11.29 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 11.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA lustrous vocal quality, combined with an alluring, exuberant stage presence, ensured the popularity of the soprano Jill Gomez, who has died aged 83, on both operatic stage and concert platform. When her talent came to the fore in the early 1970s she was hailed by Arthur Jacobs inOperamagazine, along with Josephine Barstow, as “the most exciting of our newer female singers”, while reviews of the time hailed her Governess in Britten’s The Turn of the Screw and Anne Trulove in Stravinsky’s The Rake’s Progress as among the finest.View image in fullscreenJill Gomez as Anne Trulove, second from left, in The Rake’s Progress at Glyndebourne, 1975.Photograph: Donald Cooper/AlamyThe latter role was one of those she took, along with Mélisande, Calisto and Helena (A Midsummer Night’s Dream), atGlyndebourne, where Gomez enjoyed her first major successes, appearing between 1969 and 1984. At Covent Garden her roles included Lisa in La Sonnambula, Titania in A Midsummer Night’s Dream and Lauretta in Puccini’s Gianni Schicchi.English National Opera appearances included War and Peace, where she took the part of Natasha Rostova in the 1984 revival, and, in the same year, the Governess. She also appeared regularly with Scottish Opera, the English Opera Group, Wexford and Kent Opera, and major houses abroad including Frankfurt, Vienna, Zurich, Lyons and Florence.Recordings documenting her performances in the 1970s demonstrate animmaculately schooled tone and exquisite legato line in Mozart, and well-turned ornamentation with genuine trills in Handel. Later, too, in French repertoire (as indeed in all languages) her emotional warmth and impeccable diction engendered idiomatic and affecting performances. Herrecording of Canteloube’s Songs of the Auvergne, underVernon Handley, in which the voice sensually enwraps each seamlessly joined phrase, was critically lauded and became a bestseller.Having grown up in Trinidad, Gomez felt a special affinity for Latin American music, and one of the recordings she most enjoyed making – a pleasure evident in the high-spirited renditions – was South of the Border (1990), a crossover disc of music from the so-called Latin American Songbook, largely featuring numbers written for the silver screen or cabaret in the interwar period. Her razor-sharp articulation is mordantly deployed in Noël Coward’s wittyNina from Argentina, while songs such asLa CucarachaandLa Palomaare delivered in captivating style.View image in fullscreenGomez, centre, on a chair, with fellow cast members of Tippett’s The Knot Garden, 1970.Photograph: Mike McKeown/Getty ImagesJill was born in New Amsterdam, British Guiana (now Guyana), where her father, Albert Gomez, a Spanish Trinidadian, was working as a technologist (later managing director and vice-chairman) for Angostura, the distillers. Her British mother, Denise (nee Denham), was an actor and broadcaster in Trinidad.She attended St Joseph’s Convent in Port of Spain, the capital ofTrinidad and Tobago, where her musical talents were nurtured by a persuasive and influential nun, Mother Helen de Verteuil, who encouraged her to try opera. When Jill moved to the UK at the age of 13 she studied first at the Royal Academy of Music in London and later the Guildhall School of Music and Drama, where her teacher was Walther Gruner. She then joined the Glyndebourne festival chorus (1966-68).Inevitably, perhaps, her name is invariably linked to a pair of operatic scandals. Her creation of the role of Flora in Michael Tippett’s The Knot Garden (1970) caused a sensation when, inPeter Hall’s production, she became the first female singer to appear topless at Covent Garden.Then in 1995 came the premiere production ofPowder Her FacebyThomas Adès, with libretto byPhilip Hensher, which drew its material from the scandalous 1963 divorce proceedings of the society hostess Margaret Campbell, Duchess of Argyll – the role taken by Gomez.View image in fullscreenGomez as the Duchess in an Almeida Opera production of Powder Her Face at the Cheltenham music festival, 1995.Photograph: Donald Cooper/AlamyThe behaviour of the duchess, who gives oral satisfaction to hotel staff while treating all around her with arrogant contempt, was depicted in the score and production in graphic detail. Whatever one’s reservations about the work, it is undeniable that it offered the soprano ample opportunity to display her consummate acting skills as well as her vocal versatility.Other colourful productions in which she appeared included a Giulio Cesare at Frankfurt Opera, where Gomez shared the stage with a pair of boa constrictors, which turned out to be less somnolent than she had been promised.But, in general, as her career developed, she chose to avoid what she called the “international opera circus”, opting for the more artistically satisfying rehearsal schedules of smaller venues such as Zurich Opera, where she appeared in Jean-Pierre Ponnelle’s production of Mozart’s Lucio Silla in 1981, conducted byNikolaus Harnoncourt.Significant roles she created included the countess in Thea Musgrave’s The Voice of Ariadne at the Aldeburgh festival (1974) and the title role in William Alwyn’s Miss Julie (1977), a radio premiere underVilem Tauskysubsequently commercially recorded.She also gave the well-received world premiere, at the 1998 BBC Proms, of Cantiga: The Song of Inês de Castro, which she suggested to and commissioned from David Matthews. In the same year she scored a similar success with Granados’s Goyescas, the composer’s dramatisation of his own piano pieces of that name.The sensuousness that Gomez radiated onstage was integral to her real-life persona, which was enchanting but also deeply compassionate. She was a devastating mimic and a sparkling conversationalist who regaled her friends with hilarious anecdotes drawing on her convent upbringing and stage career.It was in 1967, when she was participating in the Bayreuth youth festival as Lore in Wagner’s early opera Die Feen, that she met Patrick Carnegy, later a distinguished writer on music, editor, dramaturg and theatre critic, who was there reporting for the Times. When they finally married in 2010, Carnegy had recently inherited the title of 15th Earl of Northesk. Thus Gomez, after decades of portraying aristocrats on stage, in a splendid case of life mirroring art, spent her final years as a countess.She is survived by her husband.Jill Gomez, soprano, born 21 September 1942; died 11 August 2026Explore more on these topicsOperaClassical musicGlyndebourneGuyanaTrinidad and TobagoobituariesShareReuse this content

title: A Pocket Full of Slagford – a retro-futurist take on Thatcher-era northern England | Games | The Guardian
description: Developer Patrick Grant was born in Australia and lives in New Zealand, but a childhood of British TV inspired him to set a comedy game in a bleak vision of the north
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Developer Patrick Grant was born in Australia and lives in New Zealand, but a childhood of British TV inspired him to set a comedy game in a bleak vision of the north
Content: Inspired by northern English culture … A Pocket Full of Slagford.Photograph: SlumpsView image in fullscreenInspired by northern English culture … A Pocket Full of Slagford.Photograph: SlumpsSummer games previewsGamesA Pocket Full of Slagford – a retro-futurist take on Thatcher-era northern EnglandDeveloper Patrick Grant was born in Australia and lives in New Zealand, but a childhood of British TV inspired him to set a comedy game in a bleak vision of the northElliot GardnerTue 25 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 19.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSomething is amiss in the dingy town of Slagford, and curious scamp Pip Bunting is the only one who can find out what. So quit your mithering, it’s time to discover just how grim it truly is up north.A Pocket Full of Slagford is an upcoming retro-styled 3D puzzle adventure game set in a surreal alternative-reality near-future northern England that never escaped the clutches of Thatcherism. The story follows the misadventures of a young local lad from the eponymous Slagford after he takes ownership of a mysterious relic that lets him wreak havoc on reality.It’s the passion project of Australia-born, New Zealand-based artist Patrick Grant, who formed solo-developer studio Slumps to create a game inspired by the point-and-click classics from the late 80s and early 90s, such asLucasArts’ catalogueandGrim Fandango.View image in fullscreenReminiscent of point-and-click adventures of the past … A Pocket Full of Slagford.Photograph: Slumps“They’re just a great format for narrative-heavy games, like an interactive story,” says Grant. “I like designing puzzles as well, so I always wanted to make a point-and-click. But from playing a lot, I know how samey they can be. From the start I was thinking about what I could do differently.”The result of Grant’s prototyping is what he describes as a “jigsaw sticker book kind of thing.” As you navigate the nasty industrial hellscape, you collect imprints of the game’s scenery. If, along the way, you spot a place where these imprints align, you can paste them into the world to solve puzzles. Grant is also committed to evoking the oft-forgotten CD-Rom era of the late ’90s, complete with looping CG-rendered backgrounds and janky 3D models with far too many sharp edges.Yet he’s keen to emphasise that his main focus is the narrative. While the trailer andSteam store pagefeature a fair few Yorkshire-isms, A Pocket Full of Slagford’s story and dialogue take inspiration from various aspects of northern English culture, despite Grant admitting to having never actually spent any real time in the area.“In the colonies we get a lot of BBC English programming,” he explains. “So when I was growing up there was so much British telly that I’d be watching. There’s this BBC miniseries from the 80s calledBoys from the Blackstuff, about this group of scousers getting up to mischief, set in the Thatcher years, just trying to make ends meet. It’s incredibly well written – this mix of sad and funny – against that whole big economic collapse. I got interested in that, reading about the Thatcher years.”That interest is what inspired A Pocket Full of Slagford’s bleak setting. While Grant says he wasn’t trying to make a political point when he went into the project, he’s not shying away from the issues of the time: “Because of that working-class setting, you end up naturally touching on points like the wealth disparity, which I show in the game, and the class conflict. Specifically, from watching stuff like Boys from the Blackstuff, or Billy Elliot, I was interested in the infighting that goes on within these classes.”Despite touching on these themes, Grant stresses that he’s going for a comedic, surrealist angle. As he puts it: “I was like, what if I set it in the future and, instead of coal, they’re mining shit out of the ground?” He may not be trying to make a political statement about Thatcherism, but some might say he has hit on an apt analogy.A Pocket Full of Slagford is in development forPC, with no confirmed release dateExplore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsPCfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The ear witness: Turner-winner Lawrence Abu Hamdan and his ‘sound evidence’ exposés of human rights abuses | Art and design | The Guardian
description: From killings in Gaza to the alleged use of a sonic weapon on a vigil in Belgrade, the Lebanese-British artist reveals how his work for activist group Earshot is inseparable from his art
Author: Charlotte Higgins
Headline: From killings in Gaza to the alleged use of a sonic weapon on a vigil in Belgrade, the Lebanese-British artist reveals how his work for activist group Earshot is inseparable from his art
Content: ‘The idea of figuring things out through sound didn’t occur until Earshot’ … Abu Hamdan.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘The idea of figuring things out through sound didn’t occur until Earshot’ … Abu Hamdan.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianArt and designInterviewThe ear witness: Turner-winner Lawrence Abu Hamdan and his ‘sound evidence’ exposés of human rights abusesCharlotte HigginsFrom killings in Gaza to the alleged use of a sonic weapon on a vigil in Belgrade, the Lebanese-British artist reveals how his work for activist group Earshot is inseparable from his artTue 25 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 11.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLawrence Abu Hamdan has a double identity. He is an artist who, in 2019, jointly won theTurner prize; and one of his works is, for my money, among the most strikingon showat this year’s Venice Biennale. But he is also the director of a young NGO, founded in 2023, calledEarshot, which investigates human rights abuses using sound evidence. In less euphemistic language, that means, on occasion, investigating horrific killings. He and his team might analyse the direction and position of bullets Israeli soldiers have fired at emergency workers in Gaza, or build evidence that a sonic weapon was likely used to disperse a mass silent vigil in Belgrade.Thefoundational workhe did in this field was a project with the London-based research agency Forensic Architecture for Amnesty International. Back in 2016, he interviewed rare survivors of the unimaginably barbaric conditions in Syria’s Sednaya prison. There was a paradox at play in this murderous place – prisoners were held in complete darkness, and enforced silence, killed for making any sound. Listening was boththe inmates’ only source of information, and a tool for survival and resistance. Their acute sonic memories of screams of distress and pain; keys turning in locks; bread being slapped down outside their cells; even of lice being snapped – helped Abu Hamdan and his colleagues build a picture of the prison architecture and its conditions, nearly a decade before it was opened to the light after the fall of the bloody Assad regime.double quotation markInto the silence came a noise that felt as if it came from inside the protestors’ bodiesIn fact, these identities of Abu Hamdan’s – artist and audio investigator – are not separate. Instead, they are interlocking, the art forming a sensory, aesthetic and emotional expression of the hard-nosed research. The Sednaya projectprofoundly influenced Abu Hamdanas an artist. The cases Earshot now take on result in formal written reports – and some of them also in artworks. “There’s the really fast, urgent stuff that we need to be doing,” says Abu Hamdan, “and then there’s the stuff where we can say, ‘OK, let’s pause. Let’s unfold it and reflect on what we did and what it meant.’ It’s a duality and it helps us sustain our ears. To keep us listening in as sharp a way as possible.”View image in fullscreenCaused by a sonic weapon? … 450XL: The Story of a Fugitive Sound.Photograph: © Marco Cappelletti e Giuseppe Miotto / Marco Cappelletti Studio/Lawrence Abu HamdanI imagine Earshot’s new offices – part of a complex of artists’ studios in south London – as something out of film noir, with the Lebanese-British Abu Hamdan as the resident private eye (or “private ear”, as he calls himself). Somehow, there should be a glass door with his name engraved on it, a fug of smoke inside. Instead he and his colleagues, mostly graduates from architecture schools, are based in a small open-plan office of impeccable bright-white tidiness, the only hint of the particular nature of the work a tiny silver pendant of an ear around Abu Hamdan’s neck.But mysterious things are happening on neighbouring computer screens as we talk. Investigator Renate Lurdesa Baumane, for example, has a computer-generated model of a street on hers. She is working a cold case – a political assassination that took place some years ago. The family of the victim recently contacted Earshot with recordings that hadn’t been analysed at the time. “The idea,” says Abu Hamdan, “that you would listen and figure out what happened from sound didn’t occur to people till we started Earshot, really.” The team is turning the case on its head: discovering that the person convicted of the shooting was likely a decoy, and that the murder weapon was wielded by another hand.Abu Hamdan describes the team’s work as building the sonic equivalent of the kind of visual reconstructions that we are used to seeing in the news. They use a combination of open-source data, “earwitness” testimonies and sound data (recordings, videos) gathered at the scene. The sonic weapon investigation, for example – which was the catalyst for the work on show in Venice – came out of an investigation into the dispersal in Belgrade of a mass silent anti-government protest.Held in March 2025, the demonstration was one of many silent vigils that have taken place in the country since a deadly accident at a railway station the previous year. The protesters keep 15 minutes of silence, one minute for every person killed. That evening as many as 300,000 people were gathered. And into that long, grief-filled silence of mourning and resistance came an intolerable, frightening noise – one that at first seemed as if a vehicle was approaching at speed, then felt as if it were being produced inside the bodies of those who experienced it. The Serbiangovernment deniedthat a sonic weapon was used to panic and disperse the crowd.View image in fullscreenA deafening whoosh … a still from Zifzafa, which explores noise pollution and wind turbines.Photograph: Lawrence Abu Hamdan“It was a really interesting case for us as an organisation because of the way we got pulled in,” says Abu Hamdan. “Generally we get requests from media organisations, or from NGOs – there’s usually an institution, except for a few random individuals telling us, ‘My wife’s trying to brainwash me with microwaves,’ or something, which we ignore. But this was the first one where we had multiple individual requests. We woke up and there were what felt like hundreds of emails.” This was the morning after the protest. A Serbian music student based in Vienna, they discovered, had suggested Earshot might help them find out what had really happened; the word had gone out among the protesters.Earshot took on the case, amassing thousands of witness statements and working in detail with individuals to reconstruct the sound. To do this they played the “earwitnesses” samples, first “eliminating sounds that were claimed by the government to have caused the panic, like firework, drone,” says Abu Hamdan. The team concluded the sound was likely produced by aUS-made devicecalled anLRAD 450XL.“To me there were two sonic weapons that night. There was the silence of the vigil, and there was the counterattack,” he says. “That silence was just so unbearable to the state that they had to find a way to undermine it.” The sheer silence of the vigil also resulted in extraordinary listening conditions. When the sound erupted into the crowd, the protesters were uniquely sensitive and alive to its quality. “It was a silent vigil that was also vigilant in its silence,” he says. “And it produced, in very similar way to the Sednaya prison, an acute type of listening.”A version of the multiscreen work that was shown in a frescoed music room in Venice – on a single screen, with a live score – will be shown at a “takeover” of the Barbican in London that Abu Hamdan and Earshot are staging in September. Earshot are also running workshops on gathering sound evidence; introducing film screenings (such as the 1955 French heist movie Rififi, which has a lengthy, almost silent robbery scene); and hosting musicians such as Busher Kanj, a composer from the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights in Syria, who is creating a new work incorporating field recordings and electronics.View image in fullscreenTraces … Earshot’s audio analysis of strikes on journalists in Lebanon in 2024.Photograph: Lawrence Abu HamdanEarshot worked with inhabitants of the area to demonstrate the levels of noise pollution that would be produced by wind turbines that are planned close to a village, building a kind of walk-through video game where the sounds of community life and of nature can be encountered against the deafening whoosh of the blades. That work, Zifzafa, can also been seen in Glasgow this summer at theCommon Guild, and Abu Hamdan and his collaborators willpresent a live versionfor the closing event of the Edinburgh art festival.I ask Abu Hamdan about how he and his team cope with the often distressing material. After our interview, for example, he is meeting New York Times journalists to look at some killings by ICE, the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency in the US. And one of their most significant works has been a year-long investigation into the killing of ambulance workers in Gaza.According to Earshot’s analysis, Israeli soldiers fired at least 910 rounds in Tel Al-Sultan, near Rafah, on 23 March 2025 – at least 789 of them directly at aid workers.Evidence included a recording made by one of the killed people, his phone exhumed with 15 bodies from a mass grave. One of the paradoxes of this investigation, says Abu Hamdan, is that the sheer destruction around – only three walls intact, everything else reduced to rubble – helped them to map the shots. “Usually in an urban environment that would be extremely complex.”But working on the cases, taking an active role, is easier than passively staring at his phone in despair, he says. “Ambiently scrolling – that is so much more destructive.” And, he points out, there’s always music to think about, not just gunshots. There is so much in the world to listen to.Zifzafais at the Common Guild, Glasgow, until 17 October, with a live performance at Leith theatre as part of the Edinburgh art festival on 29 August.Lawrence Abu Hamdan: Repercussionsis from 23-26 September at the Barbican, London.450XL: The Story of a Fugitive Soundis on show in Canicula, at Complesso dell’Ospedaletto, Venice, until 22 November.Explore more on these topicsArt and designForensic ArchitectureHuman rightsGazaSyriafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Boat trips, swimming and seafood: 10 of the UK’s best harbour towns and villages  | Travel | The Guardian
description: From smoked kippers in Northumberland to dolphin spotting in Dorset and a palm-fringed village on a sea loch in the Scottish Highlands
Author: Rachel Dixon
Headline: From smoked kippers in Northumberland to dolphin spotting in Dorset and a palm-fringed village on a sea loch in the Scottish Highlands
Content: The historic Pittenweem harbour in East Neuk, Fife, where fish is sold on the quay.Photograph: Angus McComiskey/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe historic Pittenweem harbour in East Neuk, Fife, where fish is sold on the quay.Photograph: Angus McComiskey/AlamyGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.TravelBoat trips, swimming and seafood: 10 of the UK’s best harbour towns and villagesFrom smoked kippers in Northumberland to dolphin spotting in Dorset and a palm-fringed village on a sea loch in the Scottish HighlandsRachel DixonTue 25 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 02.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePittenweem, FifeThe historic harbour is the hub of this working East Neuk fishing port, home to a fleet of about 30 small trawlers and creel boats. Their catches are sold at the covered market on the quay each weekday morning, and served at the harboursideDory BistroandChip Ahoyat the Larachmhor pub. Pittenweem (which means “place of the cave”) also has a Victorian-eraswimming poolnext to the beach, which is filled by the tide twice a day. After falling into disrepair, it was saved by a local group called the West Braes Project and reopened in 2021, along with the crazy golf course. Early each August, there is an annualarts festivalwith exhibits by nearly 200 artists in harbourside spaces, heritage buildings, homes and studios. Pittenweem is flanked by two other pretty harbour villages,St MonansandAnstruther, while a third,Crail, is a little further north; the Fife Coastal Path links them all.The Bankin Anstruther has harbour-view rooms (doubles from £120 B&B).Carnlough, County AntrimView image in fullscreenCarnlough harbour featured in Game of Thrones as the Braavos canal.Photograph: Christopher Hill Photographic/AlamyThere has been a harbour in the village of Carnlough since the late 1700s, but the one standing today dates to 1853 (Game of Thrones fans may recognise it as the Braavos canal). It was built on the orders of the Marchioness of Londonderry to transport limestone from her quarries – the town hall’sHeritage Hubtells the full story. The old railway line between the quarry and harbour is now a footpath with panoramic views, leading to Cranny Falls. The harbour is the focal point of the village, which stands at the foothills of Glencoy – one of the nine glens, or glacial valleys, of Antrim – on Carnlough Bay. It bustles with local fishers, andboat tripsset sail daily (£10 adults, £6 children; trips last 45 minutes). TheTwilight coffeeshop, directly across from the harbour, serves brunch and has bunkhouse accommodation upstairs (sleeping 14). The recently refurbishedHarbourview hoteloffers more than 200 Irish whiskeys and hosts an annual whiskey festival (doubles from £120 B&B).Solva, PembrokeshireView image in fullscreenAt low tide, Solva harbour becomes a huge stretch of sand.Photograph: Ashley Cooper/Getty ImagesSolva’s ancient harbour is at the bottom of a steep-sided valley on St Brides Bay, a few miles from St David’s. At high tide, it is popular with paddleboarders, but at low tide it becomes a huge stretch of sand, with the River Solva meandering down the middle. Then, there are rock pools and caves to explore; prime fishing, crabbing and shrimping spots; and safe, shallow places to swim. The village is split into Lower Solva, by the harbour, and Upper Solva – there are fantastic views over both ends from the Gribin headland.Cafe on the Quayand theHarbour Innhave outdoor tables overlooking the water; theHats & Barrelsserves fresh fish, and seasonal lobster and crab; and theCambrian Innis a restaurant with five rooms (doubles from £140 B&B).Craster, NorthumberlandView image in fullscreenThe small harbour at Craster, known for its smokehouse and kippers.Photograph: Jim Monk/AlamyWhile Craster’s natural haven has been used by fishers for centuries, today’s harbour was built in 1906 as a memorial to a member of the Craster family and has the ruins of Dunstanburgh Castle, a mile’s (1.6km) walk away up the coast as a backdrop. Craster is perhaps best known for its kippers, andL Robson & Sonshas been producing them at its smokehouse overlooking the harbour since 1856. They are sold in the shop next door, while thePiper’s Pitchhut serves them in a bun, and theJolly Fishermanpub turns them into paté and puts them in a scotch egg. TheCottage Inn, just outside Craster, has 10 rooms (doubles from £105 room only), and theDunstanburgh Castle Innin neighbouring Embleton has 16 (doubles from £120 B&B). The market town of Alnwick is about seven miles away.Clovelly, DevonView image in fullscreenCar-free Clovelly harbour.Photograph: Nigel Hicks/Getty ImagesBrixham, on Devon’s south coast, is probably the county’s best-known harbour town – but the village of Clovelly, on the north coast, is well worth seeking out, too. It was once the property of William the Conqueror, and is still privately owned today (entry is £10.90 adults; £6.25 children). The tiny harbour stands at the foot of a 122-metre cliff, reached via the steep, cobbled main street (known as Up-along or Down-along). Cars are not allowed, so goods are transported by sledges and donkeys. TheRed Lion hotel, right on the quay, has 17 rooms, all with sea views (doubles from £225 B&B); the restaurant serves dishes such as wild hake and local lobster, while the snug bar offers haddock and chips. TheFisherman’s Cottage & Kingsley Museumis a 1930s time capsule, and there areannual festivalscelebrating seaweed, seafaring and seafood.Staithes, North YorkshireView image in fullscreenStaithes village and harbour.Photograph: Nigel Harris/Getty ImagesNorth Yorkshire is not short of busy harbour towns and fishing villages: see Scarborough, Whitby and Robin Hood’s Bay. But Staithes, a little further north, is less well known. The name means “landing place” in Old English; Vikings landed here, and it was once one of the busiest fishing ports in the north-east. Today, there are still a handful of cobles (a traditional fishing vessel), plus boats runningwildlife-watching trips, from which minke whales can be seen in August and September. The village is a steep jumble of cottages (largely white-washed and red-roofed, with the occasional electric blue pile), threaded with cobbled snickets (narrow alleys). TheCod & Lobsterpub is right on the harbour wall; and theEndeavour B&B(refurbished in 2022) has four rooms, one with harbour views (doubles from £120 B&B). There is an annualarts festival(this year running 11-13 September), and visitors can walk a mile or so along theCleveland Wayto the ruined harbour at the abandoned hamlet ofPort Mulgrave.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPorthleven, CornwallView image in fullscreenPorthleven is one of Cornwall’s quieter harbour towns.Photograph: Jory Mundy/Getty ImagesFrom mighty Falmouth to minuscule Mousehole, harbour hunters are spoiled for choice in Cornwall. But pretty Porthleven, on the Lizard peninsula, tends to have fewer crowds. Its double harbour, which opened in 1825, is said to have beenbuilt by French prisoners of warafter the battle of Waterloo. It is lined with pubs, restaurants and galleries; there is acraft marketmost days from Easter to the end of October, and a food festival in April. The 17th-centuryShip Innstraddles the harbour and the waters of Mount’s Bay; theMussel Shoalis a seafood shack right on the harbour head; andKota Kaiserves fusion food such as Cornish fish and chips with katsu curry sauce, wasabi tartare, Asian slaw and pea puree. TheHarbour Innis a recently refurbished pub with 15 rooms (doubles from £110 B&B).Lyme Regis, DorsetView image in fullscreenLyme Regis harbour, built from Portland stone.Photograph: Travel Pics/Getty ImagesLyme Regis’s harbour includesthe Cobb, a breakwater and jetty. The first written mention of it was in 1328, when it was damaged by storms, but today’s Cobb was built from blocks of Portland stone in the late 18th and 19th centuries. It is on the west side of the town (known locally as the Pearl of Dorset), so is great for a sunset stroll. You can often see seals in the harbour and dolphins just out to sea; there are daily boat trips in late spring and summer. The beaches are fertile ground forfossil hunters– especially at Monmouth, to the west of the Cobb, and East Cliff, to the east of the town – and have thrown up many amazing discoveries, including an ichthyosaurus excavated by the paleontological pioneer Mary Anning in 1812. TheCobb Armsis the closest pub to the harbour and has three rooms (doubles £155 B&B); while theHarbour Inn, a tiny bit farther north by the beach, serves Lyme Bay seafood.Lymington, HampshireView image in fullscreenLymington is a yachting hub.Photograph: Thomas Faull/Getty ImagesThis market town on the west bank of the River Lymington, at the edge of the Solent, was first mentioned in the Domesday Book, became a hotbed for salt manufacture in the medieval era and later a shipbuilding centre in the 19th century. Today, it is ayachting hub, with two marinas as well as the old town quay. Near theRoyal Lymington Yacht Clubare the town’sseawater baths– established in 1833 and still open for swimmers (plus paddleboarding and inflatable obstacle courses). There is alively marketalong the high street on Saturdays; while waterfront pubs and restaurants include theShip InnandThe Haven, and the recently reopenedMayflower, set a little back near the seawater baths, which has seven rooms (doubles from £100 B&B). TheWightlinkferry port is just outside the town at Lymington Pier, taking passengers to Yarmouth on the Isle of Wight, another historic harbour town (with a crossing of about 40 minutes).Plockton, the HighlandsView image in fullscreenPlockton sits in a sheltered bay.Photograph: Getty Images/iStockphotoPlockton, a planned harbour village built to support the herring industry in the early 1800s, is known as the Jewel of the Highlands. It sits in a sheltered bay on the banks of Loch Carron, with a mild climate that allows incongruous-looking palm trees to thrive, and wooded hills beyond. Visitors can buy fresh fish and prawns off the pier when the boats come in at about 3pm; go onsea-kayak toursandseal-watching trips(from spring until the end of October); and watch the annualsummer regattain July. ThePlockton Innserves local langoustines and other seafood; thePlockton hotelhas six rooms with loch views and five overlooking the gardens (doubles £180 B&B); andthe bunkhouseby the railway station has budget beds (£20pp, discounts for groups). It is about an hour’s drive over the bridge to the Isle of Skye and on to its pastel-painted harbour capital, Portree.Explore more on these topicsTravelUnited Kingdom holidaysScotland holidaysEngland holidaysWales holidaysNorthern Ireland holidaysWildlife holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to use up leftover party wine | Wine | The Guardian
description: Sauces, reductions, deglazing: our expert panel has plenty of options for making the most of undrunk vino – whether you’ve got just a capful or a whole carafe to get through
Author: Anna Berrill
Headline: Sauces, reductions, deglazing: our expert panel has plenty of options for making the most of undrunk vino – whether you’ve got just a capful or a whole carafe to get through
Content: ‘A novel concept’: leftover wine can go into everything from stews to desserts.Photograph: heliography/Stockimo/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘A novel concept’: leftover wine can go into everything from stews to desserts.Photograph: heliography/Stockimo/AlamyKitchen aideWineHow to use up leftover party wineSauces, reductions, deglazing: our expert panel has plenty of options for making the most of undrunk vino – whether you’ve got just a capful or a whole carafe to get throughAnna BerrillTue 25 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat can I do with wine left over from a party?Rob,by emailThis is a novel concept, perhaps, but the answer essentially comes down to the quantity: “If we’re talking dribbles of red or white, that’s simple,” says Jon Atashroo, head chef/owner ofWhere There’s Smokein North Yorkshire. “They go into sauces, whether that’s for pasta or to deglaze a pan before making a gravy.” Joe Otway, chef/co-owner ofHigher Groundin Manchester, couldn’t agree more: “Reducing wine, be it white or red, in the base of anything is generally a good idea.” Take something tomato-based, such as ragu or chilli, as an example: “Once you’ve sweated the vegetables and there’s caramelisation on the bottom of the pan, a glass of red wine will add acidity, depth and sweetness.” And remember, you can always freeze wine dregs for later use: simply pour into ice-cube trays and stash.Moving on to medium amounts, we’re talking “stewy, fish-type things”, Atashroo says, perhaps moules marinière. Another good option is pickling: “A basic recipe is one part caster sugar, one part white-wine vinegar and one part white wine. And if you’re pickling something like beetroot, cook it in that mix, while if you’re using cucumbers, say, they go in cold.” That said, a current Atashroo go-to is altogether sweeter: “Weigh some red wine, though I don’t see why it wouldn’t work with white wine, too, add 20% of its weight in sugar, and reduce to a syrup – you’re looking for the consistency of strawberry sauce.” The result is complex and acidic, “almost like reduced port”, and great for drizzling over vanilla ice-cream. While we’re talking desserts, few things are better than fruit (peaches, figs, pears) poached in wine, either.Larger amounts of excess wine could be fermented into vinegar, although Otway has an easier route if you have any natural cider vinegar (ie, one with a mother) to hand: “Add a couple of tablespoons of vinegar to, say, a third of a bottle of wine, cover with muslin, so oxygen can get to it but flies can’t, and put in a cupboard for a month.” That’ll give you “some really interesting results” as the vinegar takes on the characteristics of the wine: “It’s perfect for pepping up dressings for these never-ending salad days.”If Rob’s party was more of a sparkling affair, Alastair Walling, head chef atBar Blondiein London, would use every last drop in a beurre blanc: “Combine vinegar, shallots and a sprig of thyme in a small, heavy-based saucepan and gently reduce the liquid by half. Add champagne and some finely diced mushrooms, then reduce by half again.” Lift out the thyme, lower the heat and whisk in chilled butter a little at a time. But be warned: “Keep the sauce just below a simmer, otherwise it may split.” Season (with salt and white pepper) and spoon that lovely sauce all over some steamed fish.All that said, maybe the most obvious solution is simply to repurpose the wine in another drink, perhaps sangria: “Add a generous amount of brandy to red wine, plus some orange juice and slices of orange and lemon, and leave to infuse,” says Jonny Lake ofTrivetandLabombe by Trivetin London. Serve straight over ice or top with soda, then sip while you plan your next party.Got a culinary dilemma?
